groups.note: All come from ところ (所) — its basic meaning is “place”; used with actions it extends to “the point” an action has reached

items.diff: たところだ ends the sentence and means “just did”; たところで sits mid-sentence and means “even if … (it's no use)”.

this.tr: The train has just left.

that.tr: Even if I run now, I won't make it in time.

items.explain: ところ basically means “place”; used with an action it becomes “the point” the action has reached. 出たところだ: the action has reached the point of “just finished”, and 「だ」 closes the sentence → “just did”. 走ったところで: 「で」 means “at this point” — even if the action gets as far as “running there”, the result that follows doesn't change → “even if …”. So look at what follows ところ: 「だ」 ending the sentence → “just did”; 「で」 followed by a useless result such as 「間に合わない」 → “even if …”.

items.diff: たところだ says an action has “just finished”; たところ、 says “I did it, and as a result found …”.

this.tr: I've just sent an email to my teacher.

that.tr: I emailed my teacher, and got a reply right away.

items.explain: ところ basically means “place”, extended to “the point or situation” an action is in. 「送ったところだ」 at the end of a sentence: you say you are at the point of “having just done it”, and the sentence stops there → “just did”. 「送ったところ、」 mid-sentence: in the situation of “having done this”, something new happens next → “I did it, and then …”. Look at what follows 「たところ」: 「だ」 ending the sentence → “just did”; another event follows (すぐ返事が来た), often an unexpected discovery → the “result” use.

items.diff: ところだ only says what point in time you are at; ところに／へ says “right at that moment, someone or something came along”.

this.tr: I'm just about to go out.

that.tag: ところに · Right then → someone came
that.tr: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came over.

that.tag: ところへ · Right then → a call came
that.tr: Just as I was about to go out, I got a phone call.

items.explain: ところ basically means “place”, extended to “the point” an action has reached. 出かけるところだ: you only say you are at the point of “about to go out”, and the sentence stops there → “about to”. 出かけるところに／へ: 「に」 and 「へ」 point at that moment, and right then another person or thing barges in → “just then, … came”. So check whether someone or something comes in afterwards (友達が来た、電話がかかってきた); if so, it's ところに／へ.

items.diff: ところだ is a real point in time; ところだった means “almost …”, and it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: I'm about to arrive at the station.

that.tr: I almost left my wallet at home.

items.explain: ところ basically means “place”, extended to “the point” an action has reached. 駅に着くところだ: you are now at the point of “about to arrive”, and it really will happen → “about to”. 忘れるところだった: the past tense 「だった」 says you had reached the point of “about to forget”, but went no further, so it never happened → “almost …”. Look at the word at the start: 「今」＋ところだ is a real point in time right now; 「危うく」「もう少しで」＋ところだった means it almost happened but didn't, often with a sense of relief.

groups.note: ところ ↔ どころ — they differ only by the voicing mark (dakuten)

items.diff: ところ means “just now”; どころか means “far from …, actually / not even …”.

this.tr: I've just finished my homework.

that.tr: Far from finishing my homework, I haven't even started it.

items.explain: First check the dakuten (゛): ど ≠ と. Then look at the structure: before どころか comes an “expectation”, and after it comes a completely opposite, even more extreme fact, so the sentence always contrasts two parts.

items.diff: たところだ means “just did”; どころではない means “no time at all for …”.

this.tr: I've just finished work.

that.tr: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.

items.explain: どころではない usually follows a noun (旅行、勉強) and ends with the negative 「ではない」; a reason often comes first (忙しくて), and it has nothing to do with a point in time. When you see ど plus a negative at the end, it's not “just did”.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たところ is objectively “this very moment”; たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”, and can even be used for something months ago.

this.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

that.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → たところ; 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → only たばかり works.

groups.note: All come from the particle ばかり — its basic meaning is limiting: “only these, nothing but this”

items.diff: ta-form + ばかり means “just did”; noun + ばかり means “nothing but, all”.

this.tr: I just bought this computer.

that.tr: This shop sells nothing but expensive things.

items.explain: It's the same ばかり, originally meaning “only this”. Look at what comes before it: a ta-form (買った) → “only this little time has passed” = just now; a noun (物) → “only this one kind” = nothing but. In casual speech ばっかり works the same way.

items.diff: たばかり means “just finished doing”; てばかりいる means “always doing, doing nothing but”, often with a complaint.

this.tr: I just ate.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play video games every day.

items.explain: The basic meaning of ばかり is limiting: “only, just”. た＋ばかり limits time: after the action, “only this little time has passed” → “just did” (さっき食べたばかりだ). て＋ばかり＋いる limits the action: “doing only this one thing and nothing else”, continuously → “always, nothing but”, often with a complaint (毎日ゲームをしてばかりいる). So look at what comes before ばかり: た形 → “just did”; て形 with 「いる」 after it → “always”.

groups.note: たばかりだ ↔ たばかりに — they differ only in the last character

items.diff: たばかりだ means “just did”; たばかりに means “just because … (it led to a bad result)”.

this.tr: I've just come to Japan.

that.tr: Just because I said one thing too many, I made her angry.

items.explain: Both are 「た＋ばかり」; only the final 「だ」 vs 「に」 differs. たばかりに is always followed by a bad result (〜てしまった), meaning “just because of that little thing …”, often with regret.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”; たところだ is objectively “this very moment”.

this.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

that.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → たばかり; 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → both たところ and たばかり work, but たところ puts more stress on “at this very moment”.

items.diff: たばかり works with any verb; たて works with only a few verbs and stresses “freshly made, still new”.

this.tr: I lost the umbrella I bought just yesterday.

that.tr: Freshly baked bread is delicious.

items.explain: たて attaches directly to the ます形 (焼き＋たて) and is used only with a few words for “something just made and still new”: 焼きたて、できたて、生まれたて、塗りたて. In all other cases use たばかり, as in 「昨日買ったばかりの傘」.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようになる is “coming to be” naturally; ようにする is deliberately “making it happen” yourself.

this.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

that.tr: For my health, I make a point of getting up early.

items.explain: よう (様) means “a state, a way things are”, so 「ように」 means “into that state”. ようになる: things “become” that way on their own, changed by circumstances or time → natural change. ようにする: you yourself “make” things become that way, a conscious effort → try to, make a point of. So check whether it ends in なる or する, then look at the first half: an outside cause (子どもが生まれてから) → ようになる; your own purpose (健康のために) → ようにする.

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ようになった is a result already achieved; ように is a goal not yet achieved that you're working toward.

this.tr: Because I practiced every day, I can now read kanji.

that.tr: I practice every day so that I can read kanji.

items.explain: よう (様) means “a state, a way things are”. ようになった: you have already “become” able to read kanji → a result, already achieved. ように＋action: you act toward the state of “being able to read kanji” → a goal, not yet achieved. So look at the form: 「ようになった」 at the end of the sentence → already achieved; 「ように、」 followed by what you do for it (毎日練習している) → a goal.

items.diff: ようになる means “a person comes to be able to / starts to …”; ようになっている means “a machine or system is designed to …”.

this.tr: My child can now get dressed by themselves.

that.tag: How a machine is set up
that.tr: This door is designed to open automatically when someone approaches.

items.explain: よう (様) means “a state, a way things are”. ようになる: “becoming” a certain way, a change that happens to a person → “can now / has started to …”. ようになっている: 「なっている」 means it has become that way and stays so; used for things, it means “set up to work that way” → how a machine or system works. Look at the subject: a person (子どもが) → a change; a machine or rule (このドアは), often together with 「〜と」 → a built-in mechanism.

groups.note: Both express “change”, but are used differently

items.diff: ようになる looks at the “end point” of a change (now you can); てくる looks at the “process” (it's changing bit by bit).

this.tr: After three months, I came to understand Japanese.

that.tr: Little by little, I've started to understand Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「３か月で」 sets an end point and describes the new state once it's reached → ようになる; 「少しずつ」 describes the process of change, which is still going on up to now → てくる is common.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようにする is deliberately “making it happen” yourself; ようになる is “coming to be” naturally.

this.tr: For my health, I make a point of getting up early.

that.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

items.explain: よう (様) means “a state, a way things are”, so 「ように」 means “into that state”. ようにする: you yourself “make” things become that way, a conscious effort → try to, make a point of. ようになる: things “become” that way on their own, changed by circumstances or time → natural change. So check whether it ends in する or なる, then look at the first half: your own purpose (健康のために) → ようにする; an outside cause (子どもが生まれてから) → ようになる.

items.diff: ようにする is making an effort yourself; ように言う is telling someone else to do it.

this.tr: I try to eat vegetables every day.

that.tr: My doctor told me to eat vegetables every day.

items.explain: よう (様) means “a state, a way things are”, so 「ように」 means “into that state”. ようにする: you “make” your own behavior become that way → try to, keep it up. ように言う: you tell someone that things “should become that way” → reporting a request, telling someone to do it. Check whether する or 「言う／言われた」 follows: something you set for yourself → ようにする; a request from someone else, often with 「〜に」 such as 「医者に」 marking who made it → ように言う.

groups.note: Both mean “keep doing … all the time”

items.title: 〜ことにする (habit)
items.diff: ようにしている means “always being careful, trying to”; ことにしている means “having set yourself a rule and always doing so”, which sounds more determined.

this.tr: I try not to eat sweets at night.

that.tr: I've made it a rule not to eat sweets at night.

items.explain: Both sentences describe a habit you keep up. Which to choose: if you mean “I'm always careful and try not to eat them”, and the occasional exception is fine → ようにしている; if you mean “this is a rule I've set for myself”, with a firmer attitude → ことにしている.

groups.note: Both come from the appearance そう — “how something looks”

items.diff: そうだ means “it looks like it's about to …”; そうになった means “almost …”, and it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: The luggage on the shelf looks like it's about to fall.

that.tr: The luggage on the shelf almost fell.

items.explain: そう means “appearance”: how something looks from the outside. 落ちそうだ: you see that it looks “about to fall” and make a guess → “looks like it's about to …”, and the situation is still in front of you. 落ちそうになった: things “became” the state of “just about to fall”, but went no further, so it is usually in the past tense 「なった」 → “almost …”, and it didn't happen. The two sentences differ only in 「だ」 vs 「になった」; when you see 「そうになった」, it means “almost”.

groups.note: Both mean “it looks like …”

items.title: 〜ようだ (inference)
items.diff: そうだ is a direct impression from how something looks; ようだ is an inference made after thinking about the signs.

this.tag: From how it looks · direct impression
this.tr: Tanaka looks sleepy.

that.tr: Tanaka seems to be sleepy.

items.explain: Both sentences can mean “Tanaka seems sleepy”. Which to choose: if you're looking at his face and manner and saying your direct impression → 眠そうだ; if you judge after thinking about some signs (he keeps yawning, he sounds tired) → 眠いようだ. They also attach differently: そうだ attaches to the stem (眠＋そう), ようだ to the plain form (眠い＋よう); in casual speech ようだ is often said as みたいだ.

groups.note: Both mean “I hear that …”

items.title: 〜らしい (guess / hearsay)
items.diff: そうだ passes on what was said, from a clear source; らしい has a vague source and a hint of guessing, and the speaker doesn't take responsibility for the content.

this.tag: Clear source · passed on as is
this.tr: According to the department manager, Yamada is quitting the company next month.

that.tr: Rumor has it that Yamada is quitting the company next month.

items.explain: Both sentences pass on news you heard. Look at where the news came from: a clear source, passed on as it was said (部長の話では) → そうだ, the speaker is just relaying it; a vague source (うわさでは), or the speaker is partly guessing too → らしい, which sounds less certain and keeps the speaker at a distance from the content.

items.title: 〜とのことだ (passing on news)
items.diff: The “I hear” そうだ is the ordinary way to pass on news and is the most common in conversation; とのことだ is more formal and used mostly in work and letters.

this.tr: The news says it's going to snow tomorrow.

that.tr: According to the news, it will snow tomorrow.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same: passing on what the news said. Which to choose: chatting with friends or family → そうだ (降るそうだよ), the most common; formal situations such as work reports, emails and letters, or passing on a message for someone else → とのことです. Used in casual chat, it sounds stiff.

groups.note: Both express an inference: “it seems …”

items.title: 〜そうだ (looks like)
items.diff: ようだ is an inference made after thinking about the signs; そうだ is a direct impression from how something looks.

this.tr: Tanaka seems to be sleepy.

that.tag: From how it looks · direct impression
that.tr: Tanaka looks sleepy.

items.explain: Both sentences can mean “Tanaka seems sleepy”. Which to choose: if you judge after thinking about some signs (he keeps yawning, he sounds tired) → 眠いようだ; if you're looking at his face and manner and saying your direct impression → 眠そうだ. They also attach differently: ようだ attaches to the plain form (眠い＋よう), そうだ to the stem (眠＋そう); in casual speech ようだ is often said as みたいだ.

items.title: 〜らしい (guess / hearsay)
items.diff: ようだ is a judgment based on clues you noticed yourself; らしい is usually based on news you heard, with a “reportedly” feel.

this.tr: There are sounds coming from the next room. Someone seems to be there.

that.tr: Rumor has it that those two are getting married.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment is based on: direct clues you heard or saw yourself (隣の部屋から音がする) → ようだ／みたいだ; indirect information such as rumors or what others said (うわさでは) → らしい. With らしい, the speaker keeps a distance from the content and doesn't take responsibility for it.

items.title: 〜ように見える (guess)
items.diff: ようだ is an inference the speaker believes; ように見える only says it looks that way on the outside, and may not be true.

this.tr: He seems to be angry.

that.tr: He looks angry, but he actually isn't.

items.explain: Both sentences infer “he seems angry” from how he looks. Which to choose: ようだ is the speaker's own judgment, which they basically believe; ように見える only says “this is how it looks on the outside” and leaves room for doubt, so it can be followed by 「が、本当は怒っていない」 to overturn it. Following ようだ that way would contradict itself.

groups.note: Both express a comparison: “just like …”

items.title: 〜かのようだ (just as if)
items.diff: ようだ is an ordinary comparison; かのようだ stresses “it isn't really, but it's just as if”, and is more exaggerated and more written.

this.tr: It's only February, but it's as warm as if spring had come.

that.tr: It's only February, but it's so warm, it's just as if spring had already arrived.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same: they make a comparison. Which to choose: in everyday speech, ような is normal (casual: みたいな); with the extra 「か」, かのような adds the tone of “it isn't really so, but it's just as if”, making the comparison more exaggerated and more written; it is common in writing.

groups.note: Both mean “judging by logic”

items.diff: はずだ has objective grounds (it stands to reason); に違いない is a strong subjective conviction (a gut feeling).

this.tr: According to the schedule, the department manager should be attending the 3 o'clock meeting.

that.tr: Judging by that smile, something good must have happened.

items.explain: Behind はずだ you can name concrete grounds (a schedule, a rule, a calculation); に違いない is the speaker's own strong feeling, and the grounds can be just an impression. That's why はずだ is more common when talking about work or in writing.

groups.note: Both mean “no wonder”

items.title: 〜わけだ (no wonder)
items.diff: はずだ focuses on “given this cause, it was bound to be so”; わけだ focuses on “the cause and the result match up, so it makes sense”, and is more common.

this.tag: No wonder · bound to be so
this.tr: Oh, the air conditioner is broken. No wonder it's so hot.

that.tr: Oh, the air conditioner is broken. No wonder it's so hot.

items.explain: Both sentences can mean “no wonder it's so hot”: after learning the cause, you feel the result makes sense. The subtle difference: はずだ keeps its original meaning of “it stands to reason”, focusing on “given this cause, it was bound to be this hot”; わけだ focuses on “the cause and the result match up, so now it makes sense”, and is more common in speech. When talking about the reason itself (なるほど、そういうわけか), only わけ works; you can't say そういうはずか.

groups.note: All come from わけ (訳) — “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけだ means “no wonder, naturally”; わけがない means “there's no way”.

this.tr: He practices every day, so no wonder he's so good.

that.tr: He has never practiced even once, so there's no way he's good.

items.explain: わけ ＝ reason, logic. わけだ: it makes sense, so “no wonder”; わけがない: there's no reason at all for it, so “there's no way”. Look at the first half: a good enough reason is given → わけだ; the reason clearly doesn't hold → わけがない.

items.diff: わけだ draws a conclusion that follows logically; わけではない means “it's not that …”, a partial denial.

this.tr: Oh, you lived there for three years? No wonder you know Japan so well.

that.tr: I did live in Japan, but that doesn't mean I know Japan well.

items.explain: The basic meaning of わけ (訳) is “reason, the logic of things”. わけだ: “logically, that's how it is”, used after learning the cause → “no wonder” (３年も住んでいたのか → 詳しいわけだ). わけではない: “that's not the logic”, denying a conclusion one might draw → “it's not that …” (having lived in Japan ≠ necessarily knowing Japan well). Look at what comes before: 「〜のか」, a sudden realization followed by a conclusion → わけだ; 「けど」 or 「からといって」 before it, turning around to correct an assumption → わけではない.

items.diff: わけだ says “logically, that's how it is”; わけにはいかない says “I can't do that, for reasons of logic or responsibility”.

this.tr: Oh, there's an exam tomorrow? That's why he isn't going out to play.

that.tr: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and play.

items.explain: The basic meaning of わけ (訳) is “reason, the logic of things”. わけだ: “logically, that's how it is”, used to explain a known fact → “I see, that's why …” (明日試験なのか → 遊ばないわけだ). わけにはいかない: 「いかない」 means “it doesn't work”; it doesn't hold up logically → you can't do it because of responsibility, rules or obligation to others, and the subject is usually the speaker (明日は試験だから → 遊ぶわけにはいかない). Look at the first half: 「〜なのか」 means you've just learned the reason → わけだ; 「〜だから」 is you giving your own reason, followed by something you can't do → わけにはいかない.

groups.note: Both mean “no wonder”

items.title: 〜はずだ (no wonder)
items.diff: わけだ focuses on “the cause and the result match up, so it makes sense”, and is more common; はずだ focuses on “given this cause, it was bound to be so”.

this.tr: Oh, the air conditioner is broken. No wonder it's so hot.

that.tag: No wonder · bound to be so
that.tr: Oh, the air conditioner is broken. No wonder it's so hot.

items.explain: Both sentences can mean “no wonder it's so hot”: after learning the cause, you feel the result makes sense. The subtle difference: わけだ focuses on “the cause and the result match up, so now it makes sense”, and is more common in speech; はずだ keeps its original meaning of “it stands to reason”, focusing on “given this cause, it was bound to be this hot”. When talking about the reason itself (なるほど、そういうわけか), only わけ works; you can't say そういうはずか.

groups.note: Both mean “in order to”

items.title: 〜には (purpose)
items.diff: ために is followed by “what you do”; には is followed by “what is needed, how much it takes”.

this.tr: I'm saving money to buy a house.

that.tr: To buy a house, you need a lot of money.

items.explain: Both sentences are about “to buy a house”. Look at the second half: an action you take for it (貯金している) → ために; what is needed or how much it takes (お金がたくさん必要だ、〜がかかる、〜なければならない) → には.

groups.note: Both mean “because”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: ために (reason) is rather written and is followed by an objective result that already happened; から is conversational and can be followed by an invitation, request or command.

this.tr: Due to an accident, the train is delayed.

that.tr: We don't have time, so let's go quickly.

wrong.why: ために expressing a reason can't be followed by an invitation or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: stating a result that already happened, as in station announcements or the news → ために; your own invitation or request, such as 「〜よう」 or 「〜てください」 → only から (or ので) works.

groups.note: ことにする ↔ ことになる — only する／なる differs

items.diff: ことにする is a decision you made yourself; ことになる is decided by others or by circumstances.

this.tr: After thinking it over myself, I decided to quit my job.

that.tr: On the company's orders, I'm being transferred to Osaka.

items.explain: The two differ only in the final する／なる. する means you settle it yourself: 「自分で考えて」 → ことにした; なる means things turn out that way, decided by others or circumstances: 「会社の命令で」 → ことになった. Also, Japanese speakers sometimes deliberately use ことになった for their own decisions, to sound modest and low-key.

items.diff: ことにしている is a rule you set for yourself; ことになっている is a rule set by a school, company or similar.

this.tr: I've made it a rule not to go out after 10 p.m.

that.tr: In this dormitory, the rule is that you can't go out after 10 p.m.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in して／なって: with ことにしている you yourself “make” it a rule, so the rule is yours; with ことになっている it has “become” a rule, set by a school, company, dormitory and so on. Check whether a source of the rule is given (この寮では): if so → ことになっている; if it's just your own habit → ことにしている.

groups.note: Both mean “decide”

items.title: 〜にする (choosing)
items.diff: ことにする follows a verb and says what you decided to do; にする follows a noun and says which one you picked from several options.

this.tr: I've decided to go to Okinawa for summer vacation this year.

that.tr: For summer vacation this year, I've picked Okinawa.

wrong.why: にする can't follow a verb directly; say 「行くことにした」

items.explain: Both sentences mean “this summer vacation, I settled on going to Okinawa”. Which to choose: if you're talking about something you decided to do, with a verb (行く) before it → ことにした; if you're only naming the place or thing chosen (沖縄、コーヒー), like picking one from several options → にした. A verb can't take にする directly.

groups.note: 安く ↔ 安くて, 静かに ↔ 静かで — they differ by just one 「て」, or by a single kana (に／で)

items.diff: く／に directly modifies the following action (how it's done); くて／で first finishes describing one quality, then moves on.

this.tr: At this shop you can buy vegetables cheaply.
I clean the room until it's spotless.

that.tr: The vegetables at this shop are cheap and fresh.
This room is clean and bright.

items.explain: Look at what comes after 「く」 or 「に」: a verb right after it (買える, 掃除する) → it directly describes how the action is done; an added 「て」, or に changed to で, followed by another quality (新しい, 明るい) → the two qualities are listed side by side. 安く／安くて and きれいに／きれいで differ by only one kana, yet one modifies an action and the other links qualities.

groups.note: 安く ↔ 安くて, 静かに ↔ 静かで — they differ by just one 「て」, or by a single kana (に／で)

items.diff: くて／で: finish one quality, then continue; く／に directly modifies the following verb.

this.tr: This bread is cheap and tasty.
This town is quiet and clean.

that.tr: I get up early every morning.
Please speak quietly in the library.

wrong.why: To modify the verb 「起きる」, use く

items.explain: Look at what follows: an added 「て」 (or に changed to で) followed by another quality (おいしい, きれいだ) → the qualities are listed side by side; no 「て」 and a verb right after it (起きる, 話してください) → it describes how the action is done. 安くて／安く and 静かで／静かに differ by only one kana, and ✗静かで話してください is wrong too.

groups.note: Both mean “both … and …”

items.diff: Both mean “both … and …”; くて joins two qualities flatly into one sentence, while し lists them one by one, hinting “and that's not all”.

this.tr: That bakery is cheap and tasty.

that.tr: That bakery is cheap, the bread is tasty, and the staff are friendly too.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “both … and …”. くて ties the two qualities tightly into one sentence and simply states them; し counts them off one by one, often paired with 「も」 (店員さんも親切だ), and carries a tone of “and that's not all — there's more”, which is why it's also often used to line up reasons. They attach differently too: くて is a conjugated adjective form (安くて), while し follows the plain form (安いし, 親切だし).

groups.note: Both express a cause: “because…”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: くて／で as a reason can only be followed by a result that comes about naturally; if a request or invitation follows, you must use から.

this.tr: It's so hot I can't sleep.
I'm so worried I can't sleep.

that.tr: It's hot, so please open the window.

wrong.why: くて can't be followed by a request or command

items.explain: Both can give a cause. Look at the second half: a result you can't control, like 「眠れない」 → くて is fine (nouns and な-adjectives use で: 心配で); a request or intention, like 「窓を開けてください」 or 「〜ましょう」 → only から (or ので).

groups.note: Both come from あまり (余り) — originally “exceeding, excess”

items.diff: あまり＋negative means “not very…”; あまりに／あまりの／〜のあまり all mean “too much…”, followed by the result it causes.

this.tr: These clothes aren't very expensive.

that.tr: These clothes are too expensive — I can't buy them.

that.tag: あまりの · N so extreme that…
that.tr: The price was so high I was left speechless.

that.tag: あまり · Out of too much…
that.tr: I was so nervous I couldn't say a thing.

items.explain: あまり comes from the verb 「余る」, whose basic meaning is “to exceed, to be left over”. Used in the direction of “going too far”: あまりに高くて＝so expensive it goes past the limit → too; あまりの値段 and 緊張のあまり are likewise “… beyond the limit” → because something is too…, followed by the result it causes. Used with a negative: あまり高くない＝not so expensive as to go beyond the usual level → not very. So look at what follows: a negative (高くない) → not very; a result (買えない, 何も言えなかった) → too much.

groups.note: Both come from the copula 「です」 — でしょう＝です＋「う」, which expresses conjecture

items.diff: です states something for certain; でしょう is a guess — “probably”.

this.tr: Tomorrow is Sunday.

that.tr: It will probably rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Ask whether it's an established fact: something fixed on the calendar → です; things you can't be sure of yourself, like the weather or someone else's situation → でしょう, often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」. The plain style works the same way: だ when certain, だろう when guessing.

groups.note: Both come from だけ (丈) — expressing “a limit, only this much”

items.diff: だけ just limits the scope; だけで says “just this alone is enough to…”.

this.tr: I'm not buying — just looking.

that.tr: Just looking at it is fun.

items.explain: だけ comes from 「丈（たけ）」, originally meaning length or height, which extended to “the limit up to this point” → only this much. 見るだけです: the action stops at “looking” and goes no further (買いません) → just; 見るだけで: で means “by means of”, so “looking” alone is enough, and a result follows directly (楽しい) → just … is enough to …. So look at what follows だけ: the sentence ends with 「です」, explaining nothing else was done → just; 「で、」 followed by a result → just … is enough to ….

groups.note: All mean “only, just”

items.diff: だけ works with both affirmative and negative and sounds objective; しか must be followed by a negative and carries a sense of “too few”.

this.tr: Only three people came to the party.

that.tr: Only three people came to the party (disappointingly few).

wrong.why: しか must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (来た) → だけ; negative (来なかった) → しか, and the speaker feels it's “too few, not enough”.

items.diff: Both mean “only, just”; だけ objectively marks out a scope, while ばかり stresses “nothing but this”, often with dissatisfaction.

this.tr: My little brother ate only the meat and left the vegetables.

that.tr: My little brother eats nothing but meat — it's a real headache.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “only, just”. だけ objectively marks out a scope: only the meat, nothing else (野菜は残した); ばかり says “so much that it's almost all this”, and the speaker feels it's too one-sided and is unhappy about it, so it's often followed by a complaint like 「困る」. So look at the speaker's attitude: simply stating a scope → だけ; complaining that it's “nothing but this” → ばかり. In casual speech, ばっかり is also used.

groups.note: All express a guess

items.diff: Same meaning; だろう is the plain form, でしょう is the polite form.

this.tr: It'll probably rain tomorrow. (talking to oneself)

that.tr: Everyone, it will probably rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: talking to yourself, diaries, written texts, or close friends (mostly men) → だろう; guests, seniors, an audience (e.g. a weather forecast) → でしょう. Saying 「だろう」 to your boss would be very rude.

groups.note: Both come from 「に」 — で was originally 「にて」 (at a place ＋ and), meaning “doing … there”

items.title: 〜に (place of existence)
items.diff: で is followed by an action (勉強する, 食べる); に is followed by existence (いる, ある, 住む).

this.tr: I study at the library.

that.tr: I'm at the library.

wrong.why: 「勉強する」 is an action, so the place takes で

items.explain: で was originally 「にて」, meaning “there, (doing something)”, so an action must follow (勉強する, 遊ぶ, 働く); に just marks a point and is followed by simple “be, exist, live” (いる, ある, 住んでいる). English uses “at / in” for both, so look at the verb that follows to tell them apart.

groups.note: Both come from 「で＋も」 — で is the copula “is” and も means “also”, so the original sense is “even if it's …”

items.title: 〜でも (even if)
items.diff: でも giving an example is followed by an invitation or suggestion; でも meaning “even if” is followed by “… all the same”.

this.tr: If you're free, how about some tea or something?

that.tr: Even if it rains, the game will go ahead.

items.explain: でも is the copula 「で」 (“is”) plus 「も」 (“also”), originally meaning “even if it's …”. The concessive use keeps that meaning: 雨でも＝even if it's rain, what follows happens all the same (試合はあります) → even if. The example use is a lighter version of it: お茶でも＝“even just tea would do” — it doesn't pin anything down, just casually offers an example, so the tone becomes softer, which is why it's often followed by an invitation or suggestion (飲みませんか, 〜ましょう). Look at the second half: an invitation or suggestion → example; something that happens unaffected, all the same → even if.

groups.note: 何でも ↔ 何も — they differ by just one 「で」

items.diff: question word＋でも takes an affirmative: “anything / everything…”; question word＋も takes a negative: “nothing…”.

this.tr: My kid eats anything.

that.tr: I haven't eaten anything since this morning.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (食べる) → 何でも、誰でも、どこでも; negative (食べていない) → 何も、誰も、どこにも. Just one 「で」 makes the meanings opposite, and the readings differ too (なんでも／なにも).

groups.note: All mean “but”

items.diff: でも starts the second sentence; けど attaches to the end of the first.

this.tr: This restaurant is expensive. But it's delicious.

that.tr: This restaurant is expensive, but it's delicious.

wrong.why: でも can't attach directly to the end of a clause

items.explain: Look at the position: the previous sentence already ended with a full stop and a new sentence begins → でも; the contrast word sticks directly onto the end of the previous clause → けど. けれども works the same way, just a little more formal than けど.

items.diff: Both start a sentence and mark a contrast; でも is spoken language, しかし is written language.

this.tr: Yesterday was really fun, wasn't it? But I'm a bit tired.

that.tr: This method is convenient. However, it also has problems.

items.explain: Look at the style of the sentence: a chatty tone with 「ね」 or 「ちょっと」 → でも; reports and papers in the 「である」 style → しかし. Using 「でも」 in an essay sounds too colloquial.

groups.note: Both come from the copula 「です」 — でしょう＝です＋「う」, which expresses conjecture

items.diff: でしょう is a guess — “probably”; です states something for certain.

this.tr: It will probably rain tomorrow.

that.tr: Tomorrow is Sunday.

items.explain: Ask whether it's an established fact: things you can't be sure of yourself, like the weather or someone else's situation → でしょう, often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」; something fixed on the calendar → です. The plain style works the same way: だろう when guessing, だ when certain.

groups.note: All express a guess

items.diff: Same meaning; でしょう is the polite form, だろう is the plain form.

this.tr: Everyone, it will probably rain tomorrow.

that.tr: It'll probably rain tomorrow. (talking to oneself)

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: guests, seniors, an audience (e.g. a weather forecast) → でしょう; talking to yourself, diaries, written texts, or close friends (mostly men) → だろう.

groups.note: Both mean “there is / have”

items.title: 〜ございます (there is / exists)
items.diff: Same meaning — “there is”; がございます is the more formal form of があります, used by shop staff or receptionists speaking to customers.

this.tr: There's a restroom on the second floor.

that.tag: がございます · More formal, to customers
that.tr: There's a restroom on the second floor. (said by staff to a customer)

wrong.why: You can't use ございます to say where a person is — use おります

items.explain: The two sentences can be swapped without changing the meaning; the difference is formality: in everyday speech or when asking directions → があります; shop staff or hotel front desks speaking to customers, or formal announcements and notices → がございます. ございます can only replace 「ある」 for things; to say a person is somewhere, use おります or いらっしゃいます.

groups.note: All come from ほしい (欲しい) — the speaker's inner feeling of “wanting”

items.diff: がほしい means wanting a thing; てほしい means wanting someone else to do something.

this.tr: I want a new bicycle.

that.tr: I want my dad to fix my bike.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ほしい」: noun＋が → you want that thing; verb て-form → you want someone else to do that action, and the person doing it is marked with 「に」. てもらいたい means the same thing (父に直してもらいたい).

groups.note: が ↔ は — only one particle differs

items.diff: Only the particle differs: が puts the answer to “who” on the subject; は first raises the person as a known topic, and the focus falls on what comes after.

this.tr: Who came? — Tanaka did.

that.tag: は · Topic first, then the question
that.tr: When did Tanaka come?

wrong.why: A question word as subject must take が

items.explain: Check whether さん is followed by が or は, then look at what's being asked: when the question is 「誰が」 and you're answering “who”, the answer word takes が (田中さんが来ました); when Tanaka is already a known topic and you go on to ask 「いつ」 he came or how he is, use は (田中さんは…). A question word as subject can only take が — you can't say 「誰は」.

groups.note: Both express contrast — “…, but …”

items.title: 〜けど (contrast)
items.diff: Same meaning — “…, but …”; が leans formal and written, けど leans casual and spoken.

this.tr: This dish is a little spicy, but it's very tasty.

that.tr: This dish is kinda spicy, but it's super good!

items.explain: Both express contrast and can be swapped without changing the meaning; the difference is register: が is more formal, usually follows 「です」「ます」, and is used in writing or when speaking to a boss or a stranger; けど is casual — saying 「辛いけど」 to a friend sounds most natural. Attaching が directly to the plain form (辛いが) sounds like written language. けれども is the full form of けど and is slightly more formal.

groups.note: Both express ability — “can”

items.title: 〜ことができる (ability)
items.diff: Both mean “can”; a noun takes ができる directly, which is common in speech; for an action, say “verb dictionary form＋ことができる”, which sounds more formal.

this.tag: Noun＋ができる · Common in speech
this.tr: My older sister knows Chinese.

that.tag: Verb＋ことができる · More formal
that.tr: My older sister can speak Chinese.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 added first

items.explain: The two sentences can be swapped without changing the meaning: ができる takes a noun directly (中国語、スキー) to say you have that skill, and is the most common in speech; ことができる takes a verb (話す、泳ぐ) to name the specific action, and sounds more formal and written. Check whether a noun or a verb comes before できる: a verb can't take ができる directly.

groups.note: Both mark where you're moving to — “to …”

items.title: 〜に (destination)
items.diff: When going somewhere, both へ and に work; へ leans toward “in that direction”, に toward “arriving at that point”.

this.tr: The train is now heading for Tokyo.

that.tr: The train will arrive in Tokyo soon.

items.explain: 「東京へ行く」 and 「東京に行く」 mean the same thing, and both are fine. The difference is nuance: へ leans toward “heading in that direction”, に toward “arriving at that point”. So look at the verb that follows: 向かっています only says which way you're going → へ is more common; 着きます says where you arrive → に is usually used.

groups.note: Both suggest that the listener do something

items.diff: ほうがいい says directly “this is better”, like a piece of advice; たらどうですか makes the suggestion as a question, so it sounds softer.

this.tr: You've got a high fever, so you should go to the hospital right away.

that.tr: If you're tired, why don't you rest a bit?

items.explain: Consider how pressing it is: if not doing it could cause trouble (熱が高い, being late) → ほうがいい; if you're just lightly offering an idea (疲れているなら) and leaving the decision to the other person → たらどうですか.

items.title: 〜ばいい (advice / how to)
items.diff: Both give the listener advice; ほうがいい compares and says “this is better”, with a note of warning; ばいい means “just do this and you're fine”, implying it's easy.

this.tr: If you don't understand, you'd better ask the teacher early.

that.tr: That's easy. Just ask the teacher.

items.explain: 「先生に聞いたほうがいい」 and 「先生に聞けばいい」 both work with the same meaning, but the feel differs: ほうがいい implies a comparison — not doing it might turn out badly, so it's “best” to do it — and it often comes with reminders like 「早めに」; ばいい means “doing just this is enough” — the matter isn't hard — and it often follows 「簡単だよ」 or 「心配しないで」 to reassure the listener.

groups.note: Both confirm “…, right?”

items.title: 〜でしょう (confirming)
items.diff: じゃないですか brings up something the listener also knows as a premise, usually to lead into what comes next; でしょう？ really asks “right?” and waits for an answer.

this.tr: You know that convenience store near the station? Please wait for me there.

that.tr: There's a convenience store near the station, right?

items.explain: Check whether you are waiting for an answer: if you just bring up something both of you know as a premise and go straight on (あそこで待っていてください) → じゃないですか, and the listener doesn't need to reply; if you are really asking “right?” and waiting for them to say 「うん」 → でしょう？. Using じゃないですか for something the listener may not know sounds pushy.

groups.note: Both mean “during…”

items.diff: 〜中 only attaches to nouns; when a verb (〜ている) comes before, use 「間」.

this.tr: Please turn off your phone during the meeting.

that.tr: It rained while I was asleep.
I was reading a book the whole time I was on the train.

wrong.why: 中 can't follow a verb; use 間

items.explain: Look at whether a noun or a verb comes before: nouns like 会議、授業、夏休み → 〜中 (会議中、夏休み中); verbs like 寝ている、日本にいる → 〜間／〜間に. Nouns can also take 間, as in 「会議の間」, but you have to add 「の」.

groups.note: Both come from the particle 「か」 — its core meaning is raising a question, putting forward something uncertain

items.diff: 何を〜か asks what exactly; 何か〜か asks “would you like … something?” and is answered with はい／いいえ.

this.tr: What will you eat? — Sushi.

that.tr: Would you like something to eat? — Yes, please.

items.explain: The core meaning of か is raising a question, putting forward something uncertain. At the end of a sentence it turns the whole sentence into a question: in 「何を食べますか」, 「何」 is a blank for the listener to fill in, so the answer is the content (すし). Attached directly to a question word, 「何か」 originally meant “what could it be? (not sure)”, so it becomes an unspecified “something”, and all that is left to ask is “will you eat or not”, so you answer 「はい／いいえ」 first. Look at what follows the question word: a particle like 「を」 or 「が」 → asking what; 「か」 directly → asking whether.

items.diff: A question with a question word just takes 「か」; without a question word, to ask “whether”, use 「かどうか」.

this.tr: I don't know when he's coming.

that.tr: I don't know whether he's coming tomorrow.

wrong.why: With a question word, you can't add 「どうか」

items.explain: The core meaning of か is raising a question. When you embed a question in a sentence: if it has a question word (いつ、どこ、誰), the uncertain part is already marked, so you just add か (いつ来るか); if there is no question word, 「来るか」 and 「どうか (or what)」 are set side by side as two possibilities, fixed as かどうか, meaning “whether”. So check whether the embedded question has a question word: a word like いつ → か; none, just asking whether he comes → かどうか.

groups.note: そうですか ↔ そうですね — they differ only in the last kana

items.diff: そうですか is “oh, I see” on hearing new information; そうですね agrees with the other person: “yes, it is”.

this.tr: Tomorrow's a day off, you know. — Oh, is it? (I see.)

that.tr: It's hot today, isn't it? — Yes, it is.

items.explain: Look at what the other person said: news you didn't know (〜よ) → そうですか (falling intonation); something you both feel, where they are looking for agreement (〜ね) → そうですね. Answering “It's so hot today” with 「そうですか」 sounds as if you doubt them.

groups.note: たから ↔ てから — they differ by just one kana

items.diff: たから is “because (I) did…”; てから is “after doing…”.

this.tr: I've eaten, so I'm full.

that.tr: I'll go out after I eat.

items.explain: Only た and て differ: ta-form＋から gives a reason, and the second half is the result (おなかがいっぱい); te-form＋から gives the order in time, and the second half is what you do next (出かける).

groups.note: Both express a reason

items.diff: から is subjective and conversational, and can also end a sentence as 「〜からです」; ので is objective and polite, and is only used mid-sentence.

this.tr: The reason I was late for class is that the bus didn't come.

that.tr: The bus didn't come, so I was late for class.

wrong.why: ので can't end a sentence followed by 「です」

items.explain: Look at the position and the situation: at the end of a sentence answering “why” → only から (〜からです); explaining a reason mid-sentence to a teacher or boss → ので sounds more objective and less like an excuse; talking casually to friends, or followed by a command or invitation → から is more natural.

groups.note: The 「まで」 in から〜まで ↔ までに — only one 「に」 apart

items.diff: から〜まで is doing something continuously over a period; までに is a deadline — it's fine as long as it's done before then.

this.tr: I work from nine to five.

that.tr: I'll be back by five.

wrong.why: Handing in homework is a one-off action, so use までに

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: actions that go on continuously, like 働く、待つ、寝る → the まで of から〜まで, meaning you keep doing it up to that time; actions completed in one go, like 帰る、出す、終わる → までに, meaning “by then at the latest”.

groups.note: Both express a range “from… to…”

items.diff: から〜まで has a clear start and end; から〜にかけて only gives a rough range and is common in weather reports and the news.

this.tr: Class is from nine to twelve.

that.tr: It will probably rain from tonight through tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether you mean an exact time: things with a clear start and end, like classes or business hours → から〜まで; a vague stretch of time or area, like “tonight through tomorrow” in a weather forecast → から〜にかけて.

groups.note: 〜方（かた）↔ 〜方（ほう）がいい — the same kanji, but different readings and meanings

items.diff: masu-stem＋方 is read 「かた」 and means “the way of doing…”; ta-form＋方がいい is read 「ほう」 and means “you'd better…”.

this.tr: Please teach me how to write this kanji.

that.tr: You'd better write kanji by hand.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「方」: verb masu-stem (書き、読み)＋方 → read 「かた」, a noun meaning “way of writing”, preceded by 「の」; verb ta-form (書いた)＋方がいい → read 「ほう」, advising “you'd better do this”.

groups.note: All express a contrast — “although…, but…”

items.title: 〜が (contrast)
items.diff: けど is more casual and used between friends; が is more formal and used in formal situations, writing and emails.

this.tr: This place is pricey, but it's really delicious!

that.tr: This restaurant's prices are high, but the food is truly excellent.

items.explain: Look at the tone of the whole sentence: a chatty tone with 「よ」 and dropped particles → けど; formal wording with 「です・ます」 and words like 「大変」, in reports, emails or speeches → が. 「高いですけど」 is also possible, but formal writing generally uses が. けれども is a little more formal than けど, but formal writing still mostly uses が.

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: けど is a neutral contrast and can be followed by an intention or invitation; のに carries surprise and dissatisfaction and can't be followed by an intention or invitation.

this.tr: It's a bit expensive, but let's buy it.

that.tr: Even though it was expensive, it broke right away.

wrong.why: のに can't be followed by an intention or invitation like 「〜よう」

items.explain: Look at the second half: the speaker's own plan, invitation or request (買おう, 〜てください) → only けど; a result that goes against expectations, with frustration or regret (すぐ壊れた) → only のに can express that “even though…” feeling. けれども works the same way, just a bit more formal than けど.

items.title: でも (sentence-initial: but)
items.diff: けど attaches to the end of the first clause, joining the two into one sentence; でも goes at the start of the next sentence, after the first one is finished.

this.tr: These clothes are expensive, but cute.

that.tr: These clothes are expensive. But they're cute.

wrong.why: でも can't attach to the end of a clause; first end the sentence with 「。」

items.explain: Look at the position: 「けど」 sticks right onto the end of the previous clause (高いけど、); 「でも」 needs a complete sentence before it, closed with 「。」, and then starts the next sentence. Since English uses “but” for both, it's easy to write ✗高いでも. けれども works the same way, just a bit more formal than けど.

groups.note: この ↔ ここ — only the last kana differs

items.diff: この is followed directly by a noun and points to the one right in front of you; ここ means “here”, and to modify a noun you say 「ここの」.

this.tr: This ramen is really good.

that.tr: The ramen here is really good!

items.explain: Only the last kana differs: この already contains 「の」, so it takes a noun directly and points to the one thing in front of you; ここ is the place “here”, and like any other noun it needs an extra 「の」 to modify a noun. So check whether 「こ」 or 「ここ」 comes before 「の」: saying “this bowl” while eating → このラーメン; recommending the ramen “of this restaurant (this place)” → ここのラーメン. その／そこの and あの／あそこの work the same way.

groups.note: Only one kana apart: どこ ↔ どこか, ここ ↔ これ, ここ ↔ この

items.diff: どこ asks “where”, and the answer is a place; どこか means “somewhere”, so you answer “yes / no” first.

this.tr: Where are you going on Sunday?

that.tr: Are you going anywhere on Sunday?

items.explain: Just one 「か」 makes the answers completely different: どこへ → “To Kyoto”; どこかへ → “Yes, to Kyoto” or “No, nowhere”. When you hear 「どこか」, answer 「はい／いいえ」 first.

items.diff: ここ refers to a place, and you ask about it with 「どこ」; これ refers to a thing, and you ask about it with 「何」.

this.tr: Where are we? (What place is this?)

that.tr: What is this?

items.explain: Only the last kana differs: ここ is the place “here”, これ is the thing “this”. Look at the question word: asking what place it is, with どこ → ここ; asking what thing it is, with 何 → これ. You can't use ここ for something you are holding or pointing at in front of you. そこ／それ and あそこ／あれ work the same way.

items.diff: ここの＋noun means “of this place”; この＋noun points to the one right in front of you.

this.tr: The ramen here is really good!

that.tr: This ramen is really good.

items.explain: Only the last kana differs: ここ is the place “here”, and to modify a noun it needs an extra 「の」, becoming ここの; この already contains 「の」, so it takes a noun directly and points to the one thing in front of you. So check whether 「ここ」 or 「こ」 comes before 「の」: recommending the ramen “of this restaurant (this place)” → ここのラーメン; saying “this bowl” while eating → このラーメン. その／そこの and あの／あそこの work the same way.

groups.note: All come from the old Japanese pronoun 「こ」, whose basic meaning is “near the speaker (this)”

items.diff: これ is a noun by itself, directly followed by 「は・が・を」; この must be followed by a noun.

this.tr: This is my older brother's bag.

that.tr: This bag is my older brother's.

wrong.why: To modify a noun, use 「この」

items.explain: The basic meaning of 「こ」 is “near the speaker (this)”. Add 「れ」, which points to a thing, and you get 「これ」 — “this thing”. It is a noun on its own, so 「は」 follows directly. Add 「の」, meaning “of / …'s”, and you get 「この」 — “of here”, which can only hang in front of a noun, so a noun like 「かばん」 comes next. Just check whether the word right after it is the particle 「は」 or a noun like 「かばん」. The same goes for 「それ／その」.

items.diff: これ refers to a thing, asked about with 「何」; ここ refers to a place, asked about with 「どこ」.

this.tr: What is this?

that.tr: Where is this (place)?

items.explain: The basic meaning of 「こ」 is “near the speaker (this)”. Add 「れ」, which points to a thing, and you get 「これ」 (this thing); to ask about a thing, use 「何」. Add 「こ」, which marks a place, and you get 「ここ」 (this place); to ask about a place, use 「どこ」. So whether the question uses 「何」 or 「どこ」 tells you if it's about a thing or a place. The same goes for 「それ／そこ」.

groups.note: Both mean “can, be able to”

items.title: 〜られる (potential)
items.diff: ことができる is formal and written, often used for rules and explanations; the potential form is short and more common in everyday conversation.

this.tr: At this library, you can borrow up to five books.

that.tr: You can borrow five books at this library, you know.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the setting and the particle: notices, explanations, formal settings → ことができます, and the object keeps 「を」 (本を借りる); chatting with friends → the potential form sounds more natural, and the object often changes to 「が」 (本が借りられる).

items.title: 〜ができる (can, know how to)
items.diff: Nouns attach directly to 「ができる」; actions must be expressed as “verb＋ことができる”.

this.tr: I can play the piano.

that.tr: I can play the piano.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 added first

items.explain: Same meaning — “can, know how to”. Look at what comes before 「ができる」: a noun (ピアノ、日本語) attaches directly; a verb (弾く、書く) must first take 「こと」 to become a noun. ことができる spells out the actual action and also sounds more formal; when you just mean having a skill, noun＋ができる is shorter. English says “can…” for both, so it's easy to leave out こと.

groups.note: Both mean “like doing …”

items.diff: こと is slightly formal and leans written; の is more colloquial and more common in everyday conversation.

this.tr: I like taking photos.

that.tr: I like taking photos.

items.explain: Before 「好き・嫌い・得意」 both work and the meaning doesn't change: こと is slightly formal, common in essays and self-introductions; の is more colloquial, and 「〜のが好き」 sounds more natural in everyday chat.

groups.note: Both mean “about …”

items.title: 〜ばかり (about)
items.diff: Both mean “around …”: くらい is the most ordinary; ばかり is a bit more formal and a little old-fashioned.

this.tr: I bought about five apples.

that.tag: A bit formal · a bit old-fashioned
that.tr: I bought some five apples.

items.explain: After a quantity, both mean “around …” and are interchangeable: in everyday conversation くらい (ぐらい) is the most ordinary; ばかり is a bit more formal and has a slightly old-fashioned feel, so young people rarely use it in daily speech.

groups.note: Both mean “to the point of …”

items.title: 〜ほど (degree)
items.diff: Both work when using an exaggerated example to show degree: くらい is more colloquial, ほど slightly more formal.

this.tr: It was so funny I laughed until I cried.

that.tag: Slightly formal · also common in writing
that.tr: It was so funny I laughed until I cried.

items.explain: When an exaggerated example shows the degree, both work and the meaning stays the same: くらい (ぐらい) is more colloquial and casual; ほど is slightly more formal and more common in writing and formal settings.

groups.note: Both come from 「まで」, whose basic meaning is the end point “up to …”

items.diff: まで means continuing until then; までに means doing it once before then.

this.tr: I'll wait until five.

that.tr: I'll be back by five.

wrong.why: 「出す」 is a one-time action, so use までに

items.explain: Both contain 「まで」, whose basic meaning is the end point “up to …”. まで alone says the action continues all the way to that end point, so it goes with actions that can last, like 「待って」. Add 「に」, which marks a point in time, and you get までに: the end point becomes a deadline, and the action has to be done once at some moment before it, so it goes with actions completed in one go, like 「帰ります」. Check whether the verb that follows can continue over time.

groups.note: Both mean “even …”

items.title: 〜さえ (even)
items.diff: Both mean “even …”: まで stresses that the range has spread all the way to this point; さえ stresses that the example given is the most extreme.

this.tr: Even children laughed at me.

that.tr: Even children laughed at me.

items.explain: Both fit the same sentence, meaning “even children…”. まで feels like others were laughing at me and in the end even children joined in — it stresses the range spreading to someone unexpected. さえ feels like children were the last ones who should laugh at me, yet even they did — it stresses that this example is the most extreme. When a negative follows, saying you can't even do the most basic thing, さえ is the usual choice.

groups.note: Both come from 「前（まえ）」, whose basic meaning is “in front” in space

items.title: 〜の前 (position)
items.diff: Activity＋の前に is “before” in time; place＋の前に is “in front of” in space.

this.tr: I wash my hands before eating.

that.tr: There's a bank in front of the station.

items.explain: The basic meaning of 「前」 is “in front” in space: 駅の前 = the area in front of the station, often followed by 「あります・います」. If you picture time as a line, the stretch of time lined up ahead of an event is also called 「前」, which gives the time meaning “before”: 食事の前 = before eating, followed by the action you do first. To tell them apart, look at the noun before 「の前」: a place or thing like 駅、家、机 → space; an activity like 食事、会議、試験 → time.

groups.note: まえに ↔ までに: only one kana differs, 「え／で」

items.diff: まえに states the order of two events; までに states a deadline — any time before it is fine.

this.tr: Please take the medicine before going to bed.

that.tr: Please take the medicine by bedtime (any time before then).

items.explain: The two sentences differ by just one kana, え／で. 前に (まえに) is about order: take the medicine first, then go to bed. までに treats “going to bed” as a deadline: you can take it any time between now and bedtime, as long as it's not later than that. English often says “before …” for both, so they're easy to mix up.

groups.note: All mean “(do) before…”

items.title: 〜ないうちに (before … happens)
items.diff: 前に neutrally says “before …”; ないうちに carries urgency: “quickly, while it hasn't … yet”.

this.tr: Let's bring in the laundry before it rains.

that.tr: Let's bring in the laundry while it still isn't raining.

items.explain: Both work and both mean “before it rains”: 前に just states the order neutrally; ないうちに carries the urgency of “it hasn't started yet, so hurry”, and often comes with 「早く」 or 「〜ておこう」. Note that うちに takes the negative 「降らない」, while 前に takes the affirmative 「降る」.

groups.note: All invite the other person to do something together

items.diff: ませんか first asks about the other person's wishes; ましょう pushes to do something together, assuming they'll agree.

this.tr: If you'd like, would you like to see a movie together?

that.tr: Sure, sounds good. Let's watch it together.

items.explain: Look at the order in the conversation: a first invitation, not knowing if the other person wants to → ませんか (often with 「よかったら」); they've already agreed, or everyone has already decided → ましょう. Opening with ましょう can sound like you're deciding for them.

items.title: 〜ましょうか (suggesting doing it together)
items.diff: ませんか leaves the decision to the other person and is more indirect; ましょうか is you proposing “let's …” yourself, then asking for agreement.

this.tag: Indirect · asks if they want to
this.tr: It's about time — why don't we head home?

that.tr: It's about time — shall we head home?

items.explain: Both fit the same sentence, meaning “it's about time we went home, isn't it?”: ませんか uses a negative question to leave the decision to the other person, so it's more indirect and suits superiors or cases where you're not sure what they think; ましょうか is you putting forward the plan yourself and then asking whether they agree.

items.title: 〜ない？ (invitation)
items.diff: ませんか is polite, used with superiors and people you don't know well; 〜ない？ is casual, used among friends and family.

this.tr: Sensei, would you like to have lunch together?

that.tr: Hey, wanna grab lunch together?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: elders and superiors like 「先生」「部長」 → ませんか; friends and family (ねえ, 〜くん) → 「〜ない？」 with rising intonation. Both invite by asking a negative question.

groups.note: Both offer the other person something to eat, drink or enjoy

items.title: 〜はいかがですか (offering)
items.diff: Both offer the other person something to drink: いかがですか names only the thing and is more formal; ませんか says the action and sounds a bit more relaxed.

this.tr: Would you like to have some coffee or something?

that.tr: How about some coffee?

items.explain: Both sentences offer the other person coffee, and both often take 「でも」 (“… or something”): いかがですか doesn't mention the action — it just puts the thing in front of the other person, a formal phrase hosts and shop staff use with guests; ませんか spells out the action 「飲み」, sounds a bit more relaxed than いかがですか, and sometimes also implies “let's drink together”.

groups.note: ましょう ↔ ましょうか: only one 「か」 apart

items.diff: ましょう means “let's all … together”; add one 「か」 to get ましょうか, and it becomes “shall I …?”.

this.tr: Let's all clean up together.

that.tr: Shall I do the cleaning?

items.explain: Check whether the sentence ends with 「か」, then who does it: no 「か」, done 「みんなで」 → ましょう, “let's all … together”; with 「か」, done by 「私が」 → ましょうか, “shall I …?”, offering to help. Saying 「手伝いましょう」 outright sounds as if you've already decided for the other person; when offering help, people usually say 「手伝いましょうか」.

groups.note: Both invite the other person to do something together

items.diff: ましょう pushes to act together, assuming the other person agrees; ませんか first asks whether they want to.

this.tr: Sure, sounds good. Let's watch it together.

that.tr: If you'd like, would you like to see a movie together?

items.explain: Look at the order in the conversation: they've already agreed, or everyone has already decided → ましょう; a first invitation, not knowing if they want to → ませんか (often with 「よかったら」). Usually you ask 「〜ませんか」 first, and say 「〜ましょう」 once they agree.

items.title: 〜(よ)う (suggestion, invitation)
items.diff: ましょう is polite; the volitional form 「〜(よ)う」 is its casual form, used between friends.

this.tr: Sir, shall we get going soon?

that.tr: Hey, let's get going soon.

items.explain: Same meaning — both draw the other person into doing something together. Look at who you're talking to: a superior like 「部長」, an elder, or someone you don't know well → 行きましょう; friends or family, often opening with 「ねえ」 → 行こう, 食べよう.

groups.note: Both offer help: “Shall I…?”

items.title: 〜(よ)うか (casual)
items.diff: ましょうか is polite; 「〜(よ)うか」 is its casual form, used with family and friends.

this.tr: Professor, shall I carry that bag for you?

that.tr: Mom, shall I carry that bag?

items.explain: Same meaning — it depends on who you're talking to: a teacher like 「先生」, a boss, a customer → 持ちましょうか; family like 「お母さん」 or friends → 持とうか (for godan verbs, the final -u sound changes to the -o row, plus う).

groups.note: Both mean “Shall we… together?”

items.title: 〜ましょう (let's do it together)
items.diff: Both suggest doing something together; ましょうか asks for the other person's agreement and is more respectful; ましょう is a direct call to action that assumes they'll agree.

this.tr: Look at the time. Shall we head home soon?

that.tr: Look at the time. Let's head home soon.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence ends with 「か」: with 「か」, said with rising intonation as “…okay?”, you leave the decision to the other person → ましょうか; without 「か」, the speaker takes the lead and calls everyone to act, sounding more upbeat and assuming agreement → ましょう.

items.title: 〜ませんか (inviting someone to join)
items.diff: Both politely suggest doing something together; ましょうか is “So, shall we…?”, while ませんか first asks “Would you like to…?”, showing more respect for the other person's wishes.

this.tr: That movie we talked about the other day — shall we go see it together?

that.tr: If you'd like, would you like to go see a movie together?

items.explain: Check whether the other person already wants to do it: if you've both talked about it already, like 「この前話した」, and it just needs settling → ましょうか, with a positive “let's do it, then” tone; if you're bringing it up for the first time and asking if they're willing, like 「よかったら」 → ませんか, which leaves the decision entirely to them and is more polite.

groups.note: ません ↔ ませんか: the only difference is one 「か」 at the end

items.diff: ません is a negative, “don't…”; adding 「か」 to make ませんか usually turns it into an invitation, “would you like to…?”.

this.tr: I'm not going to the movies tomorrow.

that.tr: Would you like to go to the movies tomorrow?

items.explain: Just one 「か」 makes the difference: a sentence ending in 「ません。」 → you say you won't do it; ending in 「ませんか」 → usually an invitation, answered with 「いいですね」 or 「ええ、ぜひ」 — not 「はい、行きません」.

groups.note: Both express the negative, differing only in politeness

items.diff: ません is the polite negative; ない is the plain negative, with the same meaning.

this.tr: Professor, I won't drink today.

that.tr: Sorry, I'm not drinking today.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: a teacher like 「先生」, a boss, a stranger → 飲みません; a friend or family member, as with 「ごめん」 → 飲まない. Note the conjugation: ません attaches to the ます-form (飲み), ない to the ない-form (飲ま).

groups.note: Both come from the particle 「も」 — its core meaning is “this one counts too”

items.diff: Noun＋も means “…too”; question word＋も＋negative means “nothing / nobody at all”.

this.tr: I don't drink coffee. I don't drink juice either.

that.tr: I haven't drunk anything since this morning.

items.explain: The core meaning of 「も」 is “this one counts too”: after a specific thing (ジュース), when a similar item has already been mentioned (コーヒーは…), it adds one more → “too / either”; after the question word 「何」, it counts in “any one of them at all”, and with a following negative → not a single one → “nothing at all”, a total negation. So check whether 「も」 follows a specific thing or a question word.

groups.note: Both come from the nominalizer 「の」 — its core meaning is presenting something as “the situation”

items.diff: んです presents the situation and stops there, giving a reason; んですが presents the situation and pauses with 「が」, leading into a request or question.

this.tr: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped.

that.tr: Excuse me, I'm lost — where is the station?

items.explain: 「の（ん）」 originally presents something as “the situation”: 「んです。」 lays out the situation and ends → explaining a reason (遅れてすみません。電車が止まったんです); 「んですが、」 lays out the situation, then pauses at 「が」 without concluding and leaves room for what follows → a lead-in to a request or question (駅はどこですか). So check whether 「ん」 is followed by 「です。」 that ends the sentence or by 「ですが、」 that keeps going. The same goes for written のです and casual んだ.

groups.note: Both ask “What's wrong?” after noticing something

items.title: 〜の？ (caring question)
items.diff: んですか politely asks about the situation; 〜の？ is its casual form, used with friends and family.

this.tr: Professor, what's wrong?

that.tr: Hey, what's wrong?

items.explain: Both ask for the reason after seeing how someone looks; it depends on who you're talking to: a teacher like 「先生」, a boss, someone you don't know well → 〜んですか; calling out to a friend or family member with 「ねえ」 → 「〜の？」 with rising intonation. A more formal written version is のですか.

groups.note: Both come from classical 「なり」 (に＋あり) — its core meaning is “to be in the state of…”

items.title: 〜に (な-adjective modifying a verb)
items.diff: A な-adjective uses 「な」 to modify a noun, but 「に」 to modify a verb.

this.tr: I study in a quiet room.

that.tr: Please speak quietly in the library.

wrong.why: Use 「に」 to modify a verb

items.explain: In classical Japanese, 「静かなり」 meant “is quiet (state)”. Its form before nouns, 「静かなる」, was later shortened to 「静かな」 → 静かな部屋 (a quiet room); its form before verbs was 「静かに」 all along → 静かに話してください (please speak quietly). So look at the word right after it: a noun (部屋, 人, 町) → な; a verb (話してください, 歩く) → に.

groups.note: Both come from the sentence-final exclamatory 「な」 — its core meaning is voicing your feelings to yourself

items.diff: なあ blurts out a feeling as an exclamation; かな adds the question marker 「か」 before it, making it an unsure question to yourself.

this.tr: The ramen at this place is so good.

that.tr: I wonder if the ramen at this place is good.

items.explain: 「な」 originally voices your feelings to yourself: attached right after the feeling → おいしいなあ, you've already tasted it and exclaim “this is so good”; add the question marker 「か」 first, then 「な」 → おいしいかな, you voice a doubt to yourself: “I wonder if it's good”. So check whether 「か」 comes before 「な」: no → exclamation; yes → an unsure question to yourself.

groups.note: Both are exclamations: “How…!”

items.diff: なあ is mostly an exclamation to yourself; ね is said to a listener, seeking agreement.

this.tr: Ugh, it's so hot.

that.tr: It's really hot today, isn't it?

items.explain: Check whether there's someone you're talking to: talking to yourself with something like 「ああ」, not expecting a reply → なあ, usually after the plain form; making small talk and hoping the other person will say “It sure is” → ね, which can follow 「です」.

groups.note: Both are prohibitions: “Don't…”

items.diff: Dictionary form＋な is a rude, forceful prohibition; ないでください is a polite request.

this.tr: Don't take photos in this room!

that.tr: Excuse me, please don't take photos in this room.

items.explain: Consider who you're speaking to and the situation: politely addressing a customer, a stranger, or a superior, starting with 「すみません」 → ないでください; scolding angrily, shouting a warning in an emergency, or on signs → 〜な. Saying 「〜な」 to someone's face is very rude.

groups.note: Both can express “at the same time”

items.title: 〜間 (throughout)
items.diff: ながら is one person doing two things at once; 間 uses a stretch of time as the background, and the two halves can be about different people.

this.tr: I cooked while listening to music.

that.tr: While my mother was cooking, I was listening to music.

wrong.why: With ながら, both actions must be done by the same person

items.explain: Look at the subjects of the two actions: the same person → ながら; different people (母が……, 私は……) → 間.

items.title: 〜つつ (while doing)
items.diff: Both mean one person doing two things at once; ながら works in everyday speech and writing, while つつ is written language and more refined.

this.tr: I walked along the seaside road, chatting with a friend.

that.tr: I strolled along the seaside road, listening to the sound of the waves.

items.explain: Same meaning — it depends on the style: chatting and everyday conversation → ながら; writing, speeches, news and other formal language → つつ, which sounds refined. A very colloquial verb like 「しゃべる」 sounds awkward with つつ. With both, the two actions must be done by the same person.

groups.note: Both mean “not (do)…”, differing only in politeness

items.title: 〜ません
items.diff: ない is the plain negative; ません is the polite negative, with the same meaning.

this.tr: Sorry, I'm not drinking today.

that.tr: Professor, I won't drink today.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: a friend or family member, as with 「ごめん」 → 飲まない; a teacher like 「先生」, a boss, a stranger → 飲みません. Note the conjugation: ない attaches to the ない-form (飲ま), ません to the ます-form (飲み).

groups.note: Both come from 「いけない」 (行けない = “won't do / no good”) — not doing it is no good = must; doing it is no good = forbidden

items.diff: ないといけない is “not doing it won't do” = must; てはいけない is “doing it won't do” = must not.

this.tr: I have to take medicine every day.

that.tr: You must not drink alcohol while taking medicine.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「いけない」: 「ないと」 (if you don't) → you must do it; 「ては／では」 (if you do) → you must not do it. The only difference is the negative in front, yet the meanings are exact opposites.

groups.note: Both mean “must”

items.diff: ないといけない is conversational, mostly about your own specific situation; なければならない is more formal, mostly used for rules and in writing.

this.tr: It's already ten o'clock. I have to go home.

that.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

items.explain: Look at what you're talking about: your own immediate situation (もう10時だ) → ないといけない sounds more natural; laws, rules, or objective obligations in writing, as with 「日本では」 → なければならない. Both mean the same, and swapping them isn't wrong.

groups.note: Both come from the negative 「ないで」 — its core meaning is “without doing…”

items.diff: ないで＋ください asks someone not to do something; ないで＋another verb means “did … without …”.

this.tr: Please don't forget your umbrella.

that.tr: I went out without taking an umbrella.

items.explain: 「ないで」 originally means “in a state of not doing…”: followed by another verb (出かけた, 寝た), it means doing B without having done A → “did B without A”; followed by 「ください」, it asks the other person to stay in the “not doing” state → “please don't…”. So check whether 「ないで」 is followed by 「ください」 or by some other verb.

groups.note: Both mean “don't… / not allowed to…”

items.diff: ないでください is a polite request; てはいけません announces a rule and can sound condescending when said to customers or superiors.

this.tr: Excuse me, please don't take photos here.

that.tr: Taking photos is not allowed inside the museum.

items.explain: Consider the speaker's position: asking someone face to face to cooperate, starting with 「すみません」, especially customers or strangers → ないでください; explaining the rules of a place, as with 「美術館の中で」, or a teacher to students or a parent to a child explaining what's right → てはいけません.

items.title: 〜な (prohibition)
items.diff: ないでください is a polite request; dictionary form＋な is a rude, forceful prohibition.

this.tr: Excuse me, please don't smoke here.

that.tr: Don't smoke here!

items.explain: Consider who you're speaking to and the situation: a customer, a stranger, or a superior, starting with 「すみません」 → ないでください; scolding angrily, shouting a warning in an emergency, or on signs → 〜な. Note that 〜な follows the dictionary form (吸う), not the ない-form.

groups.note: ないで ↔ なくて — only 「いで」 vs 「くて」 differs

items.diff: ないで means “without doing … (did something else instead)”; なくて gives a reason: “because … didn't happen, …”.

this.tr: I didn't take the bus; I walked.

that.tr: The bus didn't come, and I was stuck.

items.explain: ないで is 「ない＋で」; なくて turns 「ない」 into 「なく」 and adds 「て」. Look at the second half: if it is another action you go on to do (歩いて行った) → ないで; if it is the result or feeling caused by something not happening (困った, 遅れた) → なくて.

groups.note: Both mean “without doing …”

items.title: 〜ずに (without doing)
items.diff: Same meaning, “without doing …”: ないで is everyday speech; ずに is more formal/written, and 「する」 becomes 「せずに」.

this.tr: I took the exam without studying.

that.tr: I took the exam without studying.

wrong.why: 「する」 must become 「せずに」

items.explain: Both sentences say “I took the exam without studying”; the difference is register and how they attach. In conversation, ないで is more common (勉強しないで); in writing and formal settings, ずに is common. ずに replaces 「ない」 in the ない形 (言わ＋ずに), but する verbs like 「勉強」 are the exception: say 「勉強せずに」, never 「勉強しずに」.

groups.note: Both mean “must, have to”

items.diff: なければならない is more formal, used for rules and in writing; ないといけない is spoken, usually about your own concrete situation.

this.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

that.tr: It's already ten. I have to go home.

items.explain: Look at what is being talked about: an objective obligation from laws, rules or texts (「日本では」) → なければならない; your own situation right now (もう10時だ) → ないといけない sounds more natural. The meaning is the same, so swapping them is not wrong.

items.diff: なければならない is the full, formal form; なきゃ is a spoken contraction that drops the second half 「ならない」.

this.tr: According to the rules, the report must be submitted by Friday.

that.tr: Oh no, I've got to hand in the report by Friday.

items.explain: Both sentences say the same thing: the report is due by Friday. Look at the situation: stating a rule (「規則で」), writing it in a document, or speaking formally → the full なければならない; muttering to yourself (「やばい」) or talking with friends and family → shorten it to なきゃ (＝なければ) or なくちゃ (＝なくては), dropping 「ならない」/「いけない」. Don't use なきゃ with your boss or clients.

groups.note: Both come from 「いい」 — 「ても + いい」 = “it's fine even so”: fine to do it (てもいい) / fine not to (なくてもいい)

items.title: 〜てもいい (permission)
items.diff: てもいい means “you may do it”; なくてもいい means “you don't have to do it” — check whether the part before 「ても」 is affirmative or negative.

this.tr: If you have a fever, you don't have to go to school tomorrow.

that.tr: Your fever's gone, so you can go to school tomorrow.

items.explain: Look before 「ても」: 「行って」 is affirmative → permission to do it; 「行かなく」 is negative → fine not to do it, no need. When someone asks 「〜なくてもいいですか」, answering 「はい」 means you really don't have to.

groups.note: Both mean “no need to / don't have to”

items.diff: なくてもいい objectively says “it's fine not to”; ことはない urges the listener “there's no need to do that”, often to comfort them.

this.tr: Tomorrow is a day off, so you don't need to come to the office.

that.tr: There's no need to worry so much.

items.explain: ことはない follows the 辞書形 and often goes with 「そんなに」 or 「わざわざ」 to tell someone not to do something unnecessary; なくてもいい follows the negative form, simply states there's no need, and can also be used to ask 「〜なくてもいいですか」.

items.title: 〜ずに済む
items.diff: なくてもいい says “there's no need to”; ずに済む says “I would have had to, but luckily I didn't”.

this.tr: The station is close, so there's no need to take a taxi.

that.tr: A friend drove me, so luckily I didn't have to take a taxi.

items.explain: Look at tense and tone: ずに済んだ is usually past tense and means something you would have had to do was avoided thanks to some circumstance, with a sense of relief; なくてもいい just states there's no need now or in the future.

groups.note: Both are used to check with the listener

items.title: 〜よね (confirming)
items.diff: ね just re-checks something both people already know; よね first states your own belief and then asks the listener to confirm.

this.tr: So the meeting starts at three, right.

that.tr: If I remember right, the meeting was from three, wasn't it?

items.explain: Both sentences check with the listener that the meeting starts at three. ね just goes over something both sides already know, like wrapping up a discussion with 「じゃあ」; よね first puts forward your own judgment (“I think that's right”) and then asks for confirmation, so it often goes with 「確か」.

groups.note: Both come from the case particle 「に」 — its core meaning is the point an action is directed toward and finally lands on

items.diff: Place + に行く: に marks where you arrive → where you go; ます形 + に行く: に marks the action the movement aims at → what you go to do.

this.tr: I go to the library.

that.tr: I go to borrow a book.

items.explain: The core meaning of に is the point an action is directed toward and lands on. 「図書館に行く」: that point is a place, and you move there → where you go. 「本を借りに行く」: the point becomes an action, and you move in order to land on “borrowing a book” → what you go to do. So look before 「に」: 「図書館」 is a place → destination; 「本を借り」 is a verb in ます形 (or an action noun like 「買い物」) → purpose. The two can be combined: 「図書館へ本を借りに行く」.

groups.note: に ↔ で — only one particle differs, and both are often translated as “at/in”

items.title: 〜で (place of action)
items.diff: に is where a person or thing is; で is where an action takes place.

this.tr: There are lots of books in the library.

that.tr: I read books at the library.

wrong.why: The place where you do an action takes で

items.explain: Look at the verb at the end: verbs of existing or staying like 「ある」, 「いる」, 「住む」 → に; action verbs like 「読む」, 「食べる」, 「勉強する」 → で. Both translate as “at/in the library”, which is why they're so easy to mix up.

groups.note: Both mark the destination of movement

items.title: 〜へ (direction of movement)
