items.diff: For where you go, に and へ are mostly interchangeable; に focuses on the point of arrival, へ on the direction you head in.

this.tr: I finally got to the station.

that.tr: I'm heading to the station now.

items.explain: Look at the verb: 「着く」 and 「入る」 stress the point of arrival → usually に; 「向かう」 and 「出発する」 only say which way you're heading → usually へ; with 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 either works with no change in meaning.

groups.note: Both mark the other person in an action

items.title: 〜と (partner in a mutual action)
items.diff: に is something I do toward the other person, one way; と is something two people do together as equals.

this.tr: Tomorrow I'll consult my teacher.

that.tr: Tomorrow I'll talk it over with my teacher.

items.explain: The two sentences differ by just one particle. 「先生に相談する」 means I go to the teacher on my own side to ask for advice; 「先生と相談する」 means the teacher and I discuss it and decide together. 「話す」 works the same way: 母に話す is telling Mom something, 母と話す is chatting with Mom. 「結婚する」 and 「けんかする」 need two people, so only と works; 「あげる」 and 「教える」 go only one way toward the other person, so only に works.

groups.note: Both come from the case particle 「に」 — its core meaning is the point an action is directed toward and finally lands on

items.title: 〜に (destination)
items.diff: ます形 + に行く: に marks the action the movement aims at → what you go to do; place + に行く: に marks where you arrive → where you go.

this.tr: I go to borrow a book.

that.tr: I go to the library.

items.explain: The core meaning of に is the point an action is directed toward and lands on. 「図書館に行く」: that point is a place, and you move there → where you go. 「本を借りに行く」: the point becomes an action, and you move in order to land on “borrowing a book” → what you go to do. So look before 「に」: 「本を借り」 is a verb in ます形 (or an action noun like 「買い物」 or 「散歩」) → purpose; 「図書館」 is a place → destination. に来る and に帰る work the same way (遊びに来る).

groups.note: Both mean “in order to do something”

items.title: 〜ために (purpose)
items.diff: Before 「行く」 both work: 買いに行く is the everyday phrasing, 買うために行く is more formal and stresses the purpose; if the verb after isn't movement, only ために works.

this.tr: I'm going to the department store to buy clothes.

that.tr: I'm going to the department store in order to buy clothes.

wrong.why: Purpose 「に」 can only be followed by movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」; here you need 「買うために」

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: with movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 both work and the meaning is the same — ます形 + に行く is the everyday way to say it; 辞書形 + ために行く sounds more formal and stresses “specifically for this”. With actions that aren't movement, like 「アルバイトをする」 or 「貯金する」, only ために works.

groups.note: Both express “how often”

items.diff: に〜回 says how many times within a period; おきに says how much is skipped in between — 「１日おき」 = 「２日に１回」.

this.tr: I take this medicine once every two days.

that.tr: I take this medicine every other day.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same, yet the numbers differ. おきに counts the days skipped in between: １日おき = skipping one day = once every two days (２日に１回). When you see おきに, add one to the number to get “once every N days”. Expressions like 「１日に３回」 (times per day) can only use に〜回.

groups.note: Both come from 「にする」 — core meaning “to set … as”

items.diff: Noun + にする means picking one of several options; verb + ことにする means deciding to do something.

this.tr: For our summer trip, we picked Okinawa.

that.tag: Verb + ことにする · deciding to do
that.tr: I've decided to go to Okinawa for the summer break.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 before it can take 「にする」

items.explain: The core meaning of にする is “to set … as”. 沖縄にした: set the trip destination as Okinawa → picking one of several places. ことにする: first 「こと」 turns 「行く」 into a matter, then that matter is set as your plan → deciding to do something. So look before にする: a noun (沖縄) → choosing; verb + こと (行くこと) → deciding to do. A verb cannot attach to にする directly.

groups.note: Both mean “like doing …”

items.title: 〜こと (as an object)
items.diff: Same meaning: のが好き is everyday; ことが好き is a bit more written and formal.

this.tr: I like cooking on weekends.

that.tr: I like cooking on weekends.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “I like cooking on weekends”, and swapping them doesn't change the meaning. Look at the setting: in everyday conversation or chatting with friends, 「〜のが好き」 sounds more natural; in formal settings like essays or introducing yourself at an interview, 「〜ことが好き」 is common. The same goes before 「嫌い」 and 「得意」.

groups.note: Both come from the position word 「前（まえ）」 — core meaning is “in front” in space; with actions and events it is borrowed for “before” in time

items.title: 〜まえに (before an action)
items.diff: If what comes before 「前」 is a place or thing → “in front of” in space; if it is an action → “before” in time.

this.tr: I waited for my friend in front of the station.

that.tr: I bought a ticket before getting on the train.

wrong.why: A verb attaches directly to 「前に」 without 「の」

items.explain: The core meaning of 「前（まえ）」 is the side a person faces — “in front” in space: 駅の前 = in front of the station. Borrow that direction for time, and whatever is in front happens first: 電車に乗る前に = before getting on the train. So look at what comes before 「前」: places and things like 駅 or 家 → position; actions like 乗る (and events like 「会議」 or 「食事」) → time. A verb attaches directly to 「前」, with no 「の」.

groups.note: の中（なか） ↔ 中（じゅう） — the same kanji 「中」, but different readings and meanings

items.title: 〜中（じゅう）
items.diff: の中（なか） is the “inside” of something; 「中」 attached directly after a noun is read じゅう and means “throughout the whole …”.

this.tr: There's a cat in the box.

that.tr: It rained all day long.

items.explain: Check whether there's an 「の」 before 「中」: with 「の」 → read なか, meaning the inside of a space; attached directly after a time or place noun (一日中, 世界中) → read じゅう, meaning “all of, throughout”.

groups.note: Both express “the most…”

items.title: 〜ほど〜はない (nothing is more … than)
items.diff: の中で〜が一番 first draws a circle around a range, then objectively names number one; ほど〜はない draws no range and uses a negative to say “no one can match it”, carrying the speaker's strong personal admiration.

this.tr: In my family, my mother is the kindest.

that.tr: There's no one as kind as my mother.

items.explain: Both sentences say Mom is the “most” kind. Check whether the sentence first draws a range: with a range like 「家族の中で」, use the affirmative 「〜が一番」 → it objectively says who ranks first within that range, and it can also be used to ask questions (誰が一番〜？); with no range, use the negative 「〜ほど…はいない／はない」 → it says “no one can compare”, a subjective high evaluation by the speaker, with a stronger tone.

groups.note: Both mark the subject inside a clause that modifies a noun

items.title: 〜が (subject in a clause)
items.diff: In a clause that modifies a noun, marking the subject with 「の」 or 「が」 means the same; の is slightly more literary and soft, が is more common and neutral.

this.tr: This is a picture my older brother drew.

that.tr: This is a picture my older brother drew.

items.explain: The two sentences mean exactly the same. First check whether 「描いた」 is followed by a noun it modifies, 「絵」: if so, the subject in the clause can take either の or が; の is slightly more literary and soft, が is more common. When an object like 「絵を」 comes between the subject and the verb, の is easily read as “my brother's picture”, so が is normally used; when the sentence ends at the verb with no noun after it (兄が絵を描いた), only が is possible.

groups.note: Both mean “the act of doing…”

items.title: 〜こと (as subject)
items.diff: Both turn an action into a noun used as the subject; の is more conversational and often voices personal feelings, こと is slightly more formal and sounds more like a general truth.

this.tr: Traveling alone is fun.

that.tr: Traveling alone is an enjoyable thing.

items.explain: Both sentences turn 「一人で旅行する」 into the subject, and before evaluative words like 「楽しい」 either の or こと works. When chatting about your own feelings, の is more common; when stating a general truth in writing or a speech, こと is more common and sounds a bit more formal.

groups.note: Both come from 「の＋だ」 — 「の」 turns what comes before into a single fact, and 「だ」 asserts “that's how it is”

items.diff: ので is the mid-sentence form of 「の＋だ」: it first sets out the reason as a fact, and a result must follow; んです puts 「の＋だ（です）」 at the end of the sentence to explain the situation to the listener on its own.

this.tr: The roads are crowded, so I'll be a little late.

that.tr: Sorry I'm late. The traffic was bad, you see.

items.explain: Both come from 「の＋だ」: 「の」 wraps the event 「道が混んでいる」 into a noun, and 「だ」 asserts “that's the situation”. Placed at the end of a sentence as 「んです／のだ」, it lays the situation before the listener and explains the reason behind it; when 「だ」 continues in its connective form 「で」 to become 「ので」, it first sets out the reason as an established fact and then adds the result (遅れます), which is why ので sounds objective. To tell them apart, look at what follows 「の」: 「です」 or 「だ」 ending the sentence → explaining a situation; 「で」 with a result after it → because.

groups.note: Both express a reason, “because…”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: Both mean “because”; ので presents the reason as an objective circumstance, sounds gentle, and suits polite requests; から highlights the speaker's own reason and can be followed by a blunt command.

this.tr: It's raining, so please take an umbrella with you.

that.tr: It's raining — take an umbrella!

items.explain: Both sentences say “because it's raining”. Look at the second half: for a polite request to a guest or a superior (お持ちください), use ので, which sounds objective and not pushy; with a blunt command or prohibition like 「持っていけ」, から is natural, while ので paired with a rough command sounds awkward.

items.title: 〜て (reason)
items.diff: ので can be followed by a request or an intention; when て marks a reason, only a feeling or an uncontrollable result can follow.

this.tr: We're out of time, so please hurry.

that.tr: I had no time and was at a loss.

wrong.why: 「て」 marking a reason can't be followed by a request

items.explain: Look at the second half: a 「〜てください」 request like 「急いでください」 or a 「〜ましょう」 intention → only ので (or から) works; a feeling or natural result like 「困った」「びっくりした」 → て is fine.

groups.note: 何か ↔ 何も ↔ 何でも: only the particle after the question word differs (か／も／でも)

items.diff: Question word + か means “some (one)”; question word + も + negative means “not a single one”.

this.tr: Is there anything in the fridge?

that.tr: There's nothing in the fridge.

wrong.why: 「何も」 must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Just look at the one kana after the question word: 「何か」 → something, followed by an affirmative or a question; 「何も」 → nothing at all, always followed by a negative (ない). If asked 「何かある？」 and there's nothing, answer 「何もない」.

items.title: 疑問詞＋でも
items.diff: Question word + か is “some (one)” (unspecified); question word + でも is “any at all” (everything counts).

this.tr: I'm hungry. I want to eat something.

that.tr: I'm hungry. I want to eat — anything is fine.

items.explain: Look after the question word: with 「か」 → something, just without saying which; with 「でも」 → any one will do, often followed by 「いい」. The readings differ too: 何か is read なにか, 何でも is read なんでも.

groups.note: 何も ↔ 何か ↔ 何でも: only the particle after the question word differs (も／か／でも)

items.title: 疑問詞＋でも
items.diff: 何も + negative means “nothing at all”; 何でも + affirmative means “anything at all”.

this.tr: I don't feel like eating anything today.

that.tr: I can eat anything.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: negative → 何も (total negation); affirmative → 何でも (total affirmation). The readings differ too: 何も is read なにも, 何でも is read なんでも.

items.diff: Question word + も + negative means “not a single one”; question word + か means “some (one)”.

this.tr: There's nothing in the fridge.

that.tr: Is there anything in the fridge?

wrong.why: 「何も」 must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Just look at the one kana after the question word: 「何も」 → nothing at all, always followed by a negative (ない); 「何か」 → something, followed by an affirmative or a question. If asked 「何かある？」 and there's nothing, answer 「何もない」.

groups.note: Both mean “not a single one”

items.title: 〜として〜ない (not a single thing)
items.diff: 何も〜ない is the everyday total negation; 何一つとして〜ない is more formal and stresses “not even one”.

this.tr: Nothing was stolen from the room.

that.tr: Not a single thing was stolen from the room.

items.explain: Both sentences say nothing at all was taken from the room. 何も〜ない is the most ordinary way to say it, used in both speech and writing; 何一つとして〜ない negates even 「一つ」, stressing “not even one”, with a heavy tone, and is mostly used in writing, news or formal narration. In everyday chat, 「何もない」 is enough.

groups.note: Both mean “only…”

items.diff: だけ objectively says “only”, and works with affirmative or negative; しか must be followed by a negative and carries a sense of “too little, not enough”.

this.tr: I've only got 1,000 yen left in my wallet.

that.tr: There's just 1,000 yen in my wallet.

wrong.why: 「しか」 must always be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: しか is always followed by a negative (ない, 〜ません), the speaker feels it's too little, and it often goes with 「もう」; だけ can be followed by an affirmative and simply states the amount.

groups.note: All express contrast, “but”

items.title: でも (sentence-initial: but)
items.diff: しかし is formal, used in writing and speeches; でも is conversational, used in everyday chat.

this.tr: The exam was difficult. However, everyone passed.

that.tr: The exam was so hard. But everyone passed!

items.explain: Look at the tone of the whole sentence: chat with 「よ」「ね」 at the end and words like 「みんな」 → でも; written language as in reports, news or essays → しかし. Saying 「しかし」 when chatting with friends sounds stiff.

items.diff: けど sits mid-sentence, attached right after the first clause; しかし goes at the start of a new sentence.

this.tr: This restaurant is expensive. But the food is delicious.

that.tr: This restaurant is expensive, but the food is delicious.

wrong.why: しかし is a stand-alone conjunction — end the previous sentence with a period first

items.explain: Look at the position: right after the first clause → けど (けれども); after the sentence has been ended with 「。」, at the start of a new sentence → しかし.

items.diff: しかし is a general contrast; ところが is used specifically when the outcome is unexpected.

this.tr: This plan is good. However, it costs too much.

that.tr: I rushed over there. But, to my surprise, the shop was already closed.

items.explain: Look at the second half: giving your own view or raising a problem (お金がかかりすぎる) → しかし; telling something that already happened, contrary to expectations (店は閉まっていた, usually past tense) → ところが. ところが can't be followed by your own opinion or a request.

groups.note: Both mean “first…, then…”

items.title: そして (sequence: and then)
items.diff: Both mean doing one thing after finishing another; それから is common in speech when recounting what happened and highlights “after that”; そして is slightly more formal and mostly used in writing and storytelling.

this.tr: I ran into a friend at the station. After that, we watched a movie together.

that.tr: I ran into a friend at the station. And then we watched a movie together.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same: first meeting a friend, then seeing a movie. When chatting and recounting what you did one thing at a time, それから is more common, and it can also stand alone as a question, 「それから？」 (And then?); when writing a diary or an essay, or telling a story, そして is more natural, with a slightly more formal tone.

items.diff: てから links “first A, then B” within one sentence; それから goes at the start of a sentence and links two sentences.

this.tr: First I'll do my homework. Then I'll play.

that.tr: I'll play after I do my homework.

items.explain: The meaning is the same: homework first, then play. Look at the position: with 「てから」 attached directly to the verb → it's all said in one sentence and puts more stress on “only after A is done, B”; when 「まず」 introduces the first thing, a period ends the sentence and 「それから」 starts the next → it's split into two sentences, common when you list things one by one as you think.

groups.note: Both mean “also, one more thing” (adding an item)

items.diff: Both add one more item to what's already been said; for one more thing to buy or do, それから is more common; to add another point in the same direction, good or bad, to an evaluation, use それに, with the sense of “what's more”.

this.tr: Buy some milk on your way back. Oh, and eggs too, please.

that.tr: This restaurant is cheap. What's more, the food is good too.

items.explain: Look at what's being added: one more thing to buy or do → それから (それに also works); one more good or bad point in the same direction about the same thing (after 安い, adding 料理もおいしい) → それに, with the sense of “what's more”; using それから here sounds like reading out a list.

groups.note: Both mean “and then”

items.title: 〜て (sequence of actions)
items.diff: Consecutive actions in one sentence are linked with て; そして goes at the start of a sentence, where you want a pause.

this.tr: I ate breakfast. And then, I went to school.

that.tr: I ate breakfast and then went to school.

items.explain: Both mean the same — look at the period: several actions done in a row by the same person are most naturally linked with the て-form in one sentence; そして needs a 「。」 before it, and suits writing when you want to stress “what comes next”. Linking every action with 「〜た。そして、」 reads very stiffly.

items.title: それから (and then)
items.diff: Both mean “and then”: それから focuses on the order in time; そして is slightly more formal and more common in writing and storytelling.

this.tag: Slightly formal · links the next event
this.tr: Work was over. And then I stopped by the bookstore in front of the station.

that.tr: Work was over. After that, I stopped by the bookstore in front of the station.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “and then,” and swapping them doesn't change the meaning. それから focuses on time: you do the next thing “after” finishing the previous one, so it is the most common choice in everyday speech when describing your day or a series of steps. そして simply links the next event; it is a little more formal than それから and more common in writing and storytelling.

groups.note: Both mean “and also”

items.title: それに (adding a similar point)
items.diff: Both mean “and also”: そして is smooth and neutral; それに is more conversational, with a “not only that, but also…” feel of piling on.

this.tr: This hotel is close to the station. And the rooms are spacious too.

that.tr: This hotel is close to the station, and on top of that, the rooms are spacious too.

items.explain: Both sentences add one more good point about the hotel. そして just smoothly links the next feature and is common in descriptions and written text; それに is conversational, with a “not only that, there's also…” tone of piling on, and is often used together with 「し」 (近いし、それに).

groups.note: Both mean “and so”

items.title: それで (therefore, so)
items.diff: Both mean “and so”: それで states outright that what came before is the cause; そして just carries the story forward, mostly in storytelling and writing.

this.tr: She studied until late every night. And then she passed the exam.

that.tr: She studied until late every night. So she passed the exam.

items.explain: Both sentences say “studied hard → passed.” それで clearly treats the previous sentence as the cause and is common in speech when explaining to someone “that's why.” そして doesn't spell out cause and effect; it just carries the events forward and lets the listener sense the connection, which is common in storytelling and writing.

groups.note: Both express the time order “do B after finishing A”

items.title: 〜てから (first A, then B)
items.diff: Both mean “after”: たあとで focuses on time, simply saying B comes after A; てから focuses on order, stressing that A is finished first and only then B.

this.tr: After taking a shower, I read a book for a while.

that.tr: I took a shower first, then read a book for a while.

wrong.why: あとで must follow the た-form: 浴びた後で

items.explain: Both sentences work, and swapping them doesn't change the meaning; only the focus differs. たあとで focuses on time: the reading happened after the shower, however long the gap. てから focuses on order: A is finished first and only then does B start, so when talking about steps or rules (まず〜てから、必ず〜てから), てから sounds more natural. They also attach differently: た-form＋あとで, て-form＋から.

groups.note: Both say something has already happened — same meaning, only plain vs. polite style

items.title: 〜ました
items.diff: た is the plain past; ました is the polite past. The meaning is the same.

this.tr: I saw a movie with a friend on Sunday.

that.tr: Sensei, I saw a movie with a friend on Sunday.

wrong.why: You can't add 「です」 directly after a verb's た-form; use 「ました」

items.explain: Look at who you are talking to: friends, family, a diary → た; a 「先生」, your boss, someone you don't know well → ました. To make it polite, change 「見た」 as a whole into 「見ました」; you can't just add 「です」 after it.

groups.note: た-form＋ことがある ↔ dictionary form＋ことがある — the only difference is whether 「た」 or 「る」 comes before

items.title: 〜ることがある (sometimes does)
items.diff: た-form＋ことがある means “have done … before”; dictionary form＋ことがある means “sometimes does …”.

this.tr: When I was a child, I was late for school once.

that.tr: Even now, I'm occasionally late for work.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ことがある」: the た-form (遅刻した) → an experience from the past, “have done … before,” often with 「子どもの時」 or 「一度」; the dictionary form (遅刻する) → something that still happens now and then, “sometimes does …,” often with 「たまに」 or 「時々」. On the surface only 「た」 and 「る」 differ, but the meanings are completely different.

groups.note: Both express “having had a certain experience”

items.title: 〜ている (experience, record)
items.diff: Both mean “has had this experience”: たことがある is the everyday way to say it; ている presents the past event as a record, objectively, like a résumé or a news report.

this.tr: This athlete has won a world championship before.

that.tr: This athlete won the world championship in 2018.

items.explain: Both sentences say he has won before. たことがある is the everyday expression, focusing on “whether it has ever happened,” and is used in conversation and when talking about yourself. ている lays out the past event as an item on record, objective like a résumé or news report, and often comes with a specific year (２０１８年に).

groups.note: Both make a plural of people, “the …s”

items.title: 〜ら (… and others)
items.diff: Both make a plural of people: たち is the everyday, neutral form; ら is mostly found in news and official documents, with an objective, distant tone.

this.tr: The athletes smiled and waved.

that.tr: The athletes smiled and waved.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “the athletes.” たち is the most ordinary everyday form, fine in conversation and letters; ら is the objective form used in news and official documents (選手ら、山田教授ら). It feels a little distant, so it isn't used to someone's face for elders or people you should show respect to.

groups.note: Both come from 「たい」, which at its core expresses what the speaker personally wants to do

items.diff: たい says you yourself want to do something; たがる says someone else seems to want to.

this.tr: I want to buy a new game.

that.tr: My little brother wants to buy a new game.

items.explain: たがる comes from the stem 「た」 of たい plus 「がる」; がる shows an inner feeling showing on the outside (寒がる、ほしがる). At its core, たい expresses what the speaker personally wants, so after 「私は」 you use たい. You can't see what is in someone else's mind; you can only describe how they appear to want something, so がる is added, and after 「弟は」 you use たがっている (usually in the ている form).

groups.note: Both mean “want to do”

items.title: 〜たいものだ (strong wish)
items.diff: Both mean “want to”: たい is an ordinary wish, fine even for small things right in front of you; たいものだ carries deep feeling and usually refers to a long-term wish that can't easily come true right away.

this.tr: I want to travel around the world at least once.

that.tr: I really hope I can travel around the world at least once someday.

items.explain: Both sentences say “I want to travel around the world.” たい is the general expression, usable for any wish, even small immediate ones (水が飲みたい). たいものだ carries emotion, like sighing to yourself, and refers to a long-term wish that can't easily come true right away; it isn't used to answer an immediate question like 「何が食べたい？」.

groups.note: Both give a few examples and imply there are others

items.title: 〜とか〜とか (listing actions)
items.diff: Both give examples: たり〜たりする is the standard form, with verbs in the た-form; とか〜とか is more casual and conversational, with verbs simply in the dictionary form.

this.tr: In the evenings I listen to music, read books, and so on.

that.tr: In the evenings I just listen to music, read books, stuff like that.

wrong.why: たり must attach to the verb's た-form: 聞いたり、読んだり

items.explain: Both sentences list a few things done in the evening and imply there are others; swapping them doesn't change the meaning. たり〜たりする is the standard form, with the verb in the た-form＋り (聞いたり、読んだり), and works in writing and formal situations. とか〜とか is more conversational and casual, with the verb simply in the dictionary form (聞くとか、読むとか).

groups.note: Both mean “first…, then…”

items.title: 〜てから (first A, then B)
items.diff: Both mean “and then”: て just strings actions together in order; てから stresses that A is finished first and only then B.

this.tr: I took some medicine and went to sleep.

that.tr: I took some medicine first, and only then went to sleep.

items.explain: Both sentences say “take medicine → sleep,” and swapping them doesn't change the meaning. て just strings actions together in order and can link several in one go (帰って、浴びて、寝た). てから stresses “finish A first; B waits until after A,” is often used with 「まず」 or 「必ず」 for rules and steps, and usually links only two actions.

groups.note: Both express a reason, “because”

items.diff: Both mean “because”: after て only a result that has already happened or a feeling can follow; after ので a request or a plan can follow as well.

this.tr: I had a fever, so I stayed home from school.

that.tr: I've come down with a fever, so please let me take the day off.

wrong.why: The 「て」 of reason can't be followed by a request

items.explain: Look at the second half: a result that has already happened, like 「学校を休んだ」, or a feeling, like 「困った」 → て is fine; ので also works, it just sounds more like giving an explanation. A request like 「休ませてください」, or something you plan to do → only ので (or から).

groups.note: Both mean doing something “while in a certain state”

items.title: 〜まま (keeping a state)
items.diff: Both mean doing something “while in a state”: て just plainly describes how you did it; たまま stresses that a state that should have changed didn't, with a sense of something being off or unexpected.

this.tr: I went into the room wearing my coat.

that.tag: Should have taken it off but didn't
that.tr: I went into the room without even taking my coat off.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “went into the room wearing a coat.” て just plainly describes how you came in; たまま stresses “should have taken it off but didn't” — the earlier state stayed unchanged — with a sense of something being off or unexpected, so たまま is common in reminders and regrets (電気をつけたまま寝てしまった).

groups.note: ている ↔ てある — just one character apart

items.diff: An intransitive verb like 開く＋ている only says “it is open” as a state; a transitive verb like 開ける＋てある means someone did it on purpose and the result has remained.

this.tr: The window is open.

that.tr: The window has been opened (by someone) for the cleaning.

wrong.why: After 「窓が」, use 「開いている」 or 「開けてある」

items.explain: First look at the verb: 開く (intransitive)＋ている → simply “is open”; 開ける (transitive)＋てある → someone opened it for some purpose and it has stayed open. If you see a purpose like 「掃除のために」, it is most likely てある. This test only applies to paired intransitive/transitive verbs like 開く／開ける; action verbs like 走る or 泣く＋ている mean “is doing.”

groups.note: Both mean “be doing …”

items.title: 〜ているところだ
items.diff: Both mean “be doing”: ている is the everyday way to say it; ているところだ stresses being in the middle of the process right now.

this.tr: My dad is reading the newspaper now.

that.tr: My dad is in the middle of reading the newspaper right now.

items.explain: Both sentences say Dad is reading the paper. ている is the everyday expression; ているところだ stresses “right now, in the middle of the process, not finished yet,” and is often used to answer 「今、何をしているの？」 or to explain that you can't get away at the moment.

groups.note: Both express an ongoing state

items.title: 〜まま (state unchanged)
items.diff: Both express an ongoing state: ている just describes the state in front of you; たままになっている says a state that should have changed has stayed as it was, just left that way.

this.tr: The lights in the meeting room are on.

that.tr: The lights in the meeting room have been left on.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “the lights are on.” ている just describes the state you see; たままになっている says they should have been switched off, but nobody has dealt with them and they have been left that way, often with a tone of annoyance or a reminder. When you want to say “why are they still on?”, use まま.

groups.note: し・て・から ↔ し・た・から: just て vs. た — one means “after”, the other “because”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: て-form＋から is “after doing…”; た-form＋から is “because…”.

this.tr: I'll go out to play after I finish my homework.

that.tr: I've already done my homework, so I can go out to play.

items.explain: Only one kana is different: し・て・から is time order, followed by what you will do next (遊びに行く); し・た・から is a reason, often preceded by 「もう」, and followed by the resulting outcome or judgment (行ける、大丈夫だ).

groups.note: Both mean “first…, then…”

items.title: 〜たあとで (after an action)
items.diff: Both mean “after”: てから focuses on order, stressing that A is finished first and only then B; たあとで focuses on time, simply saying B comes after A.

this.tr: I ate dinner first, then did my homework.

that.tr: After eating dinner, I did my homework.

wrong.why: あとで must follow the た-form: 食べたあとで

items.explain: Both sentences work, and swapping them doesn't change the meaning; only the focus differs. てから focuses on order: A is finished first and only then does B start, which sounds more natural for steps and rules (まず〜てから、必ず〜てから). たあとで focuses on time: B happens after A, however long the gap. They also attach differently: て-form＋から, た-form＋あとで.

items.title: 〜て (sequence of actions)
items.diff: て just strings several actions together in order; てから stresses “finish A first, and only then do B”.

this.tr: Wash your hands first, then eat.

that.tr: In the morning I get up, wash my face, and eat breakfast.

items.explain: A series of everyday actions done in order → link them one after another with て; to stress “finish A first, B waits until after A”, often with 「まず」 → use てから, which usually links only two actions.

groups.note: Both mean “ever since…”

items.diff: Both mean “since…”: てから is the ordinary expression; てからというもの is written language, stressing a big change that has lasted ever since.

this.tr: It's already been three years since I came to Japan.

that.tr: Ever since my child was born, every day has been incredibly busy.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “since….” If you are just saying how much time has passed since then (もう３年になる), use the ordinary てから. てからというもの is followed by a marked change that has continued “ever since” (毎日が本当に忙しい); it carries emotion and is mostly used in writing.

groups.note: Both come from 「くださる」 — originally “(someone) gives me”; ください is its imperative, “please give me”

items.diff: te-form + ください asks someone to “do” something; noun + をください asks someone to “give” you something.

this.tr: Excuse me, could you bring me some water?

that.tr: Excuse me, some water, please.

items.explain: ください is the imperative of 「くださる」 (someone gives me), so its basic meaning is “please give me.” Asking for a thing directly → noun + を + ください (水をください) = please give me this thing; treating the other person's action as a favor done for you → verb te-form + ください (持ってきてください) = please do this for me. Look at what comes before ください: “noun + を” asks for a thing; a te-form asks for an action.

groups.note: All ask someone to do something

items.diff: てください is a polite instruction that the listener basically can't refuse; ていただけませんか uses a question to leave the decision to the listener, and is softer.

this.tr: Please write your name here.

that.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you write your name here?

items.explain: Look at who you're asking and the tone: instructions from a service counter or teacher → てください; asking a superior or client to do something extra for you, often after 「お忙しいところすみませんが」 → ていただけませんか.

items.diff: Both ask someone to do something; てください works with anyone, while お〜ください is the respectful form used toward customers.

this.tr: Please wait a moment.

that.tr: I'm sorry, but please wait just a moment.

items.explain: Both sentences ask the listener to wait; which one to use depends on who you're talking to and where. Speaking to customers in shops, announcements or notices, often after 「恐れ入りますが」 or with 「少々」 → お + masu-stem + ください (お待ちください); between friends or coworkers → 待ってください is enough, and お〜ください would sound distant.

items.diff: Both tell someone to do something; てください is polite and works with anyone, while なさい is an instruction from above to below and leaves less room for discussion.

this.tr: Please read the following sentence aloud.

that.tr: Read the following sentence aloud.

items.explain: Both sentences are instructions, and the choice depends on the relationship between the speakers: teacher to student, parent to child, or exam questions → なさい, never used to equals or superiors; to customers, coworkers or people in general → てください. They also attach differently: なさい follows the masu-stem (読みなさい), while てください follows the te-form (読んでください).

groups.note: Both come from 「ても + いい」 — “it's fine even if…”: fine to do it = may; fine not to = needn't

items.diff: てもいい is “you may do it”; なくてもいい is “you don't have to do it”.

this.tr: You can come tomorrow, you know.

that.tr: You don't have to come tomorrow, you know.

items.explain: Look at what comes before て: an affirmative te-form (来て) → permission to do it; the negative 「なくて」 (来なくて) → it's fine not to, i.e. “needn't” — the opposite of 「来なければならない」 (must come).

groups.note: Both express permission, “may… / it's fine if…”

items.diff: Both express permission; てもかまわない is more formal, used mostly with customers and in business.

this.tr: You can pay next month, no problem.

that.tr: It's perfectly fine to make your payment next month.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: between friends, casually with 「よ」 → てもいい; staff to customers or in business, often with honorifics like 「お支払い」 → てもかまいません, which sounds more formal.

groups.note: Both come from 「いけない」 (no good) — doing it is no good = forbidden; not doing it is no good = must

items.diff: てはいけない means “doing it won't do” = prohibition; ないといけない means “not doing it won't do” = obligation.

this.tr: You may not use English in this class.

that.tag: Not doing it won't do · must
that.tr: You have to use English in this class.

items.explain: いけない originally means “it won't work, it's no good.” Preceded by the affirmative 「〜ては」 (使っては = if you use it) → doing it is no good = prohibition; preceded by the negative 「〜ないと」 (使わないと = if you don't use it) → not doing it is no good = obligation. The two sentences differ only in 使っては / 使わないと, yet mean exact opposites.

groups.note: All express prohibition, “don't / must not”

items.diff: Both express prohibition; てはならない is used in laws, maxims and formal writing, and sounds more solemn.

this.tr: You may not chew gum in the classroom.

that.tr: Whatever the reason, you must never hurt others.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the topic: everyday rules at school or work (教室で) → てはいけない; statements of principle in laws, maxims or speeches (どんな理由があっても) → てはならない, which is rare in everyday conversation.

items.diff: てはいけない announces a rule; ないでください asks the listener not to do something, and is more polite.

this.tr: This is a no-smoking area. Smoking is not allowed.

that.tr: Excuse me, please don't smoke here.

items.explain: てはいけない speaks from the rule's standpoint and states a conclusion, often after the rule has been given (ここは禁煙です); said directly to a customer or a superior, it can sound like a scolding. ないでください makes a request to the listener, often starting with 「すみません」, and sounds gentle. When asking someone face to face not to do something, ないでください is the usual choice.

items.title: 〜な (prohibition)
items.diff: てはいけない explains a rule; dictionary form + な is a very blunt, command-style prohibition.

this.tr: It's dangerous, so you may not swim in the river.

that.tr: Danger! Don't swim in the river!

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: な added straight after the dictionary form (泳ぐな) is a command-style prohibition used on signs, when yelling at someone, or in men's casual speech; it often bursts out right after 「危ない！」 and is quite rude when said to a person. てはいけない gives a reason or states a rule (危ないから、〜てはいけません) and is much less harsh.

groups.note: Both come from 「言う」 — originally “to say”

items.diff: という is followed by a noun and means “(a person or thing) called …”; と言う is a predicate and means “(someone) said …”.

this.tr: This is a food called 「もち」 (rice cake).

that.tr: My grandmother said, “I want to eat rice cakes.”

items.explain: 言う originally means “to say.” When と marks what was said and the sentence ends at 「言いました」 → quoting what someone said (「もちが食べたい」と言いました); when a name is said and then attached to the following noun → 「X という + noun」 = a … called X (「もち」という食べ物). Look at what follows という / と言う: a noun → introducing a name, usually written in kana; the sentence ends there → what someone said, usually written with the kanji 「言う」.

items.diff: という is followed by a noun and introduces a name; というのは makes a word the topic and then explains its meaning.

this.tr: Do you know the word 「スマホ」?

that.tr: 「スマホ」 means a smartphone.

items.explain: 言う originally means “to say.” 「という + noun」 says a name and attaches it to a noun (「スマホ」という言葉 = the word called スマホ); adding 「の」 and 「は」 turns “the word just mentioned” into the topic, followed by an explanation, giving “what is called … is …”. The sentence often ends with 「〜のことです」 or 「〜という意味です」. Look at what follows: a noun → introducing a name; 「のは」 followed by an explanation → a definition.

groups.note: Both come from 「言う」 — originally “to say”

items.diff: と言う is a predicate and means “(someone) said …”; という is followed by a noun and means “(a thing or person) called …”.

this.tr: My grandmother said, “I want to eat rice cakes.”

that.tr: This is a food called 「もち」 (rice cake).

items.explain: 言う originally means “to say.” When と marks what was said and the sentence ends at 「言いました」 → quoting what someone said (「もちが食べたい」と言いました); when a name is said and then attached to the following noun → 「X という + noun」 = a … called X (「もち」という食べ物). Look at what follows と言う / という: the sentence ends there → what someone said, usually written with the kanji 「言う」; a noun → introducing a name, usually written in kana.

groups.note: Both report what someone said: “(someone) said …”

items.diff: Both report what someone said; と言いました narrates what was said at the time, while と言っていました passes a third person's words on to the listener.

this.tr: At the meeting, the department head said we would start a new project.

that.tr: The department head said we're starting a new project, you know.

items.explain: Both sentences report the same words; look at the purpose: describing who said what in a particular scene (会議で) → と言いました; passing someone's words on to the person in front of you, “that's what he said” → と言っていました, often ending with 「よ」.

items.title: 〜って (sentence-final hearsay)
items.diff: Both report what someone said; と言いました is the full, formal form, while sentence-final って is a casual shortened form.

this.tr: The teacher said there's no class tomorrow.

that.tr: The teacher said there's no class tomorrow, apparently.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same and differ only at the end: the full 「と言いました」 works with anyone and suits formal situations; ending with just 「って」, dropping the 「言っていた」 that would follow, is casual speech among friends and family, not used with teachers or bosses or in formal settings.

groups.note: 行くと思う ↔ 行こうと思う — just one sound apart, with completely different meanings

items.diff: Plain form＋と思う is a guess or opinion; volitional form＋と思う is your own plan.

this.tr: I think Tanaka-san will go tomorrow.

that.tr: I'm thinking of going tomorrow.

items.explain: The only difference is 「行く」 vs. 「行こう」: plain form (行く) → a guess or opinion about something; volitional form (行こう) → the speaker's own plan, “I intend to do it”.

groups.note: Both mean “I think …”

items.diff: Both state your own opinion; と思います is what you think right now, while と思っています is what you have thought all along.

this.tr: I think this town is a nice place to live.

that.tr: I've always thought this town is a nice place to live.

items.explain: In both sentences the subject is “I”; look for words showing continuity: stating what you think right now → と思います; having thought so all along, with words like 「昔から」 or 「ずっと」 → と思っています. Also, when talking about someone else's thoughts (兄, 彼), と思っている is generally used.

groups.note: Both express a guess: “probably …”

items.diff: と思う carries the speaker's personal opinion; でしょう sounds objective and is common in weather forecasts.

this.tr: I think it will rain tomorrow.

that.tr: Tomorrow, rain is expected across most of the country.

wrong.why: A noun needs 「だ」 before と思う: 雨だと思います

items.explain: と思う means “I think” and suits giving your own view in conversation; でしょう doesn't put “I” forward and makes an objective guess, like a weather forecast. Note how they attach: after a noun, と思う needs 「だ」 (雨だと思う), while でしょう attaches directly (雨でしょう).

groups.note: Both mean “do something like …”

items.title: 〜ように (like …)
items.diff: Both mean “do something like …”; と同じように stresses doing it exactly the same way, while のように only says “similar” and can also be used for figurative comparisons.

this.tr: I read the newspaper every morning, exactly as my father does.

that.tr: Like my father, I read the newspaper every morning.

items.explain: Both sentences work; choose by what you want to stress: doing it in exactly the same way as someone, following their example → と同じように; just saying “like …”, with a hint of taking that person as a model → のように. Figurative comparisons (鳥のように空を飛ぶ) can only use のように, not と同じように.

groups.note: Both list things: “… and …”

items.diff: と lists everything; や〜など gives just a few examples and implies there are others.

this.tr: There's a book and a notebook in my bag (just those two).

that.tr: There are books, notebooks and so on in my bag.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the particles, and both list things one by one: if that's the whole list (only a book and a notebook) → と; if you're picking a few representative items and implying there are others → や, often paired with など.

groups.note: Both mark the other party of an action: “with …”

items.title: 〜に (target of an action)
items.diff: Both mark the person you meet; と means both sides arranged to meet each other, while に means going to see someone one-sidedly or running into them.

this.tr: As arranged, I met Mr. Tanaka at the station.

that.tr: I happened to run into Mr. Tanaka at the station.

wrong.why: 結婚する needs both people to take part, so the partner is marked with 「と」

items.explain: 「会う」 works with both; look at the clues before it: arranged, meeting each other (約束どおり) → と; going to see someone from your side alone, or meeting by chance (偶然) → に. Actions that need two people to happen, like 「結婚する」 or 「けんかする」, can only use と.

groups.note: Both mean “as soon as … / when …”

items.diff: と can only be followed by something that happens naturally; たら can also be followed by requests and intentions.

this.tr: When you get to the station, there's a bank right in front of you.

that.tr: Please call me when you get to the station.

wrong.why: と cannot be followed by a request or a command

items.explain: The first halves are the same, so look at the second half: a result that naturally appears as soon as A happens, like 「目の前に銀行があります」 → と; if the second half is a request like 「電話してください」, or an intention such as 「〜たい」 or 「〜よう」 → only たら works.

groups.note: Both mean “when …”

items.diff: Both mean “when …”; とき is used in everyday conversation, while 際（は） is more formal and common in notices, announcements and business settings.

this.tr: Remember to turn off the light when you leave the room, OK?

that.tr: Please turn off the lights when leaving the room.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting and the ending: said casually to family or friends, ending with 「ね」 → とき; in notices, announcements or business emails, ending with a formal phrase like 「お消しください」 → 際（は）. Using とき in formal situations isn't wrong, but 際 sounds more formal; in everyday conversation 際 sounds stiff.

items.title: 〜間に (at some point during)
items.diff: Both mark when something happens; とき only says when, while 間に treats it as a period that will end and stresses getting something done before it ends.

this.tr: When I was in Japan, I climbed Mt. Fuji once.

that.tr: While I was in Japan, I took the chance to climb Mt. Fuji once.

items.explain: Both sentences work and differ only in とき / 間に: とき simply says when it happened; 間に treats 「日本にいる」 as a period that will end sooner or later and stresses getting something done before it does, so “while I still can” plans usually use 間に (日本にいる間に登りたい). Note that 「間」 without 「に」 means something continues throughout the whole period (その間ずっと) and can't be used for one-time events.

groups.note: All express “intend / plan”

items.diff: (よ)うと思う is usually an idea that has just come to mind; つもりだ is a firmer plan decided well in advance.

this.tr: I've been planning for a while to study abroad next year.

that.tr: It's raining, so I think I'll take a taxi home today.

items.explain: Look at when the decision was made: thought of on the spot after seeing the rain (雨だから) → (よ)うと思う; a plan settled long ago and already being prepared for (前から) → つもりだ.

items.diff: つもり is a personal intention in someone's mind; 予定 is a schedule that has already been set.

this.tr: I plan to go back to my home country for summer vacation.

that.tr: The plane is scheduled to arrive at three.

wrong.why: A plane has no “intentions”; use 予定 for schedules

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person's own intention → つもり; something already scheduled, like a flight (飛行機), a meeting or an event, or arrangements decided by a company or someone else → 予定.

groups.note: Both come from 「どう」 (how) — asking what someone thinks: how about this thing = recommending; how about doing it = suggesting

items.diff: Noun + はどうですか recommends a thing; verb た-form + らどうですか suggests that the listener do something.

this.tr: If you have a cold, how about this medicine?

that.tr: If you have a cold, why don't you take some medicine?

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「どう」: noun + は (この薬は) → putting a thing forward for the listener to judge or accept; verb た-form + ら (飲んだら) → urging the listener to take action, which can sound preachy toward a superior. With guests or superiors, the more polite はいかがですか is used.

groups.note: Both are used to offer the listener something to eat or drink

items.title: 〜ませんか (offering food or drink)
items.diff: Both offer the listener something to eat or drink: はいかがですか presents the item directly and is formal; ませんか uses a verb to ask whether they'd like it, and is more easygoing.

this.tr: Would you care for a cold juice?

that.tr: Why don't you have some cold juice or something?

items.explain: Both sentences offer the listener juice. Look at what comes before: noun (ジュース) + はいかがですか puts the item right in front of the listener and is formal — common when staff serve customers or hosts serve guests; verb ます-stem (飲み) + ませんか, often with 「〜でも」, sounds like a casual suggestion between friends or colleagues and is more relaxed. With guests and superiors, はいかがですか is the first choice.

groups.note: Both mark the subject of a clause that modifies a noun

items.title: 〜の (subject in the clause)
items.diff: In a clause that modifies a noun, the subject can take either が or の, with の slightly more literary and softer; other kinds of clauses only allow が.

this.tr: I love the cake my older sister baked.

that.tr: I love the cake my older sister baked.

wrong.why: A 「〜たら」 conditional clause doesn't modify a noun, so its subject can't switch to の — say 「雨が降ったら」

items.explain: The two sentences mean exactly the same: in 「姉が焼いたケーキ」 and 「姉の焼いたケーキ」, the clause 「焼いた」 modifies the following noun 「ケーキ」, so its subject can take either が or の; の is slightly more literary and softer. Check what follows the clause: if it's a noun, both work; in clauses like 「〜たら」 or 「〜から」, or for the subject of the whole sentence, only が works.

groups.note: Both use 「ある／いる」 for existence — the difference is whether they answer “where is it?” or “what is there?”

items.diff: Nは〜にある／いる answers “where is N?”; 〜にNがある／いる answers “what is there?”.

this.tr: The key is on the desk.
Mr. Tanaka is in the meeting room.

that.tr: There's a key on the desk.
There's Mr. Tanaka in the meeting room.

items.explain: Look at which part is new information: asking where something already known (my key) is → 鍵は机の上にあります, with the question 「鍵はどこにありますか」; describing what's in a place → 机の上に鍵があります, with the question 「机の上に何がありますか」. The same goes for people and animals with いる: the questions are 「田中さんはどこにいますか」 and 「会議室に誰がいますか」 respectively.

groups.note: 「私は田中です」↔「私が田中です」 differ only in は／が: one is an introduction, the other means “I'm the one who is Tanaka”

items.diff: は brings up a known topic, with the focus on what follows; が puts the focus on the noun before it, answering “who” or “which”.

this.tr: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka.

that.tr: Which one of you is Mr. Tanaka? — I'm Tanaka.

wrong.why: When a question word is the subject, it must be followed by が

items.explain: Look at the context: introducing yourself after 「はじめまして」, you make “I” the topic and then say something about it → は; when someone asks 「田中さんはどの方ですか」 (which one is Tanaka), the answer is the noun “I” itself → が, meaning “I'm the one who is Tanaka.” When a question word (誰, 何, どれ) is the subject, it is always followed by が too.

groups.note: Both come from 「より」 — originally “from…”: measuring from B = comparison; from a certain time or place = starting point

items.diff: When より is followed by an adjective, it means “than”; after a time or place, followed by 「始まる・出発する」, it's a formal “from”.

this.tr: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.

that.tr: The meeting begins at 2 p.m.

items.explain: Look at what follows より: an adjective (大きい, 速い) → the standard of comparison; an action like 「始まります」 or 「出発します」 → the starting point in time or place, a more formal version of 「から」, often seen in notices and announcements.

groups.note: Both mean “A is more … than B”

items.diff: AはBより〜 talks about A as the topic; BよりAのほうが〜 puts the focus on A, the winner, and is mostly used to answer “which is more …?”

this.tr: Trains are faster than buses.

that.tr: Which is faster, the train or the bus? — The train is faster than the bus.

items.explain: When simply describing something, use 「AはBより〜」; when someone asks 「どちらが」, answer with 「〜のほうが」 to put the chosen one in focus. Note that the item before より is the one that loses the comparison.

items.title: 〜に比べて (compared with…)
items.diff: Same meaning: より is the everyday expression; に比べて is more formal and leans toward writing.

this.tr: This winter there's more snow than last year.

that.tr: Compared with last year, there's more snow this winter.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; only より and に比べて are swapped. より is the most basic form and sounds most natural in daily conversation; に比べて literally means “compared with…”, sounds more formal and written, and is common in news, reports and when presenting data. Use より when chatting with friends; に比べて suits reports or formal speeches.

groups.note: Both come from 「くださる」 — its command form 「ください」 originally means “please give me”

items.diff: Noun + をください asks the listener to give you something; て-form + ください asks the listener to do something.

this.tr: Excuse me, some water, please.

that.tr: Excuse me, could you bring me some water, please?

items.explain: ください is the command form of 「くださる」 (to give me), so its basic meaning is “please give me”. Noun + を (水を) → asking directly for the item; verb て-form (持ってきて) → asking for the listener's action as a “favor given to me”, which becomes “please do … for me”. So look at what comes before ください: noun + を means you want a thing; verb て-form means you want the listener to do something.

groups.note: Both mean “please give me …”

items.title: 〜をお願いします (ordering, shopping)
items.diff: Both work when asking for things: をください is direct and clear; をお願いします is softer and more polite.

this.tr: Excuse me, please give me a small plate.

that.tr: Excuse me, could I trouble you for a small plate?

items.explain: Both sentences ask a server for a small plate. をください says “please give me” outright — short and clear; をお願いします literally means “I ask this of you” and doesn't say “give” directly, so it sounds softer and more polite. Both are common for ordering and paying; choose をお願いします when you want to sound more polite.

items.title: 〜てちょうだい (give me something)
items.diff: Both mean “please give me”: をください is polite and works with staff and strangers; をちょうだい is intimate and used only with family or very close people.

this.tr: Excuse me, could I have some juice, please?

that.tr: Mommy, give me some juice!

items.explain: Both sentences ask for juice; look at who is being addressed: calling 「すみません」 to staff or strangers → をください, polite; calling 「ママ」 to family or very close people, especially a child to a parent → をちょうだい, with an affectionate, coaxing tone. ちょうだい must not be used with superiors or guests.

groups.note: Both mean “leaving from …”

items.title: 〜から (starting point in space)
items.diff: When a person leaves a place, both を and から work; when something without a will of its own comes out, only から works.

this.tr: My father left the kitchen at eight.

that.tr: Smoke is coming out of the kitchen.

wrong.why: 煙 (smoke) has no will of its own, so coming out of somewhere can only take から

items.explain: When a person leaves a place on their own, both を and から work: 「台所を出た」 and 「台所から出た」 mean the same; を talks about leaving that place, while から stresses the point you set out from. Look at the subject: when something without a will (煙, 水) comes out, only から works. Also, abstract leaving such as 「家を出る」 (leaving home to live on your own) or 「大学を出る」 (graduating) only uses を.

groups.note: Both mean “please give me …”

items.diff: Both work when asking for things: をお願いします is softer and more polite; をください is direct and clear.

this.tr: Excuse me, could I trouble you for a hand towel?

that.tr: Excuse me, please give me a hand towel.

items.explain: Both sentences ask a server for a hand towel. をお願いします literally means “I ask this of you” and doesn't say “give” directly, so it sounds softer and more polite; をください says “please give me” outright — short and clear. Both are common for ordering and paying; choose をお願いします when you want to sound more polite.

groups.note: Both are used to ask someone to do something

items.diff: をお願いします follows a noun and is concise and polite; ていただけませんか follows a verb and makes the request as a question, which is more indirect.

this.tr: Please check this document.

that.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you check this document for me?

items.explain: Look at what comes before: noun (確認, 説明) + をお願いします is concise and polite, and very common at work; verb て-form + いただけませんか leaves the decision to the listener by asking a question, which suits asking for an extra favor or speaking to someone of much higher status.

groups.note: 「本やノート」↔「本とノート」 differ only in や／と: one implies there's more, the other means that's all

items.title: 〜と (listing)
items.diff: や〜など gives only a few examples, implying there's more; と lists everything.

this.tr: In my bag there are books, notebooks and so on.

that.tr: In my bag there are a book and a notebook (just those two).

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in や／と: 「本やノート」 (often with など) picks out a few representative items, and there are other things in the bag too; 「本とノート」 is the complete list, and the bag holds only these two.

groups.note: Both give a few examples, implying there's more

items.title: 〜たり〜たりする (listing actions)
items.diff: Both give a few examples: や〜など lists nouns; たり〜たりする lists actions, and it's the only option for ordinary verbs.

this.tr: On my days off, I do laundry, cleaning and so on.

that.tr: On my days off, I do things like washing clothes and cleaning.

wrong.why: や only attaches to nouns; for an action like 「映画を見る」, say 「映画を見たり買い物をしたりする」

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same: both list a few things done on days off, with more besides. With nouns that can take 「する」, such as 洗濯 and 掃除, both patterns work: や〜などをする lists the activities as nouns, while たり〜たりする describes them as separate actions. Ordinary verbs like 「映画を見る」 or 「友達に会う」 can only use たり〜たりする.

items.diff: や〜など works in both writing and speech, and only takes nouns; とか〜とか is spoken and can also take verbs.

this.tr: There's milk, eggs and so on in the fridge.

that.tr: Hey, is there milk or eggs or anything in the fridge?

items.explain: Look at the tone: です・ます sentences and writing → や〜など; casual talk among friends → とか〜とか. Also, とか can follow verbs (掃除するとか), but や can't.

groups.note: Both give an example or two to make a suggestion

items.title: 〜なんか (casual examples)
items.diff: Both give a few examples to make a suggestion: 〜などはいかがですか is formal; 〜なんかどう？ is casual speech.

this.tr: Would you care for some cake, cookies or the like?

that.tr: How about some cake or cookies or something?

items.explain: Both sentences offer a few kinds of snacks for the listener to choose from. Look at the sentence ending and who is being addressed: with guests or elders, use 「〜などはいかがですか」, which is formal; between friends or family, say 「〜なんかどう？」, which is casual. なんか is simply the spoken form of など.

groups.note: Both are used to call the listener's attention to something

items.title: 〜ぞ (reminder, warning)
items.diff: Both call the listener's attention to something: よ can be used with anyone; ぞ is forceful and mainly used by men toward equals or juniors.

this.tr: Sensei, the floor over there is slippery.

that.tr: Hey, the floor over there is slippery!

items.explain: Both sentences warn that the floor is slippery; look at who is being addressed: to a 「先生」, an elder or someone you don't know well → よ, which can follow です・ます; a man calling out 「おい」 to a friend or junior → ぞ is possible, with a forceful, rough tone. ぞ isn't used toward elders or superiors, and women rarely use it.

groups.note: Both come from 「ほう（方）」 — “that side” of two

items.diff: より〜のほうがいい compares two things and says which is better; た-form + ほうがいい gives the listener advice: “you'd better …”.

this.tr: The train is better than the bus.

that.tr: If you have a fever, you'd better go to bed early.

items.explain: 「ほう（方）」 originally means “direction, that side”. When comparing two things, 「電車のほう」 is “the train side”, and より marks the other side → saying which side is better; when giving advice, 「寝たほうがいい」 sets “sleeping” and “not sleeping” up as two sides and says “the side where you've slept is better” → extended to “you'd better …”. To tell them apart, look at what comes before ほう: noun + の (電車の) together with 「より」 → comparison; verb た-form (寝た) → advice for the listener.

groups.note: Both say that one thing is more … than another

items.diff: BよりAのほうが〜 puts the focus on A, the winner, and is mostly used to answer “which is more …?”; AはBより〜 talks about A as the topic.

this.tr: Which is faster, the train or the bus? — The train is faster than the bus.

that.tr: Trains are faster than buses.

items.explain: When someone asks 「どちらが」, answer with 「〜のほうが」 to put the chosen one in focus; when simply describing something, use 「AはBより〜」. Note that the item before より is the one that loses the comparison.

items.title: 〜に比べて (compared with…)
items.diff: Same meaning: より〜のほうが is the everyday expression, with the focus on the winner; に比べて is more formal and leans toward writing.

this.tr: Prices are higher now than they used to be.

that.tr: Compared with the past, prices are high now.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “prices are higher now than in the past.” より〜のほうが is the everyday conversational form and puts the winner (今) in focus, often used to answer 「どちらが」; に比べて takes the first item as the standard for describing the second, sounds more formal and written, and is common in news and reports.

groups.note: All mean “not … at all”

items.diff: Both mean “not at all”; 全然 is conversational, まったく is more formal, used in writing and business.

this.tr: I had no idea about that at all!

that.tr: I was entirely unaware of that matter.

items.explain: Look at the register: casual talk among friends with 「よ」 → 全然; honorific language, business or writing (存じませんでした, 問題ございません) → まったく.

items.diff: Both mean “not … one bit”; ちっとも is more emotional, often used to complain, and must always be followed by a negative.

this.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son doesn't study at all.

that.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son doesn't study one bit.

wrong.why: ちっとも must be followed by a negative; unlike 全然, it can't go with an affirmative

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the adverb and mean the same. ちっとも carries the speaker's feelings, so when complaining about someone like this it sounds more annoyed; 全然 is more neutral and used more widely, and in casual speech it can even go with an affirmative (全然大丈夫) — ちっとも can't.

groups.note: Both mean “during …”

items.title: 〜中 (in the middle of)
items.diff: Both mean “during …”; 〜中 attaches directly to an action noun and is short and formal, common on notices; 〜の間 sounds more like everyday speech and highlights the whole stretch of time.

this.tr: Please don't use your phone during class.

that.tr: No phone use during class, please.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; they differ only in 「の間」 and 「中」. 授業中 attaches 「中」 straight to the action noun — short and formal, a set phrase on notices and announcements; 授業の間 needs 「の」 after the noun, sounds more like everyday speech, and highlights “the whole stretch from the start of class to the end”.

groups.note: Both mean “while … (taking the chance)”

items.title: 〜うちに (while … still)
items.diff: Both mean “do something while …”; 間に just states objectively that it happened during that time, while うちに adds “hurry, before that state changes”.

this.tr: While the baby was sleeping, I went shopping.

that.tr: I hurried out shopping while the baby was still asleep.

items.explain: Both sentences work; they differ only in 「間に」 and 「うちに」. 間に simply states objectively that it was done “during the time the baby was sleeping”; うちに adds a sense of urgency — “the baby could wake up any moment, so it had to be done before then”. When what comes before is a state that changes quickly and can't be got back once it's gone, like 「温かい」 or 「若い」, うちに is normally used.

groups.note: All express a condition, “if…, then…”

items.diff: When the second half is a request or command and the first half is an action, only たら works; ば mostly follows states.

this.tr: If you have time, please help me.

that.tr: When you get to the station, please give me a call.

wrong.why: ば can't be used when an action comes first and a request follows

items.explain: First check whether the second half is a request or intention like 「〜てください」「〜よう」; if so, look at the first half: states like ある, いい or adjectives → both ば and たら work; actions like 着く, 終わる → only たら.

items.title: 〜と (whenever / as soon as)
items.diff: Both mean “when … then …”; と stresses that once the first part happens the second inevitably follows, and the second half can't be a request or intention; ば puts the focus on the first part as a condition.

this.tr: If you press this button, the light comes on.

that.tr: When you press this button, the light comes on.

wrong.why: After と the second half can't be a request or command; say 「暇なら」 or 「暇だったら」

items.explain: Both sentences work; they differ only in 「押せば」 and 「押すと」. と says “press it and the light inevitably comes on”, like describing a machine's fixed response or a law of nature; ば puts the focus on “as long as the condition of pressing the button is met”. When the second half is a request or intention such as 「〜てください」 or 「〜よう」, と can't be used.

items.title: 〜なら (if that's the case)
items.diff: Both mean “if …”; なら has a judging tone of “if that's so”, as if accepting the premise first and then stating a plan; ば simply states a condition.

this.tr: If the weather is nice, let's go for a walk.

that.tr: If the weather's nice, then let's go for a walk.

wrong.why: When the second half has to happen before the first, ば can't be used; say 「日本に行くなら」

items.explain: Both sentences work and mean nearly the same. ば just says we'll go once the condition “nice weather” is met; なら is more like accepting the premise “the weather's nice” first and then stating your plan, and is heard more in conversation. When the first part is an action and the second half has to be done before it, only なら works (日本に行くなら、先に日本語を勉強しておこう).

groups.note: Both come from ほど (程) — meaning “degree, extent”

items.diff: ほど on its own says “to the extent that…”; ば〜ほど says “the more…, the more…”.

this.tr: The more I walk, the more my feet hurt.

that.tr: My feet hurt so much I could cry.

items.explain: The original meaning of ほど is “degree”. If there's only one thing before it describing the degree (泣きたい) → it hurts to that extent; if there's 「〜ば」 before it and the same word (歩く) appears twice → “to whatever extent I walk, to that extent it hurts”, i.e. the more…, the more….

items.diff: ば〜ほど means “the more …, the more …”; noun＋ほど〜ない means “not as … as …”.

this.tr: The colder beer is, the better it tastes.

that.tr: Today's beer isn't as cold as yesterday's.

items.explain: ほど originally means “degree”. ば〜ほど says the same word twice: 冷たければ冷たいほど ＝ “however cold it gets, that's how good it gets” — the degrees rise together, hence “the more …, the more …”. Noun＋ほど〜ない uses the degree of the thing compared as a yardstick: “doesn't reach yesterday's level”, hence “not as … as”. To tell them apart, look before ほど: the ば形 with the same word repeated → “the more …, the more …”; the thing being compared (昨日) with 「ない」 at the end → “not as … as”.

groups.note: Both express “changing along with…”

items.diff: Both mean “change as … changes”; ば〜ほど repeats the same word, is common in speech, and stresses both degrees rising together; につれて is more written and stresses step-by-step change over a process.

this.tr: The higher you climb the mountain, the colder the air gets.

that.tr: As one climbs the mountain, the air grows colder.

items.explain: Both sentences work. ば〜ほど says 「登る」 twice (登れば登るほど), stressing that the higher you climb, the colder it gets — very common in speech; につれて says it only once (登るにつれて), like an objective account of a gradually changing process, and is more written. When the second half is not a change but an evaluation like 「いい」, only ば〜ほど works (返事は早ければ早いほどいい).

groups.note: Both come from 「ば＋いい（良い）」 — “it's good if…”

items.diff: ばいい gives advice for the future: “just do this”; ばよかった is regret: “I should have done that”.

this.tr: Tomorrow you can just take a taxi.

that.tr: I should have taken a taxi yesterday.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in いい vs. よかった. Look at the time word: 「明日」 → you can still do it, so it's advice; 「昨日」 plus the past tense よかった → you didn't do it then, and regretting it now is too late.

groups.note: Both are used to give someone advice

items.diff: ばいい tells the other person a way to do it: “just do this and you're fine”; ほうがいい compares and recommends: “this is better”.

this.tr: How do I get to the station? — You can just take that bus.

that.tr: It looks like rain, so you'd better take an umbrella.

items.explain: Check whether it's answering “what should I do?”: the other person asks for a way (どうすればいいですか) → ばいい, meaning “doing this will do”; you warn them on your own initiative, having judged that doing it is better → ほうがいい, which is stronger and sometimes a warning.

groups.note: Both come from 「ば＋いい（良い）」 — “it's good if…”

items.diff: ばよかった is regret: “I should have done that”; ばいい gives advice for the future: “just do this”.

this.tr: I should have taken a taxi yesterday.

that.tr: Tomorrow you can just take a taxi.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in よかった vs. いい. Look at the time word: 「昨日」 plus the past tense よかった → you didn't do it then, and now you regret it; 「明日」 → there's still time, so it's advice.

groups.note: All express regret: “I should have …”

items.title: 〜たほうがよかった (regret)
items.diff: Both regret not having done something; ばよかった is regret voiced directly, while たほうがよかった involves a comparison, like calm reflection afterwards.

this.tr: I wish I'd checked the weather forecast before going out.

that.tr: It would have been better to check the weather forecast before going out.

items.explain: Both sentences regret not checking the forecast. ばよかった is “if only I had …”, a direct expression of regret, often with 「なあ」; たほうがよかった is “doing that would have been better”, comparing two courses of action — it sounds more like calm reflection after the fact, and is also often said to others: “that would have been better back then”.

items.title: 〜べきだった (should have)
items.diff: Both regret not having done something; べきだった is “by rights I should have done it”, with stronger self-blame and a more written feel; ばよかった is just “if only …”.

this.tr: If only I'd seen a doctor sooner.

that.tr: I should have consulted a doctor sooner.

items.explain: Both sentences regret not seeing a doctor sooner. べきだった measures things against “what by reason or duty should have been done”, so the self-blame is strong — said about someone else it becomes criticism — and it's more written; ばよかった just says “it would have been nice if …”, a lighter tone, more common in everyday speech.

groups.note: All mean “if …”

items.title: 〜たら (hypothetical condition)
items.diff: Both are a hypothetical “if …”; 場合は is used in notices and rules with a formal tone; たら is the everyday spoken form.

this.tr: In case of rain, the sports day will be canceled.

that.tr: If it rains, the sports day'll be canceled, I guess.

wrong.why: After a noun, 場合 needs 「の」: 雨の場合は

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same, so look at the setting: school or company notices, rules, manuals → 場合は; chatting with friends or family → たら. After a noun, 場合 needs 「の」 (雨の場合は), while たら becomes 「雨だったら」.

items.title: 〜際は (on the occasion of)
items.diff: Both mean “in the event of …”; 際は is more formal and written, common on notices and in announcements; 場合は is the general form, used in both speech and writing.

this.tr: If something breaks down, please let a staff member know.

that.tr: In the event of a malfunction, please inform a staff member.

items.explain: Both sentences work; they differ only in 「場合は」 and 「際は」, so it's about how formal it sounds: 際は sounds more formal and is common on notices, in manuals and in station announcements; 場合は is the general form, also used in everyday speech. Also, when what comes before is 「〜ない」 (連絡がない場合は), normally only 場合は is used.

groups.note: All come from 「ばかり」 — derived from 「量る」, originally meaning a measured amount or limit

items.diff: Noun＋ばかり means “nothing but, all”; た形＋ばかり means “just did”.

this.tr: This shop sells nothing but expensive things.

that.tr: I just bought this computer.

wrong.why: To mean “just did”, ばかり must follow the た形: さっき駅に着いたばかりです

items.explain: ばかり comes from the verb 「量る」 (to measure); its original sense is a measured amount or limit, extended to “only this much”. After a noun (物) → the kinds of things are limited to this one ＝ nothing but; after the た形 (買った) → only this little time has passed since it happened ＝ just. Saying 「ばっかり」 in casual speech means the same.

items.diff: Noun＋ばかり limits the “thing”: eats only this; て形＋ばかりいる limits the “action”: is always eating.

this.tr: My little sister eats nothing but sweets.

that.tr: My little sister does nothing but eat all day.

items.explain: ばかり originally means a measured limit, “restricted to just this”. Limiting the thing: noun＋ばかり (甘い物ばかり) → what she eats is limited to this one kind ＝ eats only this; limiting the action: て形＋ばかりいる (食べてばかりいる) → all her time goes into this one action ＝ is always doing it. To tell them apart, check whether ばかり follows a noun or a verb's て形. Both often carry dissatisfaction.

items.diff: ばかり means “nothing but”; ばかりでなく means “not only … (but also …)”.

this.tr: My older brother eats nothing but meat.

that.tr: My older brother not only eats meat, he eats plenty of vegetables too.

items.explain: ばかり originally means a measured limit, “restricted to just this”. ばかり alone (肉ばかり) → the range is only meat ＝ nothing but; add the negative 「でなく」 → “not limited to meat” ＝ not only …, usually followed by something like 「野菜も」 adding another item. When reading, check whether 「でなく」 follows ばかり, and don't take 「ばかりでなく」 as “nothing but”.

groups.note: All mean “only, nothing but”

items.diff: ばかり is “nothing but, always this”, often with dissatisfaction; だけ is “only this, nothing else”.

this.tr: My little brother always eats nothing but meat.

that.tr: I didn't have time this morning, so I only ate bread.

items.explain: Check for a sense of repetition, as with 「いつも」: complaining that there's too much of something, that it's always like that → ばかり (casually ばっかり); just objectively saying the scope this time was small → だけ. English can say “only / just” for both, which makes them easy to mix up.

items.diff: ばかり is “nothing but, always”, where other things may also exist, often with dissatisfaction; しか〜ない means nothing apart from it.

this.tr: My older brother eats nothing but meat.

that.tr: My older brother only eats meat (he won't eat anything else).

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: ばかり is followed by an affirmative (食べている), saying there's too much of something or it's too frequent; しか is always followed by a negative (食べない), excluding everything else.

groups.note: Both mean “about, approximately”

items.diff: Quantity word＋ばかり doesn't mean “only” but “about”, like ぐらい, just more formal and a bit old-fashioned.

this.tr: Please wait about ten minutes.

that.tr: Please wait ten minutes or so.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ばかり: quantity words like 10分, 千円, 一週間 → “about”, so don't misread it as “wait only ten minutes”; a noun (肉, ゲーム) → nothing but. In everyday speech just say くらい／ぐらい — the two spellings mean the same.

groups.note: All are plain-style yes/no questions “…?”

items.title: 〜か (plain-form question)
items.diff: 〜の？ is soft, used by everyone, and shows concern; adding か directly to the plain form sounds blunt and is mostly used by men.

this.tr: Are you really okay?

that.tr: You really okay? (male speech)

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same but sound different: 〜の？ is soft, used by both men and women, and carries concern like “what's wrong?”; adding 「か」 straight after the plain form is direct and blunt, mostly used by men to friends or juniors — in everyday speech people usually say 「〜の？」 or just use rising intonation. Note that nouns and な-adjectives need 「な」 before it: 大丈夫なの？

items.title: 〜かい (yes/no question)
items.diff: 〜の？ is the most general; 〜かい has the friendly tone of an older person or a man talking to someone younger, and is mostly found in novels and anime.

this.tr: Are you coming tomorrow too?

that.tr: Coming tomorrow too, are you? (elder's tone)

items.explain: Both sentences ask “are you coming tomorrow too?” and differ only in the ending. かい has the friendly tone of an older person or a man speaking to someone younger, mostly found in novels and anime; when you speak yourself, 「〜の？」 is the most natural.

groups.note: Both press for a reason: “why …?”

items.title: 〜んですか (asking for reasons)
items.diff: Both ask the other person to explain why; 〜の？ is plain style, for friends and family; 〜んですか is polite, for teachers, bosses and people you don't know well.

this.tr: Why didn't you answer the phone?

that.tr: Why was it that you didn't answer the phone?

items.explain: Both sentences press for a reason and differ only in the ending, so it depends on who you're talking to: friends, family → 「〜の？」 with rising intonation; teachers, bosses, people you don't know well → 〜んですか. In writing it also appears as 「のですか」.

groups.note: All come from the causative 「せる・させる」 — “make / let (someone) do”

items.diff: させる takes the person who makes someone do it as the subject; させられる takes the person forced to do it as the subject, with a sense of reluctance.

this.tr: My mother made me eat vegetables.

that.tr: I was made to eat vegetables by my mother.

items.explain: Both describe the same event — look at the subject: 「母は私に〜させた」 takes the side of the person giving the order; 「私は母に〜させられた」 takes the side of the person forced, adding 「られ」 and a grumble of “I didn't really want to”. Godan verbs use せる (行かせる), ichidan verbs use させる; the usage is the same.

items.title: 〜させてください (please let me do)
items.diff: The causative on its own means “make someone else do it”; change the person made to act to 「私に」 and add 「ください」, and you are asking the other person to let you do it.

this.tr: The department manager had his subordinate prepare the documents.

that.tr: Manager, please let me prepare those documents.

items.explain: The basic meaning of the causative is “make (someone else) do”: 「部下に作らせた」 means the manager had a subordinate do it. Replace the person made to act with yourself, 「私に」, and add the request 「ください」, and it becomes “please let me do it” — asking the other person for permission to do it yourself. Look at who comes before 「に」 and whether 「ください」 follows: 「部下に〜せた」 → making someone else do it; 「私に〜せてください」 → asking to be allowed to do it yourself.

groups.note: Both mean “tell someone else to do it”

items.title: 〜ように言う (tell someone to do)
