items.diff: The causative means you actually had the person do it; ように言う only reports the instruction “told him to do it” — whether it got done is unclear.

this.tr: My mother had my little brother tidy his room.

that.tag: Only told him · maybe not done
that.tr: My mother told my little brother to tidy his room, but he still hasn't.

items.explain: Ask whether the result matters: 「弟に片付けさせた」 means she had him do it and it got done; 「弟に片付けるように言った」 only states the instruction “told him to do it”, so whether he did is open — that is why 「まだ片付けていない」 can follow it, while it cannot follow させた. ように言う reports an instruction and also sounds more indirect than the causative.

groups.note: Both come from the causative 「させる」 — basic meaning “make / let (someone else) do”

items.diff: させられる takes the person forced to do it as the subject; させる takes the person who makes someone do it as the subject.

this.tr: I was made to eat vegetables by my mother.

that.tr: My mother made me eat vegetables.

items.explain: The basic meaning of the causative 「させる」 is “make (someone else) do”. From the side of the person giving the order, 「母は私に」 → させた: my mother made me eat. Turn that sentence into the passive and make the person being ordered the subject, 「私は母に」 → させられた: “was made to do it” — that is, forced — which is why it carries the grumble “I didn't really want to”. Look at the subject, then check for 「られ」: present → forced to do it; absent → making someone else do it.

groups.note: Both mean “be forced to do”

items.title: 〜を余儀なくされる (be forced to…)
items.diff: させられる is usually being pushed by a person, conversational, with resentment; を余儀なくされる is being forced by circumstances to have no choice, formal and objective.

this.tr: I was made to change the plan by the department manager.

that.tr: Due to heavy rain, the plan was forced to change.

items.explain: Look at what is forcing you: a specific person, like 「部長に」 → させられた, conversational, with the resentment of “I didn't want to”; circumstances you cannot resist, like 「大雨で」 — natural disasters, accidents, economic conditions → を余儀なくされた, formal and objective, common in news and reports.

groups.note: All express total negation, “not … at all”

items.title: ぜんぜん〜ない (not at all)
items.diff: Same meaning; ちっとも carries stronger feeling and is often used to complain; 全然 is the most common everyday way to say it, with a flatter tone.

this.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son doesn't study one bit.

that.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son doesn't study at all.

items.explain: Both sentences are natural and equally strong negations. The difference is nuance: ちっとも carries the speaker's frustration or impatience, like grumbling “why won't he ever…”; 全然 is the most common everyday expression and can be used to complain or just to state flatly “not at all”. To stress your annoyance → ちっとも; just describing the situation → 全然.

items.diff: The negation is equally strong; ちっとも is conversational and often complaining; 少しも is neutral and can be used in writing too.

this.tr: I took the medicine, but my fever isn't going down one bit!

that.tr: I took the medicine, but the fever did not go down in the least.

items.explain: Both mean “not even a little”, with the same strength. Choose by situation: talking to someone in a complaining tone → ちっとも; neutral narration such as a diary or report → 少しも. ちっとも is generally not used in writing.

items.title: まったく〜ない (not at all…)
items.diff: ちっとも carries personal feeling and is only conversational; まったく sounds objective and works in formal situations too.

this.tr: This machine won't work one bit!

that.tr: Manager, this machine does not work at all.

items.explain: Look at who you are talking to and how the sentence ends: grumbling among friends, ending in a plain form like 「〜ないよ」 → ちっとも is natural; reporting to a superior like 「部長」 or a customer, ending in 「〜ません」, or writing a report → use まったく; ちっとも is too casual. まったく works in both speech and writing.

groups.note: Both come from 「だけ（丈）」 — originally “length, height”, extended to “a limit, up to this point”

items.diff: だけ simply limits the scope, “only…”; add 「で」 and follow it with a result, and it means “just… alone is enough to…”.

this.tr: Just looking at it is fun.

that.tr: I'm not buying. I'm just looking.

items.explain: 「だけ」 comes from 「丈（たけ）」, originally “length, height”, extended to “up to this limit”, so だけ means “only this, nothing more”. On its own, だけ stops at limiting: 「見るだけです」 means just looking and doing nothing else (買いません). Add 「で」, which marks means or condition, and it becomes “with only this”, followed by a result: 「見るだけで楽しい」 — just looking is fun. Look at what follows: a result (楽しい) → だけで; explaining that you did nothing else (買いません) → だけ.

groups.note: だけで ↔ だけでなく — the only difference is 「なく」

items.diff: だけで is “just… alone is enough to…”; だけでなく is “not only… but also…”.

this.tr: Just the bread filled me up.

that.tr: I ate not only bread but salad too.

items.explain: The only difference is 「なく」: だけで is followed by the result that this one thing alone brings about (お腹がいっぱいになった); だけでなく means “not just this one thing” and adds another item after it, often with 「〜も」 (サラダも). When you read 「だけで」, check carefully whether 「なく」 follows: one means “just… alone is enough to…”, the other “not only… but also…”.

groups.note: Both mean “all you need is…”

items.diff: Both mean “all you need to do is…”; さえ〜ば stresses more strongly that “this one condition is all, nothing else is needed”.

this.tr: On this form, you only need to write your name.

that.tr: On this form, as long as you write your name, that's all you need.

items.explain: The structures differ: だけでいい attaches after a verb's dictionary form (書くだけでいい); さえ〜ば puts さえ after the noun and turns the verb into the ば-form (名前さえ書けば), with a stronger tone, as if saying “you don't need to worry about anything else”.

groups.note: Both express a guess, “probably…”

items.title: 〜と思う (guess)
items.diff: Both are guesses; と思う sounds more straightforward; だろうと思う adds the hedge “probably”, so it is softer.

this.tr: I think he has probably got home by now.

that.tr: I think he has got home by now.

items.explain: Both sentences guess about something uncertain and are interchangeable. と思う states the guess directly and sounds more straightforward; inserting 「だろう」 to make だろうと思う adds a layer of “probably” — you don't commit fully, so it sounds softer. To say it plainly → と思う; to leave yourself some room → だろうと思う.

items.diff: でしょう states a guess directly to the listener; だろうと思います stresses “this is my personal guess” and is softer.

this.tr: I think it'll rain tomorrow.

that.tr: It'll probably rain tomorrow.

wrong.why: でしょう can't be followed by 「と思う」

items.explain: でしょう is the polite form of 「だろう」 and states a guess directly, like a weather forecast; when you add 「と思います」, the part before it must be the plain form 「だろう」 — you can't say ✗でしょうと思います.

groups.note: Both mean “to start…”

items.diff: 出す is starting suddenly, beyond control; 始める is an ordinary start and can also be used for things you intend to do.

this.tr: Suddenly, the baby burst out crying.

that.tr: Everyone's here, so let's start eating.

wrong.why: 出す means starting suddenly, so it cannot be used in an invitation like 「〜ましょう」

items.explain: Check for 「急に」 or 「突然」, or whether it is something you intend to do: it happens suddenly and can't be controlled (泣き出す, 降り出す, 笑い出す) → 出す; something you planned or are inviting others to do together (みんな揃ったので〜ましょう, 〜たい, 〜つもり) → only 始める.

groups.note: Both come from 「ござる」 — originally “to be (present)”, said of a noble person

items.diff: でございます equals 「です」 (is); に + ございます equals 「にあります」 (is located).

this.tr: This is the reception desk.

that.tr: The reception desk is on the first floor.

items.explain: 「ござる」 comes from 「御座ある」, originally meaning a noble person “is (somewhere)”; it later became the formal way to say 「ある」, so ございます alone = あります, meaning “is located, there is”: 「一階にございます」. On the other hand, just as 「である」 is 「で＋ある」 meaning “is”, 「で＋ござる」 also means “is”, so でございます = です. Look at what comes before ございます: 「で」 → is; 「に」 or 「が」 → is located, there is.

groups.note: Both express the judgment “is”

items.title: 〜です (noun judgment)
items.diff: でございます is a more formal way of saying 「です」, used mostly by shop staff, hotels and announcements when addressing customers.

this.tr: Your room is on the fifth floor.

that.tr: The room is on the fifth floor.

items.explain: The meaning is exactly the same; it depends on the setting: speaking to customers at a hotel, in a shop or over an announcement → でございます; with your boss or colleagues in everyday situations, です is enough — being overly formal actually sounds distant.

groups.note: Both mean “is (doing) right now”

items.title: 〜ている (in progress)
items.diff: ております is the humble form of ています, used only for your own side, never for customers or superiors.

this.tr: The person in charge is checking it right now.

that.tr: The person in charge is checking it now.

wrong.why: ております only describes your own side; to ask a customer, use honorific language: 「何をなさっていますか」

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same: “is checking it right now”. ております makes the actions of your own side (yourself, people at your company) sound more formal, and is used when speaking to customers or in business emails; ています is ordinary politeness and works for anyone's actions. When the subject is a customer or a superior, never use ております — use honorific language (〜ていらっしゃいます).

groups.note: Both come from 「で + も」 — “even if it's…”

items.diff: でも〜でも appearing in pairs after nouns means “whether A or B”; でも at the start of a sentence means “but”.

this.tr: Rain or snow, the match will go ahead.

that.tr: It's raining. But the match will go ahead.

items.explain: Both carry the sense “even so…”. Look at where でも is: after nouns (雨でも雪でも), appearing as a pair → whether A or B; at the start of a sentence, following on from the previous one (雨が降っている。でも、……) → but.

items.title: 〜でも (何でも・誰でも)
items.diff: AでもBでも lists specific options; 何でも uses one question word to cover everything.

this.tr: Meat or fish — please choose whichever you like.

that.tr: Anything is fine — please take whatever you like.

items.explain: The basic meaning of 「で＋も」 is “even if it is…”. After two specific nouns, “even if it's meat, even if it's fish” → both are fine, giving AでもBでも “whether A or B”; after a question word, “even if it's what” → whatever it is, it's fine, giving 何でも “anything”. Look at what comes before でも: two specific nouns side by side (肉, 魚) → AでもBでも; a question word like 何, 誰, どこ → “all of them…”.

groups.note: Both mean “whether A or B”

items.diff: でも〜でも is conversational and follows nouns; にしろ〜にしろ is more written and can also follow verbs.

this.tr: Beer or wine — please drink whatever you like.

that.tr: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: nouns like ビール、ワイン in everyday speech → でも〜でも; verbs like 「行く／行かない」, or formal settings → にしろ〜にしろ (にしても〜にしても works the same way).

groups.note: が見られる ↔ と見られる — only the particle before it differs: 「が」 or 「と」

items.diff: が見られる means “a phenomenon can be observed”; とみられる means “it is presumed / believed that”.

this.tr: In this town, a growth in population can be seen.

that.tr: The cause of the accident is believed to be excessive speed.

items.explain: Both are common in the news, and 「とみられる」 is also often written 「と見られる」. Look at the particle before 見られる: 「が」 follows a phenomenon that is seen (増加, 変化) → observed; 「と」 follows a judgment (事故の原因は〜) → presumed, believed — talking about something not yet fully confirmed.

groups.note: Both mean “can be seen”

items.title: 〜が見える
items.diff: が見られる introduces something you have a chance to see at a certain place or time; が見える is something naturally coming into view right in front of you.

this.tr: On this beach, you can see sea turtles once summer comes.

that.tr: Look, I can see a sea turtle over there!

items.explain: Both mean “can be seen”. Ask what kind of seeing it is: introducing what you can see if you go to a certain place or season (夏になると, この海岸では) → が見られる, like a travel guide; right in front of you now, naturally coming into view (あそこに) → が見える.

groups.note: Both mean “hear a sound”

items.title: 〜が聞こえる
items.diff: 音がする stands on the side of the sound: “a sound is coming out”; 音が聞こえる stands on the side of the person: “the ears can hear it”.

this.tr: A strange noise is coming from the TV.

that.tag: The listener · can hear or not
that.tr: My grandfather is hard of hearing and can't hear the TV.

items.explain: Both can describe hearing a sound: 「テレビから変な音がする」 can also be said as 「変な音が聞こえる」 with no change in meaning. The difference is whose side you take: 音がする stands on the side of the sound, “a sound is coming out”; 聞こえる stands on the side of the listener, “whether the ears can hear it”. So when talking about the listener's conditions such as hearing or distance (祖父は耳が遠くて), only 聞こえる works; saying 「音がしない」 would mean the TV makes no sound at all.

groups.note: Both mean “feel / think”

items.diff: 気がする is just a feeling with no reason you can name; と思う is your own judgment and you can give a reason.

this.tr: Somehow I have a feeling it'll rain tomorrow.

that.tr: There are a lot of clouds, so I think it'll rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: 「なんとなく」 — no reason you can name, just a feeling → 気がする; 「雲が多いから」 — backed by a reason → と思う.

groups.note: Both come from 「がる」 — “to show signs of…”

items.diff: がり is a noun describing someone's personality; がる is a verb describing how someone behaves at a given moment.

this.tr: My little brother has always been sensitive to the cold, ever since he was a kid.

that.tr: When I opened the window, my little brother complained of the cold.

items.explain: Look at how it's used: 「寒がりだ」「寒がりの人」 used as a noun → a person who's naturally sensitive to cold, always like that; 「寒がった」「寒がっている」 used as a verb → showing signs of being cold this time, right now.

groups.note: Both describe a personality that “tends to…”

items.diff: がり attaches to feeling adjectives like 「寒い・怖い」 and is a noun; っぽい attaches to a verb's masu-stem and is an adjective.

this.tr: My older sister is sensitive to the cold and brings a jacket even in summer.

that.tr: My grandfather has become forgetful lately.

wrong.why: がり doesn't attach to verbs

items.explain: First look at the word before it: feelings like 寒い、怖い、恥ずかしい → がり (寒がり、怖がり); verbs like 忘れる、怒る → っぽい (忘れっぽい、怒りっぽい). っぽい conjugates like an i-adjective: 忘れっぽくなった.

groups.note: Both come from 「がる」 — “to show signs of…”

items.diff: がる attaches to adjectives: ほしがる is wanting a thing; たがる attaches to verbs: 買いたがる is wanting to do an action.

this.tr: My little brother wants the new game.

that.tr: My little brother wants to buy the new game.

wrong.why: A verb must first become 「たい」, then take がる

items.explain: Look at what comes before がる: an i-adjective minus い (ほし、怖、寒) → がる; a verb first becomes 「〜たい」, then 「〜たがる」 (買いたがる). Both describe someone else's wishes from the outside; がっている is just the progressive form of がる.

items.diff: がる is a verb describing how someone behaves at a given moment; がり is a noun describing someone's personality.

this.tr: When I opened the window, my little brother complained of the cold.

that.tr: My little brother has always been sensitive to the cold, ever since he was a kid.

items.explain: Look at how it's used: 「寒がった」「寒がっている」 used as a verb → showing signs of being cold this time, right now; 「寒がりだ」「寒がりの人」 used as a noun → a person who's naturally sensitive to cold.

groups.note: All express someone's feelings or wishes

items.diff: がっている means the other person shows it through words and actions; そうだ is the speaker's judgment from appearances.

this.tr: My little sister calls every night — she's feeling lonely.

that.tr: My little sister, sitting there alone, looks lonely.

items.explain: Look at the basis: the person shows their feelings through actions or words (毎晩電話してくる、帰りたいと言う) → がっている; you only see how they look and judge for yourself → そうだ. When you're not sure, そうだ is the safer choice.

items.diff: To say someone else wants something, use ほしがっている, and 「が」 changes to 「を」; がほしい is only about yourself.

this.tr: My little brother wants the new game.

that.tr: I want the new game.

items.explain: Look at the subject: a brother, a friend or anyone else → をほしがっている; me (or asking the listener in a question) → がほしい. ほしい is a feeling inside yourself; other people's feelings can only be read from how they appear.

groups.note: Both are くださる・いただく themselves — after a noun it's giving a thing, after the te-form it's doing something for someone

items.thisTitle: いただく（receive from a superior）
items.diff: noun + を いただく is receiving a thing; te-form + いただく is having the other person kindly do something for me.

this.tr: My teacher gave me a book.

that.tr: My teacher kindly lent me a book.

items.explain: Look at what comes before いただく: noun + を (本を) → you received a thing from a superior; a verb's te-form (貸して) → what you received is their help, “you kindly…”.

items.thisTitle: くださる（a superior gives me）
items.diff: noun + を くださる is a superior giving me a thing; te-form + くださる is a superior doing something for me.

this.tr: The company president gave me a souvenir.

that.tr: The company president kindly drove me to the station.

items.explain: Look at what comes before くださる: noun + を → a thing is given; a verb's te-form (送って) → an action is given, “(a superior) did … for me”. Either way the direction is from the superior to me.

groups.note: Both express giving and receiving, in exactly the same directions

items.diff: The directions are exactly the same; only the other person differs: for teachers, bosses and customers use さしあげる・くださる・いただく; for friends and family use あげる・くれる・もらう.

this.tag: さしあげる · I give a superior
this.tr: I gave my teacher flowers.

this.tag: くださる · a superior gives me
this.tr: My teacher gave me a book.

this.tag: いただく · receive from a superior
this.tr: I received a souvenir from my teacher.

that.tr: I gave my friend flowers.
My friend gave me a book.
I received a souvenir from my friend.

items.explain: They pair up one to one: あげる→さしあげる、くれる→くださる、もらう→いただく. Look at who the other person is: a teacher, boss or customer → the honorific set; friends or family → the ordinary set. Using あげる・くれる with elders sounds rude.

groups.note: Both are あげる・くれる・もらう themselves — after a noun, a thing is given; after the te-form, “help” is given

items.diff: noun + を あげる is giving a thing; te-form + あげる is doing something for someone.

this.tr: I gave my little sister a picture book.

that.tr: I read a picture book to my little sister.

items.explain: Look at what comes before あげる: noun + を → a thing is given; a verb's te-form (読んで) → an action is given, “doing … for someone”. Either way the direction is from me to others.

items.diff: noun + を くれる is someone giving me a thing; te-form + くれる is someone doing something for me.

this.tr: My friend gave me an umbrella.

that.tr: My friend lent me an umbrella.

items.explain: Look at what comes before くれる: noun + を → the umbrella was given to me; a verb's te-form (貸して) → it was only lent, and what I received is their kindness. Either way the direction is from others to me, often with a sense of gratitude.

items.diff: noun + を もらう is getting a thing; te-form + もらう is getting someone's help.

this.tr: I got a dictionary from my senior.

that.tr: My senior lent me a dictionary.

items.explain: Look at what comes before もらう: noun + を → the dictionary is now mine; a verb's te-form (貸して) → what I got is the help of “lending it to me”. In both, the subject is the receiver (me), and the other person is marked with 「に」.

groups.note: Both express giving and receiving, in exactly the same directions

items.diff: The directions are exactly the same; only the other person differs: for friends and family use あげる・くれる・もらう; for teachers, bosses and customers switch to さしあげる・くださる・いただく.

this.tr: I gave my friend flowers.
My friend gave me a book.
I received a souvenir from my friend.

that.tag: さしあげる · I give a superior
that.tr: I gave my teacher flowers.

that.tag: くださる · a superior gives me
that.tr: My teacher gave me a book.

that.tag: いただく · receive from a superior
that.tr: I received a souvenir from my teacher.

items.explain: They pair up one to one: あげる→さしあげる、くれる→くださる、もらう→いただく. Look at who the other person is: friends or family → the ordinary set; a teacher, boss or customer → the honorific set. Using あげる・くれる with elders sounds rude.

groups.note: Both come from 「ござる」 — originally “to be (present)”, said of a noble person

items.title: 〜でございます
items.diff: に + ございます equals 「にあります」 (“is located at”); でございます equals 「です」 (“is”).

this.tr: The reception desk is on the first floor.

that.tr: This is the reception desk.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ございます: 「に」 or 「が」 → ございます＝あります, meaning “is located / there is”; 「で」 → でございます＝です, meaning “is…”. Both are formal expressions used toward customers.

groups.note: Both mean “there is, is located”

items.title: 〜がある（things）
items.diff: ございます is a more formal way of saying 「あります」, used toward customers and superiors — but only for things, not people.

this.tr: The restroom is on the second floor.

that.tr: The toilet is on the second floor.

wrong.why: ございます can't be used for people

items.explain: Same meaning; it depends on the setting: shop staff or receptionists speaking to customers → ございます (even the noun changes to the more refined お手洗い); normally あります is enough. Note that you can't use ございます to say where a person is: for people on your side use 「おります」, for the other side 「いらっしゃいます」.

groups.note: Both come from 「始める」 — “to begin”

items.diff: verb masu-stem + 始める means “start doing”; noun + をはじめ means “starting with…, led by…”, used to name a representative example.

this.tr: I started taking piano lessons last month.

that.tr: It snowed in Tokyo, and also in Osaka, Kyoto and elsewhere.

items.explain: Look at what it attaches to: a verb's masu-stem (習い) → the start of an action; noun + をはじめ, followed by a list of similar things (大阪や京都でも) → that noun is treated as “the representative at the head of the list”, nothing to do with an action starting.

groups.note: Both have to do with an action “starting”

items.diff: 始める is an ordinary start and can also be used for things you intend to do; 出す is starting suddenly, involuntarily.

this.tr: Everyone's here, so let's start eating.

that.tr: The baby suddenly burst out crying.

wrong.why: 出す means a sudden start and can't be used in an invitation like 「〜ましょう」

items.explain: Check whether it's something you intend to do: planned, or inviting others to do it together (〜ましょう、〜たい、〜つもり) → only 始める; something sudden that can't be helped (急に泣き出す、降り出す) → 出す is more vivid.

items.diff: With 始める, the action continues after starting; かける／かけの means it was started and then stopped, not finished.

this.tr: I started reading this novel last week.

that.tr: He started to say something, then stopped.
There's a half-read novel on the desk.

items.explain: Look at what happens to the action afterwards: 始める only marks the starting point, and the action goes on; かける is often followed by 「やめた」「途中で」, meaning it stopped right after starting; 「〜かけの + noun」 means “a half-done…” (読みかけの本、食べかけのパン).

groups.note: Both are about whether something needs to be done

items.diff: 必要がある objectively explains that “this needs to be done”; なければならない carries a sense of obligation, “have to”.

this.tr: To get a visa, you need to go to the embassy.

that.tr: To get my visa, I have to go to the embassy tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether it's explaining a condition or describing your own situation: telling others “what needs to be done”, like in instructions or notices → 必要がある; the speaker feels they “must do it”, under pressure → なければならない. They also attach differently: dictionary form + 必要がある, nai-form + なければならない.

items.diff: Both mean “you don't have to”; 必要はない is objective and formal, なくてもいい is conversational and soft.

this.tr: There are plenty of seats, so there's no need to reserve.

that.tr: There are plenty of seats, so you don't have to reserve.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: staff or notices addressing customers → 必要はありません; between friends → なくてもいいよ. They also attach differently: dictionary form + 必要はない (予約する必要はない), nai-form + なくてもいい (予約しなくてもいい).

groups.note: Both come from 「ほど（程）」 — “degree, extent”

items.diff: ほど〜ない says “doesn't reach B's level” and must end in a negative; ほど on its own says “to the point of…”, followed by an affirmative.

this.tr: This summer isn't as hot as last year.

that.tr: It's so hot today I feel like I might collapse.

items.explain: Look at what's before ほど and at the end of the sentence: another thing being compared (去年) before it and a negative at the end → ほど〜ない “not as… as”; an exaggerated description (倒れそうな) before it and an affirmative at the end → ほど “so… that…”, stressing a high degree.

groups.note: Aほど〜ない ↔ Aほど〜はない — just one 「は」 apart; one means “not as… as”, the other “the most…”

items.diff: 「AはBほど〜ない」 means “A is not as … as B”; 「BほどAはない」 means “there's no A more … than B” — a superlative.

this.tag: A not as good as B
this.tr: This shop's ramen isn't as good as the one in front of the station.

that.tr: There's no ramen as good as this shop's.

items.explain: Look at what 「ない」 negates: if the adjective becomes 「おいしくない」 → the degree is negated, A is not as good as B; if the adjective stays affirmative 「おいしい」 and is followed by a noun plus 「はない」 → what's negated is “anything else”, meaning B is the best. A slight change in word order flips the evaluation.

groups.note: Both are used to compare two things

items.diff: ほど〜ない is the negative “not as… as”; より is “more… than”, usually followed by an affirmative.

this.tr: Today isn't as cold as yesterday.

that.tr: Today is colder than yesterday.

wrong.why: When ほど is used to compare, it must be followed by a negative; to say “as cold as yesterday”, use 「昨日と同じくらい寒い」

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: affirmative (寒い) → より; negative (寒くない) → ほど, meaning “doesn't reach yesterday's level”. When ほど is used to compare, it's always followed by a negative.

items.diff: ほど〜ない says it from the negative side, “A isn't as… as B”; より〜のほうが says it from the positive side, “B is more…”.

this.tr: Buses aren't as fast as trains.

that.tr: Trains are faster than buses.

items.explain: Both sentences say the same thing: ほど is always followed by a negative (速くない) and speaks from the side that loses, so it sounds softer; より〜のほうが is followed by an affirmative (速い) and focuses on the side that wins.

groups.note: All tell someone to do something, with different degrees of force

items.diff: The imperative form is blunt and harsh; なさい is an elder's command to a younger person — gentle and well-mannered.

this.tr: Hey, get up already!

that.tr: It's already seven. Get up now.

items.explain: Look at the speaker and the sentence-ending particles: a man to someone younger, a fight, an emergency (おい) → imperative form (起きろ、書け、来い); a mother to a child or a teacher to students, often with 「〜よ」 → なさい (attaches to the masu-stem: 起き + なさい). Never use the imperative form with superiors or strangers.

items.diff: The imperative form is a harsh command; てください is a polite request you can use with anyone.

this.tr: Look out! Stop!

that.tr: Excuse me, could you stop for a moment?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to and how urgent it is: an emergency, or the listener is younger or an opponent → imperative form (止まれ); asking an ordinary person to do something → てください. In English both can just be “stop”, but in Japanese they're several politeness levels apart.

items.title: 〜てくれと言う
items.diff: 「〜ろ／〜えと言われた」 reports a command; 「〜てくれと言われた」 reports a request, which is milder.

this.tr: The department manager told me to go home early.

that.tr: The department manager asked me to go home early.

items.explain: Look at what was originally said: a command like 「帰れ！」 → 帰れと言われた; a request like 「帰ってくれ／帰ってください」 → 帰ってくれと言われた. Using the imperative form when reporting isn't rude — it simply conveys the content of the command as it was, e.g. 「医者に酒をやめろと言われた」.

groups.note: Both let a “thing” be the subject (〜が) to describe its change or state

items.diff: intransitive verb + ている just describes the state in front of you; transitive verb + てある says “someone deliberately set it up this way”.

this.tr: I wondered why it was so cold — the window is open.

that.tr: The window has been left open (on purpose) to let in fresh air.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: you've simply discovered a state (寒いと思ったら) → intransitive verb + ている (開いている); there's a purpose and someone deliberately did it (空気を入れるために) → transitive verb + てある (開けてある). Note that てある takes a transitive verb, yet the particle is 「が」.

items.title: 〜れる・〜られる（passive）
items.diff: An intransitive verb says “the thing changed by itself”; the passive of a transitive verb says “someone did something to it”.

this.tr: The windowpane broke in the wind.

that.tr: The windowpane was broken by someone.

items.explain: Check whether a “person” is involved: a natural cause like wind or an earthquake, or you only want to state the result → intransitive verb (割れた); you're sure someone did it (誰かに) → passive of the transitive verb (割られた). Even without 「誰かに」, a passive sentence implies someone was behind it.

groups.note: Both come from the question particle 「か」 — its original meaning is “being unsure, asking”

items.title: 〜か (embedded question)
items.diff: With no question word, asking “whether or not” needs 「かどうか」; a question with a question word just takes 「か」.

this.tag: Whether or not → かどうか
this.tr: I don't know whether he's coming tomorrow.

that.tr: I don't know when he's coming.

wrong.why: When there's a question word, you can't add 「どうか」 as well

items.explain: 「か」 originally expresses being unsure and asking: it puts a question into the sentence as it is. If the question has a question word (いつ、どこ、誰、何), the unsure part is that word, so just add 「か」: いつ来るか. With no question word, only asking “yes or no”, you say 「来るか、どうか」 — “is he coming, or how is it?” Putting the two sides side by side gives “whether”: 来るかどうか. That's why you can't add 「どうか」 when there's a question word.

groups.note: Both mean “whether or not”

items.diff: かどうか is the everyday expression; か否か means the same but is very formal and written.

this.tr: I don't know whether this story is true.

that.tr: This study examines whether this drug is effective.

items.explain: The meaning is exactly the same; it depends on the setting: speech and ordinary writing → かどうか; academic papers, news, official documents (本研究では、〜である) → か否か. 「否」 means “not”, so it literally says “yes, or not”.

groups.note: Both ask “…?” out of concern

items.diff: かい has the warm tone of an older person speaking to a younger one and is now mostly seen in novels and anime; の？ is used by everyone.

this.tr: Are you not feeling well, dear?

that.tr: Are you not feeling well?

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same: asking out of concern after seeing how the other person looks. Look at the speaker: a grandfather, father or teacher speaking to a child with an affectionate, elderly tone → 〜のかい; most people, especially young people and women → 〜の？. かい only asks “yes or no”; with a question word, switch to だい.

groups.note: Both mean “might …”

items.diff: かもしれない works for good or bad things, spoken or written; おそれがある is only for bad things and is common in news and announcements.

this.tr: It might snow tomorrow, you know.

that.tr: Due to the typhoon, the river is in danger of overflowing.

wrong.why: おそれがある can only be used for bad things

items.explain: Look at the content and the setting: news, weather forecasts or announcements saying a disaster or danger may happen (台風の影響で) → おそれがある; everyday conversation, or something good (合格できるかもしれない) → かもしれない. おそれがある can't be used for good things.

groups.note: 「かな」＝ the question 「か」 + the exclamatory 「な」

items.title: 〜なあ（exclamation · wish）
items.diff: かな has the extra question 「か」 and is a self-question, “I wonder if…”; なあ is just an exclamation or a wish.

this.tr: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

that.tr: It'd be nice if it's sunny tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether there's a 「か」 before 「な」: with 「か」 → you're unsure and asking yourself; without 「か」 → a simple exclamation (きれいだなあ) or a wish (〜たらいいなあ).

groups.note: Both ask oneself “I wonder …”

items.diff: かな is used by both men and women; かしら is traditionally feminine — soft and a bit old-fashioned.

this.tr: I wonder if these clothes suit me.

that.tr: I wonder if these clothes suit me. (feminine tone)

items.explain: The meaning is basically the same; look at the speaker: anyone, especially young people → かな; middle-aged or older women, or elegant female characters in novels and TV dramas → かしら. Young women today mostly say かな too.

items.diff: かな is a relaxed, spoken way of asking yourself; のだろうか leans written and sounds serious.

this.tr: I wonder if we can win tomorrow's game.

that.tr: Why do people dream?

items.explain: Look at the setting and the topic: small matters when chatting with friends or talking to yourself → かな; serious questions pondered in writing or speeches (なぜ、本当に) → のだろうか (in speech, 「んだろうか」).

groups.note: Both ask oneself “I wonder …”

items.diff: かしら is traditionally women's language — soft and a little old-fashioned; かな is used by both men and women.

this.tr: I wonder if this skirt suits me. (feminine tone)

that.tr: Does this skirt suit me, I wonder?

items.explain: The meaning is basically the same; look at the speaker: middle-aged or older women, or elegant female characters in novels and TV dramas → かしら; men and women of all ages, especially young people → かな. Today young women also mostly say かな.

items.diff: かしら is women's spoken language; のだろうか is used by anyone and leans written.

this.tr: Oh my, I wonder if Tanaka isn't coming today.

that.tr: Why isn't Tanaka coming?

items.explain: Look at the speaker and the style: a woman in everyday conversation with a soft tone (あら、〜のかしら) → かしら; a written expression anyone can use, or asking yourself in writing → のだろうか.

groups.note: Both come from the near demonstrative 「こ」 — originally “this side, near the speaker”

items.diff: こんな means “this kind of, like this”, focusing on type and nature; この points to this specific one.

this.tr: I'd love to have a bag like this someday.

that.tr: Excuse me, I'll take this bag, please.

items.explain: この = 「こ」 + 「の」, “of this side” → points to the specific one in front of you; こんな is contracted from 「このような」, “like this side” → refers to this type, this kind of nature. So look at 「いつか」: wanting one someday means you want not this exact one but one of the same kind → こんな; saying 「ください」 in a shop means you want the one right in front of you → この. そんな／その, あんな／あの, どんな／どの differ in the same way.

items.diff: これ points directly to a thing; こんなの means “this sort of thing”, focusing on its nature and often carrying feeling.

this.tr: I don't want this sort of thing.

that.tr: I don't need this.

items.explain: これ = 「こ」 + 「れ」 (marking a thing), pointing directly to the thing on this side; こんな is contracted from 「このような」 and means “like this side”, focusing on nature, so 「こんなの」 is “this sort of thing” and often carries feeling — distaste (こんなのいらない) or surprise (こんなの初めて). If you're just pointing out which one you want or don't want → これ. そんなの／それ, あんなの／あれ work the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “like this”

items.title: このような
items.diff: こんな is conversational; このような means the same but is more formal, used in writing and formal settings.

this.tr: Don't make this kind of mistake again, OK?

that.tr: We will never make such a mistake again.

items.explain: It depends on the setting: talking with friends or family → こんな; formal settings like letters of apology, meetings or official documents (今後は) → このような. そんな／そのような、あんな／あのような、どんな／どのような likewise; there's no difference in meaning.

groups.note: する ことがある ↔ した ことがある — only る／た differs

items.diff: Dictionary form + ことがある is “sometimes …”; た-form + ことがある is “have … before”.

this.tr: Even now I'm occasionally late for work.

that.tr: I was late for school once when I was a kid.

items.explain: Look at whether 「ことがある」 comes after 「る」 or 「た」: dictionary form (遅刻する) → something that happens now and then at present, often with 「たまに」 or 「時々」; た-form (遅刻した) → an experience you had in the past, often with 「子どもの時」 or 「一度」.

groups.note: Both come from 「見える」 — originally “to naturally come into view”

items.diff: Adjective く／noun に + 見える is “looks …”; noun + が見える is “can be seen”.

this.tr: Our teacher looks younger than his age.
He always looks full of energy.

that.tr: You can see Mt. Fuji from the window.

items.explain: 「見える」 originally means something naturally comes into view. The thing itself comes into view → 「noun + が見える」, “can be seen” (富士山が見える); a person or thing comes into view looking a certain way and leaves an impression → 「adjective く／noun or な-adjective に + 見える」, “looks …” (若く見える、元気に見える), often with words that compare with reality, like 「年より」. So check whether 「見える」 comes after 「が」 or 「く／に」. 聞こえる works the same way: 「変に聞こえる」 is “sounds strange”, 「音が聞こえる」 is “I can hear a sound”.

groups.note: Both mean “looks…”

items.title: 〜そうだ (looks like)
items.diff: く／に見える describes the impression something's appearance gives, even when you know the reality is different; そうだ is a guess from appearance about a quality not yet confirmed.

this.tr: Thanks to the mirror, this room looks bigger than it really is.

that.tag: そうだ · guessing an untried taste
that.tr: Wow, this cake looks delicious.

items.explain: Look at whether the speaker knows the actual situation: already knowing what it's really like and only describing the impression its appearance gives (実際より広く見える) → く／に見える; guessing on the spot from appearance about a quality not yet confirmed, such as the taste of something you haven't tried → そうだ (おいしそう). Facts you can confirm at a glance (colour, etc.) don't take そうだ.

items.diff: く／に見える attaches to adjectives and nouns; ように見える attaches to verbs or whole clauses.

this.tr: That person looks scary.
That person looks serious.

that.tr: That person looks like he's angry.

wrong.why: After a verb you need 「ように見える」

items.explain: Look at the word before 「見える」: i-adjective → く見える; na-adjective or noun → に見える; verb (怒っている、疲れている) → only ように見える.

groups.note: Both mean “not …”

items.diff: くない is a plain negation; くはない adds the contrastive 「は」, softening the tone and hinting “other aspects are another matter”.

this.tr: This place isn't expensive, but it isn't tasty either.

that.tr: This place isn't expensive. It's cheap and tasty.

items.explain: Check whether a “but …” follows: くはない is often followed by 「けど」 or 「が」, bringing in another aspect (高くはないけど、おいしくもない); くない is just a flat denial and can carry on in the same direction (高くない。安くておいしい). This 「は」 is the same contrastive 「は」 as in 「肉は食べるが、魚は食べない」.

groups.note: Both “first concede, then turn”

items.diff: くはあるが leans written; ことは〜が is the more common way to say it in everyday speech, with the same meaning.

this.tr: This room is small, but it is close to the station and convenient.

that.tr: This room is small, sure, but it's close to the station, so it's handy.

items.explain: Both first admit one fact and then give the other side. Look at the setting and the form: writing or formal speech → 「adjective く + はあるが」; everyday speech → say the adjective twice: 「狭いことは狭いけど」.

groups.note: Both come from 「まで」 — the “limit” reached

items.diff: までに means doing something once before that point; まで means continuing until that point.

this.tr: I'll be back by five.

that.tr: I'll wait until five.

wrong.why: 「出す」 is a one-time action, so it takes までに

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: actions completed in a moment, like 帰る、出す、着く → までに; actions that can continue, like 待つ、働く、勉強する → まで.

groups.note: All set a time for an action: at that moment, or before it

items.diff: までに draws a deadline; 前に only says which of two things comes first.

this.tr: Finish your homework by bedtime.

that.tr: Brush your teeth before going to bed.

items.explain: Both sentences start with 「寝る」; the difference is what follows: までに is a deadline — the homework can be done any time before bed; 前に only gives the order — brush your teeth first, then sleep.

items.title: 〜ないうちに
items.diff: までに takes a clear point in time as the deadline; ないうちに means “quickly, while the situation hasn't changed yet”.

this.tr: Let's head back by six.

that.tr: Let's head back before it gets dark.

items.explain: Look at what comes before it: a clock time or date → までに; a state that's about to change, like 「暗くならない」「雨が降らない」「冷めない」 → ないうちに, with a sense of urgency: “do it now, or it'll be too late”.

items.title: 〜に（point in time）
items.diff: までに means any time before that moment; に means exactly at that moment.

this.tr: Please come by nine tomorrow.

that.tr: Please come at nine tomorrow.

items.explain: Only 「まで」 differs: 「９時までに」 is a deadline — coming at eight or eight-thirty is fine, as long as it's no later than nine; 「９時に」 is exactly at nine o'clock.

groups.note: Both come from 「まま（儘）」 — originally “just as it is”

items.title: 〜られるままに
items.diff: たまま means doing something else while keeping a certain state; 言われるままに means “doing whatever others say”, letting yourself be pushed around.

this.tr: I went out leaving the window open.

that.tr: I did whatever the salesclerk told me and ended up buying expensive clothes.

items.explain: 「まま」 originally means “as it is”. Look at what comes before it: ta-form (開けた) → the state after the action is left as it is; words like 「言われる」「思う」「気の向く」 + ままに → doing things just as others say or as you feel like.

groups.note: Both have to do with “keeping a certain state”

items.diff: たまま can just describe objectively; っぱなし stresses “leaving it as is”, usually with displeasure.

this.tr: I was so tired I fell asleep with the light on.

that.tr: You left the light on again! Turn it off properly.

items.explain: たまま is often followed by another action (寝てしまった) and only says “in what state”; っぱなし is itself the focus of criticism, often as 「〜っぱなしにする」, with displeasure that something that should have been finished wasn't (また、ちゃんと).

items.diff: Two ways of saying the same thing: たまま says “keeping a state”, ないで says “without doing something”.

this.tr: I went into the room with my shoes on.

that.tr: I went into the room without taking off my shoes.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; look at the verb: 履いた (put on) + まま → keeping the state of “having them on”; 脱が (take off) + ないで → not doing the action of “taking off”.

items.diff: たまま means doing something else while keeping a certain state; ている at the end of a sentence describes a state.

this.tr: I fell asleep with my glasses on.

that.tr: He's wearing glasses.

items.explain: Check whether another action follows: doing something else in that state (寝てしまった), often implying “it shouldn't have been like that” → たまま; the state itself is the point and the sentence ends there → ている. In English, both can use “with … on / wearing”.

groups.note: All pair with a negative to say something “doesn't happen much”

items.diff: めったに is only about frequency, and very low — close to “once in a blue moon”; あまり can describe frequency or degree, and the frequency isn't as low.

this.tr: I rarely go to the movie theater.

that.tr: I don't go to the movie theater very often.

items.explain: For frequency both work, with めったに being rarer (once or twice a year). For the degree of an adjective (甘くない、高くない) only あまり works: 「このりんごはあまり甘くない」 — you can't swap in めったに here.

items.diff: めったに〜ない means “rarely”, still happening occasionally; 全然〜ない means “not at all, never”.

this.tr: My older brother rarely drinks. He only has a little at New Year's.

that.tr: My younger brother doesn't drink at all.

items.explain: Check for “occasional exceptions”: if it can be followed by “only at New Year's…” → めったに; not even once → 全然 (まったく).

items.diff: めったに〜ない is about low frequency in general; なかなか〜ない is about something expected that just won't happen.

this.tr: Buses rarely come to this village.

that.tr: I've been waiting twenty minutes already, and the bus still isn't coming.

items.explain: Check whether it's about “usual frequency” or “waiting right now”: two buses a day, once a month → めったに; you're waiting and your expectation keeps failing (待っているのに) → なかなか, with a sense of impatience.

groups.note: Both come from 「見える」 — originally “to naturally come into view”

items.diff: noun + が見える means “can be seen”; adjective く／noun に + 見える means “looks…”.

this.tr: You can see the sea from the window.

that.tr: This room has big windows, so it looks spacious.
He always looks full of energy.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「見える」: 「noun + が」 → that thing comes into view (can be seen); the く-form of an adjective or 「noun / na-adjective + に」 → the impression given (looks). 聞こえる is the same: 「声が聞こえる」 is “can hear a voice”, 「変に聞こえる」 is “sounds strange”.

items.diff: が見える means actually seeing with your eyes; とみえる infers “it seems…” from visible signs.

this.tr: It's the middle of the night, but I can still see the light in the next room.

that.tr: The light is still on in the next room. It seems he's still up.

items.explain: が見える is about the thing you see right in front of you (明かり); とみえる follows a complete clause (まだ起きている) and is a conclusion drawn from visible signs — it's rather written, and in speech people mostly say 「〜みたいだ」.

groups.note: Both mean “can be seen”

items.diff: 見える is scenery naturally coming into view; が見られる is being able to see something given the conditions or a chance, and in writing it also means “(a phenomenon) is observed”.

this.tr: On clear days you can see Mt. Fuji from here.

that.tr: You can watch old movies at this theater.
A population decline can be seen in this region.

items.explain: Look at what is “seen”: scenery that naturally comes into view, like mountains, the sea or stars → 見える; things you need an opportunity or a particular place to see, like movies or exhibitions → が見られる; abstract phenomena like 「減少」「変化」「傾向」, in a report or news tone → also が見られる. 聞こえる／聞ける work the same: 「波の音が聞こえる」 is “can hear the waves”, 「ここで昔の歌が聞ける」 is “you get to hear old songs here”.

groups.note: Both come from the explanatory 「んです（のです）」 — first laying out the situation

items.diff: んですが first states the situation, then makes a request or asks a question; んです only explains the situation, and the sentence ends there.

this.tr: Excuse me, I'm lost — where's the station?

that.tr: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped.

items.explain: Check whether something follows: after 「んですが、」 comes a request or question (駅はどこですか、〜てもいいですか) → it's a lead-in; the sentence ends at 「んです。」, explaining a reason → んです.

groups.note: the けど in 「んですけど」 ↔ the contrastive けど — written exactly the same

items.title: 〜けど（contrast）
items.diff: The けど in 「んですけど」 doesn't express contrast; it just leads into the request that follows; ordinary けど means “although…, but”.

this.tr: Excuse me, I'd like to borrow this book — is that OK?

that.tr: This book is interesting, but a bit difficult.

items.explain: Check whether what's before and after けど are “opposites”: 面白い↔難しい, one positive and one negative → contrast; your own situation before it (借りたい) and a request or question after it, or nothing at all → just a lead-in; don't translate it as “but”. When 「んです」 comes before it, it's almost always a lead-in.

groups.note: 〜ない？ ↔ 〜ない。 — written the same, differing only in the question mark and intonation

items.title: 〜ない（negative）
items.diff: 「〜ない？」 with rising intonation is an invitation; 「〜ない。」 said flat is a negation.

this.tr: Want to see a movie together tomorrow?

that.tr: I'm not watching a movie tomorrow. I'm studying at home.

items.explain: In writing they differ only by a question mark; spoken, only by intonation. Look for 「一緒に」「ねえ」 and the question mark: inviting someone → 〜ない？ (rising); saying you won't do it → 〜ない。 (falling). Watch the question marks especially carefully when reading chat messages.

groups.note: All can be used to invite someone to do something together

items.diff: 〜ない？ is plain style, used among friends and family; ませんか is polite style, used with superiors and people you don't know well.

this.tr: Hey, want to have lunch together?

that.tr: Professor, would you like to have lunch with us?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: friends or family (ねえ、〜くん) → rising 「〜ない？」; elders or superiors like 「先生」「部長」 → ませんか. Both use a negative question to invite.

items.diff: 「行かない？」 first asks whether the other person wants to, which is softer; 「行こう」 is a direct call, assuming they'll agree.

this.tr: Hey, want to go to the beach this weekend?

that.tr: All right, let's go to the beach this weekend!

items.explain: Check whether it's already been agreed: you don't know yet if they want to go, so you sound them out → 〜ない？; they'll surely want to, or it's already settled, and you decide decisively (よし、じゃあ) → 〜(よ)う. When asked 「行かない？」, people often answer 「うん、行こう！」.

groups.note: Both are 「〜ない…はない」 double negatives that look very similar

items.diff: ない人はいない means “there's nobody who doesn't…” ＝ everyone; ないことはない means “it's not that I can't…”, leaving some leeway.

this.tr: There's no one who doesn't know this song.

that.tr: This song… well, it's not that I can't sing it, but…

items.explain: Look at what's sandwiched between the two negatives: a noun like 「人」「日」「もの」 → it denies that “there are exceptions”, concluding “all of them…”, with a strong tone; 「こと」 → it denies “being unable”, concluding “it's not impossible”, often followed by 「けど」, with a reluctant tone.

groups.note: Both mean “all, without exception”

items.title: 疑問詞＋でも（no matter who/what…）
items.diff: 誰でも says it positively, “everyone…”; 〜ない人はいない uses a double negative to stress “not a single exception”.

this.tr: There's no one who doesn't know this song.

that.tr: Everyone knows this song.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; look at the phrasing: 「誰でも／何でも + affirmative」 states “all” directly; 「〜ない + 人／もの + はいない／はない」 takes a detour, using a double negative to stress “you can't find a single exception” — stronger, with an exclamatory flavor.

groups.note: Both come from 「おく（置く）」 — leaving something, taking care of it for later

items.diff: ないでおく means deliberately not doing something for now, for later's sake; ておく means doing something in advance for later.

this.tr: I'll drink it later, so I'll leave the beer unopened.

that.tr: I'll drink it later, so I'll chill the beer now.

items.explain: Both sentences give the same reason (後で飲むから) and are both thinking ahead. Look at what comes before 「おく」: nai-form + で → deliberately not doing it yet, leaving things as they are; te-form → doing it in advance.

groups.note: Both can express leaving things as they are

items.diff: ないでおく is deliberately not doing something; たまま only says a state stayed as it was, often by accident.

this.tr: It wasn't cold, so I left the window open.

that.tr: I carelessly went out with the window open.

items.explain: Check whether it was on purpose: a reason, a conscious choice not to do it (寒くないので) → ないでおく; 「うっかり」「〜てしまった」, left that way without noticing → たまま. Also, ないでおく focuses on “which action you don't do” (閉めない), while たまま focuses on “which state is kept” (開けた).

groups.note: All pair with a negative to say something “doesn't happen much, or just won't happen”

items.diff: なかなか〜ない means “just won't…”, with the impatience of waiting; まだ〜ていない just objectively says “not yet”.

this.tr: I've been waiting thirty minutes, and the bus still isn't coming.

that.tr: The bus hasn't come yet.

items.explain: Check for the feeling of “impatient waiting”: you've waited a long time and keep being let down (30分も待っているのに) → なかなか来ない; just reporting the current situation → まだ来ていない. Also, なかなか is followed by a plain 「ない」, not 「ていない」.

items.diff: なかなか〜ない is about something expected that just won't happen; めったに〜ない is about low frequency in general.

this.tr: I've been waiting twenty minutes already, and the bus still isn't coming.

that.tr: Buses rarely come to this village.

items.explain: Check whether it's about “waiting right now” or “usual frequency”: you're waiting and your expectation keeps failing (待っているのに) → なかなか; two buses a day, once a month → めったに.

items.diff: なかなか〜ない is usually something objectively hard to achieve; ようとしない means the subject “refuses to”, the cause being their will.

this.tr: The child is so excited he just can't fall asleep.

that.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, the child won't go to sleep.

items.explain: Look at where the cause lies: something the person can't control, like excitement or illness → なかなか寝ない (can't fall asleep); they won't listen and simply don't want to → 寝ようとしない (refuses to sleep). ようとしない is mostly used about others, with displeasure.

groups.note: Both come from 「なければ／なくては」 — “if (I) don't… (it won't do)”

items.diff: なきゃ／なくちゃ are spoken contractions whose second half is often dropped, used only with people you know well; なければならない is complete and formal.

this.tr: Oh, it's already eight. I've gotta go.

that.tr: Students must attend class.

items.explain: なきゃ＝なければ, なくちゃ＝なくては, and the following 「ならない／いけない」 is often dropped. It depends on the setting: talking to yourself or with friends and family → なきゃ・なくちゃ (the two are the same); rules, writing, formal settings → なければならない.

groups.note: なくて ↔ ないで — both are 「ない」 joined to the te-form, just a kana or two apart

items.diff: なくて expresses a reason, “because… didn't…, so…”; ないで means “without…, (did something else instead)”.

this.tr: The bus just wouldn't come, and I was stuck.

that.tr: I didn't take the bus — I walked.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a result or feeling caused by the “not…” (困った、遅れた) → なくて; another action you then did yourself (歩いて行った) → ないで.

groups.note: Both express a reason, “because…”

items.diff: After なくて only a natural result or a feeling can follow; after ないので you can also put a request or an intention.

this.tr: I didn't have time, so I didn't make it.

that.tr: We're short on time, so please hurry.

wrong.why: なくて can't be followed by a request or a command

items.explain: Look at the second half: a request, invitation or intention such as 「〜てください」 or 「〜ましょう」 → use ないので (or ないから); a result or feeling you can't control (間に合わなかった、困った、残念だ) → なくて sounds natural.

groups.note: All express a hypothetical condition, “if…”

items.diff: なら only assumes you “plan to do it”, so the second part can happen first; たら requires the first part to happen first.

this.tr: If you're going to Hokkaido, you'd better buy a coat in Tokyo.

that.tr: Once you get to Hokkaido, you can just buy a coat there.

items.explain: Look at where the second half happens: with なら it happens before going (東京で), and the first part is only a “plan”; with たら it happens after going (向こうで), so the first part has to happen first.

items.diff: なら takes what the other person just said as a premise and responds to it; ば sets up a condition of your own — “if this is met, then…”.

this.tr: If it's that cheap, maybe I'll buy one too.

that.tr: If it were a little cheaper, I'd buy it.

items.explain: Both mean “if…”, so look at where the first half comes from: 「そんなに」 points to what the other person just said, and the speaker takes it as a premise to respond to → なら; you put forward a condition of your own that isn't met yet (もう少し安ければ) and say “if it were met, I would…” → ば, which stresses that the first half is a necessary condition for the second.

groups.note: Both come from 「なさる」 — the honorific of 「する」

items.title: なさる
items.diff: なさる is honorific, “(you) do”; yet its imperative なさい has turned into a command from a superior to someone below.

this.tr: Hurry up and do your homework!

that.tr: Professor, what will you be doing this weekend?

items.explain: 「なさい」 was originally the imperative of the honorific 「なさる」 and carried some politeness; with long use the respect faded and it became a command from parents or teachers to children. Look at the sentence: asking the other person 「なさいますか」 → honorific; attached to a verb's masu-stem to tell someone to do something, 「〜しなさい」 → command.

groups.note: All tell someone to do something, at different levels of politeness

items.diff: なさい is a command from an elder to a younger person — gentle and well-mannered; the imperative form is rough and forceful.

this.tr: It's already seven. Get up now.

that.tr: Hey, get up!

items.explain: Look at the speaker and the particles: a mother to her child or a teacher to students, often with 「〜よ」 → なさい; a man to someone younger, in a quarrel, or in an emergency (おい) → the imperative form (起きろ、書け、来い).

items.diff: なさい is a command from above to below; てください is a polite request.

this.tr: It's already ten. Go to bed!

that.tr: It's late, so please get some rest early.

items.explain: Look at the relationship between the speakers: parent to child, teacher to student → なさい, which can't be used to equals or superiors; a polite request to people in general → てください.

items.diff: お〜なさい is said by an elder to a younger person; お〜ください is a respectful request to customers or superiors.

this.tr: Come on, sit over here.

that.tr: Please have a seat over here, sir.

items.explain: Look at who is being addressed: a clerk to a customer, or someone to a superior → お〜ください; a grandmother to her grandchild, or a teacher to students → お〜なさい. Only 「なさい」 and 「ください」 differ, yet the direction of politeness is completely different.

groups.note: Both come from the appearance 「そう」 — “how something looks”

items.diff: Both are appearance そう plus a negative: なさそう is the look of “not…” = seems not…; そうもない means there isn't even a sign of “about to…” = doesn't look like it will….

this.tr: Looking at the questions, the test doesn't seem difficult.

that.tr: The sky is pitch dark. The rain doesn't look like it'll stop.

items.explain: Both sides are appearance 「そう」 (how something looks) plus a negative; only the position of the negative differs. なさそう negates first and then adds そう — the look of 「難しくない」 → “doesn't look difficult”, describing a quality. そうもない adds そう first and then negates — there isn't even the look of “about to stop” (やみそう) → “doesn't look like it will stop”, judging whether something will happen. So look at what comes before そう: the negative of an adjective or noun (難しくない、学生じゃない) → なさそう; a verb's masu-stem (やみ) → そうもない.

groups.note: なさそう ↔ ないそう — just one kana apart, 「さ」 vs 「い」

items.title: 〜そうだ（hearsay）
items.diff: When 「ない」 attaches to the “looks like” そう, it becomes なさそう; saying ないそう directly turns it into “I hear there isn't”.

this.tag: なさそう · looks like there isn't
this.tr: The manager has been on the phone since this morning. He doesn't seem to have time.

that.tag: ないそう · I hear there isn't
that.tr: According to the manager, he doesn't have time today.

items.explain: Look at whether そう is preceded by 「なさ」 or 「ない」: なさそうだ → a judgment from what you see, “looks like there isn't”, often preceded by what you observed (部長は朝からずっと電話している); ないそうだ → passing on something you heard, “I hear there isn't”, often together with 「〜の話では」 or 「〜によると」.

groups.note: Both come from 「気」 — “mind, feeling”

items.diff: に気がつく means you actually “noticed” a fact; ような気がする is only “I have a feeling that…” and isn't certain.

this.tr: After I left the shop, I realized I'd forgotten my umbrella.

that.tr: Somehow I have a feeling I left my umbrella somewhere.

items.explain: Look at how sure the speaker is: 「なんだか」 or 「どうも」 + ような気がする → just a feeling, which may be wrong; 〜ことに気がついた → the fact has been confirmed (the umbrella really was left behind). Both are built on 「気」 (mind): 気がつく is the mind “attaching” to something = noticing; 気がする is “having a certain feeling” in your mind.

groups.note: Both express purpose, “in order to…”

items.diff: には says “to achieve…, you need to…”, followed by a required condition; ために says “do… in order to…”, followed by an action you take yourself.

this.tr: To buy a house, you have to save money.

that.tr: I'm saving money every month to buy a house.

wrong.why: には must be followed by a condition needed to reach the goal (必要だ、なければならない), not by a concrete action in progress

items.explain: When the second half is a condition needed to reach the goal, such as 「必要だ」 or 「なければならない」, both work: には talks about the condition, “to… you have to…”, while ために talks about the purpose, “in order to…”. When the second half is a concrete action you are doing or have done (貯めている), only ために works.

items.title: 〜のに（it takes… to）
items.diff: Both work when saying how much time or money something takes; のに is basically followed only by 「かかる・必要だ・使う」, while には can also take requirements like 「なければならない」.

this.tr: To pass the N2, you have to study every day.

that.tr: It took me a year to pass the N2.

wrong.why: のに followed by 「しなければならない」 is heard as “even though…, still…”; to state a requirement that has to be met, use には

items.explain: When the second half is 「かかる」 or 「必要だ」, both work (合格するには一年かかる／合格するのに一年かかった), with のに sounding more like an objective statement of how much time or money it took; when the second half is a requirement like 「しなければならない」, only には works, because 「〜のに、〜しなければならない」 would be heard as “even though…, still…”.

groups.note: Both mean “for (someone)”

items.diff: Both can mean “for…”: には mostly comes with direct judgments measured against someone, like how hard or big something is; にとって mostly talks about value or meaning to someone.

this.tr: This book is too difficult for elementary school kids.

that.tr: This book is an important one for elementary school kids.

items.explain: Look at the second half: whether something is hard, big or possible (難しすぎる、無理だ) → には is more natural, though にとって also works; what value or meaning something has for someone (大切な、ありがたい、問題だ) → にとって is more natural, and には sounds awkward.

groups.note: Both come from 「よる（拠る・因る）」 — “based on, by means of”

items.title: 〜によって（cause · means）
items.diff: によると gives the source of information, with 「そうだ」 at the end; によって gives a cause or means, and the sentence ends directly with the result.

this.tr: According to the news, the trains have stopped because of the typhoon.

that.tr: Many houses were destroyed by the typhoon.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: if it has 「そうだ」, 「らしい」 or 「ということだ」 and what comes before is the news, a weather forecast or a person → によると (によれば works the same), meaning “according to…”; if the end states directly what happened and what comes before is a cause or means → によって. Both come from 「よる」 (to be based on): based on information → “reportedly”; based on a cause → “due to”.

groups.note: Both mean “according to…”

items.diff: によると relays data or what others said, often ending with 「そうだ」; 限りでは is the speaker's own judgment within that scope, implying it may not hold beyond it.

this.tr: According to this survey, the number of users is increasing.

that.tag: Own judgment · as far as this goes
that.tr: As far as this survey shows, the number of users is increasing.

items.explain: Both sentences are “according to this survey”, so look at the speaker's stance and the sentence ending: によると relays what the data says, often ending with 「そうだ」 or 「らしい」, without drawing a conclusion of one's own; 限りでは is the speaker's own judgment based on the data, while leaving room — “only within this scope; I can't speak for anything else” — and the sentence doesn't take 「そうだ」.

groups.note: Both mean “hard to…”

items.diff: Both can mean “… is hard going”: にくい objectively says the thing itself is hard to deal with; づらい focuses on the speaker's own physical or emotional burden and is more colloquial.

this.tr: This road has lots of stones, so it's hard to walk on.

that.tr: I hurt my foot, so walking is a struggle.

items.explain: Look at where the cause lies: the road, the handwriting or the tool itself is hard to use (石が多くて) → にくい, an objective description; a burden from your own body or feelings (足をけがして) → づらい fits better and sounds more colloquial. The two sentences could also swap; only the nuance changes.

items.diff: With mental acceptance such as 「信じる」 or 「理解する」, both work: にくい is colloquial and lighter; がたい is written and heavier.

this.tr: That story is a bit hard to believe.

that.tr: That story is utterly impossible to believe.

items.explain: The same verb 「信じる」 takes both, so look at the tone and the setting: in conversation, “a bit hard to believe”, often with 「ちょっと」 → にくい; in writing or formal speech, “hard to… no matter what”, often with 「到底」 → がたい (信じがたい、許しがたい、理解しがたい).

groups.note: Both come from 「だろう」 — originally the guess “probably…”

items.diff: のだろうか is asking oneself, a doubt; のではないだろうか is a roundabout way of saying “I think…”.

this.tr: Is it really OK to carry on like this?

that.tag: Indirect claim · I think it's fine
that.tr: Wouldn't it be fine to carry on like this?

items.explain: Both come from the guessing 「だろう」 (probably…). のだろうか adds 「か」 to the guess, putting a question mark on “is it so?” → asking oneself; add 「本当に」 and it becomes doubt, implying “probably not OK”. のではないだろうか first guesses “it isn't so” and then puts a question mark on that negative → “isn't it so?” → circling back to give your own view indirectly, “I think it is”. So check for 「ではない」: present → leans toward “it's OK”; absent, with 「本当に」 → leans toward “it's not OK”.

groups.note: Both ask oneself “I wonder…?”

items.diff: かな is casual talking to oneself in speech; のだろうか is more formal and serious, and mostly appears in writing.

this.tr: Why do people work?

that.tr: I wonder if it'll be sunny for tomorrow's school outing.

items.explain: Look at the style: chatting with friends or talking to yourself in short, casual sentences → かな (women also often say かしら); seriously pondering a question in writing or a speech, often with 「なぜ」 or 「本当に」 → のだろうか.

items.title: 〜だろうか（asking oneself）
items.diff: Both can be used to ask oneself; のだろうか usually comes when you see a situation and want to know what's behind it; だろうか simply wonders how something will turn out.

this.tag: Seeing a situation · wanting the reason
this.tr: The lights are off. Has he already gone to bed?

that.tr: I wonder if we can win tomorrow's game.

items.explain: Both ask oneself “I wonder…?”, so check whether there's a situation in front of you as grounds: seeing something like 「電気が消えている」 and wanting to work out what's going on → のだろうか, where 「の」 carries the sense of “explaining a situation”; with no concrete grounds, just wondering how 「明日の試合」 will go → だろうか is enough. The latter can also take のだろうか; it just adds a layer of “what's really going on”.

groups.note: Both emphasize “it is precisely…”

items.diff: Both can mean “it's precisely…”: のは〜だ puts the answer at the end, like a calm explanation; こそ attaches directly to the emphasized word, with a strong “this and nothing else” tone.

this.tr: What I've been looking for all along is this book.

that.tr: This is exactly the book I've been looking for!

items.explain: Both sentences say “this is the very book I've been looking for”, so look at the tone: のは〜だ puts the known part (ずっと探していた) first and the answer at the end, before 「〜だ」, like a calm account; こそ keeps the word order and attaches straight after the emphasized word, adding exclusiveness and excitement — “this and nothing else”. Calm explanation → のは〜だ; emotional assertion → こそ (今度こそ、健康こそ).

groups.note: のに ↔ ので — just one kana apart

items.diff: のに means “even though…”, the result goes against expectations; ので means “because… so”, the result follows naturally.

this.tr: Even though it was raining, my little brother went out.

that.tr: Because it was raining, my little brother didn't go out.

items.explain: They differ only in に vs. で, and the first half is identical (雨なのに / 雨なので), so look at how the second half relates to the first: a result that defies common sense (going out in the rain, 出かけた) → のに; a result that follows naturally (not going out because of the rain, 出かけなかった) → ので. Don't miss this single kana when reading.

groups.note: Both mean “in order to do…”

items.title: 〜には (what it takes / costs)
items.diff: Both can say how much it takes to do something; のに is mostly followed by a cost or a need, while には means “to achieve…” and can also be followed by a condition that must be met.

this.tr: Getting my driver's license cost 300,000 yen.

that.tr: To get a driver's license, you have to take lessons at a driving school.

items.explain: Both 「免許を取るのに30万円かかる」 and 「免許を取るには30万円かかる」 are fine. The difference is in the second half: if you just state how much money or time it took (かかった) → のに sounds natural; if you state a condition or advice, “to achieve it, you have to…” (通わなければならない, 〜たほうがいい) → use には. のに is usually not followed by such requirements or advice; if it is, it can easily be heard as “even though…”.

items.title: 〜ために (purpose)
items.diff: Both work for saying what something takes, and のに is more common there; when what follows is an action you take yourself for that purpose, only ために works.

this.tr: Getting a visa required a lot of documents.

that.tr: I went to the embassy to get a visa.

items.explain: Look at the second half: if it says what is needed or how much it takes (必要だった, かかる) → use のに; you could also say 「ビザを取るために書類が必要だった」, but のに is more common. If the second half is something you did yourself for that purpose (行った) → only ために works; のに is not followed by your own action.

groups.note: Both express a contrast: “although…, still…”

items.diff: のに carries surprise and dissatisfaction and can't be followed by intentions or invitations; けど is a neutral “but” and can.

this.tr: Even though it was so expensive, it broke right away.

that.tr: It's a bit pricey, but let's buy it.

wrong.why: のに can't be followed by an intention or invitation like 「〜よう」

items.explain: Look at the second half: a result contrary to expectations, with dissatisfaction or regret (すぐ壊れた) → のに; the speaker's own plan, invitation or request (買おう, 〜てください) → only けど works.

items.diff: のに can express your own regret and works for both people and things; くせに is only used to criticize others, and sounds harsher.

this.tr: I practiced every single day, and still I lost the match.

that.tr: He didn't even come to practice, and yet all he does is complain.

items.explain: Look at who it's about and the feeling: you yourself (私は) tried hard but it didn't pay off, and you simply feel regret → のに; criticizing or looking down on someone else (彼は), “he didn't even come to practice, and yet…” → くせに, and both halves must be about the same person. のに can also be used about others, but it isn't as blunt as くせに; don't use くせに about people above you.

items.diff: のに is spoken and carries personal dissatisfaction or surprise; にもかかわらず is written and objectively says “despite…”.

this.tr: Even though it was raining, lots of people came.

that.tr: Despite the rain today, a great many people have joined us.

items.explain: Look at the setting: talking among friends, with feelings of happiness or dissatisfaction → のに; formal settings like speeches, news or reports (本日, お越しいただきました) → にもかかわらず. With nouns, のに needs 「な」 (雨なのに), while にもかかわらず attaches directly (雨にもかかわらず).

items.title: 〜ながら (even though one knows…)
items.diff: のに is conversational, carries dissatisfaction, and its two halves can be about different people; ながら is more formal, and both halves must be about the same person.

this.tr: I asked him again and again, but he didn't help me.

that.tr: He knew the answer, yet he didn't tell me.

wrong.why: ながら in the sense of “even though” must have the same person in both halves

items.explain: Check whether both halves are about the same person: 「私が頼んだ」 and 「彼は手伝ってくれなかった」 involve two different people → only のに works; when one person does something despite knowing better (彼は知っていながら) → ながら also works and sounds more formal than のに. のに is more conversational and voices dissatisfaction more directly.

groups.note: Both come from 「くださる」, which originally means “(someone of higher status) gives to me”

items.diff: お〜ください is the respectful form used with customers and is more deferential; てください is an ordinary request.

this.tr: I'm sorry, but please wait a moment.

that.tr: Please wait a sec.

items.explain: The 「ください」 in both is the imperative form of くださる. くださる originally means “(someone of higher status) gives to me”; placed after an action, it becomes “do it for me”: て-form + ください = “please do it for me” → an ordinary request (待ってください); お + ます-stem (お待ち) first turns the action into a respectful expression, and adding ください then means “would you kindly do it” → a more polite request to customers. Look at the form and the setting: お + ます-stem + ください often appears together with 「少々」 and 「恐れ入りますが」 in shops and announcements; between friends or coworkers, 「待ってください」 is enough.

groups.note: Both politely ask the other person to do something

items.diff: お〜ください is a polite instruction that the listener simply follows; ていただけませんか is a request in question form that leaves the decision to them, so it's softer.

this.tr: Please write your name at the reception desk.

that.tr: Excuse me, but could you look over this document by tomorrow?

items.explain: Look at whether the listener has a choice: staff or announcements telling customers what to do (お書きください, お待ちください) → お〜ください; asking a boss or client to do something extra for you → use the question form ていただけませんか, which lets them say no and is therefore more polite.

items.title: お〜願います (kindly…)
items.diff: Same meaning; お〜ください is the ordinary respectful request and sounds natural face to face; お〜願います is more formal and stiffer, and is mostly seen on notices and in announcements.

this.tag: Said to customers face to face
this.tr: Please line up in a single row here.

that.tr: Kindly form a single line here.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same thing — asking customers to line up — and differ only at the end. A clerk speaking directly to customers → お並びください, polite and gentle; a posted notice, a recorded announcement, or a rule announced to many people → お並び願います, more formal and closer to laying down a rule. When in doubt, お〜ください is always safe.

groups.note: お〜になる ↔ お〜する — differing only in 「になる／する」

items.diff: お〜になる is respectful language for the other person's action; お〜する is humble language for what you do for them.

this.tr: Sensei, did you bring an umbrella?

that.tr: Let me carry your umbrella for you.

wrong.why: お〜になる is respectful language that elevates the other person, so it can't be used for your own action; say 「お持ちします」

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in になる／する after お持ち, yet the honorific points in exactly opposite directions. Look at who does the action: the other person, such as a teacher or a customer (先生は) → お〜になる, elevating them; I or my side (私が) → お〜する, humbling yourself. Mixing them up is rude: saying お持ちになります about your own action amounts to elevating yourself. ご〜になる／ご〜する work the same way.

groups.note: Both are respectful language, elevating the other person's action

items.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
items.diff: お〜になる is highly respectful and can't be misread; れる・られる is slightly less respectful and easily confused with the passive or potential.

this.tr: The president is reading the newspaper.

that.tr: The president is reading the newspaper.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same. By form alone, 読まれる could also be the passive “be read”, so you have to judge from the subject that it's respectful; when speaking directly to clients or superiors, お〜になる is clearer and more polite, while news and in-house communication often use れる・られる.

items.title: 〜お〜です (in progress / state)
items.diff: Same meaning; お〜です is a short form of お〜になっている and is very common in reception settings.

this.tr: The company president is waiting in the reception room.

that.tr: The company president is waiting in the reception room.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same: the president is waiting in the reception room right now. お〜です is a short form of お〜になっている and is used most often by receptionists and secretaries relaying things to visitors; to talk about a single completed action (お読みになりました) or to ask someone to do something (お掛けになってください), use お〜になる.

groups.note: お〜する ↔ お〜になる — differing only in 「する／になる」

items.diff: お〜する is humble language for what you do for the other person; お〜になる is respectful language for their action.

this.tr: Let me carry your umbrella for you.

that.tr: Sensei, did you bring an umbrella?

wrong.why: お〜になる is respectful language that elevates the other person, so it can't be used for your own action; say 「お持ちします」

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in する／になる after お持ち, yet the honorific points in exactly opposite directions. Look at who does the action: I or my side (私が) → お〜する, humbling yourself; the other person, such as a teacher or a customer (先生は) → お〜になる, elevating them. Mixing them up is rude: saying お持ちになります about your own action amounts to elevating yourself. ご〜する／ご〜になる work the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “(I) ask you about something”

items.title: 伺う (humble form of 聞く)
items.diff: Same meaning; 伺う is the special humble verb for 聞く and is more formal; お聞きする is a humble form built with the お〜する pattern and sounds slightly lighter.

this.tr: There's something I'd like to ask you about that matter, sensei.

that.tr: There is something I would like to ask you regarding that matter, sensei.

wrong.why: 見る can't take the お〜する pattern; use the special humble verb 「拝見します」

items.explain: Both sentences humbly ask the teacher about something and mean the same. 聞く has a special humble verb, 伺う, which shows more respect and is the usual choice in business emails and when talking to clients; お聞きする is also correct humble language, just slightly lighter. Not every verb allows both: 送る and 持つ have no special form, so you can only say お送りする; 見る and 言う can only use their special forms 拝見する and 申す, never the お〜する pattern.

groups.note: Both mean “every so often, once every…”

items.diff: おきに counts the gap left in between; ごとに means “once every…”. So 「1日おき」 equals 「2日ごとに」.

this.tr: I go to the gym every other day.

that.tr: I go to the gym once every two days.

items.explain: Look at how the number is counted: おき comes from 「置く」 (間を置く = leave a gap) and counts the days “skipped” in between, so add one to get “once every N days” (1日おき = 2日ごとに). With continuous units like 「分」 or 「メートル」, the two are the same: 「10分おき」 and 「10分ごとに」 both mean every 10 minutes.

groups.note: Both can mean doing an action “to the end, all the way”

items.title: 〜てしまう (get it done completely)
items.diff: 〜終わる objectively says an action reached its end; てしまう has the feel of “getting something done and over with”.

this.tr: It took two hours, but I finally finished my homework.

that.tr: Let's get that annoying homework out of the way first.

items.explain: Both can express “finishing”. If you're just describing an action from start to end (二時間かかって) → 終わる, with an objective tone; if you want to get something done and be through with it, often with 「面倒な」, 「先に」, 「全部」 or 「〜てしまおう」 → てしまう. てしまう also means “ended up doing… by accident”, but that's a different usage and isn't compared here.

items.title: 〜上げる (finish / complete)
