items.diff: 〜終わる only says the action ended; 〜上げる stresses putting in effort to produce a complete result, with a sense of accomplishment.

this.tr: I finished writing my thesis.

that.tr: After a whole year of work, I finally completed my thesis.

wrong.why: 食べる doesn't produce a finished product, so it can't take 上げる; say 「食べ終わったら」

items.explain: For finishing a thesis, both are fine. 書き終わった only says the act of writing came to an end; 書き上げた stresses that you put in effort (一年かけて) and finally produced a complete piece of work, with a sense of accomplishment. 上げる only attaches to actions that create something (書く, 作る, 育てる); for finishing a meal, a book, or using something up, only 終わる works.

items.diff: 〜終わる just says the action ended; 〜抜く stresses overcoming difficulty and sticking with it to the end, with a note of praise.

this.tr: After finishing the marathon, I drank some water.

that.tr: Even though my feet hurt, I ran all the way to the finish.

items.explain: Look for a “difficulty”: just stating the point in time when the running ended → 終わる; a difficulty before it like 「足が痛くても」 or 「苦しくても」, stressing that you didn't give up → 抜く.

groups.note: All use the auxiliary 「れる・られる」 — meaning “to undergo someone else's action”

items.diff: The passive is “someone did … to me”; させられる is “I was made to do … myself”.

this.tag: Someone else did it · I suffered
this.tr: My cake got eaten by my little brother.

that.tr: My mom made me eat my vegetables.

items.explain: Look at who does the eating: in the passive 食べられた, the eater is my little brother (弟に), and I'm the one who suffers; in させられた, I'm the one eating, because my mom (母に) made (forced) me. With the extra 「させ」, the doer switches from the other person to yourself. Godan verbs use れる (読まれる) the same way.

groups.note: 読まれる ↔ 読ませる — just one kana apart: れ / せ

items.diff: 読まれる is “be read”; 読ませる is “make/let (someone) read” — the direction of the action is exactly reversed.

this.tag: れる · read by someone else
this.tr: My essay was read aloud by the teacher.

that.tr: The teacher had me read my essay aloud.

items.explain: 読まれた and 読ませた differ only in れ / せ. Look at who does the action: in the passive, the teacher before 「に」 is the one reading (先生に), and I'm on the receiving end; in the causative, I, before 「に」, am the one reading (私に), because the teacher had me read. Misread this one kana and the meaning flips entirely. Ichidan verbs work the same way: 食べられる / 食べさせる.

groups.note: Both mean “can / be able to”

items.diff: The potential form is short and more common in everyday conversation; ことができる is formal and written, mostly used for rules and explanations.

this.tr: You can borrow up to five books at this library, you know.

that.tr: At this library, you may borrow up to five books.

items.explain: The meaning is the same; it mainly depends on the setting: chatting with friends (with 「よ」 at the end) → the potential form 借りられる, short and natural; notices, explanations of rules, formal occasions → ことができます, formal and written. With the potential form, the object is also often marked with 「が」 (本が借りられる), while ことができる keeps 「を」 before it. For godan verbs, the potential form looks like 読める, 書ける.

groups.note: Both elevate the other person's action

items.diff: れる・られる is slightly less respectful and easily confused with the passive or potential; お〜になる is highly respectful and can't be misread.

this.tr: The president is reading the newspaper.

that.tr: The president is reading the newspaper.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same. On its own, 読まれる could also be the passive “be read”, so you rely on the subject (社長は) to tell that it's respectful; news and in-company talk often use れる・られる (出席される, 来られる), while お〜になる is clearer and more polite when speaking directly to clients or superiors.

items.diff: 言われる and 来られる are respectful too, but only mildly, and are easily confused with the passive; for verbs with a special respectful form, おっしゃる and いらっしゃる are more appropriate.

this.tr: That's what the president said.

that.tr: That's what the president said.

items.explain: 「言われました」 can be respectful (the president said it) or passive (someone was told something), so look at whether the particle before it is 「が」 or 「に」 (社長が); おっしゃる has only one meaning and also shows more respect. 来られる → いらっしゃる and 食べられる → 召し上がる work the same way. When speaking to clients or superiors, prefer the special forms.

groups.note: “Noun + でも” is written exactly the same: “even if it's” ↔ “… or something”

items.title: 〜でも (soft invitation / suggestion)
items.diff: Concessive でも is followed by “… anyway”; example-giving でも is followed by an invitation or suggestion.

this.tr: Even if it rains, the game will still go ahead.

that.tr: If you're free, how about some tea or something?

items.explain: Both sentences are “noun + でも” and look exactly the same, so look at the second half: if it's something that happens anyway, unaffected (試合はあります) → concessive “even if it's…, still”; if it's an invitation or suggestion such as 「〜ませんか」 or 「〜ましょう」 (飲みませんか) → a casual example, “… or something”, which softens the tone.

groups.note: Both mean “even if…, still”

items.diff: Same meaning; たって / だって are more casual spoken versions of ても / でも.

this.tr: Even if you run now, you won't make it.
I'll go even if it rains.

that.tr: Even if you run now, you're not gonna make it.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; look at the style: casual talk with friends or family → たって (nouns and na-adjectives use だって: 雨だって); writing, or speaking to superiors → ても / でも. たって is only used in speech.

items.title: 〜とも (adjective + とも)
items.diff: Same meaning; ても is the ordinary form, used in both speech and writing; とも is a written form with a classical flavor, mostly used in speeches and texts.

this.tr: No matter how hard it gets, I'll run to the very end.

that.tr: However painful it may be, I shall run to the end.

wrong.why: とも doesn't attach to a verb's て-form; say 「降っても」 or the written 「降ろうとも」

items.explain: The meaning is the same; look at the register: everyday speech (with 「よ」 at the end) → 苦しくても; speeches, written texts, declarations of resolve and other formal settings → 苦しくとも, with a classical flavor. とも only attaches to the 「く」 form of adjectives and to the volitional form (言おうとも); after a verb's て-form you can't swap in とも.

groups.note: Both make people plural (“we”, “they”)

items.diff: ら on personal pronouns (僕ら, 俺ら) is casual and not used toward people above you; たち is neutral and can be used with anyone.

this.tr: Let's go home together tomorrow too.

that.tr: Sensei, may we go home with you too?

items.explain: Both mean “we”; look at who you're talking to: casually between friends → 僕ら, 俺ら, which are more casual; to a teacher or someone above you (先生, …いいですか) → use 僕たち or 私たち. たち is neutral and works in any setting, so when in doubt, use たち.

groups.note: Both express a guess: “it seems…”

items.diff: らしい is mostly based on information you heard or got indirectly; そうだ (appearance) is how something looks to your own eyes.

this.tr: According to my friend, the cakes at that shop are apparently delicious.

that.tr: This cake looks delicious.

items.explain: Look at where the information comes from: you only heard it from someone else (友達の話では) and haven't tried it yourself → おいしいらしい; the cake is right in front of you → おいしそう. Also note how they attach: らしい attaches to the plain form (おいしい + らしい), while そうだ attaches to the stem (おいし + そう).

items.diff: らしい is mostly based on news you heard, with an “apparently / I hear” flavor; ようだ is a judgment based on clues you perceive yourself.

this.tr: Rumor has it those two are getting married.

that.tr: There are sounds from the next room. Someone seems to be there.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment is based on: indirect information such as rumors (うわさでは) or what others said → らしい, which makes the speaker sound detached, as if not taking responsibility; direct clues you heard or saw yourself (音がする) → ようだ／みたいだ.

groups.note: Both mean “like…”

items.diff: らしい is “just as a … should be”, usually positive; っぽい is “kind of like…”, usually negative or casual.

this.tr: My five-year-old brother is lively — a real kid.

that.tr: He's already a college student, but my big brother still thinks like a child.

items.explain: Check whether the person actually is what the noun says: a five-year-old brother (５歳の弟は) is a child to begin with and is just as a child should be → 子どもらしい (innocent and sweet, positive); a university student is no longer a child (もう大学生なのに) yet acts like one → 子どもっぽい (childish, negative). 「春らしい」 and 「男らしい」 likewise mean “just as … should be”.

groups.note: Both mean “the quality of …” and turn an adjective into a noun

items.diff: さ talks about degree, “how sweet”, which can be compared and adjusted; み talks about the taste or sensation itself that you actually perceive.

this.tr: This cake is just the right sweetness.

that.tr: This cake has the sweetness of fruit.

items.explain: Both sentences are about the cake’s sweetness. Look at what follows: if it judges how sweet it is, with degree words like 「ちょうどいい」「控えめ」「足りない」 → 甘さ; if it describes the taste itself that comes through, with 「〜がある」「〜が広がる」 → 甘み. Almost every adjective can take さ, but only a few words such as 甘い、苦い、重い、深い can take み.

groups.note: Both mean “I heard that …”

items.diff: ってさ casually passes on something you heard, with a slightly offhand “that’s what they say” feel; んだって is the ordinary spoken way to report hearsay, neutral in tone.

this.tag: ってさ · casually passing it on
this.tr: I heard tomorrow’s game is canceled.

that.tr: I heard tomorrow’s game is canceled.

wrong.why: A noun before んだって needs 「な」: 中止なんだって

items.explain: Both sentences pass on news you heard. First, the connection: ってさ attaches directly to a plain-form sentence (中止だってさ); んだって needs 「ん」 before it, and nouns and な-adjectives take 「な」 (中止なんだって). Then the tone: ってさ is more casual, as if you are just passing along what someone said; んだって is the ordinary way to say it, and for a slightly politer version you can say 「んですって」.

groups.note: Both come from the causative 「させる」 — meaning “make/let … do”

items.title: 〜せる・〜させる (make/let others do)
items.diff: させる means having someone else do something; add 「ください／もらう／いただく」 after it, and the person who gets “let” do it becomes yourself.

this.tag: せてください · please let me
this.tr: Please let me do that job.

this.tag: せてもらう · was allowed to
this.tr: I had a fever, so I was allowed to take the day off work.

this.tag: せていただく · humbly doing
this.tr: Well then, allow me to explain.

that.tr: My mother made my little brother clean the room.

items.explain: Look at what follows the causative: the causative alone (掃除させた) → having someone else do it, and the doer is the little brother before 「に」; causative + ください／もらう／いただく → the doer is the speaker: a request “let me do it”, having been allowed “I was let do it”, or a formal announcement “allow me to do it”.

groups.note: Both ask for permission to do something yourself

items.diff: させてください carries an eager “please let me do it”; てもいいですか just asks whether it is OK and leaves the decision to the other person.

this.tr: That role, please let me play it.

that.tr: That role, may I play it?

items.explain: Both sentences ask for permission; look at the tone: 「ぜひ」 + させてください actively pushes for it, meaning “I really want to do it”, and is also often used to ask for time off (休ませてください); てもいいですか just checks whether it is OK, and if the answer is no, that’s that. Note the doer: the causative sentence uses 「私に」, while てもいい uses 「私が」.

groups.note: Both mean “… and also …”, listing several things in the same direction

items.title: 〜くて (linking い-adjectives)
items.diff: し sets out the good points one by one, as if “counting the merits”, and hints there are more; くて／で links two qualities into one smooth description.

this.tag: し · setting out point by point
this.tr: This shop is cheap, and the food is good too.

that.tr: This shop is cheap and the food is good.

wrong.why: A な-adjective needs 「だ」 before し: 静かだし

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; the difference is in feel and connection. Feel: し presents each feature as a separate point, sounding like you are listing merits, and often pairs with 「も」; くて simply links two qualities in a flowing description. Connection: し attaches to the plain form (安いし、静かだし), with nouns and な-adjectives taking 「だ」; くて is a form of い-adjectives, while な-adjectives and nouns use 「で」 (静かで).

items.diff: し follows the plain form and lists the next feature within the same sentence; それに goes at the start of a sentence and adds one more after the previous sentence has ended. The two are often combined: 「〜し、それに〜」.

this.tr: This room is spacious and close to the station, too.

that.tr: This room is spacious. And it’s close to the station, too.

items.explain: Look at the position: attached to a plain form while the sentence continues → し; the previous sentence already ended with 「。」 and a new sentence starts by adding one more point → それに. The two are also often used together: 「広いし、それに駅にも近い」.

items.diff: し presents each thing you did as a fact, one by one; たり〜たり just picks a few as examples, in a relaxed tone.

this.tr: On Sunday I cleaned, and I went shopping too.

that.tag: たり · giving a few examples
that.tr: On Sunday I did some cleaning, some shopping and so on.

items.explain: Both sentences list what was done on Sunday. Look at the form and the feel: たり〜たり just picks a few things as examples, with a relaxed “doing this and that” feel, and must end with 「する」; し presents each thing as a complete fact, often pairs with 「も」, and sounds like stressing “I did this, and I did that too”.

groups.note: Both express a reason: “because …”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: し lists several reasons, or gives one while hinting “there's more”, in a soft tone; から states one reason clearly.

this.tr: It's cheap and it's close, so let's go with this shop.

that.tr: It's cheap, so let's go with this shop.

items.explain: Look at how many reasons there are and how firmly they're stated: listing them one by one like 「安いし、近いし」, or giving just one while hinting at others → し; presenting a single decisive reason → から. When turning someone down, し (今日は雨だし…) is softer than から.

groups.note: （に）いらっしゃる ↔ でいらっしゃる — both have 「いらっしゃる」, differing only by one 「で」

items.diff: いらっしゃる means “to be (somewhere), come, go”; with 「で」 in front, でいらっしゃる means “to be …” (the honorific of である).

this.tr: Professor Tanaka is in his office right now.

that.tr: Excuse me, but are you Professor Tanaka?

items.explain: Look at the particle before it: place + 「に」 + いらっしゃる → someone is somewhere (or comes, goes); noun + 「で」 + いらっしゃる → saying someone “is …”, the honorific counterpart of 「です」 (お元気でいらっしゃいますか is the same usage).

groups.note: Both are respectful language, elevating the other person's action

items.title: 〜れる・〜られる (honorific)
items.diff: おっしゃる and いらっしゃる are special honorific verbs: highly respectful and impossible to misread; 言われる and 来られる are lighter in respect and easy to confuse with the passive.

this.tr: The company president said so.

that.tr: The company president said so.

items.explain: 「言われました」 can be honorific (the president said it) or passive (someone said it to me); you have to check whether 「が」 or 「に」 comes before it. おっしゃる has only one meaning. The same goes for いらっしゃる／来られる and 召し上がる／食べられる. When speaking to clients or superiors, prefer the special forms.

groups.note: それで ↔ それから: only the ending で／から differs

items.diff: それで means “so”: the previous sentence is the cause; それから means “and then”: the previous sentence is just what happened first. On the surface only the ending で／から differs.

this.tr: It started raining, so I bought an umbrella at a convenience store.

that.tr: I arrived at the station, and then I bought an umbrella at a convenience store.

items.explain: Look at how the two sentences relate: 「雨が降ってきた」 is the reason for buying the umbrella → それで (so); 「駅に着いた」 is just what happened first → それから (and then). Both words start with 「それ」 and differ only in the ending で／から, so they are easy to mix up when reading quickly.

groups.note: Both mean “so”

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: Both mean “so”; それで starts a new sentence and narrates a result that has already happened; から attaches after the reason, and the second half can even be a command, request or intention.

this.tr: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

that.tag: から · followed by a command
that.tr: You’re tired, so go to bed early.

wrong.why: それで is not followed by a command or request

items.explain: Look at the second half: a result that already happened (早く寝た) → both それで and から work (疲れていたから、早く寝た); if the second half is a command, request or intention such as 「〜なさい」「〜てください」「〜よう」 → only から. In form, それで begins a new sentence, while から attaches to the end of the reason clause.

items.diff: Both mean “therefore”; それで is more conversational and mostly used about your own experiences; そのため is more formal and mostly used in news and reports.

this.tr: I overslept. So I missed the train.

that.tr: There was heavy snow last night. As a result, the trains stopped.

items.explain: Look at the register: telling a friend about something that happened to you (寝坊しちゃって、〜んだ) → それで; objectively stating a cause in news, notices or reports (昨夜は大雪だった) → そのため.

groups.note: Both mean “also, besides”, adding one more item to what came before

items.diff: Both mean “besides”; それに is more conversational, casually adding one more point; その上 is slightly more formal, with a “not only that, but also …” tone.

this.tr: This room is close to the station, and besides, the rent is cheap too.

that.tr: This room is close to the station. On top of that, the rent is also cheap.

items.explain: Both sentences add a second merit to the first. Look at the setting and tone: casually adding one more point while chatting with a friend (〜し、それに〜よ) → それに; formally stressing “not only that” when introducing or explaining something → その上, which is somewhat more formal than それに.

items.diff: Both mean “and also”; それに has an add-on “and there’s one more thing” tone and leans conversational; そして just smoothly moves on to the next item and is slightly more formal.

this.tr: He is kind. Besides, he’s smart too.

that.tr: He is kind. And he is also smart.

items.explain: Both sentences describe his good points; look at the tone: それに has an add-on “and one more thing” feel, is common in conversation, and is often preceded by 「〜し」; そして just moves smoothly to the next item, is more common in writing and speeches, and can also stand before the last item in a list (日本語と英語、そして中国語).

items.diff: それに adds one more point, “besides”, to reasons or evaluations; それから just means “one more thing”.

this.tr: Let’s go with this room. It’s spacious, and besides, it’s close to the station.

that.tr: Go buy some milk. Oh, and eggs too, please.

items.explain: Look at what is being added: one more merit or reason, to persuade someone → それに, often used with 「〜し」; one more errand or item to buy → それから.

items.diff: それに goes at the start of a sentence and adds one more item in a new sentence; し follows the plain form and links similar items within the same sentence. The two are often combined: 「〜し、それに〜」.

this.tr: This room is spacious. And it’s close to the station, too.

that.tr: This room is spacious and close to the station, too.

items.explain: Look at the position: the previous sentence already ended with 「。」 and a new sentence starts by adding one more point → それに; attached to a plain form while the sentence continues → し. The two are also often used together: 「広いし、それに駅にも近い」.

groups.note: Both come from 「過ぎる」 — meaning “to pass, to exceed”

items.diff: すぎる means “going past the limit” = too …; にすぎない means “not going past” = nothing more than ….

this.tr: I ate too many sweets, and now my stomach hurts.

that.tr: I am nothing more than a student.

items.explain: Both come from 「過ぎる」 (to pass beyond): passing the limit → すぎる, “too …, overdo”, attached to the ます形 stem of verbs or the stem of adjectives; adding the negative gives にすぎない, “not going beyond this level” → “nothing more than …”, which follows nouns and often goes with 「ただ」. Check whether a negative 「ない」 follows and you can tell them apart.

groups.note: Both express degree, “too…”

items.title: 〜あまりに (too…)
items.diff: すぎる attaches after a word and means “beyond the limit”; あまりに is an adverb placed in front, with an exclamatory “really too…” feel.

this.tr: This curry is too spicy.

that.tr: This curry is just too spicy — I can't eat it.

items.explain: Look at the position: すぎる sticks to the end of a word (辛すぎる, 食べすぎる) and can end a sentence on its own; あまりに goes before the adjective and is usually followed by a resulting consequence (食べられない), sounding stronger and more written.

groups.note: All mean “not at all”

items.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない (degree)
items.diff: Both mean “not at all”; 全然 is the most common, casual way to say it in speech; 少しも is slightly more formal and firmer, stressing “not even a little”.

this.tr: This book wasn’t the least bit interesting.

that.tr: This book was totally boring.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting and tone: casually talking with friends → 全然 sounds most natural; in writing or to stress “not even a little” → 少しも, which is firmer. Note that 少しも is always followed by a negative; in casual speech 全然 also appears in phrases like 「全然大丈夫」, but that is a different usage.

items.diff: ちっとも is very colloquial and often carries dissatisfaction or complaint; 少しも is neutral and can also be used in formal situations.

this.tr: At that time, I was not the least bit afraid.

that.tr: I’ve been waiting a whole thirty minutes, and the bus just won’t come.

items.explain: Look at the register and the feeling: complaining among friends that something “still hasn’t come after all this time” → ちっとも sounds most natural; narrating in です・ます style or in writing → 少しも fits better, as ちっとも is rarely used in formal situations.

items.title: 〜も (not even one)
items.diff: Both mean “not even a little”; 少しも vaguely says “a little”; 「一円も」-type “one + counter + も” names a concrete smallest unit, so it is more specific.

this.tr: There’s not a bit of money left in my wallet.

that.tr: There’s not a single yen left in my wallet.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “not even the smallest amount”. Look at what is used as the smallest amount: 少しも vaguely says “a little” and works for money, time or feelings; 「一円も」「一人も」「一つも」 use “one + counter” to name a concrete smallest unit, which sounds more specific, like saying “not even one yen”. When counting people or things, 「一人も」「一つも」 are usually used.

groups.note: Both come from 「がる」, whose basic meaning is “showing an inner feeling on the outside”

items.diff: たがる is 「たい」 + がる: someone else seems to want to do something; 欲しがる and 怖がる are adjective + がる: someone else seems to want something or be afraid.

this.tr: My little brother wants to go play outside.

that.tr: My little brother wants a new toy.

items.explain: Both rely on 「がる」: its basic meaning is showing a feeling that only the person themselves knows, so that others can see it. Attached to feeling adjectives like 欲しい or 怖い (dropping 「い」) → 欲しがる、怖がる, “(seem to) want, be afraid”; attached to the desire form 「たい」 → たがる, “(seem to) want to do”. So for wanting a thing use 欲しがっている, and for wanting to do something use the verb ます形 stem + たがっている.

groups.note: Both mean “want to do”

items.diff: Both mean “want to do”; たい is your own inner wish, stated directly; たがる is seeing from the outside that someone else wants to do something.

this.tr: My little brother wants to buy a new game.

that.tr: I want to buy a new game.

items.explain: Look at who wants it: 「私は」, your own inner wish → たい (also used to ask the listener “do you want to …?”); a third person like 「弟は」, whose mind you cannot see, so you can only tell from what they say and do → たがる, usually as 「たがっている」. For other people you can also say 「〜たいと言っている」, reporting たい as something they said.

groups.note: たら ↔ ったら — an extra 「っ」 in front, yet it attaches to a noun

items.title: 〜ったら (speaking of someone)
items.diff: Verb た形 + ら means “if … / after …”; noun + ったら brings up a person with annoyance or exasperation.

this.tr: Once Mom gets home, let’s eat.

that.tr: Honestly, my mom went into my room without asking again.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ったら」: a verb た形 (帰った + ら), followed by what will happen next → a condition, “once …, then …”; a noun such as a name or a form of address (お母さん + ったら), usually followed by a complaint → “honestly, that person …”, with nothing to do with conditions. In speech people also often just exclaim 「もう、お母さんったら！」.

groups.note: Both mean “if”

items.title: 〜ば (hypothetical condition)
items.diff: Both mean “if”; たら is the most versatile and the most common in speech; ば puts the focus on “as long as this condition holds”, and when the first half is an action, it cannot be followed by a request.

this.tr: If you have time, please give me a hand.

that.tag: ば · as long as the condition holds
that.tr: As long as you have time, please give me a hand.

wrong.why: When the first half is an action like 「着く」 and the second half is a request, ば sounds unnatural; say 「着いたら」

items.explain: When the first half is a state such as 「ある」 or 「安い」, both can be followed by a request: たら is casual and the most common in speech; ば puts the focus on “as long as this condition is met”. When the first half is an action such as 「着く」 or 「来る」 and the second half is a request or intention such as 「〜てください」「〜たい」「〜よう」, only たら works.

items.title: 〜なら (if that’s the case)
items.diff: Both mean “if”; with たら you set up a condition yourself; なら picks up what the other person just said or something already known, then gives your response.

this.tr: If it’s cheap, I’ll buy it.

that.tr: If it’s that cheap, I’ll buy it.

items.explain: Look at whether the first half is picking up the other person’s words: you set up a condition yourself, “(when the time comes) if it’s cheap” → たら; the other person just said it, or it is already known, and you pick it up with 「そんなに」 or 「それ」 before responding → なら, with a “since you say so” feel. The connection also differs: たら uses the た形 (安かったら), while なら attaches directly to the plain form (安いなら、雨なら).

groups.note: Both mean “when …, then …”

items.title: 〜と (whenever …, then)
items.diff: たら can be followed by an invitation or a plan; と can only be followed by a result that naturally happens.

this.tr: When spring comes, let’s go cherry-blossom viewing together.

that.tr: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

wrong.why: と cannot be followed by an invitation or intention

items.explain: The first halves are the same, so look at the second half: a result that inevitably appears when the time comes, like 「桜が咲く」 → と (たら also works); if the second half is an invitation like 「一緒に花見に行こう」, or a request or intention → only たら.

groups.note: Both come from 「どう」 (how) — asking what the other person thinks: “how about this thing?” = a recommendation, “how about doing it?” = a suggestion

items.diff: Verb ta-form + らどうですか suggests the other person do something; noun + はどうですか recommends a thing.

this.tr: If you have a cold, why don't you take some medicine?

that.tr: If you have a cold, how about this medicine?

items.explain: Look before 「どう」: verb ta-form + ら (飲んだら) → urging the other person to take action, which can sound preachy toward superiors; noun + は (この薬は) → offering something for them to evaluate or accept. The polite version 「〜はいかがですか」 works the same way.

groups.note: Both are used to give the other person advice

items.diff: たらどうですか makes a suggestion in question form, with a lighter tone; ほうがいい says directly “it's better to do this”, like a warning.

this.tr: If you're tired, why don't you take a little break?

that.tr: You have a high fever, so you'd better go to the hospital right away.

items.explain: Look at how serious the matter is: just lightly offering an idea and letting them decide → たらどうですか; something might go wrong if they don't (a high fever, being late) → ほうがいい.

items.diff: たらどう pushes a suggestion on the other person with a rhetorical question and can sound impatient; たらいい calmly tells them “just do this”.

this.tr: Stop dawdling — why don't you just hurry up and decide?

that.tr: When you don't understand, just ask the teacher.

items.explain: Look at the tone: urging like 「〜ていないで」 before it, with the other person dragging their feet → たらどう, which easily sounds annoyed; the other person doesn't know what to do and you're telling them how → たらいい (〜といい works the same). When answering 「どうしたらいいですか」, use たらいい, not たらどう.

groups.note: Both mean “that would be good”: giving advice, or expressing a wish

items.diff: たらいい calmly tells the other person “just do this”; たらどう pushes a suggestion on them with a rhetorical question and can sound impatient.

this.tr: When you don't understand, just ask the teacher.

that.tr: Stop dawdling — why don't you just hurry up and decide?

items.explain: Look at the tone: the other person doesn't know what to do and you're telling them how → たらいい (〜といい works the same); urging like 「〜ていないで」 before it, with the other person dragging their feet → たらどう, which easily sounds annoyed. When answering 「どうしたらいいですか」, only たらいい works.

items.diff: といいね wishes the other person well from their side, in a gentle tone; てほしい is the speaker's own wish for someone else, and said to that person's face it sounds like a demand.

this.tr: I hope you pass your exam tomorrow.

that.tr: I really want my daughter to pass, no matter what.

items.explain: Look at who it's said to and whose wish it is: saying 「〜といいね」 to a friend (〜たらいいね works the same) is wishing them well; 「人に〜てほしい」 (〜てもらいたい works the same) is my own wish for someone else to achieve something, and saying 「合格してほしい」 to the person directly puts pressure on them.

items.diff: といいな calmly says “it would be nice if…”; ないかな is longing and waiting, with a sense of impatience — negative in form, yet expressing a wish.

this.tr: I hope it's sunny this weekend.

that.tr: I wish the weekend would hurry up and get here.

items.explain: Look for an impatient word like 「早く」: longing for something to come soon → 〜ないかな (negative in form, but meaning “I really wish…”); just stating a wish → 〜といいな (〜たらいいな works the same).

groups.note: Both come from 「上げる（あげる）」 — originally “raise up, offer up”, which later came to mean “give”

items.title: 〜をあげる (giving things)
items.diff: te-form + あげる gives an “action”, doing something for someone; noun + をあげる gives a thing.

this.tag: Giving an action · reading to her
this.tr: I read a book to my little sister.

that.tr: I gave my little sister a book.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「読んで」: 「noun + を」 right before あげる → giving a thing away; a verb te-form before it → giving “doing this” to the other person as a gift. くれる and もらう work the same way.

items.diff: てあげる is used for equals and juniors; てさしあげる (差し + 上げる) is the humble version, used when doing something for superiors or customers.

this.tr: I showed my friend the way to the station.

that.tr: I showed the customer the way to the station.

items.explain: Look at who benefits: friends or family → てあげる; customers or superiors → てさしあげる. Both carry a “doing you a favor” nuance, so when speaking directly to a superior, switch to 「お〜します」 (駅までご案内します).

groups.note: Both mean “I do something for someone else”; the difference is in who it's for and the tone

items.diff: てあげる is neutral in tone; てやる is used for your own younger siblings, children or pets, and is casual.

this.tr: I lent my notes to a friend.

that.tr: I lent my notes to my little brother.

items.explain: Look at who it's for: friends or people in general → てあげる; your own little brother, kids or pets → てやる also works, but it's rather blunt, and in polite settings people now mostly use てあげる instead. てやる also has meanings like “I'll show you!” or “I'll do it anyway”, which てあげる doesn't.

groups.note: てある ↔ ている — just one character apart

items.diff: てある (with transitive verbs) means someone did it on purpose and the result remains; ている (with intransitive verbs) just describes a state.

this.tr: The window has been (left) open for cleaning.

that.tr: The window is open.

wrong.why: After 「窓が」, use 「開いている」 or 「開けてある」

items.explain: Look at the verb first: 開ける (transitive) + てある → someone opened it for a purpose and has left it open; 開く (intransitive) + ている → just says “it's open”. When you see a purpose like 「〜のために」, it's most likely てある.

groups.note: Both have to do with “preparing in advance”

items.diff: てある describes the state left after preparing; ておく describes the action of “doing it in advance”.

this.tr: The meeting materials have already been copied.

that.tr: I'll copy the meeting materials by tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at the time word and the particle: 「もう」 + てあります describes a state that's already prepared now, with the object usually marked by 「は／が」; 「明日までに」 + ておきます describes an action you'll do in advance, with the object marked by 「を」. The usual order is: first ておいた, so now てある.

groups.note: Both come from 「ばかり」 — originally “only this much”

items.diff: てばかりいる means “always doing, doing nothing but”, often with dissatisfaction; たばかり means “just finished doing”.

this.tr: My little brother does nothing but play games every day.

that.tr: I just ate.

items.explain: They differ only in て vs. た: て + ばかり + いる means doing the same thing over and over, often to the speaker's dissatisfaction; た + ばかり means only a short time has passed. If you see 「ている」, it's “always”.

items.diff: てばかりいる limits the action, “always doing…”; noun + ばかり limits the object, “nothing but…”.

this.tr: My little brother is always eating sweets.

that.tr: My little brother eats nothing but sweets.

items.explain: Look at what 「ばかり」 directly follows: after a noun (物ばかり) → eats only this kind of thing; after a verb te-form (食べてばかり) → does only this one action and nothing else. The two sentences are very close in meaning, but てばかりいる stresses more that “they aren't doing what they should”. In speech, ばかり is often pronounced ばっかり.

items.diff: てばかりいる goes at the end of the sentence and is a criticism in itself; ばかりで goes mid-sentence, followed by an explicit “but doesn't…”.

this.tr: My little brother is always playing.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play and doesn't study at all.

items.explain: Look at where the sentence ends: てばかりいる closes the sentence by itself, leaving “not doing what they should” unsaid; ばかりで follows the dictionary form and has another clause after it, spelling out “but doesn't…” (全然勉強しない).

groups.note: Both come from 「ほしい（欲しい）」 — the speaker's inner feeling of “wanting”

items.diff: てほしい means wanting someone else to do something; がほしい means wanting a thing.

this.tr: I want my dad to fix my bike.

that.tr: I want a new bike.

items.explain: Look before 「ほしい」: a verb te-form → wanting someone else to do that action, with the doer marked by 「に」; noun + が → wanting that thing.

groups.note: Both express “want / wish”; the difference is who you want to do it and how you say it

items.diff: てほしい means wanting someone else to do something; たい means wanting to do it yourself.

this.tr: I want my husband to come home early today.

that.tr: I want to go home early today.

items.explain: Look at who does the action: wanting the other person or someone else to do it → 「人に + te-form + ほしい」 (夫に〜てほしい; 〜てもらいたい works the same); doing it yourself → たい. In English both are “want”, but “want someone to…” needs てほしい.

items.diff: てほしい states your own wish; てもらえませんか makes a request to the other person, and is what you use when asking someone for help face to face.

this.tr: I really wish Tanaka would help me with this job.

that.tr: Tanaka, could you help me with this job?

items.explain: Look at whether you're speaking to the person themselves: 「田中さんに〜てほしいな」 states your own wish (to yourself or to a third party); calling out 「田中さん、〜」 and asking for help → てもらえませんか (てくれませんか works the same). Saying 「手伝ってほしい」 to their face sounds like a demand.

items.diff: てほしい is my own wish for someone else; といいね wishes the other person well from their side, in a gentle tone.

this.tr: I really want my daughter to pass, no matter what.

that.tr: I hope you pass your exam tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at whose wish it is and who it's said to: 「人に〜てほしい」 is my wish for someone else to achieve something, and saying it to the person directly puts pressure on them; saying 「〜といいね」 to a friend (〜たらいいね works the same) is wishing them well.

items.title: 〜てほしいものだ
items.diff: てほしい is an ordinary wish; てほしいものだ is reflective, usually a strong hope directed at society or people in general.

this.tr: I want my son to read more books.

that.tr: I really wish young people would read more books.

items.explain: Look at the target and the tone: stating your own expectation of a specific person around you → てほしい; a reflective, slightly preachy hope directed at a group like 「若い人」 or 「政府」 → てほしいものだ, mostly used in writing and speeches.

groups.note: Both come from 「行く」 (go) — ていく is doing something and then “going”, に行く is “going” in order to do it

items.title: 〜に行く
items.diff: ていく is “do it, then go”; に行く is “go in order to do it”.

this.tr: Let's buy some souvenirs at the station before we go.

that.tr: Let's go to the station to buy some souvenirs.

items.explain: Look at the verb form: te-form (買って) + いく → do this first, then leave with it; masu-stem (買い) + に行く → the purpose of going out is to do this. The location particle also differs: 「駅で買っていく」 (where you buy), 「駅へ買いに行く」 (where you go). に来る works the same way.

groups.note: Both come from 「いただく（頂く）」 — originally “to put on top of one's head”, i.e. to receive respectfully

items.diff: ていただけませんか is a direct request; ていただく is mostly used to describe a favor already received.

this.tr: Sensei, could you please look over this essay for me?

that.tr: Yesterday, my teacher kindly looked over my essay.

items.explain: Both sentences come from the same 「ていただく」: turned into the negative potential question 「いただけませんか」 → a direct request to the other person (literally “could I not receive your…?”); in the past tense 「いただいた」, with the doer marked by 「に」 → telling others about a favor you received.

items.diff: ていただけませんか asks directly; ていただけるとありがたい doesn't ask, only says “I'd be grateful if you could…”, which is softer.

this.tr: Could you send me the materials by next week?

that.tr: I would be grateful if you could send me the materials by next week.

items.explain: Look at whether the sentence ends in a question: 「〜ませんか」 asks the other person “can you or not”, requiring an answer; 「〜とありがたいです」 turns the request into a statement of your own feelings without pressing them to commit, and is common in emails.

groups.note: Both are used to ask the other person to do something

items.diff: ていただけませんか is used with superiors and clients; てもらえませんか is slightly less polite, used with coworkers, shop staff and strangers.

this.tr: Sensei, could you please check this document for me?

that.tr: Tanaka, could you check this document for me?

items.explain: Look at who you're speaking to: a teacher, superior or client → ていただけませんか; a coworker, friend or shop staff → てもらえませんか (てくれませんか works the same). The structure is exactly the same; 「もらう」 is just replaced with the humble 「いただく」.

items.diff: ていただけませんか uses a question to leave the decision to the other person, so it's softer; てください is a polite instruction that the other person basically can't refuse.

this.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you write your name here?

that.tr: Please write your name here.

items.explain: Look at the listener and the tone: asking a superior or client to do something extra for you, often preceded by 「お忙しいところすみませんが」 → ていただけませんか; instructions given at a service counter or by a teacher → てください.

items.diff: ていただけませんか follows a verb and makes a request in question form, which is softer; をお願いします follows a noun and is concise and polite.

this.tr: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you check this document?

that.tr: Please check this document.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: verb te-form + いただけませんか uses a question to leave the decision to the other person, better suited to asking for extra help or to someone of very high status; noun (確認, 説明) + をお願いします is concise and polite, and very common at work.

groups.note: Both come from 「いただく（頂く）」 — originally “to put on top of one's head”, i.e. to receive respectfully

items.title: 〜をいただく (receiving things)
items.diff: te-form + いただく receives the other person's “action”; noun + をいただく receives a thing.

this.tr: My teacher kindly lent me a book.

that.tr: My teacher gave me a book.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「貸して」: 「noun + を」 right before いただく → receiving a thing from a superior; a verb te-form before it → receiving something a superior did for you. With equals, just say 「貸してもらった」 or 「本をもらった」.

items.diff: ていただく is mostly used to describe a favor already received; ていただけませんか is a direct request.

this.tr: Yesterday, my teacher kindly looked over my essay.

that.tr: Sensei, could you please look over this essay for me?

items.explain: Both sentences come from the same 「ていただく」: in the past tense 「いただいた」, with the doer marked by 「に」 → telling others about a favor you received; turned into the negative potential question 「いただけませんか」 → a direct request to the other person.

groups.note: Both mean “someone did something for me and I benefited”

items.diff: ていただく is the humble version of てもらう: use ていただく with superiors and customers, てもらう with friends and family.

this.tr: My teacher kindly corrected my essay.

that.tr: I had a friend correct my essay.

items.explain: The structure and particles are exactly the same (人に + te-form); just look at who helped: a teacher, boss or customer → ていただく; a friend, family member or junior → てもらう.

items.diff: For the same event, ていただく takes “me” as the subject, with the doer marked by 「に」; てくださる takes the other person as the subject, with the doer marked by 「が」.

this.tr: (I) had my teacher kindly show me the way.

that.tr: My teacher kindly showed me the way.

wrong.why: After 「先生が」, use てくださった

items.explain: Look at the particle after the teacher: 「先生に」 → the subject is me, followed by ていただく; 「先生が」 → the subject is the teacher, followed by てくださる. Same meaning, but the particle and verb must always match.

items.diff: ていただく attaches to a verb's te-form; お〜いただく / ご〜いただく replaces the verb with 「お＋masu-stem」 or 「ご＋Sino-Japanese noun」 and is more formal.

this.tr: I had Mr. Tanaka check the materials.

that.tr: We had the client check the materials.

items.explain: Look at the verb form: 確認し + ていただく is the ordinary humble expression; replacing the verb with 「ご＋確認」 or 「お＋待ち」 and attaching いただく directly is more respectful, and common in business emails and announcements (ご確認いただけますか, お待ちいただけますか). Native Japanese verbs take 「お」, Sino-Japanese words take 「ご」.

groups.note: Both come from 「くださる（下さる）」 — originally “(a superior) bestows”

items.diff: てくださる describes a superior doing something for me; てください is its imperative form, used to ask someone to do something.

this.tr: My teacher explained it to me very patiently.

that.tr: Please explain it once more.

items.explain: 「ください」 is simply the imperative form of 「くださる」, so 「〜てください」 literally means “please bestow on me the act of…”. Check whether the sentence describes what the other person did (〜てくださった) or makes a request to their face (〜てください).

items.title: 〜をくださる (a superior gives me a thing)
items.diff: て-form + くださる gives an action; noun + をくださる gives a thing.

this.tr: My teacher lent me a book.

that.tr: My teacher gave me a book.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「貸して」: if くださる comes straight after 「noun + を」 → a superior gives me a thing; if it follows a verb's て-form → a superior did that for me. With equals, say 「貸してくれた」「本をくれた」.

groups.note: Both mean “someone does something for me”

items.diff: てくださる is the honorific of てくれる: use てくださる when a superior does something for me, てくれる when a friend or colleague does.

this.tr: The department head helped me with my work.

that.tr: My colleague helped me with my work.

items.explain: Same structure, same direction (person が + て-form); just look at who's helping: superiors, teachers, customers → てくださる; friends, colleagues, family → てくれる.

items.diff: For the same event, てくださる makes the other person the subject, marking the doer with 「が」; ていただく makes me the subject, marking the doer with 「に」.

this.tr: My teacher showed me the way.

that.tr: (I) had my teacher show me the way.

wrong.why: After 「先生が」 you need てくださった

items.explain: Look at the particle after the teacher: 「先生が」 → the teacher is the subject, followed by てくださる; 「先生に」 → I am the subject, followed by ていただく. Same meaning, but particle and verb must always match.

groups.note: Both come from 「くれる」 — someone else “gives to me”

items.title: 〜をくれる (gives me a thing)
items.diff: て-form + くれる means someone does something for me; noun + をくれる means someone gives me a thing.

this.tr: My older sister made me a cake.

that.tr: My older sister gave me a cake.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「作って」: if くれる comes straight after 「noun + を」 → someone gives me a thing; if it follows a verb's て-form → someone did that for me. Either way, the receiver is “me” or my side.

groups.note: Both describe someone's action directed at me; they differ in viewpoint, respect and feeling

items.diff: For the same event, てくれる makes the helper the subject; てもらう makes me the subject and can also imply “I asked them to”.

this.tr: My friend helped me with my homework.

that.tr: I got my friend to help me with my homework.

wrong.why: With てくれる, the helper takes 「が」

items.explain: Look at the particle after the friend: 「友達が」 → stresses the friend's own kindness, so てくれた; 「友達に」 → told from my side, so てもらった, often implying “I asked them to”.

items.diff: てくれる is for friends and colleagues; when a superior does something for me, use the honorific てくださる.

this.tr: My colleague helped me with my work.

that.tr: The department head helped me with my work.

items.explain: Same structure, same direction (person が + て-form); just look at who's helping: friends, colleagues, family → てくれる; superiors, teachers, customers → てくださる.

items.title: 〜てくる (action toward me)
items.diff: てくれる carries gratitude; てくる only says the action comes toward me, often neutral or annoyed.

this.tr: My friend was worried and called me.

that.tr: A stranger called me in the middle of the night.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's feelings: the action benefits me and I'm grateful → てくれる; it just comes at me, maybe even bothering me (夜中に, 知らない人が) → てくる.

groups.note: Both thank someone for what they did for you

items.title: 〜てすみません (apology + thanks)
items.diff: てくださってありがとうございます is a simple thank-you; てくださってすみません adds an apology for “putting you to trouble” to the thanks.

this.tr: Thank you for coming in the rain.

that.tr: I'm sorry you had to come all the way out in the rain.

items.explain: The two sentences are equally polite (both use 「てくださって」); only the ending differs: if you just want to express gratitude → ありがとうございます; if you also want to say “sorry for the trouble you went to” → すみません, which sounds humbler. When the other person went to extra effort for you (coming in the rain, from far away, or despite being busy), both are common; when you simply feel happy and grateful, use ありがとうございます.

groups.note: Both mean “go and do something”

items.title: 〜に行く
items.diff: てくる says you'll go do something and then come back here; に行く only says what you're going out to do.

this.tr: I'm going to get a drink at the convenience store. I'll be right back.

that.tr: I'm going to the convenience store to buy a drink. Want to come along?

items.explain: Both mean “go and buy”; look at where the focus is: followed by 「すぐ戻るから」, stressing that you'll come back here once it's done → てくる; followed by the question 「一緒に行く」, the focus is on going out to do it → に行く (the same goes for に来る).

groups.note: All describe a change starting to appear

items.diff: てくる looks at the “process” of change (changing little by little); ようになる looks at the “end point” (now you can).

this.tr: Little by little, I've started to understand Japanese.

that.tr: In three months, I became able to understand Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the time expression: 「少しずつ」 describes the process of change, still going on and continuing up to now → usually てくる; 「３か月で」 marks an end point and talks about the new state once it's reached → ようになる.

items.title: 〜始める (start of a change)
items.diff: てくる carries a felt sense that “the change has reached me and I notice it”; 始める objectively states when the change begins.

this.tr: Oh, it's started snowing.

that.tr: According to the weather forecast, it will start snowing in the evening.

items.explain: Both can say “it starts snowing”; check whether the speaker experiences it firsthand: with 「あっ」, watching the change arrive and blurting it out → てくる; with 「天気予報によると」, passing on information and objectively stating when the change begins → 始める.

groups.note: Both mean “someone does something toward me”

items.diff: てくる only says someone's action is directed at me, neutrally or with some annoyance; てくれる carries gratitude.

this.tr: My friend called me at three in the morning.

that.tr: My friend was worried and called me.

items.explain: Both 「友達が電話をかけてきた／くれた」 are possible; the difference is the speaker's feelings: like 「夜中の三時に」, when it's a nuisance, or when you're just reporting that the action came your way → てくる; 「心配して」 shows the friend was thinking of you and you're grateful → てくれる.

groups.note: Both come from 「見る」 — originally “to look”; 「見せる」, derived from it, means “to let someone see”

items.title: 〜てみせる (determination: “I'll definitely do it”)
items.diff: てみる is trying something yourself to see the result; てみせる is doing it for others to see, or vowing “I'll definitely do it”.

this.tr: I don't know if I can, but I'll give it a try.

that.tr: I'll do it, just you watch.

items.explain: 「見る」 originally means “to look”, and 「見せる」, derived from it, means “to let someone see, to show”. てみる comes from 「見る」: do it once, then look at how it turns out → try doing, which is why 「できるか分からないけど」 often comes before it; てみせる comes from 「見せる」: do it so others can see → demonstrate → the determination “I'll do it and show you”, which is why it often goes with 「絶対に」 or 「必ず」.

groups.note: Both come from 「構う（かまう）」 — originally “to mind, to care about”

items.diff: てもかまわない means “I don't mind” = permission; もかまわず means “regardless of…”, describing someone who ignores what they should care about.

this.tr: Nobody's watching, so it's okay to cry.

that.tr: She cried without caring who saw.

items.explain: かまう originally means “to mind, to care about”. 「〜てもかまわない」 = I don't mind even if you do this → extended to permission, “it's okay to…”; it follows a verb's て-form and is said by the speaker to the listener. 「〜もかまわず」 = not even minding… → extended to “regardless of…”; it follows a noun (人目, 雨) and is followed by something someone does heedlessly, often with surprise or criticism. Look at what comes before 「も」: a verb's て-form → permission; a noun → regardless.

groups.note: Both give permission: “it's okay if…”

items.diff: Both give permission; てもかまわない is more formal, often used with customers or in business.

this.tr: You may pay next month if you wish.

that.tr: You can pay me next month, no problem.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: a clerk to a customer or business situations, often with honorifics like 「お支払い」 → てもかまいません, which sounds more formal; between friends, casual speech with 「よ」 → てもいい.

items.diff: てもかまわない is for ordinary polite situations; ても差し支えない is more written and formal, seen in documents and official instructions.

this.tr: Is it all right to write in pencil?

that.tr: The application form may be filled in with pencil.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: asking a clerk or teacher in person, 「〜てもかまいませんか」 is already very polite; formal instructions written on application forms, manuals and company documents, like this one starting with 「申込書は」, often use the stiffer 「〜ても差し支えありません」.

groups.note: All ask someone to do something for you

items.diff: てもらえませんか is for colleagues, clerks and strangers; ていただけませんか is politer, for superiors and clients.

this.tr: Tanaka, could you check this document for me?

that.tr: Professor, would you be so kind as to check this document for me?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: a colleague like 「田中さん」, friends, clerks → てもらえませんか (てくれませんか works too); 「先生」, superiors, clients → ていただけませんか. The structure is identical; 「もらう」 is just swapped for the humble 「いただく」.

items.title: 〜てください (asking for help)
items.diff: てもらえませんか asks a question that leaves the choice to the other person, so it's softer; てください states the request directly, leaving them little room to refuse.

this.tr: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?

that.tr: Excuse me, please tell me the way to the station.

items.explain: Both ask a stranger for help; only the ending differs: てください states the request directly — polite, but it leaves the other person little room to refuse; てもらえませんか asks “could you?”, leaving the choice to them, so it's softer. When asking someone to do something they have no obligation to do, てもらえませんか is more appropriate.

items.title: 〜てもらえるとありがたい
items.diff: てもらえませんか asks directly whether they can do it; てもらえるとありがたい asks nothing and just says “I'd be grateful if you could”, which is softer.

this.tr: Could you put these materials together for me by tomorrow?

that.tr: If you could put these materials together for me by tomorrow, I'd really appreciate it.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence ends in a question: 「〜てもらえませんか」 asks directly whether they can do it, so they have to answer yes or no; 「〜てもらえるとありがたいんですが」 asks nothing and just says “I'd be grateful if you could”, leaving the decision entirely to them. It's softer and suits cases where they have no obligation or the request is a bit of a stretch.

groups.note: Both come from 「もらう」 — to “receive” from someone

items.title: 〜をもらう (receive a thing)
items.diff: て-form + もらう receives something someone did for me; noun + をもらう receives a thing.

this.tr: My friend lent me an umbrella.

that.tr: My friend gave me an umbrella.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「貸して」: if もらう comes straight after 「noun + を」 → you receive a thing from someone; if it follows a verb's て-form → you receive something someone did for you. In both, the giver takes 「に」.

groups.note: てもらう ↔ させてもらう: just an extra 「させ」, yet the person doing the action changes

items.title: 〜させてもらう
items.diff: てもらう is someone else doing it for me; させてもらう is me doing it myself, with the other person's permission.

this.tag: Someone else does it · I benefit
this.tr: I didn't understand, so I had my teacher explain it again.

that.tr: At the meeting, I (was allowed to) present the new plan.

items.explain: Check whether the verb has 「させ」: 説明して + もらう → the other person did the action and I benefit; 説明させて + もらう → I did the action myself, and the “with your permission” phrasing just makes it humble — very common in business (説明させていただきます).

groups.note: Both mean “someone does something for me”

items.diff: For the same event, てもらう makes me the subject, marking the helper with 「に」; てくれる makes the helper the subject, with 「が」.

this.tr: I got my friend to help me with my homework.

that.tr: My friend helped me with my homework.

wrong.why: With てくれる, the helper takes 「が」

items.explain: Look at the particle after the friend: 「友達に」 → told from my side, so てもらった, often implying “I asked them to”; 「友達が」 → stresses the friend's own kindness, so てくれた.

items.diff: てもらう is for friends and family; with superiors and customers use the humble ていただく.

this.tr: I had a friend correct my essay.

that.tr: I had my teacher correct my essay.

items.explain: Same structure and particles (person に + て-form); just look at who's helping: 「友達」, family, juniors → てもらう; 「先生」, bosses, customers → ていただく.

groups.note: Both come from 「置く（おく）」 — originally “to put something there and leave it”

items.diff: ておく is doing something and leaving it that way; ないでおく is deliberately not doing it and leaving things as they are.

this.tr: I'll let the department head know in advance that I'll be late tomorrow.

that.tr: It's a surprise, so I won't tell him about the party yet.

items.explain: おく originally means “to put something there and leave it”. ておく = leave the result of a finished action in place for later → do in advance (letting the department head know first); ないでおく = don't do the action and leave things as they were → deliberately hold off (サプライズだから, so not telling him yet). Check whether 「おく」 follows the て-form or ないで.

groups.note: Both mean “have something ready in advance”

items.title: 〜てある (already prepared)
items.diff: ておいた talks about the action — “who made the preparations”; てある talks about the state of being ready now, without caring who did it.

this.tr: I've already booked the restaurant.

that.tr: The restaurant's already booked.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “it's already been booked in advance”, and swapping them doesn't change the meaning; only the focus differs: ておいた talks about the act of preparing and can name who did it (「私が」); てある talks about the state of being ready now and usually doesn't say who did it.

groups.note: Both mean “leave something in a certain state”

items.title: 〜っぱなし (left undone)
items.diff: ておく is deliberately keeping it that way, with no criticism; っぱなし is leaving alone something that should have been dealt with, with regret or dissatisfaction.

this.tr: I left the window open to air out the room.

that.tr: I carelessly left the window open.

items.explain: In both sentences the window stays open; look at the speaker's attitude: 「換気のために」 shows it was left open on purpose, for a reason, with no criticism → ておく; 「うっかり」 shows it should have been closed but was forgotten and left as is, with regret or dissatisfaction → っぱなし.

groups.note: All come from 「上げる（あげる）」 — originally “to lift up”, extended to “to give, to offer”

items.diff: てさしあげる is the humble form, used when doing something for superiors or customers; てあげる is for equals and juniors.

this.tr: I showed the customer the way to the station.

that.tr: I showed my friend the way to the station.

items.explain: 「上げる」 originally means “to lift up”, extended to sending something up to someone, giving it → あげる “give”; offering an action as a kindness → てあげる “do for someone”. 「差し上げる」 is raising something in both hands to offer it → humbly “present” to a superior → てさしあげる “do for a superior or customer”. So look at who benefits: 「お客様」, superiors → てさしあげる; 「友達」, family → てあげる. Both carry a hint of “doing someone a favor”, so when speaking directly to a superior, switch to 「お〜します」 (駅までご案内します).

items.title: 〜をさしあげる (offer a thing)
items.diff: て-form + さしあげる offers an action; noun + をさしあげる offers a thing.

this.tr: I drew a map for the customer.

that.tr: I gave the customer a map.

items.explain: さしあげる = 差し + 上げる, originally raising something in both hands to “offer” it. If what you offer is a thing → 「noun + を」 さしあげる; if it's something you do for the other person → verb て-form + さしあげる. The two sentences differ only by 「書いて」: 「お客様に地図をさしあげた」 means you gave the customer a map; add 「書いて」 and it means you drew a map for them. With equals, say 「書いてあげた」「地図をあげた」.

groups.note: Both mean “I do something for a superior or customer”

items.diff: てさしあげる still carries a hint of “doing a favor”; お〜する just lowers yourself, and is the first choice when speaking directly to a superior or customer.

this.tr: I carried the department head's bags for him.

that.tr: Let me carry your bags for you, sir.

items.explain: Check whether you're saying it to the person themselves: when telling a third party what you did for a superior (部長の荷物を持ってさしあげた), you can use てさしあげた; when saying “let me… for you” directly to 「部長」 or a customer, use お〜します (likewise ご〜します: ご案内します); saying 「持ってさしあげます」 sounds like you're doing them a favor.

groups.note: Both mean “finish doing”

items.diff: てしまう stresses doing it all in one go, completely, so the matter is settled; 終わる only objectively states that an action ended in time.

this.tr: I read this whole book in a single night.

that.tr: I finally finished reading this book.

items.explain: Look at what the speaker wants to stress: with 「一晩で」 and 「全部」, stressing that it was done in one go, completely, and the matter is settled → てしまう; with 「やっと」, simply stating that the act of reading has ended → ます-stem + 終わる, with no emotional coloring. Also, 終わる only attaches to actions that last a while, like reading, writing or eating.

groups.note: Both thank someone for what they did for you

items.diff: てくださってすみません adds an apology for “putting you to trouble” to the thanks; てくださってありがとうございます is a simple thank-you.

this.tr: I'm sorry you had to come all the way out in the rain.

that.tr: Thank you for coming in the rain.

items.explain: The two sentences are equally polite (both use 「てくださって」); only the ending differs: if you also want to say “sorry for the trouble you went to” → すみません, which sounds humbler; if you just want to express gratitude → ありがとうございます. When the other person went to extra effort for you (coming in the rain, from far away, or despite being busy), both are common; when you simply feel happy and grateful, use ありがとうございます.

groups.note: Both mean “doing something for someone”

items.diff: てやる is used for your own younger siblings, children or pets, and is casual; てあげる is neutral in tone.

this.tr: I lent my notebook to my little brother.

that.tr: I lent my notebook to a friend.

items.explain: Look at who it's for: your own younger siblings, children or pets, like 「弟に」 → てやる is possible, casual and somewhat masculine in tone; equals or people in general, like 「友達に」 → use てあげる, since てやる would sound condescending. These days people often use てあげる even with children and pets, as it sounds gentler.

groups.note: Both express determination to “get it done no matter what”

items.title: 〜てみせる (resolve)
items.diff: てやる is spiteful, gritted-teeth defiance with a rough tone; てみせる declares to others “I'll show you”, and can be said to someone's face.

this.tr: Argh, I'm so frustrated! Next year I'll pass, no matter what.

that.tr: Don't worry. Next year I'll pass for sure, you'll see.

items.explain: Look at who it's said to: gritting your teeth out of spite, as with 「悔しい」 → てやる, rough in tone and mostly said to yourself; promising in front of someone that they'll see you succeed, as with 「心配しないで」 → てみせる, which you can say even to family or a teacher.

groups.note: Both come from 「よかった (it was good)」 — judging an outcome

items.diff: てよかった is relief about something you did; ばよかった is regret about something you didn't do.

this.tr: It's raining. Good thing I brought an umbrella.

that.tr: It's raining. I should have brought an umbrella.

items.explain: The same 「よかった」: て-form + よかった → you did it and it turned out well = glad I did; ば-form + よかった → it would have been good if you had, implying “but I didn't” = regret. Check whether the verb is in て-form (持ってきて) or ば-form (持ってくれば).

groups.note: Both report something you heard

items.title: 〜そうだ (I hear)
items.diff: と言っていた names who said it; hearsay そうだ just means “apparently”, often without naming the source.

this.tr: The department head said tomorrow's meeting is canceled.

that.tr: I hear tomorrow's meeting is canceled.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence names the speaker: 「部長が〜と言っていました」 clearly states who said it; 「〜そうです」 only means “apparently”, and the source can be left out — if you want to name it, use 「〜によると」. Note that hearsay そうだ attaches to the plain form (中止だ + そうだ); don't confuse it with the “looks like” そうだ in 「降りそうだ」.

items.diff: と言っていた is neutral and works in polite speech; んだって is a very casual “I heard…”, only said to people you're close to.

this.tr: Professor, Tanaka said he's taking today off.

that.tr: Hey, I heard Tanaka's off today.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: passing a message to a teacher (先生) or boss → 「〜と言っていました」; chatting casually with friends → 「〜んだって」, often starting with 「ねえ」. んだって also doesn't necessarily say who said it.

groups.note: Both express the judgment “you could say…”

items.diff: と言ってもいい has an evaluative “it's no exaggeration to say” tone; と言える is an objective judgment drawn from analyzing facts.

this.tr: Her Japanese is so good you could practically call her Japanese.

that.tr: From the results of this survey, it can be said that young people are reading less and less.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment rests on: the speaker's own, slightly exaggerated evaluation (もう日本人と言ってもいい) → と言ってもいい; preceded by evidence like 「調査の結果から」「データによると」 leading to an objective conclusion → と言える, mostly in writing.

groups.note: Both check “So you mean…?”

items.title: 〜ということ (checking what someone means)
items.diff: という意味ですか zeroes in on a particular remark and presses for what it means; ということですか sums up what the other person said into a conclusion and checks it — the more common of the two.

this.tag: Pressing for what a remark means
this.tr: Does what you just said mean you're leaving the company next month?

that.tr: So you're saying you're leaving the company next month?

items.explain: Both sentences check what the other person means. Focusing on one particular remark and asking what exactly it means (「今の話は」「その言葉は」) → という意味ですか, sometimes with a probing, slightly disbelieving tone; summing up what they said into a conclusion and checking it, often after 「つまり」「じゃあ」 → ということですか, more neutral and more common in everyday speech.

groups.note: Both mean “the fact of…”

items.diff: ということ highlights the content itself and sounds a little more formal; こと simply turns the action into a noun and is more concise. Content ending in 「だ」 can only take ということ.

this.tag: Stresses the content · a bit formal
this.tr: What matters is the very act of keeping at it a little every day.

that.tr: It's important to keep at it a little every day.

wrong.why: こと can't come directly after 「だ」; say 「学生だということ」 (or, in writing, 「学生であること」)

items.explain: Both sentences are correct and mean the same. ということ presents what comes before as a piece of information or a principle, highlighting the content itself, with a slightly more formal tone; こと simply turns the action into a noun — concise, and more common in everyday speech. Then check how the part before it ends: when a noun or な-adjective ends in 「だ」, only ということ works — 「学生だということ」 is fine, 「学生だこと」 is not.

groups.note: Both report what others or society say or think, not the speaker's own judgment

items.diff: と言われている is usually something passed along by word of mouth (old sayings, legends); と考えられている is usually a view based on research or reasoning — a tendency, not a hard rule.

this.tr: Since long ago, people have said that ginger warms the body.

that.tr: Based on many studies, ginger is thought to warm the body.

items.explain: Look at the clues before it: 「昔から」, legends, sayings → usually と言われている; reasoned inferences like 「研究から」「調査によると」 → mostly と考えられている, common in scientific writing. The two are often interchangeable, just with a different feel: 言われている is like “everyone says so”, 考えられている like “it's reasonably believed”.

items.title: 〜とされている (is regarded as)
items.diff: と言われている is “everyone says so” and is common in speech too; とされている is “is regarded as”, more formal and closer to a settled conclusion.

this.tr: People say this hot spring is good for stiff shoulders.

that.tr: This hot spring is regarded as effective for stiff shoulders.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same, passing on a widely accepted view; the difference is register: と言われている is “everyone says so” and works both in conversation and in writing; とされている is “is regarded as”, more formal and like an official conclusion, common in news, textbooks and descriptions of tourist spots — in casual conversation it would sound stiff.

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: と言われている is a belief that's been widely held for a long time; そうだ passes on one specific piece of news you heard.

this.tr: Since ancient times, it has been said that gods dwell on Mt. Fuji.

that.tr: According to the news, Mt. Fuji got its first snow this morning.

items.explain: Look at the time and source: 「昔から」「一般に」 — many people have said it for a long time → と言われている; 「ニュースによると」「今朝」 — a piece of news you just heard from somewhere → そうだ.

groups.note: 書いてある ↔ 書いている: just one kana apart

items.diff: 書いてある is “it says / is written”, the words are already there; 書いている is “is writing”, someone has pen in hand.

this.tr: The blackboard says “No class tomorrow.”

that.tr: The teacher is writing “No class tomorrow” on the blackboard.

items.explain: Just あ vs. い: てある doesn't say who wrote it, and the sentence starts from where it's written (黒板に); ている has the writer in front (先生が), describing an action in progress. When reading a notice or manual and saying “it says…”, always use 書いてある.

groups.note: Both report what people generally say or think, not the speaker's own judgment

items.diff: と考えられている is usually a view based on research or reasoning; と言われている is usually something passed along by word of mouth (old sayings, legends) — a tendency, not a hard rule.

this.tr: Based on many studies, ginger is thought to warm the body.

that.tr: Since long ago, people have said that ginger warms the body.

items.explain: Look at the clues before it: reasoned inferences like 「研究から」「調査によると」 → mostly と考えられている, common in scientific writing; 「昔から」, legends, sayings → usually と言われている. The two are often interchangeable, just with a different feel: 考えられている is like “it's reasonably believed”, 言われている like “everyone says so”.

items.title: 〜とされている (is regarded as)
items.diff: と考えられている stresses that it's a view inferred from evidence; とされている is more formal, like a conclusion accepted by scholars or authorities.

this.tr: This mural is thought to have been painted 2,000 years ago.

that.tr: This mural is held to have been painted 2,000 years ago.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; the difference is tone: と考えられている stresses that this is a view inferred from evidence, leaving some room for doubt, common in scientific explanations; とされている is more formal, like a view already endorsed by scholars or authorities, common in descriptions of history, cultural artifacts and traditions.

groups.note: Both pass on news you got from someone else

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: と聞いた highlights “I heard it” and can say who you heard it from; そうだ just passes the news itself on to the listener.

this.tr: I heard from a friend that Tanaka is getting married.

that.tr: I hear Tanaka is getting married.

items.explain: Check whether it says who you heard it from: 「友達から」「先生に」 + と聞いた, the subject is “me”, the one who heard; with そうだ the focus is on the news itself, and the source is usually given with 「〜によると」. Also, と聞いた is an ordinary past tense, while hearsay そうだ has no past form (you don't say 「結婚するそうだった」).

groups.note: なると思っている ↔ なろうと思っている — plain form and volitional form differ by just one sound

items.diff: Plain form + と思っている is an opinion or expectation about how things will be; volitional form + と思っている is an intention to do something yourself.

this.tr: He's convinced he'll become a doctor.

that.tr: He's planning to become a doctor.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in 「なる」 vs. 「なろう」 — said quickly, just one 「う」 apart: plain form (なる) → he believes things will turn out this way, an opinion or expectation; volitional form (なろう) → he intends to do it himself, a plan. With 「ている」, both mean the thought has been held for some time, and both can describe someone else's thoughts.

groups.note: Both mean “to think that…”

items.diff: と思っている is a thought held over a period of time and can also describe others' thoughts; と思う is the speaker's view at this moment.

this.tr: I've always thought this method is the best.

that.tr: After all, I think this method is the best.

items.explain: Check whether the thought has been there all along: with 「ずっと」「前から」, describing a thought held for some time → と思っている; stating your view on the spot, say in a discussion → と思う. Also, to describe someone else's thoughts you need と思っている (兄は〜と思っている); you can't say 「兄は〜と思う」.

groups.note: Both come from 「AをBとする」 — “to treat A as B, to set A as B”

items.diff: 「AをBとする」 actively says “set A as B”; 「AはBとされている」 is its passive, not saying who set it, only the result.

this.tr: In this exam, 60 points or more counts as a pass.

that.tr: The school sets 60 points or more as a pass.

items.explain: Look at the particles: 「〜を〜とする」 can have the deciding party before it (学校は, 会社は), common in the original text of regulations; 「〜は／が〜とされている」 hides the decision-maker and just states the accepted or established result, so it's more common in explanatory writing and news. The mid-sentence 「〜として」 (AをBとして) is the same expression.

groups.note: Both report generally accepted statements or views, not the speaker's own judgment

items.diff: とされている is more formal and sounds more settled, and can also mean “defined as” by law or rule; と考えられている is a view reached by reasoning.

this.tr: Under the law, people aged 18 and over are defined as adults.

that.tr: Based on fossil research, birds are thought to be descendants of dinosaurs.

items.explain: Look at the basis: something set by law, rules or authorities → only とされている (here it's not a “guess” but a “rule”); a view inferred from fossils, data or research → と考えられている. とされている can also express a generally accepted view, but it's more formal and sounds more settled than と考えられている.

items.diff: とされている is “is (officially) regarded as”, and only it can be used for laws, rules and definitions; と言われている is “everyone says so”.

this.tr: Under the law, people aged 18 and over are defined as adults.

that.tr: Since long ago, people have said ginger is good for colds.

items.explain: Look at where the statement comes from: officially set by laws, rules, definitions (法律では, 規則では) → only とされている; passed along by word of mouth, sayings (昔から) → と言われている. For general beliefs either works, and it's just a tendency: とされている is more formal and sounds more settled, common in news and textbooks.

groups.note: Both are written 「とか」: in pairs mid-sentence it lists; alone at the end it's hearsay

items.diff: とか in pairs mid-sentence → listing “…and… and such”; a single とか at the end → uncertain hearsay, “I hear…”.

this.tr: I bought meat, vegetables and stuff at the supermarket.

that.tr: I hear Tanaka is getting married next month.

items.explain: Look at where とか is and how many there are: mid-sentence, often in a pair (AとかBとか), with a predicate after → listing; a single one at the end with nothing after → passing on hearsay you're not sure of, close to 「〜そうだ」 but vaguer.

groups.note: Both list a few examples, implying there are others

items.diff: とか〜とか is casual and can also attach to verbs; や〜など works in both speech and writing but only attaches to nouns.

this.tr: Hey, is there milk or eggs or something in the fridge?

that.tr: There's milk, eggs and so on in the fridge.

items.explain: Look at the tone: casual talk between friends → とか〜とか; です・ます sentences and writing → や〜など. Also, とか can attach to verbs (掃除するとか), but や can't.

items.diff: とか〜とか attaches to both nouns and verbs and is fairly casual; たり〜たりする only attaches to verbs and is the standard way to list actions.

this.tr: On my days off I go to movies, shopping and stuff.

that.tr: On my days off I watch movies, go shopping and so on.

wrong.why: たり can only follow a verb's た-form

items.explain: Look at what it attaches to: nouns like 映画, 買い物 just take とか; to list actions, use the verb's た-form + り (見たり, したり), and add 「する」 at the end. たり can't attach to nouns; とか can attach to both, but it's more casual.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — “in that situation” (ところが was originally 「〜たところが」)

items.diff: ところが starts a sentence and the result always goes against expectations; たところ follows a verb, “after doing it, (I found)…”, and the result isn't necessarily surprising.

this.tr: I took the medicine. But the fever didn't go down.

that.tr: I took the medicine, and the fever went down.

items.explain: Look at position and result: ところが starts a new sentence on its own, followed by something contrary to expectations (took the medicine but the fever stayed); たところ comes right after a verb's た-form, and the result can be surprising or perfectly natural (took the medicine and the fever went down).

groups.note: ところが ↔ ところで: only the last character differs

items.diff: ところが is “unexpectedly, but”, the next sentence overturns what was expected; ところで is “by the way”, switching to another topic.

this.tr: I thought the exam would be easy. But I couldn't do it at all.

that.tr: Good job on the exam. By the way, are you free this weekend?

items.explain: Check whether the two sentences are related: the second overturns what the first expected (thought it was easy → couldn't do it at all) → ところが; the second starts an unrelated topic, often a question → ところで. When reading, just check whether the last character is が or で.

groups.note: Both express contrast: “but, however”

items.diff: ところが is only for unexpected outcomes; しかし is general contrast and can also introduce an opinion.

this.tr: I rushed over, only to find the shop already closed.

that.tr: This plan is good. However, it costs too much.

items.explain: Look at the second half: something that already happened, contrary to expectations (usually past tense) → ところが; stating your own view or raising a problem → しかし. ところが can't be followed by your own opinion or a request.

items.title: でも (contrast)
items.diff: ところが only narrates an unexpected fact; でも is casual contrast and can also be followed by your own decision or excuse.

this.tr: The forecast said it would be sunny. But it started raining in the afternoon.

that.tr: These clothes are expensive. But I'm buying them.

wrong.why: ところが can't be followed by your own will or decision

items.explain: Look at the second half: a fact that already happened and was unexpected → ところが (でも also works in speech); your own decision, wish or excuse (買う, 頑張る) → only でも. でも leans casual, ところが leans narrative.

groups.note: Both mean “in accordance with…”

items.title: 〜にしたがって (in accordance with)
items.diff: とおりに is “doing it exactly as…” and can directly follow 「言った」「書いてある」; にしたがって follows nouns like 「指示」「規則」, stresses compliance, and is more formal.

this.tr: I wrote it just as the teacher said.

that.tr: I wrote it following the teacher's instructions.

wrong.why: In the sense “in accordance with”, にしたがって must follow a noun

items.explain: First look at what comes before: verbs like 「言った」「書いてある」 → とおりに; nouns like 「指示」「ルール」「命令」 → にしたがって (with nouns you can also say 指示どおりに). にしたがって is common in announcements and regulations (係員の指示に従って…); everyday speech mostly uses とおりに.

groups.note: Both mean an action or state “keeps going”

items.diff: 続けている stresses a long duration without stopping; ている only says the action is in progress.

this.tr: He's been talking for three whole hours already.

that.tr: He's on the phone right now.
