items.explain: Look at the time words: 「三時間も」「ずっと」 stress it's gone on a long time without a break → 続ける (attaches to the ます-stem: 話し + 続ける); 「今」 just says it's happening right now → ている.

items.diff: 続ける is continuously doing an action; っぱなし is doing something and then leaving it, so the state just stays, usually with annoyance.

this.tr: I walked for two whole hours in the rain.

that.tr: I went out and left the window open.

items.explain: Look at the action itself: actions you can keep doing, like 歩く, 話す → 続ける; one-off actions like 開ける, つける, never undone afterward so the state stays (window left open, light left on) → っぱなし, often with a “that's sloppy” tone.

groups.note: Both come from casual 「って」 — equivalent to 「と／という」

items.title: 〜って (quoting at sentence end)
items.diff: Adding 「感じ」 at the end gives your own impression; 「って」 alone passes on what someone else said (I hear).

this.tr: The new teacher seems kind of nice.

that.tr: I hear the new teacher is nice.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「感じ」: just 「って」 at the end → equivalent to 「と言っていた」, passing on what someone said; with 「感じ」 after → that's 「という感じ」, describing an impression you yourself got.

groups.note: Both express your own feelings or impressions

items.title: 〜感じがする
items.diff: Similar meaning: って感じ is young people's casual speech and follows a sentence directly; 感じがする is standard, preceded by a noun-modifying form.

this.tr: This place feels kind of pricey.

that.tr: I somehow get the feeling this place is pricey.

items.explain: Look at the setting and how it attaches: casual talk with friends → って感じ, right after a sentence (高そうって感じ); talking to elders or in writing → 感じがする, with a noun-modifying form before it (高そうな感じ, 静かな感じ).

items.title: 〜みたいだ (comparison)
items.diff: って感じ is “that's exactly the vibe”, summing up your overall impression; みたいだ is usually “it isn't really, but it's like…”.

this.tr: Blue sky, white clouds. Now that's summer.

that.tr: It's only April, but it feels like summer.

items.explain: Look at the clues before it: 「まさに」「いかにも」 — what's in front of you has exactly that feel, and you sum up the impression in a phrase → って感じ, casual and vague; 「まだ４月なのに」 — you know it's not summer but compare it to summer → みたいだ (ようだ in writing).

groups.note: Both come from the quotative 「と」 — って is the casual form of 「と／という」

items.diff: って at the end of a sentence is a casual shortcut; と言っていました is a complete, polite report.

this.tr: Hey, I heard there's no class tomorrow.

that.tr: The teacher said there's no class tomorrow.

items.explain: って can replace 「と」, and at the end of a sentence it can even drop 「言っていた」, meaning “(someone) said… / I hear…” — only between friends and family; to a teacher or boss, or in formal settings, say the full 「と言っていました」.

items.diff: Same meaning, both bring up a term to be explained: って is casual among friends; というのは is the formal version.

this.tr: Hey, what's 「おでん」?

that.tr: Professor, what is 「おでん」?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: friends → 〜って何？; teachers, bosses, or in writing → 〜というのは何ですか. って is also often used to share impressions (日本の夏って暑いね), where it's equivalent to 「は」 but with a “speaking of…” nuance.

items.diff: 「って」 alone at the end passes on what someone else said (I hear); adding 「感じ」 gives your own impression.

this.tr: I hear the new teacher is nice.

that.tr: The new teacher seems kind of nice.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「感じ」: just 「って」 at the end → equivalent to 「と言っていた」, passing on what someone said; with 「感じ」 after → that's 「という感じ」, describing an impression you yourself got.

groups.note: Both come from the volitional 「う」 (classical 「む」) — ましょう = ます + う

items.diff: 〜(よ)う is plain style, used with friends and family; ましょう is polite style.

this.tr: Hey, let's get going soon.

that.tr: Sir, shall we get going soon?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: friends, family → 行こう, 食べよう; superiors, elders, people you don't know well → 行きましょう. Same meaning: both voice your own intention while inviting the other person to join in.

items.diff: 「〜(よ)うか」 is plain style, for family and friends; ましょうか is polite style.

this.tr: Mom, want me to carry that bag?

that.tr: Professor, shall I carry that bag for you?

items.explain: Same meaning; look at who you're talking to: family, friends → 持とうか (for godan verbs, the う-row sound changes to the お-row + う); teachers, bosses, customers → 持ちましょうか.

items.diff: 〜(よ)う on its own is an on-the-spot decision or an invitation; adding 「と思う」 tells someone else about your plan.

this.tr: All right, I'm going to Japan this summer vacation!

that.tr: I'm thinking of going to Japan over summer vacation.

items.explain: Look at who it's for: making up your own mind (よし、〜しよう) or inviting someone to join → volitional form on its own; telling someone else your plan → 〜(よ)うと思います. If you just say 「夏休みは日本に行こう」 to someone, it sounds like you're inviting them to come along.

groups.note: Both express your own will or intention

items.diff: 〜(よ)う is a decision made at the moment of speaking and only about yourself; つもりだ is a plan already in place and can describe others too.

this.tr: All right, starting tomorrow I'll run every morning!

that.tr: My older brother plans to run every morning starting tomorrow.

wrong.why: The volitional form can't describe someone else's intention

items.explain: Look at the subject and setting: making up your own mind on the spot, talking to yourself → 走ろう; describing a plan decided long ago, or someone else's (兄, 彼) intention → 走るつもりだ.

groups.note: Both contrast two things

items.title: 〜に対して (contrast)
items.diff: This pattern is the most common contrast in everyday speech; のに対して is more formal, used for objective comparisons.

this.tr: My older brother is tall, but my younger brother is short.

that.tr: My older brother is tall, whereas my younger brother is short.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: in speech or a diary use 「〜は〜が、〜は〜」; objective comparisons in reports, news and papers mostly use 「〜のに対して」. のに対して follows the plain form — don't drop the 「の」 (高いのに対して).

groups.note: Both come from the sense of 「する」 meaning “to have, to show a certain appearance” (not “to do”)

items.diff: をしている describes visible looks, shapes and colors; がする describes things you smell, hear or taste.

this.tr: This cat has blue eyes.

that.tr: This flower has a sweet scent.

items.explain: Neither 「する」 means “do”; they mean “have, show”. Look at the noun: visible features like 目, 髪, 形, 色 → 〜をしている (with を, usually in ている); sensory impressions like 匂い, 音, 味 → 〜がする (with が).

groups.note: Both can describe what a person or thing looks like

items.diff: 「長い髪をしている」 depicts “long hair” as one overall feature; 「髪が長い」 states “long” as the predicate.

this.tr: She has long hair.

that.tr: Her hair is long.

wrong.why: The noun before をしている must have a modifier

items.explain: Similar meaning; look at where the adjective is: before the noun (長い髪) + をしている paints a picture, often used to describe a character; at the end of the sentence (髪が長い) is a direct statement. With をしている the noun must have a modifier — you can't just say 「髪をしている」.

groups.note: Both mean “easy to…, tends to…”

items.diff: やすい says “easy to do” or “likely to happen”; がち says “often, tends to (do something bad)”, stressing frequency.

this.tr: This book has large print, so it's easy to read.

that.tr: When I'm busy, I tend to skip breakfast.

wrong.why: がち only describes a frequent bad tendency, not “easy to read”

items.explain: Ask whether it's about “ease” or “frequency”: judging whether something is easy to do (読みやすい, 使いやすい) → only やすい; something bad that happens often (抜きがち, 遅れがち) → がち. がち can also attach directly to nouns (病気がち); やすい can't.

items.title: 〜っぽい (quick to…)
items.diff: やすい works for both things and people; っぽい only describes a person's character, “quick to…”, and is casual.

this.tr: Katakana words are easy to forget.

that.tr: My dad has gotten forgetful lately.

wrong.why: っぽい can only describe a person's character

items.explain: Look at the subject: things and matters (カタカナの言葉, このコップ) → やすい (忘れやすい, 割れやすい); a person's character or habits (父, 彼) → っぽい (忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい), though 忘れやすい also works here. っぽい only attaches to a few verbs.

groups.note: Both have to do with “things you'll do in the future, plans”

items.diff: 予定 is an already-scheduled plan; つもり is a personal intention.

this.tr: The plane is scheduled to arrive at three.

that.tr: I plan to go back to my home country over summer vacation.

wrong.why: A plane has no “intentions”; schedules use 予定

items.explain: Look at the subject: scheduled things like flights, meetings and events, or arrangements set by a company or other people → 予定; a person's own thinking → つもり.

items.diff: 予定だ is something already on the schedule; (よ)うと思う is a current intention, possibly one that just occurred to you.

this.tr: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Osaka next Monday.

that.tr: The weather's nice, so I think I'll go for a walk this afternoon.

items.explain: Check for a specific date and arrangement: something already on the calendar like 「来週の月曜日に」 → 予定です; something that just came to mind because the weather's nice and isn't settled yet → (よ)うと思う.

items.diff: 予定 is a one-off scheduled plan; ことになっている is a rule, or an arrangement fixed in advance by others that must be followed.

this.tr: There's a meeting scheduled for ten tomorrow.

that.tr: In this dorm, the gate is closed at ten every night.

items.explain: Ask whether it's a one-off arrangement or a standing rule: a specific schedule for tomorrow or next week → 予定; dorm or company rules, arrangements to be followed every time (毎晩, いつも) → ことになっている. 予定 can't express a rule.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — “a certain appearance or manner”

items.diff: ように is a goal not yet reached, still being worked toward; ようになった is a result already achieved.

this.tr: I practice every day so that I can read kanji.

that.tr: Because I practiced every day, I can now read kanji.

items.explain: Both sentences are about the same thing, seen from different points in time. Look at what follows ように: if it's followed by what you're doing for it (毎日練習している) → that's a goal; if 「なった」 follows directly and ends the sentence → it has already come about.

items.diff: ように + a specific action is “doing something so that…”; ようにしている is “making a habit of trying to…”.

this.tr: I'm wearing a mask so I won't catch a cold.

that.tr: I try to make sure I don't catch colds.

items.explain: Look at what follows ように: another specific action (マスクをしている) → purpose, “so that…”; ending directly with 「している」 → ようにしている, meaning you're always careful and make an effort to do it.

items.diff: ように + an ordinary action is doing something yourself for a purpose; ように言う is telling someone else to do it.

this.tr: I wrote it down in my planner so I wouldn't forget.

that.tr: My teacher told me not to forget.

items.explain: Look at the verb after ように: things you do yourself for a purpose, like メモする, 練習する → purpose ように; speech verbs like 言う, 頼む, 伝える → ように言う, reporting someone else's request, often with 「〜に」 before it showing who said it.

items.diff: ような／ように／みたいな are modifier forms derived from ようだ, mostly used mid-sentence for comparisons; ようだ／みたいだ at the end of a sentence can also express inference (seems like…), besides comparison.

this.tr: It's like something out of a dream.
It was a day as fun as a dream.
It's just like something out of a dream, huh.

that.tr: The lights are off. Looks like no one's home.

items.explain: Look at the position and 「まるで」: followed by a noun (話) or an adjective/verb (楽しい), often with 「まるで」 before → comparison; at the end, closing the sentence, with an observed clue before it (電気が消えている) → the speaker's inference, “it seems…”. Casual みたいだ works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “like…” or “so that…”, and are easy to mix up

items.diff: のように is an ordinary comparison; かのように is “as if…” when you know it isn't so, with a sharper contrast.

this.tr: He's as excited as a little kid.

that.tr: He's smiling as if nothing had happened.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: 「noun + の」 (子ども) → ordinary ように, a simple comparison; a sentence that isn't actually true (何もなかった) + か → かのように, stressing the gap between appearance and reality, rather formal.

items.title: 〜らしい (typical)
items.diff: のような is “like…”, not actually being it; らしい is “having the qualities of…”, actually being it, and a typical one at that.

this.tr: She talks like a man.

that.tr: He's a very manly guy.

items.explain: Check whether the subject and the noun after are the same kind of thing: 彼女 isn't a man, so comparing her to one → 男のような; 彼 is a man, and very much like one → 男らしい. Likewise, 「春らしい天気」 is very typical spring weather in spring, while 「春のような天気」 is usually spring-like weather in another season.

items.diff: ように follows states like the potential or negative form; ために follows actions you can control.

this.tr: I study every day so that I can speak Japanese.

that.tr: I study every day in order to pass N1.

wrong.why: The potential form needs ように

items.explain: Look at the verb before ように／ため: potential forms, negative forms, states that happen on their own like 「話せる」「忘れない」「見える」 → ように; 「合格する」 is an action you decide to do → ために.

items.diff: のように is “like…”, and can be followed by an adjective or verb; と同じ says things are actually “the same”.

this.tr: My older sister is as kind as my mother.

that.tr: My older sister graduated from the same university as my mother.

wrong.why: 同じ can't directly modify an adjective

items.explain: Look at what follows: to say “as (kind, pretty) as…”, followed by an adjective or verb → のように; 「同じ」 is followed by a noun (大学, 色) or 「だ」 → the two really are the same. Since both can come out as “just like…” in English, it's easy to write ✗母と同じ優しい.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — “a certain appearance or manner”

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ように言う is telling someone else to do it; ように + an ordinary action is doing something yourself for a purpose.

this.tr: My teacher told me not to forget.

that.tr: I wrote it down in my planner so I wouldn't forget.

items.explain: Look at the verb after ように: speech verbs like 言う, 頼む, 伝える → ように言う, reporting someone else's request, often with 「〜に」 before it showing who said it; things you do yourself for a purpose, like メモする, 練習する → purpose ように.

items.diff: ように言う is telling someone else to do it; ようにする is making an effort to do it yourself.

this.tr: My doctor told me to eat vegetables every day.

that.tr: I try to eat vegetables every day.

items.explain: Look at who made the request: a demand from a doctor, teacher or boss → ように言う／ように言われた, often with 「〜に」 before it showing the speaker; a goal you set for yourself → ようにする.

groups.note: Both report someone else's request or instruction

items.diff: ように言う only reports the content of the request, objectively and softly; てくれと／なと言う keeps the tone of the original words (“please…”, “don't…”), and is more direct.

this.tr: The department head told me to come in early tomorrow.
The department head told me not to be late tomorrow.

that.tag: くれと · tone of a request
that.tr: The department head said to me, “Come in early tomorrow.”

that.tag: なと · tone of a prohibition
that.tr: The department head said to me, “Don't be late tomorrow.”

items.explain: Check whether what's before 「と」 keeps the tone of the original words: 「来てくれ」「遅れるな」 are what the other person actually said → と言う; rephrasing the content as 「来るように」「遅れないように」 → indirect report, more common with bosses and in formal settings.

groups.note: Both come from the volitional 「う」 (classical 「む」) — “going to…”

items.diff: 〜(よ)うと思う tells someone else about your plan; the volitional form on its own is an on-the-spot decision or an invitation.

this.tr: I'm thinking of going to Japan over summer vacation.

that.tr: All right, I'm going to Japan this summer vacation!

items.explain: Look at who it's for: telling someone else your plan → 〜(よ)うと思います; making up your own mind (よし、〜しよう) or inviting someone to join → volitional form on its own. If you just say 「夏休みは日本に行こう」 to someone, it sounds like you're inviting them to come along.

groups.note: 行こうと思う ↔ 行くと思う: just one sound apart

items.diff: Volitional form + と思う is your own intention; plain form + と思う is a guess or opinion.

this.tr: I'm thinking of going tomorrow.

that.tr: I think Tanaka will go tomorrow.

items.explain: Just 「行こう」 vs. 「行く」: volitional form (行こう) → the speaker's own intention, “I want to do it”; plain form (行く) → a guess or opinion, “I think (he) will go”. One sound apart when read, completely different meanings.

groups.note: Both express intentions or plans for the future

items.diff: (よ)うと思う is usually a thought that just came to you as you speak; つもりだ is a firmer plan decided long ago.

this.tr: It's raining, so I think I'll take a taxi home today.

that.tr: I've been planning to study abroad next year for a while.

items.explain: Look at when it was decided: thought of on the spot because it's raining → (よ)うと思う; a plan settled long ago that you're preparing for (前から) → つもりだ.

items.diff: (よ)うと思う is a current intention, possibly one that just occurred to you; 予定だ is something already on the schedule.

this.tr: The weather's nice, so I think I'll go for a walk this afternoon.

that.tr: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Osaka next Monday.

items.explain: Check for a specific date and arrangement: something that just came to mind because the weather's nice and isn't settled yet → (よ)うと思う; something already on the calendar like 「来週の月曜日に」 → 予定です.

items.diff: (よ)うと思う is just an intention in your head and may still change; ことにした is a decision formally made after thinking it over.

this.tr: I'm thinking of studying abroad next year.

that.tr: After thinking it over a lot, I decided to study abroad.

items.explain: Check for a “making up your mind” process: a decision made after 「いろいろ考えて」「迷ったけど」 → ことにした; just voicing what you're thinking while still considering it → (よ)うと思う, softer in tone.

groups.note: Both come from the classical negative 「ず」 + 「に」 — “in a state of not doing…”

items.title: 〜ずに済む
items.diff: ずに is followed by “what you did instead”; ずに済む is “got by without having to…”, with relief.

this.tr: I didn't take a taxi today; I walked home.

that.tr: The trains were still running, so I didn't have to take a taxi.

items.explain: Look at what follows ずに: another action (歩いて帰った) → “instead of A, did B”; 「済む」 → something you thought you'd have to do turned out unnecessary, often with a “luckily, thank goodness” feeling.

items.diff: ずに is “without doing…”; ずにはいられない is “can't stay without doing” → “can't help doing” — the opposite meaning.

this.tr: I listened to the end without laughing.

that.tr: It was so funny I couldn't help laughing.

items.explain: Check whether 「はいられない」 follows ずに: followed by an action (話を聞いた) → didn't do the first thing; followed by 「はいられない」 → “can't stay without doing it”, i.e. couldn't help doing it, often with a reason like 「あまりに〜て」 before it.

groups.note: Both mean “without doing… (and instead…)”

items.diff: Same meaning: ずに is more formal, and 「する」 becomes 「せずに」; ないで is for everyday speech.

this.tr: I took the exam without studying.

that.tr: I took the exam without studying.

wrong.why: 「する」 must become 「せずに」

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the register and how it attaches: writing and formal settings often use ずに; speech mostly uses ないで (しないで). ずに replaces 「ない」 in the ない-form (言わ + ずに), but 「する」 is an exception: say 「せずに」. Also, only ないで can take 「ください」.

items.diff: ずに is for everyday “without… did…”; ことなく is more formal, often stressing “not once” over a long period.

this.tr: I went to school without eating breakfast.

that.tr: For ten years, he kept working without taking a single day off.

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: not doing something in daily life → ずに; in writing or speeches, stressing “never once over a long time” (一日も, 一度も) → ことなく. ことなく follows the dictionary form (休む + ことなく); ずに follows the ない-form (休ま + ずに).

groups.note: Both can be translated as “each / every…”

items.diff: ずつ gives the amount per time or per person; ごとに says how often, once per interval or unit.

this.tr: Take two tablets each time.

that.tr: Take the medicine every six hours.

items.explain: Look at what the number word expresses: an amount handed out or used (２錠, 一人３個) → ずつ; a time interval or unit (６時間, 一駅) → ごとに. They can be used together: 「６時間ごとに２錠ずつ飲む」.

items.diff: ずつ is the amount actually given to each person; 当たり is a value calculated per unit, “per person (in total)…”.

this.tr: I gave the children three mandarins each.

that.tr: The party fee is 3,000 yen per person.

items.explain: Look at what the sentence is doing: actually handing things out one by one, like 配る, あげる → ずつ; calculated figures like amounts of money, ratios, statistics (会費, 消費量) → 当たり, usually as 「一人当たり + amount」.

groups.note: Both come from 「上げる」 — originally “to lift up, send up”

items.diff: ます-stem + 上げる is “to finish, complete”; て-form + あげる is “to do for someone”.

this.tr: I finished writing the report in a single night.

that.tr: I wrote the letter for my little sister.

items.explain: Look at what's before 「あげる」: directly joined to the ます-stem (書き), it's a compound verb meaning finishing a laborious task; て-form (書いて) + あげる is giving and receiving, doing something for someone, often with 「〜のために」「代わりに」 in the sentence. Both were originally 「上げる」: push up to the top → finish; hand up to someone → do for them.

groups.note: Both mean “finishing” an action

items.diff: 上げる stresses putting in effort to produce a finished piece; 終わる only objectively says an action ended.

this.tr: After three months, I finally finished writing my graduation thesis.

that.tr: I finally finished reading this book.

items.explain: Check whether the action produces a “work”: writing a thesis, building a model, raising a child → 上げる, with a sense of achievement, “finally done”; eating, reading, watching a movie, where the action simply ends → 終わる. Note that 「読み上げる」 means “to read aloud”, not “to finish reading”.

items.diff: 上げる is producing a finished work; 切る is using up completely or seeing it through, with nothing left.

this.tr: It took a year, but I finished knitting a sweater.

that.tr: Knitting the sweater used up all my yarn.

items.explain: Look at the object of the action: something produced (セーター, 論文) → 上げる; something consumed (毛糸, お金, 体力), or a process from start to finish (走り切る) → 切る, often with 「全部」「最後まで」. The negative 「〜切れない」 (食べ切れない) carries the same “all of it” meaning.

groups.note: All come from あまり (余り) — originally “exceeding, surplus”

items.diff: あまりに／あまりの／〜のあまり all mean “so much that…”; あまり + negative means “not very…”.

this.tr: These clothes are too expensive for me to buy.

this.tag: あまりの · because of such…
this.tr: The price was so high that it shocked me.
I was so nervous I couldn't even get my voice out.

that.tr: These clothes aren't very expensive.

items.explain: Look at whether what follows is a negative or a result: a negative like 「高くない」 → あまり = not very; a result of “it went too far, so…” (買えない、驚いた、声が出なかった) → あまりに／あまりの／〜のあまり. 「余り」 originally means “exceeding”: exceeding the limit = too much; negated, “not exceeding by much” = not very.

groups.note: All mean “too, excessively”

items.diff: Same meaning; あまりに leans written, with a feeling of “really far too…”, and often leads to a result; すぎる is the most common everyday way to say it.

this.tag: あまりに · written · leads to result
this.tr: This year's exam was so difficult that half of the candidates failed.

that.tr: This question is way too hard. I don't get it at all.

items.explain: Look at the register and the position: あまりに is an adverb placed before the adjective, common in writing and narration, and often followed by a “so…” result (不合格となった); すぎる sticks onto the stem (難しすぎる、食べすぎた) and is most common in chat and complaints. The two are also often used together: あまりにも難しすぎる.

groups.note: All mean “per…, every…”

items.diff: 当たり calculates an “amount” averaged over each unit; ごとに describes an “action” repeated at every interval.

this.tr: This machine can make 100 pieces per hour.

that.tr: This machine is stopped for inspection every hour.

items.explain: Look at what follows: a quantity (100個、3000円、5キロ) → 当たり, used to calculate rates and averages; a repeated action (点検する、休憩する、バスが来る) → ごとに.

items.title: 〜につき (per…)
items.diff: 当たり is mostly used for averages worked out in statistics; につき is used for rules about how much is charged or given per unit, and is very formal.

this.tr: Rice consumption per person in Japan is decreasing year by year.

that.tr: The participation fee is 1,000 yen per person.

items.explain: Look at where the number comes from: data obtained by averaging a total and used for comparison (消費量、収入、売り上げ) → 当たり; notices and price lists that set how much is charged or handed out per unit → につき.

items.diff: ずつ means actually giving each person the same amount; 当たり is a rate calculated per unit.

this.tr: There are 12 in total, so that makes 3 per person.

that.tr: I gave the children three sweets each.

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: actions of actually handing things out, like 配る、もらう、食べる → ずつ, attached directly to the quantity being distributed (３個ずつ); a calculated average or rate → 当たり, preceded by a unit such as 「一人」「１時間」 and often followed by 「〜になる」 or 「〜の + noun」.

groups.note: Both come from 合う — originally “two things coming together”

items.title: 〜に合わせて (to match)
items.diff: 〜合う means both sides doing the same action to each other; 〜に合わせて means adjusting yourself to some standard.

this.tr: The two of them danced holding hands.

that.tr: We danced to the music.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: masu-stem + 合う (取り合う、助け合う) — the subject is two or more people and the action goes back and forth between them; noun + に合わせて (音楽に、相手の都合に) — one side adjusts to the other. Both come from 「合う」: either both sides' actions come together, or you make yourself fit the other.

groups.note: Both come from the contrastive のに — “even though…, (in reality)…”

items.title: 〜のに (even though)
items.diff: 〜のに states that “the reality turned out the opposite”; with 〜ば〜のに it's a hypothesis, and the sentence-final のに drops the second half, leaving only regret.

this.tr: If I'd gotten up a bit earlier, I would have made it.

that.tr: Even though I got up early, I still didn't make it.

items.explain: Look at whether the first half is a fact or a hypothesis: 「起きたのに」 — you really did get up → even though… still…; 「起きれば」 is a hypothesis and you didn't actually get up early → the sentence-final のに brings out regret that “it sadly didn't happen”.

groups.note: Both express regret about something that didn't happen

items.diff: 〜ばよかったのに is usually pity or reproach toward someone else; 〜ばよかった is usually your own regret.

this.tr: You should have come too. It was so much fun.

that.tr: I should have gone too.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: said to someone else (君も、あなたも) → add のに, with a tone of “what a shame” or “why didn't you…”; the subject is yourself (私も) → ばよかった, simple regret.

groups.note: Both come from ばかり — originally “only about this much”

items.diff: ばかりで sits mid-sentence and is followed by “so (they) don't do…”; てばかりいる ends the sentence and only says “always doing”.

this.tag: Mid-sentence · followed by what's not done
this.tr: My little brother does nothing but play and doesn't study at all.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play every day.

items.explain: Look at what follows ばかり: 「で、」 followed by something that should be done but isn't, or a bad result (勉強しない、何もしない) → ばかりで; 「いる」 closing the sentence → てばかりいる, which just describes always doing it.

items.diff: ばかりで means “only has this, lacks what it should have”; noun + ばかり means “nothing but this one thing”.

this.tr: This restaurant is just expensive; the taste is nothing special.

that.tr: This shop has nothing but expensive things.

items.explain: Look around ばかり: adjective or verb + ばかりで, followed by another clause saying “what it should have is missing” (味は普通だ) → it only has this, nothing else good about it; noun (物、肉) + ばかりだ → everything is of this one kind. (In speech, ばっかり works the same way.)

groups.note: ばかりで ↔ ばかりでなく ↔ ばかりに — only the last kana or two differ

items.diff: ばかりで is “only… and doesn't…”, with criticism; ばかりでなく is “not only… but also…”, adding on top.

this.tr: He does nothing but complain and doesn't help at all.

that.tr: Not only does he complain a lot, he often takes days off work too.

items.explain: Only 「なく」 is different: ばかりで is followed by something that should be done but isn't (何も手伝わない); ばかりでなく adds one more thing with 「も」 or 「まで」 (仕事も休む). Check whether the second half has 「も」 and you can tell them apart.

items.diff: ばかりで is “only… and doesn't…”; ばかりに is “just because…, it ended badly”.

this.tr: My older brother is all talk and never actually does anything.

that.tr: Just because I told one lie, I lost my friend's trust.

items.explain: Look at 「で」 vs. 「に」, then at the second half: ばかりで is followed by “what should be done isn't”, criticizing how things have been all along; ばかりに is mostly preceded by the ta-form (ついた、言った) and followed by an irreversible bad result caused by it, often with regret.

groups.note: ばかりでなく ↔ ばかりで — only 「なく」 is different

items.diff: ばかりでなく is “not only… but also…”, adding on top; ばかりで is “only… and doesn't…”, with criticism.

this.tr: Not only does he complain a lot, he often takes days off work too.

that.tr: He does nothing but complain and doesn't help at all.

items.explain: Only 「なく」 is different: ばかりでなく adds one more thing with 「も」 or 「まで」 (仕事も休む); ばかりで is followed by something that should be done but isn't (何も手伝わない). Check whether the second half has 「も」 and you can tell them apart.

groups.note: All mean “not only… but also…”

items.diff: Same meaning; だけでなく is the most common, often said as 「だけじゃなくて」 in speech; ばかりでなく is slightly more formal.

this.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap but tasty too.

that.tr: This place isn't just cheap, the food's good too.

items.explain: The two are basically interchangeable. Look at the register: chatting with friends, people usually say 「だけじゃなくて」; in writing and formal speech, both ばかりでなく and だけでなく work. In speech, ばかりでなく also becomes 「ばかりじゃなく」.

items.diff: ばかりでなく can be followed by a command or advice; ばかりか cannot, and it often carries a surprised “on top of that, even…”.

this.tr: Don't just eat vegetables — eat meat too.

that.tr: Not only did he not apologize, he even came to complain.

wrong.why: ばかりか cannot be followed by a command or advice

items.explain: Look at the second half: a command or advice like 「〜なさい」「〜てください」「〜ましょう」 → only ばかりでなく works; stating a surprising fact that goes even further, often paired with 「まで」 or 「さえ」 → ばかりか is more forceful.

items.diff: Same meaning; のみならず is more written and formal, common in news, speeches and academic papers.

this.tr: This song is popular not only with children but with adults too.

that.tr: This technology is highly rated not only in Japan but overseas as well.

items.explain: Look at the setting: everyday explanations → だけでなく／ばかりでなく; news reports, speeches, papers → のみならず, which goes well with stiffer expressions like 「評価されている」. のみならず can also stand alone at the start of a sentence, meaning “not only that”.

groups.note: All come from the classical べし — meaning “naturally, as it should be”

items.title: 〜べからず (prohibition)
items.diff: べきだ is “should do”; べからず is the classical “must not do”, found only on notices and in sayings.

this.tr: Promises should be kept.

that.tr: Keep off the grass.

items.explain: べき and べからず are both forms of the classical 「べし」 (ought to): べき = ought to do; べからず = べし + the classical negative 「ず」, ought not to do = must not. Look at where it appears: stating an opinion in everyday life → べきだ; park notices and sayings (働かざる者食うべからず) → べからず.

items.diff: べき is “should”; べく is the written “in order to…”, followed by the action you take.

this.tr: I should study Japanese more.

that.tr: I study every day in order to pass the exam.

items.explain: Only the last kana is different: べき is followed by 「だ」 or a noun (すべきこと), meaning should; べく is followed by a comma and the action you take for that purpose, equivalent to 「ために」, and common in news and writing. Both come from 「べし」.

groups.note: All used to say “you should do this”

items.diff: べきだ says “that's how it ought to be” from principle or duty; ほうがいい is advice given with the other person's interest in mind, and softer.

this.tr: If you've caused someone trouble, you should apologize.

that.tr: If you have a cold, you'd better go to bed early.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a general principle or the listener's specific situation: what's right for people in general, responsibilities → べきだ; “this would be good for you”, aimed at the person in front of you → ほうがいい. Using べきだ about someone else's private affairs sounds preachy.

items.diff: べきだ is the speaker's personal opinion that something “should” be done; なければならない is a rule or an objective obligation.

this.tr: I think young people should read more books.

that.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

items.explain: Look at whether it's an opinion or a rule: the speaker's own position, often with 「と思う」 → べきだ; laws, rules, things you can't not do → なければならない. English “should” usually corresponds to べきだ, and “must / have to” to なければならない.

items.title: 〜ものだ (is supposed to)
items.diff: べきだ is the speaker's own position; ものだ states common social sense — “that's just how it's supposed to be”.

this.tr: I think companies should give more days off.

that.tr: You're supposed to use keigo with your superiors.

items.explain: Look at whether the sentence has a personal “I” stance: 「私は〜と思う」, putting forward your own opinion, even one that differs from the general view → べきだ; rules and manners everyone agrees on (目上の人には、人に会ったら挨拶する) → ものだ, like an elder explaining common sense.

items.diff: べきだ mostly states a general principle; ことだ is advice to a specific person in front of you: “the best thing is to…”.

this.tr: Politicians should listen to the voice of the people.

that.tr: If you want to get good at Japanese, the best thing is to speak it every day.

items.explain: Look at who it's said to: how a group of people or society should behave → べきだ; to the person in front of you, about their specific goal (〜たいなら、〜ためには) → ことだ, like advice from a senior, and not used toward superiors.

groups.note: All come from the classical べし — meaning “naturally, as it should be”

items.title: 〜べからず (prohibition)
items.diff: べきではない is a reasoned “should not”; べからず is the classical “must not”, used on notices and in sayings.

this.tr: You shouldn't smoke in front of children.

that.tr: Keep off the grass.

items.explain: べからず is 「べし」 + the classical negative 「ず」 and, like べきではない, means “ought not to do”, but it's much stiffer and appears almost only on notices, signs and in sayings (働かざる者食うべからず). Look at where it appears: stating your own view → べきではない; a posted prohibition or old-style sign → べからず.

groups.note: All mean “shouldn't do, mustn't do”

items.diff: べきではない is “shouldn't” on principle, not necessarily backed by a rule; てはいけない is an explicit prohibition.

this.tr: It's not against the law, but you shouldn't make loud noise in the middle of the night.

that.tr: Diving is not allowed in this pool.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a rule behind it: an explicit ban such as a law, school rule or pool rule → てはいけない; no rule, but inappropriate in terms of morals or common sense → べきではない, often carrying an “I think” stance.

items.title: 〜ものではない (admonition)
items.diff: べきではない is the speaker's own judgment; ものではない lectures people based on common sense: “(people) just shouldn't do that”.

this.tr: I don't think we should push this plan forward now.

that.tr: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a specific matter or general decency: a specific plan or method, judged by the speaker from their own analysis (〜と思う) → べきではない; rules of decent behavior (人の悪口、目上の人に), like an elder lecturing → ものではない.

groups.note: Both come from 別 — meaning “separate, set apart”

items.diff: 別に〜ない is “not particularly…”; 〜は別として is “setting… aside for now”.

this.tr: These clothes aren't particularly expensive.

that.tr: Price aside, the design is nice.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「別」: 「別に」 + a sentence-final negative → nothing “separately worth mentioning” = not particularly; 「noun + は別として」, followed by another aspect → put this matter “separately to one side” = setting aside.

groups.note: Both pair with a negative, expressing the degree or tone of the negation

items.diff: あまり〜ない only states the degree, “not very”; 別に〜ない is “not really, nothing special”, with an indifferent tone.

this.tr: Do you like fish? — Not especially, but I can eat it.

that.tr: I don't like fish very much.

items.explain: Look at whether the speaker cares: あまり just says the degree is low; 別に means “no particular feeling about it”, often used to reply to someone and show indifference. Asked 「怒ってる？」, answering with just 「別に。」 means “it's nothing”, which sounds a bit cold.

items.diff: 全然〜ない is “not at all”, a strong negation; 別に〜ない is “not really…”, a light negation.

this.tr: Are you tired? — Not really.

that.tr: Are you tired? — Not at all.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the adverb. Look at the strength of the negation: 全然 is a complete denial, “not at all”; 別に just says “nothing special”, a flat tone that sometimes sounds like not wanting to talk about it.

groups.note: Both come from 振る — originally “to wave”, extended to body movements and outward appearance

items.diff: ぶり is how someone actually comes across; ふりをする is a deliberately put-on appearance that isn't really true.

this.tr: He works very conscientiously.

that.tr: He pretends to be diligent, but he's actually slacking off.

items.explain: Both come from 「振り」 (behavior, appearance). Look at whether a “but actually…” follows: ぶり describes real behavior and is often followed by an evaluation (真面目だ、見事だ); ふりをする is often followed by 「本当は」 or 「実は」, which overturns it.

items.diff: ぶり is a noun for how someone actually comes across; ぶる is a verb meaning to deliberately put on airs, and is negative.

this.tr: From the way he talks, he seems to know something.

that.tr: He's always acting the senior and talking as if he's so important.

items.explain: Look at the part of speech: 「〜ぶり」 is followed by particles (から、は、を) and used as a noun; 「〜ぶる」 conjugates (ぶって、ぶらないで) and is a verb meaning “to put on the air of…”, almost always critical (先輩ぶる、上品ぶる、偉ぶる).

groups.note: Both describe the “manner, way” of doing something

items.diff: ぶり is the “performance, manner” you actually observe, usually with an evaluation; 方 is a “way of doing” that can be taught and learned.

this.tr: I was impressed by the way Tanaka works.

that.tr: Tanaka taught me how to do the job.

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: evaluations like 感心する、驚く、すばらしい → 〜ぶり; words related to “method” like 教える、習う、分からない → 〜方. Likewise, 話し方 is how you speak (wording, accent), while 話しぶり is your manner while speaking.

groups.note: Both come from ては (said ちゃ in speech) — “if you do / don't do it, (it's no good)”

items.diff: 〜ちゃだめ directly says “don't do it”; 〜ちゃ、+ second half says “if you do that, …”, stating the consequence.

this.tr: Don't eat that much.

that.tr: If you eat that much, you'll get fat.

items.explain: ちゃ = ては, meaning “if you do it”. Look at what follows: directly 「だめ」 or 「いけない」 → doing that is no good = prohibition (ちゃいけない works the same); a bad result (太る、遅れる、困る) → just a warning about the consequence. After a noun or an 「ん」 sound it becomes では／じゃ (飲んじゃ = 飲んでは), on the same principle.

items.diff: 〜ちゃだめ is “doing it is no good” = prohibition; 〜なくちゃ is “not doing it is no good” = must.

this.tag: Doing it is no good · prohibition
this.tr: It's already late, so no video games.

that.tag: Not doing it is no good · must
that.tr: It's already late, I've got to go to bed.

items.explain: Both are contractions of ては: ちゃ = ては, なくちゃ = なくては. Look at whether 「なく」 comes before 「ちゃ」: しちゃだめ → doing it is no good = prohibition; 寝なくちゃ(いけない) → not doing it is no good = must, and the 「いけない」 at the end is often dropped. In speech people also say なきゃ (寝なきゃ), with the same meaning.

groups.note: ちゃ (= ては) ↔ ちゃう (= てしまう) — both are 「ちゃ」

items.diff: ちゃだめ is a prohibition, “don't…”; ちゃった is the casual form of てしまった, meaning “(accidentally) went and…”.

this.tr: Don't you eat the whole cake, okay?

that.tr: I ate the whole cake.

items.explain: Look at what follows ちゃ: 「だめ」「いけない」 → ちゃ = ては, a prohibition; 「う」「った」 → ちゃう = てしまう, meaning it's done or was done by accident, often with regret. Both are very common in speech and differ only in the next kana or two.

groups.note: All express prohibition: “don't…, you mustn't…”

items.diff: Same meaning; ちゃだめ／ちゃいけない are casual contractions, while てはいけない is the full form and can be used in formal settings.

this.tr: Hey, no running there!

that.tr: Running in the corridors is not allowed.

items.explain: Look at who's being addressed and the setting: parents to children or a casual reminder between friends → ちゃだめ (ちゃいけない works the same); school rules, notices, explaining to many people → てはいけません. Don't use ちゃ in essays.

items.diff: ちゃだめ is a direct prohibition, only for children or people you're close to; ないでください is a polite request that can be used with anyone.

this.tr: Ah, don't touch that!

that.tr: Excuse me, please don't touch the exhibits.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: your own child, people close to you → ちゃだめ; visitors, strangers, superiors → ないでください. Saying 「触っちゃだめ」 to a visitor would be very rude.

groups.note: All mean “not only…, but also…”

items.diff: Same meaning; だけでなく is the most common and works in both speech and writing; ばかりでなく is slightly more formal.

this.tr: Tanaka can speak not just English but Chinese too, you know.

that.tr: This study is useful not only in medicine but also in engineering.

items.explain: The two mean basically the same and are mostly interchangeable. Look at the setting: chatting and everyday explanations → だけでなく (often 「だけじゃなくて」 in speech); ばかりでなく is also common in reports and writing.

items.diff: Same meaning; のみならず is written language, common in news, speeches and academic papers.

this.tr: This town gets lots of tourists not only in summer but in winter too.

that.tr: This problem is an issue not only for Japan but for the whole world.

items.explain: Look at the register: everyday speech and ordinary explanations → だけでなく; 「である」-style writing, news, speeches → のみならず, which sounds formal and weighty. Saying のみならず in everyday conversation sounds very stiff.

items.diff: だけでなく adds a B on top of A; に限らず means “not limited to A — the same goes for everything of that kind”.

this.tr: This festival can be enjoyed not only by children but by adults too.

that.tr: This festival isn't just for children — anyone can enjoy it.

items.explain: Look at the second half: naming one more specific B (大人も) → だけでなく; saying “anyone, anywhere, many…” (誰でも、どこでも、多くの国で) → に限らず, which widens the scope to everything at once.

items.diff: だけでなく can be followed by a request or advice; 上に only states facts, and the two things point in the same direction (good on top of good, bad on top of bad).

this.tr: Don't just eat vegetables — please eat fruit too.

that.tag: Statement · bad on top of bad
that.tr: This room is not only small but also gets little sunlight.

wrong.why: 上に cannot be followed by a request or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: a request or advice like 「〜てください」「〜なさい」 → only だけでなく works; stating two features in the same direction (狭い + 日当たりが悪い), often with a tone of “to make matters worse” or “even better” → 上に.

groups.note: だって ↔ んだって — both end in 「だって」

items.diff: Noun + だって is “even…”; sentence-final んだって is “I heard that…”.

this.tr: Even a child knows something like that.

that.tr: I heard Tanaka is getting married next month.

items.explain: Look at the position and the word before it: after a noun with the sentence still continuing (子どもだって知ってる) → even; at the end of the sentence, preceded by 「ん」 (するんだって) → passing on news you heard, “I heard”.

groups.note: All mean “even…”

items.title: 〜でも (even)
items.diff: Same meaning; だって is spoken, more casual and more emphatic; でも can be used in any setting.

this.tr: A problem this easy — even an elementary schooler could solve it.

that.tr: This problem is simple, so even elementary school students can solve it.

items.explain: Look at the register: with 「よ」, said to someone close, with a hint of retort → だって; polite 「〜ます」 form, formal explanations → でも. Don't use だって in writing.

items.title: 〜さえ (even)
items.diff: だって is spoken and stresses “this is no exception either”; さえ names the most basic thing, and is usually followed by a negative.

this.tr: Even Grandpa knows this song.

that.tr: I was so busy I didn't even have time to drink water.

items.explain: Look at the second half: さえ names the most basic, easiest thing and is usually followed by a negative (時間がなかった、できない), and can be used in writing too; だって is spoken, mostly used in positive sentences, stressing “this person too, no exception”.

items.title: 〜まで (even)
items.diff: だって stresses “this is no exception either” and is often used to push back; まで stresses “surprisingly, even this…”, with a sense of surprise.

this.tr: Something like this, even I can do it.

that.tr: Even the teacher, who is usually strict, laughed.

items.explain: Look at how the speaker feels: まで is “surprisingly, even this…”, mostly used to narrate something surprising that already happened (先生まで笑った); だって is “this too, no exception”, often used to persuade or push back (私だってできる).

groups.note: All belong to the 「で + ある」 family — ある contracts to だ, becomes でございます in polite language, and でいらっしゃる in respectful language

items.diff: Same meaning, both are assertions; である is written language used in papers and newspapers; だ is the casual plain form.

this.tr: Japan is an island nation.

that.tr: It's Sunday today, you know.

items.explain: だ is originally a contraction of である (である → であ → だ). Look at the register: papers, newspapers, expository writing → である, which sounds objective and dignified; speaking, writing a diary → だ (the polite version is です). In である-style writing, verb sentences end with 「のである」.

items.title: 〜でございます
items.diff: である is a neutral written assertion with no respect; でございます is the formal-polite version of です, used toward customers.

this.tr: The purpose of this book is to solve problems.

that.tr: Sir, this is our new product.

items.explain: Both are 「で + ある」: である keeps it as is and is used in writing; でございます replaces 「ある」 with the formal 「ござる」 and is used when speaking to customers. Look at the setting: writing → である; shop staff or receptionists talking to customers → でございます.

items.diff: である is just a written “is”; でいらっしゃる respectfully says someone else “is…”.

this.tr: He is a famous writer.

that.tr: This gentleman is a famous writer.

items.explain: Replace the 「ある」 in で + ある with the respectful 「いらっしゃる」 and you get でいらっしゃる. Look at the subject: someone to be respected (こちらの方、先生、お客様) → でいらっしゃる; objective statements in writing → である.

groups.note: Both add an “explaining, emphasizing” tone to a sentence

items.diff: のである is the written version of のだ, used in writing; in speech you use んです／んだ.

this.tr: And so, this problem cannot be solved easily.

that.tr: Sorry, I have a headache.

items.explain: Look at the register: reasoning and drawing conclusions in papers and editorials → のである; explaining your situation or reasons to someone while speaking → んです (んだ). Both carry an explanatory tone of “the thing is…”.

groups.note: Both belong to the 「で + ある」 family — ある becomes でございます in polite language, and でいらっしゃる in respectful language

items.title: 〜でございます
items.diff: でいらっしゃる is respectful language, used only about the other person; でございます is polite language, used about yourself, your own side and things.

this.tr: Excuse me, but are you Mr. Tanaka?

that.tr: Yes, I'm Tanaka.

wrong.why: You can't use respectful language to elevate yourself

items.explain: Look at who the subject is: the other person, someone to be respected (田中様、先生) → でいらっしゃる; yourself, people from your own company, products → でございます. Both are honorific versions of 「です」, but they point in opposite directions, and mixing them up is very rude.

items.diff: でいらっしゃる respectfully says someone else “is…”; である is just a written “is”, with no respect.

this.tr: This gentleman is a famous writer.

that.tr: He is a famous writer.

items.explain: Replace the 「ある」 in である with the respectful 「いらっしゃる」 and you get でいらっしゃる. Look at the subject: introducing or talking about someone to be respected, face to face (こちらの方、先生) → でいらっしゃる; objective statements in writing → である.

groups.note: でいらっしゃる ↔ (に)いらっしゃる — both have 「いらっしゃる」, differing only by 「で」

items.title: いらっしゃる (to be, come, go)
items.diff: でいらっしゃる means “is…”; いらっしゃる on its own means “to be (somewhere), come, go”.

this.tr: The teacher is in very good health.

that.tr: The teacher is in the research office now.

items.explain: Look at what comes before いらっしゃる: 「で」 after a noun or na-adjective (お元気で、先生で) → the respectful way of saying “is…”; 「に」 after a place (研究室に) or used alone (いらっしゃいませ) → to be (somewhere), come, go.

groups.note: Both go with 「有名」, saying what something is famous for

items.diff: With で有名, what comes before is the reason or feature it's famous for; with として有名, what comes before is the identity it's famous as.

this.tr: This town is famous for its hot springs.

that.tr: This town is famous as a hot-spring resort.

items.explain: Look at the relationship between the noun before it and the subject: 温泉 is something the town has, a feature → で有名; 温泉地 is the town's identity itself (the town = a hot-spring resort) → として有名. Likewise: 「小説で有名な人」 (famous for novels), 「作家として有名な人」 (famous as a writer).

groups.note: Both mean “no matter…, still…”

items.diff: どんなに is “no matter how much”; たとえ is “even if it's the case”, and doesn't need a degree before it.

this.tr: No matter how busy I am, I call every day.

that.tr: Even as a joke, you mustn't say something like that.

items.explain: Look at whether you can say “how…” about the word before it: 忙しい、寒い、頑張る have degrees → どんなに; things like 冗談、子ども、雨 that are only “is or isn't” → use たとえ to suppose it's true. たとえ can also take a degree (たとえ忙しくても), but どんなに must be followed by something with a degree.

groups.note: Both attach to nouns referring to people, meaning “several people”

items.diff: 同士 stresses “among each other” within a group of the same kind; たち only marks the plural.

this.tr: Even with no adults around, the children are playing among themselves.

that.tr: The children are playing in the park.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 同士 is often followed by 「で」 or 「の」 and then interaction or a relationship between them (同士で遊ぶ、同士の付き合い), stressing “all the same kind, nobody else”; たち only says there's more than one person. 「恋人同士」 means they are lovers to each other; 「恋人たち」 means several couples.

groups.note: Both come from 振る — originally “to wave”, extended to body movements and outward appearance

items.title: 〜ぶり (manner)
items.diff: ふりをする is a deliberately put-on appearance; ぶり is how someone actually comes across.

this.tr: He pretends to be diligent, but he's actually slacking off.

that.tr: He works very conscientiously.

items.explain: Both come from 「振り」 (behavior, appearance). Look at whether a “but actually…” follows: ふりをする is often followed by 「本当は」 or 「実は」, which overturns it; ぶり describes real behavior and is often followed by an evaluation (真面目だ、見事だ).

items.diff: ふりをする means pretending, is used widely and isn't necessarily negative; ぶる attaches to only a few words, means putting on airs or acting important, and is strongly negative.

this.tr: My mom called me, but I pretended to be asleep.

that.tr: He's quick to act the senior and talk as if he's so important.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: verbs (寝た、知らない) and all sorts of nouns and adjectives → ふりをする, pretending to be in some state; only words for status or character like 「先輩、大人、上品、偉」 → ぶる, meaning putting on airs, almost always critical.

groups.note: Both mean “treating as, pretending” — when it isn't actually so

items.diff: ふりをする is putting on a show for others; たつもり is treating something as already done in your own mind.

this.tr: I actually knew, but I pretended not to.

that.tr: I told myself I'd already been on the trip, and saved that money instead.

items.explain: Look at who it's aimed at: ふりをする is acting for others, getting them to believe it (知らないふり、寝たふり); たつもり is what you think or tell yourself (行ったつもりで貯金する、言ったつもりだった), and doesn't need anyone to see it.

groups.note: Both can be translated as “…-style, …-like”

items.diff: 〜風 focuses on appearance and style; 〜的 focuses on inner nature and way of thinking.

this.tr: We made the garden in Japanese style.

that.tr: His way of thinking is very Japanese.

items.explain: Look at whether it's about the outside or the inside: visible styles like gardens, cooking, buildings and interiors → 〜風; inner qualities like 考え方, personality and habits → 〜的. 〜的 is a na-adjective (「日本的な」); 〜風 is followed by 「の」 or 「に」 (日本風の庭).

items.diff: 〜風 objectively describes style and appearance; 〜っぽい is spoken and subjectively says “kind of like”, often with a negative judgment.

this.tr: At the station, a man who looked like a student asked me for directions.

that.tr: He's already 30, but his way of thinking is childish.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: just objectively describing what something looks like (学生風の人、洋風の部屋) → 〜風; adding your own judgment that it's “like…”, often critical (子どもっぽい、安っぽい) → 〜っぽい. 〜っぽい is an adjective; 〜風 is followed by 「の」.

groups.note: Both attach to nouns, meaning “…-type, …-kind”

items.diff: 〜型 is a noun that puts something into a type; 〜的 is a na-adjective meaning “having the quality of…”.

this.tr: I switched to a morning-person lifestyle.

that.tr: I lead a healthy life.

wrong.why: 〜型 is a noun and must be followed by 「の」

items.explain: Look at whether 「の」 or 「な」 follows: 〜型 is a noun that sorts things into a category (朝型、大型、最新型) and takes 「の」; 〜的 is a na-adjective describing a quality (「健康的」「積極的」) and takes 「な」.

items.diff: 〜型 classifies by habit, specification or type; 〜風 is a style or look that resembles….

this.tr: I'm a morning person, so I go to bed early at night.

that.tr: A man who looked like an office worker was standing there.

items.explain: Look at whether it's “classifying” or “describing appearance”: sorting people or things into a category by habit, constitution or specification (朝型、血液型、大型) → 〜型; looking like some identity or style from the outside (サラリーマン風、和風) → 〜風, meaning “looks like”.

groups.note: All mean “hard to…”

items.diff: がたい is only for something hard to accept psychologically; にくい is the broadest, covering things that are hard to use and actions that aren't easy.

this.tr: It's hard to believe that he lied.

that.tr: This pen is hard to write with.

wrong.why: がたい can't be used for physical inconvenience

items.explain: Look at where the difficulty lies: hard to accept emotionally or logically (信じる、許す、理解する) → がたい, leaning written; things that are hard to use, actions that aren't easy to do (書きにくい、分かりにくい) → にくい.

items.diff: がたい is hard to accept by reason or feeling, leaning written; づらい is the doer feeling physically or emotionally uncomfortable, leaning spoken.

this.tr: Such terrible behavior is hard to forgive.

that.tr: This is a bit hard to bring up with my teacher.

items.explain: Look at how the subject feels: づらい is the speaker feeling uncomfortable or awkward doing it (言いづらい、歩きづらい), common in everyday speech; がたい is an evaluation of something, hard to do on reasonable grounds (許しがたい、理解しがたい), common in writing.

items.diff: がたい evaluates something as “hard to…”; かねる means you can't do it because of your position, and is often used to refuse politely.

this.tr: Those conditions are hard to accept.

that.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to answer regarding that matter.

items.explain: Look at the setting: turning someone down face to face in business (お答えしかねます、お引き受けしかねます) → かねる, meaning “I'd like to, but my position doesn't allow it”; expressing your own view of something (受け入れがたい、信じがたい) → がたい.

groups.note: Both express a (usually bad) tendency

items.diff: 気味 is “a bit…” right now, about degree; がち is “often…, tends to…”, about frequency.

this.tr: Work has been running a bit behind lately.

that.tr: He always tends to be late for appointments.

items.explain: The same 「遅れ」: 遅れ気味 means progress is a bit slow right now; 遅れがち means being late often, again and again. Look for frequency words like 「いつも」「よく」: if there is one → がち; if it's about the current state → 気味.

items.diff: 気味 only describes a bad state of the body or a situation, “a bit…”; っぽい is broader and can also mean “like…”.

this.tr: I have a bit of a cold today, so I'll go to bed early.

that.tr: He talks like a child.

wrong.why: 気味 cannot mean “like…”

items.explain: For having “a bit of a cold”, both 風邪気味 and 風邪っぽい work, with 気味 more formal; to say a person or thing is “like…” (子どもっぽい、白っぽい) → only っぽい works.

groups.note: All mean “every…”

items.diff: ごとに counts “each unit”; おきに counts “the gap in between” — ２日ごとに = １日おきに.

this.tr: I water the flowers every two days.

that.tr: I water the flowers every other day.

items.explain: The two sentences say the same thing. Look at what the number counts: ごとに means doing it once each time this unit comes around (２日ごと = day 1, day 3, day 5…); おきに means leaving this much space in between (１日おき = skipping one day). With larger units of time or distance (10分ごと／10分おき), the two are often treated as the same.

items.diff: ごとに can follow quantities and nouns, meaning each unit or every so often; たびに only follows verbs or 「noun + の」, meaning “every time…”.

this.tr: The bus comes every 10 minutes.

that.tr: Every time I see this photo, I remember the old days.

wrong.why: たびに cannot directly follow a quantity

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a quantity (10分、３時間) or a unit noun (国、クラス) → only ごとに; a verb (見る、会う) → たびに is the most common, stressing “every single time…”; when ごとに follows a verb, it's usually followed by gradual change (回を重ねるごとに上手になる).

items.diff: ごとに describes an action repeated at every interval; 当たり calculates an amount averaged over each unit.

this.tr: I take a break every hour.

that.tr: This machine can make 100 pieces per hour.

items.explain: Look at what follows: a repeated action (休憩を取る、バスが来る) → ごとに; a quantity (100個、1000円) → 当たり, used to calculate rates and averages.

groups.note: Both come from はず (筈) — meaning “by reason, it should be”

items.diff: はずがない is “by all logic, there's no way”; はずだ is “by all logic, it should be”.

this.tr: He's never studied it even once, so there's no way he can speak Japanese.

that.tr: He's lived in Japan for ten years, so he should be able to speak Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the reason given in the first half: the reason clearly can't lead to the conclusion → はずがない; the reason supports the conclusion → はずだ. Note that 「話せないはずだ」 only means “logically he shouldn't be able to speak it”, much weaker than はずがない (absolutely impossible).

groups.note: All mean “impossible, can't be”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; はずがない leans toward a calm judgment based on facts and reasoning, わけがない is more spoken and more emotional.

this.tr: I locked the door properly, so there's no way it's open.

that.tr: We practiced so hard — there's no way we'll lose!

items.explain: The two are mostly interchangeable. Look at the basis and the tone: calm inference from certain facts or memory (鍵はかけた) → はずがない sounds more natural; with emotions like confidence or defiance, often said 「〜わけない(じゃん)」 in speech → わけがない.

items.diff: はずがない is judging something impossible by logic; っこない is casual speech, “there's just no way…”.

this.tr: He's overseas right now, so there's no way he'll come to today's meeting.

that.tr: A problem this hard — there's no way I could ever solve it.

items.explain: Look at how it attaches and the tone: っこない follows the masu-stem (解け + っこない、分かり + っこない), is only used in casual speech among friends, and mostly says “can't do it”; はずがない follows the plain form, can be used in formal settings, and is a calm judgment based on facts.

groups.note: All come from ほど (程) — originally “degree”

items.diff: ほど on its own says “to the extent that…”; Aほど〜ない is a comparison, “not as… as A”.

this.tr: It's so hot today that I can't stop sweating.

that.tr: Today isn't as hot as yesterday.

items.explain: Look at what's before ほど and at the end of the sentence: an exaggerated situation before it (汗が止まらない) and a positive ending → it shows how far the degree goes; a noun being compared (昨日) before it and a negative ending → comparison, “not as… as”.

items.diff: ほど describes a particular degree; 〜ば〜ほど says “the more…, the more…”, with both sides changing together.

this.tr: I practiced until my hands hurt.

that.tr: The more you practice, the better you get.

items.explain: Look at whether the same word appears in the 「ば」 form before ほど: すればするほど、高ければ高いほど → the more…, the more…, followed by a result that changes with it (上手になる); no ば, just a situation before it (手が痛くなる) → describes degree.

items.diff: ほど says “to the extent that…”; Aほど〜はない says “nothing is more… than A”, a superlative.

this.tr: The scenery was so beautiful it brought tears to my eyes.

that.tr: There's no mountain more beautiful than Mt. Fuji.

items.explain: Look at what's before ほど and at the end of the sentence: a situation before it (涙が出る), describing degree → ほど; a noun before it (富士山) and 「〜はない／はいない」 at the end → nothing is more… than it, i.e. “the most…”.

groups.note: Both can use an exaggerated example to express “degree”

items.title: 〜くらい (degree)
items.diff: When expressing degree, the two are mostly interchangeable; when naming the bare minimum (“at least this much”), only くらい works.

this.tr: My feet hurt so much I can't walk anymore.

that.tr: However busy you are, you can at least make a phone call, right?

wrong.why: Only くらい can mean “at least, at the very least”

items.explain: Look at whether the example is exaggerated or trivial: using something extreme to show degree (歩けないほど／くらい) → both work, with ほど slightly more formal; using the most basic, easiest thing to make a demand (電話ぐらい) → only くらい works (ぐらい is the same), often with reproach.

groups.note: All come from ほど (程) — originally “degree”

items.diff: Aほど〜はない is “nothing is more… than A”; ほど on its own only says “to the extent that…”.

this.tr: There's no mountain more beautiful than Mt. Fuji.

that.tr: The scenery was so beautiful it brought tears to my eyes.

items.explain: Look at what's before ほど and at the end of the sentence: a noun before it (富士山) and 「〜はない／はいない」 at the end → nothing is more… than it, i.e. “the most…”; a situation before it (涙が出る) → it just describes degree.

groups.note: Aほど〜はない ↔ Aほど〜ない — only 「は」 is different, but one means “the most…” and the other “not as… as”

items.diff: Aほど〜はない is “nothing/no one is more… than A” (A is the best); Bは Aほど〜ない is “B is not as… as A”.

this.tr: Nobody is a better cook than my mom.

that.tag: B is not as… as A
that.tr: I'm not as good a cook as my mom.

items.explain: Look at what the negative at the end denies: 「人はいない」「ものはない」 deny “existence” → there's no person or thing more… than A, A is number one; 「上手ではない」 negates the adjective, with the subject 「私は」 before it → I'm not as good as A. Both sentences have 「母ほど」, but one praises Mom and the other says I'm worse.

groups.note: Both mean “the most…”

items.diff: ほど〜はない subjectively stresses “nothing is more… than it”, with stronger feeling; の中でいちばん objectively picks out number one within a range.

this.tr: Nothing tastes better than my mom's cooking, after all.

that.tr: Tanaka is the tallest in the class.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a fact or a feeling: a ranking that can be compared objectively, like height or grades, often with the range stated explicitly (クラスの中で) → いちばん; with emotion, memories or praise (やっぱり、こんなに) → ほど〜はない, where the range of comparison often goes unstated.

items.title: 〜に限る (… is best)
items.diff: ほど〜はない evaluates a thing: “nothing is more… than it”; に限る asserts “doing… is the best choice”.

this.tr: When you're tired, nothing feels better than a hot spring.

that.tr: When you're tired, there's nothing like a hot spring.

items.explain: Both sentences praise hot springs. Look at the sentence structure: ほど〜はない needs to say in between which point is being compared (気持ちいい、おいしい); に限る ends the sentence right after a noun or verb, meaning “at times like this, this is what you should do”, with a recommending tone.

groups.note: All express concession: “even if / no matter…, still…”

items.diff: いくら〜ても is “no matter how (much)…, still”, and needs a degree or number of times before it; たとえ〜ても is just “even if (supposing)…”, and can directly suppose something.

this.tr: No matter how hard it rains, the match won't be canceled.

that.tr: Even if it rains, the match won't be canceled.

items.explain: いくら is originally a word asking “how much”, so it must be followed by something that can be more or less (雨が強くても、何度言っても); たとえ only strengthens the hypothetical tone and can directly take a noun: 「雨でも」「子どもでも」. Check whether what comes before ても has degrees or can be repeated, and you can tell them apart.

items.diff: Same meaning; 〜たって is the spoken form of 〜ても, common when talking with friends.

this.tr: No matter what I say, my little brother won't listen.

that.tr: No matter what you say, my little brother just won't listen.

items.explain: Only ても → たって has changed: 「言っても」 → 「言ったって」, 「高くても」 → 「高くたって」. The meaning is exactly the same; たって is more casual and only used in speech; use ても in writing or when speaking to superiors.

groups.note: Both come from 一方 (いっぽう) — originally “one direction, one side”

items.diff: 一方だ ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means “more and more…”; 一方で is followed by another clause and means “on the other hand…”.

this.tr: The population of rural areas keeps decreasing.

that.tag: 一方で · on the other hand
that.tr: While the urban population is increasing, the rural population is decreasing.

items.explain: Look at what follows 一方: 「だ」 ending the sentence → change in only one direction (more and more…); 「で、」 followed by another matter → putting two sides side by side for contrast. 「一方」 literally means “one direction / one side”, and both meanings come from there.

groups.note: Both say a change is moving steadily in one direction

items.diff: Both mean “more and more…”; ばかりだ is used almost only for bad changes, with worry; 一方だ is more objective and also works for good changes.

this.tr: This app keeps getting more and more popular.

that.tr: My father's illness keeps getting worse.

items.explain: Look at whether the change is good or bad: for good changes like 人気が高まる、売り上げが伸びる, 一方だ is the most natural; for worrying changes like 病気が悪くなる、物価が上がる, both work, but ばかりだ carries more of the speaker's anxiety and dissatisfaction.

items.diff: 一方だ says “keeps changing in one direction and won't stop”; つつある only says “is gradually changing”, written and neutral.

this.tr: Prices just keep going up.

that.tr: The economy is gradually recovering.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's tone: 一方だ has a feeling of “endless, no end in sight”; つつある just objectively describes a change in progress, often appears with 「少しずつ」 or 「徐々に」, and attaches to the masu-stem (回復し + つつある).

groups.note: Both come from 一方 (いっぽう) — originally “one direction, one side”

items.diff: 一方で is followed by another matter and means “on the other hand”; 一方だ ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means “more and more…”.

this.tag: 一方で · on the other hand
this.tr: While the urban population is increasing, the rural population is decreasing.

that.tr: The population of rural areas keeps decreasing.

items.explain: Look at what follows 一方: 「で、」 followed by another matter → contrasting or running two things side by side; 「だ」 ending the sentence → change in only one direction (more and more…). 「一方」 literally means “one direction / one side”, and both meanings come from there.

groups.note: Both can put two things together (contrasting two sides, or doing both at once)

items.diff: 反面 only describes the good and bad sides of the same thing; 一方で can also contrast two different things.

this.tr: In cities the population is increasing, while in rural areas it is decreasing.

that.tr: Smartphones are convenient, but on the other hand they tire your eyes easily.

items.explain: Look at whether both halves are about the same thing: the pros and cons of スマホ → both 反面 and 一方で work; 都会 and 地方 are two different places → use 一方で. 反面 is specifically about “two sides of the same coin”, usually one good and one bad.

items.title: 〜ながら (while…)
items.diff: ながら is doing two actions at the same moment; 一方で is doing two things in parallel over a period of time, not necessarily at the same moment.

this.tr: He works at a company during the day while attending university at night.

that.tr: I always study while listening to music.

items.explain: Look at whether the two actions can happen at the same moment: listening to music and studying can be done at once → ながら; working and attending university happen in the 「昼」 and the 「夜」 respectively, only during the same period → 一方で. Also, ながら attaches to the masu-stem (聞き + ながら), while 一方で attaches to the dictionary form (働く + 一方で).

groups.note: Both come from 何か (なにか) — “something”

items.title: 〜なんか
items.diff: か何か is “X or something like it”; なんか is simply 何か said quickly, and besides giving examples it often carries contempt.

this.tr: You must be tired. Shall we have some coffee or something?

that.tr: I'm so busy I have no time to sit around drinking coffee.

items.explain: なんか is a spoken contraction of 何か, so it can also casually give an example; but when followed by a negative or a complaint (〜なんか…ない、〜なんか嫌いだ), it becomes “stuff like…, not even worth mentioning”. か何か just objectively says “this or something similar”, without emotion. The written form など works the same way (など also comes from 「何と」).

groups.note: Both give vague examples, meaning “… and the like”

items.diff: か何か gives only one example and loosely covers similar things with 「何か」; とか can list examples one after another (〜とか〜とか).

this.tr: When you get to the station, let me know by phone or something.

that.tr: When you get to the station, let me know by phone, email or whatever.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in how the examples are given: naming just 「電話」 and covering similar means like texting with 「何か」 → か何か; laying out 「電話」 and 「メール」 one by one → とか〜とか. Also, か何か can express an uncertain guess (風邪か何かで休んでいるらしい).

groups.note: かというと ↔ かといって — only the last two kana differ

items.diff: かというと asks a question and then answers it; かといって is a contrast: “that said, you can't…”.

this.tr: As for why I quit, it's because I ruined my health.

that.tr: Work is hard. That said, I can't just quit.

items.explain: First look at whether it ends in 「と」 or 「って」, then at the second half: かというと is followed by the answer (〜からだ); かといって first concedes a situation, then is followed by a negative like “can't… either” or “it's not that…”. かといって also often stands alone at the start of a sentence.

groups.note: All explain a reason (… is because…)

items.diff: なぜなら states the conclusion first and then adds the reason, and is somewhat written; なぜ〜かというと first restates the question and then answers it, common in both speech and writing.

this.tr: As for why I was late, it's because the train stopped.

that.tr: I was late. That's because the train stopped.

items.explain: Look at the order: the conclusion 「遅れてしまった」 comes first, then the reason is added starting with なぜなら → なぜなら; the whole question 「なぜ遅れたか」 is put first, then the answer is given → かというと. Both often end with 「からだ」.

items.diff: のは〜からだ makes the result the topic and states the reason directly; かというと first raises a question with 「なぜ……か」, giving more of a “here comes the explanation” feel.

this.tr: As for why I was late, it's because the train stopped.

that.tr: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the beginning: the question word 「なぜ」 and 「か」 → かというと, building a bit of suspense before answering; 「遅れたのは」 directly makes the result the topic → のは〜からだ, more concise.

groups.note: All come from と思う — “to think so”

items.diff: と思う states an opinion directly; adding the question particle 「か」 makes it かと思う, with a “might it be…?” tone that's softer and more modest.

this.tr: I think this plan might be better.

that.tr: I think this plan is better.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「か」. With 「か」, the opinion becomes a “question” and sounds less assertive, so 「〜かと思います」 is common in business emails and when offering opinions to superiors; when you're sure and want to state your position clearly, use 「と思います」.

items.title: 〜かと思ったら (no sooner… than)
items.diff: かと思った ends the sentence and means “I thought…”; かと思ったら sits mid-sentence and means “no sooner… than…”.

this.tr: It was so quiet I thought nobody was here.

that.tr: No sooner had it started raining than it stopped again.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「思った」: a period ends it → it describes a misunderstanding at the time, “I thought”; followed by 「ら」 and something that happened right after (すぐやんだ) → two things happening in quick succession, “no sooner… than…”.

items.diff: かと思った is spoken, and the result after “I thought…” can be left unsaid; かと思いきや is written and must be followed by an unexpected result.

this.tr: I thought today was a day off.

that.tr: I thought today was a day off, but there were classes as usual.

items.explain: Look at whether the sentence goes on to state the result: かと思った can end right there, and the listener naturally understands “it actually wasn't”; かと思いきや can't end the sentence and must be followed by something unexpected; it's common in writing and news.

groups.note: Both use a questioning tone to tentatively offer an opinion: “might it be…?”

items.diff: Both use a questioning tone to offer an opinion tentatively; かと思います is mostly used in business reports and emails, のではないか mostly in discussions and writing, and in speech it's んじゃない.

this.tr: At this rate, we might not make the deadline.

that.tr: At this rate, I'm afraid we won't make the deadline.

items.explain: The two sentences mean almost the same; the difference is the setting: when reporting to clients or bosses, 「〜かと思います」 is the most appropriate; raising concerns in writing or at meetings, 「〜のではないか」 is common; between friends, 「〜んじゃない？」.

groups.note: All describe a stage where an action isn't finished yet (about to, nearly, halfway through)

items.diff: ようとする is “about to do”, and the action hasn't started; with かける the action has already started, got partway, and stopped.

this.tr: He started to say something, then stopped.

that.tr: He was about to say something, then held back.

items.explain: Only what follows the verb is different: 言い + かけて → had already started speaking and got halfway; 言お + うとして → was just about to say it but hadn't yet. When you see 「〜かけて、やめた」, it was done halfway.

items.diff: かける says a state has already begun to appear; そうになる says something was about to happen but in the end didn't.

this.tr: I had already half forgotten my childhood dreams.

that.tr: I nearly forgot an important promise.

items.explain: Look at the adverb and the tense: 「もう〜かけていた」 says the forgetting was already under way and the memory had grown hazy; 「危うく〜そうになった」 says you very nearly forgot but actually didn't. 死にかけた (really was in danger of dying once) vs. 死にそうになった (nearly died) is the same difference.

items.diff: かけの modifies an object, meaning “something left half-done”; 途中で refers to a point in the middle of a process, followed by what happened then.

this.tr: There's a half-read book on the desk.

that.tr: I fell asleep in the middle of reading a book.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「〜かけの + noun」 is followed by a thing (本、コーヒー), saying it was left unfinished; 「〜途中で」 is followed by what happened at that moment (眠ってしまった、電話が来た). 途中 can also mean on the way (帰る途中で), but かけ can't.

groups.note: Both mean “not necessarily” (partial negation)

items.diff: とは限らない can mean “not necessarily” on its own; 必ずしも is an adverb that must be followed by a negative, and is often used together with とは限らない for emphasis.

this.tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.

that.tr: Expensive things aren't always good.

wrong.why: 必ずしも must be followed by a negative

items.explain: とは限らない is itself a negative and is enough on its own; adding 必ずしも before it makes the “not necessarily” meaning clearer. Conversely, 必ずしも can't be used alone and must be followed by a negative such as 「〜ない」「〜とは限らない」「〜わけではない」 (必ずしも〜ない works too).

groups.note: Both express the angle or basis of a judgment (judging from…)

items.diff: にとって is “for…”, followed by an evaluation (important, difficult); からすると is “judging from…”, and can be followed by a guess.

this.tr: Judging from the sky, it'll probably rain tomorrow.

that.tr: For farmers, rain is important.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and after: evidence like 「様子」「表情」 before it, and a guess with 「だろう」「ようだ」 after → からすると; the person affected before it, and an evaluation like 「大切だ」「難しい」「ありがたい」 after → にとって. から見ると works the same as からすると.

items.diff: から見ると can directly follow a person; からいうと usually follows abstract nouns like 「立場」「経験」「点」.

this.tr: To children, the adult world must seem strange.

that.tr: From my experience, this method won't work.

items.explain: Look at what comes before から: a specific person like 「子ども」「親」 → から見ると／からすると; abstract nouns like 「経験」「立場」「点」 → からいうと is most natural, focusing on “by a certain standard”. (からいえば works the same.)

items.diff: からすると follows a noun; ところを見ると follows a whole clause describing what you see.

this.tr: Judging from his expression, it seems he passed the exam.

that.tr: Seeing him grinning like that, it seems he passed the exam.

items.explain: The second halves of the two sentences are identical, so look only at the first: 「表情」 is a noun → からすると (から見ると works too); 「にこにこしている」 is a whole clause describing the scene in front of you → ところを見ると. Both are often followed by 「らしい」 or 「ようだ」.

groups.note: にかけて ↔ にかけては — only 「は」 is different

items.diff: から〜にかけて describes a rough range of time or place; にかけては means “when it comes to… (no one is better)”.

this.tr: It will probably snow from evening into the night.

that.tag: When it comes to… · the best
that.tr: When it comes to cooking, no one can beat my mom.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: time or place (夕方から夜、関東から東北) → range; an ability or field (料理、数学) + は, followed by “no one can match” or “confident” → when it comes to…. にかけては is generally not preceded by 「から」.

groups.note: Both express a range “from… to…”

items.diff: から〜にかけて only describes a rough range, common in weather forecasts and news; から〜まで has a clear start and end.

this.tr: It will probably rain from tonight through tomorrow.
