that.tr: Class is from 9 to 12.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a precise time: a vague stretch of time or area like “tonight through tomorrow” in a weather forecast → から〜にかけて; things with clear start and end times like classes or business hours → から〜まで.

items.diff: にかけて is a rough range between two points; にわたって stresses covering the entire period or area, on a large scale.

this.tr: There's a festival in town from Friday to Sunday.

that.tr: The town festival went on for three whole days.

items.explain: Look at the words before it: 「金曜から日曜」 are two points → から〜にかけて; 「３日間」「10年」「全国」 are a whole length or a whole area → にわたって, stressing it went on from start to finish, common in news and formal settings.

groups.note: Both come from 代わる — “to replace, take the place of”

items.diff: の代わりに is the everyday expression; に代わって is more formal, mostly used in speeches and formal settings, and only means “in place of”.

this.tr: I attended the meeting in place of my father.

that.tr: On behalf of my father, I would like to say a few words.

items.explain: Look at the particle before it and the setting: 「noun + の代わりに」 is the most common and is what you use in everyday speech; 「noun + に代わって」 is formal, common in speeches and news (社長に代わって、人に代わってロボットが働く). Also, 代わりに can mean “in exchange” or “there's a trade-off”, which に代わって can't.

groups.note: Both mean “there are advantages, and also disadvantages”

items.diff: 代わりに carries a sense of “equal exchange”: to get this, you give up that; 反面 just objectively points out two opposite sides of the same thing.

this.tr: This job pays well, but in return there are few days off.

that.tr: Smartphones are convenient, but on the other hand they tire your eyes easily.

items.explain: With 代わりに, the two halves are in a “price paid” relationship, like a deal (high pay ↔ paid for with days off), and it's common in speech; 反面 objectively states the positive and negative sides of the same thing, and leans written. When setting a condition, 「その代わり」 at the start of a sentence is also common: 手伝うよ。その代わり、昼ご飯おごってね。

groups.note: All mean “after going through a process, in the end…”

items.diff: 結果 is neutral and objective, often used in reports; 末に stresses that the result came only after a long time of agonizing and going back and forth.

this.tr: After talking it over with my family, I decided to quit my job.

that.tr: After agonizing over it for months, I finally decided to quit my job.

items.explain: The second halves are the same, so look at the first: a long, hard process like 「何か月も悩んだ」「いろいろ考えた」 → 末に; an ordinary process like 「話し合った」「調べた」「検査した」, objectively reporting the conclusion → 結果. 結果 is also common in news and survey reports (調査の結果).

items.diff: 結果 can be good or bad; あげく means that after a lot of fuss, it ended badly, with dissatisfaction.

this.tr: After comparing lots of models, I settled on this computer.

that.tr: After dithering for ages, I ended up not buying anything.

items.explain: Look at whether the result is disappointing: 「このパソコンに決めた」 is an ordinary conclusion → 結果; an outcome where all the effort was wasted, like 「何も買わなかった」「けんかになった」, often preceded by 「さんざん」「長い間」 → あげく, with a complaining tone.

items.diff: た結果 is a conclusion reached after carefully going through a process; たところ means you tried doing something and happened to discover a fact.

this.tr: After a thorough examination, it turned out to be just a cold.

that.tr: I asked the doctor, and it turned out to be just a cold.

items.explain: Look at the action before it: 「詳しく検査した」「話し合った」 are a careful process, followed by the conclusion drawn from it → 結果; 「聞いてみた」「行ってみた」 are just a simple try, followed by a fact you happened to learn, often with a bit of surprise → たところ.

groups.note: Both pair with a negative to mean “not at all / never”

items.diff: 全然〜ない describes degree, “not at all”, and is casual; 決して〜ない usually expresses will or a firm assertion, “never”, and sounds formal.

this.tr: I will never forget this kindness.

that.tr: I don't remember anything about yesterday.

items.explain: Ask whether it's about “resolve” or a “state”: will and prohibition, like won't forget, won't give up, must not do → 決して; a current state or degree, like don't remember, don't understand, doesn't taste good → 全然. 決して sounds formal and is also common in warnings (決して触らないでください).

groups.note: Both come from 「切る（きる）」 — “to cut off, to stop there”

items.diff: きり means “cut off, stop there” → only, and nothing after that; 切る means “cut all the way through” → do completely.

this.tr: Tonight it's just my wife and me.
My brother went out this morning and still hasn't come back.

that.tr: I spent my whole paycheck.

items.explain: The same 「切る」 developed in two directions: “cut off, stop there” → 二人きり (stops at just two people), 出かけたきり (after going out, all news was cut off); “cut all the way through” → 使い切る, 疲れ切る (completely, to the extreme). Look at the position: after a number word or the ta-form it's きり; after the masu-stem, as a compound verb, it's 切る. 「〜切れない」 (can't finish eating, too many to count) also comes from “cut all the way through” — just not managing to get to the end.

groups.note: Both can mean “only” or “stayed that way ever since”

items.diff: だけ is the everyday “only”; きり stresses “just this, nothing more”, often with feeling, and attaches only to number words and a few words like これ・それ.

this.tr: You only live once.

that.tr: You can only take this test once.

items.explain: Listen to the tone: 「人生は一度きり」 carries the feeling “just this once, never again”; 「一度だけ受けられる」 just states a rule objectively. Also, だけ attaches to any noun (野菜だけ, 私だけ), while きり generally attaches only to number words (一度, 二人) and これ・それ.

items.diff: たまま means doing something else while a state is kept; たきり means after doing something, nothing more ever followed — usually followed by a negative.

this.tr: My brother left home three years ago and we haven't heard from him since.

that.tr: I fell asleep with the window open.

items.explain: Look at the second half: “never… again” like 「連絡がない」「帰ってこない」 → たきり, with worry or surprise; another action done in that state (寝てしまった, 出かけた) → たまま.

groups.note: Both come from 「切る（きる）」 — “to cut off, to stop there”

items.diff: 切る means “cut all the way through” → do completely; きり means “cut off, stop there” → only, and nothing after that.

this.tr: I spent my whole paycheck.

that.tr: Tonight it's just my wife and me.
My brother went out this morning and still hasn't come back.

items.explain: The same 「切る」 developed in two directions: “cut all the way through” → 使い切る, 疲れ切る (completely, to the extreme); “cut off, stop there” → 二人きり (stops at just two people), 出かけたきり (after going out, all news was cut off). Look at the position: after the masu-stem, as a compound verb, it's 切る; after a number word or the ta-form it's きり. 「〜切れない」 works the same way: can't cut all the way through → can't finish.

groups.note: Both relate to “finishing” or “not managing to” (matching 切る and 切れない)

items.diff: 終わる just objectively says an action ended; 切る stresses doing it all, completely, often with a sense of “in one go, impressive”.

this.tr: I read the whole thick novel in a single night.

that.tr: I finished reading the novel yesterday.

items.explain: Look for a sense of “all of it, in one go, to the very end”: 「厚い」「一晩で」 stress a large amount finished completely → 切る; just reporting that it's done → 終わる. 切る can also describe a state reaching its extreme (疲れ切る); 終わる can't.

items.diff: 切れない means there's too much to finish; かねる means you “can't very well” do it because of your position or propriety — often used to decline politely.

this.tr: There's too much — I can't eat it all.

that.tr: I'm afraid I can't answer that question.

items.explain: Look at why it can't be done: too much, or not enough capacity (多くて, 数が多い) → 切れない; you're able to, but your position or the rules make it inappropriate → かねる, the set phrase for politely declining customers or superiors.

items.diff: 切れない means you can do it, but there's too much to finish; ようがない means there's no way to even start.

this.tr: There are so many stars in the sky that I can't count them all.

that.tr: I don't know his contact details, so there's no way to reach him.

items.explain: Look at the reason: 「多くて」 → there's a way to do it, it just can't be finished → 切れない; 「連絡先が分からない」 → the means are missing, so you can't even begin → ようがない (attaches to the masu-stem: し＋ようがない).

groups.note: Both are used when asking yourself, checking, or recalling the past

items.diff: かな asks yourself about something you don't know yet; っけ checks something you used to know but can't recall right now.

this.tr: What day is it tomorrow again?

that.tr: I wonder if it'll rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Ask whether the speaker “already knew”: the day of the week, someone's name, an agreed time — you knew it and just forgot → っけ; the weather, an outcome, things not yet known → かな. っけ is usually preceded by 「だ」 or 「た」 (何曜日だっけ, 言ったっけ).

items.diff: っけ is a casual recollection in speech; たものだ looks back with emotion on things you used to do, and can also be used in writing.

this.tr: We used to play in this river a lot as kids, didn't we.

that.tr: As kids, we used to play in this river so often.

items.explain: Only the sentence ending changes: っけな sounds like talking to yourself, light and casual; たものだ carries the feeling “those were the days” and is common when older people tell stories or in writing. Both often go with 「よく」 for things done repeatedly in the past.

items.title: 〜じゃない (confirming)
items.diff: じゃない？ means you're fairly sure and want the other person to agree; っけ means you can't remember clearly and want them to remind you.

this.tr: Was this yours?

that.tr: Isn't this yours?

items.explain: Both sentences ask the other person, but with different confidence: 「じゃない？」 (rising intonation) is “I think it's yours, right?”; 「だっけ？」 is “I don't quite remember — is it yours?”. Note that with falling intonation, じゃない becomes the plain negative “it's not yours”.

groups.note: Both come from 「込む」 — “put inside, pack in”

items.diff: 〜込む attaches to the masu-stem of a verb and says the action “goes inside” or “goes deep”; を込めて attaches to a noun and says feelings or intentions are “packed into” an action.

this.tr: I wrote the important points into my notebook.

that.tr: I wrote a letter to my mother with all my heart.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「込」: verb masu-stem (書き, 飛び, 考え)＋込む → the action goes inside, or sinks in deep; noun＋を込めて (心, 愛, 願い) → invisible feelings are “packed into” the action that follows. 込める is simply the transitive verb of 込む, “to put in”.

groups.note: Both follow the masu-stem of a verb and add a sense of “degree” or “continuation”

items.diff: 冷え込む says the cold gradually deepens, mostly about weather; 冷え切る says something is completely chilled through, to the extreme.

this.tr: It got really cold this morning, didn't it.

that.tr: I got soaked in the rain and was chilled to the bone.

items.explain: 〜込む focuses on the “process of going deeper”, and 冷え込む is used almost only for temperatures dropping and weather turning cold; 〜切る focuses on the “result of reaching the end”, and 冷え切る says a body or a relationship has gone completely cold (二人の関係は冷え切っている). Ask whether it's “the weather getting colder” or “something already chilled through”.

items.diff: 考え込む means being lost in thought and unable to get out; 考え続ける just objectively means thinking about something continuously.

this.tr: He said nothing and sat lost in thought.

that.tr: I thought about that problem all night long.

items.explain: 〜込む stresses how deeply someone has sunk into it, often with 「黙って」「じっと」 — anyone watching can tell they're agonizing over it; 〜続ける stresses no break in time, often with 「一晩中」「ずっと」「10年」.

groups.note: Both come from the emphatic particle 「こそ」 — “exactly this, nothing else”

items.diff: Noun＋こそ emphasizes a person or thing; からこそ specifically emphasizes a reason, “precisely because…”.

this.tr: Health is what matters most.

that.tr: It's precisely because I'm healthy that I can work every day.

items.explain: Look at what comes before こそ: a noun (健康, 今度, こちら) → emphasizes “this very thing”; 「から」 (健康だから) → emphasizes “this very reason”, followed by the result it brings. Starting from こそ ＝ “this very one”, からこそ ＝ “this very reason”.

items.diff: Noun＋こそ emphasizes the thing itself; te-form＋こそ emphasizes a condition, “only by… can…”.

this.tr: This year I'm definitely going to climb Mt. Fuji.

that.tr: Only by climbing it yourself can you appreciate how great Mt. Fuji really is.

items.explain: Check whether the te-form comes before こそ: 「登ってこそ」 ＝ only by doing this does the result that follows hold true; noun＋こそ just emphasizes that word itself, as in 「今年こそ」, “this time for sure”.

items.diff: こそ alone emphasizes “precisely”; こそ〜が is a concession, “…is certainly…, but…”.

this.tr: Taste is this restaurant's pride.

that.tr: This restaurant is admittedly pricey, but the food is superb.

items.explain: Check whether こそ is followed by a turn with 「が／けれど」: no turn → emphasis, “it's exactly this”; 「値段こそ高いが、……」 first concedes a drawback, then uses が to turn to the strength you really want to point out → concession. こそ〜が is mostly found in writing.

groups.note: Both give someone advice or a word of warning

items.diff: ほうがいい is general advice usable with anyone; ことだ sounds like guidance from an elder — more direct and assertive.

this.tr: If you want to pass, study every day.

that.tr: If you want to pass, you'd better study every day.

items.explain: Look at the relationship: teacher to student, senior to junior, in a “just listen to me” tone → ことだ, often as 「〜たければ〜ことだ」; between friends or to people in general → ほうがいい (attaches to the ta-form: 勉強した＋ほうがいい). You can't use ことだ to your boss.

items.title: 〜ものだ (should, by nature)
items.diff: ものだ states social common sense, “that's just how it should be”; ことだ is specific advice for the other person's current situation.

this.tr: If you want to get over your cold, just rest well today.

that.tr: You should listen to people until they've finished speaking.

items.explain: Look at who it's for and when: 「今日は」 targets this person and this situation → ことだ; common sense or manners that apply to everyone → ものだ. The negative works the same way: 無理をしないことだ (don't push yourself) / 人の悪口を言うものではない (one shouldn't speak ill of others).

items.diff: ないことだ means “you'd better not…”, clearly discouraging; ことはない means “there's no need to…”, reassuring the other person.

this.tag: ないことだ · you'd better not
this.tr: You'd better not worry too much.

that.tr: There's no need to worry so much.

items.explain: Look before and after こと: 「しない＋ことだ」 gives an instruction, “don't do this”; 「する＋ことはない」 tells someone “there's no need to do this”, sounding more like comfort. The meanings are close, but ことはない is always preceded by an affirmative dictionary form.

groups.note: Both can mean “by… / because of…” — one thing leads to a result or a judgment

items.title: 〜で (means)
items.diff: The meaning is the same — both express a means; the difference is in how they attach: a noun takes で directly, but an action (a verb phrase) first needs こと to turn it into a noun before で.

this.tr: By taking the train, you can save time.

that.tr: I go to work by train every day.

wrong.why: A verb can't take で directly — add こと first

items.explain: Look before で: a noun like 「電車」 → just add で; a whole action like 「電車を使う」 can't take で directly — add 「こと」 first → ことで. So ことで means “by doing this”, usually followed by the effect it brings (節約できる, 仲良くなった).

items.title: 〜によって (means)
items.diff: Basically the same meaning; ことによって is more formal and common in papers and news, while ことで works in both speech and writing.

this.tr: By walking every day, I lost five kilos.

that.tr: Through daily walking, body weight decreased by five kilograms.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: 「ことによって」「ことにより」 sound formal and are used in reports and news, often followed by written-style words (減少した); in everyday speech ことで is more natural.

items.diff: ことで says a method brings an effect; ことから says a judgment is drawn from a fact, or explains the origin of a name.

this.tr: By practicing every day, I got better.

that.tr: The fact that he practices every day shows he's serious.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「上手になった」 is a change brought about by the method → ことで; 「本気だと分かる」「〜と呼ばれる」 is a judgment or origin drawn from the fact → ことから.

groups.note: Both say one thing leads to a result or a judgment (because of… / judging from…)

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: から can give a subjective reason and can be followed by a command or request; ことから only states an objective fact, leans written, and isn't followed by commands.

this.tr: Being close to the station, this shop is always crowded.

that.tr: It's dangerous, so don't play here.

wrong.why: ことから can't be followed by a request or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: requests, commands and invitations (〜ないで, 〜てください, 〜しよう) can only follow から; ことから appears mostly in news and explanatory writing to give an objective cause or basis for a judgment, followed by an objective statement or 「と分かる」「と考えられる」.

items.diff: ところを見ると infers from what you see in front of you, usually followed by 「らしい」「ようだ」; ことから is more formal, usually followed by 「と考えられる」「と分かる」.

this.tr: Given that the window is broken, the culprit is thought to have entered from here.

that.tr: Seeing that the window's broken, it looks like someone got in.

items.explain: Look at the second half and the register: the speaker guesses from what they see, followed by 「らしい」「ようだ」 → ところを見ると, fine in speech; reports and news stating the basis objectively, followed by 「と考えられる」「と分かる」 → ことから. ことから can also explain the origin of a name (〜ことから「…」と呼ばれる); ところを見ると can't.

items.diff: ことから takes a fact as the basis or cause; ことで uses a method as the means that brings about the effect that follows.

this.tr: The fact that he practices every day shows he's serious.

that.tr: By practicing every day, I got better.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「本気だと分かる」「〜と呼ばれる」 is a judgment or origin drawn from the fact → ことから; 「上手になった」 is a change brought about by the method → ことで.

groups.note: Both come from 「こと（事）」 — treating a matter as the content of a decision

items.diff: ことになる means it was decided by others or by circumstances; ことにする means you decided it yourself.

this.tr: On the company's orders, I'm being transferred to Osaka.

that.tr: After thinking it over myself, I decided to quit.

items.explain: Look at who made the decision: 「会社の命令で」 → ことになった; 「自分で考えて」 → ことにした. Also, Japanese speakers sometimes deliberately use ことになった for their own decisions, to sound modest and low-key.

items.diff: ことになった reports the change “it's just been decided”; ことになっている describes a rule or arrangement that remains in force.

this.tr: Starting next month, pets will no longer be allowed in this dorm.

that.tr: Pets have never been allowed in this dorm.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「来月から」 announces a new decision → ことになった; 「昔から」「ここでは」 explain a rule that's always in force → ことになっている. ことになっている is often used to explain rules to others: 「規則でそういうことになっています」.

groups.note: Both mean “a conclusion that follows logically”

items.diff: ことになる infers a consequence that hasn't happened yet, often as a warning; わけだ reacts to an already-known result with “no wonder”.

this.tr: If you keep this up, the teacher's going to scold you again.

that.tr: You study two whole hours a day? No wonder your grades are going up.

items.explain: Ask whether it's about the future or something already known: 「このままだと」 infers a consequence that hasn't happened yet → ことになる, often a reminder or warning; after hearing 「毎日２時間も」 you suddenly understand a result that already exists → わけだ (no wonder).

groups.note: Both come from 「こと（事）」 — treating a matter as the content of a decision

items.diff: ことになっている describes a rule or arrangement that remains in force; ことになった reports the change “it's just been decided”.

this.tr: Pets have never been allowed in this dorm.

that.tr: Starting next month, pets will no longer be allowed in this dorm.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「昔から」「ここでは」 explain a rule that's always in force → ことになっている; 「来月から」 announces a new decision → ことになった.

items.diff: ことになっている is an external rule or an arrangement others made; ことにしている is a habit you set for yourself.

this.tr: Company rules say we have to be at work by eight every morning.

that.tr: For my health, I make a point of getting up at six every morning.

items.explain: Look at who set it: 「会社の規則で」「法律で」 → ことになっている (なる: I didn't decide it, it came to be this way); 「健康のために」, decided and kept up by yourself → ことにしている (する: I set it myself).

groups.note: Both mean “by the rules / by design, this is how it is”

items.diff: ことになっている describes rules and arrangements made by people; ようになっている says a machine or system is designed to work that way.

this.tr: In this building, the doors are to be closed at 10 p.m.

that.tr: This door is set to close automatically at 10 p.m.

items.explain: Look at the subject and the verb: 「ビルでは…閉める」 is people doing something according to a rule (transitive verb) → ことになっている; 「ドアは…自動で閉まる」 is a machine acting on its own (intransitive verb) → ようになっている, describing how it's built or works.

groups.note: Both come from 「こと（事）」 — treating a matter as the content of a decision

items.diff: ことにしている is a personal rule kept up over time; ことにした is a decision made at a particular moment.

this.tr: For five years now I've made a point of running every morning.

that.tr: I've decided to start running every morning from today.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「もう５年」「いつも」 show it's been kept up for a long time → ことにしている; 「今日から」 is the moment the decision is made → ことにした.

items.diff: ことにしている is a habit you set for yourself; ことになっている is an external rule or an arrangement others made.

this.tr: For my health, I make a point of getting up at six every morning.

that.tr: Company rules say we have to be at work by eight every morning.

items.explain: Look at who set it: 「健康のために」, decided and kept up by yourself → ことにしている (する: I set it myself); 「会社の規則で」「法律で」 → ことになっている (なる: I didn't decide it, it came to be this way).

groups.note: Both describe a practice you stick to

items.diff: ことにしている is a clearly set rule, kept more firmly; ようにしている means “try to as much as possible” — missing it now and then is fine.

this.tr: I've made it a rule not to look at my phone before bed.

that.tr: I try not to look at my phone before bed.

items.explain: Look at the adverbs: 「なるべく」「できるだけ」 often go with ようにしている, showing what you're aiming for — missing it occasionally is OK; ことにしている is a clear rule you've set yourself and generally isn't preceded by 「なるべく」.

groups.note: Both express a concession, “although…, …”

items.diff: ことは〜が repeats the same word, is casual, and sounds like a grudging admission; ものの doesn't repeat and leans written.

this.tr: I did go to the party, but I came right back.

that.tr: Although I went to the party, I came back soon after.

items.explain: Check whether the verb is repeated: 「行くことは行った」 says the same verb twice, with a grudging sense of “I went, all right (but it wasn't much)”, and in speech often uses けど; ものの says it only once and reads more formal and objective.

items.diff: ことは〜が means “it's true that…, but it falls short”; といっても means “even though…, it's actually not that impressive”, correcting what the listener imagines.

this.tr: I can cook, sure, but only simple things.

that.tr: I may say I can cook, but it's really only simple things.

items.explain: The second halves are identical; look at the first half: ことは〜が is the speaker honestly admitting first, “I can, sure”; といっても often picks up something the listener said or might assume, meaning “don't think it's that impressive”. When someone praises you, replying 「できるといっても……」 is the most natural.

groups.note: ことはない ↔ ないことはない — one extra 「ない」 in front completely changes the meaning

items.diff: ことはない means “there's no need to…”; ないことはない is a double negative, “it's not that I won't…”.

this.tr: It's raining — there's no need to force yourself to go.

that.tr: If someone invited me, it's not that I wouldn't go…

items.explain: Check whether what comes before こと is affirmative or negative: 「行く＋ことはない」 → no need to go; 「行かない＋ことはない」 → the two negatives cancel out, “it's not that I won't go”, sounding reluctant and not very keen. When reading, a single 「ない」 can flip the meaning completely.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no need to…”

items.diff: なくてもいい just objectively says “you don't have to”; ことはない carries a comforting, encouraging (or sometimes reproachful) tone.

this.tr: Tomorrow's a day off — there's no need to come in to work.

that.tr: Tomorrow's a day off, so you don't have to come in to work.

items.explain: The meanings are close; look at the speaker's feelings: ことはない has a comforting “don't go out of your way” tone, often used to reassure or encourage (謝ることはないよ); なくてもいい just objectively gives permission not to, and can also be used in questions (行かなくてもいいですか) — ことはない isn't used to ask like that.

items.title: 〜には及ばない (no need)
items.diff: ことはない is everyday speech; には及ばない is more formal and polite, often used to graciously decline someone's kindness.

this.tr: I'll be better soon — there's no need to come all the way over.

that.tr: I will recover soon, so there is no need for you to take the trouble of coming.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at who's being addressed: to friends and family say ことはない; when graciously declining kindness from guests or superiors say 「〜には及びません」, as in the common 「ご心配には及びません」 — it can also come directly after a noun.

items.diff: ことはない tells someone “there's no need to do that”; までもない means “it's obvious or simple, so there's no need to bother”.

this.tr: You did nothing wrong. There's no need to apologize.

that.tr: It goes without saying that health is important.

items.explain: Look at the reason: ことはない targets the other person's action, telling them “don't do that”; までもない means the matter is so obvious or simple that “there's no need to say / check it”, as in the common 「言うまでもない」「言うまでもなく」.

groups.note: Both express “not as expected” — “even though…, still…”

items.title: 〜のに (even though)
items.diff: のに just expresses surprise or regret, and the subjects of the two halves can differ; くせに needs the same subject in both halves and carries strong reproach.

this.tr: He knows perfectly well, but (deliberately) won't tell me.

that.tr: Even though it was raining, the match went ahead.

wrong.why: くせに needs the same person in both halves, and it's criticizing them

items.explain: Check whether both halves are about the same person: 「彼は知っている」 and 「（彼は）教えてくれない」 are both him → くせに, criticizing with a sense of “how outrageous”; 「雨」 and 「試合」 are different subjects and nobody is being blamed → only のに works.

items.diff: にしては evaluates against someone's status, positively or negatively; くせに is only used to criticize someone's words or actions for not matching their status.

this.tr: You're just a kid — don't talk so cheeky!

that.tr: For a child, that's very good handwriting.

items.explain: Check whether the second half praises or scolds: 「上手な字だ」 is an evaluation using “child” as the yardstick → にしては (it can be negative too: 大人にしては字が下手だ); 「生意気なことを言うな」 is contemptuous criticism → くせに.

items.diff: にもかかわらず is written language, objectively stating “despite…, still”; くせに is spoken and carries strong personal emotion.

this.tr: He promised, and yet he didn't show up.

that.tr: Despite the heavy rain, a large crowd gathered.

items.explain: Look at the register and emotion: くせに is a complaint about a particular person, mostly in speech; にもかかわらず is an objective statement in news and writing — the subjects can differ, there's no blame, and it can even be used to say thank you (お忙しいにもかかわらず、ありがとうございます).

groups.note: Both express a simile, “just like…”

items.diff: まるで〜ようだ can come directly after “noun＋の”; かのようだ follows a full sentence, usually describing “acting as if… when it isn't so”, and is more literary.

this.tr: We'd only just met, but it was as if we'd been friends for years.

that.tr: He's looking unbothered, as if he knew nothing at all.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「よう」: “noun＋の” (友達の) → まるで〜ようだ; a whole sentence (何も知らない, 〜である, 〜た)＋か → かのようだ, often describing an “act someone puts on”, mostly in novels and writing. The two are also often combined: まるで何も知らないかのように.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）＋に」 — “make it become that way”

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ように (purpose) is followed by the action taken to achieve it; ますように drops the action and leaves only the wish.

this.tr: Please let me pass the exam.

that.tr: I'm studying every day so that I can pass the exam.

items.explain: Look after ように: if it continues with “what I'm doing for it” (毎日勉強している) → purpose, “so that I can…”; if the sentence stops at 「ますように」, often with 「どうか」 in front → a prayer, “please let…”. Prayers mostly use the masu-form (できますように); purpose uses the plain form (できるように).

items.diff: ますように is a wish that doesn't name who should act; ように言う asks a specific person to do something.

this.tr: Please let my mother get well soon.

that.tr: The doctor told me to go to bed early.

items.explain: Check whether 「言う／お願いする」 and the person making the request (医者に) follow: if so → a request or a reported request; if the sentence stops at 「ますように」 → your own wish. In notices, 「ご協力くださいますようお願いいたします」 is really a formal version of 「ようにお願いする」, always followed by 「お願いいたします」.

groups.note: Both express “hoping something comes true”

items.diff: ますように is formal, like making a wish; といいね is a hope said lightly in everyday chat.

this.tr: Please let it be sunny tomorrow.

that.tr: Hope it's sunny for tomorrow's field trip.

items.explain: Look at the setting: at a shrine, on an ema plaque, a Tanabata wish strip or a greeting card, often with 「どうか」 in front → ますように; chatting with friends, with 「ね／な」 at the end → 〜といいね (〜たらいいね works the same).

items.diff: ますように is a prayer to the heavens or in your heart; てほしい voices your expectation aloud, often hoping a particular person will do something.

this.tr: Please let my father's surgery go well.

that.tr: I want my father to take better care of himself.

items.explain: Look at who the wish is addressed to: making a wish, praying, writing on an ema, often with 「どうか」 → ますように; voicing what you expect of someone, often with 「（人）に」 → てほしい (てもらいたい works the same). You can also say 「晴れてほしい」 about the weather, but it has no feeling of prayer.

groups.note: Both pair with a negative to form a strong negation

items.diff: Both mean “not at all”; まったく is more formal and works in writing and business, while 全然 leans casual.

this.tr: I was entirely unaware of that matter.

that.tr: I had no idea about that at all!

items.explain: Look at the register: in keigo, business or writing (存じませんでした, 問題ございません) → まったく (often written 「全く」); casual talk between friends, with 「よ」 → 全然.

items.diff: まったく carries no particular emotion and works in writing too; ちっとも is only used in speech and often carries dissatisfaction.

this.tr: The test results showed no abnormalities whatsoever.

that.tr: No matter how many times I tell him, my son just won't study at all.

items.explain: Look at the setting and emotion: objective statements in reports or news → まったく; complaining to family or friends, “why won't they ever…” → ちっとも — ちっとも isn't used in writing.

items.diff: まったく describes an objective degree, “not at all”; 決して expresses will or a firm assertion, “never, absolutely not”.

this.tr: I knew nothing at all about that.

that.tr: I will never tell anyone this secret.

items.explain: Check whether what follows states a fact or expresses resolve or a prohibition: an objective state like 「知らなかった」「問題がない」 → まったく; will, a promise or a prohibition like 「話しません」「諦めない」「〜しないでください」 → 決して.

groups.note: Both attach to an adjective stem and turn the adjective into a noun

items.diff: さ expresses a measurable degree or dimension; み expresses a quality or flavor you can sense.

this.tr: This wine has a taste with real depth.

that.tr: This pond is two meters deep.

wrong.why: み only attaches to a few adjectives — for 大きい you can only say 大きさ

items.explain: Ask whether you could answer with a number: 深さ, 重さ, 高さ can be measured (２メートル, ５キロ), and almost any adjective can take さ; 深み, 重み, 甘み are a “flavor or weight” you sense, often used with 「ある／増す」, and only a few adjectives can take み.

groups.note: Both have the shape “Aも＋conditional form, Bも”

items.title: 〜も〜なら〜も
items.diff: もばも objectively lists two things side by side; AもAならBもB criticizes “both sides are as bad as each other”.

this.tr: In this family, the parents are kind and so are the children.

that.tag: Criticism · as bad as each other
that.tr: The parents are hopeless, and the kids are just as bad.

items.explain: Check whether the same noun is repeated exactly before and after なら: 「親も親なら、子も子だ」 is 「AもAなら、BもB」, meaning neither side is any good — always a criticism; in もばも, what comes before ば is a verb or adjective (優しければ, いれば), simply listing facts.

groups.note: Both mean “both… and…”, listing two things side by side

items.diff: だけでなく has a main point and an addition, “not only A, but also B”; もばも lists the two things as equals.

this.tr: This place is cheap, and the food is good too.

that.tag: Building up · not only… but also
that.tr: This place is not only cheap, the food is good too.

items.explain: The meanings are close; look at the structure: 「Aも〜ば、Bも〜」 is symmetrical, with A and B on an equal footing; 「Aだけでなく、Bも」 says one thing and then adds another, giving a sense of building up.

items.diff: In もばも, the two things themselves are the point, in a neat structure; し is often used to list reasons, leading to a conclusion.

this.tr: He can sing, and he can dance too.

that.tr: He can sing, he can dance — he's really amazing.

items.explain: Check whether a conclusion follows: what し lists is usually reasons, often followed by an evaluation or conclusion (本当にすごい, だから人気がある), and it's casual; with もばも, the sentence ends once both things are said, with a neat rhythm, used in both speech and writing.

groups.note: Both come from 「もの（物）」 — “the natural way of things, common sense”

items.diff: ものだ urges “by common sense, you should…”; ものではない urges “by common sense, you shouldn't…”.

this.tr: You should use keigo with your elders and superiors.

that.tr: One shouldn't speak ill of others.

items.explain: The same 「もの」 (common sense), one positive and one negative: what common sense says you should do → ものだ; what common sense says you shouldn't → ものではない — both in the tone of an elder lecturing a junior. ものではない can also mean “is inherently hard to…” (人の心はわかるものではない).

groups.note: Both can be used to advise “you should…”

items.diff: ものだ persuades by invoking social common sense; べきだ is the speaker's own claim or judgment, and sounds firmer.

this.tr: When someone gives you something, you should thank them.

that.tr: The government should deal with this problem immediately.

items.explain: Look at the basis and the target: common sense about “how people should behave”, usually elders teaching juniors → ものだ; the speaker's own claim, which can be directed at governments or companies and is common in argumentative essays → べきだ.

items.diff: ものだ is a principle meant for everyone; ことだ is specific advice for the person in front of you.

this.tr: Children should go to bed early.

that.tr: If you want to get over your cold quickly, get plenty of sleep.

items.explain: Check for a condition tied to a specific situation: ことだ after 「〜たいなら」「〜なら」 is offering advice to this particular person (you'd best…); a general subject like 「子どもは」「人は」 → ものだ, stating a general principle.

groups.note: Both come from the formal noun 「もの」 — presenting a reason as “the way things already were”, with an excuse-making tone

items.diff: Same meaning; もので is shorter and more formal, common in apologies.

this.tr: Traffic was bad, so I'm late.

that.tr: The train was delayed, so I was late. I'm terribly sorry.

items.explain: Both give a reason as an excuse; look at who you're talking to: between friends → ものだから (often said 「もんだから」 in speech); apologizing to a superior or client → もので, or 「ものですから」, often followed by 「申し訳ありません」.

items.diff: ものだから is followed by a result; sentence-final もん drops the second half and leaves only the reason — casual and whiny.

this.tr: I was so busy that I couldn't get in touch.

that.tr: But I was busy!

items.explain: Check whether anything follows もの: if it continues with 「だから、＋result」 → ものだから, which adults can use in apologies too; if the sentence stops right at 「もん」, often with 「だって」 in front → it gives only the reason, not the result, like a child whining — only for people you're close to.

groups.note: Both give a reason, “because…”

items.diff: ので explains objectively and can be followed by a request; ものだから has an excuse-making tone, “circumstances forced me, there was nothing I could do”, mostly used to explain your own slip-ups.

this.tr: The roads were congested, so I'm afraid I was late.

that.tr: Traffic is heavy, so please leave early.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a bad result you've already caused, often followed by an apology → ものだから (ものですから); making a request or suggestion to the other person (〜てください) → ので — ものだから isn't normally used that way.

groups.note: Both come from the formal noun 「もの」 — presenting a reason as “the way things already were”

items.diff: Sentence-final もん gives only the reason and drops the second half; ものだから is followed by a result, and adults can use it in apologies too.

this.tr: But I was busy!

that.tr: I was so busy that I couldn't get in touch.

items.explain: Check whether anything follows もの: if the sentence stops at 「もん／もの」, often with 「だって」 in front → it gives only the reason, like a child whining — only for people you're close to (the polite feminine version is 「ですもの」); if it continues with 「だから、＋result」 → ものだから.

groups.note: Both put forward a reason with emotion

items.diff: もん is making excuses for yourself, whining; んだから uses a reason to make demands on or blame the other person.

this.tr: But I'm still just a kid!

that.tr: You're not a kid anymore, so do it yourself.

items.explain: Look at which way it points: finding a reason for yourself, with the sentence stopping at もん → an excuse, whining; using a reason to pressure the other person, followed by 「〜なさい」 or unspoken annoyance → んだから (＝のだから), meaning “since…, you should…”.

groups.note: Both come from the hypothetical adverb 「もし」 — “if”

items.diff: もしかしたら is a guess, “maybe”; もしも〜たら sets up a hypothetical condition, “if by any chance… (then…)”.

this.tag: Guess · ends in かもしれない
this.tr: It might rain tomorrow.

that.tr: If it does rain tomorrow, the match will be canceled.

items.explain: Look at how the sentence ends: もしかしたら pairs with sentence-final 「かもしれない」, so the whole sentence is an uncertain guess; もしも pairs with 「〜たら／〜ば」 and must be followed by a result, “in that case…”. Literally, もしかしたら is “if it so happens to be possible”, which is why it came to mean “maybe”.

groups.note: Both express a guess, with different levels of certainty

items.diff: もしかしたら〜かもしれない is low-confidence (maybe); だろう is fairly confident (probably).

this.tr: He might not be coming.

that.tr: It's already eight, so he's probably not coming.

items.explain: Look at the clues in the sentence: with grounds like 「もう８時だ」 plus 「たぶん」 → だろう, you think it's most likely so; with no grounds at all, just a possibility that occurred to you → もしかしたら〜かもしれない, a fifty-fifty chance or even lower.

groups.note: Both come from the hypothetical adverb 「もし」 — “if”

items.diff: もしも〜たら sets up a hypothesis, “if by any chance… (then…)”; もしかしたら is a guess, “maybe”.

this.tr: If it does rain tomorrow, the match will be canceled.

that.tag: Guess · ends in かもしれない
that.tr: It might rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at how the sentence ends: もしも pairs with 「〜たら／〜ば」 and is followed by “in that case…”; もしかしたら pairs with sentence-final 「かもしれない」, so the whole sentence is just a guess, not a conditional.

groups.note: Both express a hypothesis, “if…”

items.diff: たら works for any hypothesis; adding 「もしも」 limits it to an unlikely, unwelcome “if by any chance”.

this.tr: If a big earthquake ever struck, where should we flee to?

that.tr: Let's head out once it's ten.

wrong.why: Ten o'clock is sure to come, so you can't add もしも

items.explain: Ask whether the first event is certain to happen: ten o'clock will definitely come → you can only say 「10時になったら」 (＝when it comes, …); only for unlikely, unwelcome events (a big earthquake, an accident, illness) → use 「もしも〜たら」 to stress “if by any chance”.

groups.note: Both come from 「向（む）く・向（む）ける」 — “to face, to turn toward”

items.diff: 向け means the maker “made it especially for…”; 向き means the thing itself “suits…”.

this.tr: This magazine is made especially for young women.

that.tr: This dish is simple, so it's good for beginners.

items.explain: They come from two verbs: 向ける (turn something toward) → 向け, the maker “aims” the product at a group from the start, as in 「〜向けに作る」「〜向けの商品」; 向く (face toward) → 向き, simply evaluating whether the thing itself is suitable — it wasn't necessarily made for them — and you can also say 「不向き」.

items.diff: 向け attaches directly to a noun, meaning “aimed at…”; に向けて has 「に」 and is followed by an action, meaning working toward a target or goal.

this.tr: Developing products for overseas markets.

that.tag: に向けて · toward a goal
that.tr: Training every day for the Olympics.

items.explain: Check for 「に」: a noun plus 向け usually modifies a noun (〜向けの商品), stating who a product or program is for; 「〜に向けて」 is followed by an action (練習している, 話す), meaning preparing toward a goal, or addressing someone (国民に向けて話す).

groups.note: Both can mean “for a certain group of people”

items.title: 〜ために (for someone)
items.diff: 向け focuses on “who it's for to use or watch”; のために focuses on “who benefits”.

this.tr: We're holding an event for kids during summer vacation.

that.tr: Collecting donations for sick children.

items.explain: Ask whether that group are the “users”: kids come to take part, watch or use it → 向け, mostly used to categorize products, programs and events; kids don't necessarily take part, they just benefit → のために. Both 「子ども向けの本」 and 「子どものための本」 are fine, but 向け sounds more like a product category.

groups.note: Both come from the 「向（む）く」 family of verbs (向く・向ける・向かう) — “to face, to turn toward”

items.diff: 向き means the thing itself “suits…”; 向け means the maker “made it especially for…”.

this.tr: This dish is simple, so it's good for beginners.

that.tr: This magazine is made especially for young women.

items.explain: They come from two verbs: 向く (face toward) → 向き, evaluating whether the thing itself is suitable — it wasn't necessarily made for them — and you can also say 「不向き」; 向ける (turn something toward) → 向け, the maker “aims” the product at a group from the start, as in 「〜向けに作る」.

items.diff: 向き is the fixed direction something faces; に向かって is an action directed toward somewhere.

this.tr: South-facing rooms are bright.

that.tr: I shouted at the top of my voice toward the sea.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「〜向きの＋noun」 modifies a house or window, saying which way it always faces; 「〜に向かって＋action」 says where an action is aimed (叫ぶ, 歩く) — it can also be at a person (先生に向かって).

groups.note: Both mean “suited to…”

items.title: 〜に合った (suited to)
items.diff: 向き evaluates by group, season or use, “suited to this type”; に合った means “matches a specific thing”.

this.tag: Suited to a type of person
this.tr: This job is suited to young people with plenty of stamina.

that.tr: I'm looking for a job that suits me.

items.explain: 向き is preceded by a type of person, a season or a use (初心者向き, 子ども向き, 夏向き), like sticking on a category label; 「〜に合った」 is usually preceded by something specific like 「自分」「目的」「体質」, saying whether the two match.

groups.note: Both report something you heard: “I heard / they said”

items.title: 〜って (sentence-end reporting)
items.diff: んだって reports a fact; 「って」 on its own can also pass on someone's request or command.

this.tr: I heard Tanaka's taking tomorrow off.

that.tr: Tanaka says to come in early tomorrow.

items.explain: Look before 「って」: plain form＋んだ (休むんだ) → sharing news you heard; a request or command (来て, 来い, 来ないで) plus 「って」 → passing on what someone wants.

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: んだって is only used between people who are close; そうだ can be used in formal settings and in writing.

this.tr: Hey, I heard a new café is opening in front of the station.

that.tr: According to the news, a new café is opening in front of the station.

items.explain: Look at the setting: starting with 「ねえ」, chatting with friends or family → んだって; to superiors or in writing, often with 「〜によると」 → そうだ／そうです. Hearsay そうだ attaches to the plain form (できる＋そうだ) — don't confuse it with 「できそうだ」, which describes appearance.

groups.note: 来るかな ↔ 来ないかな — the extra 「ない」 doesn't mean “will it not come?” but rather “come already!”

items.diff: Affirmative 「かな」 asks yourself “I wonder if…”; negative 「ないかな」 is longing, “hurry up and…!”.

this.tr: Why isn't the bus here yet? Come on already.

that.tr: I wonder if the bus will come in five minutes.

items.explain: Check whether what comes before 「かな」 is affirmative or negative, and whether 「早く」 is there: 「来るかな」 is just wondering whether it will come; 「早く来ないかな」 literally looks like “I wonder if it won't come”, but actually means you're longing for it to come soon — often used with 「早く」「誰か」.

groups.note: Both express “hoping something comes true”

items.diff: ないかな takes the form of a self-question and carries impatience, “why isn't it… yet”; といいな calmly states a hope.

this.tr: Why won't this rain stop? Stop already.

that.tr: It'd be nice if the rain stopped by tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at the timing and tone: staring at what's in front of you, waiting impatiently, often with 「早く」 → ないかな; calmly hoping for the future → といいな (たらいいな works the same), and you can also say 「〜といいね」 to someone else.

items.diff: Both use “negative＋question” to express a wish; ないものか is more literary and more urgent.

this.tr: Why isn't it spring yet? Hurry up and come.

that.tr: Is there really no way this situation can be made better?

items.explain: Both have the same structure: negative (〜ない)＋question, longing for something to “be able to…”. ないかな is everyday talking to yourself, usually about small matters; ないものか leans written, often goes with 「何とか」, and expresses a serious, urgent wish to find a way (ないものだろうか is softer).

groups.note: These look a lot like 「〜ことはない」 and 「〜ない〜はない」: just one 「ない」 or one word in the middle differs, and the meaning is completely different

items.diff: 行かないことはない means “it's not that I won't go”; 行くことはない means “there's no need to go”.

this.tr: If I have time, it's not that I wouldn't go.

that.tr: There's no need to go all the way there — a phone call will do.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ことはない」: nai-form (行かない) → the two negatives cancel out, “it's not that I won't…”, often followed by 「けど」; dictionary form (行く) → “there's no need to…”, often with 「わざわざ」「そんなに」「心配する」.

items.diff: ないことはない means “it's not that I don't…”, leaving room; ない人はいない means “there's no one who doesn't…” ＝ everyone.

this.tr: This song… well, it's not that I don't know it…

that.tr: There's no one who doesn't know this song.

items.explain: Look at what sits between the two negatives: 「こと」 → the conclusion is “it's not that I don't…”, often followed by 「けど」, sounding reluctant; a noun like 「人」「日」「もの」 → it denies “there are exceptions”, so the conclusion is “all…”, very strong.

groups.note: Both are indirect ways of saying “not entirely…”

items.diff: ないことはない grudgingly admits “I can” from the direction of “can't”; わけではない corrects the other person's inference, “it's not that…”.

this.tr: I'm not great with spicy food, but it's not that I can't eat it.

that.tr: It's not that I dislike spicy food — I'm just skipping it today.

items.explain: Look at what comes first: nai-form (食べられない)＋ことはない → grudgingly admits it's possible, without much enthusiasm; plain form (嫌いな)＋わけではない → corrects “you think I…, but that's not it”, often followed by the real reason.

items.diff: Same meaning — both “it's not that I can't…”; ないものでもない is more literary and stiffer.

this.tr: If someone asked me, it's not that I couldn't take it on.

that.tr: Depending on the conditions, it is not out of the question that we accept.

items.explain: The two are interchangeable; look at the setting: everyday conversation and ordinary writing → ないことはない (なくはない); negotiations and formal writing, in a rather stiff, guarded tone → ないものでもない (in speech also ないでもない).

groups.note: Both mean “if a precondition isn't met, it's no good”

items.diff: ないと just says “if you don't, it's no good”; てからでないと stresses order, “only after finishing A can you B”.

this.tr: If you don't finish your homework, you can't go out and play.

that.tr: You can't go out and play until you've finished your homework.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「て＋から」: てからでないと stresses that B comes only “after A is done”, focusing on order, usually followed by 「できない」「だめ」; ないと isn't about order — it just says that without the condition it's no good, and can also be followed by a bad result (遅れるよ).

items.diff: Same meaning; ないことには is more literary, stresses the “precondition” more, and is always followed by a negative.

this.tr: You won't know until you try.

that.tr: Unless you actually try it, you can't know anything.

items.explain: Both sentences mean “unless you first…, you can't…”: ないことには leans written, and the second half is always negative (わからない, 始まらない, 決められない); ないと is more casual, and the second half can also be a bad result (遅れるよ, 困る).

groups.note: Both mean “must, have to”

items.diff: なければならない is a general obligation or rule; ないわけにはいかない comes from social obligation or your position — “it wouldn't be right not to”.

this.tr: It's my best friend's wedding, so however busy I am, I can't not go.

that.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left.

items.explain: Look at where the “must” comes from: law, rules or objective need → なければならない, with no emotion; social obligation, face or position making it “wrong not to” → ないわけにはいかない, with reluctance and resignation.

items.diff: ざるを得ない is written and stresses having objectively no other choice; ないわけにはいかない leans spoken and stresses that, by social norms, you can't not do it.

this.tr: If a senior asks me, I can't very well refuse to help.

that.tr: Due to the typhoon, the match had to be canceled.

items.explain: Look at the reason: objective circumstances like a typhoon or a lack of budget leave no other choice → ざるを得ない, common in news and formal settings; human relationships like seniors, friends or your own position → ないわけにはいかない.

groups.note: Both come from 「何（なに）」 — なんか ＝ 何か, なんて ＝ 何と, originally “…or something”

items.diff: なんか attaches to nouns and can give a casual example or belittle; なんて can also attach to a whole sentence to express surprise or shock.

this.tr: How about a hot spring or something for our next day off?

that.tr: Those two are getting married? I can't believe it.

wrong.why: To express surprise after a whole sentence, only なんて works

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun (温泉, 私) → なんか, a casual example or belittling; a whole sentence (結婚する) → なんて, surprise, “to think that…”. Both can belittle, but なんて sounds stronger.

groups.note: Both can give an example, “…and the like”

items.diff: なんか／など after a single person or thing often belittle or sound self-deprecating; や〜など just gives neutral examples.

this.tr: Someone like me could never do that.

that.tr: I prepared tea, sweets and so on.

items.explain: Look before など／なんか: a single person or thing, usually followed by something negative (無理だ, 嫌いだ) → belittling or self-deprecating, “the likes of…, not worth mentioning”; several items listed (お茶やお菓子) → just “and so on”. In formal settings, swapping なんか for など works the same (私などには無理です).

items.title: 〜でも (gentle suggestion)
items.diff: Close in meaning when giving a casual example; なんか is casual, でも is more polite.

this.tr: Let's take a break. How about some tea or something?

that.tr: Shall we take a short break? Would you care for some tea?

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: a casual suggestion between friends → なんか; to guests or superiors, with 「いかがですか」 → でも is the safer choice. What comes before なんか can sometimes sound a little “not worth mentioning”; でも doesn't.

groups.note: Both come from 「何（なに）」 — なんか ＝ 何か, なんて／なんと ＝ 何と, originally “…or something”

items.diff: なんて can attach to a whole sentence to express surprise or shock; なんか only attaches to nouns, giving a casual example or belittling.

this.tr: Those two are getting married? I can't believe it.

that.tr: How about a hot spring or something for our next day off?

wrong.why: To express surprise after a whole sentence, only なんて works

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a whole sentence (結婚する) → なんて, “to think that…”; a noun (温泉, 私) → なんか, a casual example or belittling. Both work for belittling, but なんて sounds stronger.

items.title: なんと〜 (exclamation)
items.diff: Same meaning when exclaiming “how…!”; なんて is spoken, なんと leans written.

this.tr: What a beautiful view!

that.tr: What a truly beautiful view!

items.explain: Both come from 「何と」, placed at the start of the sentence and paired with sentence-final 「だろう」 to exclaim. Use なんて in everyday speech, なんと in writing and speeches. なんと can also stand alone to mean “believe it or not” (なんと100万円！), while なんて at the end of a sentence expresses surprise (合格するなんて).

groups.note: Both express surprise or shock, “I never thought that…”

items.title: 〜とは (surprise)
items.diff: Same meaning; とは is written and composed, なんて is spoken and more openly emotional.

this.tr: Him, of all people — failing the exam!

that.tr: That someone as able as he should fail the exam.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the last word: chatting with friends, showing emotion → なんて, often followed by 「信じられない」; news, writing and formal settings → とは, which sounds more composed.

groups.note: Both are used to explain a reason

items.diff: なぜなら states the conclusion first, then adds the reason in a new sentence; のは〜からだ makes the result the topic and puts the reason at the end, all in one sentence.

this.tr: I run every morning. That's because it's good for my health.

that.tr: The reason I run every morning is that it's good for my health.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the sentence structure: 「なぜなら」 at the start of a sentence always has a conclusion in the sentence before → two sentences; 「〜のは」 puts the result up front as the topic and says it all in one sentence. のは〜からだ is more common; なぜなら feels more like reasoning in an essay or speech.

items.diff: なぜなら sounds like a logical argument; というのも is lighter, like filling in background or inside details while chatting.

this.tr: I'm against this plan. That's because it costs too much.

that.tr: I haven't been sleeping well lately. The thing is, there's construction going on next door.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's purpose: to persuade others or support your own position (反対だ) → なぜなら, common in essays and debates; just mentioning how things came about in passing → というのも, more casual and relaxed.

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: から usually comes before the conclusion, all in one sentence; なぜなら〜からだ moves the reason after the conclusion to emphasize it separately.

this.tr: The match was canceled. That's because the rain was too heavy.

that.tr: The rain was too heavy, so the match was canceled.

items.explain: Look at where the reason is placed: before the conclusion, linked with 「から、」 → an ordinary cause-and-effect sentence, used in both speech and writing; conclusion stated first, then a new sentence starting with 「なぜなら」 and ending in 「からだ」 → deliberately singling out the reason for emphasis, leaning written or speech-like.

groups.note: Both come from 「当（あ）たる」 — originally “to hit, to match up exactly”

items.diff: に当たる means “falls exactly on, is equivalent to”; にあたって means “on the occasion of… (doing something)”.

this.tr: This year marks exactly the company's 50th anniversary.

that.tr: On the occasion of the company's 50th anniversary, the president gave a speech.

items.explain: Look at what follows: if the sentence ends at 「に当たる」 (or it modifies a noun), it says something “matches up exactly” with a date or thing; 「にあたって、」 is followed by an action (挨拶した), meaning “at this occasion, (do…)”, used in formal settings like openings and speeches (in writing, 「にあたり」).

items.diff: Noun＋に当たる means “is equivalent to”; verb＋には当たらない means “there's no need to…”.

this.tr: One foot is equivalent to about 30 centimeters.

that.tr: A mistake this small is nothing to be surprised about.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a quantity or noun (30センチ, 兄) → に当たる, “is equivalent to”; verb dictionary form (驚く, 心配する, 非難する)＋には当たらない → “there's no need to…, it doesn't warrant…”, saying things haven't reached that point.

items.diff: に当たる has 「に」 in front and means “is equivalent to”; 当たり attaches directly to a number word and means “per…”.

this.tr: This amount is equivalent to three months of an employee's salary.

that.tr: The membership fee is 3,000 yen per person.

items.explain: Check whether 「に」 comes before 「当たる」: with 「に」 → “is equivalent to”; attached directly to a number word like 「一人」「１時間」「１日」 → “per…”, used to work out averages.

groups.note: Both come from 「合（あ）う」 — “to match, to agree”: matching a target ＝ fitting in with / suiting it; matching each other ＝ mutually

items.diff: に合わせて／に合った mean “matching a particular target”; masu-stem＋合う means “both sides do it to each other”.

this.tag: に合わせて · fitting in with
this.tr: Everyone danced along to the music.
Choose shoes that suit you.

that.tr: When times are tough, let's all help each other out.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「合」: noun＋に → matching a target — 「に合わせて」 means adjusting yourself to fit it, 「に合った」 means it suits it to begin with; verb masu-stem directly＋合う → two or more people doing the same thing to each other (助け合う, 話し合う).

groups.note: Both mean “based on / fitting a certain standard” or “matching it”

items.diff: に合わせて means actively adjusting to fit one particular target; に応じて means the result changes correspondingly as the first item varies.

this.tr: Change the way you talk to suit the other person's level.

that.tr: The fee varies depending on age.

items.explain: に応じて is preceded by something with several possible cases (年齢, 能力, 人数), each matched with a different result — common in rules and price lists; に合わせて means adjusting yourself to match a target (音楽, 相手, 予定), the focus being on “fitting in”.

items.diff: に合わせて means adjusting yourself to a target; に沿って means following a policy or plan set in advance, without straying.

this.tr: We put together a plan to fit the customer's budget.

that.tr: We push the project forward in line with company policy.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a “route set in advance” such as a policy, plan, manual or expectations → に沿って, meaning not straying from it; a “target to accommodate” such as the other person's budget, height or schedule → に合わせて, meaning adjusting yourself to fit.

items.diff: に合った means matching a specific thing; 向き evaluates by group, season or use, “suited to this type”.

this.tr: I'm looking for a job that suits me.

that.tag: Suited to a type of person
that.tr: This job is suited to young people with plenty of stamina.

items.explain: 「〜に合った」 is usually preceded by something specific like 「自分」「目的」「体質」, saying whether the two match; 向き is preceded by a type of person, a season or a use (初心者向き, 子ども向き, 夏向き), like sticking on a category label.

groups.note: Both are used to guess or make a judgment

items.diff: Exactly the same meaning; に相違ない is more literary and stiffer.

this.tr: The way he's acting, he must know something.

that.tr: Judging from the fingerprints left at the scene, the culprit can be none other than this man.

items.explain: The structure is exactly the same: 「違い」 and 「相違」 both mean “a mistake/discrepancy”, so both literally mean “there can be no mistake”. Everyday speech and ordinary writing → に違いない; a more solemn phrasing in novels and reports → に相違ない.

items.diff: に違いない is a strong subjective conviction (a gut feeling); はずだ has objective grounds (by logic).

this.tr: Look at that smile — something good must have happened.

that.tr: According to the schedule, the department head should be attending the 3 o'clock meeting.

items.explain: に違いない is the speaker's own strong feeling, and the basis can be just an impression; with はずだ, you can name concrete grounds behind it (a schedule, a rule, a calculation). That's why はずだ is more common when talking about work or in writing.

items.diff: に違いない infers from clues and leans written; に決まってる is spoken, dogmatic and often emotional.

this.tr: The light's on in the room. Someone must be there.

that.tr: A deal that good? It's obviously a lie.

items.explain: Look at the tone: a calm inference from the clues at hand, mostly in writing and narration → に違いない; talking with friends with a “it goes without saying” feeling, often to push back, where the basis can be mere prejudice → に決まってる (に決まっている).

items.diff: に違いない is the most certain (it must be); かもしれない is the least certain (maybe).

this.tr: The fingerprints matched too. That person must be the culprit.

that.tr: That person might be the culprit.

items.explain: Look at how much evidence the speaker has: plenty of evidence, total conviction (指紋も一致した) → に違いない; just a suspicion (もしかすると) → かもしれない. Literally they're opposites too: に違いない ＝ “there can be no mistake”, かもしれない ＝ “there's no way to know”.

groups.note: Both say the result was the opposite of what was expected

items.diff: に反して is preceded by the “expectation or hope” itself; にもかかわらず is preceded by a fact that already holds.

this.tr: Contrary to expectations, the team lost.

that.tr: Despite practicing every day, the team lost.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a “prior idea” like 「予想」「期待」「予報」＋に反して → the result went against the idea; a fact that has already happened (練習した, 雨が降っている)＋にもかかわらず → that fact made no difference.

items.title: 〜のに (even though)
items.diff: のに attaches to a full sentence, is spoken and carries dissatisfaction; に反して attaches only to nouns like “hope, expectation”, and is written and objective.

this.tr: Contrary to his parents' expectations, he did not go to university.

that.tr: His parents had such high hopes, but he didn't go to university.

items.explain: Check whether a noun or a sentence comes before: a noun like 「期待」「予想」＋に反して, objective like a news report; a sentence like 「期待していた」＋のに, carrying the speaker's dissatisfaction or regret.

groups.note: Both can be translated “toward… / about…”, marking the target or topic of an action

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; に関して is more formal and used mostly in reports, news and business.

this.tr: I will explain this matter.

that.tr: I talked with a friend about the movie I saw yesterday.

items.explain: Look at the setting: everyday chat and ordinary writing → について; reports, news and business emails (本件に関して、ご説明いたします) → に関して. The same goes when modifying a noun: 「〜に関する＋noun」 is more formal than 「〜についての」.

items.diff: に関して just raises a topic neutrally; をめぐって is usually followed by dispute or conflict.

this.tr: I read a book on environmental issues.

that.tr: The brothers are fighting over the inheritance.

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: words for several parties arguing back and forth, like 争う, 議論する, 対立する, もめる → をめぐって; neutral actions like explaining, investigating or reading → に関して (に関する when modifying a noun).

items.title: 〜に対して (target)
items.diff: に関して points to the “content or topic” (about); に対して points to the “target” of an attitude or action (toward).

this.tr: Reporting on customer complaints.

that.tr: Speak politely to customers.

items.explain: Look at the action that follows: the “content” of an explanation, report or investigation → に関して; an attitude or reaction toward that person or thing (丁寧に話す, 反対する, 怒る) → に対して. Saying 「お客さまに関して丁寧に話す」 doesn't make sense.

groups.note: All come from 「代（か）わる」 — “to replace, to take over for”

items.diff: に代わって only means “in place of, replacing”, and sounds formal; 代わりに is broader and can also mean “in exchange”.

this.tr: The department manager attended the meeting in place of the president.

that.tr: Someone helped me move, so in return I treated them to lunch.

items.explain: Look at what comes before it: noun ＋ に代わって → only “standing in for someone, replacing something”, common in speeches and the news (in writing, the mid-sentence form is 「に代わり」); verb ＋ 代わりに → can also mean “in exchange” or “doing B instead of A”, and に代わって can't be used for either of these.

groups.note: Both are built on 「決（き）まる」 — “to be decided, not going to change”

items.diff: に決まってる is a judgment about one thing: “it's bound to…”; と決まって is a pattern: “whenever…, always…”.

this.tr: After practicing that much, of course he'll pass.

that.tr: Whenever it rains, I always get a headache.

items.explain: Only 「に」 vs 「と」 differs: 「〜に決まってる」 comes at the end of the sentence as a strong judgment about one thing; in 「〜と決まって〜」, 「決まって」 is actually an adverb meaning “always, without fail”, preceded by the conditional 「と」, and describes something that happens every time.

groups.note: Both express a confident judgment

items.diff: に決まってる is casual and dogmatic, often emotional; に違いない is an inference from evidence, and leans written.

this.tr: A deal that good? It's obviously a lie.

that.tr: The light in the room is on. Someone must be there.

items.explain: Look at the tone: talking with friends, with a “goes without saying” feeling, often to push back, and the basis can be mere prejudice → に決まってる (に決まっている); calmly inferring from the clues in front of you, mostly in writing and narration → に違いない.

items.diff: に決まってる is a subjective judgment that needs no basis; はずだ is a calm calculation based on reasoning.

this.tr: Knowing him, he's bound to be late again.

that.tr: He left home at seven, so he should have arrived by now.

items.explain: Look at the basis: reasons you can state clearly, like times, schedules or rules → はずだ, calm in tone and fine in formal settings; impressions or prejudices like 「彼のことだから」, with a mocking or impatient feel → に決まってる, used only in speech.

groups.note: Both come from 「比べる」 — “to put two things side by side and compare”

items.diff: に比べて finds “a bit higher, a bit lower”; とは比べものにならない means the gap is so huge they “can't even be compared”.

this.tr: Compared with last year, this year is a little hotter.

that.tr: This year's heat is nothing like last year's — there's no comparison.

items.explain: Look at what follows: に比べて is followed by the result of the comparison, often with 「少し」 or 「ずっと」 saying by how much; とは比べものにならない is itself the conclusion — the gap is too big to put them side by side — and no further comparison result follows.

groups.note: Both are used to compare two things

items.diff: AはBより is the most basic comparison, common in speech; Bに比べて sets B as the baseline, is a little more formal, and is common in the news and when explaining data.

this.tr: Compared with ten years ago, this town's population has doubled.

that.tr: Today is colder than yesterday.

items.explain: Both can compare: 「今日は昨日より寒い」 can also be said as 「昨日に比べて、今日は寒い」. The difference is in feel: より is everyday speech; に比べて is more objective and formal, especially suited to explaining “how much numbers or conditions have changed compared with the past”, and the baseline often comes at the start of the sentence.

items.title: 〜のに対して (contrast)
items.diff: に比べて measures higher or lower on the same scale; のに対して places two opposite facts side by side for contrast.

this.tr: Compared with his older brother, the younger brother is taller.

that.tr: The older brother is tall, whereas the younger brother is small.

items.explain: Look at the second half: に比べて is followed by a description of just one side being “more…” (弟は背が高い) — a comparison of degree; with のに対して, each half describes one side (兄は背が高い／弟は小柄だ), with opposite meanings — a contrast. When attached to a clause, に対して needs 「の」 before it.

items.diff: に比べて neutrally compares degree; にひきかえ says the two are exact opposites, and carries the speaker's praise, blame or feelings.

this.tr: Compared with his older brother, the younger brother studies harder.

that.tr: In stark contrast to his serious older brother, the younger brother does nothing but play.

items.explain: With にひきかえ, the two people are one good and one bad, exact opposites (真面目な兄／遊んでばかりの弟), and the sentence carries the speaker's dissatisfaction or exasperation — it's a written expression; に比べて just says who has more or less of something, with no judgment.

groups.note: 慣れる ↔ なれる (potential form of なる) — pronounced exactly the same

items.title: 〜になる (になれる: can become)
items.diff: 先生に慣れた means “got used to the teacher”; 先生になれた means “managed to become a teacher”.

this.tr: I've finally gotten used to the new teacher.

that.tr: I finally became a teacher, just as I'd dreamed.

items.explain: Both are read 「せんせいになれた」. Written with the kanji 「慣れる」, it means getting used to; written in kana 「なれる」, it's usually the potential form of 「なる」, “can become”. When listening, look at what comes before: a new environment or new person (新しい先生, 新しい生活) → getting used to; a role or a dream (夢だった) → becoming.

groups.note: Both mean “as… (changes)” or “in accordance with…”

items.diff: In the sense of “as…”, the two are interchangeable; にしたがって can also mean “in accordance with (rules, instructions)”, and につれて can't.

this.tr: The farther north you go, the lower the temperature gets.

this.tag: In accordance with · only this one
this.tr: Please evacuate following the staff's instructions.

that.tr: The farther north you go, the lower the temperature gets.

wrong.why: につれて doesn't have the meaning “in accordance with”

items.explain: Look at what comes before にしたがって: changes like 「行く」 or 「年をとる」 → “as…”, and につれて works too; rules and instructions like 「指示」, 「規則」 or 「矢印」 → “in accordance with”, and only にしたがって works.

items.diff: にしたがって describes proportional, step-by-step change; に伴って is more formal and can also be used for the result of a one-time event.

this.tr: As you get older, your stamina declines.

that.tr: With the company's relocation, the phone number changed.

items.explain: Check whether what comes before is “changing gradually”: 年を取る is an ongoing change → both work; 会社の移転 is a one-time event, followed by the result it brought → use に伴って, and にしたがって sounds unnatural. に伴って is common in notices and the news.

items.diff: にしたがって means acting in “obedience” to rules or instructions; とおりに means “exactly as”, doing it identically to what was said or written.

this.tr: Sort and put out the garbage according to the rules.

that.tr: I assembled it exactly as the manual said.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: rules, instructions, orders — “things to obey” → にしたがって; specific content like 「言った」, 「書いてある」 or 「見た」 that you copy exactly → とおりに, which can attach directly to a verb (言ったとおりに).

items.diff: にしたがって means “acting” according to rules or instructions; に基づいて means using data or facts as the “basis” for making a judgment or creating something.

this.tr: Act according to the teacher's instructions.

that.tr: I wrote the report based on the survey data.

items.explain: Look at the verb after it and the noun before it: following orders to 「行動する」, 「避難する」, 「進む」 → にしたがって; using 「データ」, 「事実」 or 「経験」 as a foundation to 「書く」, 「判断する」, 「作る」 → に基づいて.

groups.note: にしても ↔ にしては — only the last character differs

items.diff: にしても means “even if… still”; にしては means “for a…, (surprisingly)”.

this.tr: Even if it's your first time, that's just too awful.

that.tr: For a first time, that's pretty good.

items.explain: Only 「も」 vs 「は」 differs; look at the second half: にしても first concedes “it's the first time”, then says “it's still too…”, usually criticism or a demand (ひどすぎる); にしては uses “the first time” as a yardstick, followed by an evaluation that exceeds (or falls short of) expectations (上手だ). Both come from 「に＋する (treat as)」.

groups.note: All express a concession: “even if… still”

items.diff: にしても usually first concedes an actual situation and then gives an opinion; としても leans toward pure hypothesis: “even supposing…”.

this.tag: Concede a fact · give an opinion
this.tr: Even if you're busy, I'd like you to at least get in touch.

that.tr: Even if I won the lottery, I wouldn't quit my job.

items.explain: Check whether the first half is a fact: the other person really is busy, and you concede that before saying “you should still…” → にしても, usually followed by the speaker's complaint or request; 「たとえ……としても」 is an imagined situation that may not happen → としても.

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; にしろ／にせよ are more formal and harder-sounding, while にしても is also common in everyday speech.

this.tr: Whatever the reason, hitting people isn't OK, you know.

that.tr: Whatever the reason, violence cannot be permitted.

items.explain: Look at the tone of the second half: something friends say, like 「よくないよ」, sounds most natural with にしても; drawing a conclusion (許されない) in the news, speeches or writing usually uses にせよ／にしろ. These are imperative forms of 「する」, so they sound harder, more like a final verdict. にしろ and にせよ mean the same, with にせよ more written.

items.title: 〜ても (even if)
items.diff: ても is the most ordinary “even if”, just stating a condition and a result; にしても is usually followed by the speaker's opinion or advice.

this.tr: Even if you failed, there's no need to be so down about it.

that.tr: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.

items.explain: Look at how it attaches and the second half: ても attaches to the te-form (降っても) and just says “even if the condition changes, the result is unaffected” — quite neutral; にしても attaches directly to the plain form (失敗したにしても), first concedes something, then gives your own opinion, advice or criticism (落ち込むことはない).

groups.note: にしては ↔ にしても — only the last character differs

items.diff: にしては means “for a…, (surprisingly)”; にしても means “even if… still”.

this.tr: For a first time, that's pretty good.

that.tr: Even if it's your first time, that's just too awful.

items.explain: Only 「は」 vs 「も」 differs; look at the second half: にしては uses “the first time” as a yardstick, followed by an unexpected evaluation (上手だ); にしても first concedes “it's the first time”, then says “it's still too…”, usually criticism or a demand (ひどすぎる). Both come from 「に＋する (treat as)」.

groups.note: Both mean “not in keeping with one's status or degree”

items.diff: にしては usually follows a status or a concrete fact; わりに usually follows a degree that can be higher or lower (年齢, 値段), and nouns need 「の」.

this.tr: For an elementary school kid, his handwriting is really good.

that.tr: She looks young for her age.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: statuses and concrete facts like 小学生, 初めて, プロ → にしては, attached directly to the noun; degrees that can be more or less, like 年齢, 値段, 勉強した時間 → わりに, with 「の」 after the noun (年齢のわりに), and it can also attach directly to adjectives (高いわりに).

items.diff: にしては is a neutral evaluation, positive or negative; くせに carries strong blame and contempt.

this.tr: For a kid, he's quite mature.

that.tr: He's just a kid, yet he's so cheeky.

items.explain: Look at the evaluation in the second half: 「しっかりしている」 can be praise → にしては; accusations like 「生意気だ」 or 「偉そうに」 → くせに. Also, くせに needs 「の」 after a noun, while にしては attaches directly to the noun.

groups.note: Both put two things side by side to compare or contrast them

items.diff: のに対して places two opposite facts side by side for contrast; に比べて measures higher or lower on the same scale.

this.tr: The older brother is tall, whereas the younger brother is small.

that.tr: Compared with his older brother, the younger brother is taller.

items.explain: Look at the second half: with のに対して, each half describes one side (兄は背が高い／弟は小柄だ), with opposite meanings; に比べて is followed by a description of just one side being “more…” (弟は背が高い) — a comparison of degree. When attached to a clause, に対して needs 「の」 before it.

groups.note: All mean “from someone's standpoint or point of view”

items.title: 〜としては (standpoint)
items.diff: にとって is followed by an evaluation (大切だ, 難しい); としては is followed by your own opinion or stance (賛成だ, 困る).

this.tag: Evaluation · what it means to me
this.tr: This plan is important to me.

that.tr: Personally, I'm in favor of this plan.

wrong.why: にとって can't be followed by opinions like agreeing or opposing

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「大切だ」 or 「難しい」 say what the matter means to me → にとって; 「賛成だ」, 「反対だ」 or 「困る」 are a stance or opinion I'm stating → としては.

items.diff: にとって is a general “for…, to…”; にしたら means putting yourself in someone else's shoes, mostly to guess how they feel.

this.tr: This problem is difficult for children.

that.tr: If you don't come home until that late, your parents are bound to worry.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: にしたら (also にすれば) often goes with 「だろう」 or 「と思う」, stepping into someone else's position to guess how they feel (心配だ, うれしい); にとって is an evaluation of the matter itself, with no need to guess someone's feelings.

items.diff: にとって says what this matter “means to that person”; から見ると says “how it looks through that person's eyes”.

this.tr: For international students, part-time work is an important source of income.

that.tr: To foreigners, Japanese customs seem strange.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「大切だ」, 「必要だ」 or 「ありがたい」 say what the matter means to that person → にとって; 「不思議だ」, 「おかしい」 or 「〜ように見える」 describe the impression you get looking through that person's eyes → から見ると (also からすると).

groups.note: Both come from 「就く（つく）」 — “to attach to, to follow”

items.diff: について means “about”; につき, in signs and notices, usually means “due to” or “per…” — an old, formal expression.

this.tr: I'll explain about the construction work.

that.tr: Road closed due to construction.

items.explain: Both are 「に＋就く」: について is 「就いて」, attaching to a topic to talk about it; につき keeps the old continuative form and is common in signs and notices. Look at what follows: 「話す」 or 「説明する」 → “about”; a result (通行止め) or a quantity (一人につき三枚) → “due to” / “per”.

groups.note: Both introduce the topic being discussed: “about…”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; に関して is more written and formal, while について is the most common in everyday use.

this.tr: I talked with my friend about tomorrow's trip.

that.tr: Does anyone have any questions regarding the new system?

items.explain: Look at the setting: chatting with friends or writing a diary → について; reports, official documents and formal remarks mostly use に関して. When modifying a noun, に関する＋noun (環境に関する問題) is more formal and concise than についての＋noun.

items.diff: について simply states the topic; をめぐって is used for disputes and conflicts surrounding that matter.

this.tr: I consulted a lawyer about the inheritance.

that.tr: The siblings are fighting over the inheritance.
