items.explain: Look at the verb after it: 「話す」, 「相談する」, 「調べる」 → について; clashes between parties like 「争う」, 「対立する」, 「議論が起きる」 → をめぐって.

groups.note: Both mean “as… (changes)”

items.diff: In the sense of “as…”, the two are interchangeable; にしたがって can also mean “in accordance with (rules, instructions)”, and につれて can't.

this.tr: The farther north you go, the lower the temperature gets.

that.tr: The farther north you go, the lower the temperature gets.

that.tag: In accordance with · only this one
that.tr: Please evacuate following the staff's instructions.

wrong.why: につれて doesn't have the meaning “in accordance with”

items.explain: In the sense of “as…”, the two are interchangeable (北へ行くにつれて／にしたがって); にしたがって also means “in accordance with”, and when what comes before is an instruction or rule, only it works — it can't be swapped for につれて.

items.diff: につれて only describes gradual, proportional change; とともに is more formal, works with one-time events too, and means “at the same time as…”.

this.tr: As I've gotten older, my memory has declined.

that.tr: Upon graduating, I moved to Tokyo.

wrong.why: 卒業 is a one-time event, so につれて can't be used

items.explain: Check whether what comes before is an ongoing change: 年を取る or 時間が経つ change little by little → both につれて and とともに work; events that happen all at once, like 卒業 or 結婚 → only とともに (at the same time) works, not につれて.

items.diff: につれて describes a change that actually happened over a period of time; ば〜ほど means “the more…, the more…”, says the same word twice, and often states a general truth.

this.tr: As time passed, the sadness gradually faded.

that.tr: The more you practice, the better you get.

items.explain: First look at the form: ば〜ほど repeats the same word (練習すれば練習するほど) and sounds like a general truth; につれて mentions the change only once, usually describes a change that really happened over some period, and often goes with 「〜ていく」 or 「〜てきた」.

groups.note: Both come from 「よる（因る・依る）」 — “to rely on, to depend on”; によると means “according to (a source)”

items.diff: によって expresses a cause, a means, or “varies depending on…”; によると is only for an information source: “according to…”.

this.tr: Many houses were destroyed by the typhoon.

that.tr: According to the news, a typhoon is coming.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: によると usually pairs with 「そうだ」, 「らしい」 or 「ということだ」 and conveys something you heard (によれば works the same way); によって is followed by an actual result or change (壊れた).

groups.note: All introduce a cause, means, basis or agent (due to / by means of / based on…)

items.diff: によって says “differs depending on…”; によっては says “depending on the case, some…”.

this.tr: Customs differ from country to country.

that.tr: In some countries, tipping is expected.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: によって is usually followed by 「違う」, 「異なる」 or 「さまざまだ」, saying things vary overall; によっては singles out just some of them, often followed by 「〜もある」 or 「〜こともある」.

items.diff: で is the most ordinary everyday marker of means or cause; によって is more formal, common in the news and reports, and isn't used for everyday transport.

this.tr: The problem was solved through discussion.

that.tr: I go to school by bus.

wrong.why: Everyday means like transport take 「で」

items.explain: Look at the setting and content: everyday tools and ways of getting around (バスで, ペンで) → で; in reports and the news, explaining by what method something major was achieved (話し合いによって解決した) → によって.

items.diff: によって only says “differs according to A”; に応じて says “adjusted to match A”.

this.tr: Everyone's tastes are different.

that.tr: The amount of tax is set according to income.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「違う」 or 「異なる」 just state a difference → によって; 「決める」, 「変える」 or 「選ぶ」 mean someone adapts or adjusts to the situation → に応じて.

items.title: 〜に〜（ら）れる (passive)
items.diff: Ordinary passive sentences use 「に」 for the doer; passives of “creating something” — writing, inventing, building — need によって.

this.tr: This novel was written by Natsume Soseki.

that.tr: My little brother was scolded by the teacher.

items.explain: Look at the verb: for actions that create something new, like 「書く」, 「建てる」, 「発明する」, 「発見する」, the doer in a passive sentence takes によって; for actions done directly to a person, like 「叱る」, 「ほめる」, 「頼む」, use に.

groups.note: Both mean “since… / because…”, giving a reason

items.diff: のだから uses a fact both sides know to persuade or reproach the listener; からには is usually followed by your own resolve or duty: “now that…, I'll see it through”.

this.tr: We made a promise, so you'd better show up.

that.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

items.explain: Look at who the second half is aimed at: demanding something of the listener (来てよ, 早くしなさい) or blaming them → usually のだから; expressing your own resolve or responsibility (最後までやる, 〜なければならない) → usually からには, which sounds more serious.

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: から can give a new reason the listener doesn't know; with のだから, the reason is a fact the listener also knows, with a persuading or reproachful tone.

this.tr: You're the one who suggested it, so you do it.

that.tr: I have a headache, so I'll take today off.

items.explain: Check whether the listener already knows the reason: “you suggested it” is clear to both, and is used to pressure them → んだから; “I have a headache” is new information for the listener → から. Using んだから to explain your own reasons to a superior sounds pushy and rude.

groups.note: 〜んじゃない ↔ 〜じゃない — only one 「ん」 differs

items.diff: 学生なんじゃない？ is a guess: “isn't he a student?”; 学生じゃない says “he's not a student”.

this.tr: Isn't that guy a student? (I think he is)

that.tr: That person is not a student.

items.explain: んじゃない, with 「ん（の）」, is a guess that leans positive (I think it's…), often ending with a rising 「？」; the formal version is のではないか. じゃない without 「ん」 is plain negation: “is not”. When reading, first look for that 「ん」.

groups.note: All express a guess or a tentative opinion without being definite

items.diff: のではないか is んじゃない in speech; のではないだろうか is softer and more written, common in commentary and essays.

this.tr: Shouldn't you rest a bit more?

that.tr: Isn't young people's drift away from reading largely due to smartphones?

items.explain: Look at the setting: reminding or advising a friend → んじゃない？; tentatively putting forward your own claim in an essay or speech → のではないだろうか, where the added 「だろう」 makes it less assertive.

items.diff: かもしれない just presents a possibility; のではないか means the speaker leans toward believing it, and states their judgment tentatively.

this.tr: Judging by how he's acting, doesn't he already know?

that.tr: Maybe he already knows.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: 「あの様子だと」 gives an observed basis, and the speaker already leans toward “yes” → のではないか; 「もしかしたら」 just raises a possibility, with no telling either way → かもしれない.

groups.note: のでしょうか ↔ のではないでしょうか — just 「ではない」 added

items.title: 〜のではないでしょうか
items.diff: のでしょうか is a real question; のではないでしょうか tentatively states your own view: “I'd say it's…”.

this.tr: Is this plan impossible?

that.tr: I'm afraid this plan may be impossible.

items.explain: Adding 「ではない」 actually makes it lean positive: のではないでしょうか ≈ “I think it's impossible”, a tentative opinion; のでしょうか means you don't know the answer and are asking or doubting. When reading, don't take のではないでしょうか as the negative “it's not…”.

groups.note: All are used to ask a question or express doubt

items.diff: Same meaning; のでしょうか is polite and can be used to ask others; のだろうか is plain, mostly talking to yourself or in writing.

this.tr: Excuse me, why is this train stopped?

that.tr: Is he really going to come? (wondering to myself)

items.explain: Look at who's meant to hear it: asking someone else, like station staff or a teacher → のでしょうか; wondering to yourself, or a self-question in a diary or essay → のだろうか (んだろうか in speech).

items.title: 〜んですか
items.diff: んですか directly confirms or presses for an answer; のでしょうか adds a guessing tone, softer and more polite.

this.tr: Excuse me, sir — has the meeting been canceled?

that.tr: What? The meeting's been canceled?

items.explain: With people you need to be polite to, like bosses and clients, or when unsure whether they know → のでしょうか; confirming directly on the spot after just hearing news → んですか. Asking 「どうして」 with んですか can easily sound like you're interrogating someone.

items.title: 〜でしょうか
items.diff: でしょうか just politely asks about something; のでしょうか asks about the reason or background behind a situation in front of you.

this.tr: Why is this shop always so crowded?

that.tr: Will it be sunny tomorrow?

items.explain: のでしょうか usually follows a fact you've already seen (いつも込んでいる) and asks “why is it like this”, often with 「なぜ」 or 「どうして」; でしょうか just politely asks whether something will happen or is right, with no need for a situation in front of you.

groups.note: Both are used to explain a reason

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: In AからB, the reason comes first and the focus is the result; BのはAからだ states the result first and puts the reason at the end as the focus.

this.tr: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.

that.tr: The train stopped, so I was late.

wrong.why: At the end of a sentence, a reason can only be given with 「からだ」, not ので

items.explain: Both sentences say the same thing with a different focus: when someone asks “why were you late?” or you want to stress the reason, put the known result in 「〜のは」 and the reason at the end → のは〜からだ; in ordinary narration, cause comes before effect → から.

items.diff: のは〜からだ says it all in one sentence; なぜなら first finishes the conclusion, then adds the reason in a separate sentence.

this.tr: The reason the match was canceled is that the rain was heavy.

that.tr: The match was canceled. That's because the rain was heavy.

items.explain: Count the sentences: the result goes inside 「〜のは」 and the reason is given in one sentence → のは〜からだ; the conclusion is stated in one sentence, then a second sentence beginning with 「なぜなら」 explains it → なぜなら〜からだ, common in essays and speeches. Both end in 「からだ」.

groups.note: All come from 「お＋ます-stem」 — turning an action into a respectful noun; what follows decides the meaning: お待ちです (you are waiting), お待ちになる (you wait), お待ちします (I will wait)

items.diff: お〜になる is the standard respectful form and works in any tense; お〜です is more concise and mainly describes the other person's current state or plans.

this.tr: The manager has already gone home.

that.tr: The manager went home a little while ago.

items.explain: お〜です corresponds to 「〜ている」 or 「〜する予定だ」, describing the person's state right now (もうお帰りです = already not here); for an action done at a certain point in the past (さっき帰った), お〜になりました is more natural. Also, お〜です is only used with a handful of common verbs (お待ち, お持ち, お探し, お帰り).

items.diff: お待ちです respectfully says “(you/they) are waiting”; お待ちします humbly says “(I) will wait”.

this.tr: The president is waiting for you in the reception room.

that.tr: I'll wait for you at the station tomorrow.

items.explain: Both start with 「お待ち」, so look at what follows: 「です」 → respectful language, the one waiting is the other person (社長がお待ちです); 「します」 → humble language, the one waiting is me (私がお待ちします). When reading, find the subject first and it's clear who is waiting. ご〜です／ご〜します work the same way.

groups.note: Both respectfully describe someone else's action

items.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
items.diff: れる・られる attaches to almost any verb and is lighter in respect; お〜です is more respectful but only used with a few verbs.

this.tr: Are you looking for something, sir?

that.tr: The teacher reads the newspaper every morning.

items.explain: Look at the setting: when great politeness is needed, like shop staff serving customers, set phrases like お探しです, お待ちです, お持ちですか are common; れる・られる is lighter in respect and simple to form, often used when talking about bosses or teachers, but easily confused with the passive and potential forms.

groups.note: Both come from 「お＋ます-stem」 — turning an action into a respectful noun: with いただく, the other person does it for me; with する, I do it for them

items.diff: お〜いただく means the other person does it for me; お〜する means I do it for them.

this.tr: Thank you very much for sending the materials the other day.

that.tr: I'll send you the materials tomorrow.

items.explain: Both start with 「お送り」, so look at what follows: 「いただく」 → the action is done by the other person and benefits me, often followed by 「ありがとうございます」; 「する／します」 → the action is done by me. Misread it in a business email and you'll mix up “who sent what to whom”. ご〜いただく／ご〜する work the same way (ご連絡いただく／ご連絡する).

groups.note: Both are used to formally ask someone to do something (for me)

items.diff: Same meaning; ていただく attaches to almost any verb, while お〜いただく is more formal, mostly used with customers and in business.

this.tr: Could you wait just a moment, please?

that.tr: Could you wait a moment, please?

items.explain: The action and its direction are exactly the same; only the level of formality differs: to guests and clients, say 「少々お待ちいただけますか」; to colleagues or teachers, ていただけますか is enough. Native Japanese verbs take お (お待ち), Sino-Japanese words take ご (ご確認いただく); 「来る」 and 「見る」 use special forms (お越しいただく, ご覧いただく).

items.diff: お〜ください is a direct request or instruction; お〜いただけますか uses a question form and is softer.

this.tr: I'm sorry to trouble you, but could you write your name here?

that.tr: Please write your name here.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: お〜ください announces a procedure or gives an instruction, common in signs and explanations; お〜いただけますか uses a question to leave the decision to the other person, suited to making an extra request of a customer, often preceded by 「恐れ入りますが」.

items.diff: お〜願います is mostly used in announcements and notices, addressed to everyone; お〜いただけますか is mostly used to ask one person face to face.

this.tag: Face to face · to one person
this.tr: Mr. Tanaka, could you wait here, please?

that.tr: Ladies and gentlemen, please wait a moment.

items.explain: Look at who it's addressed to: speaking to an unspecified audience in station announcements or notices → お〜願います (ご注意願います, お待ち願います); speaking face to face to a specific person → お〜いただけますか.

groups.note: Both express a cause

items.diff: おかげで is used for good results, with gratitude; せいで is used for bad results, with blame.

this.tr: Thanks to the rain, it's cooled down.

that.tr: Because of the rain, the match was canceled.

items.explain: The cause can be the same (雨), so look at the result that follows: cooling down is good → おかげで; the match being canceled is bad → せいで. Using おかげで with a bad result is sarcastic: “thanks a lot”.

items.title: 〜ために (cause)
items.diff: おかげで carries the speaker's gratitude; ために just objectively states the cause, mostly in writing and notices.

this.tr: Thanks to all of you, the event was a success.

that.tr: School was closed due to the typhoon.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence carries feeling: to express gratitude (皆さんのおかげで) → おかげで; to just state the cause without emotion, like the news or a notice (台風のため休校) → ために, which works for both good and bad results.

groups.note: The same 「との」, written the same, with completely different meanings

items.diff: との in 友達との約束 means “with…”; との in 中止との連絡 is a quote: “saying that…”.

this.tr: I forgot my promise with my friend.

that.tr: We got word that the match was canceled.

items.explain: Look at what comes before との: a person (友達, 先生) → “with…”, usually followed by 約束, 関係 or 会話; the content of a statement (試合は中止) → a quote, usually followed by 連絡, 知らせ, 返事 or 意見.

groups.note: Both modify nouns, meaning “toward…” or “in…”

items.title: 〜に対する (modifying nouns)
items.diff: への focuses on “directed at, given to”; に対する is more formal and often also means “against, in opposition to”.

this.tr: I wrote my gratitude to my teacher in a letter.

that.tr: Criticism of the government is growing.

wrong.why: の can't be attached directly to に; say 「先生への手紙」

items.explain: To say “to…, for…” (手紙, 感謝, プレゼント) → への; for things “aimed against” someone, like 批判, 反対 or 態度, or in formal writing → に対する. Note that 「の」 can't attach directly to 「に」 — only への is possible.

items.title: 〜における (modifying nouns)
items.diff: での works in both everyday speech and writing; における is a written expression, common in academic papers and official documents.

this.tr: I've been getting used to life in Japan.

that.tr: I research the role of women in modern society.

items.explain: Same meaning, “in…”: in conversation and compositions, use での (日本での生活, 学校での出来事); in academic papers, reports and official documents, use における. When modifying a verb, they become で and において respectively.

groups.note: 〜っ放し（ぱなし）↔ 〜放題（ほうだい） — both written with 「放」 and attached to the ます-stem, yet they mean different things

items.diff: っぱなし means doing something and then “leaving it be”, or a state that stays unchanged; 放題 means “limits removed”, doing as much as you like.

this.tr: I went out and left the window open.

that.tag: As much as you like · unlimited
that.tr: At this restaurant, it's all-you-can-eat for 2,000 yen.

items.explain: Both use 「放」: っぱなし is 「放し」 with a small っ, meaning you do the action and then let go and leave it (開けっぱなし); 放題 means the limits are released, with no restraint at all (食べ放題, 言いたい放題). Check whether there's a sense of “as much as you like, unlimited” to tell them apart.

groups.note: All mean a state or action continues

items.diff: たまま neutrally says “left as it is”; っぱなし stresses leaving something that should have been dealt with, with dissatisfaction. They also attach differently.

this.tr: I fell asleep with the TV left on.

that.tr: Don't come into the room with your shoes on.

wrong.why: っぱなし attaches to the ます-stem: つけっぱなし

items.explain: First look at how they attach: まま takes the ta-form (つけたまま), っぱなし takes the ます-stem (つけっぱなし). Then look at the tone: まま just describes an unchanged state; っぱなし means something that should have ended (turned off, put away) is left as is, carrying the speaker's dissatisfaction.

items.diff: ておく means deliberately keeping something a certain way for a purpose; っぱなし means leaving it because of carelessness or laziness.

this.tr: I carelessly left the window open.

that.tr: I left the window open to air out the room.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: 「換気のために」 gives a clear purpose — kept that way on purpose → ておく; 「うっかり」 or 「忘れて」 mean it happened by accident → っぱなし.

items.diff: 続ける is mostly actively keeping something going; っぱなし is mostly being stuck in a state, unwillingly or by force.

this.tr: The train was so crowded that I was standing for a whole hour.

that.tr: I kept running all the way to the finish without a break.

items.explain: Check whether it's what the person wants: the train was packed and there were no seats, so you had no choice but to stand → 立ちっぱなし; you pushed yourself to keep running to the finish → 走り続けた. っぱなし is also common for losing out or being helpless, as in 「負けっぱなし」 or 「言われっぱなし」.

groups.note: All mean “having a certain look or tendency”

items.title: 〜らしい (typical)
items.diff: らしい means “truly like a…” (living up to the name, usually praise); っぽい means “not actually one, but giving that feeling” (usually negative).

this.tr: He's a grown-up, yet he thinks so childishly.

that.tr: Lively and full of energy, she's a real kid.

items.explain: Check whether the subject actually has that identity: an adult who seems like a child → っぽい (子どもっぽい = childish); a child who has the qualities a child should have → らしい (子どもらしい = innocent and sweet).

items.diff: 気味 is mostly used for physical conditions or states, “a bit…”, and is slightly formal; っぽい is very casual and can also describe colors and personality.

this.tr: I feel like I'm coming down with a cold today.

that.tr: I've had a bit of a cold since yesterday.

items.explain: Both work for feeling unwell, but when asking your boss for time off, 「風邪気味です」 is more appropriate; 風邪っぽい is only for people you're close to. 気味 usually attaches to bad states (疲れ気味, 太り気味); っぽい can also describe colors and personality (白っぽい, 忘れっぽい), which 気味 can't.

items.diff: がち says something “tends to happen often”; っぽい with a verb describes a person's character: “quick to…”.

this.tr: My grandmother has become forgetful lately.

that.tr: When I'm busy, my replies tend to be late.

items.explain: っぽい only attaches to a few verbs describing character (忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい, 飽きっぽい), talking about someone's natural disposition; がち attaches to more verbs and nouns (遅れがち, 病気がち), saying something is prone to happen, often preceded by a condition like 「忙しいと」 or 「冬は」.

items.diff: For guesses, っぽい is very casual speech; みたいだ／ようだ are the ordinary ways to guess.

this.tr: Looks like those two are going out, huh.

that.tr: It seems those two are going out.

items.explain: The meaning is about the same; the difference is the setting: っぽい is a casual expression used by young people, not used with superiors or in formal settings; みたいだ is ordinary speech; in writing, use ようだ (付き合っているようだ).

groups.note: Both are used to join two sentences

items.diff: Same meaning; て／で is used in speech and ordinary writing; the continuative-form link drops 「て」, making it more concise and formal, common in the news and reports.

this.tr: I got off at the station and transferred to a bus.
He is a doctor, and also a writer.

that.tr: I got off at the station and transferred to a bus.
He is a doctor, and also a writer.

items.explain: Both forms mean the same; look at the style: in speech and everyday writing, 「降りて」 and 「医者で」; in the news, reports and academic papers, 「て」 is often dropped, written as 「降り、」 and 「医者であり、」. In writing, 「〜ている」 becomes 「〜ており、」 when linking.

groups.note: さえ ↔ さえ〜ば — the same 「さえ」, but adding 「ば」 after it changes the meaning

items.diff: さえ on its own means “even…”; paired with 「ば」 it becomes “as long as…”.

this.tr: I'm so busy I don't even have time to sleep.

that.tr: As long as I have time to sleep, I'll be fine.

items.explain: The same 「さえ」 — look for the conditional 「ば」 after it: no 「ば」 and a negative after it (ない) → not even something this basic; with 「〜あれば」 or 「〜すれば」 → as long as this one condition is met, nothing else matters.

groups.note: Both mean “even…”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; すら is more written and stronger in tone.

this.tr: He can't even write his own name.

that.tr: He can't even write his own name.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable; the difference is style: さえ is common in both speech and writing; すら is mostly written and heavier in tone. Also, さえ can form 「さえ〜ば (as long as…)」, which すら can't.

items.title: 〜まで (even)
items.diff: さえ names the most basic, minimal thing (not even this); まで names the extreme the range has spread to (even that…).

this.tr: I'm so busy I can't even eat lunch.

that.tag: Spreads to the extreme · adding on
that.tr: Not just my friends — even my family opposed it.

items.explain: さえ often goes with a negative, saying “can't even do the most basic thing”; まで often goes with 「〜だけでなく」 or 「〜も」, saying things escalate step by step, reaching people or things you'd never expect.

groups.note: さえ ↔ さえ〜ば — the same 「さえ」, but adding 「ば」 after it changes the meaning

items.title: 〜さえ (even…)
items.diff: さえ〜ば means “as long as…”; drop the 「ば」, and さえ on its own means “even…”.

this.tr: As long as I have time to sleep, I'll be fine.

that.tr: I'm so busy I don't even have time to sleep.

items.explain: The same 「さえ」 — look for the conditional 「ば」 after it: with 「〜あれば」 or 「〜すれば」 → as long as this one condition is met, nothing else matters; no 「ば」 and a negative after it (ない) → not even something this basic.

groups.note: All mean “as long as…”

items.title: 〜限り (as long as…)
items.diff: さえ〜ば stresses “just this one condition”; 限り stresses “for as long as this state continues”.

this.tr: As long as I'm healthy, I don't need money or anything.

that.tr: As long as I'm healthy, I want to keep working.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「お金はいらない」 says no other condition matters → さえ〜ば; 「ずっと働き続けたい」 says “I'll keep this up for as long as my health lasts” → 限り, often followed by an intention or resolve.

items.title: 〜だけで (just… is enough)
items.diff: だけでいい says “you only need to do this (it's easy)”; さえ〜ばいい says “as long as this is met, nothing else matters”.

this.tr: As long as you write your name, you don't need to do anything else.

that.tr: Applying is easy — you just write your name.

items.explain: They attach differently: だけで takes the dictionary form (書くだけで), while さえ needs the conditional form (書けば). In meaning, だけで stresses “there's little to do, it's easy”; さえ〜ば stresses “this is the only key, nothing else matters”, often followed by 「あとは……」.

groups.note: Both come from 「際（さい）」 — originally “edge, boundary”, extended to “critical moment, occasion”

items.diff: 際に is used for everyday procedures and the like, “when…”; に際して is more formal, mostly used on the occasion of starting something important.

this.tr: Please watch your step when getting off.

that.tr: When I went abroad to study, many people helped me.

items.explain: Look at what kind of event comes before it: everyday procedures like getting off, using something or applying → 〜の際に／際は; big life or career events like studying abroad, entering school or opening a business, mostly in speeches and documents → に際して. They also attach differently: 際 needs 「の」 after a noun, while に際して attaches directly to the noun.

groups.note: Both mean “when…”

items.diff: とき is the most ordinary way to say it; 際 is formal and written, mostly used in notices and business.

this.tr: When using this, please let a staff member know.

that.tr: Turn off the light when you go home, OK?

wrong.why: 際 only follows actions or events — it can't be used for a period like “when I was little”

items.explain: Look at the setting: between family and friends, とき; in notices, manuals and business emails, 際 (ご利用の際, お帰りの際). Also, 際 is only used for the moment of doing something; states and periods like 「子どものとき」 or 「暇なとき」 can only take とき.

groups.note: All mean “while in the middle of…”

items.title: 〜中 (ちゅう: in the middle of…)
items.diff: 〜中 objectively describes the state of “being in the middle of…”; 最中に stresses being halfway through, followed by something that suddenly cuts in.

this.tr: Right in the middle of the meeting, a cell phone rang.

that.tr: The manager is in a meeting right now.

items.explain: 〜中 sticks directly onto a noun and states a status like a door sign (会議中, 工事中, 電話中), and the sentence ends there; 最中に needs 「の」 before it and is always followed by something that cuts in, usually inconvenient or troublesome.

items.title: 〜ているところだ (in the process of doing)
items.diff: ているところだ just says the action is in progress; 最中だ stresses being busy in the middle of it and not wanting to be disturbed now.

this.tr: I'm right in the middle of cooking, so I'll call you back later.

that.tr: I'm cooking right now.

items.explain: Both sentences say “I'm cooking”. ているところだ just objectively says what stage you're at; 最中だ has a sense of “right at the crucial point, can't step away”, often followed by words explaining the inconvenience or interruption, like 「だから後で」 or 「なのに」.

items.title: 〜間に
items.diff: 最中に stresses being interrupted while busy in the middle of something; 間に just says something happened “during this time”, with no sense of interruption.

this.tr: In the middle of the exam, I suddenly felt sick.

that.tr: While I was asleep, the snow piled up.

items.explain: 最中に follows something in progress and important (試験, 会議, 食事), followed by something unexpected that interrupts it; 間に follows a stretch of time (寝ている間, 留守の間), and what follows is often something the person didn't notice, happening on the side.

groups.note: All come from the causative 「させて」 — “let (me) do”

items.title: 〜させてください／〜させてもらう
items.diff: させてください asks for permission; させてもらう says afterwards “I was allowed to do it”; させていただく states what you're going to do with a “by your kind permission” stance — the most humble.

this.tr: I'm not feeling well, so I'll be taking today off, if I may.

that.tag: させてください · asking permission
that.tr: I'm not feeling well, so please let me take today off.

that.tag: させてもらう · was allowed to
that.tr: I asked the store manager, and he let me take the day off.

items.explain: All have the causative 「させて (let me do)」; the difference is the second half: ください is asking, and the other person hasn't agreed yet; もらった says afterwards that you got permission, common among equals and in speech; いただきます means you've already decided to do it, and uses “by your kind permission” to show humility, common at work and in speeches.

groups.note: していただく ↔ させていただく — just one 「させ」 differs, and the person doing it switches

items.diff: 説明させていただく means “I will explain”; 説明していただく means “I'll ask the other person to explain”.

this.tr: Well then, allow me to explain.

that.tr: Well then, I'll ask Mr. Tanaka to explain.

items.explain: Only 「させ」 differs: with the causative 「させ」 → the doer is me (allow me to explain); no 「させ」 and 「〜に」 before it → the doer is the other person (Mr. Tanaka will explain). When listening to a meeting's chair, this one spot tells you who speaks next.

groups.note: Both humbly describe something you're going to do

items.title: いたす
items.diff: いたします is concise and appropriate; させていただきます adds a layer of “with your permission”, more polite, but overusing it sounds wordy.

this.tr: Well then, allow me to go over the materials.

that.tr: Well then, I will go over the materials.

items.explain: Both sentences humbly describe your own action. させていただく was originally used when you really need the other person's permission or are benefiting yourself (休ませていただく); to simply state what you're going to do, いたします is enough, and using させていただく over and over in one speech actually sounds wordy. The same goes for other humble verbs like 参る and 申す.

groups.note: Both come from 「せい（所為）」 — “the result caused by (someone or something)”

items.diff: せいで names a cause you're sure of, with blame; せいか means “maybe because of…”, with the cause uncertain.

this.tr: Because I didn't get enough sleep, I made a mistake at work.

that.tr: Maybe because I didn't get enough sleep, my head feels foggy today.

items.explain: Only 「で」 vs 「か」 differs: with せいで, the speaker is sure this is the cause, and blames it; せいか, with the questioning 「か」, means “probably because of…”, the speaker isn't sure, and the result isn't necessarily bad (気のせいか、少し痩せたみたい).

groups.note: Both express a cause

items.diff: せいで is used for bad results, with blame; おかげで is used for good results, with gratitude.

this.tr: Because of the rain, the match was canceled.

that.tr: Thanks to the rain, it's cooled down.

items.explain: The cause can be the same (雨), so look at the result that follows: the match being canceled is bad → せいで; cooling down is good → おかげで.

items.title: 〜ために (cause)
items.diff: せいで carries blame; ために just objectively states the cause, suited to the news and notices.

this.tr: Because you were late, everyone had to wait.

that.tr: Due to an accident, trains are running late.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence carries emotion: complaining about someone or something (君が遅れたせいで) → せいで; station announcements and the news just state the cause without assigning blame → ために (ため). Using せいで in formal settings sounds like you're shifting the blame.

groups.note: It's the same 「しかない」, but whether a noun or a verb comes before it changes the meaning

items.title: 〜しか〜ない (only)
items.diff: noun ＋ しか〜ない says the amount or range is small: “only”; verb ＋ しかない says there's no other choice: “have no choice but to”.

this.tr: The last train's gone, so I have no choice but to walk home.

that.tr: I only have 1,000 yen in my wallet.

items.explain: Written the same — look at what comes before 「しかない」: a noun or quantity (千円しかない) → there's only this much; a verb in the dictionary form (帰るしかない) → there's no way other than doing this, so you have to. Both literally mean “there is nothing except…”.

groups.note: All mean “can only, have no choice but to”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; しかない is the go-to in everyday speech, while ほかない is more written and formal.

this.tr: Nobody will help me, so I'll just have to do it myself.

that.tr: With no one to help, there is no choice but to do it oneself.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting: in speech and chat, しかない; in writing and formal remarks, ほかない (also よりほかない).

items.diff: しかない rules out other options, leaving only this one path; ざるを得ない means being forced by circumstances to do something against your wishes.

this.tr: There's no bus, so I'll have to walk.

that.tr: With a typhoon approaching, the tournament has to be canceled.

items.explain: Look at the tone: しかない is spoken, focusing on “there's no other way”, and can also be used to psych yourself up (やるしかない！); ざるを得ない is written, stressing “I didn't want to, but the situation leaves no choice”. Note the form: する becomes 「せざるを得ない」.

groups.note: Both come from 「ため（為）」 — expressing “purpose, cause”

items.diff: そのため stands at the start of a sentence and refers back to the previous one; ために sits inside the sentence, with the cause or purpose directly before it.

this.tr: There was heavy snow last night. As a result, the trains stopped.

that.tr: The trains stopped due to heavy snow.

items.explain: Same meaning, different position: そのため is a standalone conjunction that needs a sentence before it, and 「その」 refers to that sentence's content; ために comes right after the cause (大雪の＋ために), all in one sentence. The same goes for purpose: 「そのために」 = “for that purpose”.

groups.note: All mean “therefore, so” — following up on a cause just mentioned

items.title: それで (so)
items.diff: そのため is written and objective, mostly in the news and reports; それで is spoken, mostly used when telling someone how things went.

this.tr: It rained heavily all day yesterday. As a result, many roads were closed.

that.tr: I overslept yesterday, you know. So I was late for the meeting.

items.explain: Look at the style: objective narration like the news, reports and explanatory texts → そのため; chatting with friends about your own experiences (with 「〜ちゃって」 or 「さ」) → それで. それで can also be said alone as 「それで？」 to prompt the other person to go on, which そのため can't.

items.title: ゆえに (therefore)
items.diff: Both mean “therefore” at the start of a sentence; ゆえに is extremely formal, mostly found in academic papers and math proofs.

this.tr: It's far from the station. Because of that, rents in this area are cheap.

that.tr: The two angles are equal. Therefore, this triangle is isosceles.

items.explain: Look at the type of text: rigorous reasoning like math proofs and academic papers (often with 「である」) → ゆえに; the news, explanatory texts and general writing → そのため. Using ゆえに in everyday speech sounds extremely stiff.

groups.note: All come from 「上（うえ）」 — “on top of…”

items.diff: その上 stands at the start of a sentence and refers to the previous one; 上に sits inside the sentence, saying it all in one go.

this.tr: This restaurant is cheap. On top of that, it's delicious.

that.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap but also delicious.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the position: the previous sentence has already ended with a period and a new one begins → その上 (「その」 refers to the previous sentence); attached directly after an adjective or verb (安い＋上に), all in one sentence → 上に. With nouns, say 「noun＋の上に」.

items.title: 〜上で (on the basis of…)
items.diff: その上 means “moreover, on top of that”; その上で means “on that basis (take the next step)” — one extra 「で」 changes the meaning.

this.tr: I read the materials, and I also watched the video.

that.tr: Please read the materials first, and then ask your questions based on them.

items.explain: Look for 「で」 and the words around it: その上 is often followed by 「も」, adding another thing of the same kind on top of the first; その上で often has 「まず」 before it, meaning “do the first thing properly, then use it as a foundation for the next step”. Both come from “on top of that”: stacked on top = moreover; standing on top = on that basis.

groups.note: All express addition: “moreover, not only… but also…”

items.diff: その上 is a bit more written, often used in descriptions and introductions; それに is spoken, often used in chat to add another reason.

this.tr: This room is spacious and bright. On top of that, the rent is cheap too.

that.tr: I'm not going today. It's raining, and besides, I'm tired.

items.explain: Look at the setting: describing a home or writing an essay → その上; adding another reason in chat with 「〜し、それに〜し」 → それに. その上 is also often used when bad things happen one after another (道に迷い、その上雨まで降ってきた), and sounds heavier than それに.

items.diff: その上 splits into two sentences, finishing one point before adding another; だけでなく links the two items within one sentence.

this.tr: He can speak English. On top of that, he can speak Chinese too.

that.tr: He can speak not only English but also Chinese.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: the previous sentence has finished (話せる。), and a new sentence adds to it → その上; 「A＋だけでなく、B＋も」 links two items in the same sentence, with A attached directly as a noun or plain form.

groups.note: Both express a choice: “A or B”

items.title: AかB (choice)
items.diff: それとも links two questions and is only used in questions; AかB links nouns directly and also works in statements.

this.tr: Would you like coffee to drink, or would you prefer tea?

that.tr: This weekend I want to go to a movie or go shopping.

wrong.why: それとも can only be used in questions

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: both options end in 「〜か」 and you're asking someone → put それとも between the two questions; just stating “A or B” (行きたい) → use AかB. Since English “or” covers both, the most common mistake is slipping それとも into a statement.

groups.note: All come from the 「そう」 of appearance — “how something looks”

items.diff: そうもない means “doesn't look like it will…”; そうだ means “looks like it will…”.

this.tr: It doesn't look like this work will be done today.

that.tr: It looks like this work will be done today.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the final 「もない」 vs 「だ」. For the negative of そうだ (appearance), the most natural way is to put the negation after そう: 終わりそうもない／終わりそうにない, meaning “there's no sign at all that it will…”.

items.diff: そうにない means “doesn't look like it will…”; そうになる means “almost…” — only the final 「ない」 vs 「なる」 differs.

this.tr: It doesn't look like this rain will stop anytime soon.

that.tr: My foot slipped and I almost fell.

items.explain: Look at the last word after 「そうに」: ない → it doesn't look like it will happen (そうもない works the same); なる, almost always in the past tense 「なった」 → something that was about to happen but in the end didn't. Just one kana apart, with completely different meanings.

items.title: 〜なさそう
items.diff: そうもない only attaches to verbs; to say “doesn't look…” with adjectives and nouns, use なさそう.

this.tr: With it this crowded, it doesn't look like I'll get a seat.

that.tr: This dish doesn't look spicy.

items.explain: First look at the word before it: verbs like 座れる, 来る, 終わる → そうもない／そうにない; adjectives like 辛い, 高い (for nouns, 「〜じゃなさそう」) → なさそう. Also, そうもない is stronger, with a feeling of “no way it'll happen, however you look at it”.

groups.note: Both express a negative judgment: “won't…”

items.diff: そうもない guesses from what you see: “doesn't look like it will”; はずがない concludes by reasoning: “there's no way”.

this.tr: It's already eight. It doesn't look like he's coming.

that.tr: He's overseas right now, so there's no way he'll come to today's party.

items.explain: Look at the basis in the first half: the situation in front of you, like 「もう８時だ」 → そうもない, just a guess that leaves a little possibility; a fact that makes it logically impossible, like 「海外にいる」 → はずがない, very certain in tone. They also attach differently: 来＋そうもない (ます-stem), 来る＋はずがない (dictionary form).

groups.note: All come from the 「そう」 of appearance — “how something looks”

items.diff: そうになる means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen; そうだ means “looks like it's going to…”.

this.tr: I slipped and almost fell.

that.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

items.explain: そうになった describes something that happened to you that “was about to happen but in the end didn't”, almost always in the past tense 「なった」; そうだ is a judgment based on what you see, and it hasn't happened yet.

items.diff: そうになる means “almost…”; そうにない means “doesn't look like it will…” — only the final 「なる」 vs 「ない」 differs.

this.tr: My foot slipped and I almost fell.

that.tr: It doesn't look like this rain will stop anytime soon.

items.explain: Look at the last word after 「そうに」: なる, almost always in the past tense 「なった」 → it was about to happen but in the end didn't; ない → it doesn't look like it will happen (そうもない works the same). Just one kana apart, with completely different meanings.

groups.note: All mean “about to happen” or “almost…”

items.diff: Both can mean “almost…”; そうになった describes how things were about to spin out of control at the time, while ところだった states the consequence: “if not for…, I would have…”.

this.tag: How it was at the time
this.tr: My foot slipped on the stairs and I almost fell.

that.tr: If you hadn't told me, I would have been late for the meeting.

wrong.why: After an “if not for…” hypothesis, only ところだった can be used

items.explain: Look at the first half and how it attaches: your body or feelings about to go out of control at that moment, as in 「足が滑って」 → ます-stem＋そうになった; with 「〜なかったら」, 「もう少しで」 or 「危うく」 before it, describing a consequence that nearly happened → dictionary form＋ところだった.

items.diff: そうになる means something is involuntarily “about to happen”; ようとする means you're deliberately “about to do” something.

this.tr: I almost got caught in the train doors.

that.tr: Just as I was about to get on the train, the doors closed.

items.explain: Check whether the verb is something you want to do: things you can't control, like 挟まれる, 転ぶ, 泣く → ます-stem＋そうになる; actions you intend to do, like 乗る, 出かける → volitional form＋とする (乗ろうとする).

groups.note: Both can mean “used to often…”

items.title: 〜っけ (reminiscing)
items.diff: たものだ tells others about the past, with emotion; っけ is reminiscing to yourself, as if thinking aloud.

this.tr: Back when I was a student, I used to drink at this place a lot.

that.tr: Back when I was a student, I used to drink here a lot, didn't I…

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: っけ often goes with 「なあ」, talking to yourself while remembering, very colloquial; たものだ tells others about past habits, with nostalgia and emotion, and also works in speeches and writing.

items.title: 〜ていた (past habit)
items.diff: Both can describe past habits; ていた is just an objective statement, while たものだ adds the speaker's nostalgia and emotion.

this.tr: When I was young, I'd often work through the night.

that.tr: When I was young, I often worked through the night.

items.explain: The facts in both sentences are the same; look at the speaker's tone: たものだ carries a nostalgic, wistful “back then…” feeling, mostly used for your own past; ていた just objectively states a past habit, with no emotional coloring, and is natural for talking about others too (父はよく徹夜していた).

groups.note: All come from ところ (所, “place”) — placing an event at a certain point in time

items.diff: たところ、 says “I did it, and as a result found…”; たところだ says an action has “just finished”.

this.tr: I emailed my teacher, and got a reply right away.

that.tr: I've just sent an email to my teacher.

items.explain: Mid-sentence, 「たところ、」 is always followed by a result (often an unexpected discovery), and the whole sentence is in the past tense; at the end of a sentence, 「たところだ」 only marks a point in time, and the sentence ends there. If something happens after 「たところ、」, it's the “result” use.

items.diff: たところ、 means “I tried it, and as a result…” (it really happened); たところで、 means “even if you do it, (it's no use)”.

this.tr: I looked it up in the dictionary and understood the meaning right away.

that.tr: Even if you look it up in a dictionary, you probably won't understand what this word means.

items.explain: Only one 「で」 differs. Look at the second half: たところ、 is followed by a result that already happened, in the past tense (わかった); たところで、 is usually followed by a negative or a guess (わからないだろう, 無駄だ), describing a hypothesis — it may not have actually happened.

groups.note: All mean “after doing…, it turned out…”

items.diff: たところ leans written, mostly for results after investigating or inquiring; たら〜た is spoken, and also works for everyday chance discoveries.

this.tr: I contacted the hotel, and they still had rooms available.

that.tr: When I opened the window in the morning, there was snow on the ground.

items.explain: Look at the action before it and the setting: purposeful actions like 「問い合わせる」, 「調べる」 or 「聞いてみる」, when reporting or writing a report → たところ; doing something casually in daily life and discovering something by chance → たら (「窓を開けると、雪が積もっていた」 works too, leaning written, like in novels).

items.diff: たところ means “I did it once and found out…”; た結果 means “after much discussion or effort, in the end…”.

this.tr: I tried talking it over with my mother, and to my surprise she agreed.

that.tag: After a process → in the end
that.tr: After talking it over with my family many times, I decided not to study abroad.

items.explain: Check whether the first half has a “process”: going through a process like 「何度も話し合った」 or 「よく考えた」 → た結果, followed by a final decision or conclusion; done just once, with 「試しに」 or 「〜てみた」, followed by something you learned only after doing it (usually unexpected) → たところ.

groups.note: All mean “as soon as…”

items.title: 〜次第 (immediately upon…)
items.diff: たとたん is followed by something unexpected; 次第 is followed by something you intend to do (contact someone, set off).

this.tr: The moment I arrived at the station, it started to rain.

that.tr: I'll call you as soon as I get to the station.

wrong.why: たとたん can't be followed by your own plans

items.explain: Look at the second half: something unexpected that you can't control, like 「雨が降り出した」, in the past tense → ta-form＋とたん; something you plan to do right away, like 「電話します」 or 「連絡します」 → ます-stem＋次第, common in business settings.

items.diff: With たとたん, the first event has just finished; with か〜ないかのうちに, the first event hasn't completely finished yet — almost simultaneous.

this.tr: The moment the bell rang, the students dashed out of the classroom.

that.tr: The bell had barely started ringing when the students dashed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Look at the structure: 「鳴るか鳴らないか」 says the same verb once in the affirmative and once in the negative, meaning “you can't even tell whether it has rung or not”, stressing near-simultaneity, with a strong written feel; たとたん uses the ta-form — the first event has already happened, and the next follows immediately.

items.diff: なり is only used when the same person does something “and immediately (does something unexpected)”, and leans written; たとたん can also be followed by other people, things or natural phenomena.

this.tr: The moment I opened the door, the cat rushed in.

that.tr: As soon as he entered the room, he collapsed onto the bed.

items.explain: Check whether both events are done by the same person: with なり, it's the same person in both (he entered → he collapsed), followed by an unexpected action, attached to the dictionary form, common in novels; たとたん can be followed by another person, thing or natural phenomenon (猫が飛び込んできた, 雨が降り出した), attached to the ta-form.

items.diff: たとたん carries a sense of “sudden, unexpected”; と同時に objectively says two things happen at the same time, and can also be followed by your own plans.

this.tr: As soon as we graduated, he stopped contacting me.

that.tr: I plan to go back to my country as soon as I graduate.

items.explain: Look at the second half: something unexpected that the speaker can't control → たとたん; plans or intentions like 「つもりだ」 or 「〜ます」, or just objectively stating that things happen at the same time → と同時に. They also attach differently: と同時に can attach directly to a noun (卒業と同時に), while たとたん only takes the ta-form of a verb.

groups.note: Both come from つもり (積もり) — originally “a mental estimate, a reckoning”

items.diff: た-form + つもりだった means “I thought I had done it (but hadn't)”; dictionary form + つもりだった means “I meant to do it (but didn't)”.

this.tag: Thought it was done · it wasn't
this.tr: I thought I'd locked the door, but it was open.

that.tr: I meant to lock the door, but I forgot.

items.explain: Only た vs る differs: かけた + つもりだった → you believed all along you'd done it, and only later found out it wasn't so (開いていた); かける + つもりだった → the plan fell through, and you know you didn't do it (忘れてしまった).

items.diff: た-form + つもりで means “acting as if it were already done”; dictionary form + つもりで means “with the intention of doing it”.

this.tr: Acting as if I were already studying abroad, I live using only English every day.

that.tr: I'm saving money every day with the intention of studying abroad.

items.explain: Look at what comes before つもりで: する (dictionary form) → you genuinely intend to do it in the future, and what follows is preparation for it; した (た-form) → you haven't actually done it, you're just treating it as done, and what follows is a “substitute” action (旅行に行ったつもりで貯金する).

groups.note: Both mean “treating as / pretending” — when it isn't actually so

items.diff: たつもり is treating something as done in your own mind; ふりをする is putting on a show for others.

this.tr: I told myself I'd already gone on the trip and saved that money instead.

that.tr: I actually knew, but pretended not to.

items.explain: Look at who it's for: たつもり is what you yourself believe or treat as so (行ったつもりで貯金する、言ったつもりだった), and nobody needs to see it; ふりをする is acting for others so they'll believe it (知らないふり、寝たふり).

groups.note: All mean “whenever…, …”

items.diff: たびに only follows verbs or “noun + の” and means “whenever”; ごとに can follow quantities and nouns, meaning “per unit” or “every so often”.

this.tr: Whenever I look at this photo, I remember the old days.

that.tr: The bus comes every 10 minutes.

wrong.why: たびに can't directly follow a quantity

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a verb (見る、会う) → たびに is most common, stressing “every single time…”; a quantity (10分、３時間) or a unit noun (国、クラス) → only ごとに works.

items.title: 〜につけ (whenever)
items.diff: たびに is neutral, and anything can follow it; につけ is more literary, and what follows is usually a feeling or memory that wells up.

this.tr: Every time I go to Tokyo, there are a few more new buildings.

that.tr: Whenever I look at this photo, I think of my mother back home.

items.explain: Look at the second half: feelings and recollections like 「思い出す」「心配になる」「〜と思う」 → につけ (usually after 見る、聞く、考える); objective changes or events (ビルが増えている) → use たびに.

items.title: 〜ては (every time…, …)
items.diff: たびに states objectively that it happens every time; verb te-form + は depicts a repeated “as soon as A, B” pattern, often with a sense of exasperation.

this.tr: Every time my father drank, he'd fight with my mother.

that.tr: My father would drink and then fight with my mother, over and over.

items.explain: The two sentences mean almost the same; look at the form and the tone: dictionary form + たびに is a neutral “whenever”; te-form + は (飲んでは、会っては) depicts “A, then right away B” as a recurring pattern, mostly when recounting the past, with a weary “here we go again” feel.

groups.note: Both mean “when I did…, it turned out…”

items.diff: たら〜た is conversational and works for chance everyday discoveries; たところ leans written and is mostly used for the result of an inquiry or investigation.

this.tr: When I opened the window this morning, I found snow had piled up.

that.tr: I contacted the hotel, and it turned out they still had rooms available.

items.explain: Look at the action and the setting: something you did casually in daily life, then happened to notice → たら (novels often use 「〜と〜た」); a purposeful action like 「問い合わせる」「調べる」「聞いてみる」, especially when reporting or writing it up → たところ.

groups.note: Both come from listing たり — “for example, things like…”

items.diff: Sentence-final たりして names just one possibility, meaning “maybe…, who knows”; たり〜たりする lists several actions.

this.tr: Maybe it'll snow tomorrow, who knows.

that.tr: On my days off, I do things like watch movies and go shopping.

items.explain: Look at the position: たり in mid-sentence, followed by 「〜たりする」, lists things you usually do; たりして at the very end of the sentence, with nothing after it, casually tosses out one possibility, often with 「もしかして」「なんて」 and a joking tone.

groups.note: Both guess “maybe…”

items.diff: たりして is a half-joking offhand remark you don't really take seriously yourself; かもしれない is a serious guess.

this.tr: Those two are always together lately. Maybe they're dating?

that.tr: They're always together lately, so those two might be dating.

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: たりして is only used in chats with friends, as if joking or teasing (often with 「もしかして」「なんて」); かもしれない is an ordinary guess that works both in chat and formal settings, and the speaker is judging seriously.

groups.note: Both mean “just now”

items.diff: たて only attaches to a few verbs and stresses “freshly made, still new”; たばかり works with any verb.

this.tr: Freshly baked bread is delicious.

that.tr: I lost the umbrella I'd only just bought yesterday.

items.explain: たて attaches directly to the masu-stem (焼き + たて) and is used only with a few words about “something made that's still new”: 焼きたて、できたて、生まれたて、塗りたて; everywhere else use たばかり, as in 「昨日買ったばかりの傘」.

items.diff: たて modifies a noun, stressing “freshly made”; たところだ goes at the end of the sentence and states a point in time.

this.tr: I bought freshly baked bread.

that.tr: The bread has just finished baking.

items.explain: たて works like an adjective in 「〜たての + noun」, saying a thing is still fresh; to say “something has just happened” or report progress, use たところだ (今、着いたところです).

groups.note: All express concession: “even if…”

items.title: 〜ても (even if)
items.diff: ても can also describe something that already happened; adding たとえ generally limits it to hypotheticals, with a stronger tone.

this.tr: Even if I have a fever, I'm taking tomorrow's exam.

that.tr: Even after a night's sleep, my fever didn't go down.

items.explain: Look at the tense of the second half: a fact that already happened (下がらなかった) → use ても; something that hasn't happened, a hypothetical, often followed by resolve or judgment (受ける、変わらない) → you can add たとえ to stress “even if that really happens”. たとえ is basically only for hypotheticals. Nouns and na-adjectives take 「たとえ〜でも」 (たとえ雨でも).

items.diff: たとえ means “even if it's that”, and what comes before needn't have a degree; どんなに means “no matter how (much)”.

this.tr: Even as a joke, you mustn't say something like that.

that.tr: No matter how busy I am, I call every day.

wrong.why: 冗談 has no degree, so どんなに can't be used

items.explain: See whether the word before can take “how…”: things like 冗談、子ども、雨, which simply are or aren't → use たとえ to suppose it's so; 忙しい、寒い、頑張る have degrees → どんなに. たとえ can also take degrees (たとえ忙しくても), but どんなに must be followed by something with a degree.

items.title: 〜とも (even if)
items.diff: Same meaning; たとえ〜とも is a written, classical-style expression, common in speeches, novels and song lyrics.

this.tr: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead as planned.

that.tr: No matter what happens, I will fight to the very end.

items.explain: Look at the ending and the style: ordinary conversation, notices and writing use 「たとえ〜ても」; solemn settings like speeches, novels and lyrics use 「たとえ〜とも」, preceded by the volitional form (あろう) or an adjective's く-form (苦しくとも).

groups.note: 「〜たって」 is written exactly the same: even if… ↔ I heard…

items.title: 〜って (I heard)
items.diff: たって followed by another clause means “even if…”; sentence-final 「〜たって」 is 「〜た + って」, meaning “I heard that…”.

this.tr: Even if the match is canceled, we're not skipping practice, you know.

that.tr: Hey, I heard the match got canceled.

items.explain: 「中止になったって」 looks exactly the same in writing. Look at what follows: another clause comes after it (練習は休まない) → even if…; the sentence ends right there → 「なった + って」 = passing on news you heard. When reading, first check whether anything follows 「たって」.

groups.note: All express concession: “even if…”

items.title: 〜ても (even if)
items.diff: Same meaning; たって is very casual speech, while ても works in any setting.

this.tr: Even if you run now, you won't make it.

that.tr: Even if you run now, you won't make it in time.

items.explain: The meaning is exactly the same; look at who you're talking to: casually among friends and family → たって (読んだって、急いだって are sound changes, written 「だって」); to superiors, customers, or in writing → ても. With i-adjectives it's 「高くたって」, equivalent to 「高くても」.

items.diff: Both are spoken concessions; たって follows verbs and adjectives, だって follows nouns.

this.tr: Even if it rains tomorrow, I'm going.

that.tr: Even if it's rainy tomorrow, I'm going.

items.explain: First look at the word before: verbs and adjectives like 降った、高く → たって (sound changes like 読んだ + って are also written 「だって」); nouns like 雨、子ども → attach だって directly, equivalent to 「でも」 (子どもだって知ってる = even a kid knows).

items.diff: Both can mean “even if…”; たところで leans written and can only be followed by “it's no use, nothing will change”, while たって can also be followed by resolve.

this.tr: Even if it rains, I'm going.

that.tr: Even if I apologize now, after all this, I probably won't be forgiven.

items.explain: Look at the second half: resolve like 「行くよ」「やるよ」 → たって (or ても) is most natural; a “it's pointless even if you do it” judgment like 「許してもらえない」「無駄だ」「変わらない」 → たところで fits better, often with 「今さら」「どうせ」「いくら」.

groups.note: Both come from 見る (to see) — 「ご覧」 is the honorific of 「見る」

items.diff: てごらん urges the listener “(you) try…”, said only to juniors and children; てみる is “trying something” yourself.

this.tr: It's yummy. Try a bite.

that.tr: I tried eating natto for the first time.

items.explain: てごらん is short for 「〜てご覧なさい」, just like 「〜てみなさい」, telling the listener to try something, usually said by parents or teachers to children; てみる is the speaker trying something, and works in any tense (食べてみた、行ってみたい).

groups.note: Both get the listener to do something

items.diff: てごらん encourages the listener to “give it a try”; なさい instructs them to “do it”.

this.tr: It's okay, you can do it. Try doing it yourself.

that.tr: Hurry up and do your homework.

items.explain: Both are said by elders to juniors. Look at the surrounding words: encouragement like 「大丈夫」「できるよ」, getting a child to try → てごらん, with a gentle tone; urging like 「早く」, demanding they do what they should → なさい.

items.diff: てください is a polite request you can use with anyone; てごらん has a senior's tone and can't be said to superiors or elders.

this.tr: Look, take a look at this picture.

that.tr: Teacher, please take a look at this picture.

wrong.why: てごらん can't be said to teachers or superiors

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: children, students, juniors → てごらん; teachers, bosses, customers → てください, and to say “please try…” use 「〜てみてください」.

groups.note: Both are read 「はじめて」: 〜て初めて ↔ 〜始めて

items.diff: Te-form + 初めて means “only after… (for the first time)”; masu-stem + 始める means “start to…”.

this.tr: Only after actually eating it did I realize how good it was.

that.tr: I started eating at seven and finished at eight.

items.explain: The reading is the same; check two places: is the form before it the te-form (食べて) or the masu-stem (食べ)? Is the kanji 「初」 (first time) or 「始」 (start)? 食べて初めて is usually followed by a realization like 「分かった」「気づいた」; 食べ始めて just says the action began.

groups.note: Both mean “first A, and only then B”

items.diff: て初めて puts it positively: “only after… did I understand”; てからでないと puts it negatively: “unless you first…, you can't”.

this.tr: Only after becoming a parent myself did I understand how hard my parents had it.

that.tr: Until you become a parent yourself, you can't understand how hard parents have it.

items.explain: Look at the second half: affirmative, usually past tense (分かった、気づいた), saying “only at that moment did I first understand” → て初めて; negative (分からない、できない), saying “without doing A first, it won't work” → てからでないと. Both sentences express the same truth.

items.title: 〜てから (sequence)
items.diff: てから only states the order of events; て初めて stresses “never… before that, and only then for the first time…”.

this.tr: It was only after coming to Japan that I saw real snow for the first time.

that.tr: Since coming to Japan, I've been studying Japanese every day.

items.explain: See whether the second half is a “first time”: an experience or realization you never had before and only got then, like 本物の雪を見た、大切さが分かった → て初めて; just ordering events, or something you've been doing ever since → てから.

groups.note: All mean “ever since…”

items.title: 〜てから (since)
items.diff: て以来 only means “from some point in the past up to now”; てから can also be used for future sequences.

this.tr: Since coming to Japan last year, I've lived in Tokyo the whole time.

that.tr: I plan to go to Japan after I graduate from university next year.

wrong.why: て以来 can't be used for future events

items.explain: Look at the time words and the second half: 「去年」「ずっと〜ている」, continuing from the past up to now → て以来 (てから also works); future plans like 「来年」「〜つもりだ」 → only てから. て以来 is somewhat more formal than てから.

items.diff: て以来 just states objectively “ever since then…”; てからというもの stresses that life changed dramatically after that, with deep feeling.

this.tr: Since joining the company, I haven't taken a single day off.

that.tr: Ever since I started keeping a dog, every day has been an absolute joy.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a plain, ongoing state like 「一度も〜ない」「ずっと〜ている」 → て以来; an emotional “since then, I and my life have changed completely” (毎日が楽しくてたまらない、すっかり変わった) → てからというもの, which has a strong written flavor.

items.diff: Both mean “ever since…”; てこのかた is more literary and old-fashioned, mostly used for very long spans like 「生まれてこのかた」.

this.tr: Since coming to Japan, I haven't caught a single cold.

that.tr: Never once in my life have I caught a cold.

items.explain: Look at the starting point: a long span counted from birth like 「生まれて」, with a touch of feeling → てこのかた, rarely used in everyday conversation; ordinary “since coming to Japan / joining the company” → て以来.

groups.note: Both come from 場合 (ばあい) — “situation, occasion”

items.diff: ている場合じゃない means “now is not the time to…”; 場合は is a neutral “in the case of…”.

this.tr: The exam is tomorrow. This is no time to be playing games.

that.tr: In case of rain, the match will be canceled.

items.explain: 「場合」 originally means “situation, occasion”. 場合は is followed by what to do in that case, often in notices and rules; ている場合じゃない rejects “what you're doing right now” — in the current situation, this is not the moment for it, with a sense of urgency or prodding.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no room for… now, can't keep…”

items.diff: ている場合じゃない is a subjective “I shouldn't be doing this now”; どころではない is an objective “there's simply no room for it, it can't be done”.

this.tr: The exam is tomorrow. This is no time to be chatting about trips.

that.tr: Work is so busy that a trip is out of the question.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: ている場合じゃない follows an action in progress (話をしている), with the speaker reminding themselves or others to “get down to business”; どころではない usually follows a noun (旅行、勉強), often preceded by a reason like 「忙しくて」, saying there's objectively no capacity left.

items.diff: ている場合じゃない stresses “it's the wrong time”, often used to prod others; てはいられない stresses that the speaker “can't sit still, has to act”.

this.tr: It's already eight! This is no time to be sleeping.

that.tr: My rivals are working hard too. I can't keep taking it easy.

items.explain: Both say “can't go on like this”. てはいられない is usually the speaker's own inner urgency, often followed by “I've got to… too”; ている場合じゃない is often shouted at or used to scold others (〜てる場合か！), with a more urgent tone.

groups.note: Both mean “first A, and only then B”

items.diff: てからでないと puts it negatively: “unless you first…, you can't”; て初めて puts it positively: “only after… did I understand”.

this.tr: Until you become a parent yourself, you can't understand how hard parents have it.

that.tr: Only after becoming a parent myself did I understand how hard my parents had it.

items.explain: Look at the second half: negative (分からない、できない), saying “without doing A first, it won't work” → てからでないと; affirmative, usually past tense (分かった、気づいた), saying “only at that moment did I first understand” → て初めて. Both sentences express the same truth.

groups.note: Both report what someone told me to do (or not do)

items.diff: てくれと／なと quote the original words, sounding vivid and direct; ように言う rephrases the content when reporting it, with a calmer tone.

this.tr: The department head told me, “Copy these documents for me.”
The department head told me, “Don't be late again.”

that.tr: The department head told me to copy the documents.
The department head told me not to be late again.

items.explain: Look before 「と」: 「コピーしてくれ」「遅刻するな」 are the department head's actual words, placed directly before 「と」, so it sounds like a live replay; rephrasing as 「コピーするように」「遅刻しないように」 reports only the content of the request without the original tone, which is more common when relaying a superior's words.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no point in…”

items.diff: Both can mean “there's no point in…”; ても仕方がない can also mean “it's only natural that…”, while ても始まらない can't.

this.tr: There's no use regretting it now.

that.tr: You broke your promise, so you can't blame anyone if you get scolded.

items.explain: Look at the reason before it: when you were at fault first, like 「約束を破った」, and what follows is a result like being scolded or disliked → “it's only natural”, and only ても仕方がない works (しょうがない too); after 「今さら」, saying doing it won't change the situation → both work, and ても始まらない stresses more that “it gets you nowhere at all”.

items.diff: ても始まらない is itself the conclusion “it's no use” and goes at the end of the sentence; たところで is the first half, and must be followed by a concrete result.

this.tr: There's no use apologizing now. Let's just hurry up and fix it instead.

that.tr: Even if I apologize now, after all this, I probably won't be forgiven.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: ても始まらない directly concludes “it's no use”, often followed by a suggestion like 「それより〜しよう」; たところで must be followed by a concrete result (許してもらえない、何も変わらない), with a more written tone.

groups.note: Both come from 仕方がない (there's no way / nothing can be done)

items.diff: ても仕方がない means “there's no point in…”; て仕方がない means “unbearably…” — the only difference is one 「も」.

this.tr: There's no point worrying about it already.

that.tr: I'm terribly worried about tomorrow's interview.

items.explain: 「仕方がない」 originally means “there's no way”. With 「も」 → even doing it, there's no way to change anything = it's no use (心配してもしょうがない); without 「も」, attached right after a feeling word → the feeling is so strong you can't help yourself = unbearably… (心配でしょうがない). 仕方がない and しょうがない are used exactly the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no point in…”

items.diff: Both can mean “there's no point in…”; ても仕方がない can also mean “it's only natural that…”, while ても始まらない can't.

this.tr: You broke your promise, so you can't blame anyone if you get scolded.

that.tr: There's no use regretting it now.

items.explain: Look at the reason before it: when you were at fault first, like 「約束を破った」, and what follows is a result like being scolded or disliked → “it's only natural”, and only ても仕方がない works; after 「今さら」, saying doing it won't change the situation → both work, and ても始まらない stresses more that “it gets you nowhere at all”, often followed by 「それより〜しよう」.

groups.note: Both come from 仕方がない (there's no way / nothing can be done)

items.diff: て仕方がない means “unbearably…”; ても仕方がない means “there's no point in…” — the only difference is one 「も」.

this.tr: I'm terribly worried about tomorrow's interview.

that.tr: There's no point worrying about it already.

items.explain: 「仕方がない」 originally means “there's no way”. Attached right after a feeling word → the feeling is so strong you can't help yourself = unbearably… (心配でしょうがない); with an extra 「も」 in between → even doing it, there's no way to change anything = it's no use (心配してもしょうがない). 仕方がない and しょうがない are used exactly the same way.

groups.note: Both express an intense feeling or sensation: “unbearably…”

items.diff: Same meaning; てならない is more written and usually follows 「気がする」「思える」, while everyday chat mostly uses てしょうがない.

this.tr: Living alone is so lonely, I can't stand it.

that.tag: Written · wells up on its own
that.tr: I can't shake the feeling that something bad is going to happen.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the word before: in chat, with 寂しい、眠い、気になる → てしょうがない is most natural; in writing, with feelings that arise involuntarily like 「〜気がする」「〜と思えて」 → てならない is common.

groups.note: All come from 済む (すむ) — originally “for a matter to be settled”

items.diff: ずに済む means “it got settled without doing it” = luckily spared; ずにはすまない means “it can't be settled without doing it” = must do it — the only difference is one 「は」.

this.tr: The rain stopped, so I didn't have to buy a new umbrella.

that.tr: I broke my friend's umbrella, so I can't get away without buying him a new one.

items.explain: 「済む」 = a matter is settled. ずに済む: it got settled without doing it → luckily spared, often preceded by a lucky reason with 「〜ので」; ずにはすまない: it can't be settled without doing it → you're morally obliged to, often preceded by a reason you're responsible for with 「〜のだから」. Just one 「は」 apart, and the meanings are exact opposites.

items.diff: て済む means “doing… settled the matter”; the 「すみません」 in てすみません is just 「済まない」 — “this can't be settled, I feel bad” = an apology.

this.tr: I was late, but a quick apology was all it took.

that.tr: Sorry I'm late.

items.explain: すみません is originally 「済みません」, the negative of 「済む」, meaning “as things stand this can't be settled, and I feel bad about it”, which is why it's used to apologize; て済む uses the affirmative 「済む」, saying “doing… settled the matter”, often with a “luckily that was all” feel.

groups.note: Both mean “don't have to do”

items.diff: ずに済む means “I would have had to, but luckily didn't need to in the end”; なくてもいい says “there's no need to”.

this.tr: A friend drove me, so luckily I didn't have to take a taxi.

that.tr: The station is close, so you don't need to take a taxi.

items.explain: Look at the tense and tone: ずに済んだ is usually past tense, saying “something I'd have had to do was avoided thanks to some circumstance”, with relief; なくてもいい just explains there's no need now or in the future.

groups.note: Both express a feeling or sensation too strong to control

items.diff: てたまらない is mostly used for physical sensations and strong emotions; てならない is more written and mostly used for feelings that well up on their own, like 「気がする」「思える」.

this.tr: I walked all day, and my feet hurt like crazy.

that.tr: I can't shake the feeling that something bad is going to happen.

items.explain: Look at the word before: physical sensations like 痛い、暑い、おなかがすく, or strong emotions like うれしい、会いたい → てたまらない; thoughts that arise naturally in the mind, like 「気がする」「〜に思える」「残念だ」, in writing → てならない.

items.diff: てたまらない describes the “state” of a feeling or sensation; ずにはいられない describes an “action” you can't help doing.

this.tr: His story is hilarious.

that.tr: When I heard his story, I couldn't help laughing.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: an adjective (おかしい、うれしい) or 「〜たい」 → the feeling itself is intense → てたまらない; a verb's nai-form (笑わ、泣か、言わ) → you uncontrollably did some action → ずにはいられない.

groups.note: Both mean “so as not to…, in case…”

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: てはいけないから takes an affirmative before it (忘れては) and gives “worry” as the reason; ないように takes a negative before it (忘れない) and states the purpose directly.

this.tr: It'd be bad if I forgot the appointment, so I'll write it in my planner.

that.tr: I'll write the appointment in my planner so I don't forget it.

items.explain: The two sentences mean almost the same; look at the verb before: てはいけないから is preceded by the affirmative 「忘れて」 (it'd be bad if I forgot), and in speech 「忘れるといけないから」 is also common; ように is preceded by the negative 「忘れない」 (so as not to forget).

items.diff: てはいけないから is conversational and voices your own worry; ことのないように is very formal, mostly used in notices and speeches.

this.tr: It'd be bad to catch a cold, so let's take a jacket.

that.tr: To ensure the same accident never happens again, we will thoroughly enforce safety measures.

items.explain: Look at the setting: among family and friends, preparing for your own small matters (上着を持っていく) → てはいけないから; formal settings like company notices, public apologies and school rules → ことのないように, preceded by the dictionary form, often with 「二度と」.

groups.note: Both come from 「て + は」 — “if… (then it's no good)”

items.diff: てはいけない has become a fixed prohibition: “you must not…”; ては + a specific bad result means “if this goes on, …”.

this.tr: If you do nothing but play games every day, your grades will drop.

that.tr: You must not play games during class.

items.explain: Look after 「は」: the fixed 「いけない」「だめ」 → a prohibition; a specific bad result (成績が下がる、間に合わない、体を壊す) → a warning about what will happen if things go on like this. In speech, both become 「〜ちゃ」.

groups.note: Both express a supposition: “if…”

items.title: 〜たら (if)
items.diff: たら is a neutral “if”, and either good or bad can follow; ては can only be followed by a bad result.

this.tr: With it raining this hard, the match is out of the question.

that.tr: If it's sunny tomorrow, let's play the match.

wrong.why: ては can only be followed by a bad result

items.explain: Look at the second half: a negative result or evaluation like 「無理だ」「困る」「間に合わない」 → ては, with a “this won't do” tone; a good result, invitation or intention (しよう、うれしい) → only たら.

items.diff: Both mean “if it's like this, it won't do”; ようでは follows the dictionary form or nai-form and often has a lecturing tone; ては follows the te-form.

this.tr: If you're late every day, people won't trust you.

that.tr: If you get even a simple question like this wrong, you won't pass.

items.explain: First look at the form: ては follows the te-form (遅刻していては), ようでは follows the dictionary form or nai-form (間違えるようでは、できないようでは). ようでは usually describes behavior the speaker disapproves of, often with 「こんな」, like a teacher scolding a student; ては just points out the consequence of carrying on like this.

groups.note: Both mean “having the nature of…, …-style”

items.diff: 〜的 focuses on inner nature and way of thinking; 〜風 focuses on appearance and style.

this.tr: His way of thinking is very Japanese.

that.tr: We made the garden in Japanese style.

items.explain: See whether it's about the inside or the outside: inner qualities like ways of thinking, personality and habits → 〜的; visible styles like gardens, food and architecture → 〜風. Also, 〜的 is a na-adjective (「日本的な考え方」), while 〜風 is followed by 「の」「に」 (「日本風の庭」).

items.diff: 〜的 only follows Sino-Japanese nouns and is more written and objective; 〜っぽい is conversational, attaches to native words, adjectives and verbs, and often carries a negative judgment.

this.tr: His way of thinking is realistic.

that.tr: His way of thinking is childish.

items.explain: First look at the word before: Sino-Japanese nouns like 現実、積極、経済 → 〜的; native words, verbs and adjectives like 子ども、男、忘れる、安い → 〜っぽい (子どもっぽい、忘れっぽい、安っぽい). 〜っぽい is conversational and usually implies “a bit…, not quite good enough”; 〜的 just describes the nature objectively.

groups.note: Both mean “in terms of…”, limiting the scope of an evaluation

items.diff: 点で evaluates one aspect of something, good or bad; にかけては is only used for strengths: “when it comes to…, no one can beat them”.

this.tr: This car is a bit expensive in terms of price, but it gets good mileage.

that.tr: When it comes to cooking, no one can beat him.

wrong.why: にかけては must be followed by a strength or confidence, not a weakness

items.explain: Look at the evaluation that follows: good or bad points about some aspect (値段の点では高い) → 点で; praising someone's (or something's) forte, usually followed by 「誰にも負けない」「一番だ」 → にかけては.

groups.note: All mean two things happen right after each other (at the same time, as soon as…)

items.diff: と同時に just says two things happen at once, and what follows can be something you do on purpose; たとたん must be followed by something unexpected.

this.tr: As soon as I got home, I called my mom.

that.tr: The moment I got home, it started raining.

wrong.why: たとたん can't be followed by your own plan or will

items.explain: Look at the second half: something beyond your control and unexpected, like rain starting or a phone ringing → たとたん (with the た-form before it); something you deliberately do (making a call, starting work) → use と同時に.

items.title: 〜次第 (as soon as)
items.diff: と同時に narrates two things happening at once; 次第 means “as soon as… (I'll do it right away)”, for arrangements that haven't happened yet.

this.tr: As soon as the rain stopped, the children rushed outside.

that.tr: We'll set off as soon as the rain stops.

wrong.why: 次第 can't be used to narrate something that already happened

items.explain: Look at the tense of the second half: a scene that already happened (飛び出した) → と同時に; an upcoming arrangement or promise, usually in a business tone (出発します、ご連絡します) → 次第. The forms differ too: 次第 follows the masu-stem (止み次第), と同時に follows the dictionary form (止むと同時に).

items.diff: と同時に only means “at the same moment”; とともに can also mean “gradually changing along with…” and “together with…”.

this.tr: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.

that.tr: As I've gotten older, my stamina has gradually declined.

items.explain: Look for words of gradual change like 「少しずつ」「だんだん」: happening simultaneously in an instant → と同時に (とともに also works); as one thing changes, the other slowly follows → only とともに (close to 「につれて」). とともに can also follow a person to mean “together with…” (仲間とともに); と同時に can't.

groups.note: All come from conditional forms of 「と言う」 — “speaking of…”

items.diff: For associations, といえば and というと are basically interchangeable; for checking with the listener “by…, do you mean…?”, only というと works.

this.tr: Speaking of Tanaka, I hear he's getting married next month.

that.tr: Tanaka — you mean that tall guy?

items.explain: Look at the second half: following the topic to say something it reminds you of (〜らしいよ、〜が有名だ) → といえば (というと also works here); a question checking with the listener who or what they mean → only というと.

items.diff: といえば is a calm association; といったら often carries exclamation, stressing “so… it's beyond words”.

this.tr: Speaking of Hokkaido, it's got to be crab, right?

that.tr: The cold of a Hokkaido winter — it's so cold you don't even want to go outside.
