items.explain: Look at the noun before it: an ordinary noun, followed by a typical thing it brings to mind → といえば; a 「〜さ」 noun like 「寒さ」「美しさ」 or an emotion noun, followed by a description of degree (〜ほどだ、言葉にできない) → といったら. といったら can also express association (北海道といったらカニだ), but といえば can't exclaim a degree.

items.diff: といえば brings up a topic neutrally; ったら is a casual contraction of 「と言ったら」, used when bringing up someone close with annoyance or affection.

this.tr: Speaking of my mom, I always picture her smiling face.

that.tr: Honestly, my mom — she tidied up my room without asking again.

items.explain: Look at the tone of the second half: saying what it brings to mind → といえば; going on to complain about the person's behavior (また、勝手に) → ったら, often as 「もう、〜ったら」 in speech. ったら usually follows people close to you (母、あなた), not general topics.

groups.note: All are the speaker's judgment: “it can be said… / it can't be said…”

items.diff: と言える draws an objective conclusion from facts; と言ってもいい has an evaluative “it's no stretch to say” tone, slightly exaggerated.

this.tr: Judging from the survey results, it can be said that young people are increasingly turning away from cars.

that.tr: You could say her Japanese is already as good as a native speaker's.

items.explain: Look at the basis: evidence before it like 「調査の結果から」「データによると」, a cool-headed analysis → と言える, common in writing; the speaker's own impression, a bit exaggerated (もう…と同じ) → と言ってもいい.

items.diff: と言える is a plain conclusion; と言っても過言ではない means “it's no exaggeration to say…”, deliberately overstating for emphasis, the strongest tone.

this.tr: It can be said that smartphones are now indispensable to daily life.

that.tr: It's no exaggeration to say that smartphones are now part of our bodies.

items.explain: See whether what's said is exaggerated: a reasonable judgment (生活に欠かせない) → と言える; deliberately strong wording (体の一部だ) for emphasis → と言っても過言ではない, common in speeches and writing.

items.diff: とは言えない means “can hardly be called, doesn't count as”, rejecting the evaluation; とは限らない means “not necessarily”, admitting it's usually so but there are exceptions.

this.tr: The food at this restaurant can by no means be called good.

that.tr: Food at famous restaurants isn't necessarily good.

items.explain: Look at what's being talked about: one specific restaurant, being given a verdict → とは言えない (often paired with 「決して」); a category (有名な店), generally thought to be so but with exceptions → 必ずしも〜とは限らない. The two are also often combined: 「必ずしも正しいとは言えない」.

groups.note: All come from conditional forms of 「と言う」 — “if we're talking about…”

items.diff: といったら first presents the subject, then describes the degree; といったらない ends the sentence right there: “incredibly…”.

this.tr: The beauty of Mt. Fuji that day — it was beyond words.

that.tr: Mt. Fuji that day was incredibly beautiful.

items.explain: Look after といったら: followed by a description like 「言葉にできない」「〜ほどだ」 → といったら; immediately followed by 「ない／なかった」 to end the sentence → といったらない, which itself means “… to the extreme”. Same meaning, just a different sentence structure.

items.diff: といったら often carries exclamation, stressing “so… it's beyond words”; といえば is a calm association.

this.tr: The cold of a Hokkaido winter — it's so cold you don't even want to go outside.

that.tr: Speaking of Hokkaido, it's got to be crab, right?

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: a 「〜さ」 noun like 「寒さ」「美しさ」 or an emotion noun, followed by a description of degree → といったら; an ordinary noun, followed by a typical thing it brings to mind → といえば. といったら can also express association (北海道といったらカニだ), but といえば can't exclaim a degree.

items.diff: といったら is the full form and can exclaim a degree; ったら is its casual contraction, mostly used to bring up someone close with annoyance or affection.

this.tr: How cute my kid is — I just can't stand it.

that.tr: Honestly, my kid — he kicked off his shoes and left them lying around again.

items.explain: Look before and after: a quality noun like 「かわいさ」 before it and a description of degree after → といったら; a person directly before it (うちの子、母、あなた) and a complaint or mock reproach after → ったら, very conversational.

groups.note: Both exclaim how extreme something is: “how…!”

items.diff: といったら puts a quality at the start of the sentence as the topic, then describes its degree; ことか goes at the end, pairs with 「どんなに」, and expresses emotion through a rhetorical question.

this.tr: The joy when I passed — I couldn't help crying.

that.tr: How happy I was when I passed!

items.explain: Look at the position: 「〜さといったら」 raises the topic at the start, and another clause must follow describing how intense it was; 「どんなに〜ことか」 closes the sentence, expressing “how…!” through a rhetorical question, often with 「どんなに」「何度」 before it.

groups.note: All derive from 「と言う」 — “although it's called… (but)”

items.diff: といっても leans conversational, focusing on “it's not actually that much”; とはいえ leans written, and anything contrary to expectations can follow.

this.tr: I say “trip”, but I just stayed one night at a nearby hot spring.

that.tr: It may be spring, but the cold days are continuing.

items.explain: Look at the second half: correcting the listener's idea of scale or degree (〜だけだ、〜ぐらいだ) → といっても; just pointing out another side that differs from expectations, common in writing and news → とはいえ. In speech, to lower the listener's expectations, people generally use といっても.

items.diff: といっても means “although it's…, it's not really that…”; といえども is written language for “even… (is no exception)”.

this.tr: He may be a teacher, but he's only just graduated from university.

that.tr: Even teachers make mistakes sometimes.

items.explain: Look at the second half: lowering the listener's impression (まだ…たばかりだ) → といっても; saying “however special their status, the same applies” (間違うことはある、ルールは守るべきだ) → といえども, with a strong classical flavor, common in 「子供といえども」「プロといえども」.

items.diff: といっても corrects the impression of “degree”; からといって rejects a conclusion drawn from what came before, usually followed by 「〜とは限らない」.

this.tr: It's expensive, but only about 1,000 yen.

that.tr: Just because it's expensive doesn't mean it's good.

items.explain: Only 「から」 differs: 〜といっても is followed by the actual degree (〜ぐらいだ、〜だけだ); 〜からといって treats what came before as a reason and then rejects the inference “so therefore…” (〜とは限らない、〜わけではない).

groups.note: Both are built on 「と言う」 — rephrasing around “what to call it”

items.diff: というか is self-correcting while thinking, light and conversational; というより compares and clearly picks the second wording.

this.tr: He's kind… or rather, kind of too soft on people, you know?

that.tr: He's not so much kind as indulgent.

items.explain: Look at the tone: in speech, with 「ちょっと」「〜んだよね」, as if swapping words while thinking → というか; putting two wordings side by side and clearly judging the second more accurate, also usable in writing → というより (often with 「むしろ」).

groups.note: Both are used to “put it another way”

items.diff: というか corrects yourself because the first wording felt off; つまり restates the previous words more concisely with the same meaning.

this.tr: He's serious… or rather, stubborn.

that.tr: He's my mother's older brother — in other words, my uncle.

items.explain: See whether the two parts mean the same thing: 母の兄 = おじ, exactly the same content, just said more concisely → つまり; まじめ ≠ 頑固, replacing the first word because it didn't fit → というか.

groups.note: All report hearsay: “I hear that…”

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: Both mean “I hear”. ということだ is more objective and formal, common in news and notices; そうだ is the most common in daily life.

this.tr: According to those involved, the construction will continue until next month.

that.tr: A friend told me a new café has opened in front of the station.

items.explain: Both mean “I hear”; look at the setting: news, notices, formal reports → ということです is more objective; chatting with friends → そうだ is most natural. Also, ということだ can follow 「つまり」 to draw a conclusion (つまり、中止ということだ), while そうだ has no “in other words” use.

items.diff: ということだ relays general information; とのことだ is more written and mostly used to pass on someone's message.

this.tr: According to the weather forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

that.tr: The department head asked me to let you know he'll be a little late for the meeting.

items.explain: Look at the source: general information like news and forecasts → ということだ (とのことだ also works); words someone asked you to pass on (部長から、〜さんから) → とのことです is the most idiomatic, common at work and in letters, as in 「よろしくとのことです」.

groups.note: Both come from 「という」 — treating what comes before as “the thing called…”

items.diff: というのは is the full form, usable in formal settings too; って is its casual contraction, used among friends.

this.tr: “Karoshi” means dying from overwork.

that.tr: Hey, what does “karoshi” mean?

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: explanations, lectures, writing → というのは; chatting with friends, short casual sentences (ねえ、〜の？) → って. The topic-raising って in 「日本語って難しい」 is also a casual form of というのは.

groups.note: Both are used to explain — a word's meaning or a reason

items.diff: For definitions, というのは is common in both speech and writing; とは is more written, common in dictionaries and essays.

this.tr: “Shukatsu” just means job hunting.

that.tr: “Job hunting” refers to the activities students undertake to find work.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: spoken endings like 「〜ことだよ」「〜って意味」 → というのは; dictionary or academic tone like 「〜である」「〜を指す」 → とは. Also, とは can express surprise (彼が犯人だとは), which というのは can't.

items.diff: To give a reason at the start of a sentence, というのは is natural in speech; なぜなら is more formal, like making an argument, usually with 「〜からだ」 at the end.

this.tr: I'm going home early today. You see, my child has a fever.

that.tr: I'm against this proposal. That's because it costs too much.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the ending: in everyday conversation, explaining “it's because this happened”, usually ending in 「〜んです」「〜んだ」 → というのは; presenting arguments in meetings or essays, ending in 「〜からだ」 → なぜなら.

groups.note: Both come from conditional forms of 「と言う」 — “speaking of…”

items.diff: For associations the two are basically interchangeable; checking with the listener “by…, do you mean…?” uses only というと, while taking up a topic yourself usually uses といえば.

this.tr: Tanaka — you mean that tall guy?

that.tr: Speaking of Tanaka, I hear he's getting married next month.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a question checking with the listener who or what they mean → only というと; following the topic to say something it reminds you of (〜らしいよ、〜が有名だ) → といえば (というと also works here).

items.diff: というと focuses on association and checking, with a calm tone; といったら often carries exclamation, stressing degree.

this.tr: Summer makes me think of fireworks.

that.tr: The heat this summer — it's just unbearable.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: an ordinary noun (夏), followed by an association → というと; a 「〜さ」 noun like 「暑さ」「美しさ」, followed by how intense it is → といったら.

groups.note: Both are built on 「と言う」 — rephrasing around “what to call it”

items.diff: というより compares and clearly picks the second wording; というか is self-correcting while thinking, light and conversational.

this.tr: He's not so much kind as indulgent.

that.tr: He's kind… or rather, kind of too soft on people, you know?

items.explain: Look at the tone: putting two wordings side by side and clearly judging the second more accurate, also usable in writing → というより (often with 「むしろ」); in speech, with 「ちょっと」「〜んだよね」, as if swapping words while thinking → というか.

groups.note: Both correct the first wording with the second — “not A; B is right”

items.diff: というより corrects the “wording” for the same thing; よりむしろ compares two options and picks the latter.

this.tr: Today it's not so much cool as cold.

that.tr: In summer, I'd rather go to the mountains than the beach.

items.explain: Look at what's being compared: finding a more accurate word for the same state (涼しい → 寒い) → というより; comparing two different options (海と山) and choosing the latter → よりむしろ. The two are also often combined: 「涼しいというよりむしろ寒い」.

items.diff: というより doesn't reject A, just says B fits better; じゃなくて rejects A entirely: “not A but B”.

this.tr: He's less a teacher than something like a friend.

that.tr: He's not a teacher, he's an office clerk.

items.explain: See whether A is true: he really is a teacher, but “friend” describes the relationship better → というより; A is simply wrong (he's not a teacher) and you're correcting a misunderstanding → じゃなくて (ではなく in writing).

groups.note: Both come from 見る (to see) — extended from “see” to “appear, be regarded as”

items.diff: とみえる is the speaker's own guess; とみられる is the news phrase “it is believed, it is thought”, objective and impersonal.

this.tr: The book on the desk is still open. It seems he was studying until just now.

that.tr: According to police, the fire is believed to have been caused by a cigarette.

items.explain: Look at the tone: the speaker sees signs and judges for themselves → とみえる; in news reports, a guess by police or experts without saying who's guessing → とみられる (the passive of 「みる」, “be regarded as”).

items.diff: とみえる infers “it seems…” from visible signs; が見える means you actually see it with your eyes.

this.tr: The light is on in the next room. It seems he's still up.

that.tr: It's the middle of the night, but I can still see the light in the next room.

items.explain: Look before 見える: “noun + が” → that thing comes into view (明かりが見える); a full sentence + と (まだ起きているとみえる) → a conclusion drawn from signs, more written; in speech people mostly say 「〜みたいだ」.

groups.note: All give a judgment based on how things look: “it seems, it looks like…”

items.diff: とみえる leans written, with a detached, commentator's tone; ようだ is the most common everyday guess, and みたいだ in casual speech.

this.tr: His shoes aren't in the entryway. It appears my brother has gone out.

that.tr: His shoes aren't in the entryway. Looks like my brother went out.

items.explain: The meaning is almost the same; the difference is register: in novels and writing, with a calm, observing tone → とみえる, often with 「よほど」; in everyday speech → ようだ, or more casually みたいだ (出かけたみたいだ). Also, ようだ can make comparisons (氷のようだ), while とみえる can't.

items.diff: とみえる goes at the end of the sentence and is itself the conclusion; ところを見ると puts the evidence first, “judging from…”, and must be followed by a guess.

this.tr: She keeps smiling. It seems something good happened.

that.tr: Judging from how she keeps smiling, something good seems to have happened.

items.explain: Both go “see signs → guess”. Look at the structure: ところを見ると itself introduces the evidence and must be followed by 「らしい」「ようだ」「にちがいない」; とみえる goes at the end of the sentence and is itself the conclusion, with the evidence in the previous sentence.

items.diff: とみえる draws the conclusion “it seems…” from signs; ように見える just describes an outward impression, “looks like…”, which may not be true.

this.tr: He keeps yawning. He must be really tired.

that.tr: He looks tired, but he's actually full of energy.

items.explain: ように見える only describes the impression given by appearance, and is often followed by 「が、実は……」 to overturn it; とみえる is a judgment drawn from signs (何度もあくびをしている) that the speaker basically believes, often paired with 「よほど」, more written.

groups.note: Both come from 「並ぶ」 — originally “to line up in a row”

items.diff: と並んで says two things are equally famous or of equal standing; 並み attaches directly after a noun, meaning “on par with…”.

this.tr: Like Nara, Kyoto is known as a city with many old temples.

that.tr: His cooking skills are on a professional level.

items.explain: Look at the form and meaning: 「Aと並んで」 is followed by B being as famous or important as A, the two standing side by side; 「noun + 並み」 sticks right after the noun (プロ並み、平年並み), saying something reaches that level, followed by 「だ」 or 「の + noun」.

groups.note: Both come from 「とする」 — “to treat as, to set as…”

items.title: 〜としても (even if)
items.diff: Noun + として means “as…”; plain form + としても is a hypothetical concession, “even if…”.

this.tr: As a mother, I worry about my child's future.

that.tr: Even if people oppose it, I'm going to study abroad.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun (母、教師) → として indicates a role; a verb or adjective in plain form (反対された、高い) + としても → supposes a situation, followed by “the outcome won't change”. Noun + としても can also mean “as… too” (母としても), so check the second half.

groups.note: Both are written 「として」, but with “一 + counter” before and a negative after, the meaning is completely different

items.diff: Noun + として means “as…”; 一 + counter + として〜ない means “not a single…”, and must be followed by a negative.

this.tr: He took part in the meeting as an interpreter.

that.tr: Not a single person took part in the meeting.

items.explain: Look before として: a role or position (通訳、教師) → “as”; “一 + counter” like 「誰一人」「一日」「一つ」, always followed by a negative (なかった) → “not a single one”.

groups.note: Both indicate the role or standpoint from which something is viewed

items.diff: として means “in the capacity of… (doing something)”; にとって means “for… (how it is)”, followed by an evaluation.

this.tr: As a teacher, I have a responsibility to protect my students.

that.tr: For a teacher, students' smiles are the greatest joy.

items.explain: Look at the second half: what someone in this role should do, or did in this capacity (責任がある、参加する) → として; evaluating how important, hard or pleasing something is for this person (大切だ、難しい、喜びだ) → にとって.

items.diff: として just indicates a role; にしては means “by the standard of…, (surprisingly)”.

this.tr: He's taking part in this project as a new hire.

that.tr: For a new hire, he's very good at his job.

items.explain: See whether the second half contains a “surprise”: just stating in what capacity someone acts → として; saying their performance differs from what's typical for that role (新人なのによくできる) → にしては, with evaluation and surprise.

groups.note: Both come from 「とする」 — “to suppose…”

items.diff: としても is contrastive: “even supposing…, (it doesn't change)”; とすれば follows on: “supposing…, then…”.

this.tr: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead as planned.

that.tr: If it rains, the match will probably be canceled.

items.explain: Only 「も」 vs 「ば」 differs: としても is followed by “all the same…”, the premise doesn't affect the outcome; とすれば (としたら、とすると) is followed by a conclusion drawn from the premise, often with 「だろう」「はずだ」.

items.title: 〜としたところで
items.diff: としても is a neutral hypothetical concession; としたところで is more negative, stressing “even so, it's no use / nothing changes”.

this.tag: Neutral · can be followed by good things
this.tr: Even if I fail, it'll be a good experience.

that.tr: Even if I go and apologize now, I probably won't be forgiven.

items.explain: Look at the second half: the outcome can be good or bad (いい経験になる) → としても; a negative conclusion of “no use, nothing will change” (許してもらえない、無駄だ) → としたところで, with a “wasted effort” flavor; in speech people usually say 「〜たところで」.

groups.note: All express concession: “even if…”

items.diff: としても leans toward pure hypotheticals; にしても usually addresses a known fact: “granted that…, (still…)”.

this.tr: Even if he's busy, he should at least reply.

that.tr: Granted he's (really) busy, it's strange not to reply for three whole days.

items.explain: See whether the premise is a fact: starting with 「仮に」, not knowing if he's really busy → としても; knowing full well he's busy, granting that first and then voicing criticism or dissatisfaction (〜のはおかしい、〜すぎる) → にしても.

items.title: 〜ても
items.diff: としても is only for hypotheticals; ても works for both hypotheticals and things that already happened.

this.tr: Even if I waited all day, he probably wouldn't come.

that.tr: Yesterday I waited all day, but he didn't come.

items.explain: Look at the clues: starting with 「仮に」, something that hasn't happened → both としても and ても work (としても sounds more clearly hypothetical); a fact that already happened, like with 「昨日」 → generally ても.

groups.note: Both come from 「とする」 — “to suppose…”

items.diff: とすれば follows on: “supposing…, then…”; としても is contrastive: “even supposing…, (it doesn't change)”.

this.tr: If it rains, the match will probably be canceled.

that.tr: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead as planned.

items.explain: Only 「ば」 vs 「も」 differs: とすれば is followed by a conclusion drawn from the premise, often with 「だろう」「はずだ」 (としたら and とすると are the same); としても is followed by “all the same…”, the premise doesn't affect the outcome.

groups.note: All express a hypothetical condition: “if…”

items.diff: たら can be used for things certain to happen (“after…”); としたら is only for “supposing, for the sake of argument”, with an uncertain or unrealistic premise.

this.tr: If you won the lottery, what would you spend it on?

that.tr: Please call me when you get to the station.

items.explain: See whether the premise will happen: things that will happen sooner or later, like arriving at a station or finishing work → use たら; uncertain or unrealistic things like winning the lottery or turning into a bird, supposed for the sake of argument → としたら (とすれば、とすると are the same). としたら is often followed by a question.

items.diff: なら usually picks up what the other person said to give advice; とすれば sets up a premise yourself and draws a conclusion, with a strongly logical feel.

this.tr: If what he says is true, then the culprit is someone else.

that.tr: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a good time.

items.explain: Look at the second half: advice or a request (〜がいいですよ、〜てください) → なら; a conclusion reasoned step by step from the premise (〜ことになる、〜はずだ) → とすれば. なら often picks up what the other person just said, while とすれば sets up a premise yourself to reason from.

items.diff: The premise of とすれば is just a supposition and can be unrealistic; となると means “once it actually comes to…”, and the premise is usually already, or about to become, reality.

this.tr: If I were to live abroad, which country would be good, I wonder?

that.tr: If I'm being posted overseas from next month, it'll be hard on my family too.

items.explain: See whether the premise is real: 「仮に」, just imagining → とすれば; already decided or about to come true (来月から海外勤務) → となると, followed by the speaker's judgment or worry. となれば and となったら are the same.

groups.note: Both come from 「共 (とも)」 — “together”: 伴う = 共 + なう (to appear together), とともに = と + 共に

items.diff: に伴って is only used for changes in things and can't follow a person; とともに can also mean “together with someone”.

this.tr: I fought to the very end together with my comrades.

that.tr: With the population increase, housing has become scarce.

wrong.why: に伴って can't follow a person

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: people or groups (仲間、家族) → only とともに (“together with…”); changes like 人口増加、経済の発展 → both に伴って and とともに work, with に伴って sounding more like news or official documents.

groups.note: Both can mean “along with…” or “at the same time as…”

items.diff: とともに can also mean “gradually along with…” and “together with…”; と同時に only means “at the same instant”.

this.tr: As I've gotten older, my stamina has gradually declined.

that.tr: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Look for words of gradual change like 「少しずつ」「だんだん」: as one thing changes, the other slowly follows → only とともに; an instant like a bell ringing or a door opening → と同時に (とともに also works).

items.diff: につれて only expresses gradual change and is more conversational; とともに is more written and can also be used for one-off simultaneous events.

this.tr: Upon graduating, I returned to my home country.

that.tr: As I got used to life in Japan, I made more friends.

wrong.why: Graduating is a one-off event; につれて is only for gradual change

items.explain: See whether what comes before is “gradual”: slowly progressing changes like 慣れる、年を取る、増える → both につれて and とともに work; one-off events like 卒業、結婚 → only とともに (meaning “at the same time”).

groups.note: Both refer to when something is “halfway through”

items.diff: 途中で focuses on “not finished yet, partway through”, most often followed by leaving or giving up midway; 最中に focuses on “right in the thick of it”, often followed by an unexpected interruption.

this.tr: Halfway through the movie, I got bored and left.

that.tr: Right in the middle of the movie, my phone started ringing.

items.explain: Look at the second half: stopping or giving up midway yourself (帰った、やめた) → 途中で; something unexpected suddenly cutting in while it's going on (携帯が鳴った、停電した) → 最中に fits better. Also, 途中で can mean “on the way” (駅へ行く途中で), which 最中に can't. 途中に is usually followed by existence verbs like 「ある」「いる」, with the same meaning.

items.title: 〜かけの (half-done)
items.diff: 途中で says “something happened partway through”; かけの modifies a noun, saying the thing itself is “half-done, not finished”.

this.tr: I fell asleep halfway through reading the book.

that.tr: There's a half-read book on the desk.

items.explain: Look at what follows: another event (寝てしまった) → 途中で, “partway through that”; a noun directly (本、コーヒー) → masu-stem + かけの, saying the thing itself isn't finished.

groups.note: Both are written 「とか」: a single one at the end of a sentence is hearsay, a pair mid-sentence is a list

items.diff: A single とか at the end of a sentence → uncertain hearsay, “I heard…”; paired とか mid-sentence → a list, “… and … and such”.

this.tr: I heard Tanaka's getting married next month.

that.tr: I bought things like meat and vegetables at the supermarket.

items.explain: Look at where とか is and how many there are: a single one at the end with nothing after it → passing on hearsay you're unsure of, close to 「〜そうだ」 but vaguer; mid-sentence, often a pair (AとかBとか), with a predicate after → a list.

groups.note: All report hearsay: “I hear that…”

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: そうだ is ordinary hearsay, usable in formal settings too; とか is vaguer, with an “I don't quite remember” tone, used only in casual chat.

this.tr: Electricity bills are going up from next month, or something like that.

that.tr: According to the news, electricity bills are going up from next month.

items.explain: See whether there's a clear source: a clear source like 「ニュースによると」 and definite content → そうだ; not saying where you heard it, not quite sure yourself, just mentioning it in passing → とか.

items.diff: とか is vague and doesn't vouch for the truth; んだって shares news you heard as fact, in casual speech.

this.tr: I'm not really sure, but I heard a new shop opened in front of the station or something.

that.tr: Hey, guess what — a new shop opened in front of the station!

items.explain: Look at the lead-in: 「よく知らないけど」 → とか, unsure of the content; eagerly telling someone, as with 「ねえ聞いて」 → んだって, with a confident, friendly tone (women also often say 「んですって」).

items.diff: とか is vague hearsay in casual chat; とのことだ is formal reporting, mostly used to pass on a message.

this.tr: I heard Yamada's off sick with a cold today.

that.tr: Yamada called to say he's off today with a cold.

items.explain: Look at the setting and source: casual chat among coworkers, not quite sure → とか; reporting to your boss “so-and-so called to say…”, with a clear source → とのことです. Using とか at work can sound careless.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ (所)」 — placing an event at a certain “point in time”

items.diff: ところだった means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen; ところだ is a real point in time right now.

this.tr: I very nearly missed the train.

that.tr: I'm just about to arrive at the station.

items.explain: Look for words like 「もう少しで」「危うく」 and the past tense 「だった」: ところだった is about something that nearly happened but didn't, often with relief or a lingering scare; ところだ is about a real point in time right now.

groups.note: Both mean “almost…”

items.diff: ところだった stresses “it was one step away from becoming reality”, with “that was close” relief; そうになった focuses on the signs that appeared at the time, usually an involuntary bodily reaction.

this.tr: If you hadn't woken me up, I'd have been late.

that.tr: The sad movie almost made me cry.

wrong.why: A hypothetical like 「〜なかったら」 must be followed by ところだった

items.explain: Look for 「〜なかったら」「もう少しで」 before it: a hypothetical “if not for…, would have…”, or stressing it was just one step away → ところだった (after the dictionary form); a bodily reaction at the time like tears, falling or dozing off, often with 「思わず」 before it → そうになった (after the masu-stem: 泣き + そう).

items.title: 〜かける (nearly)
items.diff: かけた focuses on something that had already begun and was partway along; ところだった focuses on something that didn't happen at all, just came close.

this.tr: If I hadn't been wearing a life jacket, I'd have drowned.

that.tr: I nearly drowned in the sea, but someone nearby saved me.

items.explain: See whether it had started: 溺れかけた means you were already struggling in the water and were rescued partway through, often followed by 「が、助けられた」; 溺れるところだった means some condition (ライフジャケット) kept you from going under, often with 「〜なかったら」 before it.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ (所)」 — “the very scene where… is happening”

items.diff: ところに／へ are followed by something that “came or happened”; ところを is followed by an action directly acting on that scene (見る、起こす、助ける).

this.tr: While I was sleeping, a friend called.
While I was sleeping, my little brother came home.

that.tr: I was sleeping when my mom woke me up.

items.explain: Look at the verb in the second half: “arriving, happening” like 電話がかかってくる、帰ってくる → ところに／ところへ (へ stresses “coming to” more); actions aimed directly at “me while sleeping” like 起こす、見る、助ける, often in the passive → ところを.

items.diff: ところに／へ say “just at that moment, someone or something came”; ところだ only says what point in time you're at.

this.tag: ところに · just then → a call
this.tr: Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.

this.tag: ところへ · just then → someone came
this.tr: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came over.

that.tr: I'm just about to go out.

items.explain: ところに／ところへ must be followed by a person or event that “barges in” (電話がかかってきた、友達が来た), often upsetting your plans; ところだ only states your own situation, and the sentence ends there.

groups.note: Both mean “just as… (something else happened)”

items.diff: ところに／へ can follow “about to” or “just did”, and are usually followed by “someone came, a call came”; 最中に only refers to when something is in full swing.

this.tag: ところに · just about to…
this.tr: Just as I was about to leave the house, the phone rang.

this.tag: ところへ · just did… someone came
this.tr: I'd just gotten home when a friend came to visit.

that.tr: The phone rang while I was in the middle of cooking.

items.explain: Look at the form before it: 「〜ようとした」 (about to) and the た-form (帰った = just did) can both take ところに／へ; 最中に only follows 「noun + の」 or 「ている」, referring to when something is halfway through and you're busy with it.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — “the very scene where something is going on”

items.diff: ところを is followed by an action aimed directly at that scene (見る、起こす、助ける); ところに／へ is followed by something that “arrives or happens”.

this.tr: I was sleeping when my mother woke me up.

that.tr: I was sleeping when a friend called me.
I was sleeping when my little brother came home.

items.explain: Look at the verb in the second half: actions aimed straight at “me while I was sleeping”, like 起こす、見る、助ける, often in the passive → ところを; “arriving, happening” like 電話がかかってくる、帰ってくる → ところに／ところへ.

groups.note: Both mean “in the middle of a situation”

items.title: 〜中を (in spite of…)
items.diff: In polite phrases about the other person being busy, the two are basically interchangeable; only 中を can attach directly to a weather or surroundings noun to mean “braving…”.

this.tr: Thank you so much for taking the time to come despite being so busy.

that.tr: Thank you so much for coming all this way in the rain.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: the other person's situation, like 「お忙しい」「お休みの」 → both ところを and 中を work (ところを is more polite; the set phrase 「お足元の悪いところを」 belongs here too); a weather or surroundings noun attached directly, like 「雨の中を」「寒さの中を」 → only 中を; you don't say 「雨のところを」.

items.diff: 最中に can be followed by anything that suddenly happens; ところを must be followed by an action aimed directly at that scene.

this.tr: I was sleeping when the phone woke me up.

that.tr: The power went out in the middle of the meeting.

items.explain: Look at the verb in the second half: transitive verbs aimed at that scene, like 起こす、見る、捕まえる, often in the passive → ところを; something that simply happens, like 停電する、地震が起きる → 最中に.

groups.note: ところで ↔ ところが ↔ たところで look almost identical

items.diff: ところで means “by the way” and switches to another topic; ところが means “but unexpectedly”, and the second sentence overturns what the first expected.

this.tr: Good job on the exam. By the way, are you free this weekend?

that.tr: I thought the exam would be easy. But I couldn't do any of it.

items.explain: Check whether the two sentences are related: the second starts an unrelated topic, often a question → ところで; the second overturns the first's expectation (thought it was easy → couldn't do any of it) → ところが. When reading, just look at whether the last kana is で or が.

items.diff: ところで on its own at the start of a sentence means “by the way”; たところで after a verb's ta-form means “even if… (it's no use)”.

this.tr: It's cold today, isn't it. By the way, what time does tomorrow's meeting start?

that.tr: Even if you run now, you won't make it.

items.explain: Look at what's before ところで: it stands alone after a period or comma → change of topic; it's glued to a verb's ta-form (走った、謝った) and followed by a negative or “no use” result → even if….

groups.note: Both are used to change the topic

items.diff: ところで simply moves to another topic, often with a casual question; はさておき explicitly “sets aside” the previous topic, usually to get back to the main point.

this.tr: Nice weather, isn't it. By the way, how is Mr. Tanaka?

that.tag: Set aside · back to the point
that.tr: Joking aside, let's get down to business.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun like 「冗談」「挨拶」＋はさておき, often followed by 「本題に入る」「まず〜」 → shelving it to get back to what matters; ところで sits at the start of a sentence with no noun before it and just changes the topic, usually followed by a question.

groups.note: Both come from 「通す」 — originally “make… pass through”

items.diff: Verb masu-stem＋通す means “keep… up to the end”; noun＋を通して means “through…” or “throughout…”.

this.tr: He kept up the lie right to the end.

that.tr: I got to know him through a friend.

items.explain: Look at what's before 通す: a verb's masu-stem (つき、やり、守り) → carrying the action through from start to finish; noun＋を (友達を、一年を) → through some medium, or 「一年を通して」 for a whole period. In writing 「を通じて」 is common, with the same meaning.

groups.note: Both mean keeping an action going to the end

items.diff: 〜通す stresses going from start to finish without stopping or changing; 〜抜く stresses overcoming difficulty or taking it to the limit.

this.tr: I ran the whole 42 km without taking a single break.

that.tr: My feet hurt, but I ran all the way to the end.

items.explain: Look at the clue: 「一度も休まずに」「ずっと」 stress no breaks and no change → 通す (守り通す、黙り通す); 「痛かったが」「苦しい中」 stress overcoming difficulty, or going to the limit as in 「考え抜く」 → 抜く. The two are often interchangeable; only the emphasis differs.

items.diff: 〜続ける only says you kept doing it, whether or not you reached the end; 〜通す stresses that you kept going all the way to the end.

this.tag: All the way to the end
this.tr: I walked the mountain path all the way to the end.

that.tr: I kept walking along the mountain path for three hours.

items.explain: Look at the clue: 「最後まで」「全部」 point to an end → 通す; 「3時間」「ずっと」 only say how long it lasted, and you may keep going afterwards → 続ける. That's why 「今も走り続けている」 is fine, while 通す is normally used once it's done.

groups.note: Both pair with a negative to mean “can't do it, can't happen”

items.diff: とても〜ない works in speech and writing and sounds measured; 〜っこない is very colloquial and casual.

this.tr: There's no way I can solve a problem this hard.

that.tr: No way I could ever solve a problem this hard.

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: casual speech with 「俺」「〜よ」 → っこない; something more formal, or in writing → とても〜ない. Also, っこない attaches directly to the masu-stem (解けっこない), while とても has to pair with a negative form (とても解けない).

items.diff: とても〜ない means “impossible no matter what”; なかなか〜ない means “not easily, takes a long time to…” — with time it might happen.

this.tr: There's no way I can read a book this thick in one day.

that.tr: I read it every day, but I just can't seem to finish this book.

items.explain: Look at the clue: under a condition like 「一日で」 it's completely beyond your ability → とても〜ない; 「毎日読んでいるけど」, you keep trying but progress is slow and it takes a long time → なかなか〜ない.

items.diff: とても〜ない means ability or conditions fall far short; 〜ようがない means there's no way or method to do it.

this.tr: There's no way one person can finish this much work.

that.tr: I don't know their phone number or address, so there's no way to contact them.

items.explain: Look at the reason: too much work, too little time, not enough human effort → とても〜ない; no number, no address, no means at all → ようがない (attaches to the masu-stem: し＋ようがない).

groups.note: Both mean taking the chance while doing one thing to do another “while you're at it”

items.diff: ついでに is common in speech, attaches freely, and has a clear main task and side task; がてら is more written, usually follows action nouns like 「散歩」「買い物」, and is usually followed by going somewhere.

this.tr: When I went to the post office, I picked up some bread on the way.

that.tr: I went out for a walk and bought some bread along the way.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a verb's dictionary form, ta-form, or 「noun＋の」 all work → ついでに (行くついでに、散歩のついでに); 「散歩」「買い物」 with がてら attached directly, usually followed by movement like 「〜に行く」, with a more written tone.

items.diff: ついでに means doing something extra alongside the main task, with a clear main and side; を兼ねて means one action serves two purposes at once — killing two birds with one stone.

this.tr: While on a business trip, I took the chance to see some temples in Kyoto.

that.tr: I went to Kyoto for both business and sightseeing.

items.explain: Check whether it's one thing or two: 「出張のついでに」 → the business trip is the main task and the temples are a side thing; 「AとBを兼ねて」 → one trip fulfills two purposes at once, with neither more important (趣味と実益を兼ねて).

groups.note: Both are used to “rephrase or sum up”

items.diff: つまり restates what came before in a shorter way with the same meaning; というか corrects yourself because the first wording didn't feel right.

this.tr: He's my mother's older brother — in other words, my uncle.

that.tr: He's serious — or rather, stubborn.

items.explain: Check whether the two parts mean the same thing: 母の兄＝おじ, exactly the same content, just said more briefly → つまり; まじめ ≠ 頑固, the first word didn't fit, so you swap it → というか.

items.title: 〜ということだ (conclusion)
items.diff: つまり goes at the start of a sentence and signals “here comes the conclusion”; ということだ goes at the end and wraps the conclusion up. They're often used together.

this.tr: The trains have stopped. In other words, I'll be late today.

that.tr: The trains have stopped. That means I'll be late today.

items.explain: Look at the position: つまり is at the start, so as soon as you hear it you know a conclusion is coming; ということだ is at the end and sums the whole sentence up as “that means…”. The fullest version uses both: 「つまり、今日は遅刻ということだ」.

groups.note: Both come from 「つもり（積もり）」 — “a mental estimate”: estimating the future＝intending; estimating the present＝believing (wrongly) about yourself

items.diff: Dictionary form＋つもりだった means “I had planned to do it”; ta-form＋つもりだった means “I thought I had already done it”.

this.tr: I meant to lock the door before going out, but I forgot.

that.tr: I thought I'd locked the door, but it wasn't locked at all.

items.explain: The only difference is whether つもり follows 「かける」 or 「かけた」: the dictionary form is a plan made beforehand, and the second half says you didn't do it (忘れてしまった); the ta-form means you believed it was done, and the second half says reality was different (かかっていなかった).

groups.note: Both mean “was supposed to… (but didn't)”

items.title: 〜はずだった
items.diff: つもりだった is what a person “had intended”; はずだった is what “should have happened according to plan” but didn't.

this.tr: I had planned to take the three o'clock train.

that.tr: The train was supposed to arrive at three.

wrong.why: A train can't “intend” anything — use はずだった

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person's own plan by choice → つもりだった; things like trains, packages, or schedules that “should” happen as arranged → はずだった. People can take はずだった too (今日は休みのはずだった), but then it's about the arrangement, not the person's will.

groups.note: Both come from 「つもり（積もり）」 — “a mental estimate”: estimating the future＝intending; estimating the present＝believing (wrongly) about yourself

items.diff: Dictionary form＋つもりで means “intending to do it”; ta-form＋つもりで means “treating it as already done” when it actually wasn't.

this.tr: I'm saving money every month because I plan to travel next year.

that.tr: I pretended I'd already gone on the trip and put that money in the bank.

items.explain: The only difference is whether つもり follows 「する」 or 「した」: the dictionary form is something you really will do, and you're saving for it; the ta-form means “pretend it's already done” — you don't actually do it, and use the money or time saved for something else.

groups.note: Both come from quoting with 「と言う」 — “speaking of…”

items.diff: ったら follows a person and complains about their habits in exasperation; といったら brings up a topic and names the most typical example, or stresses a degree.

this.tr: Honestly, my husband went out and forgot his umbrella again.

that.tr: When it comes to Japanese mountains, it has to be Mt. Fuji.

items.explain: ったら is just a contraction of 「と言ったら」. Look at what follows: someone's exasperating behavior (また忘れた) → ったら, usually after family or people you know; a typical answer (富士山だ) or “incredibly…” → といったら, with a neutral tone.

items.title: 〜って (topic)
items.diff: って is just a colloquial 「は」 that raises a topic neutrally; ったら raises the topic with a feeling of “they're hopeless”.

this.tr: Honestly, Tanaka's late again.

that.tr: What kind of person is Tanaka?

items.explain: Both are 「と言う」 shortened in speech, and both can follow a name as the topic. Look at what follows: a neutral question or introduction → って; a complaint about their habits (また遅刻、いつも〜) → ったら, with annoyance or affection.

groups.note: Both carry an emotion when bringing someone up

items.diff: ったら means “they're hopeless”, often with affection; なんて expresses contempt or disdain.

this.tr: Honestly, my kid came home with dirty clothes again.

that.tr: I'm done with someone like that.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude toward the person: small annoying habits of family or friends, with closeness behind the complaint → ったら; someone you look down on or dislike, like 「あんな人」 → なんて, usually followed by a negative or a bad opinion.

groups.note: Both come from 「うち（内）」 — “within a certain range”

items.diff: うちに is “within” a time (while…); うちに入らない is “within” a category — “doesn't even count as…”.

this.tr: Let's go home while it's still light.

that.tr: Being five minutes late doesn't even count as late.

items.explain: うち just means 「内」. Check whether 「入らない」 follows: if not, it's a time range → while…; with 「入らない」, it's whether something counts as part of that category → the degree is too small to count at all.

groups.note: 〜ないうちに ↔ 〜か〜ないかのうちに: the only difference is whether 「〜か」 comes before

items.diff: 〜ないうちに means “before… happens (hurry)”; 〜か〜ないかのうちに means “no sooner had… than…”.

this.tr: Let's go home before it gets dark.

that.tr: The bell had barely rung when everyone rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: The key is 「か」: just 「ならないうちに」 with no 「〜か」 before it means “before it becomes…”, often followed by something to do quickly like 「〜よう」「〜なさい」; 「鳴るか鳴らないか」 puts the same verb in positive and negative to mean “the instant it did or didn't ring”, followed by something that already happened.

groups.note: Both mean doing something “during or before” a time

items.title: 〜間に
items.diff: うちに carries urgency — “now, before it's too late”; 間に just says something was done during that period.

this.tr: Let's get the laundry done while the kids are asleep.

that.tr: I got my driver's license during summer vacation.

items.explain: Check whether the state could end at any moment: the kids could wake up any time → うちに, often followed by a race against time like 「〜てしまおう」; a period with a clear start and end like summer vacation, just saying what you did in it → 間に.

items.diff: ないうちに means “hurry before… happens”, with urgency; 前に only gives the order in time.

this.tag: ないうちに · before it happens
this.tr: Let's hurry and bring the laundry in before it rains.

that.tr: I brush my teeth every night before going to bed.

items.explain: Check for urgency: you're worried something unwelcome (rain, food getting cold) is about to happen, and you act before it → ないうちに, often with 「急いで」; a daily habit or a simple order of events (毎晩寝る前に) → 前に. Note the forms: here うちに takes the negative form (降らない), while 前に takes the dictionary form (寝る).

groups.note: Both come from 「上（うえ）」 — “on top of…”

items.diff: 上に follows the first point and finishes in one sentence; その上 starts a sentence and links back to the previous one.

this.tr: This room is not only spacious but also close to the station.

that.tr: This room is spacious. On top of that, it's close to the station.

items.explain: Same meaning, different position: 上に attaches directly to the plain form of the first point (広い上に); その上 is a standalone conjunction that needs a sentence before it, and 「その」 refers to that sentence.

items.diff: 上に means “on top of…, in addition”; た上で means “after…, and on that basis…”.

this.tr: He not only works fast but also makes few mistakes.

that.tr: I'll decide after talking it over carefully with my family.

items.explain: The only difference is に vs. で. 上に joins two judgments in the same direction (速い＋ミスが少ない), often paired with 「も」; 上で usually follows a step in the ta-form (相談した), followed by the action taken on that basis (決める) — it's about order, not adding.

items.diff: 上に means “and also, on top of that”; 上は means “now that… (you must)…”.

this.tr: I failed the exam, and on top of that I even lost my wallet.

that.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I have no choice but to see it through.

items.explain: Look at the second half: after 上に comes another fact in the same direction (〜まで、〜も); after 上は comes a resolve or obligation (〜しかない、〜なければならない). It means the same as 「以上は」「からには」 and sounds quite formal.

groups.note: Both add something: “not only… but also…”

items.diff: 上に can only state facts; だけでなく can also be followed by a request or suggestion.

this.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap but also tasty.

that.tr: Don't just look — please actually touch it too.

wrong.why: 上に can't be followed by a request or suggestion

items.explain: Look at the second half: a request or suggestion like 「〜てください」「〜ましょう」 → only だけでなく; for stating facts (おいしい) both work, and 上に stresses the piling up — “even better” or “even worse”.

items.diff: 上に simply says “on top of that”; し lists reasons, often leading to the speaker's conclusion or decision.

this.tr: This room is not only spacious, but the rent is cheap too.

that.tr: This room is spacious, and the rent is cheap — let's go with this one.

items.explain: Check whether a conclusion follows: し is often used two or three times (〜し、〜し) and finally leads to a decision like “so let's…”, with a strongly spoken feel; 上に usually joins just two points and simply says “and also”, leaning toward writing.

groups.note: Both come from 「別（べつ）」 — “a separate matter”

items.diff: は別として just sets the first item aside; なら別だが means “if it were…, that would be another matter”, with the focus on the general conclusion that follows.

this.tr: Children aside, all adults please take part.

that.tr: It would be one thing if it were a child, but it's strange for an adult to do something like that.

items.explain: Look at the second half: after は別として, you go straight on to the rest (大人は全員参加); なら別だが first supposes an exception, then turns with 「が」 to criticize or stress the general case (大人がするのはおかしい).

groups.note: Both mean “leaving out” one item

items.diff: は別として sets a topic or issue aside for now; を除いて objectively removes one item from a group, with everything else the same.

this.tr: Results aside, everyone did their best.

that.tr: We're open every day except Monday.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a “topic” like results, costs, or jokes, set aside for now → は別として; one member removed from a set such as weekdays or people, followed by “all the rest” → を除いて, common in notices and rules.

groups.note: Both mean “not to mention A, B too…”

items.diff: Same meaning; は言うまでもなく is more written and more formal.

this.tr: This amusement park is fun for adults, not to mention children.

that.tr: This tournament will feature many athletes from overseas, to say nothing of domestic ones.

items.explain: Look at the setting: everyday conversation → はもちろん; speeches, news, writing → は言うまでもなく. はもとより also leans written, with a tone close to は言うまでもなく.

items.diff: はもちろん works in both positive and negative sentences; はおろか is used almost only with negatives or bad outcomes, with surprise or frustration.

this.tr: This shop is crowded on weekdays too, not just on weekends.

that.tr: I'm so busy that I don't even have time to rest on weekends, let alone travel.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: はおろか is almost always followed by a negative like 「〜もない」「〜もできない」, with the surprise or frustration of “this is too much”, and it can't take a request or intention; はもちろん (はもとより) is neutral and works in positive sentences and requests alike.

items.diff: はもちろん stresses that the first item is “a given”; だけでなく just means “not only…”, with neither part more important.

this.tr: This temple is popular with foreigners, not to mention Japanese people.

that.tr: Don't just talk — listen to the other person too.

items.explain: はもちろん follows a noun (a verb needs 「の」), and it's the most obvious one (a Japanese temple → Japanese people); だけでなく just widens the scope, can attach directly to a verb (話す), and is often followed by a suggestion like 「〜ましょう」.

groups.note: Both come from 「わけ（訳）」 — “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけではない means “it's not that…”, denying only part of something; わけだ draws a conclusion that follows from the reasoning.

this.tr: I lived in Japan, but that doesn't mean I know a lot about it.

that.tr: Oh, you lived there for three years? No wonder you know so much about Japan.

items.explain: わけだ follows the reason to conclude “no wonder”; わけではない is exactly what corrects that kind of “obvious” inference: lived in Japan ≠ must know Japan well. When you see 「けど」「からといって」 before it, what follows is most likely わけではない.

items.diff: わけではない just means “not (all)…”, a soft tone; わけがない means “absolutely impossible”, a strong tone.

this.tr: Expensive things aren't all good.

that.tr: There's no way something this cheap is any good.

items.explain: Only では vs. が differ, but the tone is very different. わけではない often goes with 「全部」「いつも」「別に」 and denies only part, or the other person's misunderstanding; わけがない means “there's no reason at all for that”＝absolutely impossible, often with 「こんなに」「あの人が」.

items.diff: わけではない means “it's not that…”; わけにはいかない means “can't do… (because of duty or decency)”.

this.tr: It's not that I want to quit — I just want to rest a bit.

that.tr: I have a family to support, so I can't quit my job now.

items.explain: Look at what follows: わけではない is often followed by 「けど／が」 and then your real feelings, to clear up a misunderstanding; わけにはいかない often has 「〜から」 before it explaining a duty or obligation, and means the speaker “can't do that”. When you see 「いかない」, it means “can't”.

groups.note: Both are partial denials: “not necessarily…”

items.diff: とは限らない says a general rule “isn't always true”; わけではない can also deny what others assume about you.

this.tr: I'm not angry or anything.

that.tr: Expensive medicine isn't necessarily effective.

items.explain: Look at what's being talked about: a general rule like “expensive＝effective” has exceptions → とは限らない (わけではない also works here); the other person has misunderstood you (they think you're angry), and you clear it up with 「別に〜わけではない」 → use わけではない. Both are often preceded by 「必ずしも」.

groups.note: Both come from 「わけ（訳）」 — “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけにはいかない is about an action you “can't do”; わけがない is a guess that something is “impossible”.

this.tr: I promised, so I can't turn it down now.

that.tr: Someone as kind as him would never turn it down.

items.explain: Look at what is being judged: whether the speaker can do something themselves → わけにはいかない; a guess about whether someone else or something would be that way → わけがない (＝absolutely impossible). In English both can come out as “can't”, so they're easy to mix up.

items.diff: わけにはいかない means “can't do…”; わけではない means “it's not that…”, just clarifying.

this.tr: I have a family to support, so I can't quit my job now.

that.tr: It's not that I want to quit — I just want to rest a bit.

items.explain: When you see 「いかない」, it means “can't”: it's often preceded by 「〜から」 explaining a duty or obligation; わけではない is often followed by 「けど／が」 and your real feelings, to clear up a misunderstanding, and has nothing to do with whether you can do something.

groups.note: Both mean “can't…”

items.diff: てはいけない is a rule or someone else's prohibition; わけにはいかない is your own judgment, based on the situation or your responsibilities, that you “can't do that”.

this.tr: I came by car, so I can't drink.

that.tr: People under twenty must not drink alcohol.

items.explain: Look at who is stopping it: the law, rules, or elders telling others “you mustn't” → てはいけない; the speaker, considering the situation (driving, work, obligations), feels “I can't do that” → わけにはいかない, usually with “I” as the subject.

items.diff: わけにはいかない means you could but shouldn't; ようがない means you'd like to but there's no way.

this.tr: I still have work left, so I can't go home.

that.tr: There's no last train and no taxis, so there's no way to get home.

items.explain: Look at the reason: unfinished work, a responsibility → you could go home, you just shouldn't → わけにはいかない; no train, no way to contact anyone → no means, so you can't go home even if you want to → ようがない. Note the form: ようがない attaches to the masu-stem (帰り＋ようがない).

groups.note: Both express a contrast: “different from what you'd expect”

items.diff: わりに usually follows a degree word like 「値段、年齢」, or attaches directly to an adjective; にしては follows a specific status, number, or fact.

this.tr: This dish is pretty good for the price.

that.tr: For 500 yen, this dish is pretty good.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: words like 「値段、年齢、身長」 that have no specific value of their own and express a range of degree → のわりに; a specific status or fact like 「500円」「小学生」「初めて」 → にしては. Adjectives can also attach directly to わりに (高いわりに).

items.diff: わりに is a fairly objective evaluation, positive or negative; くせに carries strong blame or contempt and is only negative.

this.tr: He eats a lot, yet he doesn't gain weight.

that.tr: He doesn't do anything himself, yet all he does is complain.

items.explain: Check whether the second half blames someone: 「太らない」 is just a bit surprising, even envious → わりに; 「文句ばかり言う」 is annoyance at a person → くせに, and the subject of both halves must be the same person.

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: わりに compares whether the “degree” matches; のに just says the result went against expectations, often with frustration.

this.tr: This place is pricey, but the food is just average.

that.tr: We'd made plans, but he didn't come.

items.explain: Check whether the first part talks about a “degree”: things that can be higher or lower, more or less, like 高い、よく食べる、年齢 → わりに, meaning “given that degree, what follows doesn't match”; a simple fact like 約束した, with a result against expectations and frustration → のに.

groups.note: Both mean “mainly / starting with A, but not only A”

items.diff: を中心に stresses that A is the core, the focus; をはじめ names A first as a representative, with the focus on “and many more”.

this.tr: This game is popular mainly among young people.

that.tr: This game is popular with all generations, young people first and foremost.

items.explain: Check whether the scope is spread out afterwards: 「幅広い世代」「多くの」「〜など」 → をはじめ, and A is just the first example; no spreading, just saying it's mainly concentrated around A (the Tokyo area, young people) → を中心に.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「始める」 — 「はじめ」 simply means “the beginning”

items.diff: をはじめ follows a noun and lists things “starting with…”; 〜始める follows a verb's masu-stem and means “start doing”.

this.tr: Everyone from the president down attended the party.

that.tr: It started to rain.

items.explain: はじめ originally means “the beginning”: on an action → the beginning of the action＝start doing (降り始めた); on a list → the beginning of the list＝the first representative named (社長をはじめ). Check whether it follows 「noun＋を」 or a verb's masu-stem.

groups.note: Both mean “naming A, but not only A”

items.diff: をはじめ names A first as a representative, with the focus on “and many more”; を中心に stresses that A is the core, the focus.

this.tr: This game is popular with all generations, young people first and foremost.

that.tr: This game is popular mainly among young people.

items.explain: Check whether the scope is spread out afterwards: 「幅広い世代」「多くの」「〜など」 → をはじめ, and A is just the first example; no spreading, just saying it's mainly concentrated around A → を中心に.

items.diff: や〜など lists a few examples equally; をはじめ singles out the first item as the most important representative, in a formal tone.

this.tr: Representatives from many countries, led by the prime minister, gathered at the venue.

that.tr: I bought vegetables, fruit, and so on at the supermarket.

items.explain: Check whether the first item is “the most important one”: the highest-ranking or most representative, like 首相、社長、東京 → をはじめ, common in news and speeches; just a few equal examples (野菜、果物) → や〜など.

groups.note: Both come from 「込む／込める」 — “go inside, put in”

items.diff: を込めて means “putting” feelings into an action; 〜込む after a verb means a person or thing itself “goes inside, goes deep”.

this.tr: I wrote the letter full of gratitude.

that.tr: It started raining, so I dashed into a shop.

items.explain: 込める is the transitive partner of 込む: 込む＝go in oneself (駆け込む、考え込む), 込める＝put something in (弾を込める＝load a bullet). Look at what comes before: noun＋を (感謝を、心を) → pouring a feeling in; a verb's masu-stem (駆け)＋込む → the action goes inside or deep.

groups.note: Both come from 「通す」 — “pass from one end to the other”

items.diff: を通して follows a noun and means via some medium, or throughout a whole period; 〜通す follows a verb's masu-stem and means carrying an action through to the end.

this.tr: I met my wife through a friend's introduction.

that.tr: I ran all the way to the end on my own.

items.explain: 通す originally means “pass from one end to the other”. Noun＋を通して: passing through a person or thing in between (a friend, the internet) → via, or through a span of time (一年を通して); verb masu-stem＋通す: one action carried from start to finish → see it through to the end. を通じて works the same way.

groups.note: を通して has several jobs, each with a close equivalent: “through (a medium)” ≈ によって, “throughout a period” ≈ にわたって

items.title: 〜によって (means)
items.diff: を通して means getting a result “step by step” via someone or something in between; によって is a means that works directly, more written.

this.tr: I got introduced to my current company through a senior colleague.

that.tr: The data is processed automatically by machine.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: a “medium you pass through”, like 先輩、ボランティア活動、テレビ → を通して; a means or method that acts directly, like 機械、法律、話し合い → によって, common in explanatory writing and often followed by the passive. を通じて works the same way.

items.diff: を通して (period) stresses that a state “stays the same” for the whole time; にわたって stresses how long or wide-ranging it is.

this.tr: This island is warm all year round.

that.tr: The conference went on for a full three days.

items.explain: Look at what follows: an unchanging state like 暖かい、人気がある → を通して (一年を通して is a set phrase); an activity like 行われる、続く、調査する, with a specific length or range before it (三日間、全国) → にわたって, stressing “that long, that wide”.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — here meaning “way, method”

items.diff: ようがない means “there's no way to do it”; てもしょうがない means “there's no point doing it” — しょうがない is really 「し＋ようがない」.

this.tr: I don't know their contact details, so there's no way to get in touch.

that.tr: There's no point regretting it now.

items.explain: しょうがない is a sound change of 「しようがない（仕様がない）」, literally “there's no way to do it”, and the 「仕方」 in 仕方がない also means “method”. Look at what comes before: masu-stem＋ようがない → no means, can't be done at all; te-form＋も＋しょうがない (仕方がない) → it can be done, but doing it is pointless.

items.diff: ようがない means “there's no way to…”; ようによっては means “depending on how you…” — a different way gives a different result.

this.tr: The parts aren't available anymore, so there's no way to fix it.

that.tr: Looked at another way, even a failure is a good experience.

items.explain: Both よう follow a masu-stem and both mean “way, method”: 直し＋よう＝a way to fix it, there isn't one → can't fix it; 考え＋よう＝a way of thinking, change it → the result changes. Check whether it's followed by 「がない」 or 「によっては」.

groups.note: Both mean “can't do it”

items.diff: ようがない simply says “there's no way”; ようにも〜ない stresses the feeling of “I want to, but I can't”.

this.tr: I don't know their address or phone number, so there's no way to contact them.

that.tr: I'd like to contact them, but I don't know their address or phone number.

items.explain: Both contain 「しよう」, but from different sources: the しよう in ようにも is the volitional form (wanting to contact), so the sentence first says you want to, then names the obstacle; the よう in ようがない means “method”, follows the masu-stem, and the sentence ends by simply saying “no way”. The meanings are close; ようにも stresses the frustration more.

items.diff: ようがない means you'd like to but there's no way; わけにはいかない means you could but shouldn't.

this.tr: There's no last train and no taxis, so there's no way to get home.

that.tr: I still have work left, so I can't go home.

items.explain: Look at the reason: no train, no way to contact anyone → no means, so you can't go home even if you want to → ようがない (attaches to the masu-stem: 帰り); unfinished work, a responsibility → you could go home, you just shouldn't → わけにはいかない (attaches to the dictionary form: 帰る).

groups.note: Both express the speaker's judgment that “it seems…”

items.diff: ようだ judges from signs you see or hear; ような気がする is based only on a feeling, with no reason you can name.

this.tr: I have a feeling it's going to rain tomorrow.

that.tr: The road is wet. It seems it rained.

items.explain: Check for a clue before it: a sign like 「道が濡れている」 → ようだ; 「なんとなく」「何だか」, a hunch you can't explain → ような気がする. ような is just the noun-modifying form of ようだ, and adding 「気がする（feel）」 makes it more subjective. In speech ようだ becomes みたいだ, used the same way.

items.diff: と思う states your opinion clearly; ような気がする presents it as a “feeling”, more softly.

this.tr: Sir, I have a feeling this plan is a bit unrealistic.

that.tr: I think this plan is a bit unrealistic.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to and what you're saying: when objecting to a superior or pointing out someone else's problem, ような気がします softens it and avoids sounding absolute; when you want to state your view clearly → と思います.

items.diff: ように見える is how something “looks” from the outside; ような気がする is how you “feel” inside.

this.tr: Lately I feel like I've put on a bit of weight.

that.tr: In the photo, he looks like he's put on a bit of weight.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment is based on: what your eyes see (写真では、顔色が) → ように見える, usually about others; no concrete basis, just your own inner feeling → ような気がする.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」＋a condition — “if it looks like…”

items.diff: ようなら is followed by what to do about it; ようでは is followed by a negative judgment (“that won't do”).

this.tr: If you're late every day, you'd better go to bed earlier.

that.tr: If you're late every day, you're not fit to be a working adult.

items.explain: The first half can be exactly the same, so look at the second half: a solution or advice (〜たほうがいい、〜てください) → ようなら; criticism or a pessimistic verdict (失格だ、合格できない) → ようでは.

groups.note: Both express a condition: “if…”

items.diff: たら works for any condition; ようなら is only for uncertain situations that “might turn out that way, depending on how things go”.

this.tr: If it looks like the train's going to be late, give me a call.

that.tr: Give me a call when you get to the station.

items.explain: Check whether the first part will definitely happen: getting to the station certainly will → たら; being late, a fever not going down, rain getting heavier — things you only know as they unfold → ようなら, with the guess “if it looks like…”, usually followed by what to do.

items.diff: 場合は is an objective condition in rules or notices; ようなら looks at how things actually go and talks over what to do with the person in front of you.

this.tr: If the rain gets heavier, let's cancel today's practice.

that.tr: In case of rain, the match will be canceled.

items.explain: Look at the setting: a condition written in advance in a notice or rule (雨天の場合は) → 場合は; talking it over with someone while watching the weather (〜ようなら〜にしよう) → ようなら.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — “a certain look or state”

items.diff: ように見える only says how something “looks on the outside”, which may not be true; ようだ is a judgment based on the evidence taken together.

this.tr: He looks angry, but he actually isn't.

that.tr: The lights are off. It seems nobody's home.

items.explain: ように見える only describes how something “looks”, and is often followed by 「が、本当は……」, which overturns it; ようだ is the speaker's judgment after putting the clues together, and they basically believe it. In speech ようだ becomes みたいだ (留守みたいだ), used the same way.

groups.note: All mean “looks…”

items.diff: All mean “looks”; the difference is what they attach to: a clause takes ように見える; an i-adjective takes く見える; a noun or na-adjective takes に見える.

this.tr: He looks tired.

that.tr: He looks younger than his age.
He looks like a student.

wrong.why: After a verb clause, use ように見える

items.explain: First look at what comes before 「見える」: 疲れている is a verb clause → ように見える; 若い is an i-adjective → drop い and add く見える; 学生、元気 are a noun and a na-adjective → に見える. With a noun you can also say 「学生のように見える」, which has a stronger “looks just like…” flavor.

items.diff: ように見える describes the impression given by appearance; とみえる “infers” from signs, more written.

this.tr: Judging just by his face, he looks tired.

that.tr: He's been yawning again and again since this morning. He must be really tired.

items.explain: Look at the basis: 「顔だけ見ると」 is just an outward impression that may be wrong → ように見える; a behavioral sign like “yawning all the time” used to infer someone's inner state → とみえる, mostly in writing or narration, often with 「よほど」.

items.diff: そうだ is a direct impression at a glance; ように見える often implies “it looks that way, but may not be”, and can attach to a whole clause.

this.tr: He looks like he has no worries, but he's actually been through a lot.

that.tr: The children are playing happily.

items.explain: そう attaches to the stem (楽し＋そう、おいし＋そう) and is a direct reaction to how things look right now; ように見える attaches to the plain form, can take a full clause with 「ない」「ている」「た」, and often pairs with 「が、実は……」 to mean “on the surface…”.

groups.note: 「しようとしない」↔「しようにも〜ない」: both are volitional form＋negative

items.diff: ようとしない means “won't do it”; ようにも〜ない means “wants to but can't” — completely different meanings.

this.tr: He has time, but he won't get in touch.

that.tr: I'd like to get in touch, but I don't know the phone number.

items.explain: Both are 「しよう＋…＋ない」, and at first glance both look like “not…”. Look at what follows しよう: とし＋ない negates the “will” → won't; にも is followed by an obstacle (電話番号が分からない) → you want to, there's just no way.

groups.note: Both mean “having no will to do it”

items.title: 〜たがらない
items.diff: たがらない means “doesn't want to” (a feeling); ようとしない means “won't do it” (doesn't act even when urged).

this.tr: Even though the doctor told him to, my father won't give up drinking.

that.tr: The child is scared of shots and doesn't want to go to the hospital.

items.explain: Check for the background “won't listen even when told”: the doctor said so, everyone urged them, and they still don't act, and the speaker is frustrated → ようとしない; just describing someone's feelings or likes and dislikes (怖がって) → たがらない. Both are used for third persons.

items.title: 〜つもりはない
items.diff: つもりはない is the speaker declaring “I don't intend to”; ようとしない describes someone else who “won't”, with frustration.

this.tr: He won't admit his mistake.

that.tr: I have no intention of quitting.

items.explain: Look at the subject: 「私」 declaring their own intention → つもりはない; describing someone else's attitude while the speaker looks on in frustration → ようとしない. ようとしない isn't normally used for your own current intentions.

groups.note: Both come from volitional form＋「と」 — having it in mind “to do”

items.diff: ようと思う is a plan in your head, with no action yet; ようとする means you've started acting or are just about to.

this.tr: Just as I was about to leave the house, the phone rang.

that.tr: I'm thinking of leaving home early tomorrow.

items.explain: Both are 「volitional form＋と」. と思う → still just a thought in your head; とする → put into action, you're already doing it or about to, so it often appears as 「〜とした時」「〜としたが」 followed by something else happening.

groups.note: Both mean “about to”

items.title: 〜ところだ (about to)
items.diff: ところだ just objectively says “I'm at the point of doing it”; ようとした is often followed by an interruption, and is also often used to describe what others do.

this.tr: Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.

that.tr: I'm just about to head out.

items.explain: ところだ tells the listener “what stage I'm at now”, and the sentence ends there; ようとした is often followed by 「時／ところ」 and then an unexpected interruption, and is also often used to narrate a third person “was about to…”.

items.diff: ようとする means you're “about to” do something on purpose; そうになる means you “almost” did something involuntarily.

this.tr: Just as I was about to get off the train, the doors closed.

that.tr: The train stopped suddenly and I almost fell over.

items.explain: Check whether it's something you wanted to do: getting off the train is something you intend → ようとする; falling over, bursting into tears, dozing off — unwanted, involuntary things → そうになる (usually in the past, 「なった」, meaning “almost”).

groups.note: 「ずには」 can be followed by いられない／おかない／すまない — only the final verb differs

items.diff: ずにはいられない means you yourself “can't help it”; ずにはおかない means something “is bound to make people…”, or a resolve of “I will definitely…”.

this.tr: Watching that movie, I couldn't help crying.

that.tr: That movie is bound to move anyone who sees it.

items.explain: Look at the subject: “I”, driven by emotion → ずにはいられない; the subject is a work or event, often with a causative before it (感動させ、考えさせ) → ずにはおかない, meaning “will certainly cause”. The spoken form ないではおかない works the same way.

items.diff: ずにはいられない means you emotionally “can't help it”; ずにはすまない means “it wouldn't be right not to” by social obligation.

this.tr: It was so outrageous that I couldn't help saying something.

that.tr: I broke someone else's things, so I can't get away without apologizing.

items.explain: Look at the reason before it: strong emotions (ひどい、おかしい、心配) you can't control → いられない; you did something wrong and common sense demands you act → すまない (the matter can't be settled otherwise), close to 「なければならない」. The spoken form ないではすまない works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “can't help it, can't hold back”

items.diff: Same meaning; only the negative form differs: ずには is more written, ないでは a bit more spoken.

this.tr: I was so worried that I couldn't help calling.

that.tag: ない · a bit more spoken
that.tr: I was so worried that I couldn't help calling.

wrong.why: The ず form of する is 「せず」: 確認せずには

items.explain: 「ず」 is the classical negative and means the same as 「ない」: かけない → かけず, 行かない → 行かず. The easiest one to get wrong is する: it becomes 「せず」 (確認せずにはいられない); you can't say ✗しず.

items.diff: ずにはいられない describes an “action” you can't help doing; てたまらない describes a strong “state” of feeling or sensation.

this.tr: I'm so anxious about the results that I can't help checking again and again.

that.tr: I'm dying to know the results.

items.explain: Check whether there's a concrete action before ずには: an action like 確認する、笑う、言う → ずにはいられない; just the feeling itself, like being anxious, wanting, or happy → てたまらない.

items.title: 〜てしまう (regret · by accident)
items.diff: ずにはいられない focuses on an impulse too strong to hold back; つい〜てしまう focuses on the result of “doing it without meaning to” and regret.

this.tr: It was so funny that I couldn't help bursting out laughing.

that.tr: In the quiet classroom, I accidentally laughed out loud.

items.explain: Look at the reason before it and the tone after: 「あまりに〜て」 shows an impulse so strong you couldn't stop it → ずにはいられない; 「つい」「うっかり」, feeling it was inappropriate and regretting it afterwards → てしまう.

groups.note: Both mean “hard to…”

items.diff: づらい is subjective and stresses the doer's physical or emotional discomfort; にくい is objective and neutral, and can also describe a thing's nature.

this.tr: My feet hurt, so walking is hard.

that.tr: This material doesn't burn easily.

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person who finds doing something painful or awkward (足が痛くて) → づらい fits better; the nature of a thing, or something that doesn't easily happen (燃える、壊れる、割れる) → usually にくい.

items.diff: づらい is spoken, meaning it's uncomfortable or awkward to do; がたい is written, meaning “hard to accept or do” on moral or emotional grounds.

this.tr: It's a bit awkward to bring it up with my teacher.

that.tr: It's hard to believe that he's the culprit.

items.explain: がたい usually follows mental verbs like 「信じる、許す、理解する、忘れる」, meaning it's nearly impossible on emotional or moral grounds, and is used in writing or formal settings; づらい is everyday speech — you can do it, it's just uncomfortable (言いづらい、聞きづらい).

items.diff: 言いづらい means you personally find it hard to say; 〜かねる means your position doesn't allow it, mostly used to politely refuse customers.

this.tr: It's hard to ask a friend to pay me back.

that.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to answer that question.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the speaker's position: a clerk or company telling a customer “we can't…” → 〜かねます, a polite refusal; finding it hard or awkward to say yourself → づらい. Saying 「お答えしづらいです」 to a customer would sound like mere personal feelings.

groups.note: Both mean “after a long process, ending up with a certain result”

items.diff: あげく usually leads to a bad result, with regret or frustration; 末に works for good or bad results, often “after effort or much thought, finally…”.

this.tr: After failing many times, I finally gave up.

that.tr: After failing many times, I finally succeeded.

items.explain: Look at the ending in the second half: a disappointing result like giving up, falling out, or getting sick → あげく, with the regret of “after all that trouble…”; a good result like 「ついに成功した」 sounds odd with あげく, so use 末に. 末に is also more written: 「努力の末」「話し合いの末」.

items.diff: あげく stresses “after all that trouble, in the end…”; 結果 just objectively says “did A, got B”, good or bad.

this.tag: After much effort · came to nothing
this.tr: I looked into it every which way, but in the end I still couldn't find the cause.

that.tr: After investigating in various ways, we found the cause.

items.explain: Look at the second half and the tone: あげく is usually followed by something that fell through or went badly (結局分からなかった), with the speaker's feelings; 結果 calmly states cause and effect, works for “found out” or “decided”, is most common in reports and news, and also appears as 「検査の結果」「その結果」.

items.diff: あげく sits mid-sentence and links the “process” to the “result”; 始末だ sits at the end and says reproachfully “and it came to this in the end”.

this.tr: After being late again and again, he got fired.

that.tr: He kept coming in late, and now he's even skipping work without a word — it's outrageous.

items.explain: Look at the position: あげく still needs a result clause after it; 始末だ closes the sentence itself, often with 「ついには」「とうとう」 before it, putting the worst thing last, with reproach or exasperation of “it's outrageous”.

groups.note: Both come from 「あまり（余り）」 — originally “excess, surplus”

items.title: 〜あまりに・〜のあまり
items.diff: あまりの is followed by a noun (あまりの驚きに); あまりに is an adverb modifying a verb or adjective (あまりに驚いて); 〜のあまり puts 「あまり」 after a noun (驚きのあまり).

this.tr: I was so shocked I couldn't even make a sound.

that.tag: あまりに · with a verb
that.tr: I was so shocked that I couldn't make a sound.
In my shock, I couldn't even make a sound.

wrong.why: あまりの must be followed by a noun (寒さ)

items.explain: All three mean the same; look at where 「あまり」 sits and what follows it: あまりの＋noun (驚き、暑さ)＋に; あまりに＋verb or adjective (驚いて、暑くて); noun＋の＋あまり (驚きのあまり). An adjective must first become a noun (暑い → 暑さ) before it can follow あまりの. (「あまりの〜で」 works the same way.)

items.diff: あまりの〜に means “so… that”; あまり＋negative means “not very…” — a low degree instead.

this.tr: It was so cold my hands were shaking.

that.tr: It's not very cold today.

items.explain: Look at what follows: あまりの takes a noun (寒さ) plus 「に」, and the second half is the reaction it caused (手が震えた); あまり followed by the negative form of an adjective or verb (寒くない) means “not very…”. 「余り」 originally means “exceeding”: exceeding the limit＝too much; in the negative, “doesn't exceed by much”＝not very. (「あまりの〜で」 works the same way.)

groups.note: Both mean “because it's too…, …”

items.diff: あまりの〜に leans written and exclamatory, usually followed by an involuntary reaction; すぎて is the most common everyday “too…, so…”.

this.tr: The heat was so intense I felt dizzy.

that.tr: It was too hot, and I felt dizzy.
