items.explain: Look at the register: in conversation, 「暑すぎて」 is most natural; 「あまりの暑さに」 is mostly used in narration and writing, with the exclamation of “unbearably hot”, followed by involuntary reactions like めまいがした、声も出なかった. すぎる is more versatile and can even end a sentence (暑すぎる！). (「あまりの〜で」 works the same way.)

groups.note: Both come from 「ばかり」 — originally “only this much”

items.diff: Noun＋ばかり means “nothing but, only”; ばかりか means “not only…, but also…”.

this.tr: This child eats not only meat but fish and vegetables too, and happily.

that.tr: This child eats nothing but meat.

items.explain: The same 「ばかり（only）」: followed directly by a verb → only this one thing (肉ばかり食べる); add the rhetorical 「か」 → “is it only this?”＝not only this, and the second half always brings in more with 「も」「まで」. Check whether 「か」 follows ばかり.

groups.note: ばかりか ↔ ばかりに: only the last kana differs

items.diff: ばかりか means “not only…, but also…”; ばかりに means “just because… (it ended badly)”.

this.tr: Not only did he forget our plans, he didn't even apologize.

that.tr: Just because he forgot our date, his girlfriend dumped him.

items.explain: Both follow 「忘れた」; only the final 「か」 vs. 「に」 differ. ばかりか is followed by another thing in the same direction, often with 「も」 (謝りもしなかった); ばかりに is followed by the bad result it brought on, often with the regret of 「〜てしまった」.

groups.note: Both mean “not only…, but also…”

items.diff: ばかりか often carries the surprise of “and even…”, and can only be followed by a statement of fact; ばかりでなく can also be followed by an order or advice.

this.tr: Not only did he not apologize, he even came to complain.

that.tr: Don't just eat vegetables — eat meat too.

wrong.why: ばかりか can't be followed by an order or advice

items.explain: Look at the second half: orders or advice like 「〜なさい」「〜てください」「〜ましょう」 → only ばかりでなく; stating a surprising fact that goes even further, often paired with 「まで」「さえ」 → ばかりか is more forceful.

items.diff: だけでなく is the most common and simply adds two things together; ばかりか is more written, and the second part usually goes a step further — “even…”.

this.tr: Not only did he forget his homework, he even lost his textbook.

that.tr: He can speak not only English but Chinese as well.

items.explain: Look at the second part and the tone: だけでなく just puts two things side by side and is the most common in daily life (in speech, 「だけじゃなくて」); ばかりか often has 「まで」「さえ」 in the second part, going a step further and more unexpected than the first, and leans written.

items.diff: のみならず is formal written language that calmly widens the scope; ばかりか carries the speaker's surprise or frustration.

this.tr: Not only was he late, he didn't even bother to let us know.

that.tr: This problem is an issue not only for Japan but for the whole world.

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: のみならず appears mostly in news, papers, and speeches, often with the 「である」 style, objectively saying “the scope goes beyond this”; ばかりか carries personal feeling, and the second part often uses 「さえ」「まで」 to mean “even…”.

items.title: 〜どころか (far from · not even)
items.diff: ばかりか calmly adds another layer; どころか means “forget A — not even B…”, and is often used to overturn the other person's expectation.

this.tr: He can't write kanji, and he can't even write hiragana.

that.tr: “Can he write kanji?” “Kanji? He can't even write hiragana.”

items.explain: Check for an expectation to overturn: the other person assumes “he can at least write kanji”, and the answer flatly rejects it with どころか — forget A, not even the more basic B…, very common in speech; just objectively stacking two things up → ばかりか, more written. Also, どころか can introduce the opposite result (熱が下がるどころか上がった), which ばかりか can't.

groups.note: Both come from 「〜ばいい」 — “it would be good if…”

items.diff: ばいい says 「いい」 out loud and suggests “you just need to…”; ばと思う drops 「いい」, turning it into a polite request or wish.

this.tr: I'd appreciate it if you could check it once.

that.tr: You just need to check with the teacher once.

items.explain: 「ばと思います」 can be seen as 「ばいい（ありがたい）と思います」 with the second half dropped: it's no longer a suggestion “just do this”, but an indirect request “it would be great if you could…”. Look at what comes before: ばいい usually follows an ordinary verb (すれば、聞けば), like giving advice; ばと思う often follows 「いただければ」「お役に立てれば」, used with superiors and clients.

groups.note: Both make a polite request or express a wish

items.diff: ばと思います doesn't even say “I'd be grateful”, so it's more indirect; ていただけるとありがたい spells out the gratitude, so it's clearer.

this.tr: I was hoping you might send me the materials.

that.tr: I'd be grateful if you could send me the materials.

items.explain: Both are very polite requests, at about the same level. Look at the end of the sentence: 「ありがたいです」「助かります」 state your own feeling and are common in speech too; 「ばと思います」 only says “I hope…”, leaving out the result entirely, and is common in business emails.

items.diff: ていただけませんか asks the other person directly “could you?” and waits for an answer; ばと思います just states a hope without pressing them to respond.

this.tr: I'd appreciate a reply by tomorrow.

that.tr: Could you reply by tomorrow?

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: 「〜ませんか」 is a question, a direct request in person or on the phone that needs an answer; 「〜ばと思います」 is a statement that only expresses your hope, softer in tone, suited to emails, and gives the other person room.

items.title: 〜といい・〜たらいい (wish)
items.diff: ばと思う is usually a modest statement of your own wish, or a request to the other person; といい is hoping for something you can't control — “I hope…”.

this.tr: I hope I can be of at least some help.

that.tr: I hope it clears up tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at what the wish is about: things nobody can control, like weather or luck → といいね／たらいいな, common in speech; wanting to do your part (お役に立てれば、力になれれば), or politely asking someone to do something → ばと思います, formal and modest, mostly in formal settings.

groups.note: Both come from 「ばかり」 — originally “only this much”

items.diff: Noun＋ばかり means “nothing but this”; dictionary form＋ばかりだ means “changing in only one direction”.

this.tr: Prices just keep going up.

that.tr: This shop has nothing but expensive things.

items.explain: The same 「ばかり（only）」: after a noun (物) → only this one kind; after the dictionary form of a verb of change (上がる、増える、悪くなる) → change in only this one direction, with no sign of improvement.

items.diff: Dictionary form＋ばかりだ usually says a situation is getting “more and more…”; てばかりいる says a person is “always doing…”, with blame.

this.tr: My mother's illness keeps getting worse.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play video games every day.

items.explain: Look at the subject and verb: a situation like an illness or a number＋a verb of change (悪くなる、増える) → ばかりだ, saying it only goes in a bad direction; a person＋the te-form of an action (して、遊んで)＋いる → てばかりいる, criticizing them for always doing the same thing. ばかりだ can also take an action verb (泣くばかりだ), where it means “can do nothing but that”, not blame.

groups.note: All are 「〜ばかり」; only 「る／た」 before or 「だ／に」 after differs

items.diff: Dictionary form＋ばかりだ means “more and more…”; ta-form＋ばかりだ means “just…”.

this.tr: Lately the shop has fewer and fewer customers.

that.tr: This shop only just opened last week.

items.explain: Only the kana before ばかり differs: る (dictionary form) → change keeps going in one direction; た (ta-form) → the action was completed only a short while ago. With a word of ongoing time like 「最近」「年々」 → more and more; with a point in time like 「先週」「さっき」 → just.

items.diff: ばかりだ at the end of a sentence means “more and more…”; ばかりに mid-sentence means “just because… (it ended badly)”.

this.tr: At this rate, the debt will just keep growing.

that.tr: Just because I became a guarantor for a friend, I ended up saddled with debt.

items.explain: Look at what follows ばかり: 「だ。」 ends the sentence → more and more…; 「に、」 has another half after it explaining the bad result → just because…. The form before it also differs: ばかりだ takes the dictionary form (増える), ばかりに usually takes the ta-form (なった、言った).

groups.note: Both mean “change continuing in one direction”

items.diff: ばかりだ is used almost only for bad changes, with worry or resignation; 一方だ is more objective and is also common for neutral changes.

this.tr: The number of unemployed just keeps growing.

that.tr: More and more people are learning Japanese.

items.explain: Both take the dictionary form of a verb of change; check whether the change is good or bad: bad things like unemployment, debt, or illness → both work, with ばかりだ sounding more worried; a neutral increase like learners or tourists → usually 一方だ; ばかりだ would make the speaker sound unhappy about it.

items.diff: ばかりだ stresses that a bad trend can't be stopped; つつある just objectively says a change is underway step by step, good or bad.

this.tr: The economy just keeps getting worse.

that.tr: The economy is gradually recovering.

items.explain: Look at the direction of change and the tone: つつある is written language, often with 「少しずつ」「徐々に」, saying a change is underway and not yet complete, and is common for good things like recovery or improvement; ばかりだ carries the speaker's worry, meaning a bad trend keeps going with no sign of improvement.

groups.note: Both come from 「ばかり」 — originally “only this much”

items.diff: Noun＋ばかり means “nothing but, only”; ばかりに applies “only” to a cause: “just because…”.

this.tr: Just because I said one word too many, I made her angry.

that.tr: He's always doing nothing but complaining.

items.explain: The same 「ばかり（only this much）」: after a noun → only this one thing in content (文句ばかり); after a ta-form etc. plus 「に」 → the cause was only this small, yet it brought big trouble (一言多かったばかりに). Check whether 「に、」 follows, leading to a bad result.

groups.note: All have 「ばかり」; only a kana or two before or after differs

items.diff: たばかりに means “just because… (it ended badly)”; たばかりだ means “just did…”.

this.tr: Just because I said something unnecessary, I made her angry.

that.tr: I've just come to Japan.

items.explain: Both are 「た＋ばかり」; only the final 「に」 vs. 「だ」 differ. たばかりに is always followed by another half with a bad result (〜てしまった), meaning “just because of that little thing…”, often with regret; たばかりだ ends the sentence and only says very little time has passed.

items.diff: たばかりに means “just because…”; んばかりに means “as if about to…”, describing how someone looks.

this.tr: Just because I told one lie, I lost their trust.

that.tr: Her eyes were brimming with tears, as if she might burst out crying any second.

items.explain: Look at what's before ばかり: the ta-form (ついた、言った) → a cause, followed by a bad result; the nai-stem＋「ん」 (泣き出さん、言わん) → 「ん」 is the classical 「む（will）」, meaning “as if about to…”, just describing how someone looks — it didn't actually happen. 「言わんばかりに（as if to say）」 is common in novels. 「んばかりの＋noun」 and 「んばかりだ」 work the same way, all meaning “as if about to…”.

items.diff: ばかりに mid-sentence means “just because…”; ばかりだ at the end of a sentence means “more and more…”.

this.tr: Just because I became a guarantor for a friend, I ended up saddled with debt.

that.tr: At this rate, the debt will just keep growing.

items.explain: Look around ばかり: 「に、」 with another half giving a bad result, usually with the ta-form before it (なった) → just because…; 「だ。」 ending the sentence, with the dictionary form of a verb of change before it (増える、悪くなる) → more and more….

groups.note: Both express “the cause of a bad result”

items.diff: せいで blames a bad result on some cause; ばかりに stresses “just because of this one thing”, usually with regret.

this.tr: Just because I took the wrong road, everyone was late.

that.tr: Everyone was late, all because the train was delayed.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: せいで pushes the responsibility onto the cause (電車のせい、あいつのせい), with blame; ばかりに means “just because of such a small thing”, often used to reflect on yourself (私が〜たばかりに), with the regret of “if only I hadn't…”. せいで can attach directly to a noun (雨のせいで); ばかりに usually isn't used that way.

items.title: 〜あまり (out of too much…)
items.diff: With ばかりに, the cause is just one small thing; with （の）あまり, an emotion or degree goes too far.

this.tr: Just because I let my guard down for a moment, I lost the match.

that.tr: I was so nervous that I couldn't show my real ability in the match.

items.explain: Look at what the cause is: one small slip or word (ちょっと油断した、一言多かった) → ばかりに, stressing “just because of that little thing”; an emotion like nerves, worry, or joy that goes “too far” (緊張のあまり、心配するあまり) → あまり.

groups.note: All come from 「だけ（丈）」 — “a corresponding amount or degree”

items.diff: だけあって sits mid-sentence: identity first, then the result; だけのことはある sits at the end: result first, then the verdict.

this.tr: As you'd expect from a professional, the food is delicious.

that.tr: This food is delicious. Just what you'd expect from a pro.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the position and order: 「identity＋だけあって、result」 says it all in one sentence; with the other, you first state the result you see (おいしいね), then add 「〜だけのことはある」 as your verdict. Both often go with 「さすが」.

items.diff: だけあって is only for positive “as expected of…” praise; だけに works for good or bad, and can also say “precisely because expectations were high, it was all the more disappointing”.

this.tr: As you'd expect from a famous restaurant, the food was superb.

that.tr: Precisely because it was a famous restaurant, I had high hopes — but the food was just ordinary.

wrong.why: だけあって can only be followed by a positive verdict that befits the identity

items.explain: Look at the second half: if the result “befits” the identity and you're praising → だけあって (だけに also works); if the result lets your expectations down and shows disappointment → only だけに. What follows だけあって is always a positive verdict.

groups.note: Both mean “the result matches the effort”

items.title: 〜かいがある (not in vain)
items.diff: だけあって is an evaluation: “the result truly matches the effort”; かいがある is the person's own feeling: “the effort wasn't wasted”.

this.tr: As you'd expect from someone who practiced every day, his piano playing is superb.

that.tr: Practicing every day paid off — I won the competition.

items.explain: Look at what the second half says: after だけあって comes an evaluation of the result (見事だ、上手だ), often praise from others; after かいがあって comes a goal finally reached (優勝できた、合格した), the person's own satisfaction that “the hard work wasn't for nothing”.

groups.note: All come from 「だけ（丈）」 — “a corresponding amount or degree”

items.diff: だけに works for good or bad, and can also say “precisely because expectations were high, it was all the more disappointing”; だけあって is only for positive “as expected of…” praise.

this.tr: Precisely because it was a famous restaurant, I had high hopes — but the food was just ordinary.

that.tr: As you'd expect from a famous restaurant, the food was superb.

wrong.why: だけあって can only be followed by a positive verdict that befits the identity

items.explain: Look at the second half: if the result lets your expectations down and shows disappointment → only だけに; if the result befits the identity and you're praising → だけあって (だけに also works). だけに often carries a sense of 「なおさら」 (all the more).

groups.note: Both mean “precisely because…”

items.diff: With だけに, the outcome can be good or bad; ばかりに is only for bad outcomes and carries regret.

this.tr: Precisely because I'd had high hopes, failing the exam hit me all the harder.

that.tr: Just because I overslept on the day of the exam, I ended up failing it.

items.explain: Look at how cause and effect relate: before ばかりに comes a small slip, and after it the bad result it directly brought on, with regret like “if only I hadn't…”; before だけに comes a situation or degree (期待していた、初めての優勝), and after it a feeling that is “correspondingly stronger” — good or bad.

groups.note: All come from 「だけ（丈）」 — “a corresponding amount or degree”

items.diff: だけのことはある sits at the end: result first, then the verdict; だけあって sits mid-sentence: identity first, then the result.

this.tr: This food is delicious. Just what you'd expect from a pro.

that.tr: As you'd expect from a professional, the food is delicious.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the position and order: first state the result you see (おいしいね), then add 「〜だけのことはある」 as your verdict; 「identity＋だけあって、result」 says it all in one sentence. Both often go with 「さすが」.

items.diff: だけのことはある is only for praise and approval; だけに sits mid-sentence and says “precisely because…, all the more…”, and can express regret or disappointment too.

this.tr: The view is stunning. All that hard climbing was worth it.

that.tr: Precisely because we'd struggled so hard to climb up, it was all the more disappointing that the fog hid everything.

items.explain: Look at the position and the verdict: だけのことはある goes at the end and says “it was worth it / it lives up to its name” about a good result you've already seen; だけに goes mid-sentence and is followed by an “all the more…” feeling, which can also be regret or disappointment (残念だった).

groups.note: Both mean “the effort or reputation matches the result”

items.title: 〜かいがある (not in vain)
items.diff: だけのことはある can also judge an identity or reputation as “living up to its name”; かいがある only says your own effort “wasn't wasted”.

this.tr: This is really good. No wonder it's such a popular place.

that.tr: Studying late every night paid off — I finally passed.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: before かいがある there can only be effort (勉強した、待った、努力の), saying “it wasn't wasted”; だけのことはある can also follow an identity, reputation or price (人気店、プロ、高い), judging that it “truly lives up to its name / is worth the money”.

groups.note: Both mean “full of, covered in”

items.diff: だらけ means “all over the place, lots of them”; まみれ means a liquid or powder “coating the surface”.

this.tr: His arms are covered in scars.

that.tr: He was working, drenched in sweat.

items.explain: Look at what the thing is: liquids and powders like sweat, blood, oil or mud stuck to the body → まみれ (「泥」 works with both); countable things scattered everywhere, like wounds, holes or mistakes → usually だらけ (傷だらけ、穴だらけ、間違いだらけ).

items.diff: だらけ is mostly about unwanted things and sounds disapproving; ずくめ means “nothing but”, often used for good things or being dressed all in one color.

this.tr: This year was one failure after another.

that.tr: This year was one good thing after another.

items.explain: Look at whether it's good or bad: unwanted things like failures, mistakes or debts → だらけ; good or happy things (いいことずくめ), or one color from head to toe (黒ずくめ) → ずくめ. ずくめ has no sense of “messy”.

items.diff: ばかり means “only this one kind, nothing else”; だらけ means “so many they're everywhere”, with a sense of mess and dislike.

this.tr: This essay is full of mistakes.

that.tr: This class is all girls.

items.explain: Look at whether it's about “many” or “only”: だらけ says something is so plentiful it's everywhere (mistakes throughout the essay), almost always bad things; ばかり says that within a range there's only this one kind and nothing else, and works with neutral things like 女の子 — 「女の子だらけ」 would sound exaggerated and chaotic.

groups.note: Both come from 「しか〜ない」 — “nothing except…”

items.diff: しか〜ない limits a quantity or range: “only…”; でしかない limits an identity or nature: “nothing more than…”.

this.tr: He's still nothing more than a child.

that.tr: I only have 1,000 yen in my wallet.

items.explain: でしかない simply puts the copula 「で（＝is）」 inside 「しか〜ない」: “he is nothing except a child” ＝ he's merely a child. Look at what's before 「しか」: a quantity or thing (千円、水) → “only”; 「noun＋で」 → a judgment of identity or worth, with a “nothing special” tone.

items.diff: Noun＋でしかない means “nothing more than…”; verb＋しかない means “have no choice but to…”.

this.tr: That's nothing more than a dream.

that.tr: I have no money, so I have no choice but to give up my dream.

items.explain: Look at what's before 「しかない」: a verb in dictionary form (諦める、待つ) → there's no other way but to do this ＝ have no choice but to; noun＋で (夢で、言い訳で) → it's nothing except this ＝ nothing more than. When reading, don't mistake 「でしかない」 for “have no choice but”.

groups.note: Both mean “nothing more than…”

items.diff: にすぎない sounds more objective and can also follow verbs; でしかない only follows nouns and carries a stronger dismissive or resigned tone.

this.tr: That's nothing more than a rumor.

that.tr: I was just asking, that's all.

wrong.why: Only a noun can come before でしかない

items.explain: The meanings are nearly identical (噂にすぎない＝噂でしかない), so first look at what comes before: a verb or clause (聞いてみた) → only にすぎない; with nouns both work. In tone, でしかない is colder, often with a dismissive or resigned “in the end, when all's said and done”; にすぎない is mostly used to state quantities or facts objectively.

groups.note: Both come from 「まい」 — a classical negative guess, “probably won't…”: ではあるまい plus the question 「か」 ＝ “isn't it probably…?”, plus the reason-giving 「し」 ＝ “it's not as if…”

items.diff: まい on its own means “probably won't… / will never…”; ではあるまいか adds the rhetorical 「か」 and becomes a tentative claim: “isn't it perhaps…?”.

this.tr: Might this not be the cause of the accident?

that.tr: That person probably won't ever come again.

items.explain: 「まい」 is a negative guess: 「来るまい」 ＝ “probably won't come”. 「ではあるまい」 ＝ “it probably isn't…”; add the rhetorical 「か」 — “isn't it…?” — and it becomes a tentative positive claim: “it's probably…”. Check the end of the sentence for 「か」: none → negative; there → actually affirming.

items.diff: ではあるまいか is a guess, “it's probably…”; ではあるまいし means “it's not as if…”, used to criticize the other person.

this.tr: Isn't this plan perhaps a little unrealistic?

that.tr: You're not a child — surely you can do it by yourself.

items.explain: The only difference is the final 「か」 or 「し」. ではあるまいか comes at the end and puts forward your own view; ではあるまいし comes mid-sentence, after an identity that clearly doesn't apply (子ども、学生), followed by advice or criticism (自分でやりなさい、〜でしょう). In speech ではあるまいし often becomes 「じゃあるまいし」.

groups.note: Both put forward a guess or claim tentatively: “it's probably…, isn't it?”

items.diff: Same meaning; のではないだろうか is used in ordinary writing and formal speech; ではあるまいか is more literary and old-fashioned.

this.tr: Might young people's turning away from reading not be due to smartphones?

that.tr: Isn't young people's turning away from reading due to smartphones?

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the setting: ではあるまいか turns up now and then in commentary and essays, sounding old-school and literary; papers, speeches and formal statements usually use のではないだろうか. Watch the connection after a noun: 影響ではあるまいか, but 影響なのではないだろうか (「な」 is needed before の).

items.diff: Nearly identical — both are tentative written guesses; ではなかろうか uses 「なかろう」, ではあるまいか uses 「あるまい」, and the latter is more old-fashioned.

this.tr: This was probably no accident, but a premeditated crime.

that.tr: This was probably no accident, but a premeditated crime.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable. Look at how they're built: ではなかろうか ＝ 「なかろう」, the conjectural form of 「ではない」 ＋か; ではあるまいか ＝ 「である」 ＋ the negative guess 「まい」 ＋か — two routes to the same “it's probably…”. Both are only used in writing; in speech, say 「〜のではないでしょうか」 or 「〜じゃないかな」.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — here meaning “point, extent”

items.diff: どころではない comes at the end: “in no position to…”; どころか comes mid-sentence: “far from…, actually…”.

this.tr: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.

that.tr: Far from taking time off, I'm working overtime every day.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「どころ」: if 「ではない／じゃない。」 ends the sentence → you have no room to do this right now; if 「か、」 is followed by a completely opposite, even more extreme fact → “far from…, actually…”. Literally both say “not at the point of…” — one stops there, the other carries on.

groups.note: どころ ↔ ところ, just one voicing mark apart

items.diff: どころではない means “in no position to…”; ところだ marks the moment of an action: “about to / in the middle of / just did”.

this.tr: The exam is coming up, so playing is out of the question.

that.tr: I'm just about to go out and have some fun.

items.explain: First check for the voicing mark: ど ≠ と. Then look around it: どころ is followed by 「ではない」, often with a busy or urgent reason before it (試験前で); ところ is followed by 「だ」, often with time words like 「今から」「今」「ちょうど」 before it.

groups.note: Both mean “no room for it right now; this isn't the time to…”

items.diff: どころではない focuses on “I have no room for it”; ている場合じゃない is often used to warn or urge: “this is no time to be doing that”.

this.tr: I've got a fever — studying is out of the question.

that.tr: The exam is almost here — this is no time to be playing games.

items.explain: Look at the tone and what it attaches to: どころではない usually follows a noun (勉強、旅行、花見), saying “the situation doesn't allow it, I can't handle it”; ている場合じゃない follows an ongoing action (している、寝ている), often said to others or yourself as “stop that and get to what matters”, very colloquial.

items.diff: どころではない means “no room at all to do…”; てはいられない means “I can't keep… like this any longer”, pushing yourself to act.

this.tr: I'm busy getting ready to move — I'm in no mood for cherry-blossom viewing.

that.tr: Only a week left until the exam. I can't keep taking it easy.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: noun (花見、旅行)＋どころではない says “doing that is out of the question”; the て-form of a state (のんびりして、じっとして)＋はいられない says “I can't stay the way I am”, often followed by action like 「早く〜しよう」.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — here meaning “point, extent”

items.diff: どころか comes mid-sentence: “far from…, actually…”; どころではない comes at the end: “in no position to…”.

this.tr: Far from taking time off, I'm working overtime every day.

that.tr: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「どころ」: if 「か、」 is followed by a completely opposite, even more extreme fact → “far from…, actually…”; if 「ではない。」 ends the sentence → you have no room to do this right now. Literally both say “not at the point of…” — one carries on, the other stops there.

groups.note: どころ ↔ ところ, just one voicing mark apart

items.diff: どころか means “far from…, actually / not even…”; ところだ means “about to / just did”.

this.tr: Far from finishing my homework, I haven't even started it.

that.tr: I've just finished my homework.

items.explain: First check for the voicing mark: ど ≠ と. Then look at the structure: before どころか is an “expectation”, and after it a completely opposite or more extreme fact, so the sentence contrasts two halves; ところだ only says what point in time the action is at, and the sentence ends there.

groups.note: Both mean “not only…, but (even more)”

items.diff: どころか means “never mind A, not even B…”, often used to overturn the other person's assumption; ばかりか just calmly adds another layer.

this.tr: “Can he write kanji?” “Never mind kanji, he can't even write hiragana.”

that.tr: Not only can he not write kanji, he can't write hiragana either.

items.explain: Look for an assumption to overturn: the other person thinks “at least he can write kanji”, and you shoot it down with どころか — never mind A, not even the more basic B…, very common in speech; when you're just objectively stacking two facts, use ばかりか, which is more written. どころか can also introduce an opposite outcome (熱が下がるどころか上がった); ばかりか can't.

items.diff: どころか is common in both speech and writing and can also mean “on the contrary”; はおろか is written language, used only for “let alone A, not even B”.

this.tr: Never mind kanji, he can't even read hiragana.

that.tr: Never mind kanji, he can't even read hiragana.

items.explain: For “let alone A, not even B…” the two are interchangeable; はおろか is more written and stiff, mostly followed by a negative or something surprising. But the “far from…, on the contrary…” use (下がるどころか上がった) only works with どころか — はおろか has no “on the contrary” meaning.

groups.note: Both mean “tend to…, be prone to…”

items.diff: やすい means “easy to do” or “likely to happen”, good or bad; がち means “tend to, often (do something undesirable)”, stressing frequency.

this.tr: When I'm busy, I tend to skip meals.

that.tr: This pen is easy to write with.

wrong.why: がち doesn't mean “easy to do”

items.explain: Ask whether it means “easy to handle”: easy to write, use or understand — this “easy to do” sense only works with やすい; がち says a person “tends to…” in some situation, mostly things they shouldn't do (食事を抜く、遅れる、休む).

items.diff: がち is about “frequency”: often…; 気味 is about “degree”: a bit… right now.

this.tr: She was often sick as a child.

that.tr: I feel like I'm coming down with a bit of a cold today.

items.explain: Look at the time words: something that recurs over a period, like 「子どもの頃」「冬になると」 → がち; a mild current state, with 「今日は」「最近少し」 → 気味 (風邪気味、疲れ気味、太り気味).

items.diff: っぽい describes someone's character: “quick to…”; がち says “tends to…” in a certain situation.

this.tr: When I'm busy, I tend to forget appointments.

that.tr: My grandfather has become forgetful lately.

items.explain: Look for a condition: がち is often preceded by a situation like 「忙しいと」「冬は」, saying it tends to happen then; っぽい describes the person's own nature, like a personality trait (忘れっぽい、怒りっぽい、飽きっぽい), attaches to only a few verbs, and is colloquial.

items.title: 〜傾向がある (have a tendency to…)
items.diff: がち is colloquial and often carries the speaker's negative judgment; 傾向がある is an objective statement, mostly in reports and news.

this.tr: My kid tends to leave his vegetables.

that.tr: Young people these days tend not to eat vegetables.

items.explain: Look at who it's about and the setting: people around you or your own habits, with a hint of complaint or self-mockery → がち; an overall trend in a group (若者、日本人), stated objectively like a survey report → 傾向がある. Watch the connection: がち follows the ます-stem (残しがち); 傾向がある follows the dictionary form or ない-form (食べない傾向がある).

items.diff: がち describes things that happen often; きらいがある is written language, criticizing someone for having a habit of… by nature.

this.tr: He often oversleeps and is late.

that.tr: He has a habit of deciding everything on his own.

items.explain: Look at whether it's about behavior or nature: things that happen often, like being late, getting sick or forgetting → がち; a person's way of thinking or character tendency, like “deciding everything alone” or “always expecting the worst”, with a critical tone → きらいがある, mostly in writing.

groups.note: Both come from 「甲斐（かい）」 — “the payoff for one's effort”

items.title: 〜かいがある (not in vain)
items.diff: 〜がい follows the ます-stem and says doing the thing itself is “meaningful, rewarding”; 〜かいがある follows the た-form and says effort already made “wasn't wasted”.

this.tr: This job is tough, but it's really rewarding.

that.tr: Practicing every day paid off — we won the match.

items.explain: It's the same 「甲斐 (payoff)」: after the ます-stem it's voiced into 「がい」 (やりがい、生きがい、教えがい) and says doing this itself brings satisfaction, mostly about something you're still doing; after the た-form or 「noun＋の」 (練習したかい、努力のかい) it says effort already made has borne fruit.

groups.note: Both come from 「掛け（かけ）」 — “an action just started or in progress”

items.title: 〜かける (about to · half-done)
items.diff: 帰りがけに means “on the way back (and while at it)”; 帰りかける means “about to leave, just starting to go back”.

this.tag: On the way · While at it
this.tr: On my way home I stopped by a convenience store.

that.tr: Just as I was about to leave, the department head called me back.

items.explain: Just one voicing mark apart — the same 「掛け」: 〜かける means an action has just begun or is half done (帰りかける、読みかけの本); voiced as 「がけ」 it's fixed in a few words like 「帰りがけに／行きがけに／出がけに」, meaning on the way there or back or just as you head out, often followed by something done along the way.

groups.note: Both have to do with “on the way, while at it”

items.diff: がけに is limited to going, returning or heading out; ついでに can follow all kinds of things, with the focus on “while you're at it”.

this.tag: Only on the way there or back
this.tr: On my way home from work, I dropped into a bookstore.

that.tr: While I was out shopping, I dropped into a bookstore.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: movement words like 「帰り」「行き」「出」 → がけに, meaning “on the way” in time; any activity like shopping, a walk or a business trip → ついでに (買い物のついでに、駅に行くついでに), the focus being “taking the chance to do something else too”.

items.diff: 途中で just objectively says “on the way”, and can also mean partway through something; がけに usually carries a sense of “doing something along the way”.

this.tr: On my way to school I mailed a letter.

that.tag: On the way · Something that happened
that.tr: On my way to school I got caught in the rain.

items.explain: Look at the second half: something you chose to do along the way (手紙を出した、寄った) → がけに sounds natural; something that happened to you (雨に降られた、事故を見た), or “partway through” (話の途中で) → use 途中で. 途中で also connects more freely: 行く途中、帰る途中、会議の途中.

items.diff: がてら means “do A and do B at the same time”, where A is itself a purpose; がけに only marks the moment on the way there or back.

this.tr: On the way there I stopped by a bakery.

that.tag: The walk is a purpose too
that.tr: I took a walk and stopped by a bakery while I was at it.

items.explain: Look at the word before: がてら follows something you want to do anyway (散歩、買い物、見物), combining two things, rather written; がけに only follows 「行き」「帰り」「出」, marking a point on the way, while the reason for going is something else.

groups.note: Both mean “how something looks from the outside”

items.diff: 〜げ mainly describes the feelings or demeanor people show, with a literary flavor; 〜そう is broad and works for people, things and the weather.

this.tr: The children are playing happily.

that.tr: This cake looks delicious.

items.explain: For people's moods the two are often interchangeable (楽しげ／楽しそう、寂しげ／寂しそう), but げ is more written and common in novels; for things, the weather or what's about to happen (おいしそう、雨が降りそう、壊れそう), only そう works.

items.diff: 〜げ is a feeling read from someone's face or manner; 〜がる is that feeling shown in actions or words.

this.tr: Mother said nothing, just smiled a lonely smile.

that.tr: Mother kept saying 「もう帰るの？」 again and again — she clearly didn't want us to go.

items.explain: Look at how the feeling is noticed: if nothing is said and it just shows in the expression or mood (何も言わず) → げ, subtle and literary; if it's clearly shown through words and actions (何度も言って、帰りたがる) → がる, often used to describe other people's feelings.

groups.note: Both contrast “on the one hand…, on the other hand…”

items.diff: 反面 only covers two opposite sides of the same thing; 一方で can also contrast different people or things, or mean doing two things at once.

this.tr: City life is convenient, but on the other hand rent is expensive.

that.tr: My older brother works in the city, while my younger brother farms in the countryside.

wrong.why: 反面 can only describe two sides of the same thing

items.explain: Look at the subjects of the two clauses: the pros and cons of the same thing (都会) → both 反面 and 一方で work; two different people or things set side by side (兄／弟) → only 一方で. 一方で can also mean “working while raising kids”; 反面 has no such use.

items.title: 〜代わりに (a trade-off)
items.diff: 反面 objectively points out two sides of the same thing; 代わりに carries a sense of “in exchange, at a price”.

this.tr: This job pays well, but on the other hand the responsibility is heavy.

that.tr: This job pays well, but the price is lots of overtime.

items.explain: Both sentences talk about gains and losses — the angle differs: 反面 simply lists “the good side / the bad side”; 代わりに has a trade-off feel, “to get this, you have to pay that”, like stating terms. 代わりに can also mean “instead of” (父の代わりに行く); 反面 can't.

groups.note: Both come from 「ほか（外）」 — “other, besides”

items.diff: ほかない means “there's no other way, so I have to…”; にほかならない means “it is nothing other than…”.

this.tr: The trains have stopped, so I have no choice but to walk home.

that.tr: Passing the exam was nothing other than the result of hard work every day.

items.explain: It's the same 「ほか (other)」: verb in dictionary form＋ほかない → there's no other way; noun＋に＋ほかならない → it's nothing else but this, used to pin down a cause or essence. The only difference is 「に〜ならない」 — when reading, check whether 「ほか」 follows a verb or 「noun＋に」. (よりほかない works the same way.)

groups.note: Both mean “have no choice but to, have to”

items.diff: Same meaning; しかない is common in both speech and writing, while ほかない is more written and formal.

this.tr: The typhoon has grounded the planes. There is no choice but to give up the trip.

that.tr: The planes aren't flying because of the typhoon, so we'll just have to give up on the trip.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the setting: chatting with friends, 「〜しかないね」 is most natural; writing, news and formal speech often use 「〜ほかない」「〜よりほかない」, which sound more formal and more strongly resigned.

items.diff: ほかない focuses on “there's no other option”, with resignation; ざるを得ない focuses on “forced by circumstances, against one's will”.

this.tr: The last train's gone too. There's nothing for it but to take a taxi home.

that.tr: It's the president's order, so I have no choice but to go.

items.explain: Look at the reason: all options are used up (終電もない、方法がない) → ほかない, “this is the only road left”; there's outside pressure and you don't really want to (命令、規則、立場) → ざるを得ない. They connect differently too: ほかない follows the dictionary form (帰る); ざるを得ない follows the ない-form (行か＋ざる; する → せざる).

groups.note: Both come from 「以上」 — originally “above this”

items.diff: 以上に means “more than, beyond”; 以上（は） means “now that…, then…”.

this.tr: The exam was even harder than I'd expected.

that.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

items.explain: It's the same 「以上 (above this)」: followed by 「に」 and then an adjective or verb → the degree goes beyond this benchmark; followed by 「は」 or a comma, then a resolve or obligation (最後までやる、〜べきだ) → taking this as a premise, “now that…”. Check whether 「以上」 is followed by 「に」 or 「は／、」.

groups.note: Both mean “even more than…”

items.diff: 以上に often pairs with 「予想」「思った」 to say something exceeded expectations; にもまして is more written and can also mean “more than anything”.

this.tr: The match was even more exciting than expected.

that.tr: More than anything, my family's health matters most.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: expectations like 「予想」「想像」「思った」 → 以上に, meaning beyond what was expected; question words like 「何」「誰」 → にもまして, meaning “more than anything / anyone”. After 「去年」「以前」 both work; にもまして is more written and implies “it was already very… to begin with”.

items.diff: より is a neutral comparison; 以上に stresses “going past the benchmark”, especially beyond expectations, and sounds stronger.

this.tr: The exam was harder than I could have imagined.

that.tr: The exam was harder than I thought.

items.explain: Both sentences work — the tone differs: より just flatly says “harder than…”; 以上に treats 「思った」 as a line and stresses that reality “broke through it”, with more surprise. For everyday comparisons of two things (AはBより高い), use より; for “beyond expectations, more than in past years”, 以上に is more forceful.

groups.note: Both come from 「以上」 — originally “above this”

items.diff: 以上（は） means “now that…, then…”; 以上に means “more than, beyond”.

this.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

that.tr: The exam was even harder than I'd expected.

items.explain: It's the same 「以上 (above this)」: followed by 「は」 or a comma, then a resolve or obligation (最後までやる、〜べきだ) → taking this as a premise, “now that…”; followed by 「に」 and then an adjective or verb → the degree goes beyond this benchmark. Check whether 「以上」 is followed by 「は／、」 or 「に」.

groups.note: Both mean “now that…, then…”

items.diff: Nearly the same meaning; からには is more subjective, carries resolve and is common in speech; 以上（は） is slightly more objective and reasoned.

this.tr: As long as you live in Japan, you should follow Japan's rules.

that.tr: Now that I've finally made it to Japan, I want to visit all kinds of places.

items.explain: They're mostly interchangeable. Look at the second half: a reasoned conclusion like an obligation or rule (守るべきだ、〜なければならない) → 以上 sounds natural; your own resolve or wish, especially with 「せっかく」 (行ってみたい、絶対に勝つ) → からには has more punch.

items.diff: 上は is more written and formal, mostly for weighty resolutions, and its 「は」 can't be dropped; the 「は」 of 以上 can be.

this.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll take responsibility to the end.

that.tr: Now that it's come to this, I have no choice but to steel myself.

items.explain: Look at how heavy the tone is: 上は is mostly used at critical moments like 「こうなった上は」「決まった上は」, followed by 「覚悟を決める」「〜しかない」, and sounds solemn; 以上 is broader and works for everyday obligations and reasoning. The 「は」 of 上は can't be dropped; with 以上 you can just say 「以上、」.

groups.note: Both mean “once…, then…”

items.diff: いったん〜ば／と works with good or bad outcomes and can also lead into a request; たら最後 only leads to irreversible bad outcomes and sounds exaggerated.

this.tr: Once you get the hang of it, the rest is easy.

that.tr: Once you start playing this game, that's it — you can't stop until morning.

items.explain: Look at the outcome in the second half: たら最後 (が最後) is always followed by an irreversible bad result like “it's all over, can't stop”, in an exaggerated tone; いったん〜ば／と can be followed by good or bad (あとは簡単だ), or by a request like 「最後までやりなさい」.

groups.note: Both come from 「上」 — extended from “on top of…” to “in terms of…”

items.diff: 〜上（じょう） just objectively sets the angle; 〜の上（うえ）では often hints “that's how it is on paper, but not necessarily in reality”.

this.tr: Legally speaking, there's no problem.

that.tr: According to the calendar it's already spring, but it's still cold.

items.explain: Look at the reading and the second half: 「〜上（じょう）」 attaches directly to Sino-Japanese nouns (法律上、健康上、教育上) and just means “from this angle”; 「〜の上（うえ）では」 often follows 「暦」「数字」「計算」「書類」 and is usually followed by 「だが、実際は……」, hinting that paper and reality differ.

groups.note: Both mean “from the standpoint of…”

items.diff: 〜上 only attaches to Sino-Japanese nouns for fields, written and concise; から見ると can follow people and positions: “seen from …'s point of view”.

this.tr: From an educational standpoint, this movie isn't really suitable.

that.tr: From a child's point of view, what adults say is hard to understand.

wrong.why: 〜上 can't attach to people

items.explain: Look at the word before: field nouns like 教育、健康、法律、仕事 → 〜上, written and concise; people or positions like 子ども、親、外国人 → から見ると／からすると.

groups.note: Both come from 「否（いな）」 — the classical word for “no”

items.diff: か否か means “whether or not…”; や否や means “no sooner…than…”.

this.tr: We don't know yet whether he's coming or not.

that.tr: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: It's the same 「否 (no)」: か否か ＝ “is it…, or not”, raising a yes-or-no question; や否や originally also meant “did it or not”, i.e. the instant of doing it, extended to “no sooner…than…”. Check whether 「か」 or 「や」 comes first, then look at what follows: か否か is followed by 「分からない」「問題だ」; や否や by an action that happens immediately.

groups.note: Both mean “whether or not…”

items.diff: Same meaning; かどうか is the everyday expression, か否か is written language, common in official documents, news and papers.

this.tr: Whether or not to hold the meeting will be decided next week.

that.tr: We'll decide next week whether to hold the meeting.

items.explain: Exactly the same meaning — look at the style: official documents, news or papers with words like 「決定する」 → か否か; everyday speech and ordinary writing → かどうか — か否か sounds very stiff in conversation. Both are only for “yes or no” and can't be used with question words like 「誰」「何」.

groups.note: 〜か〜ないかのうちに ↔ 〜ないうちに, differing only in whether 「〜か」 comes first

items.diff: 〜か〜ないかのうちに means “no sooner…than…”; 〜ないうちに means “while it's not yet… (hurry and…)”.

this.tr: The bell had barely rung when everyone rushed out of the classroom.

that.tr: Let's head home before it gets dark.

items.explain: The key is 「か」: 「鳴るか鳴らないか」 uses the same verb in positive and negative back to back, meaning “the instant between ringing and not ringing”, followed by something that already happened; with just 「ならないうちに」 and no 「〜か」 before it, it means “before it becomes…”, often followed by something to do quickly, like 「〜よう」「〜なさい」. Even in the shortened form 「鳴るか鳴らないうちに」, first check whether the same verb is repeated.

groups.note: Both mean “no sooner…than…”

items.diff: With たとたん, the first action is complete and the second is usually unexpected; with 〜か〜ないかのうちに, the first action isn't quite complete and the two happen almost simultaneously.

this.tr: I'd barely lain down when I fell asleep.

that.tr: The moment I lay down, the phone rang.

items.explain: Look at whether the first action is complete: たとたん follows the た-form — the action is done, and right after something unexpected happens (電話が鳴った、雨が降り出した); 〜か〜ないかのうちに stresses “before … was even complete, … already”, the two events nearly overlapping, often used to exaggerate how fast it was.

items.diff: Same meaning; や否や is written language and uses the verb in dictionary form only once, without repeating it.

this.tr: The kids had barely gotten home when they went out to play.

that.tr: As soon as the kids got home, they went out to play.

items.explain: The two sentences mean almost the same. Look at the form: 〜か〜ないかのうちに says the same verb once positive and once negative, and works in speech and writing; や否や says it only once (帰るや否や), is common in novels and news, and sounds more written.

items.title: 〜次第 (as soon as…, right away)
items.diff: 〜次第 is used for the future, followed by something the speaker intends to do; 〜か〜ないかのうちに only describes things that already happened.

this.tr: I'd barely gotten home when it started to rain.

that.tr: I'll contact you as soon as I get home.

wrong.why: か〜ないかのうちに can't be used for future plans

items.explain: Look at the tense and the second half: something that already happened, often unexpectedly (雨が降り出した) → 〜か〜ないかのうちに; something that hasn't happened yet that the speaker plans to do right away (連絡します、お知らせします) → 〜次第, common in business settings.

groups.note: Both mean “it isn't really so, but it looks as if…”

items.diff: かのようだ is “just as if…” when you know full well it isn't, with a stronger contrast; ようだ (simile) is an ordinary comparison.

this.tr: He's laughing as if nothing had happened.

that.tr: Her hands are as cold as ice.

items.explain: かのようだ follows a clause that “isn't actually true” (何もなかった), stressing the gap between appearance and fact, and is rather written; ordinary ようだ usually follows 「noun＋の」 as a plain comparison, and can also express a guess (誰か来たようだ) — かのようだ has no guessing use. In speech ようだ becomes みたいだ, used the same way.

items.diff: かのような means “looks as if…, but isn't really”; んばかりの means “on the verge of…”, extremely intense, nearly about to happen.

this.tag: Actually knows · Putting on an act
this.tr: She had a look as if she knew nothing (when she actually did).

that.tr: She looked as if she was about to burst into tears.

wrong.why: んばかり must follow the ない-form (泣き出さ＋ん)

items.explain: Look at the form before it and the clues: んばかり follows the ない-form (泣き出さ＋ん), often together with 「今にも」, about an action that's just about to happen; かのような follows the plain form, after a situation that isn't really true (何も知らない), the point being that “appearance and fact differ”. The same goes for んばかりに／んばかりだ.

items.diff: ふりをする directly says someone is “deliberately pretending”; かのように＋verb describes from outside how something “looks as if…”, often critically.

this.tr: He kept walking as if he hadn't heard a thing.

that.tr: He deliberately pretended not to hear.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: ふりをする is itself the predicate (〜ふりをした), often with 「わざと」, stating outright that it's deliberate; かのように must be followed by another action (歩き続けた) and only describes how things looked, leaving the reader to judge whether it was on purpose.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 — literally “even if you say so”, so both express concession

items.diff: かといって goes at the start of a sentence: “but the other way doesn't work either”; からといって follows a reason: “just because…, doesn't mean…”.

this.tr: Work is hard. That said, I can't just quit either.

that.tr: Just because work is hard doesn't mean you should quit right away.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「といって」: starting a new sentence after a full stop (かといって) → you accept the situation, but the other road is blocked too, usually followed by 「〜わけにもいかない」「〜もない」; right after a reason (辛い＋からといって) → it rejects the idea “because of this reason, you should…”.

items.diff: Both can start a sentence; after かといって comes “the other option doesn't work either”, after とはいえ comes “a reality that goes against expectations”.

this.tag: The other road won't work either
this.tr: I hate being cold. But running the heater all day long is too wasteful.

that.tr: It's already spring. Even so, mornings are still cold.

items.explain: Look at the second half: かといって is followed by “the other choice won't do either” (〜のももったいない、〜わけにもいかない), expressing a dilemma; とはいえ just states a fact contrary to expectations (まだ寒い), with no choice involved — it's rather written and can also follow a noun directly (春とはいえ).

items.diff: かといって expresses a dilemma; といっても means “although I say…, it's not really that…”, used to lower the listener's expectations.

this.tr: I'm not good at cooking. But I don't have the money to eat out every day either.

that.tr: I can cook, but only simple things.

items.explain: Look at the second half: といっても is followed by a correction to what was just said (〜だけだ、〜くらいだ), toning it down; かといって is followed by another road that's also blocked (〜もない). Also, といっても attaches directly to a clause, while かといって usually starts its own sentence.

groups.note: Both come from 「…かと思う」 — “I wondered if…”

items.title: 〜かと思った (I thought…)
items.diff: かと思った just says “I thought…”, and the sentence ends there; かと思ったら is followed by something unexpected that happened right after.

this.tag: Just… and then · More to follow
this.tr: My brother had only just come home when he went straight back out again.

that.tr: I heard the door, so I thought my brother had come home.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「かと思った」: if a full stop ends it → you're just saying what you thought at the time (and it wasn't so); if 「ら、」 and another half follows → the first thing had just happened when an unexpected change came right after.

items.diff: For “I thought…, but actually…”, かと思ったら is colloquial; かと思いきや is the written version, common in articles.

this.tr: I thought the exam would be easy, but it turned out to be surprisingly hard.

that.tr: I thought the exam would be easy, but it turned out to be surprisingly hard.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the setting: in conversation say かと思ったら; in news, essays and other writing you often see かと思いきや, with a slightly classical flavor. Also, かと思ったら／かと思うと can mean “no sooner…than…”; かと思いきや can't.

groups.note: Both mean “no sooner…than…”

items.diff: かと思うと only describes other people or things you observe; たとたん can also describe what happens to you.

this.tr: No sooner had he stood up than he walked out of the room.

that.tr: The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.

wrong.why: かと思うと isn't used for the speaker's own actions

items.explain: Look at the subject: かと思うと describes a change the speaker observes from the side, with someone or something else as subject (彼は、空が); for “the moment I…” about yourself, use たとたん. かと思ったら is the same — not used for your own actions.

items.diff: With かと思うと the first event has already happened and the focus is the unexpected change after it; か〜ないかのうちに stresses that the second began when the first was barely over.

this.tr: The sky had no sooner darkened than it started pouring.

that.tag: First not yet over · Very short
that.tr: The bell had barely rung (it hadn't even finished) when the students rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Look at the form of the first part: か〜ないかのうちに puts the positive and negative of the same verb side by side (鳴るか鳴らないか), meaning “before … was even finished”, an even tighter timing; かと思うと follows the た-form — the first event has already happened, usually followed by an unexpected change.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit or range”

items.diff: 限り follows ordinary states and means “as long as…”; 限りでは follows verbs like 「知る・調べる」 and means “as far as … knows”.

this.tr: As long as I'm alive, I'll keep this shop going.

that.tag: As far as I know · Limited scope
that.tr: As far as I know, he's still single.

items.explain: Look at the verb before 「限り」: verbs of “getting information” like 知る、調べる、聞く、見る, often followed by 「では」 → “as far as … knows”, a cautious tone; states like 生きている、元気な → as long as this state lasts, the second half holds, usually a resolve or judgment.

items.diff: Verb＋限り means “as long as … still…”; noun＋に限り means “only for…”, common in ads and notices.

this.tr: As long as we have stock, we'll accept orders.

that.tr: Today only, everything is half price.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「限り」: a verb or adjective (ある、元気な) → as long as that state continues; noun＋に (本日に、学生に) → limited to this scope only, and beyond it there's nothing.

items.diff: 限り means “as long as…, then…”; に限って means “of all times, just when…”, usually a complaint.

this.tr: As long as I'm here, there's nothing to worry about.

that.tr: Just when I'm in a hurry, of all times, the train is late.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the second half: に限って follows a time or noun like 「〜時」「今日」 and is followed by bad luck or something unexpected → “of all times”; 限り follows an ongoing state and is followed by a resolve or guarantee → “as long as”.

groups.note: Both express conditions: “as long as…, then…” / “unless…, not…”

items.diff: 限り means “for as long as this state continues”; さえ〜ば means “as long as this one condition is met”.

this.tr: As long as I'm healthy, I want to keep working.

that.tr: As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better right away.

items.explain: Look at both halves: the first part of 限り is a state lasting over time (元気な、生きている), and the second is usually a lasting resolve too (続けたい); the first part of さえ〜ば is a condition you just need to meet (飲みさえすれば), and the second is the result that follows (すぐ治る).

items.diff: After ない限り the second half can be positive or negative; after ないことには it's always a negative or discouraging result.

this.tr: Unless it rains, the match will go ahead as planned.

that.tr: Until I actually see it, I can't say anything for sure.

wrong.why: The second half after ないことには must be negative or discouraging

items.explain: Look at the second half: ないことには can only be followed by negative, discouraging results like 「〜ない」「始まらない」「無理だ」, rather colloquial; ない限り can be followed by a positive arrangement (予定通り行う) and is more written.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit or range”

items.title: 〜限り (as long as…)
items.diff: 限りでは follows verbs like 「知る・調べる」 and means “as far as … knows”; 限り follows ordinary states and means “as long as…”.

this.tag: As far as I know · Limited scope
this.tr: As far as I know, he's still single.

that.tr: As long as I'm alive, I'll keep this shop going.

items.explain: Look at the verb before 「限り」: verbs of “getting information” like 知る、調べる、聞く、見る, often followed by 「では」 → “as far as … knows”, a cautious tone; states like 生きている、元気な → as long as this state lasts, the second half holds, usually a resolve or judgment.

groups.note: Both state the basis for a judgment

items.diff: 限りでは is the speaker judging within their own limited knowledge; によると just cites a source, often paired with 「そうだ」「らしい」.

this.tr: From what I've found, this restaurant has a good reputation.

that.tr: According to a magazine, this restaurant has a good reputation.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the sentence ending: 限りでは follows your own action (調べた、知っている) and ends with your own judgment, implying “beyond that, I can't say”; によると／によれば follows a source (雑誌、ニュース) and often ends with 「そうだ」「らしい」, just passing on information.

items.diff: 限りでは stresses “only within what I've seen”; から見ると means “seen from a certain angle or standpoint”.

this.tr: From what I saw, there were no particular problems.

that.tr: From an expert's point of view, this plan has a lot of problems.

items.explain: Both sentences have 「見る」 — look at what's before it: the speaker's own experience (私が見た)＋限りでは → limited scope, cautious tone; a noun (専門家、子ども、データ)＋から見ると → judging from that angle. からすると works the same way.

groups.note: Both come from 「兼ねる」 — originally “to do two things at once”, extended to “hard to manage both → hard to…”

items.diff: かねない means “could well (lead to something bad)”; かねる means “find it hard to…, cannot…”, often used for polite refusals.

this.tr: If things go on like this, it could well lead to a serious accident.

that.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to accommodate your request.

items.explain: Just check whether the ending has 「ない」: かねる ＝ hard to do, so かねます is a polite “cannot”; かねない ＝ “not impossible”, so it means “could well happen”, and only for bad outcomes. Memory tip: かねます ＝ no can do, かねません ＝ might happen.

groups.note: Both mean “there's a chance (it will happen)”

items.diff: かねない carries the speaker's worry and warning; おそれがある is objective and calm, common in news and weather forecasts.

this.tr: If the rain keeps up like this, the river could well flood.

that.tr: Due to the typhoon, there is a risk the river will flood.

wrong.why: かねない follows the ます-stem (氾濫し＋かねない)

items.explain: Look at the setting and connection: objective reporting in news or weather forecasts → おそれがある (after the dictionary form: 氾濫する＋おそれ); the speaker's own worry or a warning to someone → かねない (after the ます-stem: 氾濫し＋かねない). Judging a person as “capable of doing it” (彼ならやりかねない) only works with かねない.

items.diff: かもしれない works for good or bad things; かねない only for bad outcomes.

this.tr: If you don't practice, you could well lose the match.

that.tr: If you practice properly, you might win the match.

wrong.why: かねない can't be used for good outcomes

items.explain: Look at whether the outcome is good or bad: good things like “winning, succeeding” only take かもしれない; bad things like “losing, having an accident” work with both, and かねない sounds more like a warning and more written.

groups.note: Both come from 「兼ねる」 — originally “to do two things at once”, extended to “hard to manage both → hard to…”

items.diff: かねる means “find it hard to…, cannot…”, often used for polite refusals; かねない means “could well (lead to something bad)”.

this.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to accommodate your request.

that.tr: If things go on like this, it could well lead to a serious accident.

items.explain: Just check whether the ending has 「ない」: かねる ＝ hard to do, so かねます is a polite “cannot”; かねない ＝ “not impossible”, so it means “could well happen”, and only for bad outcomes. Memory tip: かねます ＝ no can do, かねません ＝ might happen.

groups.note: Both mean “hard to…”

items.diff: かねる means you're not in a position to do it, often used to refuse politely; がたい is a judgment that something is “hard to…”.

this.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to accept those terms.

that.tr: Those terms are really hard to accept.

items.explain: Look at the setting: turning someone down face to face in business (お受けしかねます、お答えしかねます) → かねる, meaning “I'd like to, but my position doesn't allow it”; expressing your own feeling or judgment about something (受け入れがたい、信じがたい) → がたい.

items.diff: かねます politely says “cannot do it” — really a refusal; にくい just means it's awkward to do.

this.tr: We're very sorry, but we're unable to answer that question.

that.tr: That's a bit of a tricky question to answer.

items.explain: Look at the setting and meaning: 「申し訳ございませんが、〜かねます」 said to a customer means “cannot”, a tactful refusal; something you find hard but can still manage (答えにくい、読みにくい) → にくい. Note that かねます is affirmative in form yet means “cannot”.

groups.note: からいうと ↔ からといって — both built from 「から」 and 「言う」, yet completely different in meaning

items.diff: からいうと means “in terms of…”, setting a standard for judgment; からといって means “just because…, doesn't mean…”, usually followed by a negative.

this.tr: In terms of ability, he should win the championship.

that.tr: Just because you have the ability doesn't mean you'll win.

items.explain: Look at what's before 「から」 and the second half: directly after a noun (実力、立場、経験) → からいうと, followed by the speaker's judgment; after a full clause (実力がある) → からといって, usually followed by negatives like 「とは限らない」「わけではない」. からいえば works the same way.

groups.note: Both set out a standpoint or angle: “from the standpoint of… / for…”

items.diff: からいうと follows standards like 「品質・立場・経験」; からすると can also follow people: “in …'s eyes”.

this.tr: In terms of quality, this price is cheap.

that.tag: After a person · In someone's eyes
that.tr: From a parent's point of view, a child living alone is worrying.

items.explain: Look at the noun before: “standards, viewpoints” like 品質、立場、経験 work with both; for a person (親、外国人), to say “in someone's eyes” use からすると／から見ると — からいうと usually doesn't follow people.

items.diff: にとって follows a person or organization: “for someone”; からいうと follows a standard or viewpoint: “in terms of something”.

this.tr: Speaking from experience, this method is the best.

that.tr: For me, family is the most important thing.

items.explain: Look at the noun before: a person, company or country (私、子ども、会社)＋にとって, followed by an evaluation like 「大切だ、難しい、ありがたい」; a standard for judgment like 経験、立場、点＋からいうと.

groups.note: All rely on the emphatic particle 「こそ」 — “this, and nothing else”; after から／て／ば it emphasizes a reason or condition respectively

items.diff: からこそ specifically emphasizes a reason; こそ on its own can emphasize any element (今年こそ、あなたこそ).

this.tr: It's precisely because I care about you that I'm being so strict with you.

that.tr: This year, I'm definitely going to pass the exam.

items.explain: こそ itself means “this very one”: on a time word (今年こそ) it means “this time for sure”; only after the reason marker 「から」 does it become “precisely because…”. Check whether 「から」 comes before こそ.

items.diff: からこそ gives the reason for a specific event: “precisely because…”; てこそ gives the condition in a general truth: “only if…”.

this.tr: It was precisely because I worked hard every day that I passed.

that.tr: Only by working hard every day can you pass.

items.explain: Look at the verb form and tense: た-form＋からこそ, followed by a result that already happened (合格できた) → explaining the reason; て-form＋こそ, followed by a general truth (合格できる、意味がある) → it only works if this condition is met.

items.diff: Same meaning, “precisely because…”; ばこそ is a written, slightly old-fashioned way of saying it — in everyday use, say からこそ.

this.tr: It's precisely because I care about my child that I'm strict with him.

that.tr: It's precisely because I care about my child that I'm strict with him.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the connection and style: ばこそ follows the conditional form (思え＋ばこそ), common in writing and speeches; からこそ follows the plain form (思う＋からこそ) and is common in both speech and writing.

groups.note: Both mean “made up of…, made from…”

items.diff: からなる says which parts (members, chapters, components) a whole is made up of; から作る／で作る says what raw materials or materials something is made from.

this.tr: This team is made up of five people.

that.tr: Sake is made from rice.
This desk is made of wood.

items.explain: Look at the noun and verb: a number of people, chapters or components (５人、三章)＋からなる describes the makeup of a whole, rather written; to say “what it's made from” use 作る: raw materials (米、牛乳)＋から作る, where the original form is unrecognizable in the finished product; recognizable materials (木、紙)＋で作る.

groups.note: Both mean “now that…, then…”

items.diff: からには carries a personal resolve: “now that I've started, I'll see it through”; 以上（は） is more formal, often used for rules, contracts and official settings.

this.tr: Now that I'm entering the competition, I'm aiming to win.

that.tr: Now that you've signed the contract, we ask that you comply with the regulations.

items.explain: Basically the same meaning — look at the setting: talking about your own resolve or speaking to friends → からには; responsibilities and obligations in contracts, regulations or official notices → 以上（は）, with a harder tone.

items.diff: からには is common in everyday speech too; 上は is very written and formal, mostly for weighty decisions.

this.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

that.tr: Having accepted this task, I am resolved to give it my all.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the style: 上は belongs to writing and formal addresses, often appearing with solemn words like 「覚悟」「全力を尽くす」; in everyday speech use からには.

items.diff: からには stresses “now that it's come this far, I'll see it through”; のだから takes a fact the other person also accepts and uses it to urge or scold them.

this.tr: Now that I've come to Japan, I want to really master Japanese.

that.tag: Known fact · Urging the other person
that.tr: You're an adult now, so decide for yourself.

items.explain: Look at both halves: before からには is usually a choice you made yourself (来た、引き受けた、出る), followed by a resolve or obligation to see it through; before のだから／んだから is a fact both sides know (もう大人だ), usually followed by a demand on or reproach of the other person.

groups.note: からして ↔ からすると, both 「から＋する」

items.title: 〜からすると
items.diff: Person＋からして means “even … (let alone everyone else)”; person＋からすると means “in …'s eyes”.

this.tr: At this company, even the president isn't punctual (let alone everyone else).

that.tr: In the president's eyes, employees being late is probably unforgivable.

items.explain: Both have 「社長」 before them — look at the second half: if it's about the president's own behavior (時間を守らない), implying “never mind everyone else” → からして; if it's about the president's view or judgment (許せないだろう) → からすると. But when it means “judging from…” (口ぶりからして／口ぶりからすると), the two are interchangeable.

groups.note: Both cite one point, implying “never mind the rest”

items.diff: からして cites the most basic part, the first thing you see; さえ cites the most extreme, least likely example.

this.tr: This shop looks suspicious from its name alone.

that.tr: Even a child knows that.

items.explain: Look at what's being cited: the first, most basic thing you notice, like 名前、入口、態度＋からして, usually a negative judgment, “it's wrong from the start”; the least likely, most surprising example, like 子ども、専門家＋さえ, meaning “even this…”.

items.diff: Nearly the same meaning, “even…”; にしてからが is more written and stiff, and usually follows people.

this.tr: Even he, the leader, has no motivation (never mind the others).

that.tr: Even he, the leader, has no motivation (never mind the others).

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same — look at the style: にしてからが is mostly found in writing, almost always after a person, and specifically “the one who should be setting the example”; からして is used in both speech and writing, and can also follow things like names or clothing.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 — literally “even if you say so”, so both express concession

items.diff: からといって follows a reason: “just because…, doesn't mean…”; かといって goes at the start of a sentence: “but the other way doesn't work either”.

this.tr: Just because work is hard doesn't mean you should quit right away.

that.tr: Work is hard. That said, I can't just quit either.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「といって」: right after a reason (辛い＋からといって) → it rejects the idea “because of this reason, you should…”; starting a new sentence after a full stop (かといって) → you accept the situation, but the other road is blocked too, usually followed by 「〜わけにもいかない」「〜もない」.

items.diff: からといって rejects a conclusion drawn from a reason; といっても corrects what was just said, lowering the listener's expectations.

this.tr: Being able to cook doesn't mean you can open a restaurant.

that.tr: I can cook, but only simple things.

items.explain: Same first half — look at the second half: からといって is followed by a rejection of the inference “so you can…” (わけではない、とは限らない); といっても is followed by the real situation, toning it down (〜だけだ、〜くらいだ).

items.diff: からといって is followed by a negative; とはいえ is a written “although…, still…”, followed directly by a reality contrary to expectations.

this.tr: Just because it's spring doesn't mean it'll get warm right away.

that.tr: It may be spring, but it's still cold.

items.explain: Look at the second half: after からといって the sentence usually ends with a negative like 「わけではない」「とは限らない」「〜てはいけない」; とはいえ is followed directly by a fact contrary to expectations (まだ寒い), which needn't be negative — it's rather written and can also stand alone at the start of a sentence.

groups.note: Both mean “have a tendency / trend toward…”

items.diff: 傾向がある is objective and neutral, mostly used in surveys and reports; がち is more colloquial, mostly about undesirable things that tend to recur.

this.tr: According to a survey, people tend to get too little exercise in winter.

that.tr: In winter I always end up not getting enough exercise.

items.explain: Look at the tone and connection: objective description in surveys or news → 傾向がある (after the dictionary form or 「noun＋の」); talking about yourself or people around you, with a sense of “not good”, often with 「つい」 → がち (after the ます-stem: なり＋がち, or a noun: 病気がち).

items.diff: 傾向がある is neutral and objective; きらいがある is only for bad tendencies, critical, and very written.

this.tr: Students these days tend to look everything up online.

that.tr: He has a bad habit of deciding everything by himself.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: just describing a phenomenon or statistic → 傾向がある; displeased with someone's way of doing things, with criticism → きらいがある (mostly in writing, usually with a specific person as subject).

items.diff: 傾向にある objectively describes a statistical trend; 一方だ stresses “getting more and more… in one direction only”, often with concern.

this.tr: The population of this region is on a downward trend.

that.tr: The population of this region just keeps on falling.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: 傾向にある follows Sino-Japanese nouns like 「減少、増加、上昇」, common in news and reports, in a calm tone; 一方だ follows a verb in dictionary form (減る、悪くなる), stressing that the change won't stop, usually with the speaker's concern.

groups.note: Both mean “impossible”

items.diff: Both mean “impossible”; っこない is only for casual speech and follows the ます-stem; わけがない follows the plain form and works in any setting.

this.tr: With this much, there's no way I'll finish in a day!

that.tr: With this much, it can't possibly be finished in a day.

wrong.why: っこない follows the ます-stem (終わり＋っこない)

items.explain: Look at the connection and setting: っこない follows the ます-stem (終わり、でき、わかり＋っこない), with a “no way!” emotion, said only to people you know well; わけがない follows the plain form (終わる＋わけがない), argues more calmly, and can be used in writing too.

items.diff: っこない is casual speech: “there's just no way…”; はずがない is a calm judgment based on facts that something can't be.

this.tr: There's no way I can solve such a hard problem!

that.tr: He's overseas right now, so he can't be coming to today's meeting.

items.explain: Look at the tone and basis: っこない is only for casual talk among friends, mostly a gut feeling of “can't be done”; はずがない has concrete facts behind it (今海外にいる) and works in formal settings too.

groups.note: Both give a reason or basis for a judgment

items.diff: ことだから predicts something that hasn't happened yet from a person's usual ways; だけあって says “as you'd expect from…” about a result already seen.

this.tr: Knowing how conscientious he is, he surely won't be late.

that.tr: As you'd expect from a professional, the food is really delicious.

items.explain: Look at the second half: ことだから is usually followed by a prediction about something yet to happen, like 「きっと〜だろう」「〜に違いない」; だけあって is followed by a result already seen, often with 「さすが」, expressing admiration. They connect differently too: ことだから follows 「person＋の」; だけあって follows a noun directly (プロだけあって).

items.diff: ことだから follows 「person＋の」 and is followed by a prediction; ことだし takes the current situation as a reason and is followed by a suggestion or decision.

this.tr: Knowing her, she's surely already got everything ready.

that.tr: The rain has stopped, so let's get going.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the sentence ending: 「person＋の」 (彼女の)＋ことだから, followed by a prediction about that person (きっと〜だろう); plain form (やんだ)＋ことだし, followed by a suggestion or decision like 「〜よう」「〜ましょう」.

items.diff: ことだから predicts from the consistent traits of a person or thing; ことから uses one concrete fact as grounds to explain the origin of a name or judgment, and is rather written.

this.tr: Knowing how cautious the department head is, he won't decide right away.

that.tr: Because its shape resembles Mt. Fuji, this mountain is called 「小富士」.

items.explain: The only difference is one 「だ」 — look at what comes before: 「person＋の」＋ことだから relies on a character or nature everyone knows; a fact in the plain form (似ている)＋ことから is often used to explain where a name came from or the grounds for a conclusion (〜と呼ばれている、〜とわかった).

groups.note: Both give a reason or basis for a judgment

items.diff: ことだし takes the current situation as a reason and is followed by a suggestion or decision; ことだから follows 「person＋の」 and is followed by a prediction.

this.tr: The rain has stopped, so let's get going.

that.tr: Knowing her, she's surely already got everything ready.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the sentence ending: plain form (やんだ)＋ことだし, followed by a suggestion or decision like 「〜よう」「〜ましょう」; 「person＋の」 (彼女の)＋ことだから, followed by a prediction about that person (きっと〜だろう).

items.diff: し can list several reasons in one go; ことだし usually gives just one reason at hand, mostly followed by a suggestion or decision, and sounds softer.

this.tr: The rain has stopped — shall we go for a walk?

that.tr: The rain has stopped and the breeze is nice — shall we go for a walk?

items.explain: The 「し」 at the end of ことだし is that same reason-listing 「し」, so it also hints “there are other reasons too”. Look at how many reasons there are: two or three side by side (〜し、〜し) → し; just one ready-made situation as a reason, then a suggestion that follows naturally → ことだし, often with 「も」 before it (雨もやんだことだし).

groups.note: Both express strong feelings

items.title: 〜ものだ (exclamation)
items.diff: ことか exclaims over the degree or frequency of something you experienced, often with 「どんなに」「何度」; ものだ exclaims over human nature or general truths.

this.tr: When I heard I'd passed, how happy I was!

that.tr: Time really does fly.

items.explain: Look for a question word: ことか is a rhetorical-question exclamation, almost always preceded by 「どんなに」「どれほど」「何度」, about your own specific feelings or how many times; ものだ takes no question word and exclaims over feelings anyone would have (時間が経つのは早い).

items.diff: ことか uses a rhetorical “how…!” and needs a question word; といったらない attaches directly to a noun or adjective: “so… it's beyond words”.

this.tr: When I lost, how frustrated I was!

that.tr: The frustration I felt when I lost was beyond words.

items.explain: Look at the structure: ことか has 「どんなに／どれほど」 before it and takes the form of a question; といったらない follows a noun or adjective like 「悔しさ」「寒さ」, uses no question word, and says directly that the degree has hit the limit.

groups.note: Both come from 「こと＋ない」 — “there is no such thing as…”

items.diff: ことなく simply describes doing the second part “without…”; ことなしに is usually followed by a negative, meaning “without…, you can't…”.

this.tr: He opened his shop on his own, without relying on anyone.

that.tr: Without effort, success is impossible.

items.explain: Look at the second half: ことなしに is mostly followed by negatives like 「ありえない」「できない」, so the whole sentence means “if you don't do the first part, the second can't happen”; ことなく is followed by something that actually happened (店を開いた) and only describes it as happening “without…”.

groups.note: Both mean “without doing… (and then…)”

items.diff: ことなく is more formal and often stresses “not even once” over a long period; ずに is for everyday “did… without doing…”.

this.tr: For ten years he kept working without taking a single day off.

that.tr: I went to school without eating breakfast.

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: in writing or speeches stressing “never once over a long time” (一日も, 一度も) → ことなく; not doing something in daily life → ずに, or more casually ないで. They also attach differently: ことなく takes the dictionary form (休む＋ことなく), ずに takes the ない-form stem (食べ＋ずに).

groups.note: Both can state a feeling first, then the fact that caused it: “what's surprising is…”

items.diff: ことに is more formal: it gives the evaluation first, followed by a complete sentence stating the fact; 〜のは〜だ is common in speech and puts the fact at the end as the focus.

this.tr: Surprisingly, he finished that book in a single night.

that.tr: What surprised me was that he finished that book in a single night.

items.explain: Look at the form of the second half: after ことに comes an ordinary complete sentence (彼は〜読み終えた), with the subject marked by 「は」; after 〜のは, the fact has to be wrapped up as a noun with 「〜ことだ」, and the subject switches to 「が」. The meaning is almost the same; ことに reads more like written prose.

groups.note: Both come from 「ことになる」 — “it ends up being…”

items.diff: た-form＋ことにはならない means “doesn't count as”; dictionary form＋ことになる often means “it has been decided”.

this.tr: Apologizing just once doesn't mean you've reflected on what you did.

that.tr: I'm being transferred to Osaka starting next month.

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「こと」: た-form (謝った, 理解した)＋ことにはならない → judging whether the action counts; dictionary form (転勤する)＋ことになった → something has been decided, nothing to do with whether it “counts”.

groups.note: Both reject an inference that might seem “only natural”

items.diff: ことにはならない judges whether an action is “good enough to count as…”; わけではない corrects a misunderstanding someone may have: “it's not that…”.

this.tr: Going there only once doesn't mean you know that country.

that.tr: It's not that I dislike meat; I just don't feel like it today.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a concrete action (行った, 読んだ)＋だけでは〜ことにはならない → the action doesn't meet the standard; a feeling or state (嫌いな, 知らない)＋わけではない → correcting a possible misunderstanding, often followed by the real situation (〜だけだ).
