items.diff: とは限らない says “not necessarily”, leaving room; ことにはならない flatly rules “doesn't count”, which sounds more decisive.

this.tr: Just getting full marks on a test doesn't mean you're good at English.

that.tr: Even if you get full marks on a test, it doesn't necessarily mean you can speak English.

items.explain: Look at what the speaker is judging: whether something “is possible” → とは限らない, meaning “maybe, maybe not”; whether an action “qualifies” → ことにはならない, a straight denial.

groups.note: のことになると ↔ ことになる: they differ by just one 「と」

items.diff: のことになると means “whenever it comes to…”; ことになる means “it's been decided / it turns out that…”.

this.tr: Once the topic turns to cars, my brother can't stop talking.

that.tr: My brother is being transferred to Osaka starting next month.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「こと」: 「noun＋の」 (車の)＋ことになると, where 「こと」 means “matters concerning…”, followed by how a person behaves; verb dictionary form (転勤する)＋ことになる, a decision or natural outcome. The extra 「と」 means another half-sentence follows. こととなると also means “when it comes to”.

groups.note: Both come from 「くらい（位）」 — expressing “degree”

items.diff: Noun＋くらいなら means “if it's only this much”; verb＋くらいなら means “rather than…, I'd sooner…”.

this.tr: Rather than ask someone else, I'd be better off doing it myself.

that.tr: If it's just this much, I can carry it by myself.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「くらい」: quantity words like これ, 少し → ordinary “degree”, くらいなら＝“if it's this much”; a verb in the dictionary form (頼む) followed by 「〜ほうがましだ」 → the first part is treated as the last thing you'd want to do, so you'd rather choose the second. ぐらい works the same way.

groups.note: Both express a choice: “rather than…, I'd…”

items.diff: In AくらいならB, A is something the speaker really hates, with strong feeling; AよりむしろB is a calm comparison, judging B to be the better fit.

this.tr: Rather than ride a packed train, I'll walk.

that.tr: At this hour, walking is actually faster than taking the train.

items.explain: Look at whether the first part is “something unpleasant”: a packed train is unbearable, so you'd rather walk → くらいなら, with the second part often 「〜ほうがましだ」 or the speaker's decision; just comparing which of two ways is more suitable (早い, 正しい) → よりむしろ.

groups.note: Both come from 「まで」 — “to the point of…”

items.diff: までもない means “no need to go that far”; までして／てまで means “going so far as to…”.

this.tag: No need to go that far
this.tr: The station is close, so there's no need to call a taxi.

that.tag: までして · noun: going so far as…
that.tr: There's no need to go so far as borrowing money to buy a car.

that.tag: てまで · verb: going so far as…
that.tr: I don't want to go so far as borrowing money to buy a car.

items.explain: It's the same 「まで」 (to the point of…): までもない is “things haven't reached the point where that's needed”, after the verb dictionary form (呼ぶ); までして／てまで is “actually going to that extreme”, after a noun (借金までして) or a verb て-form (借金してまで), often with surprise or criticism. までもなく also means “no need to”.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no need to…”

items.diff: までもない usually says “it's simple and obvious, so no need to…”; には及ばない is usually a polite “you needn't…” said to the other person.

this.tr: It's simple, so there's no need to bother explaining it.

that.tr: There's no need for you to come all this way; an email will be fine.

items.explain: Look at who is being addressed: politely telling the other person “please don't trouble yourself”, ending in the polite 「〜には及びません」 → には及ばない; just saying that something is simple and obvious → までもない.

items.diff: までもない says something is obvious, so there's no need to bother; ことはない is mostly used to reassure or advise someone: “you don't need to…”.

this.tr: Something that simple doesn't even need looking up.

that.tr: You don't need to apologize. I'm the one at fault.

items.explain: Look at the context: ことはない is mostly said to the other person, reassuring or advising them (心配することはない, 謝ることはない), and is common in speech; までもない speaks from the matter itself: it's too simple or too obvious to be worth doing.

groups.note: Both come from 「まで」 — “to the point of…”

items.diff: までして／てまで means “going so far as to…”; までもない means “no need to go that far”.

this.tag: までして · noun: going so far as…
this.tr: There's no need to go so far as borrowing money to buy a car.

this.tag: てまで · verb: going so far as…
this.tr: I don't want to go so far as borrowing money to buy a car.

that.tag: No need to go that far
that.tr: The station is close, so there's no need to call a taxi.

items.explain: It's the same 「まで」 (to the point of…): までして／てまで is “actually going to that extreme”, after a noun (借金までして) or a verb て-form (借金してまで), often with surprise or criticism; までもない is “things haven't reached the point where that's needed”, after the verb dictionary form (呼ぶ).

groups.note: Both mean “paying a price to get something”

items.diff: てでも expresses the speaker's strong will: “I'll do it even if…”; てまで／までして is mostly used to judge a method as going too far, often followed by a negative or surprise.

this.tr: I don't want to go so far as borrowing money to study abroad.
I was amazed that he went so far as borrowing money to study abroad.

that.tr: I want to study abroad, even if I have to borrow money.

items.explain: Look at the second half: てでも is followed by positive intentions like 「〜たい」「〜つもりだ」, the speaker willing to pay the price; てまで／までして is mostly followed by 「〜たくない」「〜必要はない」「〜とは驚いた」, showing the price feels excessive. Note how they attach: てでも only takes a verb て-form, while までして takes a noun.

groups.note: Both come from the negative conjecture auxiliary 「まい」 — “probably won't… / will never…”

items.diff: まい on its own means “will never…”; (よ)うか〜まいか pairs the volitional form with まい to show hesitation over “whether or not to do it”.

this.tr: I made up my mind never to lie again.

that.tr: I can't decide whether or not to go to the party.

items.explain: Look at whether まい comes with a 「〜(よ)うか」 before it: まい alone shows a resolve not to do something (often with 「二度と」); 「行こうか行くまいか」 sets doing and not doing side by side, followed by 「迷う」「悩む」, showing indecision.

items.diff: まい alone is negative conjecture: “probably won't…”; ではあるまいか adds a question and flips it around to “I suspect that…”.

this.tr: A mistake this small probably won't be a problem.

that.tr: I suspect this plan is somewhat unrealistic.

items.explain: Look at whether the sentence ends with 「か」: 「〜まい。」 is “probably won't…”; 「〜ではあるまいか」 is a rhetorical “isn't it…?”, really meaning “I suspect it is…”, more formal than 「〜のではないだろうか」.

items.diff: 「〜ではあるまい」 at the end of a sentence is a guess: “probably isn't…”; 「〜ではあるまいし」 means “it's not as if…”, followed by criticism or advice.

this.tr: He's probably not a child anymore.

that.tag: It's not as if… · advice follows
that.tr: You're not a child anymore, so decide for yourself.

items.explain: Look at whether 「し」 follows: 「〜ではあるまい。」 at the end of a sentence is a guess, “probably isn't…”; add 「し、」 and another half-sentence follows, turning it into “it's not as if…”, mostly followed by criticism, an order or advice (自分で決めなさい).

groups.note: Both can express a negative guess or a negative intention (“probably won't…”, “don't intend to…”)

items.title: 〜ないだろう
items.diff: They mean the same, “probably won't…”; まい is formal and literary, while everyday conversation uses ないだろう.

this.tr: In this rain, he probably won't come either.

that.tr: In this rain, he probably won't come either.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: まい is mostly found in writing and speeches and attaches to the dictionary form (来る＋まい; する can also become すまい); in everyday speech, use 「〜ないだろう」.

items.title: 〜ないつもりだ
items.diff: まい carries the strong feeling of a firm resolve and leans formal; ないつもりだ just calmly states an intention.

this.tr: I'll never go to a shop like that again.

that.tr: I don't plan to go to that shop again.

items.explain: Look at the tone and what it pairs with: まい often goes with 「二度と」「決して」 to show a resolve of “never again…”, with the speaker as the subject; ないつもりだ just states a plan and is more common in everyday conversation.

groups.note: Both come from 「まま（儘）」 — “as it is, going along with…”

items.diff: まま means “staying as it is, unchanged”; ままに means “acting by following your mood, someone's words or someone's force”.

this.tr: I wandered through an unfamiliar town wherever my feet took me.

this.tag: れるままに · pushed by others
this.tr: The clerk kept recommending things, and before I knew it I'd bought expensive clothes.
Unable to resist, I was completely at their mercy.

that.tr: I fell asleep with the window open.

items.explain: Look at what comes before まま: a た-form or ない-form (開けたまま, 脱がないまま) → a state stays unchanged while something else is said to happen; a mood, someone's request or someone's force (気の向く, 勧められる, されるが)＋ままに → the following action is done “going along with it”.

groups.note: Both mean “doing as (someone) says”

items.diff: 言われるままに is doing “whatever you're told” without a mind of your own; 言われたとおりに is accurately “following the instructions”.

this.tag: At others' mercy · no mind of your own
this.tr: Without reading it carefully, I signed the contract just because I was told to.

that.tr: I filled in the form exactly as I was told, so it was accepted on the first try.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: ままに often appears with 「よく考えずに」「断れずに」 and carries regret or criticism about “being led along without a mind of your own”; とおりに only says “in line with the instructions” and is neutral or even positive. They attach differently too: 言われるままに (dictionary form), 言われたとおりに (た-form).

groups.note: Both mean “the same as… / like…”

items.diff: も同然だ firmly states “it's practically the same as…”; かのようだ means “as if…”, when it really isn't.

this.tr: One minute left and a three-point lead. It's as good as won.

that.tr: The game isn't even over, yet he's celebrating as if he'd already won.

items.explain: Look at whether the speaker admits “it isn't really so”: かのようだ is often preceded by 「まだ……なのに」 and describes something that looks that way but isn't; も同然だ is the speaker judging from the situation that “it's as good as done”, often after a た-form (勝ったも同然, 決まったも同然) or a noun (家族も同然).

groups.note: Both come from 「構う（かまう）」 — meaning “to mind, to care”

items.diff: もかまわず means “(doing something) without caring at all”; てもかまわない means “it's fine if…”, giving permission.

this.tr: Not caring that her clothes would get dirty, she scooped up the child who had fallen.

that.tr: These clothes are old, so it's fine if they get dirty.

items.explain: Look at what follows かまう: かまわず is followed by another action (抱き上げた), saying “ignoring that, they did it anyway”; かまわない comes at the end of the sentence and says “that's fine”, giving permission or showing indifference. They attach differently too: noun／〜の＋もかまわず, て-form＋もかまわない.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…”

items.diff: もかまわず is usually about ignoring other people's eyes or the setting, often with criticism; 顧みず is usually about ignoring danger or oneself, often with praise, and is more formal.

this.tr: He's on the phone in a loud voice on the train, without caring that he's bothering the people around him.

that.tr: With no thought for his own safety, he jumped into the river and saved the child.

items.explain: Look at what is being ignored and how it's judged: other people's eyes, inconvenience to others, the place → もかまわず, which the speaker usually disapproves of; danger, personal safety, family → 顧みず, usually sacrificing oneself for others or an ideal, common in news reports and biographies.

items.diff: もかまわず is someone “not caring” themselves; をよそに is “brushing aside” other people's worries or hopes, and is written language.

this.tr: Not caring who was watching, she burst into tears at the station.

that.tr: Ignoring his parents' worries, the son set off abroad on his own.

items.explain: をよそに is almost always preceded by other people's feelings or the surrounding situation (心配, 期待, 反対), describing like an onlooker how “the person involved stays aloof from it”; もかまわず is mostly preceded by things one would normally pay attention to, like 人目, 場所, 汚れ, saying the person simply doesn't care.

items.diff: もかまわず usually carries criticism; をものともせず means “making nothing of the difficulty”, with praise.

this.tr: Not caring that Mom will scold him, my little brother is playing and covered in mud.

that.tr: Undaunted by the heavy rain, the runners kept going all the way to the finish.

items.explain: をものともせず is preceded by a difficulty or obstacle (嵐, けが, 逆境) and followed by what was achieved by overcoming it, with the speaker giving praise; もかまわず is preceded by something one should normally care about, and the speaker is usually criticizing or surprised at how little the person cares.

groups.note: Both come from the formal noun 「もの」 — presenting a reason as “that's just how it was”, with an excusing tone

items.diff: They mean basically the same; もので is short and polite, common in formal apologies; ものだから is more colloquial and stresses the reason more.

this.tr: I'm terribly sorry for being late; the train was delayed.

that.tr: Sorry, my alarm didn't go off, so I overslept.

items.explain: The two are interchangeable; look at the setting: apologizing to a boss or client mostly uses the short 「〜もので」; explaining to friends, or stressing “it's because of this, you see”, mostly uses 「〜ものだから」 (in speech also 「〜もんだから」).

items.diff: もので sits mid-sentence and is followed by an apology or result, fine in polite settings; sentence-final もの／もん is a whiny, pouty excuse, only used with people you're close to.

this.tr: I'm sorry for the trouble; I'm not used to this yet.

that.tr: But I'm not used to it yet!

items.explain: Look at the position: もので has another half-sentence after it (an apology or result); もの／もん comes at the end of the sentence, often with 「だって」 before it, a childish excuse you can't use with a boss or customer.

groups.note: Both express a cause or reason

items.diff: ので states a cause objectively and can be followed by a request; もので has an excusing tone of “it couldn't be helped, please forgive me” and can't be followed by a request or order.

this.tr: The roads were congested, so I ended up late.

that.tr: The roads are congested, so please leave early.

wrong.why: もので can't be followed by a request

items.explain: Look at the second half: an apology or something that has already happened (遅れてしまいました) → もので works too; a request, order or invitation (〜てください, 〜ましょう) → only ので.

groups.note: Both come from 「もの」 — how things naturally are, common sense

items.title: 〜ものだ (should)
items.diff: ものだ means “by common sense, one should…”; ものではない means “by common sense, one shouldn't…”.

this.tr: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

that.tr: You should use keigo with your elders and superiors.

items.explain: It's the same 「もの」 (the way the world works): followed by an affirmative, it means “this is what one ought to do”; followed by a negative, “this is what one ought not to do”. Both sound like an elder instructing a younger person, talking about rules everyone should follow.

groups.note: Both end in 「ものではない」, but change what comes before and the meaning is completely different

items.diff: Dictionary form＋ものではない is advice: “you shouldn't…”; potential た-form＋ものではない means “simply impossible to…”, complaining that the thing is too awful.

this.tr: You shouldn't leave food that's been served to you.

that.tr: This food is so bad it's simply impossible to eat.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ものではない: the dictionary form (残す, 言う) → advice; the た-form of the potential (食べられた, 見られた, 聞けた) → complaining “it's simply impossible to…”, often with 「とても」 and a negative judgment before it (まずくて, 下手で).

items.diff: ものではない is advice: “you shouldn't…”; というものではない means “it's not as if just… is enough”, correcting a one-sided view.

this.tr: You shouldn't waste food.

that.tr: A higher price doesn't automatically make something better.

items.explain: Just adding 「という」 changes the meaning entirely: というものではない is mostly preceded by “as long as… it's fine” phrasings like 「〜ば いい」「〜ほど いい」, rebutting an oversimplified idea; ものではない directly follows a concrete action, advising someone not to do it.

groups.note: Both mean “one shouldn't…”

items.diff: ものではない is advice based on social common sense, mostly from elders to younger people; べきではない is the speaker's own position and can be used in discussions and debates.

this.tr: A child shouldn't talk back to their parents like that.

that.tr: I don't think the government should raise taxes right now.

items.explain: Look at whose standard it rests on: ものではない rests on “common sense everyone knows”, mostly used to lecture younger people and in speech; べきではない rests on the speaker's own judgment, often used with 「と思う」, and is the usual choice when discussing policies or plans.

items.diff: ものではない is advice based on common sense, with a fairly mild tone; てはならない is a rule or principle that “is absolutely not allowed”, with a solemn tone.

this.tr: You shouldn't make a racket late at night.

that.tr: Eating and drinking are prohibited in the laboratory.

items.explain: てはならない mostly appears in regulations, laws and official addresses, backed by a written rule or an unshakable principle; ものではない is common-sense advice between people, a little preachy, and isn't used to write rules.

groups.note: Both express high praise for something

items.diff: ものがある only says you sense some remarkable quality; だけのことはある means “just what you'd expect of…”, linking a good result to someone's status or effort.

this.tr: This newcomer's rate of growth is truly remarkable.

that.tr: This sushi is really good. Just what you'd expect from someone who trained for ten years.

items.explain: Look at whether a reason is given: だけのことはある is always preceded by a status, experience or effort (プロ, 十年修行した), often with 「さすが」, meaning “the result lives up to it”; ものがある gives no reason and only suggests “there's something remarkable here”.

groups.note: Both come from 「もの＋か」 — expressed as a rhetorical “as if that would happen?”

items.diff: ものか after an affirmative means “I'll never…”; ないものか after a negative means “isn't there some way to…?”, expressing a wish.

this.tr: I'm never going to a shop like that again!

that.tr: Isn't there something that can be done about this traffic jam?

items.explain: Just one 「ない」 makes the difference: 「行くものか」 asks “would I ever go?” → never going; 「ならないものか」 asks “can't something be done?” → really wishing it could. 「二度と」「絶対」 before it signal resolve; 「何とか」「どうにか」 signal a wish.

groups.note: Both express a strong denial: “never… / no way…”

items.diff: ものか carries anger or spite; わけがない calmly rules something out as “impossible” on logical grounds.

this.tr: Shut up already. Like I care about your problems!

that.tr: I haven't told anyone, so there's no way he knows.

items.explain: わけがない is often preceded by a reason (誰にも話していないから) and is a calm deduction; ものか／もんか is an emotional rhetorical question, common in arguments and fits of spite, and can also express a resolve of “I'll never…” (二度と行くものか), which わけがない can't do.

items.diff: ものか is spite said out loud; まい is a calm, formal “never again…”.

this.tr: A place this awful? I'm never coming back!

that.tr: Recalling that day's failure, I swore never to make the same mistake again.

items.explain: まい mostly appears in writing or inner monologue, often with 「と思う」「と誓う」, in a restrained tone; ものか／もんか is a rhetorical question blurted out with strong emotion, mainly used in speech.

items.diff: っこない only judges “there's no way”; ものか, when about oneself, can also express a resolve of “I'll never…”.

this.tr: There's no way I'm losing to a guy like that!

that.tr: We could never beat a team that strong.

items.explain: っこない attaches to the ます-stem (勝てっこない, 分かりっこない) and only judges “impossible”, usually sounding defeated; ものか attaches to the dictionary form and, when about oneself, means “I'll never…” (負けるもんか), with a refuse-to-lose spirit.

groups.note: Potential form＋ものなら ↔ volitional form＋ものなら: both end in 「ものなら」, differing only in the verb form before it

items.diff: Potential form＋ものなら means “if only I could…” (a wish); volitional form＋ものなら means “if you dare to…, you'll be in trouble” (a warning).

this.tr: If I could go back, I'd love to return to my student days.

that.tr: If you're ever late to a meeting, the department head will chew you out.

wrong.why: Volitional form＋ものなら is followed by a bad outcome, not a wish

items.explain: First look at the verb form before ものなら: the potential form (戻れる, できる) → “if I really could”, followed by 「〜たい」 or 「〜てみろ」; the volitional form (しよう, 言おう) → “if you were to do it”, followed by a serious consequence.

groups.note: Both express a strong wish

items.title: 〜たいものだ (I'd really love to…)
items.diff: ものなら first supposes “if it were really possible”, stressing that it's hard to achieve; たいものだ directly exclaims “I'd really love to…”.

this.tr: If I could, I'd quit my job right now and travel around the world.

that.tr: After I retire, I'd really love to travel around the world.

items.explain: ものなら comes after a potential form and first admits “this probably can't happen in reality” before stating the wish, with a sense of helplessness; たいものだ at the end of the sentence voices the wish directly, and it isn't necessarily hard to achieve (after retiring, you might really go).

items.diff: ものなら means “if I could…, I'd want to…”; ないものか means “is there really no way to…?”, anxiously searching for a way out.

this.tr: If I could, I'd gladly take my sick daughter's place.

that.tr: Is there really nothing that can cure my daughter's illness?

items.explain: ものなら is a condition and must be followed by a wish (〜たい); ないものか comes at the end of the sentence after a negative form, often with 「何とか」「どうにか」, fretting over “whether there's any way”.

groups.note: ものの ↔ ものを: they differ only in the last kana

items.diff: ものの simply and calmly says “although…”; ものを means “it would have been fine if…, but instead…”, with regret or blame.

this.tr: I did take the medicine, but the fever didn't go down.

that.tr: You should have just gone to the hospital early. It got worse because you tried to tough it out.

items.explain: Only the last kana differs, but the tone is completely different: ものを is often preceded by a supposition like 「〜ばいい」「〜ばよかった」, the speaker lamenting or complaining that the other person didn't do that; ものの is preceded by a fact that already happened, followed by a plain statement that the result fell short of expectations.

groups.note: Both express a contrast: “although…, …”

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: ものの is formal and calm, simply acknowledging the gap; のに is colloquial, with dissatisfaction or surprise.

this.tr: I did buy a new computer, but I've hardly used it.

that.tr: I finally went and bought a new computer, and it broke right away!

items.explain: のに often appears with 「せっかく」 and ends with emotional words like 「よ」「なんて」, showing dissatisfaction or surprise at the result; ものの is mostly used in writing and reports, calmly stating “I did…, but nothing came of it”, with no sense of complaint.

items.title: 〜ながらも (although…)
items.diff: ながらも is mostly preceded by an ongoing state (狭い, 知っている); ものの is mostly preceded by a one-time fact (買った, 合格した).

this.tr: I got into university, but I can't afford the tuition and don't know what to do.

that.tr: The room may be small, but it gets plenty of sunlight.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: an adjective or a state like 「知っている」「子どもながら」 → ながらも, often followed by a positive judgment; an action in the た-form (合格した, 買った) → ものの, mostly followed by a disappointing result.

items.diff: にもかかわらず stresses that something is “unexpected”, with a stronger sense of surprise or dissatisfaction; ものの just calmly acknowledges the gap.

this.tr: I made an effort, but it didn't pay off.

that.tr: Despite the heavy rain, a large crowd turned out for the game.

wrong.why: ものの can't attach directly to a noun (you'd need 「大雨であるものの」)

items.explain: にもかかわらず can attach directly to a noun (大雨にもかかわらず) and is followed by a surprising fact, common in the news; ものの can't attach directly to a noun, is mostly preceded by something that was done and followed by a result that fell short, in a flat tone.

groups.note: Both come from 「いられない」 — “can't stay (in that state)”

items.diff: ないではいられない is “can't stand not doing it” → can't help doing it; てはいられない is “can't stand keeping on doing it” → can't go on…ing any longer.

this.tag: Can't hold back → can't help it
this.tr: Watching that movie, I couldn't help crying.

that.tag: Can't keep on → can't go on…
that.tr: Only three days until the exam. I can't keep goofing off.

items.explain: Look at what comes before いられない: ないでは (negative) → “can't hold back from doing it” ＝ can't help doing it; て／では (affirmative) → “can't keep doing this” ＝ can't go on…ing anymore, often preceded by 「もう」「いつまでも」 and an urgent reason.

groups.note: ないでは＋いられない／すまない／おかない: they differ only in the last word

items.diff: ないではいられない is you yourself “can't help it”; ないではすまない is “not doing it would be unacceptable” by moral or social standards.

this.tr: I felt so sorry for them that I couldn't help speaking to them.

that.tr: I scratched the company president's car, so I can't get away without apologizing.

items.explain: Look at what's driving it: a feeling before it (かわいそうで, おかしくて) → いられない, you can't control yourself; a wrongdoing or responsibility before it (傷つけたのだから) → すまない, morally or socially you have to do it, often unwillingly. (ないではすまない is also written ずにはすまない, with the same meaning.)

items.diff: ないではいられない is a person who can't help doing something; ないではおかない is “will inevitably make people…” or a strong will of “will not rest until…”.

this.tr: Anyone who hears that story can't help laughing.

that.tr: This movie is bound to move anyone who sees it.

items.explain: Look at the subject: the subject of いられない is the person doing the action (誰でも); the subject of おかない is often a thing (この映画は), mostly preceded by a causative form (感動させ, 考えさせ), meaning “inevitably makes people…”; when the subject is a person, it shows a resolve of “I won't rest until…”. (ないではおかない is also written ずにはおかない, with the same meaning.)

groups.note: Both mean “can't help…, can't not…” — pushed along by feelings or circumstances

items.diff: They mean exactly the same; ずにはいられない uses the classical negative 「ず」 and is more formal; ないではいられない is a bit more colloquial.

this.tr: It was just so funny that I couldn't help laughing.

that.tr: It was just so funny that I couldn't help laughing.

wrong.why: する has to become 「せずには」 (or 「しないでは」)

items.explain: The two are interchangeable; it's just that 「ず」 is the classical form of 「ない」, so ずにはいられない is more formal and more common in exams and writing. Watch how する changes: しないでは／せずには.

items.diff: ないではいられない is driven by feeling, involuntary; ないわけにはいかない is “can't not do it” out of reason or obligation.

this.tr: Whenever I see someone in trouble, I can't help lending a hand.

that.tr: The department head invited me, so I can't not go to the drinking party.

items.explain: Look at the reason: a feeling welling up inside (見ると, かわいそうで) → ないではいられない, you actually want to do it; social ties, rules, responsibility (誘われたから, 約束したから) → ないわけにはいかない, often the person doesn't really want to.

items.diff: てたまらない describes the feeling itself as overwhelming: “unbearably…”; ないではいられない describes an action driven by that feeling.

this.tr: I missed him so much that I couldn't help calling him.

that.tr: I miss him so much; he lives so far away.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: てたまらない is preceded by a feeling or sensation (会いたくて, うれしくて, 痛くて), describing an inner state; ないではいられない is preceded by an action (電話をかけ, 泣か), describing something you couldn't stop yourself from doing.

groups.note: ないことには ↔ ないことはない: they differ by just one 「に」

items.diff: ないことには means “unless you first…, it won't work”; ないことはない means “it's not that I can't…”.

this.tr: You can't tell what someone is like until you actually meet them.

that.tr: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I'm not very fond of it.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「こと」: 「には」 is followed by another half-sentence, always negative (分からない, 始まらない) → a prerequisite; 「はない」 ends the sentence directly → a double negative, a roundabout yes, “I can…”, often followed by 「が」「けど」 adding a reservation.

groups.note: Both mean “without…, it won't work” — a prerequisite

items.diff: They're similar in meaning; ないと is colloquial, and anything can follow it; ないことには stresses the prerequisite, can only be followed by something negative, and sounds more serious.

this.tr: Unless the president gives approval, nothing can get started.

that.tr: If you don't leave early, you'll miss the train.

items.explain: ないことには is always followed by a negative like 「できない, 分からない, 始まらない」, stressing “if this condition isn't met, there's nothing more to discuss”; ないと can be followed by all kinds of results (遅れるよ) and can also end a sentence by itself to mean “I need to…” (もう帰らないと).

items.diff: てからでないと focuses on “the order of events”; ないことには focuses on “whether the condition is met”.

this.tr: You won't know the real reason unless you ask the person themselves.

that.tr: We can only ship the goods after confirming payment.

items.explain: てからでないと means “only after doing A can B happen”, with a clear time order between A and B (確認してから→発送); ないことには only cares whether condition A is in place, not the order, as in the common phrase 「やってみないことには分からない」.

items.title: 〜なしでは (no good without…)
items.diff: なしでは follows a noun and focuses on “lacking something”; ないことには follows a verb's negative form and focuses on “not doing some action first”.

this.tr: You won't appreciate how good it is until you actually try using it.

that.tr: Life today is simply unimaginable without a smartphone.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: a noun (スマホ, 許可, あなた) → なしでは; a verb's negative form (使ってみない, 会わない) → ないことには. Both are followed by a negative, and both mean “without it, it won't work”.

groups.note: Both come from 「もの＋か」 — expressed as a rhetorical “as if that would happen?”

items.diff: ないものか means “can't something be done…?”, expressing a wish; ものか after an affirmative form means “I'll never…”.

this.tr: Isn't there some way to deal with this noise?

that.tr: I'm never going to such a noisy shop again!

items.explain: A negative form before it (ならない, できない) → asking “can't it…?” ＝ really wishing it could; an affirmative form before it (行く) → asking “would I ever…?” ＝ never. 「何とか」「どうにか」 signal a wish; 「二度と」「絶対」 signal resolve.

groups.note: Both express a strong wish: “I really hope…”

items.diff: ないかな is a light, colloquial “it'd be nice if…”; ないものか is stronger and more formal, mostly about something hard to achieve that needs a solution.

this.tr: Hoping to somehow cure my back pain of many years, I went from hospital to hospital.

that.tr: I wish the bus would hurry up and come.

items.explain: ないかな is for small everyday hopes (バスが来る, 晴れる), talking to oneself, colloquial; ないものか is often preceded by 「何とか」「どうにか」, hoping for a solution to a long-standing hard problem, often followed by 「と思う」「と考える」, and fairly formal.

items.diff: たいものだ／てほしいものだ use a statement to say directly “I'd really love to… / I really wish…”; ないものか uses a question, with an anxious “is there any way?”.

this.tr: Can't the construction noise next door get a little quieter?

that.tag: てほしいものだ · wishing others would
that.tr: I really wish the construction next door would be a little quieter.

that.tag: たいものだ · wanting to oneself
that.tr: Just once, I'd love to try living in a quiet place in the countryside.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: 「ものだ」 → calmly stating a wish, たいものだ for something you want to do, てほしいものだ for wanting others or the situation to change; 「ないものか」 → a question, like fretfully asking “is there any way?”, often with 「何とか」「もう少し」 before it.

groups.note: All written 「中」 — read なか／じゅう／ちゅう, with different meanings

items.diff: 雨の中（なか）を means “braving…, in the middle of (a situation)”; 一日中（じゅう） means “all through”; 会議中（ちゅう） means “in the middle of (doing)”.

this.tr: I walked to the station in the rain.
Amid the ongoing recession, they increased sales.

that.tr: It rained all day long.
I can't take calls during meetings.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「中」: a noun＋「の」, or an adjective or verb directly (雨の中, 忙しい中, 続く中) → なか, being in some weather or situation; a time or range noun directly (一日中, 世界中) → じゅう “all through”; an action noun directly (会議中, 工事中) → ちゅう “in progress”.

groups.note: Both mean “still doing… despite unfavorable conditions”

items.diff: 中を is acting despite outside conditions like the weather; を押して is pushing through one's own obstacles like illness or opposition, and is more formal.

this.tr: Despite the heavy snow, our guests still came.

that.tr: Despite a high fever, he pushed himself to play in the match.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: conditions anyone might face, like 雨, 雪, 寒さ → 中を, mostly followed by 「来る, 歩く, 出かける」; obstacles of the person themselves, like 病気, けが, 反対 → を押して, stressing “forcing oneself, toughing it out”.

items.thisTitle: 〜中（を） (despite your busy schedule · polite formula)
items.diff: Both can be used when thanking someone; お忙しい中 is a soft polite formula; お忙しいにもかかわらず is a contrast, “despite…, still…”, more formal and stiff.

this.tr: Thank you very much for taking the time to come today despite your busy schedule.

that.tr: We sincerely thank you for your cooperation despite your extremely busy schedule.

items.explain: 「お忙しい中」 simply describes the situation the other person is in and is the most natural polite formula in speeches and emails; 「にもかかわらず」 carries a contrast of “one shouldn't have expected it, yet still…”, is more formal, and can also express dissatisfaction (注意したにもかかわらず、また遅れた).

groups.note: Both come from 「ともかく（兎も角）」 — “setting aside for now”

items.diff: はともかく “sets aside” a topic for now; ならともかく means “if it were…, that'd be understandable”, contrasting with reality and implying criticism.

this.tr: A child, maybe, but a grown adult crying over something like this?

that.tr: Taste aside, this place gives you big portions.

items.explain: はともかく is preceded by a topic (味, 値段) that the speaker just isn't discussing for now, then moves on to what they really want to say; ならともかく is preceded by a hypothetical case (子ども), followed by a different, real case (大人), contrasting the two, usually with dissatisfaction.

groups.note: Both mean “if it were…, that'd be forgivable, but…”

items.diff: They mean almost the same and are interchangeable in most cases; ともかく literally means “setting aside”, まだしも literally means “would still be OK”.

this.tr: Once or twice is one thing, but being late every day is a problem.

that.tr: Once or twice would be acceptable, but being late every day is a problem.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable; read both as “A is acceptable, but B isn't”. The difference is only in the literal meaning: ともかく is “let's not press A”, まだしも is “A is still better than B”, so まだしも hints more that “A isn't great either”.

items.diff: ならいざしらず is mostly preceded by a special or extreme case, and is more formal and stiff.

this.tr: A beginner, maybe, but for a pro to make a mistake like this?

that.tr: God may be another matter, but there's no way a human can know the future.

items.explain: いざしらず literally means “who can say”, often preceded by cases far removed from reality like 神様 or 昔, and mostly found in writing; ともかく is preceded by ordinary cases close to home (初心者, 子ども) and is also common in speech.

groups.note: Both come from the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 — ね, ぬ and ざる are all forms of it

items.diff: The 「ね」 in ねばならない and 「〜ぬ」 are both forms of 「ず」: ねば＝なければ, ぬ＝ない.

this.tr: Promises must be kept.

that.tr: Before I knew it, dawn had broken.

items.explain: Classical 「ず」 has several forms: ぬ (modifying a noun or ending a sentence), ね (followed by 「ば」), ざる (followed by a noun). So 「守らねばならない」 is just 「守らなければならない」, and 「知らぬ間に」 is just 「知らない間に」. Read ね・ぬ as 「ない」 and the meaning becomes clear.

items.diff: ねばならない means “must”, whether duty or resolve; ざるを得ない means “forced by circumstances to…”, with a sense of resignation.

this.tr: As the leader, I must take responsibility.

that.tr: Because of the typhoon, we have no choice but to cancel the trip.

items.explain: Both use 「ず」: ね＋ば＝“if not… (it won't do)”, ざる＋を得ない＝“can't manage to ‘not…’”. Look at the reason: one's position or responsibility → ねばならない; outside circumstances like a typhoon or budget forcing you to do something you'd rather not → ざるを得ない.

groups.note: Both mean “must, have to”

items.diff: Same structure and meaning; なければならない is the standard modern form, ねばならない is the classical form and more solemn.

this.tr: We must tackle this problem seriously.

that.tr: I have to get up at six tomorrow.

items.explain: Exactly the same meaning; look at the setting: speeches, editorials, writing, or wanting to sound solemn → ねばならない; everyday speech → なければならない (colloquially also 「なきゃ」). Using ねばならない for small everyday things sounds exaggerated, a bit humorous.

items.diff: べきだ means “should” by reason, carrying the speaker's opinion; ねばならない means “it has to be this way”, stressing necessity.

this.tr: I have to submit this document by tomorrow.

that.tr: You should gain lots of different experiences while you're young.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a hard reason that “it won't do otherwise”: a deadline, rule or responsibility → ねばならない; just the speaker feeling “this is the right thing” or giving advice → べきだ. Not doing what べきだ says has no immediate consequence; not doing what ねばならない says isn't an option.

groups.note: Both mean “worthy of…”

items.diff: に足る means “qualified, sufficient for”, focusing on whether the conditions are enough; に値する means “has the value”, focusing on whether it's worth it.

this.tr: His courageous act deserves praise.

that.tr: He is a person fully worthy of trust.

items.explain: The two are often interchangeable with words like 「信頼, 尊敬」. に足る often goes with 「十分」, appears in phrases like 「取るに足らない」 (not worth mentioning), and mostly modifies a noun (信頼に足る人物); に値する mostly follows evaluative nouns like 「称賛, 注目, 一読」, judging “whether it's worth it”.

items.diff: に堪える means “able to withstand…, up to that standard”; に値する means “worth (doing)”.

this.tr: This paper is worth reading.

that.tr: It's an amateur's work, but it's well worth viewing.

items.explain: に堪える stresses “reaching a level where it can…”, often preceded by a concession like 「素人だが」「古いが」, with common phrases like 「鑑賞に堪える, 読むに堪える, 批判に堪える」; に値する judges value and carries no sense of “just barely qualifying”.

groups.note: Both come from 「当たる」 — originally “to face directly, to hit”

items.diff: にあたって means “on the occasion of…”, followed by what's done for it; に当たる means “corresponds to, falls on”, showing a correspondence.

this.tag: On the occasion · doing something for it
this.tr: When I went to study abroad, I prepared lots of documents.

that.tr: Today happens to be the anniversary of my grandfather's death.

items.explain: The original meaning of 「当たる」 is “to line up exactly”: にあたって is “hitting this exact moment”, followed by an action taken for it (準備した, 挨拶する); に当たる comes at the end of the sentence and says two things match up exactly (今日＝命日).

groups.note: Both mean “when… / on the occasion of…”

items.diff: にあたって is mostly used for things you're about to undertake and need to prepare for; に際して only says “at that time”, and is also common for sudden events.

this.tr: When opening the new shop, I went around greeting the neighbors.

that.tr: In the event of an earthquake or fire, please do not use the elevator.

items.explain: Look at the event before it: things you're about to undertake and prepare for, like opening a shop, studying abroad or a competition → both にあたって and に際して work; sudden events you didn't plan, like an earthquake or fire → mostly に際して, while にあたって sounds unnatural. にあたり and に際し are more formal versions.

items.diff: 際（に） can be used for ordinary things (getting off a train, when using something); にあたって is only for important, special occasions.

this.tr: On taking office, the new president spoke about his aspirations.

that.tr: Please watch your step when getting off.

items.explain: Look at how weighty the event is: major life or organizational events like 入学, 就任, 開業 → にあたって; everyday situations like getting off, using something or going out → 際（に）, with 「〜の際は」 common in announcements and notices.

items.diff: に先立って clearly means “doing it before…”; にあたって focuses on “facing this moment”, without stressing what comes first.

this.tr: At the opening of the meeting, the chairman gave a speech.

that.tr: Before the opening, everyone observed a moment of silence.

items.explain: With に先立って, what follows is always done before the first event (silence first, then the opening), also written 「〜に先立ち」; with にあたって, what follows is mostly the opening act of or preparation for that moment, without stressing what comes first.

groups.note: Both come from 「ほか（外・他）」 — “other, besides”

items.diff: にほかならない means “nothing other than…, precisely…”; ほかない means “there's no other way but to…”.

this.tr: His success is nothing other than the result of hard work.

that.tag: No choice · nothing else to do
that.tr: I missed the last train, so I have no choice but to walk home.

items.explain: It's the same 「ほか」 (other): にほかならない＝“not anything else” → a firm “precisely”, mostly after a noun; ほかない＝“no other (way)” → a resigned “have no choice but to”, after a verb dictionary form. Check whether a noun or a verb comes before it to tell them apart.

groups.note: Both are used to stress “precisely…”

items.diff: こそ sits mid-sentence and highlights one item; にほかならない comes at the end as a judgment, with a stronger formal, argumentative feel.

this.tr: The cause of this failure is nothing other than a lack of preparation.

that.tr: Preparation is the very key to success.

items.explain: Look at the position: こそ comes right after the word being stressed (準備こそ, 今度こそ), is common in both speech and writing, and carries feeling; にほかならない comes at the end, and 「AはBにほかならない」 is a calm conclusion, mostly found in papers and speeches.

items.diff: Both stress “precisely because…”; からこそ carries feeling and is common in speech and writing; からにほかならない is more formal, a calm explanation.

this.tr: The reason he was able to win is precisely that he kept practicing every day.

that.tr: It's precisely because he kept practicing every day that he won!

items.explain: からにほかならない is usually in the pattern 「〜のは〜からにほかならない」, with the result first and the cause at the end; からこそ puts the cause first and the result after, often ending with 「のだ」「んだ」, carrying the speaker's feelings.

items.diff: でなくてなんだろう stresses with a rhetorical “if this isn't…, what is?”, with strong emotion; にほかならない is a calm, firm judgment.

this.tr: This isn't luck; it's nothing other than the result of hard work.

that.tr: The two of them meeting again: if that isn't fate, what is?

items.explain: でなくてなんだろう is mostly preceded by lyrical words like 「運命, 愛, 奇跡」 and is common in novels and essays; にほかならない is used in arguments and explanations, with a calm, objective tone.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit”

items.diff: に限らず means “not limited to…”, widening the scope; に限り means “only…”, narrowing the scope.

this.tr: This service isn't limited to members; anyone can use it.

that.tr: This service is free to use for members only.

items.explain: Only the last character differs: 限らず (negative) ＝ not setting a limit → often followed by 「誰でも」「〜も」; 限り (affirmative) ＝ limited to just this → followed by special treatment (無料, 割引), common in notices.

items.diff: Same meaning, both “not only…”; に限ったことではない comes at the end of the sentence and is mostly used to point out that a problem is widespread.

this.tr: The falling birth rate has become a problem not only in Japan but in many countries.

that.tag: Sentence end · pointing out it's widespread
that.tr: The falling birth rate isn't just Japan's problem.

items.explain: Look at the position: に限らず sits mid-sentence, followed by the wider scope (多くの国で…); に限ったことではない ends the sentence and is often used to say “this happens elsewhere too”, as in 「彼の遅刻は今日に限ったことではない」 (it's not just today that he's late).

groups.note: Both mean “not only… (but also)”

items.diff: だけでなく is the most common in speech and attaches to all kinds of words; に限らず is more formal, only follows nouns, and focuses on “not restricted to this scope”.

this.tr: Not just children but adults too can enjoy this festival.

that.tr: She's not only a good singer, she's a great dancer too.

wrong.why: に限らず only follows nouns

items.explain: に限らず can only be preceded by a noun (子ども, 日本, 週末), meaning “not just this category”; だけでなく can be preceded by adjectives and verbs (上手な, 歌う), and is often used to list several aspects of a person or thing.

items.diff: のみならず is more formal and can follow nouns, verbs and adjectives; に限らず only follows nouns.

this.tr: Environmental problems aren't limited to developed countries; they're a challenge for the whole world.

that.tr: He is not only an excellent researcher but also an outstanding educator.

items.explain: のみならず is the formal version of 「だけでなく」, can be preceded by all kinds of forms like 「である」「した」, and often describes two aspects of the same subject; に限らず only follows nouns and talks about the scope of the subject being “not just this category” (先進国→世界全体).

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit”

items.diff: In the sense of “only”, the two are the same; に限り only expresses a limit and is more formal; に限って also has emotional uses like “of all times…” and “surely not…”.

this.tr: Today only, everything is half price.

that.tr: Of all days, the train is late on the day I'm in a hurry.

items.explain: に限り appears almost only in ads and notices (本日に限り, 先着100名様に限り), followed by special treatment; に限って is often preceded by 「〜時, 〜日」 or a person, followed by something unwelcome or 「〜はずがない」, carrying the speaker's feelings.

items.diff: に限り sits mid-sentence and means “only”; に限る mostly comes at the end of the sentence, often meaning “…is best”.

this.tr: A small gift for the first 50 customers only.

that.tr: When you're tired, sleep is the best thing.

items.explain: Look at the position: 限り has another half-sentence after it, followed by special treatment; 限る ends the sentence, preceded by a method or thing (寝る, ビール), the speaker's claim from experience: “nothing beats…”. Only in regulations does 「〜者に限る」 mean “only”.

items.diff: に限り means “only”, narrowing the scope; に限らず means “not limited to”, widening the scope.

this.tr: Admission is free for students only.

that.tr: At this museum, not just students but anyone can get in free.

items.explain: Only the last character differs: 限り (affirmative) → only these people; 限らず (negative) → not only these people, often followed by 「誰でも」「〜も」.

groups.note: Both mean “only, just”

items.diff: Same meaning; だけ is the most ordinary, used in speech and writing; に限り is the formal word in notices and ads, mostly followed by special treatment.

this.tr: Today only, coffee is half price.

that.tr: I heard coffee is half price today only.

items.explain: Shop signs, announcements and official notices use に限り, which is more formal; chatting with friends uses だけ. だけ can be used for any limit (一人だけ, 少しだけ), while に限り is only used to say “who gets special treatment, or when”.

items.diff: のみ is a formal “only, just”, a simple limit; に限り stresses “only those who meet the condition get special treatment or an exception”.

this.tr: Only in case of rain will it be held indoors.

that.tr: Beyond this point, authorized personnel only.

items.explain: のみ just fixes the scope (関係者のみ, 現金のみ), common in rules; に限り is mostly followed by an arrangement or deal that doesn't normally apply (雨天の場合に限り室内で, 本日に限り半額), like “opening up an exception”.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit”; from “limited to just this” came “this is the best”

items.diff: に限る mostly comes at the end of a sentence, meaning “…is best”; に限り sits mid-sentence and only means “only”.

this.tr: In summer, nothing beats an ice-cold beer.

that.tr: Today only, beer is half price.

items.explain: に限る ends the sentence, preceded by a method or thing the speaker recommends, a claim from experience; に限り has another half-sentence after it and is a limiting condition in notices. Only when regulations say 「〜者に限る」 does に限る mean “only”.

items.diff: に限る means “…is best”; に限って means “of all times…”, with annoyance.

this.tr: When you have a cold, it's best to go to bed early.

that.tr: Of all days, the day I want to go to bed early is the day my work won't end.

items.explain: に限る comes at the end and is a recommendation; に限って sits mid-sentence and is followed by something unwelcome, with 「〜日に限って」「〜時に限って」 as the typical phrases.

groups.note: Both mean “…is best”

items.diff: に越したことはない means “…would of course be best (but it's not essential)”, more rational; に限る is a subjective declaration: “this is the best”.

this.tr: When you're tired, nothing beats a hot spring.

that.tr: More money is of course better, but money alone can't make you happy.

items.explain: に越したことはない is often preceded by conditions everyone agrees on, like 「早い, 多い, 安全な」, often followed by 「が」 adding “but…”; に限る is preceded by the speaker's own choice (温泉, 寝る), in a confident tone, like a recommendation.

items.diff: ほうがいい is advice for the listener's specific situation; に限る is a subjective claim from personal experience, mostly speaking in general terms.

this.tr: When something upsetting happens, the best thing is to sleep on it.

that.tr: If you have a fever, you'd better go to bed early today.

items.explain: ほうがいい is usually said to the person in front of you (〜なら、〜たほうがいいよ), specific advice; に限る mostly begins with 「〜時は」「〜ことがあったら」 and is the speaker's life experience, a general claim.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to set a limit”

items.diff: In the sense of “only”, the two are the same; に限って can also mean “of all times…” or “surely not (this one)”, while に限り is just a dry limit.

this.tr: My child would never do something like that.

that.tr: Free admission for elementary school students only.

items.explain: When に限って is preceded by a person and followed by 「〜はずがない」, it shows trust in that person; に限り only appears in notices and rules, followed by a deal or exception.

items.diff: に限って sits mid-sentence and often means “of all times…”; に限る comes at the end of a sentence and means “…is best”.

this.tr: Of all days, it rains on the day I didn't bring an umbrella.

that.tr: On rainy days, nothing beats watching movies at home.

items.explain: に限る ends the sentence, preceded by a method the speaker recommends; に限って has another half-sentence after it, followed by a bit of bad luck, often preceded by 「〜日, 〜時」.

items.diff: に限って means “this time, of all times”; に限らず means “not just this time”.

this.tr: Of all days, he was late on the day of the important meeting.

that.tr: It's not just today; he's always late.

items.explain: Just one character apart, with opposite meanings: 限って＝only this one time (and precisely when nothing should go wrong); 限らず＝not limited to this time, often followed by 「いつも」「〜も」.

groups.note: Both come from 「かかる（掛かる）」 — “to hang, to fall on…”

items.title: 〜にかかったら (once it's in his hands…)
items.diff: にかかっている means “it all depends on…”; にかかったら means “once it gets into (someone's) hands (it's easily handled)”.

this.tr: The outcome of the game depends entirely on the ace's form.

that.tr: Once he gets his hands on it, any hard problem is solved in no time.

items.explain: It's the same 「かかる」 (to fall on…): にかかっている＝the result “hangs” on this factor, with subjects like 「成功, 結果, 勝敗」; にかかったら＝a matter “falls into” someone's hands, preceded by a person, followed by how capable that person is (or how helpless others are against them).

groups.note: Both mean “depends on…”

items.title: 〜次第だ (depends on)
items.diff: 次第だ is more colloquial and common; にかかっている carries the image of “everything hinges on this”, sounding more serious and weighty.

this.tr: The company's future depends on the hard work of its young employees.

that.tr: Whether you pass or not comes down to how motivated you are.

items.explain: The two are often interchangeable. 次第だ attaches directly to a noun and is very common in everyday speech; にかかっている is often used as 「〜の肩にかかっている」「〜かどうかにかかっている」, with a sense of weight, “the whole burden rests on this”, mostly for big matters like success or failure, or someone's future.

items.title: 〜によって (varies with…)
items.diff: によって means “differs depending on…”; にかかっている means “success or failure hinges entirely on this one point”.

this.tr: Whether it succeeds depends entirely on the weather.

that.tr: The game's start time will change depending on the weather.

items.explain: によって is often followed by 「違う, 変わる, 異なる」, saying there are several possible outcomes that vary with circumstances; にかかっている is concerned with “will it succeed or not”, often preceded by 「〜かどうかは」, with the outcome depending on this single factor.

groups.note: Both come from 「関わる（かかわる）」 — “to be involved, to be related”

items.diff: にかかわらず means “regardless of…”; with an extra 「も」, にもかかわらず means “despite…”.

this.tr: The game will be held whether or not it rains.

that.tr: Despite the heavy rain, the game was held.

items.explain: Look at whether the first part is an established fact: several possibilities before it (降る降らない, 天候, 年齢) → にかかわらず, mostly followed by a rule or plan; an established fact before it (大雨) → にもかかわらず, followed by an unexpected result, usually in the past tense. 「も」＝“even this…”, which turns it into a contrast.

items.diff: にかかわらず means “unrelated to…, regardless of…”; the affirmative にかかわる means “affects…, concerns…”.

this.tr: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.

that.tr: This is a matter of life and death.

items.explain: It's the same 「関わる」: the negative かかわらず＝not involved → “regardless”, preceded by words with several possibilities like 「年齢, 天候」; the affirmative かかわる＝involved → “affecting (something serious)”, mostly preceded by 「命, 将来, 名誉」.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…, no matter…”

items.diff: They mean almost the same; を問わず is more formal, mostly used in job ads and recruiting, usually preceded by paired nouns.

this.tag: Verb: doing / not doing side by side
this.tr: Whether or not you'll attend, please be sure to reply.

that.tr: We are hiring staff regardless of age or gender.

items.explain: を問わず literally means “not asking about”, often preceded by nouns like 「年齢, 性別, 国籍, 昼夜, 男女」, and is most common in job ads; for a verb's affirmative and negative side by side, like 「する・しない」, にかかわらず is generally used.

items.diff: によらず means “not judged by…, not depending on…”, and also appears in set phrases like 「見かけによらず」.

this.tr: Whatever the weather, the event will go ahead as planned.

that.tr: He may not look it, but he's really strong.

items.explain: The 「よる」 in によらず means “to be based on”, so the point is “not judging or deciding based on…”; the set phrases 「見かけによらず」 (you can't judge by appearances) and 「何事によらず」 (no matter what it is) can't be replaced with にかかわらず; にかかわらず is preceded by words with several possibilities (天候, 年齢), saying that none of them makes a difference.

items.diff: (よ)うが〜まいが also means “whether you do it or not”, but with a feeling of “suit yourself, I don't care”.

this.tr: Whether or not you go, the cost will be split among everyone.

that.tr: Whether you go or not has nothing to do with me.

items.explain: にかかわらず is calm and objective, mostly used in rules and notices; (よ)うが〜まいが repeats the same verb in the volitional form and with 「まい」, carrying a feeling of “suit yourself, I don't care”, often followed by 「関係ない」「勝手だ」.

groups.note: Both come from 「関わる（かかわる）」 — “to be involved, to be related”

items.diff: にかかわりなく means “unrelated to…”; にかかわる means “affects…”.

this.tr: Anyone can get this illness, regardless of age.

that.tr: If it isn't treated early, it could be life-threatening.

items.explain: The same root: かかわり＋なく＝no connection → “regardless”; かかわる＝connected → “affects”, mostly preceded by serious things like 「命, 将来, 名誉」, with a grave tone.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…, no matter…”

items.diff: を問わず is mostly used in job ads and recruiting, usually preceded by paired or categorizable nouns; にかかわりなく also often follows 「する・しない」 side by side.

this.tr: Whether or not you attend, the materials will be handed out to everyone.

that.tr: We are accepting international students of any nationality.

items.explain: を問わず literally means “not asking about” and is most common in job ads and recruiting, preceded by nouns like 「国籍, 年齢, 男女, 昼夜」; にかかわりなく is mostly used in rules and notices and can be preceded by a verb's 「する・しない」.

groups.note: Both come from 「関わる（かかわる）」 — “to be involved, to be related”

items.diff: にかかわる means “affects…”; the negative にかかわらず means “regardless of…”.

this.tr: Lack of sleep affects your health.

that.tr: I go running every morning, whatever the weather.

items.explain: Look at whether it's affirmative or negative: かかわる (involved) → affects, has a bearing on, mostly preceded by 「命, 健康, 名誉」; かかわらず (not involved) → unaffected, regardless, preceded by words with several possibilities like 「天候, 年齢」, and followed by another half-sentence.

groups.note: Both mean “related to…”

items.diff: に関する only marks a topic: “about…”; にかかわる means an actual connection or serious impact, with a heavier tone.

this.tr: This is a matter that affects the company's reputation.

that.tr: I read a book about the company's history.

items.explain: Look at the noun that follows and the tone: 「〜にかかわる問題, 病気」 means “affecting, endangering”, mostly preceded by life, reputation or the future; 「〜に関する本, 資料, 質問」 only says what the content is about, with no sense of seriousness. に関して works the same way.

groups.note: にかけては ↔ にかけて: they differ by just one 「は」

items.diff: にかけては means “when it comes to… (no one can beat)”; から〜にかけて means “from… through…”, describing a range.

this.tr: When it comes to cooking, no one can beat my mother.

that.tr: Heavy rain is expected from the Kanto region through Tohoku.

items.explain: First check whether 「から」 comes before it and whether it's a place name or a time (関東から東北, 夜から朝) — that's marking out a range; then check for 「は」: にかけては is preceded by a skill or field (料理, 数学), and the second half is praise like “no one can beat…”.

groups.note: Both single out one field to talk about: “in terms of…”

items.diff: 点で neutrally points out “on the point of…”, for good or bad; にかけては is only used to praise ability: “when it comes to…, the best”.

this.tr: When it comes to speed, no one in his class can beat him.

that.tr: This car is disappointing when it comes to price.

items.explain: Look at the judgment in the second half: praising someone's ability, like 「誰にも負けない」「右に出る者はいない」 → にかけては; an ordinary judgment that can be good or bad, like 「不満がある」「優れている」, where the subject can also be a thing → 点で (after a clause, 「という点で」). にかけては isn't used to talk about weaknesses.

items.diff: にかけては says someone has “the greatest ability” in this area; こととなると says that whenever the topic comes up, “their attitude changes”.

this.tr: When it comes to fishing, my brother is second to none.

that.tr: Whenever fishing comes up, my brother gets so absorbed he's like a different person.

items.explain: Both sentences are 「釣り＋……」; look at the second half: talking about ability or skill level (誰にも負けない, 一番だ) → にかけては; talking about losing one's usual self whenever the topic comes up (夢中になる, 目の色が変わる) → こととなると (ことになると works the same way).

groups.note: Both mean “…is best”

items.diff: に越したことはない states common sense: “of course … is best (but it's fine if you can't)”; に限る is the speaker's own strong opinion: “… is the best, period”.

this.tr: Of course the more money you have for a trip, the better, but you can still have fun with less.

that.tr: When you're tired, nothing beats a good long sleep at home.

items.explain: Look at what follows: に越したことはない is often followed by 「が、〜」 — it first grants “of course that's best”, then adds “but it's fine if you can't”; it states something everyone accepts. に限る often comes with 「やっぱり」 and is a conclusion the speaker draws from their own experience; the sentence ends there, leaving no room.

items.diff: ほうがいい directly advises the listener: “you'd better…”; に越したことはない is a general truth: “of course … is best”, not aimed at anyone in particular.

this.tr: Generally speaking, the more sleep you get, the better.

that.tag: Advising the person in front of you
that.tr: If you have a fever, you'd better go to bed early today.

items.explain: Look at who it's said to: advice tailored to this person's specific situation (熱があるなら) → ほうがいい; a truth or bit of common sense that holds for anyone → に越したことはない. Saying 「早く寝るに越したことはない」 to a friend with a fever sounds like a lecture on general principles.

groups.note: Both mean acting in line with someone's expectations or requests

items.diff: にこたえて means repaying expectations with action — “living up to them”; に応じて means adjusting to someone's request or situation — “adapting accordingly”.

this.tr: To meet our customers' requests, we created a new menu.

that.tag: おうじて · adjusting to requests
that.tr: We adjust portion sizes to suit our customers' requests.

wrong.why: 応える only takes expectations, requests or support before it; for quantities that vary, like the number of people, use に応じて

items.explain: When what comes before is 「要望、リクエスト」, both work: にこたえて stresses making an effort to fulfil them, not letting people down, and is followed by something accomplished (新しいメニューを作った); に応じて stresses flexibly adapting to the request and is often followed by 「変える、対応する」. When what comes before is a varying quantity like 「人数、年齢、収入」 → only に応じて. Don't mix up the readings, either: 応えて＝こたえて, 応じて＝おうじて.

items.diff: にこたえて is a positive response, working to “fulfil” expectations; に沿って means “not straying from” a policy or wish and following it.

this.tr: The players lived up to their fans' expectations and won the championship in fine style.

that.tr: We drew up a new plan in line with company policy.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: hopes others place in you, like 「期待、声援」, followed by results that repay them → にこたえて; a set course like 「方針、計画、マニュアル」, followed by acting accordingly → に沿って. Both 「ご希望に沿って」 and 「ご希望にこたえて」 are fine, but 「方針にこたえて」 sounds unnatural.

groups.note: Both add something on: “not only… but also…”

items.diff: 上に attaches directly to adjectives and verbs and often carries the speaker's judgment; に加えて mainly attaches to nouns and is objective and formal.

this.tr: On top of its low prices, this shop also has good service.

that.tr: This shop is not only cheap, but has good service too.

wrong.why: The adjective must first become a noun (安さ) or take 「こと」

items.explain: Look at the word before it: a noun (安さ、大雨、経験) → に加えて; an adjective or verb (安い、降る) → 上に. To use に加えて with an adjective, you first have to turn it into 「安さ」 or say 「安いことに加えて」.

items.diff: だけでなく is common in both speech and writing; に加えて is more formal and objective, like news or notices “adding one more item”.

this.tr: Due to the typhoon, in addition to heavy rain, strong winds also require caution.

that.tr: It's not just raining today — it's really windy too, isn't it?

items.explain: Look at the setting: formal texts like weather forecasts, news and notices (〜の影響で、注意が必要です) → に加えて; chatting with friends (〜よね) → だけでなく, which in speech is often だけじゃなくて. だけでなく can also attach directly to verbs and adjectives (安いだけでなく); に加えて can't.

groups.note: Both come from 「かかわる（関わる）＋ず」 — “not affected by…”

items.diff: にもかかわらず means “despite (something that's already the case)…”; にかかわらず, without the 「も」, means “regardless of…”.

this.tr: Despite the heavy rain, the match went ahead.

that.tr: The match will go ahead regardless of the weather.

items.explain: The only difference is one 「も」. Look at what comes before: 「大雨」 is a specific fact that has already happened, followed by an unexpected result → にもかかわらず; words that can take various values, like 「天気」「年齢」「晴雨」, meaning it's the same whatever the case → にかかわらず.

groups.note: Both express contrast: “although…, still…”

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: にもかかわらず is written language, saying “despite…” objectively; のに is spoken, carrying personal dissatisfaction or surprise.

this.tr: Despite the rain today, a great many people came.

that.tr: Even though it was raining, so many people came for us.

items.explain: Look at the setting: formal occasions like speeches, news and reports (本日、お越しいただきました) → にもかかわらず; talking among friends, with feelings of happiness or dissatisfaction → のに. With nouns, にもかかわらず attaches directly (雨にもかかわらず), while のに needs 「な」 (雨なのに).

groups.note: Both come from 「もと（基）」 — “root, foundation”

items.diff: に基づいて means strictly “basing” a judgment on facts or rules; をもとに means using something as “material” to then rework or create from.

this.tr: We made a new plan based on the survey results.

that.tr: I wrote a novel based on a real incident.

items.explain: Look at what the second half does: making judgments or plans according to data or law, where the content can't stray from the basis → に基づいて; using it as raw material for a novel or film, which can be freely adapted → をもとに. 基づく itself is 「基（もと）＋付く」: stuck close to the foundation.

groups.note: Both mean “according to, based on…”

items.diff: に基づいて takes facts, data or laws as its “basis”; に沿って follows the “route” of a policy or plan.

this.tr: We improved the product based on the questionnaire results.

that.tr: We improved the product in line with company policy.

items.explain: The two sentences only swap the basis: things that can serve as evidence, like 「結果、データ、法律、事実」 → に基づいて; things that set a direction or route to follow, like 「方針、計画、マニュアル、ご希望」 → に沿って. 沿って can also be used literally, as in 「川に沿って歩く」 (walk along the river); 基づいて can't.

groups.note: Both come from 「向く」 — “to face”

items.diff: に向かって means you yourself are “heading toward” or facing something; に向けて means preparing “for” an upcoming goal, or directing something at someone.

this.tr: We walked slowly toward the summit.

that.tr: I'm practising every day for next month's match.

items.explain: 向かう is intransitive: you move toward a direction or face someone (頂上に向かって歩く、客に向かって話す); 向ける is transitive: you direct effort or a message at something, and it's often preceded by a goal that hasn't arrived yet, like 「来月の試合」「〜の実現」, followed by 「準備」「練習」. Check whether what comes before is a place or person, or a future event.

items.diff: 子どもに向かって means doing something “facing the child”; 子ども向け means “designed for children”.

this.tr: She spoke to the child in a loud voice.

that.tr: This is a book for children.

items.explain: Check whether there's a 「に」 and what follows: 「に向かって＋action」 means doing something while facing the other person; 「向け」 attaches directly to a noun (no に) and is followed by 「の＋noun」 (子ども向けの本、海外向けの商品), saying who the thing is made for.

groups.note: Both mark who or what an action or attitude is directed at

items.diff: に向かって means “facing” someone in person; に対して marks the target an action or attitude is “directed at”, which can be quite abstract.

this.tr: You must not say rude things to a customer's face.

that.tr: I answered the customer's question politely.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a person you're actually facing while speaking or bowing (親に向かって、客に向かって) → に向かって; abstract things like questions, opinions and policies → に対して; you can't say 「質問に向かって」.

groups.note: Both come from 「向く」 — “to face”

items.diff: に向けて means preparing “for” an upcoming goal, or directing something at someone; に向かって means you yourself are “heading toward” or facing something.

this.tr: I'm practising every day for next month's match.

that.tr: We walked slowly toward the summit.

items.explain: 向ける is transitive: you direct effort or a message at something, and it's often preceded by a goal that hasn't arrived yet, like 「来月の試合」「〜の実現」, followed by 「準備」「練習」; 向かう is intransitive: you move toward a direction or face someone (頂上に向かって歩く、客に向かって話す). Check whether what comes before is a future event, or a place or person.

items.diff: に向けて is followed by an action, “sending toward…”; 向け attaches directly to a noun, meaning “designed for…”.

this.tr: We're promoting Japanese culture to audiences overseas.

that.tr: This is a product for overseas markets.

items.explain: Look at what follows: 「に向けて」 is followed by an action (発信する、準備する); 「向け」 has no 「に」, attaches directly to a noun, and then modifies a noun with 「の」 (海外向けの商品、子ども向けの本), saying who the thing is made for.

groups.note: Both mean “for (the purpose of)…”

items.title: 〜ために (purpose)
items.diff: に向けて only takes nouns and stresses step-by-step preparation for a day that's coming; ために can take verbs and simply states a purpose.

this.tr: I'm studying every day for next month's exam.

that.tr: I'm studying every day to pass the exam.

wrong.why: に向けて can't attach directly to a verb

items.explain: Look at what comes before: nouns like 「試験」「オリンピック」「〜の実現」 for an event coming up on some future date → に向けて; verbs like 「合格する」「やせる」 → ために (with nouns, add 「の」: 健康のために).

groups.note: Both correspond to 「で」 marking a place or occasion

items.diff: で is the everyday form; において is its formal, written version, used for ceremonies, meetings and academic papers.

this.tr: The general shareholders' meeting will be held in the conference room at head office.

that.tr: Let's eat lunch in the meeting room.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the verb that follows: announcements of ceremonies, meetings or competitions (開催いたします、行われます) → において; everyday matters → で. To modify a noun, において becomes 「における」 (日本における教育), and で becomes 「での」.

items.diff: において can also mean “in the field or area of…”; にて is mostly used in notices for a place or means (メールにて).

this.tr: In modern society, English is indispensable.

that.tr: We will notify you of the results by email.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: fields or areas like 「社会、教育、経済」 → において (にて has no such use); means like 「メール、書面、電話」, or a place given in a notice (受付にて) → にて. Both are written language; にて reads more like a set phrase in notices and letters.

groups.note: Both mean producing a corresponding result according to the preceding situation or request

items.title: 〜によって (varies with…)
items.diff: に応じて means actively “adjusting according to…”; によって means objectively “differing depending on…”.

this.tr: We set our fees according to age.

that.tr: Fees differ by age.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the verb in the second half: adjusting accordingly, with verbs like 「変える」「決める」「選ぶ」 → に応じて; describing a difference that objectively exists, with 「違う」「異なる」「さまざまだ」 → によって.

items.title: 〜次第で (depending on…)
items.diff: に応じて means adjusting in proportion to “how much or to what degree…”; 次第で means “it all depends on…” — whether the outcome is good or bad is decided entirely by it.

this.tr: The scholarship amount is set according to your grades.

that.tag: All depends on it · decides success
that.tr: With enough effort, anyone can get good at it.

items.explain: Look at the second half: proportional or tiered adjustments like 「金額が決まる」「量を変える」 → に応じて; outcomes like 「できる／できない」 or whether you succeed, governed entirely by that one factor → 次第で, often rendered “it all depends on…”.

items.diff: に応じて means adjusting to someone's request or situation — “adapting accordingly”; にこたえて means repaying expectations with action — “living up to them”.

this.tag: おうじて · adjusting to requests
this.tr: We adjust portion sizes to suit our customers' requests.

that.tr: To meet our customers' requests, we created a new menu.

wrong.why: 応える only takes expectations, requests or support before it; for quantities that vary, like the number of people, use に応じて

items.explain: When what comes before is 「要望、リクエスト」, both work: に応じて stresses flexibly adapting to the request and is often followed by 「変える、対応する」; にこたえて stresses making an effort to fulfil them, not letting people down, and is followed by something accomplished (新しいメニューを作った). When what comes before is a varying quantity like 「人数、年齢、収入」 → only に応じて. Don't mix up the readings, either: 応じて＝おうじて, 応えて＝こたえて.

groups.note: Both come from 「際（さい）」 — “when…, on the occasion of…”

items.diff: の際 is the general “when…”; に際して is used for important, out-of-the-ordinary occasions and is more solemn.

this.tr: On the occasion of my marriage, I wrote my parents a letter of thanks.

that.tr: When leaving, please be careful not to forget your belongings.

items.explain: Look at the event before it: rare, major events like marriage, going abroad, starting school or signing a contract → に際して (attaches directly to the noun); everyday things like going home, using something or paying → 「〜の際（に／は）」, often seen on notices in shops and stations.

groups.note: Both mean “on the occasion of…”

items.diff: にあたって is mostly used for something you're about to undertake and need to prepare for; に際して just means “at that time” and is also common for things that happen suddenly.

this.tr: In the event of an earthquake or fire, please do not use the elevator.

that.tr: When opening my new shop, I went around greeting the neighbours.

items.explain: Look at the event before it: something you set out to do and need to prepare for, like opening a shop, studying abroad or a competition → both にあたって and に際して work; something sudden that you didn't arrange, like an earthquake or fire → mostly に際して, while にあたって sounds a bit unnatural. にあたり and に際し are even more formal versions.

groups.note: Both mean “before…”

items.diff: に先立って means doing something first, “ahead of” something in time; に先駆けて means “ahead of others or other places”, taking the lead.

this.tr: Ahead of the new product's launch, a briefing session was held.

that.tr: This town introduced the new system ahead of the rest of the country.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a single event like 「発売、会議、試合」 → mostly に先立って, saying another thing is done before it; others or other places, like 「全国、他社、世界」 → mostly に先駆けて, stressing getting a step ahead of them. A way to remember: 先＋立つ＝standing at the front, 先＋駆ける＝running at the front.

items.diff: 前に works in any situation; に先立って is written language, for things done before an important event.

this.tr: Ahead of the opening ceremony, a press conference was held.

that.tr: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

items.explain: Look at the event before it: important events like an opening ceremony, a launch or an official match, followed by formal preparations or preliminary events → に先立って; small everyday things like sleeping or eating → only 前に; saying 「寝るに先立って」 sounds comical.

groups.note: Both are concessive: whatever the case, the conclusion stays the same

items.diff: にしろ raises just one case: “even if…”; 〜にしろ〜にしろ raises two cases: “whether… or…”.

this.tr: Even if you're busy, surely you can at least make a phone call.

that.tr: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.

items.explain: Count how many times にしろ appears: once → it grants that one case, but the conclusion doesn't change; twice, with a pair of opposite or similar cases (行く／行かない) → it's the same either way. にせよ〜にせよ and にしても〜にしても work the same way.

items.diff: Both mean “even if…”; にしても works in both speech and writing, while にしろ／にせよ are more formal and stiffer.

this.tr: Even if it was a joke, that remark is unforgivable.

that.tr: Even as a joke, that was going a bit too far.

items.explain: Look at the tone of the sentence: ordinary talk with 「ちょっと」「〜だよ」 → にしても; commentary, reports or formal opinions (許されない発言だ) → にしろ／にせよ, with にせよ the most formal. All three come from する: しろ and せよ are imperative forms of する — “suppose it's…” → even if it's….

groups.note: Both are concessive: whatever the case, the conclusion stays the same

items.diff: 〜にしろ〜にしろ raises two cases: “whether… or…”; にしろ on its own raises just one case: “even if…”.

this.tr: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.

that.tr: Even if you're busy, surely you can at least make a phone call.

items.explain: Count how many times にしろ appears: twice, with a pair of opposite or similar cases (行く／行かない) → it's the same either way; once → it grants that one case, but the conclusion doesn't change. にせよ〜にせよ and にしても〜にしても work the same way.

items.diff: にしろ〜にしろ leans formal and can also take verbs; でも〜でも is spoken and takes nouns.

this.tr: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.

that.tr: Beer or wine, please drink whatever you like.

items.explain: Look at the words before it: verbs like 「行く／行かない」, or formal situations → にしろ〜にしろ (にしても〜にしても works too); nouns like ビール and ワイン in everyday talk → でも〜でも.

items.diff: にしろ〜にしろ is usually followed by a request or judgment; (よ)うが〜まいが is stronger, with a laissez-faire “do what you like, it's nothing to do with me” feel.

this.tr: Whether you're going or not, please give us an answer.

that.tr: Whether you go or not has nothing to do with me.

items.explain: Look at the second half: requests to the listener like 「返事をください」「連絡してください」 → にしろ〜にしろ; a “do as you please” attitude with 「関係ない」「勝手だ」「自由だ」 → (よ)うが〜まいが. The forms differ too: the first uses 行く／行かない, the second the volitional 行こう and 行くまい. (よ)うと〜まいと works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “for…, from …'s point of view”

items.diff: にしたら means putting yourself in someone else's shoes and guessing their feelings; にとって gives an evaluation, “for… (it's important, hard)”, and is often used about yourself.

this.tr: From my mother's point of view, she's probably worried about me living alone.

that.tr: For me, family is the most important thing.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending and the person before it: when it ends in 「〜だろう」「〜かもしれない」, guessing what someone else (母、相手) feels → にしたら (にすれば works too); when it's a value judgment like 「大切だ」「難しい」, often about yourself (私にとって) → にとって.

groups.note: Both express a confident inference: “it must be…”

items.diff: Both mean “it must be”; に違いない works in speech and writing, while に相違ない is only used in writing and is stiffer.

this.tr: Judging from the fingerprints left at the scene, the culprit must be this man.

that.tr: Seeing that smile of his, something good must have happened.

items.explain: The two mean the same; the only difference is register. Look at the setting: everyday talk → に違いない; academic papers, news, or the narration of a mystery novel → に相違ない, which sounds very stiff in conversation.

items.diff: に相違ない is a firm conclusion drawn from evidence; はずだ is an inference from reasoning, “it should be”, which may still turn out wrong.

this.tr: Judging from the evidence, the culprit must be him.

that.tag: Should by rights · may fall through
that.tr: He was supposed to come at three as promised, but he still isn't here.

items.explain: Check whether 「のに」 can follow: はずだ is an expectation based on a plan or common sense, so you can say 「はずなのに、まだ来ない」 to show it didn't happen; に相違ない is a conclusion the speaker is sure of and isn't used this way. Also, に相違ない is written language, while はずだ is common in both speech and writing.
