items.diff: に相違ない is a calm, written conclusion; に決まっている is spoken, with a dogmatic “no doubt about it” tone.

this.tr: Judging from the investigation results, this part must have caused the accident.

that.tr: Doing it that way, you're bound to fail.

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: drawing a calm conclusion from an investigation in reports or news → に相違ない; talking among friends, concluding with some emotion (〜じゃ、〜よ), often shortened to 「決まってる」 in speech → に決まっている. に決まっている isn't used in formal writing.

groups.note: Both mean acting in line with a standard, policy or request

items.diff: に沿って follows the “route” of a policy or plan; に基づいて takes facts, data or laws as its “basis”.

this.tr: We improved the product in line with company policy.

that.tr: We improved the product based on the questionnaire results.

items.explain: The two sentences only swap the basis: things that set a direction or route to follow, like 「方針、計画、マニュアル、ご希望」 → に沿って; things that can serve as evidence, like 「結果、データ、法律、事実」 → に基づいて. 沿って can also be used literally, as in 「川に沿って歩く」 (walk along the river); 基づいて can't.

items.title: 〜にしたがって (following)
items.diff: に沿って means “not straying from” a policy or wish, keeping to the same general direction; に従って means “obeying” instructions or rules, which must be followed.

this.tr: We'll put together a travel plan to suit your wishes.

that.tr: Please follow the staff's instructions and evacuate.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a direction to match and not stray from, like 「希望、方針、計画、テーマ」 → に沿って; something that must be obeyed, like 「指示、命令、規則、法律」 → に従って. 「ご希望に沿って」 has a considerate feel and is a stock phrase in the service industry.

items.diff: に沿って means “not straying from” a policy or wish and following it; にこたえて is a positive response, working to “fulfil” expectations.

this.tr: We drew up a new plan in line with company policy.

that.tr: The players lived up to their fans' expectations and won the championship in fine style.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a set course like 「方針、計画、マニュアル」, followed by acting accordingly → に沿って; hopes others place in you, like 「期待、声援」, followed by results that repay them → にこたえて. Both 「ご希望に沿って」 and 「ご希望にこたえて」 are fine, but 「方針にこたえて」 sounds unnatural.

groups.note: Both come from 「過ぎる」 — “to pass, to exceed”

items.diff: にすぎない means “not exceeding” ＝ nothing more than…; すぎる means “going past the limit” ＝ too….

this.tr: I'm just a student, nothing more.

that.tr: I ate too many sweets and now my stomach hurts.

items.explain: Both come from 「過ぎる」 (to pass): にすぎない, with a negative added, means “doesn't go past this level” → “is merely…”; it takes nouns and often comes with 「ただ」. すぎる, with no negative, means going past the limit → “too…, overdoing it”, and attaches to the ます-stem of verbs and the stem of adjectives. Check whether there's a negative 「ない」 after it.

groups.note: Both mean “merely…, only…”

items.diff: にすぎない can also take verbs; でしかない only takes nouns, sounds colder and is more disparaging.

this.tr: I only said that as a joke.

that.tr: That's nothing but an excuse.

wrong.why: でしかない can only take nouns before it

items.explain: Look at the word before it: a verb (言った、聞いた) → only にすぎない; a noun (言い訳、子ども) → both work, but でしかない is colder, with a negative judgment of “in the end it's only…”.

items.diff: にすぎない is written language with a “not worth mentioning” judgment; だけ is the neutral spoken “just”.

this.tr: This success was merely a matter of good luck.

that.tr: I just got lucky this time, that's all.

items.explain: The two sentences mean almost the same; they differ in setting and tone: in writing or speeches, playing something down as “no big deal”, with a touch of disparagement or modesty → にすぎない; talking with friends (〜よ) → だけ.

groups.note: Both come from 「共（とも）」 — “together”

items.diff: に伴って only means “along with… (something changes or happens)”; とともに can also mean “together with…”.

this.tr: As the population grew, there was no longer enough housing.

that.tr: I moved to a new town together with my family.

items.explain: 伴う＝「共（とも）＋なう」: appearing together; とともに＝「と＋共に」: together with…. Look at what comes before: people like 「家族、友人」 → only とともに (together); changes like 「増加、変化、発展」 → both can mean “as…”, with に伴って more formal and common in the news.

groups.note: Both mean “as…, along with…”

items.diff: につれて is only used for gradual change; に伴って can also be used for knock-on effects of a one-off event.

this.tr: With the relocation of our office, our phone number will change.

that.tr: As time went by, the pain gradually faded.

wrong.why: 移転 is a one-off event; につれて is only used for gradual change

items.explain: Check whether what comes before changes “bit by bit”: things that progress gradually, like 「時間が経つ、年をとる、上達する」 → both work, with につれて more common in speech; one-off events like 「移転、工事、法律の改正」 → only に伴って (に伴い), describing the changes they bring; common in notices.

groups.note: につけ ↔ につき — only the last kana differs

items.diff: につけ means “whenever… (a feeling wells up)”; につき is the “because of…” or “per…” of notices.

this.tr: Whenever I look at this photo, I remember my childhood.

that.tr: We are closed today, as it is our regular holiday.

items.explain: Only the last kana differs, but the meanings are completely different. Look at what comes before and where it's used: verbs like 「見る、聞く、思う」＋につけ, followed by memories or emotions; nouns like 「定休日、工事中」＋につき, mostly seen on shop doors and notices, giving a reason (「一人につき」, on the other hand, means “per person”).

groups.note: Each matches one of two uses: “whenever…” and “whether A or B”

items.diff: につけ is only followed by feelings or memories and is more formal; たびに is the objective “every time…”, and anything can follow it.

this.tr: Whenever I hear this song, I remember my student days.

that.tr: Every time I go on a trip, it rains.

wrong.why: につけ must be followed by feelings or memories, not objective events

items.explain: Look at the second half: feelings welling up inside, like 「思い出す、懐かしく思う、心配になる」 → につけ (たびに works too); objective events like 「雨が降る、お土産を買う」 → only たびに.

items.diff: につけ〜につけ mostly appears in set pairs like 「いいにつけ悪いにつけ」; にしろ〜にしろ can freely take all sorts of opposing pairs.

this.tr: For better or worse, parents always worry about their children.

that.tr: Whether you'll take part or not, please let us know by tomorrow.

items.explain: につけ〜につけ works with very few words — pretty much only pairs like 「いいにつけ悪いにつけ」「うれしいにつけ悲しいにつけ」, usually followed by feelings; for ordinary pairs like 「参加する／しない」「大人／子ども」, to say “either way…”, use にしろ〜にしろ (にしても〜にしても).

groups.note: Both come from 「に＋付く」 — “attached to…” → “about” (につき is the continuative form, について the て-form)

items.diff: Both mean “about”; について works in any situation, while につき is a formal written expression, usually said as 「につきまして」 aloud.

this.tr: Regarding this matter, we will contact you at a later date.

that.tr: I'm researching Japanese history.

items.explain: Both come from 「に＋付く」: について is the て-form, につき the continuative form. Look at the setting: everyday talk and writing → について; formal settings such as company announcements, meetings and dealing with clients (本件、後日、いたします) → につき／につきまして.

groups.note: につき ↔ につけ — only the last kana differs

items.diff: につき is the “because of…” or “per…” of notices; につけ means “whenever… (a feeling wells up)”.

this.tr: We are closed today, as it is our regular holiday.

that.tr: Whenever I look at this photo, I remember my childhood.

items.explain: Only the last kana differs, but the meanings are completely different. Look at what comes before and where it's used: nouns like 「定休日、工事中」＋につき, mostly seen on shop doors and notices, giving a reason (「一人につき」, on the other hand, means “per person”); verbs like 「見る、聞く、思う」＋につけ, followed by memories or emotions.

groups.note: Each matches one of two uses: “because” and “per…”

items.title: 〜ために (cause)
items.diff: につき is used almost only in notices and announcements and attaches directly to nouns; ため works in all kinds of writing and needs 「の」 after a noun.

this.tr: Road closed due to construction.

that.tr: Yesterday the road was closed because of construction work.

items.explain: Look at where it appears: signs on doors or by the roadside, giving a brief reason (工事中につき、定休日につき) → につき; ordinary sentences in news, diaries or explanations → ため. With nouns, につき attaches directly (工事中につき), while ため needs 「の」 (工事のため).

items.diff: につき is for rules on how much is charged or given per unit and is very formal; 当たり is mostly for averages calculated from statistics.

this.tr: The participation fee is 1,000 yen per person.

that.tr: Per-capita rice consumption in Japan is falling year by year.

items.explain: Look at where the number comes from: a rule in a notice or price list on how much is charged or given per unit → につき; data obtained by averaging a total, used for comparison (消費量、収入、売り上げ) → 当たり.

groups.note: Both come from 「及ぶ（およぶ）」 — “to reach”

items.diff: には及ばない ends the sentence and means “there's no need to…”; 言うに及ばず sits mid-sentence and means “… goes without saying”, with more to follow.

this.tr: It'll heal soon, so there's no need to worry.

that.tr: This singer is popular not only at home, of course, but overseas too.

items.explain: 言うに及ばず is the classical form of 「言うに及ばない」 (no need to say): it doesn't even need saying → of course. Look at the position: at the end of the sentence, politely turning aside someone's worry or kindness → には及ばない; mid-sentence, followed by 「〜でも」「〜も」 adding another layer → 言うに及ばず.

items.diff: には及ばない means “it hasn't reached the point of needing…” ＝ no need; に及んで means “things have already reached the point of…”.

this.tr: There's no need for you to come all this way — a phone call will do.

that.tr: Things have come to this, and you're still making excuses?

items.explain: 及ぶ＝to reach. The negative には及ばない: things haven't got that far → no need; the affirmative に及んで: the situation has already come to this (この期に及んで＝at this late stage), usually followed by reproach. Check whether there's 「ない／ません」.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no need to…”

items.diff: には及ばない is more formal and polite, often used to decline someone's kindness; ことはない is the casual “no need” used with people you know.

this.tr: There's no need to worry, sir.

that.tr: There's no need to worry so much.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: politely telling a superior or client “please don't trouble yourself” → には及ばない, usually in the polite form 「ご心配には及びません」; casually reassuring friends or family (〜よ) → ことはない.

items.diff: には及ばない politely tells the other person “please don't trouble yourself”; までもない means “it's obvious, so there's no need to go that far”.

this.tr: It's only a minor injury, so there's no need to visit me.

that.tr: Everyone knows this, so there's no need to explain.

items.explain: Look at the reason: politely turning aside something the other person would do for you (見舞い、心配、送迎) → には及ばない; something too obvious, like 「誰でも知っている」「明らかだ」 → までもない (「言うまでもない」 is the most common; mid-sentence it becomes までもなく).

groups.note: Both express a range in time or space

items.diff: にわたって covers the whole range, “for as long as, throughout”, stressing scale; から〜にかけて means “from… to… or thereabouts”, with fuzzy start and end points.

this.tr: It rained for ten whole days straight.

that.tr: It rained from last night through this morning.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a whole period or entire area like 「10日間」「全国」「長年」, often with a number → にわたって, stressing how long or widespread; a start point + end point like 「昨夜から今朝」「関東から東北」 → から〜にかけて, only saying roughly in that span.

items.title: 〜を通して (throughout a period)
items.diff: にわたって says an activity spans “as long as, throughout”, stressing scale; を通して says something is “the same all the way through” a whole cycle.

this.tr: The construction work went on for as long as three years.

that.tr: This island is warm all year round.

items.explain: Look at what follows: an activity or event that continues or unfolds, like 「工事が続いた」「調査を行った」 → にわたって; a state that stays the same through a whole cycle, like 「暖かい」「にぎやかだ」, usually after a complete cycle like 「一年、一生」 → を通して (を通じて works too).

groups.note: Both come from 「よる（因る）」 — “to be based on”

items.title: 〜によって (varies with…)
items.diff: によらず means “regardless of… it's the same”; によって means “differs depending on…”.

this.tr: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.

that.tr: The participation fee differs by age.

items.explain: よる＝to be based on. によって: divided by age → each is different; によらず (ず＝not): not based on age → the same for everyone. Look at the second half: 「違う」「異なる」 → によって; 「誰でも」「一律」 → によらず. 「見かけによらず」 (you can't judge by appearances) has the same meaning: unrelated to how something looks.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…”

items.diff: They mean almost the same, “regardless of”; を問わず is a stock phrase in job ads and notices and uses 「を」; によらず uses 「に」 and can also mean “not relying on…” or “contrary to…”.

this.tr: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.

that.tr: Anyone can take part, whatever their age.

wrong.why: 問う is transitive, so say 「を問わず」

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; first look at the particle before it: 「よる」 (to be based on) takes 「に」 → 〜によらず; 「問う」 (to ask) is transitive and takes 「を」 → 〜を問わず. を問わず often takes paired words or ranges like 「男女、昼夜、経験の有無」; によらず also has uses that を問わず doesn't, like 「見かけによらず」 (you can't judge by appearances) and 「話し合いによらず」 (without going through discussion).

groups.note: によっては ↔ ようによっては — just an extra 「よう」

items.diff: Noun＋によっては means “some… may”; verb ます-stem＋ようによっては means “if you change the way you…”.

this.tr: Depending on the circumstances, plans may change.

that.tag: ます-stem＋よう · change of view
that.tr: If you look at it differently, even failure is a good experience.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun like 「人、国、場合」 → によっては, meaning situations differ; a verb ます-stem＋よう, like 「考え、見、やり」 → ようによっては, meaning “change the way you see or do it, and the conclusion changes”, often followed by a surprisingly positive judgment.

groups.note: Both mean the result changes with the preceding circumstances

items.title: 〜によって (varies with…)
items.diff: によっては picks out just a part: “some… may…”; によって describes the whole: “differs depending on…”.

this.tr: For some people, this medicine may not agree with them.

that.tr: How well the medicine works varies from person to person.

items.explain: Adding 「は」 narrows the scope to “some of them”. Look at the second half: 「〜こともある」「〜場合もある」, saying a special (usually bad) result occurs in some cases → によっては; 「違う」「さまざまだ」, saying there's variation across the whole → によって.

items.title: 〜いかんによっては (possibly, depending on…)
items.diff: Both mean “depending on…, sometimes…”; いかんによっては is stiffer written language, mostly seen in official documents and regulations.

this.tr: Depending on the results, we may need to run the test again.

that.tr: Depending on the outcome of the review, qualifications may be revoked.

items.explain: Look at the type of text: a doctor or teacher explaining in person → によっては; clauses in regulations, contracts or official documents (資格を取り消す場合がある) → いかんによっては, which also needs 「の」 before it (結果のいかん).

items.title: 〜次第で (depending on…)
items.diff: によっては only says a special result “may” occur in some cases; 次第で means the outcome “all depends on…”.

this.tr: Depending on the weather, the match may be cancelled.

that.tr: Whether the match goes ahead will be decided by the weather.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「〜こともある」「〜場合もある」 only warns that a certain result “may” happen → によっては; when the outcome is entirely governed by what comes before, like 「するかどうか決める」「合否が決まる」 → 次第で.

groups.note: Both correspond to 「で」 marking a place or means

items.diff: で is the most general everyday form; にて means the same but is only used in formal documents like notices, announcements and invitations.

this.tr: The entrance ceremony will be held in Gymnasium 1.

that.tr: Let's play basketball in the gym after school.

items.explain: Look at the type of text: notices, invitations and announcements from schools or companies (〜にて行います) → にて; ordinary speech → で. 「これにて終了します」 (this concludes…) and 「メールにて」 are also set uses of にて; in speech you'd say これで, メールで.

items.diff: にて is mostly used in notices for a place or means (メールにて); において can also mean “in the field or area of…”.

this.tr: We will notify you of the results by email.

that.tr: In modern society, English is indispensable.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: means like 「メール、書面、電話」, or a place given in a notice (受付にて) → にて; fields or areas like 「社会、教育、経済」 → において (にて has no such use). Both are written language; にて reads more like a set phrase in notices and letters.

groups.note: のだろうか ↔ のではないだろうか — just an extra 「ではない」

items.diff: のではないだろうか is a gentle assertion: “isn't it… (I think it is)”; のだろうか expresses doubt: “is it really…?”.

this.tr: If anything, wouldn't this method be better?

that.tr: Is this method really all right?

items.explain: The extra 「ではない」 isn't a negation: のではないだろうか uses a rhetorical question to gently state your own view, “I think it's…”, and often appears with 「むしろ」; のだろうか often comes with 「本当に」 and expresses doubt, implying “probably not”.

groups.note: Both use a negative question to gently voice a guess or opinion: “I suspect…, perhaps…”

items.diff: They mean the same; のではないだろうか adds an extra layer of conjecture with 「だろう」, making it softer and suited to writing and speeches; のではないか is more direct, and in speech becomes んじゃない.

this.tr: This price is probably a little expensive for students, isn't it?

that.tr: Hey, isn't this price a bit high?

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: chatting with friends, you just say 「〜んじゃない？」 (in writing のではないか); in writing or speeches, when you want to state your view more politely and leave some room, add another layer of 「だろう」 → のではないだろうか.

items.diff: They mean the same; ではなかろうか is a classical form, more old-fashioned and elegant, mostly seen in editorials and academic writing.

this.tr: Surely that is the very essence of the problem.

that.tr: Surely that is the very essence of the problem.

items.explain: 「なかろう」 is just the classical form of 「ないだろう」, so the two sentences mean exactly the same; ではなかろうか is simply more old-fashioned and bookish, and almost never used in everyday conversation. Note that with nouns, のではないだろうか needs 「な」 (本質なのでは), while ではなかろうか attaches directly (本質ではなかろうか).

items.diff: They mean the same; ではあるまいか uses the classical negative conjecture 「まい」 and is even stiffer than ではなかろうか, basically found only in writing.

this.tr: If things go on like this, traditional culture may well disappear.

that.tr: If things go on like this, traditional culture may well disappear.

items.explain: 「まい」 is an old negative conjecture (＝ないだろう), so ではあるまいか is the classical version of ではないだろうか. Today it only turns up occasionally in novels and commentary; in speech, use のではないだろうか or 「んじゃないかな」.

groups.note: Both come from 「もと」 — originally “base, root”

items.diff: のもとで means “under…” (under someone's guidance, protection or control); をもとに means “using… as material or a basis”.

this.tr: I wrote my thesis under my professor's guidance.

that.tr: I wrote my thesis based on the data I collected.

items.explain: First look at the particle: の＋もとで／もとに → being “under” a person or condition; を＋もとに → using it as a “foundation” to make something new. Then look at the noun before it: people or supervision like 先生、指導、親 → のもとで; materials like データ、事実、資料 → をもとに. 「のもとに」 and 「をもとに」 differ by just one particle, so read carefully.

items.diff: のもとに describes being in a state “under” some system or condition; に基づいて describes actions taken “in accordance with” rules or data.

this.tr: All citizens are equal under the law.

that.tag: In accordance with · basis for action
that.tr: The police arrested him in accordance with the law.

items.explain: It's the same 「法」, so look at the second half: a situation or state (平等である、自由に暮らす) → のもとで／のもとに; taking action or making judgments in accordance with it (逮捕した、判断する) → に基づいて. When what comes before is a person or a regime (先生、政府), only のもとで works. 「基づく」 is originally 「基（もと）＋付く」 — stuck close to the foundation.

groups.note: Both express an extreme degree: “incredibly…”

items.diff: Both mean “incredibly…”; のなんのって is very colloquial, like telling a story; といったらない can also go in writing.

this.tr: We lost the match, and oh, was I frustrated!

that.tr: The frustration of losing that match was beyond words.

items.explain: Look at the tone: のなんのって is for chatting, telling someone about something with a bit of embellishment; what follows is often left out, and it often comes with fillers like 「もう」「いやあ」. といったらない is often preceded by a noun (悔しさ、寒さ), rounds off the sentence, and doesn't feel out of place in writing.

items.diff: てたまらない describes a feeling you can't stand “right now”; のなんのって is mostly an exaggerated account to someone after the fact.

this.tr: Yesterday my tooth hurt like crazy — I couldn't sleep all night.

that.tr: My tooth hurts unbearably right now.

items.explain: Look at the time and the audience: something you're putting up with 「今」 → てたまらない; telling someone about 「昨日」's experience, along with the consequence (一晩中眠れなかった) → のなんのって. The forms differ too: 痛くて＋たまらない, 痛い＋のなんのって.

groups.note: Both come from 「上（うえ）」 — originally “on top”, extended to “on the level of…”

items.diff: They mean the same; 上（じょう） attaches directly to Sino-Japanese nouns and is more concise and formal; の上では has 「の」 in between and also works with native Japanese nouns.

this.tag: の上では · native Japanese noun
this.tr: By the calendar it's already spring, but it's still cold.

that.tr: Legally there's no problem, but what about morally?

items.explain: Look at the noun before it and the reading: 上（じょう） can only attach directly to Sino-Japanese words (法律上、計算上、形式上); の上（うえ）では has 「の」 in between, so it also works with native Japanese nouns like 「暦（こよみ）」. Both often hint “so it seems on the surface, but not necessarily in reality”, often followed by a contrasting 「が」.

items.title: 〜上で (in terms of…)
items.diff: Noun＋の上では means “seen from this angle, it's like this”; verb＋上で means “in the course of doing this, in this respect”.

this.tag: Noun＋の上では · on the surface
this.tr: On paper we'll make it in time, but in reality it'll be hard.

that.tr: When living abroad, language is extremely important.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「上」: noun＋の上では means “seen from this angle it's like this”, often hinting at a gap with reality; verb dictionary form＋上で means “when doing this, in this respect”, usually followed by 「大切だ・必要だ・問題がある」.

groups.note: Both mean “from the standpoint of…”, limiting the angle of a judgment

items.diff: の上では often hints “so it seems on the surface, but not necessarily in reality”; 点では picks out one of several aspects to evaluate.

this.tr: On paper the economy is recovering, but nobody actually feels it.

that.tr: I'm happy with this car in terms of price, but the design is a bit lacking.

items.explain: Look at what's contrasted after 「が」: の上では is contrasted with “the actual situation” (実感はない), meaning “on paper it's like this”; 点では is contrasted with “another aspect” (デザイン), meaning “as far as this point goes”.

groups.note: Both come from the old adverbial particle 「のみ」 — equivalent to 「だけ」, meaning “only”

items.diff: のみ means “only”; のみならず is 「のみ」 plus the classical negative 「ならず（＝でなく）」, becoming “not only…”.

this.tr: This product is sold not only in Japan but overseas as well.

that.tr: This product is sold only in Japan.

items.explain: 「ならず」 is the negative of the classical copula 「なり」, equal to modern 「でなく」: のみならず＝だけでなく. Look at what follows: if the sentence fixes the scope at のみ → only; if 「〜も」「〜でも」 follows to widen the scope → not only.

groups.note: Both mean “not only…, but also…”

items.diff: They mean the same; のみならず is written language, mostly seen in news, speeches and academic papers; だけでなく works in both speech and writing.

this.tr: Our city is lively with tourists not only in summer but in winter too.

that.tr: Our town isn't just fun in summer — it's fun in winter too!

items.explain: Look at the style: chatting or ordinary explanations (うちの町、〜よ) → だけでなく; the tone of official documents, news or speeches, as with 「本市」 → のみならず, which sounds formal and weighty. Saying のみならず in everyday conversation sounds very stiff.

items.diff: のみならず just means “not only A, but B too”; にとどまらず stresses going beyond a certain scope or limit and spreading wider.

this.tr: That singer is not only good at singing but good at acting too.

that.tr: That singer's popularity isn't confined to Japan — it has spread overseas too.

items.explain: 「とどまる」 means “to stay”: にとどまらず is preceded by a scope or limit (国内、一部の地域、「一時的」) and often followed by 「広がる・及ぶ」, saying things didn't stop there; のみならず simply adds in parallel, with two similar things on either side (歌と演技).

items.diff: They mean the same; adding 「ひとり」 stresses “this isn't just one party's concern”, mostly used to widen a problem to society as a whole, and is more solemn.

this.tr: The falling birthrate has become a problem not only in rural areas but in cities too.

that.tr: The falling birthrate is not merely a rural problem but a problem for Japan as a whole.

items.explain: Check whether 「ひとり」 comes before the noun: this 「ひとり」 isn't 「一人」 (one person) but an adverb meaning “merely”, which pairs with のみならず. What follows usually widens the scope to the whole, like 「社会全体・日本全体の問題」.

groups.note: Both come from the old adverbial particle 「のみ」 — equivalent to 「だけ」, meaning “only”

items.diff: のみ means “only”; のみならず adds the classical negative 「ならず（＝でなく）」, becoming “not only…”.

this.tr: This product is sold only in Japan.

that.tr: This product is sold not only in Japan but overseas as well.

items.explain: 「ならず」 is the negative of the classical copula 「なり」, equal to modern 「でなく」: のみならず＝だけでなく. Look at what follows: if the sentence fixes the scope at のみ → only; if 「〜も」「〜でも」 follows to widen the scope → not only.

groups.note: Both limit: “only…”

items.diff: They mean the same; のみ leans formal and is mostly seen in notices, regulations and announcements; だけ works in any situation.

this.tr: Today, admission is for members only.

that.tr: Apparently only members can get in today.

items.explain: Look at the setting: notices, regulations and announcements (本日は〜いただけます) → のみ; ordinary speech (今日は〜んだって) → だけ. Using のみ in conversation sounds like reading out a notice.

items.diff: のみ is used in the affirmative and sounds objective; しか must be used with a negative and often carries a sense of “too few, not enough”.

this.tr: There were only 10 participants.

that.tr: There were a mere 10 participants.

wrong.why: しか must be followed by a negative

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: のみ is followed by an affirmative (だった), simply reporting the number objectively; しか is always followed by a negative (いなかった), bringing out regret at “too few”.

items.diff: Both can express determination; のみだ means “this is the only thing left to do”, mostly said when everything's ready; しかない means “there's no other way, so I have to…”.

this.tr: The preparations are all done. Now all that's left is to wait for the results.

that.tr: The trains have stopped. I'll have to walk to the station.

items.explain: Look at the situation before it: everything that needed doing is done and you're ready (準備は全部終わった) → のみだ, with calm or resolve; you've hit trouble and have no choice (電車が止まった) → しかない, with resignation. のみだ is written; in speech you'd say 「あとは待つだけだ」.

groups.note: Both come from 「無理（むり）」 — originally “without reason (理が無い)”

items.diff: のも無理はない means “not without reason” → understandable, no wonder; には無理がある means “there's something unreasonable about it” → far-fetched, doesn't hold up.

this.tr: He was kept waiting a full three hours, so no wonder he's angry.

that.tr: A plan to finish everything in three hours is a bit unrealistic.

items.explain: 「無理」 means “without reason”. 無理はない negates it → there's reason, used to sympathize with someone's reaction (怒る、泣く); 無理がある says there's “something unreasonable” in it, used to criticize a plan or claim as too far-fetched. Look at what comes before: a person's emotional reaction → のも無理はない; a plan, explanation or claim → には無理がある.

groups.note: Both mean “it's only natural, no wonder”

items.title: 〜のも当然だ
items.diff: のも当然だ is a cool judgment and works for good or bad outcomes; のも無理はない focuses on sympathizing with someone's feelings or reaction and is mostly used for negative situations.

this.tr: You kept them waiting three hours, so no wonder they're angry.

that.tr: She practised ten hours every day, so of course she won.

items.explain: Look at what's being described: emotional reactions like someone getting angry, crying or being disappointed, where the speaker shows understanding and sympathy → のも無理はない; results that follow naturally, especially good things (優勝する、合格する) → usually のも当然だ. People occasionally use のも無理はない for good outcomes too, but it's less natural than のも当然だ.

items.diff: わけだ is your own realization, “no wonder, so that's why”; のも無理はない sympathizes with others: “it's no wonder they reacted that way”.

this.tr: The window was open, so it's no wonder everyone felt cold.

that.tr: The window's open. No wonder it's so cold.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: when you discover the cause yourself and “now it makes sense”, often with 「どうりで」「なるほど」 → わけだ; laying out the cause to speak up for someone else's feelings or behaviour (寒がる、怒る) → のも無理はない.

groups.note: All come from the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 — 「ぬ」「ね」「ざる」 are all forms of it

items.diff: ぬ is the attributive form of 「ず」 and modifies nouns (知らぬ人); ず links to a following action (食べずに出かけた).

this.tr: A stranger spoke to me.

that.tr: I went out without even eating breakfast.

items.explain: Look at what follows: a noun (人、間、事故) → ぬ; an action, with the sentence continuing → ずに (＝ないで). Both are the same classical negative word, just in different shapes.

items.diff: The 「ね」 in ねばならない is also a form of 「ず」: 「ねば」＝“if not…”, so the whole means “must…”, not “that doesn't…”.

this.tr: Better left unsaid.

that.tr: Some things have to be said clearly.

items.explain: Check whether 「ば」 follows 「ね」: 言わぬ means “not say”; 言わねば＝言わなければ, and with 「ならない」 added it means “must say”. When you see 「〜ねば」 in written texts, just read it as 「〜なければ」.

items.diff: Both ぬ and ざる modify nouns, meaning “that doesn't…”; ざる sounds more solemn and stiffer, and is mostly used in titles and maxims.

this.tr: That is an unforgivable act.

that.tr: That is an unforgivable act.

items.explain: They attach the same way (drop 「ない」 and add it) and mean the same. ざる is a contraction of 「ず＋ある」 and sounds harder and weightier; it's common in film titles and headlines (知られざる真実); ぬ is more common in set expressions (見知らぬ、思わぬ).

groups.note: Both are negatives: “not…”

items.diff: They mean the same; ない is the standard modern negative; ぬ survives only in set expressions and in formal, old-fashioned styles.

this.tr: Before I knew it, night had fallen.

that.tr: Before I knew it, night had fallen.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same. Set expressions like 「知らぬ間に」「見知らぬ人」「思わぬ事故」 keep 「ぬ」; when making your own sentences, just use 「ない」. The 「ん」 in colloquial 「知らん」「わからん」 also comes from 「ぬ」.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「抜く」 — originally “to pull out, remove; to pierce through”

items.diff: 抜きで／抜きにして means “leaving… out”; 〜抜く means “pushing all the way through” → keeping at it to the very end.

this.tr: No wasabi, please.
Let's skip the formalities and make a toast.

that.tr: Even though my legs hurt, I kept running to the very end.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「抜き」: a noun (わさび、挨拶)＋抜きで／抜きにして → take it out; a verb ます-stem (走り)＋抜く → carry the action through to the end. It's the same 「抜く」: “pulling out” led to “leaving out”, and “piercing through to the other side” led to “seeing it through”.

groups.note: Both mean “setting… aside, not talking about…”

items.diff: 抜きにして keeps the topic out of the whole occasion; さておき just puts it aside for now and moves on to another topic.

this.tag: Not discussed at all this time
this.tr: Tonight let's leave work talk out of it and just enjoy our drinks.

that.tag: Set aside for now · change topic
that.tr: Work aside, how have you been lately?

items.explain: Look at the second half: 抜きにして is often followed by 「楽しもう・乾杯しよう」, meaning the topic simply won't come up this time; さておき is immediately followed by another topic (最近元気？本題に入ろう), and the original topic is only shelved for now and may come up again later.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「抜く」 — originally “to pull out, remove; to pierce through”

items.diff: 〜抜く means “pushing all the way through” → keeping at it to the very end; 抜きで／抜きにして means “leaving… out”.

this.tr: I'm going to see this job through to the end.

that.tr: No wasabi, please.
Let's skip the formalities and make a toast.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「抜く」: a verb ます-stem (やり)＋抜く → carry the action through to the end; a noun (わさび、挨拶)＋抜きで／抜きにして → take it out. It's the same 「抜く」: “piercing through to the other side” led to “seeing it through”, and “pulling out” led to “leaving out”.

groups.note: Both attach to the verb ます-stem, meaning doing an action “to the end, completely”

items.diff: 〜きる focuses on “finishing all of it”, with nothing left over; 〜抜く focuses on overcoming difficulty and going to the limit.

this.tr: After thinking it over for days on end, I finally came up with an answer.

that.tag: Finished all of it · nothing left
that.tr: I ate a whole big cake all by myself.

items.explain: Check whether it's about “quantity” or “difficulty”: finishing a set amount completely, with nothing left (食べきる、使いきる、読みきる) → きる; overcoming difficulty, taking thinking or perseverance to the limit (考え抜く、悩み抜く、やり抜く) → 抜く.

items.diff: 〜通す means “keeping the same state” from start to finish; 〜抜く means overcoming difficulty and holding out to the end.

this.tr: No matter how hard it gets, I'll hold on to my dream.

that.tr: On a packed train, I had to stand the whole way to Tokyo.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: something like 「ずっと」, keeping up one state (立つ、黙る、隠す) → 通す; something like 「どんなに苦しくても」, a difficulty to overcome → 抜く.

items.diff: 〜抜く stresses overcoming difficulty and holding out to the end, with a note of praise; 〜終わる just says the action ended.

this.tr: Even though my legs hurt, I kept running to the very end.

that.tr: After finishing the marathon, I drank some water.

items.explain: Check whether there's a “difficulty”: when it's preceded by difficulties like 「足が痛くても」「苦しくても」, stressing that you didn't give up → 抜く; when it only marks the point at which you “finished running” before doing the next thing → 終わる.

groups.note: Both are humble language, showing respect by lowering your own actions

items.diff: They're built the same way; お〜する is ordinary humble language, common when speaking face to face; お〜申し上げる is more solemn, mostly used in letters, speeches and announcements.

this.tr: We would now like to introduce our new products to you all.

that.tr: Sir, let me show you to your seat.

items.explain: Look at the setting: a shop assistant guiding a customer in person → ご案内します is polite enough; addressing a crowd, writing a letter or making an announcement → ご案内申し上げます, which is grander. Set greetings like 「お祝い申し上げます」「お見舞い申し上げます」 only use 申し上げる. Both use 「お」 before native Japanese verbs and 「ご」 before Sino-Japanese words.

groups.note: Both politely ask someone to do something

items.diff: お〜願います is more solemn and businesslike, mostly seen in announcements and notices; お〜ください is the ordinary honorific request.

this.tr: Please watch your step when boarding.

that.tr: For your safety, please wait behind the yellow line.

items.explain: Both are used for requests to customers at stations and shops. お〜願います is more solemn and stiffer, like a notice, addressed to the public at large; when serving someone in person, お〜ください is already quite polite. 「願う」 and 「願います」 differ only in politeness and are used the same way.

items.diff: お〜願います wraps around an action the other person is to do; 〜をお願いします can follow anything.

this.tag: Wraps an action · asking someone to do it
this.tr: Please refrain from using mobile phones inside the building.

that.tr: Excuse me, one hot coffee, please.

items.explain: Look at what sits between 「お／ご」 and 「願」: an action by the other person, like 遠慮、注意、待ち → お〜願います, used only to ask someone to do something; when 「〜を」 is preceded by a thing like a drink or a service → をお願いします, used for ordering or entrusting. Both come from the verb 「願う」 (to request).

items.diff: They mean the same; お〜願えませんか is more solemn, mostly used at counters, on the phone and in business; 〜ていただけませんか is more common for requests made in person.

this.tr: I'm sorry to trouble you, but could you kindly fill this in here?

that.tr: Excuse me, could you write your name here, please?

items.explain: Look at how formal the wording is: business phrasing like 「恐れ入りますが」「ご記入」 → お〜願えませんか; asking in person with an ordinary verb like 「書いて」 → ていただけませんか. The former sounds more like official language at a counter or on the phone.

groups.note: Both mean “when…”

items.diff: They mean the same; 〜とき is the most common and fits any situation; 〜折 is solemn and refined, mostly used in letters and speeches.

this.tr: Whenever you happen to be in the area, please do drop by.

that.tr: When you're in the area, come over to my place!

items.explain: The two sentences say the same thing; the difference is the setting: in letters, speeches or when addressing guests, with honorifics like 「お越しの」「お立ち寄りください」 → 折; casually between friends → 時.

items.diff: Both are formal versions of 「時」; 〜際 works for good and bad things and is common in instructions and notices; 〜折 is more refined, mostly used for pleasant or courteous occasions.

this.tr: When I went to Kyoto the other day, I visited my former teacher's home.

that.tr: In an emergency, please press this button.

items.explain: Look at the kind of occasion: machine instructions, regulations or emergencies (非常の際、事故の際) → 際; warm, pleasant occasions like visits, trips or meetings, common in letter greetings → 折.

groups.note: Both mean “… may happen”

items.diff: おそれがある is only for bad things and mostly used in news and announcements; かもしれない works for good or bad things, in speech or writing.

this.tr: Due to the typhoon, there is a risk of heavy rain tomorrow.

that.tr: The typhoon has veered off, so it might clear up tomorrow.

wrong.why: Clearing up is good news; おそれがある is only for bad things you're worried about

items.explain: Check whether what might happen is good or bad: bad things that call for caution, like heavy rain, earthquakes or infections → おそれがある, with a formal tone; good things like clearing up, or casual everyday guesses → only かもしれない.

items.diff: おそれがある is objective and mostly used in news and announcements; かねない carries the speaker's worry or criticism and is mostly about people's actions.

this.tr: If things go on like this, there is a risk of personal information being leaked.

that.tr: Knowing him, he could easily blab the secret.

wrong.why: かねない attaches to the ます-stem: しゃべりかねない

items.explain: Look at the subject and the tone: distrust or criticism of someone, as in 「あの人なら」 → かねない (attaches to the ます-stem: しゃべり＋かねない); news or announcements calmly warning of a risk → おそれがある (attaches to the dictionary form: 漏れる＋おそれ).

items.diff: おそれがある is only for bad things and implies “caution needed”; 可能性がある objectively says “it's possible”, good or bad.

this.tr: After an earthquake, there is a risk of a tsunami.

that.tr: This medicine may be able to cure this illness.

items.explain: Look at whether the outcome is good or bad: good things like curing an illness → only 可能性がある; the moment おそれがある appears, it's warning “something bad may happen, be careful”. Also, 可能性 is often used as 「可能性が高い・低い」 to express how likely something is.

groups.note: Both pair with a negative to express a very low degree: “hardly…／not at all…”

items.diff: ろくに〜ない means you did a little but nowhere near enough, with dissatisfaction; ちっとも〜ない means not at all.

this.tr: I was so worried I barely slept last night.

that.tr: I was so worried I didn't sleep a wink last night.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the adverb: ろくに means “properly”, so with the negative it's “didn't sleep properly” — you did sleep, but nowhere near enough; ちっとも means “a bit”, so with the negative it's “didn't sleep at all”. ろくに also often has a complaining or self-mocking tone.

groups.note: Both come from 「せい（所為）」 — meaning “because of…”, usually a bad cause

items.diff: せいか is an uncertain guess: “maybe because of…”; せいで firmly identifies the cause and blames it: “it's all because of…”.

this.tr: Maybe it's from lack of sleep, but my head feels foggy.

that.tr: Thanks to lack of sleep, I was late for an important meeting.

items.explain: Only one kana differs: か marks “uncertainty”, so せいか is a guess the speaker isn't sure about, usually followed by a physical condition or mood whose cause is hard to pin down; せいで asserts that this is the cause, with a note of blame: “it's all its fault”.

groups.note: Both express a cause

items.diff: せいか is an uncertain guess: “maybe because of…”; こともあって is certain: “partly because of… (one of the causes)”.

this.tr: Maybe it was because of the long weekend, but the roads were jammed.

that.tr: Partly because it was a long weekend, the roads were jammed.

items.explain: Check whether the speaker is sure: せいか has 「か」 and is a guess — it may or may not be the cause; こともあって is a fact the speaker has confirmed, only hinting “there are other causes too”. News and reports usually use こともあって when explaining causes.

groups.note: 次第 has two jobs, each with a close equivalent: “as soon as…” ≈ たとたん, and “depends on…” ≈ にかかっている・によっては

items.diff: 次第 is for something you'll actively do from now on; たとたん is for something that has already happened, unexpectedly.

this.tr: I'll contact you as soon as I get to the station.

that.tr: The moment I got to the station, it started raining.

wrong.why: 次第 can't be followed by an unexpected event that has already happened

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「ご連絡します」 is something not yet done that you intend to do → 次第 (attaches to the ます-stem: 着き＋次第); 「雨が降り出した」 is an unexpected event that already happened and was beyond your control → たとたん (attaches to the た-form: 着いた＋とたん).

items.diff: Both mean “depends on”; 次第だ just says “it's decided by this” and works for big or small things; にかかっている stresses that “success or failure rests entirely on it”.

this.tr: Whether we go depends on the weather.

that.tr: Whether we win the match all depends on your effort.

items.explain: Look at what's being talked about: things that depend on circumstances, like whether to go or whether to buy → 次第だ; major successes or failures, like a match or a project, resting on someone or something → にかかっている, with a sense of “a heavy responsibility on your shoulders”. 次第 can also be used mid-sentence as 「次第で」.

items.diff: 次第では focuses on how the preceding result or degree turns out; によっては focuses on picking out particular cases from several.

this.tag: Depends on how it turns out
this.tr: Depending on the test results, surgery may be necessary.

that.tr: For some people, this medicine causes drowsiness.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: things that can turn out well or badly or vary in degree, like 結果、天気、やり方 → 次第では; things that can be divided into many kinds, like 人、場所、国、場合 → によっては, meaning “some of them…”.

groups.note: Both mean “after (doing)…, …”, linking two events

items.diff: 末に is fairly neutral and formal, usable for good or bad outcomes; あげく is mostly followed by a bad outcome, with a note of frustration or resignation.

this.tr: After agonizing for a long time, I finally decided to study abroad.

that.tr: After dithering forever, I ended up buying nothing.

items.explain: Look at the outcome in the second half: careful thought or effort leading to a conclusion or achievement → 末に, common in writing; a lot of fuss ending in something disappointing like wasted effort, a quarrel or failure → あげく, with a “seriously…” tone.

items.diff: 末 stresses going through a long, winding process; 結果 just states cause and effect objectively.

this.tr: After long discussions, we finally reached a conclusion.

that.tr: As a result of the investigation, the cause of the accident was identified.

items.explain: 末に is often preceded by a time-consuming, troublesome process such as 「悩む・迷う・長い話し合い・苦労」, and followed by 「やっと・ついに」; 結果 just calmly reports “did A, so B”, and is most common in investigation, inspection and lab reports.

items.diff: 末に means “in the end” after going through a process; たあとで only gives the order in time. Plain sequence cannot use 末に.

this.tr: After failing many times, we finally completed the new product.

that.tr: I brush my teeth after eating.

wrong.why: Plain sequence can't use 末に

items.explain: Check whether the first part is a “process”: a hard-won experience like failing many times or agonizing for a long time, followed by 「ついに」 → 末に; everyday actions like eating or bathing that are just put in order → たあとで.

groups.note: 〜たものではない ↔ 〜ものではない — only one 「た」 apart

items.diff: たものではない attaches to the た-form of the potential form and means “simply can't…”; ものではない attaches to the dictionary form and means “shouldn't…”.

this.tr: This awful food is simply inedible.

that.tr: You shouldn't leave food uneaten.

items.explain: Look before 「もの」: the た-form of the potential form (食べられた、見られた、聞けた) → putting something down, “simply can't…”, often with 「こんな」; a plain dictionary form (残す、言う) → advice based on common sense, “you shouldn't…”, often said by elders to younger people.

groups.note: Both mean “simply can't…”

items.diff: たものではない means you can't because the thing is too bad, and is disparaging; とても〜ない means you can't manage it because it's too much or too hard.

this.tr: This food is so awful it's impossible to get down.

that.tr: There's so much of this food that I can't possibly finish it.

items.explain: Look at the reason: a criticism of quality like 「まずくて」「下手で」 → たものではない, implying “this thing is no good”; something beyond your ability like 「多すぎて」「難しすぎて」 → とても〜ない — the problem is that you can't manage it, not that the thing is bad.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — placing an event at a certain “point in time”

items.diff: たところで comes mid-sentence and means “even if…, (it's no use)”; たところだ comes at the end and means “just did”.

this.tr: Even if I run now, I won't make it.

that.tr: The train has just left.

items.explain: Look after ところ: followed by 「で」 with another clause after it, usually a negative or “no use” outcome → even if…; followed by 「だ」, ending the sentence → just now.

items.diff: たところで is followed by a “it's no use” judgment; たところ、 is followed by the fact “I did it, and found that…”.

this.tag: No use even if you do it
this.tr: It's too late now to ask the teacher.

that.tr: I asked the teacher, and she told me right away.

items.explain: Only a 「で」 apart: たところ、 is always followed by an outcome that has already happened, and the whole sentence is in the past; たところで is followed by a negative or “no use” judgment, often with 「今さら」「いくら」 before it.

groups.note: Both mean “even if…, (it's no use)”

items.diff: Same meaning; たところで is more formal and stresses “it would be wasted effort”; たって is colloquial.

this.tr: Even if I apologize now, I probably won't be forgiven.

that.tr: Apologizing now won't help — they won't forgive you.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the tone: talking among friends, often with 「よ」 at the end → たって; writing or fairly formal situations → たところで.

items.diff: たところで comes mid-sentence and can be followed by all sorts of negative judgments; ても始まらない is a fixed judgment at the end of the sentence.

this.tr: Even if you regret it now, nothing will change.

that.tr: There's no point regretting it now.

items.explain: Look at where “no use” goes: ても始まらない is itself the end of the sentence, meaning “doing it gets you nowhere”; たところで is only the first half, and the second half still has to state the specific outcome (何も変わらない、間に合わない).

items.title: 〜にしたところで
items.diff: たところで attaches to a verb's た-form, “even if you do…”; にしたところで attaches to a person or noun, “even for… (from that position)”.

this.tag: No use even if you do it
this.tr: Even if you ask an expert, you probably won't get an answer.

that.tr: Even an expert probably doesn't know the answer.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a verb's た-form (聞いた) → たところで, doing something would be pointless; a person or noun (専門家、私) ＋にしたところで → it's the same even from that person's position (としたところで works the same way).

groups.note: たいものだ ↔ たものだ — only one 「い」 apart

items.diff: たいものだ means “I'd really like to…”, a wish for the future; たものだ means “used to often…”, recalling the past.

this.tr: I'd really love to swim in that sea again someday.

that.tr: When I was a child, I'd often swim in that sea.

items.explain: Look at the time words and verb forms: 「いつか」＋ます-stem (泳ぎ)＋たい → a wish for the future; 「子どもの頃」＋た-form (泳いだ) → fondly recalling something you often did. Just one 「い」 apart: one looks to the future, the other to the past.

groups.note: Both express a wish: “want to… / hope…”

items.diff: たいものだ is emotional and usually refers to a long-term wish that isn't easy to fulfill; たい is an ordinary wish, usable even for small things right in front of you.

this.tr: I'd love to see the aurora at least once in my life.

that.tr: I'm thirsty. I want some water.

items.explain: Look at how big and distant the wish is: a long-term wish that can't easily come true right away, like 「一生に一度は」「いつか」 → たいものだ, with a sigh of feeling; something you can satisfy right now (drinking water, sleeping) → たい. Saying 「水が飲みたいものだ」 sounds overblown.

items.diff: てほしいものだ is emotional, usually a strong wish directed at society or others; てほしい is an ordinary hope.

this.tr: I really wish young people would read more books.

that.tr: I want my son to read more books.

items.explain: Look at the target and tone: a heartfelt, somewhat preachy wish aimed at a group like 「若い人」「政府」 → てほしいものだ, mostly in writing or speeches; your own request to a specific person close to you → てほしい. 「てもらいたい」 works the same way.

items.diff: たいものだ states the wish directly; ないものか uses the rhetorical “is there really no way to…?”, with a tone of impatience and frustration at not being able to make it happen.

this.tr: I really wish something could be done about this traffic.

that.tr: Is there really nothing that can be done about this traffic?

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: affirmative 「〜たい」＋ものだ → saying directly “I'd really like to…”; negative 「〜ない」＋ものか → indirectly asking “is there no way to…?”, revealing impatience and helplessness, often with 「何とか」 (ないものだろうか is softer but works the same).

groups.note: Both are ways of telling someone to do something

items.diff: たまえ is used by men toward equals or subordinates, with an air of authority, and sounds old-fashioned; なさい is used by both men and women, mostly by parents or teachers to children, with an instructive tone.

this.tr: Don't hold back — go ahead and eat.

that.tr: Come on, eat your vegetables properly too.

items.explain: Look at the speaker and how the listener is addressed: calling them 「君」 and calmly giving instructions like an old-school male boss or professor → たまえ, nowadays mostly in novels and dramas; a mother or teacher instructing a child → なさい.

items.diff: たまえ is also a command from above, but calm and dignified; the plain imperative form is blunt and rough.

this.tr: You there, come over here a moment.

that.tr: Hey, get over here!

items.explain: Look at the form of address and tone: 「おい」＋imperative is a gruff command between men or in an emergency; 「君」＋たまえ is a condescending but composed instruction, attached to the ます-stem (来＋たまえ). Other imperatives (食べろ、行け) are just as blunt.

groups.note: Both mean “can't go on like this”

items.diff: てばかりはいられない means “can't just keep doing…”; てはいられない means the situation is urgent: “can't… a moment longer”.

this.tr: I'm sad, but I can't just keep crying forever.

that.tr: There's no time left. I can't keep taking it easy.

items.explain: Look for 「ばかり」 and the clues before it: てばかりはいられない admits you can do it a bit, just not “only that, all the time”, often with 「いつまでも」; てはいられない is because of an urgent situation like 「時間がない」, so you can't keep doing it even a moment longer — the tone is more pressing.

items.diff: てばかりはいられない is calm, mostly used to motivate yourself; ている場合じゃない is colloquial and urgent, often used to warn someone else.

this.tr: The failure is disappointing, but I can't just keep moping.

that.tr: You've got an exam tomorrow, right? This is no time to be playing games.

items.explain: Look at who it's said to and the tone: urgently warning someone “this is no time for that”, often with 「よ」 at the end → ている場合じゃない; calmly telling yourself “I can't keep this up, time to pull myself together”, also fine in writing → てばかりはいられない.

groups.note: Both ask someone to do something

items.diff: てちょうだい is affectionate and colloquial, only for family, children and close friends; てください is the standard polite request, usable with anyone.

this.tr: Yu, write your name here, okay?

that.tr: Excuse me, please write your name here.

items.explain: Look at who's being addressed: 「〜ちゃん」, family, close friends → てちょうだい, usually from a woman or an older person; strangers, customers, superiors → only てください. Saying てちょうだい to a superior would be very rude.

items.diff: てちょうだい is a request with a soft tone, usually what the speaker personally wants the other person to do; なさい is a command or instruction that leaves no room for discussion.

this.tr: Mommy's busy right now. Could you be a bit quieter, please?

that.tr: It's already nine o'clock. Go to bed now.

items.explain: Look at whose need it is: Mom is busy or tired herself and asks the child to cooperate → てちょうだい; instructing the child to do what the rules say (寝る、勉強する) → なさい, a command not open to negotiation.

groups.note: ても ↔ てでも — just one extra 「で」

items.title: 〜ても (even if…)
items.diff: てでも means “even if it takes this means, I'll…”; ても means “even if…, the result is still…”.

this.tr: Even if I have to stay up all night, I'll finish it by tomorrow.

that.tr: Even if I stay up all night, I probably won't finish by tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at the second half: your own resolve, like 「終わらせる」「〜たい」「〜つもりだ」 → てでも, with the first part being the lengths you're willing to go to; an unaffected outcome like 「終わらない」 → ても, a plain concession.

groups.note: Both mean “going to extreme lengths”

items.title: 〜てまで
items.diff: てでも is mostly used to express your own resolve positively; てまで usually carries surprise or criticism, often saying “there's no need to go that far”.

this.tr: Even if I have to borrow money, I want to buy this house.

that.tag: Criticism · not worth going that far
that.tr: I don't want a house so badly that I'd borrow money for it.

items.explain: Look at the attitude in the second half: positive resolve (買いたい、やり遂げる) → てでも; negation, surprise or criticism (〜とは思わない、〜なんて信じられない) → てまで, meaning “going that far is too much”.

groups.note: Both mean “ever since… (continuously)”

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; てこのかた is more archaic and elegant, often with a sense of looking back; て以来 is the neutral, common written form and can also attach directly to nouns.

this.tr: Since leaving my hometown, I've never once gone back.

that.tr: Since leaving my hometown, I've never once gone back.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same, and て以来 is more common; てこのかた sounds old-fashioned and reflective, and its most common use is 「生まれてこのかた」. Also, 以来 can attach directly to nouns (卒業以来、入社以来), while てこのかた generally attaches to a verb's て-form.

items.diff: てこのかた focuses on something continuing right up to now, often paired with 「一度も〜ない」; てからというもの stresses that event as a turning point, after which things changed greatly.

this.tr: I've never once been abroad in my whole life.

that.tr: Ever since our child was born, our life has completely changed.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a state unchanged from then until now, like 「一度も〜ない」「ずっと〜」 → てこのかた; a before-and-after split with that event as the dividing line, like 「すっかり変わった」「〜ようになった」 → てからというもの.

groups.note: Both come from the binding particle 「こそ」 — putting the focus on what comes before: “this, precisely”

items.diff: てこそ states a condition: “only by doing… can…”; からこそ states a reason: “precisely because…”.

this.tr: People can only grow by experiencing failure.

that.tr: It's precisely because I failed many times when I was young that I am who I am today.

items.explain: Look before 「こそ」 and at the second half: て-form (失敗して)＋こそ, usually followed by a general truth with 「できる」「分かる」 → a condition, “only this way can…”; plain form (失敗した)＋からこそ, explaining the reason for something that already happened → a reason, “precisely because”.

groups.note: Both mean “the second part only holds once the first part happens”

items.diff: てこそ states a general truth: “only by doing this do you truly…”; て初めて describes a single experience: “only then, for the first time…”.

this.tr: Only by actually living there can you understand what's truly good about that town.

that.tag: Single experience · for the first time
that.tr: Only after actually living there did I first notice what's good about that town.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: て初めて usually describes one personal experience, often in the past (気づいた、分かった), stressing “only then, for the first time”; てこそ usually states a general truth in the present (分かる、価値がある), stressing “only this way does it truly count”.

items.diff: The same idea, one positive and one negative: てこそ says “only by doing it can…”; ないことには says “unless you do it, you won't…”.

this.tr: Only by actually doing it can you discover how interesting the work is.

that.tr: Unless you actually try it, you won't know whether it's interesting.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a positive result (分かる、できる) → てこそ; a negative result (分からない、始まらない) → ないことには. Each can be rewritten as the other: やってみてこそ分かる ＝ やってみないことには分からない.

items.diff: あってこそ is followed by a clause; あっての is followed directly by a noun and is more formal.

this.tr: It's only thanks to everyone's support that this shop has been able to keep going.

that.tr: A business exists only because of its customers.

items.explain: Look after 「あって」: followed by 「こそ、」 and then a whole clause → あってこそ; followed directly by a noun (商売、人生), with no 「が」 before it → あっての, mostly in set phrases like 「お客様あっての商売」「命あっての物種」.

groups.note: Both come from 「見る」 — みる is looking for yourself, みせる (見せる) is letting others see

items.diff: てみる means trying something yourself, with an unknown result; てみせる means doing it for others to see, declaring “I'll definitely do it”.

this.tr: I'll definitely pull it off on my own — just watch.

that.tr: I don't know if I can, but I'll try it on my own.

items.explain: Only る vs せる apart: みる = seeing the result for yourself, often preceded by 「できるかどうか分からないが」; みせる = letting others see the result, often preceded by 「絶対に」「必ず」, with a refuse-to-lose spirit.

groups.note: Both express the speaker's intention to “do something”

items.title: 〜てやる (defiance · resolve)
items.diff: Both express strong resolve: てみせる is “I'll achieve it for people to see”; てやる carries resentment or grit, usually aimed at someone.

this.tr: Someday I'll definitely become a professional singer — you'll all see.

that.tr: Someday I'll show that guy who laughed at me.

items.explain: Check whether there's an “opponent”: if there's someone who got under your skin, like 「僕を笑ったあいつ」, てやる is common — rough in tone, mostly men's casual speech; if you just want to prove you can do it, use てみせる, which is more positive and fits more situations.

items.diff: つもりだ just calmly states a plan; てみせる declares to others “I'll definitely do it”.

this.tr: Next year I'll pass the exam for sure — just watch.

that.tr: I plan to take the exam again next year.

items.explain: つもりだ only states a plan in your head, regardless of whether anyone is watching; てみせる has “someone watching me” in mind, with a competitive “just you wait” spirit, often with 「必ず」「絶対に」.

groups.note: Both give permission, “it's okay to…”, at different levels of formality

items.diff: てもいい is everyday speech; ても差し支えない is the formal version used in instructions and business.

this.tr: You may fill in the application form in pencil.

that.tr: It's just a note, so pencil is fine.

items.explain: Exactly the same meaning; look at the setting: service counters, instructions, business emails → 差し支えありません; between friends and family → てもいいよ. The same goes for asking permission: 「〜ても差し支えないでしょうか」 is far more polite than 「〜てもいい？」.

items.diff: てもかまわない leans toward “I don't mind”; ても差し支えない leans toward “there's objectively no problem”, and is more formal.

this.tr: You may also send your questions by email.

that.tr: I don't mind where I sit.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's position: saying you personally don't mind (私は〜) → かまいません; telling someone, in the voice of rules or a system, that “doing this won't cause any problem” → 差し支えありません. Formality: てもいい ＜ てもかまわない ＜ ても差し支えない.

groups.note: Both come from 「ならない」 — originally “no good, unbearable”

items.diff: Only a 「は」 apart: てならない means “terribly…, can't help…”; てはならない means “must not…”.

this.tr: I can't stop worrying about the exam results.

that.tr: During the exam, you must not look at your neighbor's answer sheet.

items.explain: First check for 「は」, then look at the word before it: feelings and sensations like 気になる、心配、悔しい、思える → てならない, “so much I can't stand it”; actions you control like 見る、入る, plus 「は」 → てはならない, “doing it is not okay” = prohibition.

items.diff: てならない is a feeling: “so… I can't help it”; なければならない is an obligation: “must do”.

this.tr: I can't help feeling that his story is a lie.

that.tr: I have to hand in the report by tomorrow.

items.explain: Both use 「ならない (no good)」: a feeling or sensation before it → the feeling is so strong it's “unbearable”; 「なければ (if you don't)」 before it → it's “no good” if you don't = must. A deadline like 「明日までに」 usually means なければならない.

groups.note: Both mean a feeling or sensation is very strong: “terribly…”

items.diff: てたまらない is colloquial, often for physical sensations; てならない leans formal and often follows 「気がする」「思える」.

this.tr: I can't help feeling there's something hidden behind this case.

that.tr: The air conditioner broke, and the heat is unbearable.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: physical sensations like 暑い、痛い、眠い, or strong desires like 「〜たくてたまらない」 → usually てたまらない; an “involuntary feeling” like 「気がする」「思える」 → usually てならない.

items.diff: てしょうがない is everyday speech; てならない is more formal, suited to speeches and letters.

this.tr: I deeply regret having to say goodbye to you all.

that.tr: Summer vacation starts tomorrow — I'm so excited I can hardly stand it.

items.explain: Look at the setting: telling friends how you feel → てしょうがない (て仕方がない works too); formal occasions like farewell speeches or letters → てならない, often in the polite form 「〜てなりません」.

groups.note: Both mean “given the cause, it's perfectly reasonable”

items.thisTitle: 〜のも当然だ・〜のももっともだ
items.diff: のも当然／のももっともだ neutrally says “it's only reasonable”; のも無理はない is mostly used to sympathize with a negative reaction or a mistake.

this.tag: のも当然 · naturally follows from the cause
this.tr: He practiced every day, so it's only natural that he won.

this.tag: のももっともだ · it's understandable
this.tr: They broke their promise three times, so it's understandable that he's angry.

that.tr: It's your first trip abroad, so no wonder you're nervous.

items.explain: のも無理はない is sympathetic, mostly used for negative reactions like being nervous, crying or failing; のも当然だ just calmly says “it naturally follows from the cause”, for good or bad outcomes; のももっともだ focuses on acknowledging that someone's feelings or opinion are justified.

groups.note: Both come from 「いられない」 — “can't stay in a certain state”

items.diff: てはいられない means “can't keep…ing any longer”; ないではいられない means “can't help…”.

this.tag: Can't keep it up any longer
this.tr: The trains have stopped. I can't just wait around any longer.

that.tr: Whenever I watch this movie, I can't help crying.

items.explain: Look before 「いられない」: て-form (待って) → can't stay in that state, can't go on like this; ない-form (泣かない) → can't stay in the state of “not doing” = can't help doing it. ずにはいられない (泣かずにはいられない) works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “I can't keep… now”

items.diff: てはいられない focuses on your own restless urgency; ている場合じゃない focuses on “getting your priorities wrong”, often critical.

this.tr: When I heard my mother had collapsed, I couldn't just sit still.

that.tr: The exam is tomorrow. This is no time to be playing games.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's feelings: you're anxious yourself and can't sit still → てはいられない; reminding (or scolding) someone else or yourself that “you should be doing something else now” → ている場合じゃない, more colloquial; in writing, ている場合ではない.

items.diff: てはいられない means can't… even a little longer; てばかりはいられない means can't “only”….

this.tr: The deadline is tomorrow. I can't rest any longer.

that.tr: I've already recovered. I can't just keep resting forever.

items.explain: The extra 「ばかり (only, nothing but)」: 休んではいられない means the situation is urgent and you can't rest even a moment longer; 休んでばかりはいられない means resting is understandable, but you can't do nothing but rest, often appearing with 「いつまでも」.

groups.note: Both come from 「ならない」 — originally “no good, won't work”

items.diff: Only a 「は」 apart: てはならない means “must not…”; てならない means “terribly…, can't help…”.

this.tr: During the exam, you must not look at your neighbor's answer sheet.

that.tr: I can't stop worrying about the exam results.

items.explain: First check for 「は」, then look at the word before it: actions you control like 見る、入る, plus 「は」 → てはならない, “doing it is not okay” = prohibition; feelings and sensations like 気になる、心配、悔しい → てならない, “so much I can't stand it”.

items.diff: てはならない is “doing it is not okay” = prohibition; なければならない is “not doing it is not okay” = must.

this.tag: Doing it is not okay · prohibition
this.tr: You must not talk loudly in the library.

that.tag: Not doing it is not okay · must
that.tr: Library books must be returned within two weeks.

items.explain: The same 「ならない (no good)」 — look at the condition before it: 「て＋は」 = if you do it → no good → prohibition; 「なければ」 = if you don't → no good → must. てはいけない／なければいけない follow the same logic.

groups.note: Both express prohibition or “shouldn't”

items.diff: てはいけない is colloquial and can be said to a specific person; てはならない is formal and solemn, mostly found in rules and speeches.

this.tr: No one other than authorized personnel may enter this room.

that.tr: It's dangerous, so you mustn't go into this room, okay?

items.explain: Look at who's addressed and the sentence ending: said to the person in front of you (especially a child), with 「よ」 at the end → てはいけない (more casually, ちゃだめ); notices, regulations and warnings to the public → てはならない.

items.diff: べきではない is the speaker's opinion, “really shouldn't”; てはならない means “absolutely not allowed”.

this.tr: War must never be started again.

that.tr: Personally, I don't think we should rush this plan.

items.explain: Look at how strong the tone is: べきではない is an opinion open to discussion, often with 「と思う」「個人的には」; てはならない is a prohibition with no room for discussion, often with 「決して」「二度と」.

items.title: 〜べからず
items.diff: Both are prohibitions with the same meaning; べからず is classical Japanese, now found only on signs and in proverbs.

this.tr: Do not enter the park lawn.

that.tr: Keep off the grass.

items.explain: Look at the style and how it attaches: べからず attaches to the verb dictionary form (入る＋べからず; する usually becomes すべからず), an old form mostly seen on signs and in proverbs (「働かざる者食うべからず」); in writing and speech, use てはならない.

groups.note: Both come from the quoting 「と言う」 — “to call…, to be called…”

items.title: 〜という (called)
items.diff: という introduces a name; といった lists a few examples and sums them up as a category.

this.tr: Dishes like ramen and curry are popular with children.

that.tr: I ate ramen at a restaurant called “Sakura”.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: before という is a name (さくら), and the noun after it is that very thing; before といった are several examples (ラーメンやカレー), and the noun after it is the category they belong to — implying there are others too.

groups.note: Both are used to list examples

items.diff: や〜など can be followed directly by a particle; といった must be followed by a summarizing noun, and is more formal.

this.tr: Tourist spots like Hokkaido and Okinawa get lots of foreign visitors.

that.tag: Can be followed directly by a particle
that.tr: I went to places like Hokkaido and Okinawa.

wrong.why: といった must be followed by a noun

items.explain: Look after 「といった／など」: if it can be followed directly by a particle like 「に」「を」 → など; if there's always a noun after it grouping the examples into a category (観光地、料理) → といった. For casual listing in speech you can also say 「〜とか〜とか」.

groups.note: Both mean “like… (in that way, in that manner)”

items.title: 〜ように (as…, like…)
items.diff: ふうに is colloquial and usually pairs with こんな、そんな; ように attaches directly to a verb clause, meaning doing it according to some reference.

this.tr: Please fold the paper in half like this.

that.tr: Please fold the paper in half as written in the instructions.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: こんな、そんな、どんな are followed by ふうに, most common when showing while explaining in person; a verb clause like 「書いてある」「言った」 is followed directly by ように, meaning “just as…”. When ふうに follows a clause, it usually needs 「という」.

items.diff: ふりをする is the subject deliberately pretending; ふうな is how something looks to the speaker, often critical.

this.tr: He doesn't know a thing, yet he talks as if he knows it all.

that.tr: I actually knew, but I pretended not to.

items.explain: ふりをする is the subject consciously pretending (知らないふりをする); ふうな is the speaker describing how the other person comes across — 「知ったふうな口をきく」 (talking like a know-it-all) is practically a set phrase, usually with a note of annoyance.

groups.note: Both come from 「というもの」 — “the thing called…”: affirmative というものだ means “that's what… is”, negative というものではない means “it's not as if… is enough”

items.diff: というものだ asserts “this is what… is”; というものではない means “it's not as if… is enough” — not a simple opposite.

this.tr: Being able to laugh together with your family — that's what happiness is.

that.tr: It's not as if having money is all it takes to be happy.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: というものだ usually follows a noun (幸せ、人生、友情), with the speaker asserting “this is its true essence”; というものではない is almost always preceded by 「〜ばいい」「〜さえ〜ば」, specifically rejecting the one-sided idea that “just… is enough”.

groups.note: というものだ ↔ というもの — only the final 「だ」 apart

items.diff: というものだ gives an evaluation at the end of a sentence; というもの follows a period of time, stressing “that entire time”.

this.tr: Making people work ten hours every day is simply unreasonable.

that.tr: For this entire week, I've hardly slept.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and where it sits: というもの follows a period of time (この一週間、ここ数年), sits mid-sentence, and is followed by a continuing state; というものだ sits at the end of the sentence, after a noun or clause, meaning “that's what you call…”.

groups.note: Both come from 「というもの」 — “the thing called…”: affirmative というものだ means “that's what… is”, negative というものではない means “it's not as if… is enough”

items.diff: というものではない rejects “just… is enough”; というものだ asserts “this is what… is” — the two are not simple opposites.

this.tr: It's not as if having money is all it takes to be happy.

that.tr: Being able to laugh together with your family — that's what happiness is.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: というものではない is almost always preceded by 「〜ばいい」「〜さえ〜ば」, specifically rejecting the one-sided idea that “just… is enough”; というものだ usually follows a noun (幸せ、人生), with the speaker asserting “this is its true essence”.

groups.note: Both end in 「ものではない」 — the only difference is whether 「という」 is there, but the meanings are completely different

items.title: 〜ものではない (shouldn't)
items.diff: ものではない is advice based on common sense, “you shouldn't…”; というものではない means “it's not as if… is enough”.

this.tag: It's not as if… is enough
this.tr: An apology alone doesn't settle it.

that.tr: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

items.explain: Check for 「という」 in the middle and the form before it: ものではない attaches directly to a verb's dictionary form and is elder-style advice, “you shouldn't do that”; というものではない is usually preceded by 「〜ばいい」, and rejects an idea rather than forbidding an action.

groups.note: Both express partial negation: “it's not that…, not necessarily”

items.diff: とは限らない objectively points out “there are exceptions”; というものではない criticizes the idea that “just… is enough”.

this.tr: It's not as if the more expensive something is, the better.

that.tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a “just… is enough” expression like 「〜ければいい」「〜さえすれば」 is followed by というものではない, with a lecturing tone; 「必ずしも」「〜からといって」 are followed by とは限らない, which just calmly says “there are exceptions”.

items.diff: わけではない corrects someone's misunderstanding about a specific situation; というものではない rejects a one-sided principle.

this.tr: With studying, it's not as if the longer you do it the better.

that.tr: It's not that I dislike studying. I just don't have time.

items.explain: Look at whose situation it's about: explaining that you or a specific situation is “not what you think”, often adding the real reason (〜だけだ) → わけではない; saying “that way of thinking is wrong” about a general idea → というものではない.

groups.note: Both mean “all, every single one”

items.diff: AというA repeats the same noun, meaning “every A”; AといわずBといわず names two or three representative examples, meaning “everywhere”.

this.tr: People were leaning out of every single window.

that.tr: Face, hands — he's covered in mud all over.

items.explain: Check whether the noun repeats: the same noun with 「という」 in between (窓という窓) → every one in that category; two different nouns each with 「といわず」 (顔といわず手といわず) → naming a few representatives, meaning “no matter where”. Both are formal, literary expressions.

groups.note: Both express a well-grounded inference

items.diff: と考えられる is objective and leaves room for doubt; に違いない is a strong subjective conviction.

this.tr: Judging from the sales trend, the economy can be considered to be recovering.

that.tr: Seeing that smile, something good must have happened.

items.explain: Look at the basis and setting: objective material like data or surveys, when writing a report and you don't want to state things too definitively → と考えられる; feeling quite sure just from someone's expression or a hunch → に違いない, common in everyday conversation too.

groups.note: Both come from 「と＋なる」 — “becoming a situation of…”

items.diff: となると means “if it actually comes to this situation”; ともなると means “once you reach such a high status or stage”.

this.tag: Specific situation · if it really comes to that
this.tr: If I'm going into the hospital tomorrow, I'll have to take time off work.

that.tag: Status or stage · once you get there
that.tr: Once you're a university student, you should make your own decisions.

items.explain: Check whether 「も」 follows 「と」 and what comes before: a status, age or period like 大学生、社長、12月 ＋ともなると → “once you reach this stage, naturally…”, describing a general tendency; a specific event like 入院、引っ越し ＋となると → “if it really comes to that”, a judgment about the situation at hand. となれば・となったら are used like となると.

groups.note: Both mean “if it's the case that…”

items.diff: としたら can be a pure hypothesis; となると usually refers to something that has become reality or that you actually have to face.

this.tr: If the typhoon really does come, tomorrow's game will probably be canceled.

that.tr: If you won the lottery, what would you buy?

items.explain: Look at how real the premise is: a fantasy that will almost never happen, like 「もし宝くじが当たったら」 → としたら／とすれば; a situation you're about to face, like a typhoon in the forecast → となると, usually followed by a judgment like 「だろう」「大変だ」.

groups.note: Both mean “I hear that…” — passing on what someone said

items.title: 〜そうだ (I hear)
items.diff: そうだ is ordinary reporting; とのことだ is more formal, mostly used to pass on a message from someone.

this.tr: I have a message from the department manager: the meeting starts at three.

that.tr: According to the news, it's going to snow tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at where the information comes from and who you're telling: general information like news or weather forecasts → そうだ; passing on a message for a boss or client, at work or in letters → とのことです. とのことだ can also carry requests and instructions (「〜てほしいとのことです」), which そうだ usually doesn't.

items.diff: んだって is casual speech between friends; とのことです is the formal version used at work and in letters.

this.tr: Mr. Tanaka got in touch to say he'll be a little late.

that.tr: I heard Tanaka's going to be a bit late.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the setting: mentioning it casually to coworkers or friends → んだって (also んですって); formally passing on a message to a boss or client → とのことです.

groups.note: Both come from the quoting particle 「と」 — raising what comes before as the topic

items.diff: とは is formal and used for definitions; って is its colloquial form, used in everyday conversation to ask “what is…?”.

this.tr: “Shūkatsu” is short for “job-hunting activities”.

that.tr: Hey, what's “shūkatsu”?

items.explain: Look at the style: the sentence ends in 「である」「のことだ」 and appears in dictionaries, textbooks or papers → とは; friends asking 「〜って何？」「〜ってどういう意味？」 → って. って is originally just the colloquial form of と（は）.

groups.note: Each matches one of 「とは」's uses — definition and surprise

items.diff: とは is concise and formal, mostly in dictionaries and titles; というのは works in both speech and writing, and can also explain something just said.

this.tr: What is happiness?

that.tag: Colloquial · explaining what was just said
that.tr: When I said “a little while” just now, I meant about thirty minutes.

items.explain: Look at the style and what's being explained: short written sentences like paper titles or dictionary definitions → とは; explaining a word in conversation, or explaining what you or the other person just said → というのは.

items.diff: Both mean “to think that…!”; なんて is colloquial and often dismissive; とは is more formal and leans written.

this.tr: To think that a friend I hadn't seen in ten years had become a company president!

that.tr: Getting such an easy question wrong — I can't believe it.

items.explain: Look at the tone: between friends, with a hint of contempt or complaint (こんな簡単な問題を) → なんて; expressing surprise or deep feeling in writing or formally, often ending in 「〜とは。」「〜とは思わなかった」 → とは.

groups.note: Both mean “although it's said that…, …”
