items.diff: Nearly the same meaning; とはいえ can be followed by advice or a command, while とはいうものの is usually followed by a disappointing reality.

this.tr: It may be spring, but it's still cold.

that.tag: Can be followed by advice or a command
that.tr: It may be spring, but it gets cold at night, so take a coat with you.

items.explain: Look at the second half: just describing that “reality isn't as expected” → either works; followed by advice or a command like 「〜なさい」「〜ましょう」 → とはいえ is more natural. とはいえ is also more concise and often stands alone at the start of a sentence (とはいえ、……).

items.diff: といっても means “it's not as impressive as it sounds”, correcting what the listener imagines; とはいうものの means “reality doesn't match the label”.

this.tr: It's supposedly a day off, but I'm actually working at home.

that.tag: Not as impressive as it sounds
that.tr: I say I can cook, but really I can only make a rolled omelet.

items.explain: Look at the second half: scaling things down with 「〜くらい」「ほんの〜」 → といっても, common in speech; the second half says reality contradicts the label (休みなのに仕事をしている) → とはいうものの, leaning formal.

groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — originally “to limit, to be restricted to”

items.diff: とは限らない means “not necessarily”; に限らず means “not just…, others too”.

this.tr: Just because someone is Japanese doesn't mean they like sushi.

that.tr: Sushi is popular not only with Japanese people but with foreigners too.

items.explain: The same 「限る (to limit)」: とは限らない = can't be limited to being that way → there are exceptions, usually at the end of a sentence; に限らず = not limited to this → the scope widens, often followed by 「〜も」「〜にも」.

groups.note: Both express partial negation: “not necessarily, it's not that…”

items.diff: とは限らない points out exceptions to a general claim; わけではない corrects a misunderstanding about a specific situation.

this.tr: Expensive restaurants aren't necessarily good.

that.tr: It's not that I dislike this restaurant. I'm just full today.

items.explain: Look at what's being discussed: a general view like 「高い店はおいしい」 → とは限らない, “there are exceptions”; explaining that you or a specific situation is “not what you think”, often adding the real reason (〜だけだ) → わけではない.

items.diff: とは限らない calmly says “there are exceptions”; というものではない criticizes the idea that “just… is enough”.

this.tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.

that.tr: It's not as if the more expensive something is, the better.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: 「必ずしも」「〜からといって」 are followed by とは限らない, which just calmly says “there are exceptions”; a “just… is enough” expression like 「〜ければいい」「〜さえすれば」 is followed by というものではない, with a lecturing tone.

groups.note: Both come from the formal noun 「ところ」 — meaning “a certain point, a certain situation”

items.diff: ところから is mostly about the origin of a name, and can be followed by an established fact; ところを見ると is always followed by a guess.

this.tr: Because they're shaped like stars, they're called “star sand”.

that.tr: Since the light is still on, it seems he's still up.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: an established fact like 「と呼ばれている」「と名付けられた」 → ところから; a guess like 「らしい」「ようだ」「に違いない」, based on what you can see in front of you → ところを見ると.

groups.note: Both mean “basis, reason” — from which a name or judgment is derived

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; ことから is the most common, ところから is more formal and focuses on a particular “feature” of something.

this.tr: Because you can see Mt. Fuji from it, this slope is called “Fujimi-zaka”.

that.tr: Because the fingerprints matched, it became clear he was the culprit.

items.explain: The two are mostly interchangeable; when you read ところから, you can understand it as ことから. ことから has the widest range, common for both judgments and causes; ところから is more formal, mostly used to explain the origin of place names or object names, focusing on a particular feature.

groups.note: Both come from the formal noun 「ところ」 — meaning “a certain point, a certain situation”

items.diff: ところを見ると is always followed by a guess; ところから is mostly about the origin of a name, and can be followed by an established fact.

this.tr: Since the light is still on, it seems he's still up.

that.tr: Because they're shaped like stars, they're called “star sand”.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: a guess like 「らしい」「ようだ」「に違いない」, based on what you can see in front of you → ところを見ると; an established fact like 「と呼ばれている」「と名付けられた」 → ところから.

groups.note: Both mean “guessing from what you see”

items.diff: ところを見ると gives the evidence in the first half of the sentence; とみえる sits at the end and is itself the guess.

this.tr: He's not answering no matter how many times I call, so he must still be asleep.

that.tr: He's not answering no matter how many times I call. He must still be asleep.

items.explain: Look at the position: ところを見ると is in the first half, and needs 「らしい」「ようだ」 after it to be complete; とみえる sits at the end, directly after the content of the guess, with the evidence usually in the previous sentence.

items.diff: からすると follows a noun; ところを見ると follows a clause, with the evidence being what's right in front of you.

this.tag: Follows a clause · what you see
this.tr: Since the lights in the room are off, it looks like nobody's home.

that.tr: Judging from his expression, the exam didn't go well.

items.explain: First check whether a noun or a clause comes before: a noun like 表情、話し方、この点 ＋からすると (から見ると works too); a clause describing a situation, like 「電気が消えている」 ＋ところを見ると. からすると can also mean “from the standpoint of…”, which ところを見ると cannot.

groups.note: Both are written 「として」, but put “一 + counter” before it and a negative after, and the meaning is completely different

items.title: 〜として (as)
items.diff: 一 + counter + として paired with a negative means “not a single one”; noun + として means “as…”.

this.tr: Not a single person objected at the meeting.

that.tr: I came to Japan as an exchange student.

items.explain: Look before 「として」 and at the sentence ending: “一 + counter” like 一人、一つ、一日, with a negative at the end → not a single one; a role noun like 留学生、教師 → as. The original sense is “even counting it as just one, there's none”, which is why the negation is so strong.

groups.note: Both express total negation: “not a single one, not at all”

items.diff: 誰も〜ない is the ordinary way to say it; 誰一人として〜ない stresses “not even one” more, and is formal and emphatic.

this.tr: Not a single person could answer that question.

that.tr: Nobody could answer that question.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the tone: in everyday speech use 「誰も〜ない」「何も〜ない」; to stress “not even the smallest amount”, or in writing and speeches, add 「一人」「一つ」 followed by として (誰一人として、何一つとして).

items.diff: として usually states a fact, “not even once”; たりとも is more formal and usually expresses resolve or prohibition, “not even a little”.

this.tr: In these ten years, I haven't taken a single day off.

that.tr: Until the exam, I can't waste a single day.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: stating a past fact, like 「休んだことはない」「いなかった」 → として is natural; expressing resolve or prohibition, like 「できない」「〜てはならない」「許さない」 → たりとも is more forceful and more formal.

groups.note: Both mean “while…” and “although…”

items.diff: The meanings match one to one: つつ ＝ ながら, つつも ＝ ながらも; つつ is more formal.

this.tag: つつ · at the same time
this.tr: I walked slowly, enjoying the scenery.
I know it's bad for my health, yet I can't quit smoking.

that.tag: ながら · at the same time
that.tr: I walked slowly, enjoying the scenery.
I know it's bad for my health, yet I can't quit smoking.

wrong.why: つつ only attaches to verbs; adjectives need ながらも

items.explain: With verbs the two are interchangeable: ながら is everyday speech, つつ is mostly found in writing and speeches. But つつ only attaches to a verb's ます-stem: uses with adjectives and nouns like 「狭いながらも」「残念ながら」「子どもながら」 can't be replaced with つつ.

groups.note: Both can express “a change in progress”

items.diff: 沈んでいる means “has already sunk”; 沈みつつある means “is in the process of sinking”.

this.tr: Right now, the evening sun is sinking into the sea.

that.tr: By the time I noticed, the sun had already sunk into the sea.

items.explain: Look at the verb: for instantaneous changes like 沈む、消える、死ぬ, adding ている shows the resulting state, “has already become…”; to say “is heading toward that result”, use つつある. つつある is written language; in speech people usually say 「沈みかけている」.

items.diff: てきている is colloquial, describing a change that has developed up to now; つつある is formal, objectively describing a change moving in a certain direction.

this.tr: Japan's population is declining.

that.tr: It's gradually been getting colder lately, hasn't it?

items.explain: Look at the style: objectively describing a trend in news or reports → つつある; saying “it's getting more and more…” in everyday chat → てきた／てきている, often with 「だんだん」「最近」.

items.diff: つつある just objectively describes a change in progress; 一方だ means “keeps on…ing”, mostly for negative trends.

this.tr: The economy is recovering little by little.

that.tr: Prices just keep going up and up.

items.explain: Look at the tone: 一方だ stresses “only in one direction, unstoppable”, with worry or dissatisfaction (上がる一方、悪くなる一方); つつある just calmly says a change is happening, good or bad. They attach differently too: 一方だ takes the dictionary form, つつある takes the ます-stem.

groups.note: Both come from 「上（うえ）」 — from “on top” extended to “on the basis of…”

items.diff: た上で means “after…, then…”; た上は means “now that…, (must)…”.

this.tr: I'll give you my answer after thinking it over carefully.

that.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

items.explain: Only で vs は apart; look at the second half: the next step to take (返事をします、決めます) → 上で; resolve or responsibility (最後まで〜、〜しかない) → 上は. 上は is fairly formal.

items.diff: 上で means “after, on the basis of…”; 上に means “not only…, but also”.

this.tr: I'll decide after talking it over with my family.

that.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap, but tasty too.

items.explain: Look before 「上」 and at the second half: a verb's た-form, followed by the next action → 上で; an adjective or a word describing a state, followed by another evaluation in the same direction → 上に, “what's more”.

groups.note: Both mean “do… first, then…”

items.diff: てから is just a plain sequence; た上で stresses that the first part is a necessary prerequisite for the second, with a careful, formal tone.

this.tr: Please check the contents carefully before signing.

that.tr: I wash my hands and then eat.

items.explain: Check whether the first part is “preparation for the second”: something done first to get the next step right, like 確認、相談、検討 → た上で (with nouns, 「確認の上で」), mostly in business and procedures; an everyday sequence like washing your hands before eating → てから.

groups.note: Both come from 「上（うえ）」 — from “on top” extended to “on the basis of…”

items.diff: 上に means “not only…, but also”; 上で means “after, on the basis of…”.

this.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap, but tasty too.

that.tr: I'll decide after talking it over with my family.

items.explain: Look before 「上」 and at the second half: an adjective or a word describing a state, followed by another evaluation in the same direction → 上に, “what's more”; a verb's た-form, followed by the next action → 上で.

items.diff: 上に means “what's more”, adding one thing on top of another; 上は means “now that…, (must)…”.

this.tag: One bad thing after another · what's more
this.tr: I got lost, and on top of that it started to rain.

that.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

items.explain: Only に vs は apart; look at the second half: adding another thing in the same direction, often with 「まで」「も」 → 上に; the speaker's resolve or responsibility → 上は.

items.diff: 上に attaches after a word and finishes the idea in one sentence; その上 comes at the start of a sentence, picking up from the previous one and adding more.

this.tr: This restaurant is not only cheap, but tasty too.

that.tag: Sentence start · follows the previous sentence
that.tr: This restaurant is cheap. What's more, it's tasty.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the position: 上に comes right after an adjective or verb, joining the two things into one sentence; その上 is a standalone conjunction, with a sentence before it, and 「その」 refers to what that sentence said: 安い上においしい ＝ 安い。その上、おいしい。

groups.note: Both express addition: “not only…, but also”

items.diff: 上に only states facts piled on top of each other; ばかりでなく can also be followed by a command or suggestion.

this.tr: He can speak not only English but Chinese too.

that.tag: Can be followed by a command
that.tr: Don't just study English — study Chinese too.

wrong.why: 上に can't be followed by a command or request

items.explain: Look at the second half: just stating “there's A and also B” → either works; if the second half is a command or request like 「〜しなさい」「〜てください」 → only ばかりでなく (だけでなく). Also, 上に requires both parts to point the same way — both good or both bad.

items.diff: 上に follows adjectives and verbs; に加えて usually follows nouns and is objective and formal.

this.tr: It's windy today, and it's raining too.

that.tr: In addition to strong winds, heavy rain is expected.

items.explain: First look at the word before it: a noun (強風、経験) → に加えて, common in news and announcements; an adjective or verb (強い、降っている) → 上に. The news says 「強風に加えて」, while in conversation you'd say 「風が強い上に」.

groups.note: Both come from 「上（うえ）」 — from “on top” extended to “on the basis of…”

items.diff: た上は means “now that…, (must)…”; た上で means “after…, then…”.

this.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

that.tr: I'll give you my answer after thinking it over carefully.

items.explain: Only は vs で apart; look at the second half: resolve or responsibility (最後まで〜、〜しかない) → 上は; the next step to take (返事をします、決めます) → 上で.

items.diff: 上は means “now that…, (must)…”; 上に means “what's more”, adding one thing on top of another.

this.tr: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.

that.tag: One bad thing after another · what's more
that.tr: I got lost, and on top of that it started to rain.

items.explain: Only は vs に apart; look at the second half: the speaker's resolve or responsibility → 上は; adding another thing in the same direction, often with 「まで」「も」 → 上に.

groups.note: Both mean “now that…, (must)…”

items.diff: 以上（は） is common in both speech and writing, and 「は」 can be dropped; 上は is more formal, and 「は」 can't be dropped.

this.tag: Formal · now that it's come to this
this.tr: Now that it's come to this, I'll just have to do it myself.

that.tr: Since you promised, you should keep your word.

items.explain: Same meaning; look at the style: 以上（は） is common in both daily life and business, and 「は」 is often dropped; 上は is mostly used in formal or grimly resolute situations (こうなった上は、かくなる上は), and 「は」 can't be dropped.

items.diff: からには is the most common in speech, positive and direct in tone; 上は is formal and written, often with a grim “now that it's come to this” feel.

this.tr: Now that I've been chosen as company president, I'm determined to give it everything I have.

that.tr: If I'm going to play in the match, I definitely want to win.

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: telling friends “if I'm going to…, then…” → からには; an inauguration speech, an official statement, or resolve when backed into a corner like 「こうなった上は」 → 上は.

groups.note: Both come from 「得る（える／うる）」 — originally “to obtain”, extended to “to be able to”

items.diff: 得ない means “impossible”; ざるを得ない means “can't not…”, in other words “have no choice but to”.

this.tr: Such a coincidence is impossible.

that.tag: Can't not → have no choice but to
that.tr: Because of the heavy rain, we have no choice but to cancel the match.

items.explain: 得る = can, 得ない = can't. ざるを得ない is 「ざる (not doing)＋を得ない (can't)」: can't not do = have no choice but to. Look before 「得ない」: directly after a verb's ます-stem (あり得ない) → impossible; with 「ざる」 before it (せざる、行かざる) → have no choice but to.

groups.note: Both are about “whether it's possible”

items.diff: Both mean “it's possible”; 得る only attaches to a verb's ます-stem and is more formal and concise; 可能性がある attaches to the dictionary form, and you can also say 「可能性が高い」.

this.tr: A major earthquake could happen at any time.

that.tr: There's a possibility of a major earthquake in the near future.

wrong.why: 得る needs the ます-stem: 起こり得る

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「得る」: it can only be the ます-stem (起こり得る、あり得る); 可能性がある takes the dictionary form (起こる可能性). To say the possibility is “high/low”, you can only use 可能性が高い／低い — 得る has no such expression.

items.diff: 得ない means objectively “impossible”; かねる means “find it hard to…” from the speaker's position, mostly used to decline politely.

this.tr: A person's heart is something others can never fully understand.

that.tag: Hard from one's position · polite refusal
that.tr: I'm very sorry, but I'm unable to agree with that opinion.

items.explain: The subject of かねる is the speaker, often appearing with 「申し訳ありませんが」: you can't do it because of your position or feelings, usually as a polite refusal; 得ない says the thing itself is objectively impossible, often preceded by 「あり」「理解し」「知り」.

groups.note: Both mean “A goes without saying, and B too…”

items.diff: Nearly the same meaning; はもちろん is also used in everyday speech, は言うまでもなく is more formal.

this.tr: Today, not to mention the safety of the athletes, we are also putting the safety of all our spectators first.

that.tr: This ramen shop — the taste goes without saying, and it's cheap too.

items.explain: Both have the same structure (Aは〜、Bも〜); the difference is the setting: chatting with friends, with 「よ」 at the end → はもちろん is most natural; in speeches, addresses and writing, は言うまでもなく is more formal. はもとより also leans formal, like は言うまでもなく.

items.diff: Same meaning; は言うに及ばず has a classical flavor and is even more formal than は言うまでもなく.

this.tr: His name is well known not only in Japan but overseas too.

that.tr: The name is known, needless to say, at home, and far and wide overseas as well.

items.explain: Look at the style of the whole sentence: the 「ず」 in 及ばず is a classical negative, often appearing with formal words like 「遠く〜にまで」「その名は」, mostly in writing and formal speeches; for ordinary formal occasions, は言うまでもなく is enough.

items.diff: は言うまでもなく focuses on “A goes without saying”; もさることながら acknowledges A but stresses that B is really the point.

this.tr: This movie has a great story, of course, and the music is wonderful too.

that.tr: The story of this movie is good, but the music is even better.

items.explain: Look at the particle after B: 「Aは言うまでもなく、Bも」 — B takes 「も」, and A and B are equally good; 「Aもさることながら、Bが」 — B usually takes 「が」, and what the speaker really wants to praise is B.

items.diff: は言うまでもなく is a neutral “and furthermore”; はおろか is mostly used for negative or bad things, with surprise or dissatisfaction.

this.tr: My older sister can read not only kanji but even difficult classical texts.

that.tr: My little brother can't write kanji — he can't even write hiragana.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a negative or bad outcome like 「さえ〜ない」「も〜ない」, with the speaker surprised or dissatisfied → はおろか; something positive or neutral → は言うまでもなく. はおろか also can't be followed by a command or invitation.

groups.note: Both mean “setting A aside for now”

items.diff: はさておき sets a topic aside to get to the main point; はともかく means “A aside, how about B”, with a contrasting evaluation.

this.tr: Joking aside, let's get down to business.

that.tr: Never mind how this dish looks — it tastes good.

items.explain: Look at what the second half is doing: moving on to the topic you really want to discuss (本題に入る) → はさておき — 「冗談はさておき」「それはさておき」 are set phrases; contrasting A and B and evaluating B (A isn't great, but B is fine) → はともかく.

items.diff: はさておき just means not discussing it for now; は別として can also mean “except for… (as an exception)”.

this.tag: Set aside → switch to main topic
this.tr: Let's leave that for now and talk about next week's trip.

that.tag: A few exceptions · all the rest
that.tr: Except for a few people, almost all the employees agreed.

items.explain: は別として is often preceded by a small exception (一部の人、子ども) and followed by what's true of the rest (ほとんど、みんな); はさておき is preceded by one topic and followed by a switch to another — it's not excluding exceptions.

groups.note: Both come from 「ともかく」 — “whatever the case, leaving it aside”

items.diff: はともかく sets the A in front of you aside for now; ならともかく is a hypothesis, “if it were A, that would be understandable”, but in reality it isn't A.

this.tr: Never mind the taste — the portions at this place are way too small.

that.tag: Hypothesis · if it were A, fine
that.tr: A child would be one thing, but a grown adult crying over something like that!

items.explain: Check whether 「は」 or 「なら」 comes before: は = A is a real topic, just not being discussed for now; なら = a hypothesis, A isn't actually the case (it's an adult in front of you, not a child), usually followed by criticism or dissatisfaction.

groups.note: Both mean “setting A aside for now”

items.diff: はともかく means “A aside, how about B”, with a contrasting evaluation; はさておき sets a topic aside to get to the main point.

this.tr: Never mind how this dish looks — it tastes good.

that.tr: Joking aside, let's get down to business.

items.explain: Look at what the second half is doing: contrasting A and B and evaluating B (A isn't great, but B is fine) → はともかく; moving on to the topic you really want to discuss (本題に入る) → はさておき — 「冗談はさておき」「それはさておき」 are set phrases.

items.diff: はともかく often implies A has a problem, but lets it slide for now; は別として neutrally sets A aside as an exception.

this.tag: A has a problem · let it slide
this.tr: The price aside (it's a bit expensive), the taste is top-notch.

that.tag: A few exceptions · all the rest
that.tr: Except for a few people, almost all the employees agreed.

items.explain: は別として can mean “except for…”: preceded by a small exception and followed by what's true of most of the rest (ほとんど、みんな); はともかく isn't used that way — it lets A slide for now (usually A isn't great, e.g. it's expensive) and turns to evaluating B.

groups.note: Both come from 「わけ（訳）」 — meaning “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけがない means “there's no way”; わけだ means “no wonder, it makes sense”.

this.tr: He's never practiced even once, so there's no way he's any good.

that.tr: He practices every day, so no wonder he's so good.

items.explain: わけ = reason. わけがない: there's simply no reason for it, so “impossible”; わけだ: there's a reason, so “no wonder”. Look at the first half: the reason clearly doesn't hold → わけがない; a sufficient reason is given → わけだ.

items.diff: わけがない means “there's no way” (total denial); わけではない means “it's not that…” (partial denial).

this.tr: He practiced that much — there's no way he'll lose.

that.tr: Just because you practiced doesn't mean you'll definitely win.

items.explain: わけがない is the speaker asserting “absolutely not”; わけではない corrects an inference that seems “only natural”, often appearing with 「からといって」「必ず」「全部」. Check for these words before it, then see whether the ending is 「が」 or 「では」.

items.diff: わけがない judges that something “can't possibly happen”; わけにはいかない says you yourself “can't do it (out of duty or decency)”.

this.tr: Someone as serious as him would never go out partying the day before an exam.

that.tr: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and play today.

items.explain: Look at the subject and perspective: inferring about someone else or a situation (彼が〜) → わけがない; the speaker themselves “would like to, but can't because of duty or rules” → わけにはいかない.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no way”

items.diff: The two are often interchangeable; はずがない leans calm, inferring from evidence, while わけがない is more subjective and emotional, often used to retort.

this.tr: How could I possibly forget my promise to you?!

that.tr: I definitely locked it, so there's no way the door is open.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's basis and tone: calmly inferring from specific evidence (鍵をかけた) → はずがない is most natural; angrily rebutting someone's suspicion, with 「だろう／じゃないか」 at the end → わけがない (in speech often わけない). Often the two are interchangeable.

items.diff: Both mean “impossible”; っこない is very casual speech and only attaches to a verb's ます-stem.

this.tr: There's no way we can beat such a strong team.

that.tr: We can't possibly beat a team that strong.

wrong.why: っこない needs the ます-stem: 勝てっこない

items.explain: Look at the verb form before it: plain form (勝てる)＋わけがない; ます-stem (勝て)＋っこない. っこない is only for casual talk between friends; in formal situations and writing, use わけがない.

groups.note: Both mean “after going through…, the result came about”

items.diff: を経て objectively says something passed through a certain stage; 末(に) stresses that after a long stretch of agonizing or effort, a result was finally reached.

this.tr: After a document screening and an interview, I was hired.

that.tr: After agonizing over it again and again, I finally decided to quit my job.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: を経て follows a noun, usually a procedure or stage (審査, 面接, 議論) or a period of time; 末に usually follows a verb in た-form or 「Nの」 — an effortful process like 「悩んだ」「考えた」, often together with 「何度も」「さんざん」, and the result didn't come easily.

groups.note: Both mean “doing one thing also serves another purpose at the same time”

items.diff: を兼ねて is one action that itself serves two purposes; ついでに is doing B on the side while doing A.

this.tr: I walked to the station, which also served as exercise.

that.tr: On my way to the station, I stopped by a bookstore.

items.explain: Count the actions in the sentence: を兼ねて has just one action (歩いて行った), and the noun before it is an extra purpose of that action; ついでに has two actions (駅に行く + 本屋に寄る), and the second is done on the side.

items.diff: がてら only links two actions, usually followed by 「行く・寄る」; を兼ねて can also be used as 「〜を兼ねた + noun」 to say one thing serves two purposes.

this.tr: This room is a bedroom that doubles as a study.

that.tr: While out for a walk, I stopped by a nearby bookstore.

wrong.why: がてら needs an action before it (散歩, 買い物); it can't say one thing doubles as something else

items.explain: がてら usually follows actions like 「散歩」「買い物」 and is followed by movement like 「行く・寄る・歩く」; to say a room or an object has two uses at once, only を兼ねた works.

items.diff: かたがた is only used in formal letters and business greetings; を兼ねて also works in everyday speech.

this.tr: On the weekend I went to the venue, partly to check it out in advance.

that.tr: I will call on you shortly to greet you and to express my thanks.

items.explain: かたがた almost always follows 「お礼」「ご挨拶」「ご報告」 and is usually followed by 「伺う」「お願いする」 — a set phrase in business letters and greetings; for everyday “while I'm at it / doubling as…”, use を兼ねて.

groups.note: Both mean “with some event as a turning point, things started to change”

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; を契機に is more formal and usually describes major social shifts; をきっかけに works in speech too, even for small personal things.

this.tr: Spurred by the oil crisis, the development of energy-saving technology advanced.

that.tr: A friend invited me, and that's how I started playing tennis.

items.explain: Look at the scale of the trigger and the register: big historical or social events, in news or academic papers → を契機に; small personal things like a friend's invitation, in everyday chat → をきっかけに (きっかけ can also be used for big events, so it's more widely applicable).

items.diff: を契機に focuses on “this triggered a change”; を機に focuses on “taking this opportunity to actively do something”.

this.tr: The big earthquake raised people's awareness of disaster prevention.

that.tag: Seizing the moment · acting on purpose
that.tr: I took my retirement as the chance to move to the countryside.

items.explain: Look at the second half: something the subject decides to do (引っ越した, 始めた) → を機に is most natural, usually after life milestones like retirement, marriage or graduation; a change that was “triggered” in society or awareness (高まった, 広まった) → を契機に.

items.diff: With を契機に, the first part is the cause of the change; を境に is just a dividing line — things are completely different before and after, with no necessary cause and effect.

this.tr: Following that accident, traffic lights were installed at this intersection.

that.tag: Dividing line · before and after differ
that.tr: From that day on, I never heard from him again.

items.explain: を境に can follow just a point in time (その日, 40歳); the focus is “before and after are completely different”; を契機に must follow an event that can cause change (事故, 地震), and what follows is a new measure or development it brought about.

groups.note: Both mean “with some event as the starting point”

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; をきっかけに works in speech too, even for small personal things; を契機に is more formal and usually describes major social shifts.

this.tr: A friend invited me, and that's how I started playing tennis.

that.tr: Spurred by the oil crisis, the development of energy-saving technology advanced.

items.explain: Look at the scale of the trigger and the register: small personal things like a friend's invitation, in everyday chat → をきっかけに; big historical or social events, in news or academic papers → を契機に (きっかけ can also be used for big events, so it's more widely applicable).

items.diff: をきっかけに usually describes a change that followed naturally; を機に stresses taking the opportunity to actively do something.

this.tr: A friend invited me along, and I came to love mountain climbing.

that.tr: I quit smoking when I got married.

items.explain: を機に usually follows life milestones like marriage, retirement or moving, and is followed by something you resolved to do (やめた, 引っ越した); with をきっかけに, the trigger is often a small chance event, and what follows can be a change that happened without you noticing (好きになった).

groups.note: Both mean “concerning a certain topic”

items.diff: について just marks the topic, “about…”; をめぐって always implies several parties arguing or clashing over it.

this.tr: Residents are divided over the construction of the new airport.

that.tr: A briefing was held on the construction of the new airport.

items.explain: Look at the verb in the second half: 対立する, 争う, もめる, 議論になる → をめぐって; things one person can do with no dispute, like 調べる, 書く, 説明する → について.

items.diff: をめぐる usually modifies disputes and conflicts; に関する just neutrally means “related to…”.

this.tr: The quarrel between the brothers over the inheritance is still going on.

that.tr: I read a book about inheritance.

items.explain: Both can come before a noun (をめぐる + N / に関する + N). Look at the noun being modified: 争い, 対立, 問題, 裁判 → をめぐる; neutral things like 本, 資料, 情報 → に関する (に関して also just means “about”). When you see 「〜をめぐる」 in a news headline, you know there's a dispute behind it.

groups.note: All come from もと (基), “foundation, basis”

items.diff: をもとに uses something as material, so you're free to build on it; に基づいて (もと + つく) sticks closely to a basis and can't stray from it.

this.tr: I wrote a novel based on a real incident.

that.tr: The penalty was decided in accordance with the rules.

items.explain: 基づく is literally 「もと (基, base) + つく (to attach)」 — clinging to the foundation, so it usually follows laws, rules or data and is followed by a judgment or a measure, with no room to stray; をもとに just uses something as a starting point — it follows material like events, experiences or documents, and is usually followed by writing, making or developing, which allows adapting and reworking.

groups.note: Both mean “using… as a basis”

items.diff: をもとに uses something as material to “make something”; を頼りに relies on it as a clue to “feel your way forward”.

this.tr: Drawing on my childhood memories, I painted the old town as it used to be.

that.tr: Relying on my childhood memories, I looked for the house I used to live in.

items.explain: The first half is exactly the same, so look at the verb that follows: “producing a work” like 描く, 作る, 書く → をもとに; “feeling your way forward” in an unclear situation, like 探す, 歩く, たどり着く → を頼りに.

groups.note: Both mean “leaving… out”

items.title: 〜抜きで (without…, leaving out…)
items.diff: を除いて removes part of a range and says “all the rest…”; 抜きで means doing something “without it”.

this.tag: Remove a part · all the rest
this.tr: Everyone except Tanaka has gathered.

that.tr: We started the meeting without Tanaka.

items.explain: を除いて is often followed by 「全員」「みんな」「毎日」 and describes “all the rest” once that part is removed; 抜きで is followed by an action and means “do it this way, without it / leaving it out”, as in the common 「わさび抜きで」「冗談抜きで」.

items.diff: を除いて removes specific members from a range; は別として sets a certain issue aside and then makes an assessment.

this.tr: Except on rainy days, I bike to work every day.

that.tr: The cost aside, I think the plan itself is good.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a fact about all the rest (毎日, 全員) → を除いて; an evaluation (いいと思う) → は別として, with an “issue or condition” set aside for now before it.

groups.note: Both mean “using… as a basis”

items.diff: を頼りに relies on something as a clue to “feel your way forward”; をもとに uses it as material to “make something”.

this.tr: Relying on my childhood memories, I looked for the house I used to live in.

that.tr: Drawing on my childhood memories, I painted the old town as it used to be.

items.explain: The first half is exactly the same, so look at the verb that follows: “feeling your way forward” in an unclear situation, like 探す, 歩く, たどり着く → を頼りに; “producing a work” like 描く, 作る, 書く → をもとに.

groups.note: All come from とする, “to set… as, to regard… as”

items.diff: AをBとして sets some other person or thing A as B; Bとして on its own states the subject's own role.

this.tr: The department head made him the leader and formed a new team.

that.tr: As the leader, he keeps the team together.

items.explain: Check whether there's 「〜を」 before 「として」: with 「Aを」, A is being set as B (彼をリーダーとして); without it, the subject is acting in that role (彼はリーダーとして).

items.diff: AをBとする actively sets A as B; AはBとされる is its passive, “A is considered / designated as B”.

this.tr: The government designated this area a danger zone.

that.tr: This area has been designated a danger zone.

items.explain: とされる is simply the passive of とする. Look at the subject and particles: someone making the decision (政府は) and A marked with 「を」 → とする; A as the subject with 「は」 and no mention of who decided → とされる, also common in news and papers to say “it is generally believed that…”.

groups.note: Both mean “to set A as B”

items.title: 〜にする (to set as)
items.diff: Same meaning; AをBとする is for written rules and notices; AをBにする is the everyday way to say it.

this.tr: Entry to this tournament is limited to those aged 18 and over.

that.tr: Let's make the meeting time nine o'clock.

items.explain: Look at the setting: in rules, notices or contracts, “set… as…” is とする (〜を対象とする, 〜を条件とする); when friends or coworkers decide something together, use にする.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; を問わず usually only follows nouns; にかかわらず can also follow paired opposites like 「する・しない」.

this.tr: Anyone can apply, with or without experience.

that.tr: Whether or not you will attend, please be sure to reply.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: nouns like 「経験の有無」「男女」「年齢」 → both work, though を問わず is more common in job ads and notices; paired verbs like 「する・しない」「行く・行かない」 → use にかかわらず.

items.diff: を問わず follows a range (age, gender); いかんを問わず follows 「Nのいかん」 and means “however N turns out / whatever N is” — stiffer.

this.tr: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.

that.tr: Unauthorized absence is not permitted, whatever the reason.

items.explain: いかん means “how / what”. Look at what comes before: nouns with “content or quality” like 理由, 結果, 事情 take 「の」 and then いかんを問わず, mostly in regulations and contracts; ranges or categories like 年齢, 男女, 国籍 take を問わず directly. いかんにかかわらず works the same way.

groups.note: All come from やら (← classical 「にやあらむ」, “might it be…?”) — originally carrying a vague, “hard to say” questioning tone

items.diff: やら〜やら lists things, “…and… and…”; のやら〜のやら means “I can't tell whether… or…”.

this.tr: What with work and housework, I'm busy every day.

that.tag: Can't tell if A or B
that.tr: I really can't tell whether he's serious or joking.

items.explain: Check for 「の」 and what follows: のやら〜のやら is often followed by 「分からない」, and the two items are usually opposite possibilities (本気/冗談, 行く/行かない); やら〜やら is followed by 「で忙しい／大変だ」 and lists several things piling up at once.

groups.note: Both list a few examples, hinting there are others

items.diff: とか〜とか is a neutral, casual way of listing; やら〜やら carries a sense of “so much going on, a total mess”.

this.tr: Before the move, what with packing and cleaning, it was really hard.

that.tr: On my days off, I do things like cleaning and laundry.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a chaotic feeling like 「〜で大変だった／忙しい」 → やら〜やら; just calmly giving a few examples → とか〜とか.

items.diff: だの〜だの usually relays someone else's complaints, with irritation; やら〜やら lists things that happened or mixed feelings.

this.tr: Being praised in front of everyone, I was both happy and embarrassed.

that.tr: He does nothing but complain — the pay is low, there aren't enough days off.

items.explain: だの〜だの lists what someone “said”, often followed by 「文句を言う」「うるさい」, and the speaker finds it annoying; やら〜やら lists things that happened, or several feelings welling up in you at once.

items.diff: たり〜たり calmly lists representative actions; やら〜やら carries a sense of “chaotic, one thing after another”.

this.tr: On the trip, what with losing my wallet and getting lost, it was a disaster.

that.tr: On the trip, I did some shopping, took some photos, and so on.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「〜で散々だった／大変だった」 → やら〜やら, after the dictionary form; just mentioning a few things you did → たり〜たりする, after the た-form.

groups.note: Both mean “after comparing, B is more fitting than A”

items.diff: というより rephrases, “it's not so much A as B”; よりむしろ chooses the latter of two options.

this.tr: On my days off, I'd rather relax at home than go out.

that.tr: Today it's not so much cool as cold.

items.explain: というより gives two descriptions of the same thing (涼しい → 寒い), and the speaker switches to the more accurate word; よりむしろ compares two choices or courses of action and is often followed by 「〜たい」「〜ほうがいい」. They're also often used together: 「〜というよりむしろ〜」.

items.diff: よりむしろ calmly compares and picks B; くらいなら follows something you really don't want to do: “rather than do that, I'd sooner…”.

this.tr: Rather than ask someone else, it's quicker to do it myself.

that.tr: Rather than ask someone like that, I'd sooner pull an all-nighter myself.

items.explain: Look at the first part and the sentence ending: with くらいなら, the first part is something the speaker hates (あんな人に頼む), and the sentence often ends in 「ほうがましだ」; with よりむしろ, A isn't necessarily bad — B is just more suitable by comparison.

groups.note: It's the same particle より — originally “from…”: setting out from a time or place = starting point; measuring from B = comparison

items.diff: より as a starting point means “from / by”; より for comparison means “than”.

this.tr: And now, a few words of greeting from our president.

that.tr: The department head talks even longer than the president.

items.explain: Look at what follows より: actions like 「挨拶・連絡・出発・始まる」 → starting point or source, “from / by”; an adjective (長い, 高い) → comparison, “than”. The formal 「〇〇より」 is easy to mistake for a comparison, so watch the verb that follows.

groups.note: Both mark a starting point, “from…”

items.title: 〜から (starting point)
items.diff: Same meaning; より is used in notices, announcements and formal documents; から in everyday speech.

this.tr: The meeting will be held from 3 p.m. today.

that.tr: The meeting starts at three, okay?

items.explain: Look at the setting and tone: notice- or announcement-style phrasing like 「本日」「行います」 → より; casual talk between friends or coworkers → から. The same goes for ranges: a notice writes 「9時より17時まで」, everyday speech says 「9時から5時まで」.

groups.note: Both come from よう (様), “that kind of state”, followed by a supposition

items.diff: ようでは can only be followed by a negative judgment; ようなら is a neutral “if”, and can be followed by advice or instructions.

this.tr: If the fever doesn't go down, tomorrow's trip is out of the question.

that.tr: If the fever doesn't go down, go to the hospital.

items.explain: The first half is exactly the same, so look at the second half: a negative evaluation like 「無理だ」「だめだ」「〜とは言えない」 → ようでは; advice or instructions like 「〜しなさい」「〜てください」 → ようなら.

groups.note: 「ようでは」 ↔ 「(よ)うではないか」 — the first few kana are identical

items.diff: ようでは means “if it's like this, (it's no good)”; (よ)うではないか is a rallying call, “let's… together!”.

this.tr: If you give up over something this small, you'll never succeed.

that.tr: Let's keep going to the very end and never give up!

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「よう」: dictionary form or ない-form (諦める) + ようでは → supposition; volitional form (続けよう, しよう) + ではないか → rallying call. Then look at the sentence ending: a rallying call ends with 「ではないか」, while ようでは is followed by a clause with a negative evaluation.

groups.note: Both mean “carrying on like this will lead to a bad result”

items.diff: ては directly says an action will bring a bad result; ようでは judges someone's behavior as a “sort of state”, and carries a stronger sense of criticism.

this.tr: Anyone who makes such a simple mistake can hardly be called a pro.

that.tr: If you stay up late every night, you'll ruin your health.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a concrete bad result (体を壊す, 太る) → ては (likewise では, ていては); an evaluation of a person or their qualifications (プロとは言えない, 失格だ) → ようでは. ようでは is often preceded by 「こんな」「この程度で」 and conveys disappointment or criticism.

groups.note: Both come from the volitional form 「〜(よ)う」, “let's…”

items.diff: The volitional form alone is an ordinary “let's…”; adding the rhetorical question 「ではないか」 turns it into a solemn, forceful rallying call.

this.tr: Let us all join forces and change this town!

that.tr: Let's head home soon.

items.explain: ではないか literally means “isn't it…?”; the rhetorical question makes it stronger, so it's mostly used in speeches and declarations addressed to a crowd; to casually say “let's…” to friends around you, just use the volitional form (帰ろう, 食べよう).

groups.note: 「(よ)うではないか」 ↔ 「ようでは」 — the first few kana are identical

items.diff: (よ)うではないか is a rallying call, “let's… together!”; ようでは means “if it's like this, (it's no good)”.

this.tr: Let's keep going to the very end and never give up!

that.tr: If you give up over something this small, you'll never succeed.

items.explain: Look at the verb form before 「よう」: volitional form (続けよう, しよう) + ではないか → rallying call; dictionary form or ない-form (諦める) + ようでは → supposition. Then look at the sentence ending: a rallying call ends with 「ではないか」, while ようでは is followed by a clause with a negative evaluation.

groups.note: Both invite or urge others to do something together

items.diff: ましょう is an everyday polite suggestion; (よ)うではありませんか is a speech-style rallying call, formal and stirring.

this.tr: Fellow citizens, let us join forces and build a beautiful city!

that.tr: Everyone, let's take a short break.

items.explain: Look at the setting and audience: an everyday suggestion in a meeting or class → ましょう; a speech or declaration to a crowd, meant to rouse people → (よ)うではありませんか.

items.diff: ませんか politely asks whether the other person would like to; (よ)うではありませんか is also a question in form, but it's actually a strong rallying call that doesn't wait for an answer.

this.tr: For the future of our planet, let us take action right now!

that.tag: Invitation · asking if they'd like to
that.tr: Would you like to see a movie together this weekend?

items.explain: Both sentences end in 「〜ませんか」. Look at what comes before: verb ます-stem + ませんか (見ませんか) asks one person's wishes, and they can say no; volitional form + ではありませんか (行動しようではありませんか) is a call out to a crowd.

groups.note: Both come from まい, a negative intention: “I won't…”

items.diff: まい alone is a resolution, “I'll never… again”; paired with the volitional form as 「〜(よ)うか〜まいか」, it becomes hesitation over “to do it or not”.

this.tr: Every night I agonize over whether to quit my job or not.

that.tr: I'm never going to that shop again.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence has a pair of “positive intention + negative intention”: 「辞めようか辞めまいか」 side by side, followed by 「悩む・迷う」 → hesitation; just one 「〜まい」 at the end of the sentence, often with 「二度と」「もう」 → resolved not to do it.

groups.note: 「〜うか〜まいか」 ↔ 「〜うが〜まいが」 — only か / が differ

items.diff: Only one kana differs: 「か」 is hesitating between doing and not doing; 「が」 is “whether or not you do (it's all the same)”.

this.tr: I still can't decide whether to go or not.

that.tr: Whether you go or not has nothing to do with me.

items.explain: The structure is identical, so just look at the particle: 「〜うか〜まいか」 is followed by 「迷う・悩む」 — the mind isn't made up yet; 「〜うが〜まいが」 is followed by 「関係ない・自由だ」 — either outcome is the same. 「〜(よ)うと〜まいと」 also means “whether or not”.

groups.note: Both mean “whether”

items.diff: かどうか is a neutral “whether”, usable for anything; (よ)うか〜まいか is only for actions you can decide yourself, and highlights inner wavering.

this.tr: I'm torn over whether to tell him the truth.

that.tr: I don't know whether it will rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Check whether the speaker can decide the action: their own actions like 言う, 行く, 辞める, with inner back-and-forth → (よ)うか〜まいか; an objective “whether”, like the weather or other people's affairs → only かどうか.

groups.note: Both mean “can't do it even though you want to”

items.diff: (よ)うにも〜ない stresses that the wish to do something is blocked; ようがない focuses on “there's simply no way to do it”.

this.tr: I don't know the phone number, so even if I want to contact them, I can't.

that.tr: I don't know the phone number, so there's no way to contact them.

items.explain: ようにも must be followed by another negative (連絡できない), splitting “want to” and “can't” into two parts; ようがない says “there's no way” in one phrase, after the ます-stem (しようがない, 書きようがない). They're also often used together: 「連絡しようにも連絡のしようがない」.

items.diff: (よ)うにも〜ない is usually about an objective obstacle that stops you; に〜ない is mostly a set phrase expressing an emotional dilemma.

this.tr: The trains stopped, so I couldn't get home even if I wanted to.

that.tr: It's a story you want to laugh at but can't.

items.explain: Look at the verb form and the reason: volitional form + にも (帰ろうにも), usually with an objective reason before it (電車が止まって); dictionary form + に (笑うに笑えない, 泣くに泣けない, 引くに引けない), mostly set phrases about the dilemma of feeling you “can't do that”.

groups.note: Both come from よう (様), “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようになっている means “a machine or system is designed to…”; ようになる means “a person comes to be able to / starts to…”.

this.tr: This door is designed to open automatically when someone approaches.

that.tr: My child can now get dressed on their own.

items.explain: Look at the subject: a machine, system or rule → a mechanism built in from the start (ようになっている), often with 「〜と」 — not a “change”; a person or animal → a change in ability or habit (ようになった).

items.diff: ようになっている says the mechanism simply works this way; ようにしている is a person consciously making a point of doing something. Only 「な」 and 「し」 differ.

this.tr: This door locks automatically when night falls.

that.tag: Person · makes a point of it
that.tr: I always lock the door when night falls (I make a point of it).

items.explain: Look at the subject and verb: a machine or system as subject, with an intransitive verb (鍵がかかる) → ようになっている; a person as subject, with a transitive verb (鍵をかける), often with 「必ず」「なるべく」 → ようにしている.

groups.note: Both mean “that's how it's set up / that's the rule”

items.diff: ことになっている is a rule or arrangement people have set; ようになっている is something that happens automatically by system or mechanism.

this.tr: With this card, every tenth use is automatically free.

that.tr: At this company, you're required to let them know if you'll be late.

items.explain: Look at who carries out what follows: a rule people must follow or carry out (連絡する) → ことになっている; a result that the machine or system produces on its own with no effort from anyone (無料になる) → ようになっている.

groups.note: Both come from the classical negative auxiliary ず, “not”

items.diff: ざる and ぬ are both forms of 「ず」 that modify nouns (“that does not…”); ぬ is more common, ざる more solemn.

this.tr: Introducing little-known masterpieces.

that.tr: A stranger spoke to me.

items.explain: Both come before a noun, equivalent to modern 「〜ない + noun」: 見知らぬ人 = 見知らない人, 知られざる名作 = 知られていない名作. ぬ is also common in novels and everyday writing; ざる sounds more solemn and is mostly seen in titles and ads (知られざる〜, 見えざる〜).

items.diff: ざる + noun means “N that does not…”; ざる + を得ない means “cannot not…”, i.e. “have no choice but to”.

this.tag: ざる + noun · that does not…
this.tr: Ceaseless effort led to success.

that.tag: ざる + を得ない · have no choice but to
that.tr: The budget fell short, so we had no choice but to cancel the plan.

items.explain: Look at what follows ざる: a noun (努力, 名作) → “that does not…”; 「を得ない」 → a double negative, “have no choice but to”. ざる is a noun-modifying form that can act like a noun, which is why it can take 「を」 after it.

items.title: 〜べからざる (that must not…)
items.diff: ざる just means “that does not…”; べからざる is 「べし (should, may) + ざる」 and means “that must not / cannot…”.

this.tr: To fight an unseen enemy.

that.tr: Water is indispensable to daily life.

items.explain: Check for 「べから」 before ざる: without it (見えざる = 見えない), it's just a negative; with it (欠くべからざる), it takes on the “should, may” of 「べし」 and becomes “that must not…”. Also, べからざる follows the dictionary form (欠く), while ざる follows the ない-form stem (見え).

groups.note: Break it down: 「ざる」 (classical negative 「ず」, “not”) + 「を得ない」 (negative of 「得る」, “cannot”)

items.diff: ざるを得ない means “cannot not…”, i.e. “have no choice but to”; ざる + noun means “N that does not…”.

this.tag: ざる + を得ない · have no choice but to
this.tr: The budget fell short, so we had no choice but to cancel the plan.

that.tag: ざる + noun · that does not…
that.tr: Ceaseless effort led to success.

items.explain: Look at what follows ざる: 「を得ない」 → a double negative, “have no choice but to”; a noun (努力, 名作) → “that does not…”. ざる is a noun-modifying form that can act like a noun, which is why it can take 「を」 after it.

items.diff: ざるを得ない means “cannot not”, i.e. “have no choice but to”; 得ない on its own means “impossible”.

this.tag: Cannot not → have no choice but to
this.tr: Because of the heavy rain, the match has to be canceled.

that.tr: There's no way such a coincidence could happen.

items.explain: 得る = to be able to, 得ない = cannot. ざるを得ない = 「ざる (not doing) + を得ない (cannot)」: cannot not do = have no choice but to. Look at what comes before 「得ない」: 「ざる」 (せざる, 行かざる) → have no choice but to; directly after a verb's ます-stem (あり得ない) → impossible.

groups.note: Both mean “have no choice but to…, can only…”

items.diff: ざるを得ない stresses being forced by pressure, against your will; ほかない means “there's no other way”, in a calm tone.

this.tr: If it's the president's order, I have no choice but to go.

that.tr: I missed the last train, so I'll just have to walk home.

items.explain: Look at the reason: someone else's order or pressure, when you don't really want to (社長の命令) → ざるを得ない; simply no other means available (終電を逃した) → ほかない (しかない in casual speech). よりほかない works the same way.

items.diff: ざるを得ない is being forced by objective circumstances; ないわけにはいかない is not being able to avoid it out of personal obligation or responsibility.

this.tr: The typhoon grounded our flight, so we had no choice but to give up the trip.

that.tr: It's my best friend's wedding, so no matter how busy I am, I can't not go.

items.explain: Look at the reason: objective circumstances like a typhoon or budget shortfall leave you no choice → ざるを得ない; friends, gratitude or responsibility, where not going would be unacceptable → ないわけにはいかない.

items.diff: ざるを得ない always carries the resignation of “I didn't want to”; なければならない is “must” based on rules or duty.

this.tr: I wasn't feeling well, so I had to miss the match I'd been looking forward to.

that.tr: In Japan, cars must drive on the left side of the road.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence is about a rule: laws, regulations, general duties (左側を走る) → なければならない, with no sense of reluctance; something you wanted to do but had to give up or change because of circumstances (楽しみにしていた試合を休む) → ざるを得ない.

groups.note: Both come from しまう (仕舞う), “to finish, wrap up”

items.diff: With ずじまい, the regret is that you “didn't do it” before it ended; with てしまう, the regret is that you “did it”.

this.tr: The book I'd meant to buy — in the end I never bought it.

that.tr: I even ended up buying clothes I had no intention of buying.

items.explain: じまい is the voiced form of 「しまい」 (end). Look at what comes before: 「ず」 = didn't do → it ended “without getting done”; 「て」 = did → finished it, or did something you shouldn't have. Both often carry regret, but in exactly opposite directions.

groups.note: Both mean “didn't do something”

items.title: 〜ないまま
items.diff: ないまま just describes something else happening “while not having done” something; ずじまい says “it never got done in the end” — a settled regret.

this.tag: Never, in the end · sentence end
this.tr: The cake I'd been looking forward to — in the end I never got to eat it.

that.tag: State of not having done · then something else
that.tr: I left the house without eating breakfast.

items.explain: Look at the position in the sentence and what follows: ずじまい usually comes at the end, often with 「結局」「とうとう」, and says something completely fell through; ないまま is followed by another action (家を出た) and just describes the state at the time, not necessarily with regret.

groups.note: Both mean “wanting to do something but not managing to”

items.diff: あぐねる is thinking or trying again and again with no result, with a hint of weariness; かねる is “can't” because of your position or feelings, often used to politely decline.

this.tag: Thinking over and over · no result
this.tr: I've been thinking for a whole week about how to reply, and I still have no idea.

that.tr: I'm very sorry, but I'm unable to answer regarding that matter.

items.explain: Check for “taking a long time”: 一週間も, 何度も, ずっと → あぐねる, focusing on the weariness and deadlock after repeated attempts; set politeness like 「申し訳ありませんが」 → 「〜しかねます」, meaning “I'm not in a position to…”, a tactful refusal — あぐねる has no such use.

items.diff: あぐねる is going back and forth on your own without being able to decide; に〜ない is being held back by a concern or obstacle, so you can't do it even if you want to.

this.tag: Going back and forth · can't decide
this.tr: I still can't make up my mind about which university to go to.

that.tag: A concern · can't decide even if I want to
that.tr: When I think about my parents objecting, I just can't bring myself to decide.

items.explain: Check for a “reason holding you back”: a concern like 「親の反対を思うと」 → に〜ない, repeating the same verb (決めるに決められない, 言うに言えない); no outside obstacle, just options that are hard to compare and no conclusion after long thought → あぐねる, often with 「ずっと」「何日も」.

items.diff: With あぐねる you're still looking for a way, still trying, just not succeeding; すべがない means there isn't even a way, so you can only give up.

this.tr: No matter how many times they attacked, they couldn't score — the attack stalled.

that.tag: No way at all · can only give up
that.tr: The opponent was too strong — we were utterly helpless.

items.explain: Look at the first half: 「何度攻めても」 shows they kept trying, just without results → あぐねる, with a sense of frustration and impatience; 「強すぎて」 shows there was simply no means available, so they could only stand by and watch → すべがない, most often as 「なすすべがない」.

groups.note: Both mean “B exists only because of A” — A is indispensable

items.diff: Same idea: あっての says it positively, “B exists because there's A”; なくして says it negatively, “without A, there's no B”.

this.tr: Without customers, there's no business — it all depends on them.

that.tr: Without customers, a business can't survive.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「AあってのB」 is followed directly by a noun, and the whole sentence is positive; 「Aなくして」 is always followed by a negative (成り立たない, ありえない). The two sentences mean the same thing — one positive, one negative.

items.diff: あっての follows a noun and says something is indispensable; てこそ follows an action and says “only by doing… can you…”.

this.tr: Passing the exam was entirely thanks to daily effort.

that.tr: Only by working hard every day can you pass the exam.

items.explain: Check whether a noun or a verb's て-form comes before: nouns like 努力, 健康, お客様 → あっての, also followed by a noun, mostly looking back on an achievement with gratitude; actions like 努力して, 苦労して → てこそ, followed by “what can only then be achieved”, mostly stating a general truth.

groups.note: Both come from 切る / 切り (きり), “cut-off point, limit”

items.diff: 数えればきりがない means “once you start counting, there's no end to it (so I won't)”; 数えきれない means “far too many to count”.

this.tag: Endless once you start · don't want to count
this.tr: If you started listing his faults, you'd never finish.

that.tr: The stars in the sky are countless.

items.explain: Both come from 「切る」. Look at the form: ば-form + きりがない → there's no place to stop; the speaker subjectively feels “once I start, I can't stop”, implying “so I won't go on”; ます-stem + きれない → objectively too many to finish. (The positive 数え切る = to count them all, likewise “cutting through to the end”.)

items.diff: ばきりがない says “there's no limit, it goes on forever”; きり says “it stops there” — only this much, or nothing more after that.

this.tr: If I started complaining, there'd be no end to it.

that.tr: I'd like to talk with just the two of us.
My son went out this morning and still hasn't come back.

items.explain: 「きり」 is 「切り」, the point where something is cut off. きりがない: no place to cut off → endless; noun + きり: cut off here → only this much; た-form + きり: cut off after this happened → nothing more after that (行ったきり, 会ったきり).

groups.note: All come from こそ, “precisely this” — attached to ば / から / て to emphasize a reason or condition

items.diff: Same meaning; ばこそ is formal and solemn, mostly for well-meant reasons; からこそ works in speech and writing, for good or bad reasons alike.

this.tr: It's precisely because I'm thinking of your future that I speak so harshly.

that.tr: It's precisely because I'm thinking of your future that I speak so harshly.

items.explain: First look at the connection: ばこそ follows the conditional form (思えば, あればこそ); からこそ follows the plain form (思う). Then look at the setting: ばこそ is solemn, mostly in speeches and writing, and mostly for well-meant, positive reasons; in everyday speech, or when the reason is something bad, use からこそ.

items.diff: ばこそ gives a reason, “precisely because…”; てこそ gives a condition, “only by doing… can you…”.

this.tr: It's precisely because parents love their children that they scold them harshly.

that.tr: Only once you become a parent yourself do you understand how much your parents did for you.

items.explain: Don't be fooled by 「ば」: the ば in ばこそ isn't “if” — what comes before is an established fact (子を愛している), and what follows explains the intention behind an action (叱るのだ); with てこそ, what comes before is something you must first experience, followed by the result that “only then can be achieved or understood” (分かる, できる).

groups.note: Both come from まで, “up to…, until…”

items.diff: ばそれまでだ means “once…, that's the end of it (all is lost)”; までだ means “if worst comes to worst, I'll just…”, showing there's still a way out.

this.tr: No matter how much you practice, if you mess up on the day, that's the end of it.

that.tag: Worst case, I'll just… · a way out
that.tr: If it doesn't work out this year, I'll just take the exam again next year.

items.explain: Both 「まで」 mean “that's where it ends”. Look at what comes before: ば-form + それまでだ → things end at that moment and everything before is wasted; verb dictionary form + までだ → “I'll just take this step, that's all”, often with 「〜なら」, showing calm and a fallback (までのことだ is the same).

groups.note: Both mean “once…, there's no going back”

items.diff: With ばそれまでだ the sentence ends there, and the conclusion is “it's all over”; たら最後 must go on to state the bad result that follows.

this.tr: However much money you save, once you get sick, that's the end of it.

that.tr: Once you start playing this game, you can't stop until morning.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「それまでだ」 is itself the conclusion (everything back to zero), often preceded by 「いくら〜ても」; 「たら最後」 must be followed by a bad result that inevitably happens (朝までやめられない, 二度と戻れない). が最後 is the same, just more formal.

groups.note: Both come from ばかり — originally “only this much”

items.diff: ばかりになっている means “only this step is left, ready to go at any time”; ばかりだ means “steadily changing in one direction”, usually for the worse.

this.tag: Only one step left · all set
this.tr: The luggage is packed. All that's left is to set off.

that.tr: Even with medicine, the illness just keeps getting worse.

items.explain: Both are 「dictionary form + ばかり」. Look at the context: followed by 「になっている」 and often preceded by 「あとは」 → everything else is ready, only this one action remains; 「ばかりだ」 right at the end, after a verb of change (悪くなる, 増える) → the situation only moves in one direction.

items.diff: Dictionary form + ばかりになっている means “not done yet, just waiting to be done”; た-form + ばかり means “just finished”.

this.tag: Dictionary form → just waiting to do it
this.tr: The food is all laid out. All that's left is to eat.

that.tr: I only just had lunch a moment ago.

items.explain: Look at the verb form before ばかり: dictionary form (食べる) → the action hasn't happened yet, “only this one thing is left”, often preceded by 「あとは」; た-form (食べた) → the action just ended, often preceded by 「さっき」「今」.

items.diff: ばかりになっている means really ready, just waiting to do it; んばかりに means “as if about to…”, and the action doesn't actually happen.

this.tr: My mother had finished packing and was all set to leave the house.

that.tag: As if about to… · didn't actually happen
that.tr: My mother begged me, practically in tears.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ばかり: dictionary form (出る) + ばかりになっている → an actual state of readiness; ない-form with ない replaced by ん (泣か + ん) → “looking as if about to…”, a figurative description followed by another action (頼んできた) — she didn't actually cry. (んばかりの + noun works the same way.)

groups.note: Both come from classical べし, “ought to be so, should”

items.diff: べからず is the negative of べし: べし means “must…”, べからず means “must not…”.

this.tr: No running in the hallway.

that.tr: Walk quietly in the hallway.

items.explain: Both are classical forms found on notices and signs. Look at the ending: ending in 「べし。」 → a rule saying “you must do this”; 「べから + ず」 (ず = not) → a rule saying “you must not do this”. The two often appear on the same notice, one positive, one negative.

items.diff: べからず is a non-negotiable “prohibited” on a notice; べきではない is “shouldn't” by reasoning — advice or a personal opinion.

this.tr: Authorized personnel only. No entry.

that.tr: I don't think you should speak ill of others in front of children.

items.explain: Look at the setting: notices and signs posted on doors or walls (立ち入るべからず) → べからず, a prohibition in command form; reasoning or giving an opinion in writing or conversation (〜と思う) → べきではない. Both come from べし; べきではない is the modern form.

items.diff: べき + noun means “… that should be”; べからざる + noun is its negative, “… that must not be / cannot be”.

this.tag: That must not… · modifies a noun
this.tr: Water is indispensable to daily life.

that.tr: This is a rule everyone should follow.

items.explain: Both べき and べからざる can directly modify nouns: べき + noun = “… that should be”; べからざる + noun = “… that must not / cannot be” (べから + ざる, ざる = that does not). べからざる is very formal; the most common are 「欠くべからざる」 (indispensable) and 「許すべからざる」 (unforgivable).

groups.note: Both mean “must not, shouldn't”

items.diff: Both mean prohibition; べからず is classical and only seen on notices and signs; てはならない is modern written language.

this.tr: Danger. No entry beyond this point.

that.tr: By law, minors are not allowed to drink alcohol.

items.explain: Look at where it appears: notices, signs, maxims → べからず, a classical form — using it in modern speech is a joke; laws, regulations, news, lecturing → てはならない, modern written language. Both mean “must not…”.

items.diff: べからざる means “that must not / cannot…” in a general sense; まじき usually appears as 「〜にあるまじき」, criticizing something as “unbefitting one's position”.

this.tr: That is an absolutely unforgivable act.

that.tr: That is conduct unbecoming of a teacher.

items.explain: Check whether a role or position comes before: 教師, 政治家, 学生 + にあるまじき → criticizes something as “unbefitting that role”; no role, just saying the thing itself is not acceptable (許すべからざる, 欠くべからざる) → べからざる.

groups.note: Both come from classical べし, “ought to, must”

items.diff: べく means “in order to…”; べくして repeats the same verb before and after, meaning “was bound to…”.

this.tr: I keep working hard to make my dream come true.

that.tr: Since safety measures had been neglected, the accident was bound to happen.

items.explain: Look at what follows べく: 「、」 followed by an action taken for that purpose → purpose, “in order to…”; followed by 「して」 and then the same verb in た-form (起こるべくして起こった) → “what was destined to happen, happened”. Both are the continuative form of べし; one takes its “intention” sense, the other its “naturally so” sense.

items.diff: べく means “in order to…”; べくもない means “there's no way to…”.

this.tr: An investigation began to uncover the truth.

that.tr: Back then, I had no way of knowing the truth.

items.explain: Look at what follows べく: 「、」 followed by an action → purpose; directly followed by 「もない」 → “not even possible”, mostly after the verbs 知る, 望む, 比べる. べし itself has senses like “intention” and “possibility”; べく takes “intention”, べくもない takes “possibility”.

groups.note: Both express purpose, “in order to…”

items.diff: Same meaning; べく is stiff written language and can't be followed by commands or requests; ために works in any situation.

this.tr: To pass the exam, he studied so hard he barely slept.

that.tr: Study every day so that you pass the exam.

wrong.why: べく can't be followed by a command or request

items.explain: Look at the second half: an action you take toward your own goal (勉強した, 全力を尽くした) → both べく and ために work, べく sounding more like news or a speech; a command or request like 「しなさい」「してください」 → only ために. Also, する + べく usually becomes すべく.

items.diff: Both are written expressions of purpose; んがため follows the ない-form and sounds more intense, often with a sense of “by any means necessary”.

this.tr: He gave it everything he had to win the championship.

that.tr: To win, they'll stop at nothing.

items.explain: First look at the connection: べく follows the dictionary form (優勝する → 優勝すべく); んがため follows the ない-form with ない replaced by ん (勝た + ん; する becomes せん). Then look at the tone: んがため is more intense and often followed by something like 「手段を選ばない」, at any cost; べく is calmer and common in news reports.

groups.note: Both come from classical べし, “should, possible”

items.diff: べくもない means “there's no way to…”; べく means “in order to…”.

this.tr: Back then, I had no way of knowing the truth.

that.tr: An investigation began to uncover the truth.

items.explain: Look at what follows べく: directly followed by 「もない」 → “not even possible”, mostly after the verbs 知る, 望む, 比べる; 「、」 followed by an action → purpose, “in order to…”. べし originally has senses like “possibility” and “intention”; べくもない takes “possibility”, べく takes “intention”.

groups.note: Both mean “can't…, impossible to…”

items.diff: ようがない is the general expression, focusing on “no way can be found”; べくもない is written language, focusing on “simply impossible given the circumstances”, and only goes with a few verbs.

this.tr: I had no way of knowing how things were in my faraway hometown.

that.tr: I don't know their address or phone number, so there's no way to contact them.

items.explain: Look at the verb and register: ようがない can follow almost any verb (連絡しようがない, 直しようがない), is common in speech too, and means “there's no method”; べくもない only goes with a few verbs like 知る, 望む, 比べる, 疑う, is stiff written language, and means “completely impossible” given the circumstances.

items.diff: Same meaning, “there's no comparison”; 比べるべくもない is more formal and stiff, while 比べものにならない is common in speech too.

this.tr: The cooking of an amateur like me can't even begin to compare with a professional chef's.

that.tr: An amateur's cooking is no match for a professional's.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same thing — the gap is so huge there's no comparison; the only difference is the setting: 比べるべくもない is a set written expression, mostly seen in reviews, narration in novels and formal speeches; everyday speech and ordinary writing use 比べものにならない. Saying 「比べるべくもない」 in conversation sounds stiff and pompous.

groups.note: Both come from classical べし, “ought to, must”

items.diff: べくして repeats the same verb before and after, meaning “was bound to…”; べく means “in order to…”.

this.tr: Since safety measures had been neglected, the accident was bound to happen.

that.tr: I keep working hard to make my dream come true.

items.explain: Look at what follows べく: 「して」 and then the same verb in た-form (起こるべくして起こった) → “what was destined to happen, happened”; 「、」 followed by an action taken for that purpose → purpose. Both are the continuative form of べし; one takes its “naturally so” sense, the other its “intention” sense.

groups.note: Both mean “only natural”

items.title: 〜のも当然だ
items.diff: べくして repeats the same verb before and after, with an analytical “it was destined” tone, very formal; のも当然だ is the general expression, simply judging that it's “not surprising”.

this.tr: We were underprepared, so this was a match we were bound to lose.

that.tr: We were underprepared, so it's only natural we lost.

items.explain: Look at the form: 「dictionary form + べくして + same verb in た-form」 is a fixed pattern used only for things that already happened, like an after-the-fact analysis that “it was doomed from the start”; のも当然だ follows the plain form, is common in everyday speech too, and just means “no wonder, only natural”.

groups.note: Both come from classical べし, “ought to be so, should”

items.diff: べし is classical and at the end of a sentence sounds like an order; べきだ is its modern form, used to state an opinion or give advice.

this.tr: The meeting time must be strictly observed.

that.tr: I think people should be on time.

items.explain: べき is the attributive form of べし. Modern Japanese uses 「べきだ」 to state opinions and give advice, and it can take 「と思う」; べし is the classical sentence-final form, appearing today only in rules, slogans and admonitions, with a commanding tone (the online phrase 「〜恐るべし」 is a joking use).

items.title: 〜べからず (must not…)
items.diff: べし means “must…”; べからず is its negative, “must not…”.

this.tr: Walk quietly in the hallway.

that.tr: No running in the hallway.

items.explain: Both are classical forms found on notices and signs. Look at the ending: ending in 「べし。」 → a rule saying “you must do this”; 「べから + ず」 (ず = not) → a rule saying “you must not do this”. The two often appear on the same notice, one positive, one negative.

items.diff: べし at the end of a sentence means “must…”; べく followed by 「、」 means “in order to…”. Only one kana differs.

this.tr: All personnel are to assemble at eight tomorrow morning.

that.tr: To make the eight o'clock assembly, I left home at six.

items.explain: Look at the kana after 「べ」 and where it sits: 「べし。」 ending the sentence → command, obligation; 「べく、」 followed by the action taken for that purpose (家を出た) → purpose. Both are inflected forms of べし.

groups.note: Both express obligation, “must…”

items.diff: べし is short and forceful, like giving an order; ねばならない states the obligation itself, “this must be done”.

this.tr: Players shall follow the rules.

that.tr: Players must follow the rules.

items.explain: Look at where it's used: slogans, regulations, articles of admonition → べし, sounding like a superior giving an order; explaining why something “must…” in academic papers, speeches or expository writing → ねばならない (the written form of なければならない).

groups.note: 大人びる ↔ 大人ぶる — only one vowel differs

items.diff: びる is an appearance that shows naturally (neutral or praise); ぶる is a deliberately put-on appearance (criticism).

this.tr: He's still in elementary school, but his face looks so grown-up.

that.tr: He's just a kid, yet he acts all grown-up and talks big.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: neutral description or praise (大人びた顔つき, 古びた家) → びる, something that shows without anyone intending it; criticism (〜くせに, 偉そうに) → ぶる, something put on on purpose for others to see.

groups.note: Both mean “having the look of…”

items.diff: 大人びた is a maturity that shows naturally, leaning written; 大人っぽい is casual and just means “looks like an adult”, usable for clothes and hairstyles too.

this.tr: He's only in junior high, but he talks like someone much older.

that.tr: In these clothes, you look really grown-up.

items.explain: Look at what's being described and the setting: びる only attaches to a few words (大人, 古, 田舎) and describes a quality a person or thing naturally takes on, mostly in writing; っぽい is casual and very widely used — clothes, colors, personality (忘れっぽい) all work.

groups.note: Both come from 振る — originally “to wave”, extended to a put-on appearance: ぶる = to put on airs of…, ふり = a pretended appearance

items.diff: ぶる attaches to nouns or stems and means putting on airs, posturing; ふりをする can follow verbs and is a neutral “pretend”.

this.tr: He's read just a few books and already acts like a scholar.

that.tr: He's actually awake but pretending to be asleep.

wrong.why: ぶる can't follow a verb

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun or adjective stem (学者, 偉, 上品) → ぶる, putting on the airs of some status, with criticism; a verb (寝た, 知らない) → only ふりをする works, a simple “pretend”, not necessarily critical.

groups.note: 大人ぶる ↔ 大人びる — only one vowel differs

items.diff: ぶる is a deliberately put-on appearance (criticism); びる is an appearance that shows naturally (neutral or praise).

this.tr: He's just a kid, yet he acts all grown-up and talks big.

that.tr: He's still in elementary school, but his face looks so grown-up.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: criticism (〜くせに, 偉そうに) → ぶる, something put on on purpose for others to see; neutral description or praise (大人びた顔つき, 古びた家) → びる, something that shows without anyone intending it.

groups.note: Both mean “showing a certain appearance”

items.diff: ぶる is deliberately putting on an air; じみる is unconsciously giving off an air (usually childish or shabby).

this.tr: He's a newcomer, yet he acts like a senior and gives orders.

that.tr: You're a grown adult — stop making childish excuses.

items.explain: Check for an intention of “wanting others to see you that way”: 先輩ぶる = wanting people to think you're like a senior, on purpose; 子供じみる is something the person doesn't notice, an air they naturally take on (子供じみた, 所帯じみた), almost always a negative judgment.

groups.note: Both come from まし (増し), “(comparatively) a bit better”

items.diff: だけましだ finds one “at least it's not that bad” point in a bad situation; ほうがましだ means “I'd rather take this one” between two bad options.

this.tr: The pay is low, but at least I have a job.

that.tag: Lesser of two evils · would rather
that.tr: Rather than work at a company like that, I'd be better off with no job at all.

items.explain: Check for 「くらいなら」「より」: comparing two options and picking the less bad one → ほうがましだ; no choice involved, just saying “at least…” about the current situation → だけましだ, often preceded by 「〜が」「けど」.

groups.note: Both mean “at least…, luckily…”

items.diff: だけましだ just expresses relief and stops there; からいいようなものの is always followed by a reproach or warning after the relief.

this.tr: My wallet was stolen, but at least nobody got hurt.

that.tr: Luckily you weren't hurt, but be much more careful from now on.

items.explain: Look at the second half: the sentence ends at 「ましだ」, consoling yourself or someone else → だけましだ; 「、」 followed by a reproach or warning like 「気をつけなさい」「〜たらどうするんだ」 → からいいようなものの.

groups.note: Both emphasize degree: “even…” or “just…”

items.diff: だに is only used in a few set phrases like 「微動だにしない」; すら can follow all kinds of nouns.

this.tr: No matter what was said to him, he didn't so much as flinch.

that.tr: He can't even write hiragana.

items.explain: Look at the word before: set combinations like 微動, 一顧, 夢に → だに, followed by a negative; ordinary nouns (ひらがな, 水, 名前) → use すら (さえ in speech); people don't normally say 「ひらがなだに」.

items.diff: だに is old-fashioned written language, only used with a few verbs like 想像する, 考える; だけで is the everyday expression and works with any verb.

this.tr: Just imagining what would happen if a big earthquake struck is terrifying.

that.tr: Just hearing her voice makes me happy.

items.explain: Look at the register and the second half: だに is mostly written and is almost only followed by negative feelings like 恐ろしい, ぞっとする; だけで is used in speech and writing, and can also be followed by something good (聞くだけで嬉しくなる).

groups.note: Both list things, “… and … and so on”

items.diff: だの lists with irritation or dissatisfaction; とか gives neutral examples.

this.tr: My mom keeps nagging — go to bed early, eat your vegetables — it drives me crazy.

that.tr: My mom told me things like going to bed early and eating more vegetables.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's judgment: followed by irritated words like 「うるさい」「文句ばかり」 → だの; just plainly giving examples → とか. だの carries a complaint, so it can't be used to give examples politely.

items.diff: だの usually lists what others said or demanded, with dissatisfaction; やら lists a pile of things, meaning “what with… and…, totally swamped”.

this.tr: He does nothing but complain — the pay is low, there aren't enough holidays.

that.tr: What with cleaning and laundry, I was busy all day.

items.explain: Look at what's being listed: other people's complaints or demands, often followed by 「と言う」「と文句を言う」 → だの; a pile of things to do or mixed emotions, often followed by 「で忙しい」「で大変だ」 → やら.

groups.note: Both express a contrast or regret: “even though…”, “would have…”

items.title: 〜のに (even though…)
items.diff: のに states a known fact; だろうに adds a layer of guessing, “(I imagine) you must be…”, which sounds more considerate.

this.tr: You must be busy, so thank you for taking the trouble to come.

that.tr: Thank you for taking the trouble to come even in the rain.
