items.explain: Check whether the first half is something the speaker knows for sure: the rain is a fact right in front of you → のに; you can't see whether the other person is busy, you're only imagining it → だろうに, putting yourself in their shoes, softer in tone.

items.diff: だろうに guesses what someone else “would probably have…”, in a gentle tone; ものを is the speaker's own strong regret or reproach.

this.tr: If you'd talked it over with him, he probably would have helped.

that.tr: Why didn't you say anything? If you'd just said a word, I would have helped you.

items.explain: Look at who “would have…”: what someone else would have done, which you can only guess → だろうに; what you yourself would have done (手伝ったものを) → ものを, with strong regret and reproach, “why didn't you tell me sooner”, heavier and more literary than のに.

groups.note: Both mean “no matter…, even if…”, with the conclusion unchanged

items.diff: Same meaning; であれ only follows nouns and question words and is more formal; にしろ can also follow verbs and adjectives.

this.tr: Even a child should follow the rules.

that.tr: However busy you are, you can at least get in touch.

wrong.why: であれ can't directly follow adjectives or verbs

items.explain: Look at the word before: a noun or question word (子ども, 誰, 何) → であれ; an adjective or verb (忙しい, 行く) → にしろ / にせよ (after verbs, 「〜(よ)うと」 also works). であれ is very formal; にしろ is also used in speech. 「AであれBであれ」 listing two items is the same use.

items.diff: であれ〜であれ is a concession, “whether A or B, the conclusion is the same”; といわず〜といわず is a description, “A, B, everywhere”.

this.tr: Adults and children alike must follow the rules.

that.tr: I fell over, and now I'm covered in mud — hands, feet, everywhere.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a claim or rule (守らなければならない, 関係ない) → であれ〜であれ; describing a fact in front of you, stressing “all over, everywhere” (泥だらけ, 傷だらけ) → といわず〜といわず, usually listing parts of one whole (手, 足; 昼, 夜). 「たとえ〜であれ」 on its own is the same kind of concession.

groups.note: Both come from 「である + う」 — であろう contracted into だろう, so they mean the same

items.diff: Both express conjecture; であろう is the written language of academic papers and editorials, だろう is for speech and ordinary writing.

this.tr: This problem will likely become increasingly serious in the future.

that.tr: This problem will probably get worse from here on.

items.explain: だろう is generally thought to be a shortened であろう, so they mean the same. Look at the wording: formal words like 今後, ますます go with であろう; in speech, say だろう / でしょう. Also, であろう can directly modify a noun (今後起こるであろう問題), which だろう normally doesn't.

groups.note: Both are conjecture in written language

items.diff: であろう states a guess directly; ではなかろうか uses the form of a rhetorical question to put your view tactfully.

this.tr: This method is probably the most effective.

that.tr: Might this method not, in fact, be the most effective?

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: であろう is the author's direct judgment, “it is probably…”; ではなかろうか is the rhetorical “isn't it…?”, used to put forward your own view tactfully, reading as if asking the reader to agree. Both are only used in written language like papers and commentary.

groups.note: Both are a complete denial: “not at all…, not in the least…”

items.diff: でもなんでもない follows nouns and な-adjectives and denies an identity or quality; くもなんともない follows い-adjectives and usually denies a sensation.

this.tr: That person is just a coworker — not a lover or anything of the sort.

that.tr: A cut like this doesn't hurt one bit.

wrong.why: い-adjectives take 「くもなんともない」

items.explain: First look at the word before: a noun or な-adjective (恋人, 好き, 簡単) → でもなんでもない; an い-adjective in its く-form (痛く, 怖く, 悲しく) → くもなんともない. Both are complete denials, “neither this nor anything else”, much stronger than just 「〜ではない」「〜くない」.

groups.note: Both are a strong assertion: “this is exactly…”

items.diff: でなくてなんだろう uses a rhetorical question and is highly emotional; にほかならない is a calm, direct assertion.

this.tr: Protecting your child at the risk of your own life — if this isn't love, what is?

that.tr: His success is nothing other than the result of years of effort.

items.explain: Look at the sentence pattern and setting: でなくてなんだろう uses the rhetorical “if not…, then what is it?”, full of emotion, mostly in novels and speeches, often after 「これが」; にほかならない calmly asserts a cause or essence (〜の結果にほかならない), common in academic papers and commentary.

items.diff: というものだ is a calm evaluation, “that's what… really is”, also used in speech; でなくてなんだろう is an impassioned rhetorical question.

this.tr: Protecting your child at the risk of your own life — if this isn't love, what is?

that.tr: Helping each other in hard times — that's what true friendship is.

items.explain: Look at the tone: というものだ sounds like calmly defining or explaining something (〜のが本当の友情というものだ) and is also used in everyday speech; でなくてなんだろう is a rhetorical question when the writer's emotions run high, appearing almost only in literature and speeches.

groups.note: Both come from 「ではあるまい」, “probably isn't…”

items.diff: ではあるまいし means “it's not as if…”, followed by criticism or advice; ではあるまいか means “I suspect it's…”, a tactful conjecture.

this.tr: I'm not a child — I can get home on my own.

that.tr: If things go on like this, I suspect the economy will worsen further.

items.explain: Both come from 「ではあるまい」 (probably isn't). Look at the last kana: 「し」 gives a reason — “it's not as if…, so…”, followed by criticism or advice, often 「じゃあるまいし」 in speech; 「か」 turns it into a question — “isn't it…?” = I suspect it is, mostly in writing.

groups.note: Both first raise a situation that doesn't match reality, then criticize reality

items.diff: じゃあるまいし flatly denies, “you're not…”, in a blunt tone; ならいざ知らず first concedes, “if it were…, that would be understandable”.

this.tr: You're not a child — don't cry over something like this.

that.tr: A child would be one thing, but a grown adult crying over something like this?

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: じゃあるまいし is immediately followed by a command or criticism aimed at the listener (泣くな); ならいざ知らず must go on to name the actual subject (大人が……), meaning “that case would be understandable, but this one isn't”, in a more formal tone (はいざ知らず is the same).

groups.note: Both are conjecture in written language

items.diff: Exactly the same meaning (なかろう = ないだろう); ではなかろうか is stiffer and only used in writing.

this.tr: I suspect the cause of the declining birthrate lies in economic insecurity.

that.tr: I suspect the cause of the declining birthrate lies in economic insecurity.

items.explain: なかろう is an old-fashioned form of ないだろう, so the two sentences mean the same; the only difference is the setting: very formal writing like academic papers and editorials uses ではなかろうか; speeches, remarks in meetings and ordinary writing mostly use ではないだろうか; everyday conversation says 「んじゃないかな」.

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; ではあるまいか is more elegant and classical, mostly seen in literature, often with a hint of worry.

this.tr: I suspect his story is made up.

that.tr: I fear his story may be made up.

items.explain: なかろう and まい both correspond to 「ないだろう」, so the two sentences mean the same. The difference is style: ではあるまいか is more classical, mostly in novels and essays, often with a worried “surely it isn't…?”; ではなかろうか is mostly in academic papers and commentary.

items.diff: ではなかろうか uses the form of a rhetorical question to put a view tactfully; であろう states a guess directly.

this.tr: Might this method not, in fact, be the most effective?

that.tr: This method is probably the most effective.

items.explain: Look at the sentence ending: ではなかろうか is the rhetorical “isn't it…?”, used to put forward your own view tactfully, reading as if asking the reader to agree; であろう is the author's direct judgment, “it is probably…”. Both are only used in written language like papers and commentary.

groups.note: Both come from 「済む」 — “a matter is settled”

items.title: 〜で済む (just … and that's the end of it)
items.diff: で済む means “just … and it's settled,” with a sense of relief; では済まない is its negative, “… alone won't settle it,” and the consequences are more serious.

this.tr: If you injure someone, an apology alone won't settle it.

that.tr: Luckily, I got off with just a minor injury.

items.explain: Both come from 「済む (to be settled)」. 「〜で済む」 = it can be settled with just …, often used with 「幸い」 or 「〜だけで」 to express relief; with the negative 「では済まない」 = … alone won't settle it, implying heavier responsibility still has to be borne. The passive 「では済まされない」 works the same way, stressing more that “others won't allow it.”

items.diff: ではすまない follows a noun and means “… alone won't settle it”; ずにはすまない follows a verb's nai-form and means “you can't get away without …”.

this.tr: I said something that can't be passed off as a joke.

that.tr: I caused trouble, so I can't get away without apologizing.

items.explain: Only one 「ず」 apart. Look at what comes before: a noun or 「〜だけ」 + では → that alone won't settle it, the matter is more serious; a verb's nai-form minus ない + ずには → you are morally obliged to do it (謝らずには済まない = I have to apologize; ないではすまない is the same). The passive 「では済まされない」 works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “two things are true at the same time”

items.diff: でもあり〜でもある lists two identities or qualities side by side; も〜ば〜も lists two traits of the same person, and is more colloquial.

this.tr: He is both a doctor and a writer.

that.tr: He's smart, and he has a good personality too.

items.explain: Look at what is being listed: identities or qualities expressed by nouns (医者, 作家) → でもあり〜でもある; two good or bad points described with adjectives or verbs (頭もよければ性格もいい) → も〜ば〜も, common in everyday speech.

items.diff: In でもあり〜でもある the two items are equal; だけでなく builds up, with the focus on the second item.

this.tr: He is both a doctor and a writer.

that.tag: Building up · focus on the second
that.tr: He's not only a doctor — he's also famous as a writer.

items.explain: Look at how the two items are weighted: in でもあり〜でもある they are completely equal, neither more important; with だけでなく the first item is already known, and the second is the new information you want to stress, often followed by 「〜も」 or 「〜としても」.

items.title: 〜やら〜やら (mixed emotions)
items.diff: くもあり〜くもある calmly states two feelings that coexist; やら〜やら is several emotions rushing in at once in a jumble.

this.tr: My daughter's getting married — I'm happy, and a little lonely too.

that.tr: Praised in front of everyone, I was happy and embarrassed at once, and my face went bright red.

items.explain: Look at the second half: with くもあり〜くもある the sentence ends after the two feelings, a calm reflection; やら〜やら is often followed by the reaction at the time (顔が真っ赤になった, どうしていいか分からない), showing someone flustered.

groups.note: Both mean “as soon as … ,” two actions happening right after each other

items.diff: が早いか is written style, and the second action is usually the subject's own eager action; たとたん is more colloquial, and the second part is usually something unexpected or involuntary.

this.tr: The moment my son got home, he tossed his bag aside and ran out to play.

that.tr: The moment I left the house, it started to rain.

wrong.why: とたん needs the ta-form before it: 出たとたん

items.explain: First look at the connection: が早いか follows the dictionary form (帰る), たとたん follows the ta-form (出た). Then look at the second half: the subject's own next action, done immediately → が早いか; something unexpected and uncontrollable, like rain starting or a phone ringing → たとたん is more natural.

groups.note: AもAなら ↔ AもBなら — both are 「も〜なら、〜も」, with exactly the same frame

items.diff: AもAならBもB repeats the same noun and criticizes both sides as “equally bad”; AもXならBもY talks about different things — “both … and …”.

this.tr: The parents are hopeless, and the kids are no better.

that.tr: She's good at singing, and a great cook too.
He drinks, and he smokes too.

items.explain: Both sentences are 「〜も〜なら、〜も〜」; look before なら: the same noun before and after 「も」 (親も親なら、子も子だ) → criticizing both sides as hopeless; different things and judgments before and after 「も」 (歌も上手なら、料理もうまい) → simply “both … and …”, and the verb ba-form (酒も飲めば、タバコも吸う) works the same way.

groups.note: Both are used to scold people and voice discontent

items.diff: ときたら singles out one person to complain about; AもAならBもB criticizes both sides together.

this.tr: The husband is hopeless, and the wife is just as bad.

that.tr: As for my husband, all he does every day is play video games.

items.explain: Count the people being criticized: only one (うちの夫) → ときたら, followed by a complaint about them; two, each with the noun repeated (夫も夫なら、妻も妻だ) → AもAならBもB, meaning “neither of them is any better.”

groups.note: Both mean “once … , it's all over”

items.diff: が最後 says that once it happens you inevitably end up in an unmanageable situation, usually a fact or habit; ようものなら is a hypothetical warning about something that hasn't happened yet.

this.tr: Once our dog bites, it absolutely won't let go.

that.tr: If you're even a little late, the department head will yell at you.

items.explain: First look at the connection: が最後 follows the ta-form (かみついた), ようものなら follows the volitional form (遅れよう). Then look at the tone: が最後 describes a fact or habit, “once …, inevitably …”; ようものなら is a hypothetical “if by any chance …, there'll be hell to pay,” often with 「少しでも」, mostly used as a warning. たら最後 is the colloquial version of が最後 and is used the same way.

items.diff: が最後 looks forward: afterwards things spiral into something that can't be stopped or contained; ばそれまでだ looks back: everything before ends there and is all wasted.

this.tr: Once my dad starts drinking, he keeps going until morning.

that.tr: No matter how much you practice, if you fail in the real match, that's the end of it.

items.explain: Look at which part is “over”: ばそれまでだ looks back — all the effort and preparation suddenly become meaningless, often preceded by 「どんなに〜ても」; が最後／たら最後 look forward — once it starts, there's no stopping or containing what follows.

items.diff: Both say “once you start, it's hard to turn back”; たら最後 is strong, with a resigned “now there's no hope”; いったん〜と／ば is a neutral explanation.

this.tr: Once my little brother starts playing games, he won't even eat.

that.tr: Once something becomes a habit, it's hard to quit.

items.explain: Look at the tone: たら最後／が最後 are often used to scold someone — “once they …, there's no hope” — followed by an exaggerated, unmanageable result; いったん〜と just objectively explains “once …, it's hard to change,” and can even be followed by advice (いったん引き受けたら、責任を持ちなさい). いったん〜ば works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “having an air of …”

items.diff: がましい attaches to words and actions, saying “the words betray an unpleasant intention”; じみる attaches to people or things, saying “like that kind of person or thing.”

this.tr: He always talks as if he's doing you a favor.

that.tr: He always makes childish excuses.

wrong.why: がましい only attaches to a few words like 恩着せ, 押し付け, 言い訳 — there is no 「子供がましい」; say 子供じみた

items.explain: Look at what comes before: words and actions like 恩着せ (acting as if doing a favor), 押し付け (imposing), 言い訳 (making excuses) → がましい, meaning “smacks of …, off-putting”; people or things like 子供, 年寄り, 芝居 → じみる, meaning “like a …”.

items.diff: がましい is almost always negative; めく is usually neutral, and 「春めく」 even has a poetic touch.

this.tr: I wish you'd stop talking in that pushy way.

that.tr: Now that it's March, it's really starting to feel like spring.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: disapproving of someone's words or actions → がましい (押し付けがましい, 恩着せがましい); just describing “taking on a hint of …,” such as a change of season → めく (春めく, 秋めいた風). Also, めく is a verb, often used as 「めいてきた」 or 「めいた + noun」; がましい is an adjective.

groups.note: がらみ has two jobs, each with a similar expression: “connected to …” ≈ にまつわる, “around … years old” ≈ くらい

items.diff: がらみ is mostly used for tangled interests like money and politics, hinting at something going on behind the scenes; にまつわる is mostly used for legends and stories, with a touch of mystery and fun.

this.tr: Money-related scandals keep cropping up.

that.tr: I heard a strange legend about this castle.

items.explain: Look at the noun it modifies: tangled interests like 事件, 汚職, トラブル → がらみ, with a sense of “murky dealings behind it,” common in the news; stories like 伝説, 話, エピソード → にまつわる.

items.diff: Both mean “about”; がらみ is only used for adults' ages and sounds old-fashioned; くらい works with any quantity.

this.tr: A man of about forty came into the shop.

that.tr: It's about ten minutes on foot to the station.

wrong.why: がらみ is only used for people's ages

items.explain: Look at what the number measures: an adult's age (四十, 五十) → both がらみ and くらい work, がらみ is more old-fashioned and mostly found in novels and the news; time, distance, money, etc. → only くらい (ぐらい is the same).

groups.note: Both mean “while at it, doubling as”

items.diff: がてら is casual and can also follow a verb's masu-stem; かたがた only follows nouns and is mostly used in formal situations like business and letters.

this.tr: While out for a walk, I stopped by the convenience store.

that.tr: I will call on you soon, both to pay my respects and to thank you.

items.explain: Look at the situation and the word before it: everyday activities like 散歩 or 買い物, or a verb's masu-stem (送り, 遊び) → がてら; courtesy nouns like お礼, ご挨拶, ご報告, followed by 「伺う」 or 「参上する」 → かたがた.

items.diff: With ついでに the first part is the main thing and the second is a small extra; with がてら the two things carry about equal weight, giving a “two birds with one stone” feel.

this.tag: Two things · two birds, one stone
this.tr: I went for a walk and enjoyed the cherry blossoms along the way.

that.tr: While I was at the supermarket, I also picked up my dry cleaning.

wrong.why: がてら follows a noun or the masu-stem, not the ta-form

items.explain: First look at the connection: ついでに can follow the ta-form, the dictionary form, or 「noun + の」 (行ったついでに, 散歩のついでに); がてら only follows a noun or the masu-stem (散歩がてら, 送りがてら). Then look at the weight: with ついでに the second part is a small side task; with がてら you want to do both.

items.diff: を兼ねて says one action also serves another purpose, and works in both writing and speech; がてら is more casual, and the second part is usually movement like “going” or “walking.”

this.tr: While shopping, I wandered around in front of the station.

that.tr: I walk to work every day, which also counts as exercise.

items.explain: Look at the role of the noun before it: with を兼ねて it's an “added purpose” (運動を兼ねて = walking to work also serves as exercise), and you can also say 「書斎を兼ねた寝室」 for one thing serving two uses; with がてら it's the thing you're doing (買い物), and what follows is something done along the way.

groups.note: ごとく ↔ ごとに, differing only in the last kana

items.diff: ごとく means “just as …”; ごとに means “every …”.

this.tr: As in every year, the cherry blossoms bloomed this year too.

that.tr: Year by year, there are fewer cherry blossoms.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the last kana: 「noun + の + ごとく」 (例年のごとく, 矢のごとく) → like …, a written-style comparison; 「noun／counter + ごとに」 attached directly with no 「の」 (年ごとに, ３日ごとに) → every …, about frequency and intervals.

groups.note: ごとし・ごとく・ごとき have several jobs, each with a similar expression: comparison ≈ ようだ, “as stated …” ≈ ように, “a mere …” ≈ なんか

items.diff: ごとし is the classical version of ようだ and can only make comparisons; ようだ can also express inference.

this.tr: Time flies like an arrow.

that.tr: The road is wet. It seems to have rained.

wrong.why: ごとし can only make comparisons, not express inference

items.explain: ごとし／ごとく／ごとき roughly correspond to ようだ／ように／ような, but are only used for comparisons and examples, mostly in proverbs and writing; when inferring from signs that “it seems …,” only ようだ works (colloquially みたいだ).

items.title: 〜ように (as stated …)
items.diff: Both mean “as stated …”; のごとく is more written and formal, mostly found in papers and official documents, while ように is used in both writing and speech.

this.tr: As stated above, this method has many problems.

that.tr: As I just explained, this method has many problems.

items.explain: Look at the style: papers, announcements, and speeches use 「前述のごとく」, 「周知のごとく」, 「例年のごとく」; everyday speech and ordinary writing use 「〜ように」. When ごとく follows a noun, add 「の」 (前述のごとく).

items.diff: Same meaning, both carrying disdain or self-deprecation; ごとき is written and stronger, なんか is colloquial.

this.tr: Someone like me is not fit for such an important role.

that.tr: Someone like me can't handle such an important job.

items.explain: Look at the situation: in everyday conversation say 「私なんか」 or 「お前なんか」; in writing, formal settings, or to show strong contempt, use 「ごとき」 (私ごとき, 素人ごときに負けない). など is the written version of なんか and is used the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “things ended up a certain way”

items.diff: ことになる just states a result or arrangement objectively, good or bad; 羽目になる only describes an unwanted bad outcome, with regret or self-mockery.

this.tr: Because I overslept, I ended up having to take a taxi to work.

that.tr: Starting next month, I'll be working at the Osaka branch.

items.explain: Look at the cause and the tone: if there's your own blunder before it (寝坊したせいで, うっかり〜て) and the result is something you don't want to do → 羽目になった, with a “just my luck” tone; just reporting a decided arrangement or result, good or bad → ことになった.

items.diff: 羽目になる is mostly about a predicament you're forced into yourself, with self-mockery; 始末だ is mostly used to scold others, saying that after a string of bad things it actually came to this.

this.tr: I forgot my umbrella, so I ended up running all the way home from the station.

that.tr: He was late again and again, and in the end he actually got fired.

items.explain: Look at the subject and the context: you had to do something unlucky because of one mistake → 羽目になる; first listing someone's string of outrageous behavior, then leading into the worst outcome with 「とうとう」 or 「ついには」 → 始末だ, with reproach.

items.title: 〜を余儀なくされる
items.diff: を余儀なくされる is news-report written style and follows a noun; 羽目になる is more colloquial, follows a verb, and carries personal regret.

this.tr: The typhoon grounded the planes, and I ended up spending a night at the airport.

that.tr: Due to the typhoon, the tournament was forced to be cancelled.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and who is speaking: nouns like 中止, 延期, 撤退, in a news report objectively saying “was forced to …” → を余儀なくされる; verbs (過ごす, 歩く), talking about your own bad luck → 羽目になる.

groups.note: Both mean “in the instant of …, something unexpected happened”

items.diff: The two are often interchangeable; はずみ focuses on the momentum of an action or a sudden impulse, 拍子 focuses on the chance trigger of that instant.

this.tr: On the spur of the moment, I said something awful to my friend.

that.tr: Out of the blue, I remembered the old days.

items.explain: When talking about the impact of an action, like 「転んだはずみで／転んだ拍子に」, either works. The difference is in set phrases: for doing something you shouldn't on a sudden impulse, say 「ものの弾みで」 or 「その場のはずみで」; for remembering or noticing something at a chance moment, say 「ふとした拍子に」 or 「何かの拍子に」.

items.diff: With はずみで, the first part must be the cause of the second; たとたん only says the times are right next to each other, not necessarily cause and effect.

this.tr: I slammed the door so hard that the vase fell off the shelf.

that.tr: The moment I opened the door, the phone rang.

wrong.why: Opening a door can't make a phone ring; with no cause and effect, you can't use はずみで

items.explain: Ask yourself: did the first action “cause” what came after? The force of shutting the door knocks down the vase → はずみで (拍子に also works); opening the door and the phone ringing just happened at the same time → only たとたん works.

groups.note: Both mean “not only … (but also …)”

items.diff: のみならず simply means “not only”; adding ひとり before it stresses “by no means just this one,” extends to a wider scope after it, and sounds more solemn.

this.tr: The declining birthrate is not just Japan's problem — it's one shared by many developed countries.

that.tr: He speaks not only English but French too.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it and the second half: ひとり is usually followed by a “party” such as a country, region, or individual, and the second half widens to a bigger scope like 「社会全体」 or 「多くの国」, common in editorials and speeches; for a simple “not only A, B also …” use のみならず (which can also follow verbs and adjectives).

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; ひとり only follows nouns for a party (a country, an individual, an organization), while ただ can also follow verbs and adjectives.

this.tr: This isn't just our company's problem — it's a problem for the whole industry.

that.tr: This place isn't just cheap — the food tastes good too.

items.explain: Look before のみならず: adjectives or verbs like 「安い」 or 「便利だ」 → only ただ works; ひとり is basically only followed by a “who” — a country, company, or individual — stressing “the problem isn't just this party's.”

items.diff: Same meaning; ひとり〜のみならず is solemn written language from editorials and speeches, while だけでなく works in both speech and writing.

this.tr: Environmental problems are not the concern of one country alone, but an issue the whole world should tackle.

that.tr: Not only kids but adults too can enjoy this movie.

items.explain: Look at the style: everyday speech and ordinary writing use だけでなく (colloquially だけじゃなくて); in editorials and speeches on social issues, when stressing “this is by no means just one party's concern,” use ひとり〜のみならず.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no need to …”

items.diff: ことはない tells someone “you don't need to …”; ほどのことではない says the matter itself “isn't serious enough for that.”

this.tr: It's just a slight fever — not worth going to the hospital over.

that.tr: You don't need to apologize. I'm the one at fault.

items.explain: Look at where the reason lies: ほどのことではない judges the matter itself as “minor” (ちょっと熱があるだけ); ことはない tells the other person “you don't have to do that,” often to comfort or encourage, and the reason isn't necessarily that the matter is minor (悪いのは僕だ).

items.diff: With までもない the reason is “it's obvious, everyone knows”; with ほどのことではない the reason is “it's not serious.”

this.tr: It's just a small mistake — not worth reporting to the department head.

that.tr: Everyone knows this, so there's no need to explain it.

items.explain: Look at the reason in the first half: 「小さなミス」 — small, not worth it → ほどのことではない; 「誰でも知っている」 — too obvious, no need to say more → までもない. The very common 「言うまでもない (needless to say)」 has this meaning, and までもなく is the same.

items.diff: には当たらない is more formal and mostly follows evaluative verbs like 驚く or 非難する, meaning “it's not worth …”; ほどのことではない is common in both speech and writing.

this.tr: I just fell and scraped my knee. Nothing to make a fuss about.

that.tr: Given his ability, it would be no surprise even if he won.

items.explain: Look at the verb after it and the style: “evaluations or reactions” like 驚く, 非難する, 悲観する, saying “it's not worth …” in commentary or news → には当たらない; saying in everyday speech that something isn't serious and there's no need to worry or panic → ほどのことではない.

items.diff: には及ばない is mostly used to politely decline someone's kind offer; ほどのことではない focuses on explaining that the matter itself is minor.

this.tr: It's just a cold, so there's no need to worry.

that.tr: There's no need for you to come all this way. An email will be fine.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to and about what: when the other person wants to do something for you (来る, 心配する) and you politely say “that won't be necessary” → には及びません, often preceded by 「わざわざ」 or 「ご〜」; explaining that the matter itself isn't that serious → ほどのことではない.

groups.note: Both come from 「まし（増し）」 — originally “more, a cut above,” extended to “(though not good) relatively better”

items.diff: ほうがましだ means “I'd rather pick this one” between two bad options; だけましだ finds the one “at least …” point in a bad situation.

this.tr: I'd rather quit than bow my head to that guy.

that.tr: My wallet got stolen, but at least nobody was hurt.

items.explain: Both use 「まし」; see whether there's something being compared: with 「〜くらいなら」 or 「〜より」 before it, picking one of two options → ほうがましだ; first stating something bad (〜けど), then finding something to be thankful for → だけましだ, often said as 「だけまだましだ」.

groups.note: Both compare two things and pick one

items.diff: ほうがいい is positive advice, “you'd better …”; ほうがましだ picks the lesser of two evils, “I'd rather …,” with distaste.

this.tr: I'd rather walk than ride a packed train.

that.tr: The weather's so nice — you should walk.

items.explain: See whether both options are bad: neither the packed train nor walking is wanted, walking is just less awful → ほうがましだ; walking is a good choice in itself and you're recommending it → ほうがいい. ほうがましだ often pairs with 「〜くらいなら」.

items.diff: よりむしろ says “B suits better than A,” and B isn't necessarily bad; with ほうがましだ both sides are bad, B is just less awful.

this.tr: I'd rather stay silent than tell a lie.

that.tr: On my days off, I'd rather relax at home than go out.

items.explain: Look at how the speaker feels about the two options: よりむしろ just feels the latter is more suitable or more wanted; with ほうがましだ neither is liked, and you'd “rather” take the less awful one, with distaste in the tone, often paired with 「〜くらいなら」 before it.

groups.note: 〜放題（ほうだい）↔ 〜っ放し（ぱなし） — both written with 「放」, both follow the masu-stem, both have a “just letting it be” feel

items.diff: 放題 is doing as you please without restraint, or letting a bad state spread unchecked; っ放し is doing something and not finishing up, so the state just stays that way.

this.tr: Since nobody lives there anymore, the garden has gone completely wild.

that.tr: I went out and left the window open again.

items.explain: Both are written with 「放」 and both mean “letting things be,” but in different ways: っ放し is doing one action and leaving it at that (開けっ放し, 出しっ放し, つけっ放し); 放題 is doing whatever you like (食べ放題, 言いたい放題), or letting a bad state run its course (荒れ放題, 伸び放題).

groups.note: Both mean “doing something to your heart's content, without restraint”

items.diff: 放題 describes a state of “free to do as much as you like, no limits”; まくる describes actually “doing it like crazy,” with a strong colloquial flavor.

this.tr: At this place it's all-you-can-eat for two hours for 3,000 yen.

that.tr: I ate tons of delicious food on my trip.

items.explain: Look at the part of speech: 放題 attaches to the masu-stem to form a noun, as in 「食べ放題の店」 or 「言いたい放題だ」, describing a rule that lets you do as you please or an unchecked state; まくる is a verb (食べまくる, 遊びまくった), describing someone actually doing something wildly and in large amounts.

items.diff: 三昧 is being immersed in something and enjoying it fully; 放題 stresses being unrestrained and doing as you please, often with criticism.

this.tr: While their parents were away, the kids ran completely wild.

that.tr: Since retiring, I spend every day fishing to my heart's content.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: being wholly absorbed in something you love, like 読書三昧 or ゴルフ三昧, usually enjoyment → 三昧; being unrestrained and doing whatever you want, like やりたい放題 or 言いたい放題, usually criticism → 放題. Also, 三昧 follows a noun, while 放題 follows a verb's masu-stem or 「〜たい」.

groups.note: Both mean “in the instant of …, something unexpected happened”

items.diff: The two are often interchangeable; 拍子 focuses on the chance trigger of that instant, はずみ focuses on the momentum of an action or a sudden impulse.

this.tr: Out of the blue, I remembered the old days.

that.tr: On the spur of the moment, I said something awful to my friend.

items.explain: When talking about the impact of an action, like 「転んだ拍子に／転んだはずみで」, either works. The difference is in set phrases: for remembering or noticing something at a chance moment, say 「ふとした拍子に」 or 「何かの拍子に」; for doing something you shouldn't on a sudden impulse, say 「ものの弾みで」 or 「その場のはずみで」.

items.diff: 拍子に requires that the first action caused the unexpected thing after it; たとたん only says the times are right next to each other, not necessarily cause and effect.

this.tr: As I stood up, I banged my head on the shelf.

that.tr: The moment I stood up, the phone rang.

wrong.why: Standing up can't make a phone ring; with no cause and effect, you can't use 拍子に

items.explain: The first half is the same; check whether the second half is caused by it: standing up makes you hit your head on the shelf → 拍子に (はずみで also works); the phone ringing just happened as you stood up → only たとたん works.

groups.note: Both come from 「いかん（如何）」 — “how”

items.diff: いかんで says “the result depends on how A turns out”; いかんにかかわらず says “however A turns out, the result stays the same” — exact opposites.

this.tr: Whether you can go on to the next school depends on your exam results.

this.tag: いかんによっては · may, depending
this.tr: Depending on your grades, you may not be able to graduate.

that.tr: Whatever the reason, lateness will not be accepted.

items.explain: 「いかん」 simply means 「如何 (how)」. Look at what follows: 「で」 or 「によっては」 → the result changes with A (決まる, 〜こともある); 「にかかわらず」 or 「を問わず」 → however A is, it doesn't affect what follows (認めない, 一律).

groups.note: Both mean “depending on …”

items.title: 〜次第で (depending on)
items.diff: Basically the same meaning; 次第で is common in both speech and writing, いかんで is stiffer and mostly found in notices, contracts, and the news.

this.tr: The number of hires will be decided based on the results of the selection process.

this.tag: いかんによっては · contracts
this.tr: Depending on the results of the review, the contract may be terminated.

that.tr: Let's decide whether to go depending on tomorrow's weather.
Depending on the weather, the match may be cancelled.

items.explain: Look at the style: talking things over with friends or everyday speech → 次第で (天気次第で); company notices, contracts, news, and other formal texts → いかんで／いかんによっては, usually preceded by nouns like 「結果」, 「審査」, 「対応」.

items.diff: Same meaning, both “depending on circumstances, may …”; によっては is the ordinary phrase, いかんによっては is more formal and stresses that it depends on the specific content or degree of A.

this.tr: Depending on how you respond from here on, we will also consider legal action.

that.tr: Depending on the circumstances, reservations may be cancelled.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it and the setting: general “different cases” like 場合, 人, 国 → によっては (人によっては, 場合によっては); how the other party's 「対応」, 「回答」, or 「結果」 actually turns out, used in formal notices and warnings → いかんによっては, with a harder tone.

groups.note: Both come from 「いかん（如何）」 — “how”

items.diff: いかんにかかわらず says “however A turns out, the result stays the same”; いかんで says “the result depends on how A turns out” — exact opposites.

this.tr: Whatever the reason, lateness will not be accepted.

that.tr: Whether you can go on to the next school depends on your exam results.

that.tag: いかんによっては · may, depending
that.tr: Depending on your grades, you may not be able to graduate.

items.explain: 「いかん」 simply means 「如何 (how)」. Look at what follows: 「にかかわらず」 or 「を問わず」 → however A is, it doesn't affect what follows (認めない, 一律); 「で」 or 「によっては」 → the result changes with A (決まる, 〜こともある).

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of …”

items.diff: にかかわらず mostly follows words like 「晴雨」 or 「年齢」, where the possible cases are obvious; いかんにかかわらず follows nouns like 「理由」 or 「結果」 whose content can vary endlessly, and is more formal.

this.tr: Regardless of the exam results, everyone will be interviewed.

that.tr: Rain or shine, the match will go ahead.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: words where “the possible cases are obvious at a glance,” like 晴雨, 男女, 経験の有無 → just にかかわらず; words whose “specific content varies endlessly,” like 理由, 結果, 事情 → add 「のいかん」 to stress “no matter what the content,” mostly found in regulations and notices.

items.diff: を問わず mostly follows nouns for a range, like 「年齢」 or 「経験」, meaning “regardless of / open to all”; いかんを問わず stresses “the specific content of A doesn't matter,” mostly found in terms and conditions.

this.tr: For whatever reason, fees once paid will not be refunded.

that.tr: Anyone may apply, regardless of age or experience.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: “ranges or categories” like 年齢, 国籍, 経験 → を問わず (most common in job ads); “specific content” like 理由, 事情, 結果 → のいかんを問わず, common in refund and breach-of-contract terms. いかんにかかわらず is the same.

groups.note: 以前 has two jobs, each with a similar expression: “before …” ≈ 前に, “not even at the level of …” ≈ どころか

items.diff: 前に means “before doing something,” followed by another action; 以前 refers to the whole period before a certain time, and is more formal.

this.tr: In Japan before the Meiji era, few people ate meat.

that.tr: Brush your teeth before going to bed.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and what's said after: action + 前に, followed by another action done before it (寝る前に歯を磨く); era or time + 以前, describing the whole period before it (明治以前の日本).

items.thisTitle: 〜以前 (not even at the level of)
items.diff: 以前 points out that the problem lies at a more basic level — “it's not even a question of …”; どころか first rejects A, then gives something more extreme — “never mind A, not even B ….”

this.tr: Forget polite language — they can't even greet people properly.

that.tr: Never mind polite language — they can't even say hello.

items.explain: The two sentences are very close in meaning; look at the tone: 以前 points out that “the problem isn't A but the more basic B,” often as 「〜以前の問題だ」, with a critical, lecturing tone; どころか is “never mind A, not even B …,” often with 「も」 or 「さえ」 in the second half, carrying surprise or exaggeration.

groups.note: Both mean “having an air of …”

items.diff: じみる attaches to people or things, saying “like that kind of person or thing”; がましい attaches to words and actions, saying “the words betray an unpleasant intention.”

this.tr: He always makes childish excuses.

that.tr: He always talks as if he's doing you a favor.

wrong.why: がましい only attaches to a few words like 恩着せ, 押し付け, 言い訳 — there is no 「子供がましい」; say 子供じみた

items.explain: Look at what comes before: people or things like 子供, 年寄り, 芝居 → じみる, meaning “like a …”; words and actions like 恩着せ (acting as if doing a favor), 押し付け (imposing), 言い訳 (making excuses) → がましい, meaning “smacks of …, off-putting”.

items.diff: Both mean “like a …”; じみる is more written, stronger, and used almost only for criticism; っぽい is colloquial, milder, and combines freely.

this.tr: You're a grown adult — stop saying such childish things.

that.tr: He talks a bit like a kid.

items.explain: Both say “childish,” but 子供じみた is strong, clearly critical, and mostly found in writing or scolding; 子供っぽい is colloquial and milder. Also, っぽい can be used as 白っぽい or 忘れっぽい, while じみる only follows a few words like 子供, 年寄り, 芝居, 狂気.

items.diff: じみる is almost always negative; めく is usually neutral, and 「春めく」 even has a poetic touch.

this.tr: He's only thirty, yet he talks like an old man.

that.tr: The wind has turned warm, and it feels more and more like spring.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: saying someone is “like an old person” or “like a child,” with displeasure → じみる; describing a season or mood “taking on a hint of …,” neither good nor bad → めく (春めく, 謎めいた).

items.diff: びる is naturally taking on a certain look, neutral or even complimentary (大人びた); じみる is “looking like what you shouldn't,” with criticism (子供じみた).

this.tr: He's a grown adult, yet he does such childish things.

that.tr: That child seems mature for his age.

items.explain: Look at who it's about and what they resemble: an adult like a child, a young person like an old one, out of keeping with who they are → じみる, critical; a child seeming mature, a thing looking old, naturally taking on that look → びる (大人びる, 古びる), not necessarily bad.

groups.note: Both come from 「限り（限る）」 — “limit, end”

items.title: 〜限り (as long as …)
items.diff: 限りだ is a feeling reaching its “limit” = extremely …; 限り draws a “range” = as long as it stays within this range ….

this.tr: With everyone's support, I feel truly reassured.

that.tr: As long as my body can move, I want to keep working.

items.explain: 限り originally means “limit.” Look before and after it: emotional adjectives like 嬉しい, 心強い, 寂しい, ending the sentence with 「です／だ」 → the feeling has reached its limit (限りだ); a verb (動く, 生きている), with another half-sentence following → stays that way within this range (限り).

groups.note: Both mean a degree has hit its peak

items.diff: 限りだ follows emotional adjectives (嬉しい限り); の極み follows nouns (感激の極み), is more solemn, and mostly used in formal speeches.

this.tr: I'm absolutely delighted to receive such an award.

that.tr: To receive this award is the greatest honor.

wrong.why: の極み must follow a noun: 感激の極み, 光栄の極み

items.explain: First look at the word before it: an i-adjective (嬉しい, 寂しい) or 「残念な」 → 限りだ; a noun (光栄, 感激, 贅沢) + の → の極み. As for the setting, の極み is more solemn, often used in award or thank-you speeches, and can also describe a state, as in 「贅沢の極み」.

items.diff: 限りだ can only express your own feelings; といったらない can also judge others or things as “incredibly ….”

this.tr: All my friends have gone back to their home countries, and I'm terribly lonely.

that.tr: That clerk's attitude is unbelievably bad.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: the speaker's own inner joy or loneliness → 限りだ; judging a trait of someone or something (態度の悪さ, 景色の美しさ) → といったらない, usually preceded by a 「〜さ」 noun.

items.diff: てたまらない stresses a feeling or sensation so strong you can't stand it, and is more colloquial; 限りだ expresses deep feeling about the present moment, and is more formal.

this.tr: I am truly grateful for everyone's warm words.

that.tr: Summer vacation starts tomorrow, and I'm so excited I can't stand it.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the connection: saying in everyday talk that you're unbearably happy or eager → adjective く-form + てたまらない, which can also describe physical sensations (暑くてたまらない); formally expressing gratitude or relief in a speech or letter → adjective + 限りです.

groups.note: Both come from 「甲斐（かい）」 — “effect, reward”

items.diff: かい stands alone and says whether a particular effort paid off (かいがある／かいもなく); がい attaches to the masu-stem to form a noun (やりがい, 生きがい), saying that doing the thing is meaningful in itself.

this.tag: かいがある · an effort paid off
this.tr: Practicing every day paid off — we finally won.

this.tag: かいもなく · effort in vain
this.tr: Despite desperate treatment, my grandfather passed away.

that.tr: This job is tough, but it's very rewarding.

items.explain: Both are 「甲斐」 (reward). Look at the position: standing alone after a verb's ta-form or 「noun の」 → かい, saying a particular effort brought results (かいがある) or came to nothing (かいもなく); attached directly to the masu-stem to form one word, read with a voiced sound → がい (やりがい, 生きがい, 教えがい), saying the activity is worthwhile and meaningful.

groups.note: かいがある／かいもなく each have a similar expression: “not in vain” ≈ だけのことはある, “in vain” ≈ にもかかわらず

items.diff: かいがあって says an effort brought a result; だけのことはある judges after seeing the result that it “lives up to the effort or reputation,” often meaning “just as you'd expect from ….”

this.tr: Waiting in line for three hours paid off — we got good seats.

that.tag: Seeing the result · judging it worth it
that.tr: This ramen is really delicious. It was worth the three-hour wait.

items.explain: Look at the sentence order and purpose: 「並んだかいがあって、いい席が取れた」 states the effort first, then the result it brought; 「本当においしい。並んだだけのことはある」 sees the result first, then judges that it “was worth” the effort, often paired with 「さすが」 to mean “just as you'd expect from ….”

items.diff: かいもなく must be preceded by an effort made to get a result, followed by the result falling through; にもかかわらず is a general contrast, and both sides can be anything.

this.tr: Despite the family's devoted care, my grandfather passed away.

that.tr: Despite the rain, a lot of people came.

wrong.why: Rain is not an effort, so かいもなく can't be used

items.explain: Check whether the first half is an “effort”: actions taken for a certain result, like 看病, 練習, 治療, where the result wasn't achieved → かいもなく, with regret; an ordinary fact like rain or opposition, followed by something contrary to expectations → にもかかわらず.

groups.note: Both mean “there's a chance that …”

items.diff: おそれがある is only used for bad things; 可能性がある works for good or bad and is more neutral.

this.tr: Sales may well grow this year.

that.tr: The typhoon may make landfall.

wrong.why: おそれ means “fear,” so it can't be used for good things

items.explain: Check whether what follows is good or bad: bad things you fear might happen, like a typhoon making landfall, infection, or accidents → おそれがある (可能性がある also works); good things like sales growth or passing, or anything neutral → only 可能性がある.

items.diff: かもしれない is the speaker's subjective guess, common in speech; 可能性がある is more objective and formal, and can be measured with 「高い／低い」.

this.tr: According to the study, there's a high chance this drug causes side effects.

that.tr: I might not be able to go tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the basis: a judgment based on data or research, used in reports and news, and can take 「高い／低い」 → 可能性がある; your own casual guess, often with 「もしかしたら」 → かもしれない.

items.diff: かねない carries the speaker's worry or criticism, “could well end up …”; 可能性がある just calmly points out a possibility, without emotion.

this.tr: According to experts, a major earthquake could occur.

that.tr: If you keep driving like that, you could end up causing an accident.

items.explain: Check whether the speaker takes a stance: citing experts or data, simply stating a possibility → 可能性がある; unhappy with someone's behavior and warning them “if this keeps up, something will happen” → かねない, often preceded by 「このままでは」 or 「そんな〜をしていたら」, and only used for bad outcomes.

groups.note: Both are “quantity + から”: one says “a whopping,” the other says “from … up”

items.diff: からある／からする／からの stress how large a quantity is — “a whole …, as much as …”; plain から just marks a starting point — “from … up.”

this.tr: I caught a fish that weighed a good ten kilos.

this.tag: からする · as much as (price)
this.tr: I bought a watch that cost a whopping million yen.
As many as ten thousand people gathered.

that.tr: Watches at this shop start from 10,000 yen.

items.explain: Look at what follows “quantity + から”: ある, する, or の, then modifying a noun → stresses “a whole …, as much as …, at least this many” — it's saying a lot; followed by an ordinary verb or 「です」 (1万円から買える, 1万円からです) → just a starting point, actually saying “it only takes this much at minimum.”

groups.note: Both stress a large quantity

items.title: 〜も (stressing a large quantity)
items.diff: quantity + も is the speaker feeling “that many!”, colloquial and flexible; からある／からする／からの stress “at least this much, maybe more,” are more written, and only modify nouns.

this.tr: I caught a fish that weighed a good ten kilos.

this.tag: からする · as much as (price)
this.tr: I bought a watch that cost a whopping million yen.
As many as ten thousand people gathered.

that.tr: I caught a fish that weighed a whole ten kilos.

that.tag: Can also modify the verb directly
that.tr: I was kept waiting at the station for a whole three hours.

items.explain: Look at what follows: quantity + も can take ある／する (10キロもある) or modify the verb directly (３時間も待たされた), and is most common in speech; quantity + から only takes ある／する／の and then modifies a noun, has a more written flavor, and means “at least, maybe even more.”

items.diff: からの goes before a noun as a modifier, “as many as … N”; にのぼる goes at the end of the sentence as the predicate, reporting a statistical total that “reached ….”

this.tr: After the accident, as many as 1,000 residents evacuated.

that.tr: The number of residents who evacuated due to the accident reached 1,000.

items.explain: The numbers in both sentences are the same; look at the position: the quantity comes before a noun and modifies it (1000人からの住民) → からの; the quantity comes at the end, reporting a statistic (住民は1000人にのぼった) → にのぼる, common in the news.

groups.note: からいいようなものの is half “luckily” and half “although … but”: the first half is close to てよかった, the second to ものの

items.diff: てよかった simply expresses relief; からいいようなものの always adds a reproach or warning after the relief.

this.tr: Luckily no one was hurt, but it nearly turned into a serious accident.

that.tr: I'm so glad nobody was hurt.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence is finished: ending at 「よかった」, just expressing relief → てよかった; 「からいいようなものの」 is always followed by another half-sentence pointing out that “it could have been bad” or “be careful next time” — the speaker isn't actually satisfied.

items.diff: ものの is just a general “although … but”; with からいいようなものの the first part must be a lucky good outcome, and the second part is criticism or “it nearly went wrong.”

this.tr: Good thing I had insurance — otherwise I'd have been in real trouble.

that.tr: I signed up for the gym, but I haven't been even once.

items.explain: Check whether the first half is “thank goodness”: something that luckily avoided a bad outcome, like 保険に入っていた or 間に合った → からいいようなものの, followed by “otherwise …” or a reproach; the first half is just an ordinary fact, and what follows falls short of expectations → ものの. The 「ものの」 at the end of からいいようなものの is this same contrast.

groups.note: Both come from 「あれ」, the imperative of the classical 「あり」 — “be it … or …”

items.diff: かれ〜かれ is only used with a few set pairs of opposite adjectives (遅かれ早かれ); であれ follows nouns and can be swapped freely.

this.tr: The truth will come out sooner or later.

that.tr: Man or woman, we hire capable people.

items.explain: かれ = く + あれ (遅く + あれ → 遅かれ), であれ = で + あれ, and 「あれ」 always means “be it ….” Look at what comes before: adjectives, and only the few pairs 遅かれ早かれ, 多かれ少なかれ, 善かれ悪しかれ → かれ〜かれ; nouns → であれ〜であれ, any noun works.

groups.note: Both mean “whether A or B, …”

items.diff: にしろ〜にしろ can follow all kinds of nouns and verbs, so you can build sentences freely; かれ〜かれ is an idiom limited to a few pairs of opposite adjectives.

this.tr: Everyone has worries, to a greater or lesser degree.

that.tr: Whether you're for or against it, please give your own opinion.

items.explain: Check whether it's one of the set pairs: 遅かれ早かれ, 多かれ少なかれ, 善かれ悪しかれ → かれ〜かれ, and you can't swap in other adjectives yourself; any other “A or B” (賛成／反対, 行く／行かない) → にしろ〜にしろ (にしても〜にしても is the same).

items.diff: (よ)うが〜まいが pairs “doing / not doing” of the same verb and can be built freely; かれ〜かれ is a set expression made from a pair of opposite adjectives.

this.tr: For better or worse, smartphones have greatly changed our lives.

that.tr: Whether you come or not, the party will go ahead as planned.

items.explain: Look at what's being paired: the affirmative and negative of the same verb (来ようが来るまいが, 行こうが行くまいが) → (よ)うが〜まいが, stressing “it's the same whether you do it or not”; set adjective pairs like 遅かれ早かれ or 善かれ悪しかれ → かれ〜かれ. ((よ)うと〜まいと is the same.)

groups.note: Both mean “while at it, doubling as”

items.diff: かたがた only follows nouns and is mostly used in formal situations like business and letters; がてら is casual and can also follow a verb's masu-stem.

this.tr: I will call on you soon, both to pay my respects and to thank you.

that.tr: While out for a walk, I stopped by the convenience store.

items.explain: Look at the situation and the word before it: courtesy nouns like お礼, ご挨拶, ご報告, followed by 「伺う」 or 「参上する」 → かたがた; everyday activities like 散歩 or 買い物, or a verb's masu-stem (送り, 遊び) → がてら.

items.diff: かたがた is usually preceded by courtesies like お礼 or ご報告, with a formal tone; を兼ねて has the widest range and works in both writing and speech.

this.tr: I have come to report to you, and also to thank you for the other day.

that.tr: I went for a short walk, partly to clear my head.

items.explain: Look at the setting and what comes before: visiting a client or writing a business letter, 「お礼」, 「ご挨拶」, 「ご報告」 + かたがた; in everyday talk or ordinary writing, saying “also to …” → を兼ねて (運動を兼ねて, 気分転換を兼ねて), and you can also say 「書斎を兼ねた寝室」.

items.diff: With ついでに the first part is the main thing and the second is a small extra; with かたがた the two purposes carry equal weight, and it's more formal.

this.tr: While visiting my hometown, I also called on my old teacher.

that.tr: When you go to the post office, could you mail this letter for me too?

items.explain: Look at the weight of the two things and the setting: with ついでに the first part is the main thing you were going to do anyway and the second is a small side task, common in speech, and it can follow verbs (行くついでに); かたがた only follows nouns, both purposes matter equally, and it's mostly used in formal settings like visits and letters.

items.diff: かたがた is “doubling as” on a single occasion; かたわら is “also doing” something else long-term alongside your main job.

this.tr: Since I was in the neighborhood, I dropped by to say hello.

that.tr: My father writes novels while working at a company.

items.explain: Look at the time span and the word before it: courtesy nouns like お礼 or ご挨拶, followed by a one-time visit like 「伺う」 → かたがた; main work like 勤める or 教える, followed by a long-term side job or hobby (〜ている) → かたわら.

groups.note: Both mean “while doing one thing, also doing another”

items.title: 〜ながら (while …)
items.diff: ながら can describe doing two things at the same moment; かたわら only means “alongside the main job, also doing something else long-term.”

this.tr: Besides working at a bank, he also writes novels.

that.tr: I do my homework while listening to music.

wrong.why: Actions done at the same moment can't use かたわら

items.explain: Check whether the two things are being done “at this same moment”: doing homework while listening to music → only ながら; “working at a bank” is a long-term main job, and “writing novels” is something done on the side → かたわら, written style, mostly used to describe someone's career. ながら also works for long-term parallel activities (働きながら大学に通う), but is more colloquial.

items.diff: がてら is doing something else “while at it” on a single outing; かたわら is doing something else long-term alongside your main job.

this.tr: Besides teaching at a university, I also do translation work.

that.tr: While out for a walk, I stopped by the bookstore in front of the station.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a one-time outing like 「散歩」 or 「買い物」, getting something else done along the way → がてら; a long-term job or role like 「教える」 or 「勤める」, plus something else on the side → かたわら.

items.diff: かたがた is one visit serving two purposes, mostly in letters and business; かたわら is two activities carried on in parallel over a period of time.

this.tr: Besides farming, my father also researches local history.

that.tr: I've come to thank you for the other day and to pay my respects.

items.explain: The two look alike too; look at what's before and after: かたがた is usually preceded by nouns like 「お礼」, 「ご挨拶」, 「お見舞い」 and followed by 「伺う」 or 「訪ねる」 — one visit achieving two purposes, a stock phrase in letters and business; かたわら is preceded by long-term work (営む, 勤める) and describes a way of life over a period of time.

groups.note: Both mean “tending to show a certain tendency”

items.title: 〜傾向がある
items.diff: 傾向がある is a neutral, objective description, for good or bad; きらいがある only describes bad habits, with the speaker's criticism.

this.tr: He has a habit of deciding everything on his own.

that.tr: According to research, women tend to live longer.

wrong.why: きらいがある is only used for bad tendencies

items.explain: Check whether it's a flaw and whether there's criticism: “deciding everything on his own” is a habit the speaker dislikes → きらいがある; an objective description based on data, like “according to research”, which can also be positive → 傾向がある.

items.diff: がち is common in both speech and writing and follows the masu-stem or a noun; きらいがある is written language, follows the dictionary form, and is mostly used to criticize someone's way of doing things.

this.tr: Young people have a tendency to think things are simpler than they are.

that.tr: In winter, people tend to catch colds.

items.explain: Look at the connection and the subject: がち follows the masu-stem or a noun (ひきがち, 病気がち) and is used for everyday things like “catching colds easily” or “often being late”; きらいがある follows the dictionary form and is mostly used in writing to comment on the thinking or style of a person or group, with clear criticism.

items.title: 〜っぽい (quick to …)
items.diff: っぽい is colloquial and only follows a few verbs (忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい); きらいがある is written commentary and can be preceded by a whole clause.

this.tr: That politician has a habit of dodging awkward questions.

that.tr: My dad's been really forgetful lately.

items.explain: っぽい attaches to the masu-stem (忘れ + っぽい) to form an i-adjective, only with a few personality verbs like 「忘れる」, 「怒る」, 「飽きる」, and is used in chat; きらいがある is written criticism of someone's style in news and commentary, and can be preceded by a whole clause (都合の悪い質問を避ける).

groups.note: Both mean “the best within a certain range”

items.diff: の中で〜がいちばん is everyday language and can compare anything; きっての is written and formal, only modifies nouns, and carries high praise.

this.tr: She is the brightest student in the whole school.

that.tr: She's the tallest in the class.

wrong.why: きっての must be followed by a noun

items.explain: Look at what follows “the most”: ordinary comparisons like 背が高い or 足が速い → の中でいちばん; followed by nouns expressing high praise like 「秀才」, 「名門」, 「実力者」 → きっての, preceded by a range like 「学内」 or 「当代」, mostly used in written profiles of people.

items.diff: きっての says “the foremost within this range”; をおいて〜ない says “there's no one else but him,” stressing he's the only suitable one.

this.tr: He's one of the most capable people in the industry.

that.tr: There's no one but him we can entrust this job to.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: きっての is preceded by a range (業界, 社内, 当代) and followed by a noun, simple praise; をおいて is preceded by the person themselves and always followed by 「ほかにいない／ない」, often with 「〜できるのは」, stressing “only he can do this.”

groups.note: Both come from 「極（きわ）」 — “end, limit”

items.diff: 極まりない follows a na-adjective stem and is used almost only for criticism; の極み follows a noun, usually saying a feeling or state has reached its peak, and is often used for good things too.

this.tr: Calling in the middle of the night — that's utterly inconsiderate.

that.tr: Getting to meet the teacher I've always admired — I'm overwhelmed with emotion.

items.explain: The 「ない」 in 「極まりない」 is not a negation; it means “no end.” Look at what comes before: na-adjective stems like 非常識, 失礼, 危険 → 極まりない, used to condemn others' words and actions; nouns like 感激, 贅沢, 疲労 + 「の」 → の極み, usually about your own feelings or state. 極まる (非常識極まる) means the same and is stiffer.

groups.note: Both mean “… to the extreme”

items.diff: 極まりない attaches directly to the stem and is used almost only for criticism; ことこの上ない needs 「なこと／いこと」 first and works for good or bad.

this.tr: That clerk's attitude is extremely rude.

that.tag: Good things too · add こと
that.tr: Winning the championship — I couldn't be happier.

wrong.why: 極まりない doesn't follow i-adjectives, and is rarely used for good things

items.explain: First look at the connection: na-adjective stems like 失礼 or 危険 attached directly → 極まりない; first turned into 「うれしいこと」 or 「不便なこと」 and then added → ことこの上ない. Then look at the tone: 極まりない is used almost only to condemn; ことこの上ない works for good and bad. 極まる is the same as 極まりない.

items.diff: 限りだ expresses the speaker's own feelings at the moment; 極まりない is mostly a negative judgment on outside events or others' behavior.

this.tr: Driving in rain this heavy — that's dangerous in the extreme.

that.tr: It's my first solo trip, and I feel really uneasy.

items.explain: Look at whose feelings it's about: i-adjectives expressing your own feelings, like 心細い, うれしい, 羨ましい → 限りだ; judgments on outside events or others' actions, like 危険, 失礼, 不愉快 → 極まりない (極まる is the same).

groups.note: Both come from the emphatic particle 「こそ」 — singling out one point

items.diff: こそ〜が is a concession, “… may be …, but …”; こそ on its own is emphasis, “precisely, it's … that.”

this.tr: This place may be pricey, but the food is top-notch.

that.tr: It's the taste that this place takes pride in.

items.explain: Check whether こそ is followed by a turn with 「が／けれど」: 「値段こそ高いが、……」 first admits a drawback, then uses が to turn to the strength you really want to talk about → concession; no turn → emphasis, “it's exactly this.” こそ〜が is mostly found in writing.

items.diff: With こそ〜が both parts are true and the focus is on the second; こそすれ is “only A, never B”; こそあれ is “though there are differences, ….”

this.tr: He may have a sharp tongue, but he's kind at heart.

that.tr: They helped me, so I can only be grateful — never resentful.
Everyone has worries, though to different degrees.

items.explain: All of these use 「こそ」 to single out one point; the difference is in the second half: with こそ〜が both the first part (口が悪い) and the second (根は優しい) are facts; こそすれ is always followed by a negation (恨むことはない), saying “only this, never that”; こそあれ mostly appears as 「程度の差こそあれ」 or 「違いこそあれ」, admitting differences and then saying the essence is the same.

groups.note: Both express a concessive turn, “although … but”

items.diff: こそ〜が uses 「こそ」 to concede just one aspect; ものの concedes the whole preceding event, and what follows is usually “didn't turn out as expected.”

this.tr: This apartment's rent may be high, but it's close to the station and convenient.

that.tr: I rented an apartment close to the station, but the rent is so high that life is a struggle.

items.explain: Look at the form before it: noun (家賃) + こそ concedes just one aspect, then turns to a positive judgment of another aspect; ものの is preceded by a whole clause about something that already happened (借りた), and what follows says the result fell short of expectations.

groups.note: Both come from the emphatic particle 「こそ」 — singling out one point

items.diff: こそ on its own just emphasizes “precisely”; こそすれ is “only A, never B,” and こそあれ is “though there's …, still,” both followed by another half-sentence.

this.tr: I feel nothing but gratitude toward my parents — never resentment.
Everyone has worries, though to different degrees.

that.tr: This time I really want to pass the exam.

items.explain: Look after こそ: the meaning is complete right there (今度こそ合格したい) → simple emphasis, “this time for sure”; こそ followed by 「すれ」 or 「あれ」, then another half-sentence with a negation or a turn → こそすれ (only grateful, never resentful)／こそあれ (there are differences, but everyone has worries). 「すれ」 and 「あれ」 are the classical realis forms of 「する」 and 「ある」, a remnant of the 「こそ + realis form」 pattern.

items.diff: こそすれ denies the opposite (only A, never B), こそあれ admits differences and then states what's the same; with こそ〜が both things are true and the focus is on the second.

this.tr: With that much practice, your results can only go up — there's no way they'll drop.
Our methods may differ, but our goal is the same.

that.tr: He may have a sharp tongue, but he's kind at heart.

items.explain: Look at the second half: with こそすれ it's the opposite of the first part, flatly denied (下がるはずがない); こそあれ admits differences, then states what's the same (目指すところは同じ); with こそ〜が the first part 「口が悪い」 is true and the second 「根は優しい」 is true too, but the focus is on the second.

groups.note: Both mean “… to the extreme”

items.diff: ことこの上ない works for good or bad and needs 「なこと／いこと」 first; 極まりない attaches directly to the stem and is used almost only for criticism.

this.tag: Good things too · add こと
this.tr: Winning the championship — I couldn't be happier.

that.tr: That clerk's attitude is extremely rude.

wrong.why: 極まりない doesn't follow i-adjectives, and is rarely used for good things

items.explain: First look at the connection: first turned into 「うれしいこと」 or 「不便なこと」 and then added → ことこの上ない; na-adjective stems like 失礼 or 危険 attached directly → 極まりない (極まる is the same). Then look at the tone: 極まりない is used almost only to condemn; ことこの上ない works for good and bad.

items.diff: ことこの上ない follows adjectives and is often used to judge things; の極み follows nouns and usually says a feeling or state has reached its peak.

this.tr: This road is dark at night and extremely dangerous.

that.tr: To receive such an award is the greatest of honors.

items.explain: Check whether what comes before is an adjective or a noun: adjectives like 危険な or うれしい + 「こと」 → ことこの上ない; nouns like 光栄, 贅沢, 疲労 + 「の」 → の極み, mostly found in formal settings like speeches and greetings.

items.diff: 限りだ only expresses the speaker's own feelings at the moment; ことこの上ない can also judge the nature of things.

this.tr: This town has only two buses a day — it's extremely inconvenient.

that.tr: My son has grown up so well — I couldn't be happier.

items.explain: Look at what it's about: 限りだ is preceded by emotional adjectives like うれしい, 心細い, 羨ましい and only expresses the speaker's own feelings; besides feelings, ことこの上ない can also judge the nature of things, like 「不便」 or 「危険」.

groups.note: Both give a reason, “because …”

items.diff: ことだし is followed by the speaker's suggestion or decision; こともあって is followed by an objective result that happened.

this.tag: One of the reasons → objective result
this.tr: Partly because it was raining, there were few customers.

that.tr: It's raining anyway, so let's head home early today.

items.explain: Both hint that “there are other reasons too”; the difference is in the second half: “few customers” is an objective result that already happened → こともあって, common in news and reports; “let's head home early” is the speaker's present suggestion or decision → ことだし, colloquial. こともあって is generally not followed by invitations or intentions.

items.title: 〜とあって (because it's)
items.diff: とあって stresses “because it's this special situation, naturally this happens”; こともあって just gives one of the reasons.

this.tr: Partly because the weather was nice, the park was packed with families.

that.tr: Because it was a long holiday weekend, the park was packed with families.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: とあって is preceded by an unusual, special situation like 「連休」 or 「人気歌手が来る」, followed by the scene you'd naturally expect, common in the news; こともあって is preceded by an ordinary reason, and 「も」 hints at other reasons too, for a softer tone.

items.diff: せいか is an uncertain guess, “maybe it's because …,” usually with bad results; こともあって is a definite reason among others.

this.tr: Partly because it's close to the station, this shop is always crowded.

that.tr: Maybe it's from lack of sleep, but my head feels foggy.

items.explain: Check how sure the speaker is: せいか carries a “… I guess” inference, the speaker isn't sure, and it's usually followed by bad results like feeling unwell or failing; こともあって is a confirmed reason, just hinting at other reasons too, and the result can be good or bad.

groups.note: Both come from 「こと + 無し（なし）」 — “without the fact of …”

items.diff: ことなしに is mostly used for a necessary condition, “without … you can't …”; ことなく mostly describes an actual situation, “without …, kept on ….”

this.tr: People can't go on living without dealing with others.

that.tag: Without … kept on · describing a fact
that.tr: He kept working without taking a single day off.

items.explain: Look at the second half: ことなしに is usually followed by 「〜できない」 or 「〜ない」, saying the first part is an essential condition; ことなく is followed by what actually happened (働き続けた), just describing “without doing …, kept on ….” ことなしに can also mean “without … , …,” but it's stiffer than ことなく.

groups.note: Both mean “without … (you can't)”

items.diff: Same meaning, different connection: nouns take なしに／なしでは; verbs take ことなしに.

this.tr: You may not enter this room without permission.
You can't read this book without using a dictionary.

that.tr: You may not enter this room without permission.

that.tag: なしでは · noun · impossible without
that.tr: You can't read this book without a dictionary.

wrong.why: A verb needs 「こと」 after it

items.explain: First check whether a noun or a verb comes before: nouns like 許可 or 辞書 → なしに／なしでは; verbs like 得る or 使う → add 「こと」 to make ことなしに(は). なしでは is always followed by “can't,” while なしに can have either meaning.

items.diff: ないことには is the more colloquial “unless you … first, you can't …”; ことなしには is the written, formal version.

this.tr: Unless you actually try it, you won't appreciate how good it is.

that.tr: If you don't actually try it, you won't appreciate how good it is.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register and the connection: ないことには follows the nai-form and works in everyday conversation (行ってみないことには分からない); ことなしには follows the dictionary form and is mostly found in speeches and writing.

groups.note: Both mean “so that … doesn't happen”

items.title: 〜ように (so as not to …)
items.diff: ないように is the ordinary phrase; ことのないように is more formal, mostly used in apologies, announcements, and pledges.

this.tr: To ensure that an accident like this never happens again, we will thoroughly strengthen our safety management.

that.tr: Be careful not to leave anything behind.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the sentence ending: between friends saying 「気をつけてね」 → ないように; a company apology, notice, or pledge, followed by 「いたします」 or 「お願いいたします」 → ことのないよう(に). Same meaning; ことのないように has an extra 「こと」, which makes it sound more formal.

groups.note: Both come from the classical particle 「とて」 — equivalent to 「と言って／として」 (saying it's …, as …)

items.diff: こととて means “since it's …, please forgive”; とて means “even if it's …, (no exception).”

this.tr: It was only a child's doing, so please go easy on him.

that.tr: Even for a child, this is unforgivable.

items.explain: Look at the second half: asking for understanding or apologizing (大目に見てください, ご迷惑をおかけしました) → こととて, giving a reason; a negation or “no exception” (許されることではない) → とて, a concession. What comes before differs too: こととて follows an event (子どものした + こと), while とて attaches directly to a person or noun. The source 「とて」 ≈ 「と言って」: saying it was a child's doing → so please forgive; even saying it's a child → still not OK.

groups.note: Both explain a reason, with an excusing, asking-for-understanding tone

items.diff: もので is a spoken excuse; こととて is a formal, old-fashioned expression, mostly used in formal apologies and letters.

this.tr: As it was so sudden, we were unable to prepare adequately.

that.tr: It was so sudden that I couldn't prepare properly.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: もので follows the plain form (急だった) and is common in spoken excuses; こととて is preceded by 「急な」, 「不慣れな」, or 「noun + の」, often appears with 「何分（なにぶん）」, and is used in formal apologies and letters — far more old-fashioned than もので.

groups.note: Both limit to “only …”

items.diff: しか〜ない limits objectively with a negative sentence; くらいのものだ uses an affirmative sentence, with an exclamatory “nobody else would.”

this.tr: In my family, the only one who gets up at five every morning is my dad.

that.tr: In my family, only my dad gets up at five every morning.

items.explain: Check whether the sentence is affirmative or negative: しか is always followed by a negative (しかいない), just objectively saying “only”; くらいのものだ is affirmative, carrying the speaker's exclamation “he's about the only one who'd do that — ordinary people wouldn't.”

items.diff: をおいて〜ない is written and formal, used for high praise, “no one but him”; くらいのものだ is more colloquial and can be praise or criticism.

this.tr: He's about the only one who'd do something that reckless.

that.tr: No one but him could play this role.

items.explain: Look at the tone and judgment: をおいて is always followed by 「ほかにいない／ない」, formal praise saying “only he is worthy”; くらいのものだ is relaxed and can be praise or a jab (あんな無茶をする), saying “he's about the only one who'd do this.”

groups.note: Both come from the particle 「まで」 — marking a limit, “up to …”

items.diff: までだ means “at worst I'll just …,” with a way out; ばそれまでだ means “once …, it's all over,” with no way out.

this.tag: At worst · still a way out
this.tr: If I fail the exam, I'll just take it again next year.

that.tr: No matter how hard you study, if you get sick on exam day, that's the end of it.

items.explain: Both rely on 「まで」 = “this far and no further”: までだ is “going this far is enough,” preceded by something you can still do (また受ける), with a determined “so be it”; ばそれまでだ is “at that point it's over,” preceded by 「〜ば」, saying that once something happens, everything before is wasted. までのことだ is the same as までだ.

items.diff: たまでだ means “I merely did …, that's all”; までもない means “there's no need to go that far.”

this.tr: I was asked, so I merely told the truth.

that.tr: There's no need to bother saying something like that.

items.explain: Look at the limit drawn by 「まで」: たまでだ is preceded by something you've already done (言った), saying “I only went this far, nothing more to it”; までもない is “no need to go that far,” saying it's unnecessary (言うまでもない, 確認するまでもない). までもなく is the mid-sentence form and works the same way; までのことだ is the same as までだ.

groups.note: Both limit things to “just …”: the only thing to do, or merely that

items.diff: ほかない is a resigned “I have no choice but to …”; までだ is a decisive “at worst I'll just … and that's that,” with a determined resolve.

this.tr: If the trains have stopped, I'll just walk.

that.tr: The trains have stopped, so I have no choice but to walk.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only at the end: ほかない means there's no other way and you have to accept it, with a resigned tone; までだ treats it as a fallback, “so what,” often paired with 「〜なら」 or 「〜たら」. よりほかない is the same as ほかない, and までのことだ is the same as までだ.

items.diff: たまでだ only follows your own actions, with an excusing or modest tone; にすぎない follows nouns and quantities, objectively saying “nothing more than that.”

this.tr: No need to thank me. I merely did what anyone should.

that.tr: That's nothing more than a rumor.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: たまでだ is preceded by something the speaker did (したまでです), used modestly or as an excuse, “nothing more to it”; にすぎない is usually preceded by nouns or quantities (噂, 一部, 10％), objectively judging “nothing more than that.” 「したまでのことです」 is the same.

groups.note: Both mean “like… (but not quite)”

items.diff: まがい modifies a noun and is only used for shady conduct or fakes; も同然だ usually comes at the end of the sentence, meaning “practically the same as”, and works for good or bad things.

this.tag: Close to something bad · modifies noun
this.tr: Pushing expensive futons on elderly people is a business that borders on fraud.

that.tag: As good as · good things OK
that.tr: One more point and this match is as good as won.

items.explain: Look at the position and the evaluation: まがい usually modifies a noun as 「〜まがいの＋noun」, preceded by something bad like 詐欺 or 脅迫, or by 「ブランド品」, stressing “looks like it but isn't — a convincing fake”; も同然だ usually comes at the end of the sentence, meaning “in effect already equal to”, and can describe good things too, as in 「勝ったも同然」.

groups.note: Both come from the classical auxiliary 「まじ」 — the negative of 「べし」, meaning “should not / will not”

items.diff: まじき modifies a noun, meaning “(for someone in that position) unacceptable”; まい comes at the end of the sentence, meaning “will never…” or “probably won't…”.

this.tr: That is conduct unbecoming of a teacher.

that.tr: I'll never go to a shop like that again.

items.explain: Look at the position: まじき must be followed by a noun (行為, 発言), and is often used as 「〜にあるまじき」 to condemn someone for not living up to their position; まい comes at the end of the sentence, expressing the speaker's resolve “I'll never… again” (二度と行くまい), or a guess “probably won't…”. まい actually developed from 「まじ」.

groups.note: Both mean “should not”

items.diff: べきではない is the everyday modern “should not” and can end a sentence; まじき is classical, only modifies nouns, and condemns much more strongly.

this.tr: For a politician, that is a remark that should never have been made.

that.tr: Politicians should not make remarks like that.

wrong.why: まじき can only modify a noun; it can't end a sentence

items.explain: Look at the position: べきではない can end a sentence directly and works in both everyday and formal speech; まじき must be followed by a noun (あるまじき発言), usually as a strong condemnation along the lines of “and this from someone who is a…!”, and is common in news commentary.

groups.note: Both mean “doing something nonstop, without restraint”

items.diff: てばかりいる means “doing only this and nothing else”, with a note of complaint; まくる stresses doing it a lot and with gusto, and when said about yourself it can sound a bit proud.

this.tag: Lots, full force · can be proud
this.tr: During summer vacation I partied to my heart's content abroad.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play and never studies at all.

items.explain: Look at what follows and the tone: てばかりいる is often followed by 「全然〜しない」 and focuses on “only doing this and not what you should”, with criticism; まくる focuses on doing it many times and with force (遊びまくった, 食べまくった), is slang, and when said about yourself it carries a sense of enjoyment or pride.

items.diff: 放題 describes a state of “no limit, as much as you like”; まくる describes actually doing something a lot and with gusto.

this.tr: During the trip, I ate tons of delicious food.

that.tr: At this restaurant, it's all-you-can-eat for two hours.

items.explain: Look at whether it's a rule or an action: 放題 is usually a state or rule of “you can… as much as you like” (食べ放題, 飲み放題) and can work as a noun; まくる is a verb saying someone actually did a lot of something (食べまくった) — so you can say 「食べ放題の店で食べまくった」.

groups.note: Both mean “covered in…, full of…”

items.diff: まみれ is liquid or powder “smeared all over the surface”; だらけ is “everywhere, far too many”.

this.tr: We played the match in the rain and got covered in mud from head to toe.

that.tr: This essay is full of mistakes.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: things that stick to the body and dirty the whole surface, like 泥, 汗, 血, 油, ほこり → まみれ; things scattered one by one in too great a number, like 傷, 間違い, ゴミ → だらけ. 「泥だらけ」 is also possible, but まみれ gives more of a “caked all over” feel.

items.diff: まみれ means being smeared with something dirty or mired in something bad — almost always negative; ずくめ means “nothing but…”, usually about good things or the color of clothes.

this.tr: I want to get out of this life buried in debt.

that.tr: This year I got married and promoted — it was nothing but good news.
