items.explain: Look at the evaluation: まみれ is preceded by unpleasant things like 泥, 汗, 借金, 嘘, with a sense of “being dirtied, sinking into it”; ずくめ is preceded by 「いいこと」, 「黒 (clothing)」, 「規則」 etc., meaning everything from start to finish is of the same kind, and is most common with good things.

groups.note: Both mean “like…, having an air of…”

items.title: 〜らしい (typical)
items.diff: めく means “starting to take on a hint of…”; らしい means “fully having the features of…, very typical”.

this.tr: It's gradually starting to feel like spring.

that.tr: Today is really typical spring weather.

items.explain: Look at the degree: めく says “not completely yet, but it's starting to have that feel”, often with 「少しずつ」 and 「〜てきた」; らしい says “it fits the typical features in every way”, often with 「本当に」 and 「いかにも」. Also, めく is a verb (春めいてきた), while らしい is an adjective (春らしい天気).

items.diff: めく is fairly neutral and often has a touch of charm; じみる is usually negative: “…-ish (in an unbecoming way)”.

this.tr: He smiled a mysterious smile.

that.tr: You're a grown adult — stop saying such childish things.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it and the evaluation: じみる is usually preceded by types of people like 「子ども」 「年寄り」 「所帯」, saying someone has taken on an air they shouldn't have — it's criticism; めく is usually preceded by 春, 謎, 皮肉, 冗談, saying something has that feel, which isn't necessarily bad.

items.diff: めく is written language and only attaches to a few words like 春, 謎, 皮肉; っぽい is colloquial and attaches to almost any noun.

this.tr: Outside the window, it's already quite autumnal.

that.tr: These clothes look a bit cheap.

items.explain: Look at the register and what it can attach to: っぽい is colloquial, attaches to 子ども, 男, 安い, 水 and more, and turns them into an い-adjective (安っぽい服); めく is written language, attaches only to a few set words, and is mostly used to describe a season or mood lyrically (秋めいてきた, 謎めいた).

items.diff: めかす means deliberately using a certain tone to hide your real intent (冗談めかして); ぶる means putting on airs, pretending — clearly negative.

this.tr: He told his true feelings half-jokingly.

that.tr: Don't act so high and mighty just because you know a little.

items.explain: Both mean “deliberately putting on an appearance of…”; look at the word before: めかす is usually preceded by 「冗談」, in the form 「冗談めかして」, meaning “it looks like a joke on the surface but is actually sincere”; ぶる is preceded by 「偉い」 「いい子」 「上品」 etc., saying someone is putting on a show or airs, with clear disapproval.

groups.note: Both mean “this is no time to care about…”

items.diff: どころではない is a neutral “have no room to think about”; もへったくれもない is a rough way of saying “… or whatever — who cares”.

this.tr: When lives are at stake, who cares about the rules!

that.tr: When lives are at stake, there's no time to worry about rules.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only at the end; look at the tone: どころではない simply says “there's no room to think about this now”, sounds calm, and works in formal settings too; もへったくれもない expresses contempt for the thing itself (rules are meaningless right now), sounds rough, and is only said when agitated or among people you know well.

groups.note: Both are strong negation: “not at all…, not … in the least”

items.diff: The meaning is the same — “not at all” — the difference is in what it attaches to: い-adjectives take くもなんともない; nouns and な-adjectives take でもなんでもない.

this.tr: A cut like this doesn't hurt one bit.

that.tr: That person is no friend of mine at all.

wrong.why: With an い-adjective, say 「痛くもなんともない」

items.explain: Look at the word before it: い-adjectives like 痛い, 怖い → change to the く-form and add 「もなんともない」; nouns and な-adjectives like 友達, 好き → add 「でもなんでもない」. The meaning is the same: “not at all…, not … in the least”.

items.diff: ちっとも〜ない is an adverb that can modify any predicate; もなんともない only negates feelings and evaluations, with more of a sense of bravado or disdain.

this.tr: Shots? They don't scare me one bit.

that.tr: No matter how long I wait, the bus just won't come.

items.explain: Look at what is being negated: ちっとも comes before the predicate and can negate an action (来ない) or a feeling; もなんともない only attaches to adjectives of feeling or evaluation like 痛い, 怖い, 面白い, with a bravado or coolness of “I couldn't care less”.

groups.note: Both mean “not to mention A, B also…”

items.diff: はもちろん means “A goes without saying, and B too”, giving both equal weight; もさることながら first acknowledges A and puts the focus on B.

this.tr: The food at this restaurant is great, of course, but the staff's service is even more outstanding.

that.tr: The food at this restaurant is great, of course, and the staff's service is excellent too.

items.explain: Look at the particle in the second part: はもちろん is often followed by 「も」, adding B so both carry equal weight; もさることながら is often followed by 「が」 or 「こそ」, meaning “A is certainly good, but what's even more worth mentioning is B”, with a dignified tone. はもとより is the same as はもちろん, but more formal.

items.diff: もさることながら is used for positive evaluations; はおろか is mostly used for negative or surprising situations (“let alone…, not even…”).

this.tr: Her English goes without saying, and her French pronunciation is also superb.

that.tr: My little brother can't even write hiragana, let alone kanji.

items.explain: Look at whether the second half is good or bad: はおろか is usually followed by a negative or shockingly bad result (〜も書けない), and A is “the harder thing, the one that goes without saying”; もさることながら is followed by praise, and A is “an aspect that's already very good”. The two can't be swapped.

groups.note: Both are emphatic negations: “not even… / not … at all”

items.diff: もしない comes at the end of the sentence or modifies a noun, simply saying “doesn't even…”; もしないで must be followed by another action, saying “without even…, did…”.

this.tr: No matter how much I try to talk to him, he doesn't even answer.

that.tr: He left the room without even answering.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「もしない」: the sentence ends there, or a noun follows (ありもしない話) → もしない; it's followed by 「で」 and another action (部屋を出て行った) → もしないで, saying he skipped the bare minimum and went straight on to something else.

items.diff: もしない adds the sense of “not even the bare minimum”; やしない is a flat denial: “absolutely not, never”.

this.tr: He didn't even read the letter I took the trouble to write.

that.tr: Nobody's going to believe a story like that.

items.explain: Look at what the speaker is blaming: the 「も」 in もしない picks out a bare-minimum action (surely you could at least read it) and blames the other person for not doing even that; やしない just makes the negation stronger and more emphatic (信じやしない = will never believe), with a strongly colloquial flavor. はしない is the same as やしない.

groups.note: Both mean “not doing…”; the difference is in the tone and how the sentence continues

items.diff: ないで simply states objectively “did B without doing A”; もしないで adds 「も」, stressing “didn't even do something as basic as A”, usually with blame.

this.tr: He stamped the document without even checking what was in it.

that.tr: He stamped the document without checking what was in it.

items.explain: The two sentences differ by just one 「も」: ないで is an objective statement; もしないで treats “checking” as the bare minimum anyone should obviously do and says the person didn't even do that, with blame or surprise. In written language, these are 「せずに」 and 「もせずに」 respectively.

items.diff: もしないで must be followed by another action; もしない comes at the end of the sentence, simply saying “doesn't even…”.

this.tr: He left the room without even answering.

that.tr: No matter how much I try to talk to him, he doesn't even answer.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「もしない」: it's followed by 「で」 and another action (部屋を出て行った) → もしないで, saying he skipped the bare minimum and went straight on to something else; the sentence ends there, or a noun follows (ありもしない話) → もしない.

groups.note: Both are non-committal written expressions: “it is thought that…”

items.diff: They're often interchangeable; as a tendency, とみられる is common in the news and often modifies a noun directly, while ものと思われる is usually the writer's own inference, placed at the end of the sentence.

this.tr: Judging from the state of the scene, the culprit appears to have entered through the window.

that.tr: The police are pursuing a man believed to have broken in through the window.

items.explain: Both are non-assertive written guesses and are often interchangeable (the news also often says 「〜したものとみられる」). As a tendency: reporting the judgment of the police or investigators, or modifying a noun directly as in 「侵入したとみられる男」 → usually とみられる; in reports and papers, when the author draws their own inference from the evidence at the end of a sentence → usually ものと思われる.

items.diff: ものと思われる is the writer's own guess; とされる relays a generally accepted view or that of an authority.

this.tr: Judging from the pottery that was excavated, this temple was probably built in the 8th century.

that.tr: This temple is generally said to have been built in the 8th century.

items.explain: Look at who is making the judgment: drawn by the writer from evidence like 「出土した土器から」 → ものと思われる; a view that is socially accepted or given by an authority, introduced by 「一般に」 or 「〜では」 → とされる, with the writer just passing it on.

groups.note: Both mean “treating… as true (and acting on that)”

items.title: 〜ものとする (deem)
items.diff: ものとして is a mid-sentence pause, followed by how things will be handled on that basis; ものとする ends the sentence and is the language of rules and contracts.

this.tr: If we haven't heard from you by the deadline, we'll treat you as absent.

that.tr: Those who do not contact us by the deadline shall be deemed absent.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: ものとして is followed by an action like 「扱います」 「考える」 「計算する」, and is used in notices and explanations; ものとする ends the sentence itself and has the tone of regulations and contracts.

items.diff: としたら means “if…”, followed by an inference; ものとして means “treating … as true for now”, followed by an action taken on that basis.

this.tr: Let's assume it'll rain tomorrow and get our umbrellas ready.

that.tr: If it rains tomorrow, the match will probably be canceled.

items.explain: Look at the second half: としたら is followed by a conclusion that's been inferred (中止だろう), often with 「だろう」 or 「かもしれない」; ものとして is followed by what the speaker will do on that basis (用意しておこう), i.e. “assume this for now, then act”. とすれば and とすると are the same as としたら.

items.diff: を前提に attaches to a noun and states explicitly “on the precondition of…”; ものとして attaches to a clause, meaning to proceed “assuming, for now, that it's so”.

this.tag: Attaches to clause · assume for now
this.tr: We set out seats assuming that everyone would attend.

that.tr: We made plans on the premise that everyone would take part.

items.explain: Look at the form before it: を前提に is preceded by a noun (全員参加, 結婚), is often used for plans and negotiations, and states a “precondition”; ものとして is preceded by a whole clause (全員が参加する), with the tone of “let's assume it's so for now”. を前提として is the same as を前提に.

groups.note: ものとする has several jobs, each with a similar alternative: “shall… (a rule's obligation)” ≈ べきだ; “shall be deemed…” ≈ AをBとする, たことにする

items.diff: ものとする is an objective provision in a legal text; べきだ is the speaker's own claim based on reason.

this.tr: Members shall pay their membership fees by the deadline.

that.tr: If you're a member, you should at least pay your fees properly.

items.explain: Look at who's talking: clauses in contracts and regulations, with no personal feeling → ものとする (not used in everyday conversation); the speaker's own view based on reason, often with criticism or advice → べきだ.

items.diff: Both mean “shall be set as / deemed” in legal texts; ものとする follows a verb clause, AをBとする follows a noun.

this.tr: Those who score 60 points or more shall be deemed to have passed.

that.tr: 60 points or more shall be the passing mark.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at what comes before 「とする」: a verb clause (合格した, 同意した) → add 「もの」 to make ものとする; a noun (合格, 1000円) → use 「AをBとする」, setting A as B. Both are very common in regulations and contracts, and the same goes for the 「として」 form.

items.title: 〜たことにする (act as if)
items.diff: ものとする is the formal “shall be deemed” in legal texts; たことにする is a private “let's just say…”, often pretending.

this.tr: If no reply is received by the deadline, you shall be deemed to have agreed.

that.tr: I'll pretend I didn't hear what you just said.

items.explain: Look at the setting and whether it's true: ものとする is used in rules and contracts to officially “deem” a situation to be a certain state according to the rules (返事がない → 同意した); たことにする is used in everyday conversation to “just treat it as” so even though you know the facts aren't so, with a sense of pretending or letting something slide.

groups.note: ものを ↔ ものの: only the last kana differs

items.diff: ものを means “it would have been fine if…, but…”, with regret or blame; ものの is just an objective “although…, …”.

this.tr: If you'd just said something, I would have helped (but you didn't).

that.tr: I bought a new computer, but I haven't used it yet.

items.explain: Look at what comes before もの: ものを is often preceded by a hypothetical 「〜ば／〜たら」 (言ってくれれば) and talks about a good outcome that didn't happen, with regret or blame; ものの is preceded by a fact that has already happened (買った) and followed by a result that goes against expectations, with no emotional coloring.

groups.note: Both mean “if only… (but it didn't happen)”

items.diff: Same meaning; 〜ば〜のに is used in both speech and writing, while 〜ば〜ものを is more literary, with stronger feelings of blame or regret.

this.tr: If you'd gone to the hospital right away, it could have been cured (but you wouldn't go).

that.tr: If you'd gone to the hospital right away, it would have been cured.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable; look at the setting: everyday speech uses のに; ものを is literary and slightly old-fashioned, mostly seen in novels and essays, often comes after 「〜ば〜た」, and can be followed by a complaint (〜ものを、無理をして悪化させてしまった).

groups.note: Each half of んばかり has its own family: 「ん」 comes from the classical 「む」 (“about to…”), like んとする・んがため; 「ばかり」 expresses degree (“almost to the point of…”), like とばかりに

items.diff: んばかり means “as if about to…”, but it doesn't actually happen; んとする means “just about to…”, and it really is about to happen.

this.tr: She begged, almost in tears.

that.tr: Right now, the sun is just about to set.

items.explain: ん = the classical 「む (about to)」. Followed by ばかり (almost to the point of…) → it just describes how something looks; she didn't actually cry; followed by とする → the action really is about to happen, often used with 「今まさに」. んばかりの + noun and sentence-final んばかりだ are exaggerations too.

items.diff: んばかり describes appearance: “as if about to…”; んがため states a purpose: “in order to… (at any cost)”.

this.tr: Thunderous applause broke out in the hall (almost enough to split it apart).

that.tr: They'll stop at nothing to win.

items.explain: It's the same 「ん (about to)」; look at what follows: ばかり → “almost to the point of…”, describing how intense a sound or feeling is (割れんばかりの拍手); が + ため → “in order to…”, with the second half being what's done to reach that goal (手段を選ばない).

items.diff: んばかりに attaches to a verb: “as if about to do some action”; とばかりに attaches to a quote: “as if to say…”.

this.tag: Verb → as if about to do
this.tr: He apologized as if he were about to press his head to the floor.

that.tag: A quote → as if to say
that.tr: The manager kept looking at the clock, as if to say, “Go home already.”

items.explain: Look at what comes before ばかりに: the ない-form stem of a verb + ん (こすりつけん, 泣かん) → almost doing that action; a sentence in 「」 + と → expressing what that sentence means through actions or attitude, without actually saying it. と言わんばかりに works the same way.

groups.note: んばかりに ↔ たばかりに: only the first character differs

items.diff: んばかりに means “as if about to…”; たばかりに means “just because… (it led to a bad result)”.

this.tr: He was so happy he almost jumped for joy.

that.tr: Just because I said one thing too many, I made her angry.

items.explain: Look at what comes before ばかりに: ない-form stem + ん (上がらん, 泣かん) → an exaggerated description of how something looks; it didn't actually happen; た-form (言った) → gives a reason, and the second half is always a bad result (〜てしまった), often with regret.

groups.note: Both are exaggerated comparisons: “just as if…”

items.diff: んばかり stresses degree, “almost about to…”; かのようだ means “as if…”, often saying appearance is the opposite of reality.

this.tr: She looked as if she was about to burst into tears.

that.tr: She looked as if she knew nothing.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: the ない-form stem of a verb + ん (泣き出さん) → an action “just about to happen”, stressing how strong a feeling or degree is; a plain-form sentence + かのよう (何も知らない) → something that isn't actually true (in fact she does know), used to point out the gap between appearance and reality.

groups.note: Both come from the classical auxiliary 「む」 (which shifted in sound to 「ん」) — meaning “about to, intend to…”

items.diff: んがため means “in order to…”, followed by what's done for that purpose; んとする means “about to, trying to…”, and doesn't itself express purpose.

this.tr: He worked desperately to protect his family.

that.tr: He lost his life trying to protect his family.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in が + ため versus と + して: with んがため, the second half is “what's done for that purpose” (必死に働いた); んとする／んとして just says “about to, trying to do”, followed by how the action went or what came of it. ん is the classical 「む (about to)」 in both; in modern Japanese these are 「〜ために」 and 「〜ようとして」.

items.diff: んがため states a purpose: “in order to…”; んばかり describes appearance: “as if about to…”.

this.tr: He practiced day after day in order to win the match.

that.tr: He won the match and was so happy he almost jumped for joy.

items.explain: Look at what follows ん: が + ため → the second half is the action taken for that goal (練習を重ねた); ばかり → just an exaggerated description; he didn't actually jump. んがための + noun and んばかりの + noun are told apart the same way.

groups.note: Both express purpose: “in order to…”

items.diff: ために is the most ordinary “in order to”; んがため is stiff written language, with a fierce resolve of “at any cost”.

this.tr: He even stole just to stay alive.

that.tr: I exercise every day in order to live a healthy life.

items.explain: Both mean “in order to”. Everyday speech and ordinary writing use ために; んがため is a classical-style written expression, often followed by all-out actions like 「手段を選ばない」 or 「〜までした」. Note the forms: ために follows the dictionary form (生きる), んがため follows the ない-form stem (生き + ん; する → せんがため).

items.diff: べく is a calm, written “in order to”; んがため shows a fiercer resolve, often with the negative nuance of “by any means necessary”.

this.tr: Just to sell their products, they ran ads that weren't true.

that.tr: An investigation is underway to determine the cause of the accident.

items.explain: Both are written-language “in order to”. べく is mostly used in the news and official documents for legitimate purposes (調査が進められている); んがため sounds fiercer and is often used to criticize “doing even what you shouldn't, just to reach your goal” (事実と違う広告). Forms: べく follows the dictionary form (する → すべく), んがため follows the ない-form stem (売ら + ん).

groups.note: Both come from the classical auxiliary 「む」 — meaning “about to, intend to…” (む later shifted in sound to 「ん」 and 「う」)

items.diff: Same meaning — “about to…, trying to…”; んとする is classical literary language, used only in writing and speeches.

this.tr: The evening sun is just about to sink below the horizon.

that.tr: The evening sun is about to set.

items.explain: The ん in 「沈まん」 and the う in 「沈もう」 both developed from the classical 「む」, so the two sentences mean the same. Everyday speech and ordinary writing use ようとする; んとする appears only in novel descriptions, speeches and commentary, sounding solemn (新しい時代を切り開かんとする). Form: んとする follows the ない-form stem (沈ま + ん), and する becomes 「せんとする」.

items.diff: んとする means something really is “about to happen”; んばかり is exaggeration, “as if about to…”, and it doesn't actually happen.

this.tr: The match is just about to begin.

that.tr: The moment he won, he was so happy he almost jumped for joy.

items.explain: Look at whether it will really happen: what んとする describes is about to become reality (the match really will start), often used with 「今まさに」; んばかり is a figure of speech saying the degree is so strong it's “almost…”; he didn't actually jump.

items.diff: んとする means “about to, trying to do”; んがため means “in order to do”, followed by the action taken for that purpose.

this.tr: He lost his life trying to protect his family.

that.tr: He worked desperately to protect his family.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in と + して versus が + ため: んとして just says “trying to do”, followed by how the action went or what came of it (命を落とした); with んがため, the second half is “what's done for that purpose” (必死に働いた).

groups.note: Both come from 「ながら」 — originally meaning “keeping… as it is”

items.title: 〜ながら (while…)
items.diff: ながら attaches to the ます-form of a verb: “while doing…”; ながらに only attaches to a few nouns and keeps the old meaning of “remaining as is”.

this.tr: With tears in her eyes, she described what happened in the accident.

that.tr: Crying, she described what happened in the accident.

items.explain: The meanings are very close; look at what comes before ながら: a verb in ます-form (泣き) → the ordinary “while doing…”, which works with any verb; a noun (涙, 生まれ, 昔) + ながらに／ながらの → limited to a few set phrases, written and formal. Both mean “staying in that state”: speaking while staying in a crying state = speaking while crying.

groups.note: Both mean “keeping the original state”

items.diff: まま attaches freely to all kinds of words and just says “unchanged”; ながらの is only used in set phrases like 「昔ながらの」, with nostalgia or admiration.

this.tr: This town still has its old-fashioned streetscape.

that.tr: This town still has streets exactly as they were long ago.

items.explain: The two sentences are close in meaning; look at the form and feel: まま can follow 「noun + の」, a verb in た-form (靴を履いたまま) and more, and simply says “unchanged”; ながらの only attaches to a few words like 「昔」 「生まれ」 「いつも」, and 「昔ながらの」 carries admiration for “keeping a tradition alive, which is rare”.

groups.note: ないまでも ↔ までもない: the same 「ない・まで・も」, but swapping the order changes the meaning completely

items.diff: ないまでも means “even if not…, at least…”; までもない means “there's no need to…”.

this.tr: Maybe not every day, but I'd like you to call at least once a week.

that.tr: We're so close by, there's no need to go to the trouble of calling.

items.explain: First look at what comes before 「まで」: ない-form (言わない) + までも → first names a high standard that can't be reached, and is always followed by a fallback minimum (週に一度は); dictionary form (する, 言う) + までもない → the matter is simple or obvious, so there's no need to go that far. まで means “as far as…” in both: not going that far, but at least… / no need to go that far. までもなく works the same way.

groups.note: Both mean “at least the bare minimum”

items.diff: ないまでも first states a high standard that can't be reached, then falls back to “at least…”; なりとも directly names the bare minimum: “even a little”.

this.tr: Maybe not the full amount, but I'd like you to pay back at least half.

that.tr: I'd be glad if I could be of even a little help.

items.explain: Look at how many standards the sentence has: ないまでも has one on each side (全額 → 半分), “stepping back by comparison”; なりとも only attaches to words for tiny amounts like 「少し」 「多少」 「一目」, and is a formal written expression, equivalent to colloquial 「少しでも」.

groups.note: Both are double negatives of the form 「〜ない + も + negative」 and look very similar

items.diff: ないものでもない means “it's not that I wouldn't (do it)”, saying you might agree; ないとも限らない means “it can't be ruled out that…”, warning that something bad might happen.

this.tag: Not that I wouldn't · reluctant yes
this.tr: Depending on the conditions, I wouldn't say no to taking it on.

that.tr: It might rain, so let's take an umbrella.

items.explain: Look at whose action is being talked about: ないものでもない is usually about yourself being “willing to do” something under certain conditions (引き受ける, 許す), and in speech ないでもない is also used; ないとも限らない is about the outside world, that “something might happen” (雨が降る, 事故が起きる), often followed by a precaution (〜から, 〜ておこう).

groups.note: Both mean “it's not that… not…”, using a double negative to tactfully leave room

items.diff: Same meaning; ないものでもない is the most formal and stiff, mostly about a conditional willingness; なくもない is more colloquial and can also describe a feeling of “a little bit”.

this.tr: Depending on the conditions, I wouldn't say no to cooperating.

that.tr: Now that you mention it, I do kind of get that feeling.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the content: negotiating conditions or stating a position with a bit of an air → ないものでもない (in speech ないでもない); everyday conversation, especially about feelings like 「気がする」 or 「分かる」 → なくもない (なくはない too), which sounds more easygoing.

items.diff: Same meaning, “it's not that… not…”; ないものでもない is more formal and stiffer.

this.tr: If you're going to go that far, I suppose I could forgive you.

that.tr: If we hurry, it's not like we can't make it.

items.explain: ないことはない is common in both speech and writing, and can also say something is objectively “doable” (急げば間に合う); ないものでもない is mostly the speaker conditionally giving in and showing they're “willing to do it” (許す, 引き受ける), with a stiffer, more formal tone.

groups.note: Both come from 「限らない」 — “not limited to this”, i.e. “not necessarily”

items.diff: ないとも限らない follows a negative: “it can't be ruled out that…”; とは限らない follows a positive: “not necessarily…”.

this.tag: Negative + 限らない → can't rule out
this.tr: An accident can't be ruled out, so let's get insurance.

that.tag: Positive + 限らない → not necessarily
that.tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good things.

items.explain: Both are 「限らない (not necessarily)」: following a negative (起きない) → “not necessarily won't happen” = can't be ruled out, used to warn that something might happen, often followed by a precaution (〜ておこう); following a positive (いい物だ) → it isn't necessarily so, used to overturn an assumption.

groups.note: Both are double negatives of the form 「〜ない + も + negative」 and look very similar

items.diff: ないとも限らない means “it can't be ruled out that…”, warning that something bad might happen; ないものでもない means “it's not that I wouldn't (do it)”, saying you might agree.

this.tr: It might rain, so let's take an umbrella.

that.tag: Not that I wouldn't · reluctant yes
that.tr: Depending on the conditions, I wouldn't say no to taking it on.

items.explain: Look at whose action is being talked about: ないとも限らない is about the outside world, that “something might happen” (雨が降る, 事故が起きる), often followed by a precaution (〜から, 〜ておこう); ないものでもない is usually about yourself being “willing to do” something under certain conditions (引き受ける, 許す), and in speech ないでもない is also used.

groups.note: Both mean “(something bad) could happen”

items.diff: かねない means “could well lead to a bad result” — high likelihood; ないとも限らない just means “can't be ruled out” — low likelihood.

this.tr: It's rare, but an earthquake can't be ruled out.

that.tag: High likelihood · caused by an action
that.tr: If you drive that fast, you could easily cause an accident.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: かねない is usually preceded by a risky action (スピードを出したら), saying “if this goes on, something could well happen”, with criticism; ないとも限らない often goes with 「めったにないが」 or 「念のため」, saying the chance is small but can't be ruled out. The forms differ too: かねない follows the ます-form stem (起こし + かねない).

items.diff: おそれがある is an objective warning in news and announcements; ないとも限らない is the speaker's own reminder that “something might…”.

this.tr: You might come down with a fever while traveling, so let's take some medicine.

that.tr: Due to the typhoon, there is a risk of the river flooding.

items.explain: Look at the setting: weather forecasts, news and announcements issuing an objective warning → おそれがある; the speaker reminding themselves or those around them that “something might happen, so let's be prepared” → ないとも限らない, often followed by 「〜から、〜ておこう」.

groups.note: Both mean “it's not that… not…”, using a double negative to tactfully leave room

items.diff: Same meaning; なくもない is more colloquial and often describes a feeling of “a little bit”; ないものでもない is more formal and stiffer, mostly about a conditional willingness.

this.tr: Now that you mention it, I do kind of get that feeling.

that.tr: Depending on the conditions, I wouldn't say no to cooperating.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the content: everyday conversation, especially about feelings like 「気がする」 or 「分かる」 → なくもない (なくはない too), which sounds more easygoing; negotiating conditions or stating a position with a bit of an air → ないものでもない (in speech ないでもない).

items.diff: ないことはない is more objective: “it's not that it can't be done”; なくもない carries more subjective reservation: “a little bit…”.

this.tr: Now that you mention it, I can sort of understand how he feels.

that.tr: It's tough, but if we hurry, it's not like we can't make it.

items.explain: Look at whether it's about a feeling or a possibility: ないことはない is often used for an objective judgment that “it can be done if conditions are met” (急げば間に合う), with a fairly strong degree of affirmation; なくもない usually goes with feelings like 「気がする」 or 「分かる」, meaning “a little bit”, with hesitation and reservation. なくはない is the same.

groups.note: Both come from the classical adjective 「なし (without)」

items.diff: なくして only says “without…, it would be impossible”, and is the most formal; なしでは means the same but is more common, and なしに can also mean “without…, (went ahead and) did…”.

this.tr: Without everyone's help, this success would not have been possible.

that.tag: なしでは · can't do without
that.tr: Without everyone's help, this job can't get done.
He took the day off work without telling anyone.

items.explain: 「なし」 just means “without”. Look at the second half: followed by a negative (できない, ありえない) → both なくして and なしでは work, saying the first part is indispensable; なくして is more formal, mostly used in speeches and writing; followed by an action that's already been done (休んだ) → only なしに works, meaning “did… without going through…”, often with blame.

groups.note: Both stress that “A is indispensable; without A there's no B”

items.diff: なくして puts it negatively: “without A, there's no B”; あっての puts it positively: “only with A is there B”.

this.tr: Without customers, a business can't survive.

that.tr: A business exists only because of its customers.

items.explain: The two sentences make the same point; look at the structure: 「AなくしてB」 must be followed by a negative or 「ありえない」; 「AあってのB」 attaches directly to a noun, and the sentence is positive. あっての is often used to express gratitude (皆さんあっての私です).

items.diff: なくして attaches to a noun and stresses that something is indispensable; ないことには attaches to the ない-form of a verb, saying “unless you first do…, you can't…”.

this.tr: Without effort, success is impossible.

that.tr: You won't know if it's any good until you actually try using it.

items.explain: First look at the word before it: a noun (努力, 協力, 愛) → なくして, formal written language; the ない-form of a verb (使ってみない, 会わない) → ないことには, more common in everyday judgments (会ってみないことには分からない).

groups.note: Both come from 「並ぶ」 — originally “to line up”

items.diff: 並み follows a noun, meaning “on the level of…”; と並んで says two things are “equally famous, of equal standing”.

this.tr: His cooking skills are on a par with a professional's.

that.tr: Like Nara, Kyoto is known as a city with many old temples.

items.explain: Both mean “lined up together”: 並み attaches directly to a noun (プロ並み, 平年並み), taking that noun as the standard and saying the degree “lines up with it”; 「Aと並んで」 puts two things side by side as equally famous or important, usually followed by a feature they share.

groups.note: Both come from 「何と (なんと)」 — “how, what a…”

items.diff: When exclaiming “how…!”, they mean the same; なんと／なんという lean formal, なんて is colloquial.

this.tr: What a beautiful view!

this.tag: なんという · before a noun
this.tr: What a beautiful view!

that.tr: What a pretty view!

items.explain: All developed from 「何と」: なんと pairs with a sentence-final 「だろう」 or 「ことか」, and なんという attaches directly to a noun; both are used in writing and speeches. In everyday speech, both become なんて (なんてきれいな景色, なんて人だ). なんと can also stand alone to mean “believe it or not” (なんと100万円！).

groups.note: Both come from 「別 (べつ)」 — “a different matter”

items.diff: なら別だが means “if it's…, that's a different story”, with the focus on the general conclusion that follows; は別として just sets the first item aside.

this.tr: It'd be one thing for a child, but for an adult to do that is just strange.

that.tr: Children aside, all adults please take part.

items.explain: Look at the second half: なら別だが first supposes an exception, then turns with 「が」 to criticize or stress the general case (大人がするのはおかしい); は別として is followed directly by the rest (大人は全員参加).

groups.note: Both mean “it'd be different if it were A, but…”

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; なら別だが can also be said on its own as 「それなら話は別だ」, meaning your stance changes once the condition changes.

this.tr: If it's urgent, that's another matter, but please don't call in the middle of the night.

that.tr: If it's urgent, fine, but please don't call in the middle of the night.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable. The difference is in the literal meaning: 「別」 is “that's an exception, a different matter”, so only 別 works on its own in 「それなら話は別だ (well, that's a different story)」; ともかく means “leaving aside” and can't be used alone like that.

items.diff: なら別だが just names an exception; ならまだしも compares the degree of the two: the first is “still bearable”, the second “even worse”.

this.tag: An exception of a different kind
this.tr: If it were for work, that'd be different, but being late because you were out having fun is unforgivable.

that.tr: Once would be one thing, but being late three times is unforgivable.

items.explain: Look at how the two items relate: with ならまだしも, both are the same thing in lighter and heavier forms (一度 → 三度も), saying “the light one is bearable, the heavy one isn't”; with なら別だが, the first is a special case of a different nature (仕事なら) — an exception, not a lesser degree.

groups.note: Both say “this really shows A's character”

items.title: 〜らしい (typical)
items.diff: らしい says “very much like A, very typical”; ならでは says “only A has this”, stressing uniqueness, with higher praise.

this.tr: This is a view you can only get in Kyoto, nowhere else.

that.tr: With old temples lined up, it's a view that's so very Kyoto.

items.explain: Look at whether it's about “being like it” or “having it”: らしい matches the typical image of A (somewhere else might have something similar), as in 「春らしい天気」; ならでは stresses that other places or people don't have it, often comes with phrases like 「ほかでは見られない」, and is mostly used as praise.

items.diff: ならではの means “… that only A has” and modifies a noun; だけあって means “as expected of A, so sure enough…”, expressing cause and effect.

this.tr: It has a warmth that only a craftsman's handiwork can give.

that.tag: As expected of A · cause and effect
that.tr: As you'd expect from a craftsman, the finish is beautiful.

items.explain: Look at the structure: ならではの is followed directly by a noun (温かみ, 味), saying that feature is found nowhere else; だけあって is followed by a clause, saying “because it's A, the result is good, just as you'd expect”, often used together with 「さすが」.

groups.note: Both mean “it'd be different if it were A, but…”

items.diff: Basically the same meaning; ならいざしらず is more literary with a classical flavor, while ならともかく is used in both speech and writing and is the most common.

this.tr: It'd be one thing for a child, but for an adult to make an excuse like that is pathetic.

that.tr: It'd be one thing for a child, but for an adult to make an excuse like that is pathetic.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable; the difference is register: ならともかく is common in both speech and writing; ならいざしらず has a classical flavor, is mostly seen in essays and commentary, and the first item is often a special case like 「神様」 「子ども」 「昔」. はいざしらず works the same way (昔はいざしらず).

items.diff: ならいざしらず excludes the first item as a “special case”; ならまだしも compares the degree of the two, with the first “still bearable”.

this.tr: It'd be one thing for a newcomer, but for a veteran to make a mistake like this…

that.tr: Once would be one thing, but making the same mistake three times…

items.explain: Look at how the two items relate: with ならいざしらず, they're different people or situations (新人 ↔ ベテラン), and the first is special so it can be treated differently; with ならまだしも, it's usually the same thing in lighter and heavier forms (一度 ↔ 三度も), saying the light one is bearable but the heavy one isn't.

groups.note: Both mean “it'd be different if it were A, but…”

items.diff: ならまだしも stresses that the first item is “just about acceptable”, comparing its degree with the second, with stronger dissatisfaction; ならともかく just sets the first item aside and has a wider range of uses.

this.tr: Being a little late would be one thing, but making someone wait two hours…

that.tr: A genius aside, ordinary people can't do it.

items.explain: Look at whether the second half is a complaint: with ならまだしも, the first item is a mild case that's “just about bearable”, and the second is a reality of greater degree that can't be accepted (二時間も), so the whole sentence is a complaint; ならともかく has wider uses and can also neutrally say “A aside, B is like this” (普通の人には無理だ).

items.diff: ならまだしも compares degrees of the same thing; ならいざしらず excludes a special person or situation, and is more literary.

this.tr: Once would be one thing, but making the same mistake three times…

that.tr: It'd be one thing for a newcomer, but for a veteran to make a mistake like this…

items.explain: Look at how the two items relate: with ならまだしも, it's usually the same thing in lighter and heavier forms (一度 ↔ 三度も), saying the light one is bearable but the heavy one isn't; with ならいざしらず, they're different people or situations (新人 ↔ ベテラン), and the first is special so it can be treated differently, with a more literary tone. はいざしらず is the same.

groups.note: All are written 「なり」, but they attach differently and mean completely different things

items.diff: Dictionary form + なり means “as soon as… (immediately did)”; た-form + なり means “after…, (stayed that way, with nothing after)”.

this.tr: As soon as he entered the room, he collapsed onto the bed.

that.tr: He went into his room and hasn't come out since.

items.explain: The only difference is る vs. た: dictionary form + なり is immediately followed by an unexpected action; た-form + なり is usually followed by a negative (出てこない, 連絡がない), meaning “stayed just like that, and nothing more happened after”, close in meaning to 「たきり」.

items.diff: Verb + なり means “as soon as…”; noun + なりに means “in … own way, within …'s abilities”.

this.tr: As soon as my mother saw my face, she burst into tears.

that.tr: Children have their own ideas about things, in their own way.

items.explain: Look at what comes before なり: a verb in dictionary form (見る) → as soon as…, followed by an unexpected action right after; a noun for a person or thing (子ども, 私) + なりに → “in a way suited to its status or abilities”, admitting limits but saying it has its own way. なりの + noun is the same (私なりの考え).

items.diff: Verb + なり means “as soon as…”; AなりBなり means “A or B — pick one and do it”.

this.tr: As soon as he hung up the phone, he rushed out of the house.

that.tr: Please get in touch, whether by phone or by email.

items.explain: Both can be “verb dictionary form + なり”; look at how many times なり appears and what follows: once, followed by an unexpected action that has already happened (飛び出した) → as soon as…; in a pair as 「AなりBなり」, followed by a request or suggestion (〜してください, 〜たらどう) → naming options, pick any one.

groups.note: Both mean “the moment…, …”

items.diff: なり usually describes the same person “doing something unexpected the moment…”; や否や is more literary, and what follows can be someone else or a natural phenomenon.

this.tr: The moment he sat down, he started snoring.

that.tr: The moment the curtain rose, applause broke out from the audience.

items.explain: Look at whether it's the same person before and after: with なり, it's the same person on both sides (he sits down → he snores), followed by an action others didn't expect; with や否や, they can be different people or things (幕が上がる → 観客が拍手する); it's a literary expression used in news and novels, also shortened to 「や」.

items.diff: なり is only used for the same person “the moment…, (did something unexpected)”, and leans literary; たとたん can also be followed by an unexpected change, and can be used about yourself.

this.tr: The moment she read the letter, she burst into tears.

that.tag: Unexpected change · can be about oneself
that.tr: The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.

items.explain: なり is followed by an action the same person actively does, and is mostly used to describe others (彼女は……泣き出した); たとたん is followed by an unexpected change, which can be a sensation in yourself (めまいがした) or something else, and is common in speech too. The forms differ too: なり follows the dictionary form, たとたん follows the た-form.

items.title: 〜次第 (as soon as…, right away)
items.diff: Both mean “as soon as…”, but なり only narrates things that have already happened; 次第 is followed by something you're going to do, or a request.

this.tr: As soon as my father got home, he shut himself up in his room.

that.tr: I'll contact you as soon as I get to the station.

wrong.why: なり can't be followed by your own intention or a request

items.explain: Look at the tense and intention in the second half: なり is followed by an unexpected action that has already happened (部屋にこもってしまった); 次第 is followed by what the speaker will do next or a request (連絡します, ご連絡ください), mostly in work settings. The forms differ too: なり follows the dictionary form, 次第 follows the ます-form stem (着き + 次第).

groups.note: Both come from the classical copula 「なり」 — equivalent to modern 「である」

items.diff: AなりBなり means “A or B, pick one”; なりとも means “even just a little”.

this.tr: I'd like to express my thanks, whether by phone or by letter.

that.tr: I'd like to express my thanks, even if only in a word.

items.explain: なり = である: 「電話なり手紙なり」 = 電話であれ手紙であれ, naming a few options to pick from; 「一言なりとも」 = 一言であっても, preceded by a tiny amount like 「一言」 「少し」 「一目」, saying “even just this little”.

groups.note: All are written 「なり」, but they attach differently and mean completely different things

items.diff: AなりBなり means “A or B — pick one and do it”; verb + なり means “as soon as…”.

this.tr: Please get in touch, whether by phone or by email.

that.tr: As soon as he hung up the phone, he rushed out of the house.

items.explain: Both can be “verb dictionary form + なり”; look at how many times なり appears and what follows: in a pair as 「AなりBなり」, followed by a request or suggestion (〜してください, 〜たらどう) → naming options, pick any one; once, followed by an unexpected action that has already happened (飛び出した) → as soon as….

items.diff: AなりBなり names options; noun + なりに means “in … own way”.

this.tr: If there's something you don't understand, ask your teacher or a senior colleague.

that.tr: I thought it over as hard as I could, in my own way.

items.explain: 「先輩なりに聞いて」 also contains 「なりに」, but here it's なり + に (the 「に」 of who you ask), meaning “ask someone like a senior colleague”; the なりに in 「私なりに」 is a single unit meaning “within my own abilities and circumstances”. Look at the context: AなりBなり in a pair, followed by a request or suggestion → pick one; attached only to a person like 「私」 or 「子ども」, followed by what they themselves do → in one's own way.

groups.note: Both are used to list examples

items.diff: なり〜なり means “pick any one of these and do it”, followed by a suggestion or request; とか〜とか just gives random examples and can also describe the past.

this.tr: If you're free, why not go for a walk or do some shopping?

that.tr: On my day off, I took a walk, did some shopping and so on.

items.explain: Look at the second half: なり〜なり is followed by a suggestion, request or resolve (〜たらどう, 〜てください), meaning “any of them is fine, just do one”; とか〜とか just gives a few random examples, and can be followed by a description of what was already done (過ごした).

groups.note: All are written 「なり」, but they attach differently and mean completely different things

items.diff: Noun + なりに means “in … own way”; verb + なり means “as soon as…”.

this.tr: Children have their own ideas about things, in their own way.

that.tr: As soon as my mother saw my face, she burst into tears.

items.explain: Look at what comes before なり: a noun for a person or thing (子ども, 私) + なりに → “in a way suited to its status or abilities”, admitting limits but saying it has its own way; a verb in dictionary form (見る) → as soon as…, followed by an unexpected action right after. なりの + noun is the same (子どもなりの考え).

items.diff: Noun + なりに means “within its own abilities”; AなりBなり means “A or B, pick one”.

this.tr: I thought it over as hard as I could, in my own way.

that.tr: If there's something you don't understand, ask your teacher or a senior colleague.

items.explain: The なりに in 「私なりに」 is a single unit meaning “within my own abilities and circumstances”; 「先輩なりに聞いて」 also contains 「なりに」, but it's actually なり + に (the 「に」 of who you ask), meaning “ask someone like a senior colleague”. Look at the context: attached only to a person like 「私」 or 「子ども」, followed by what they themselves do → in one's own way; AなりBなり in a pair, followed by a request or suggestion → pick one.

groups.note: Both come from the classical copula 「なり」 — equivalent to modern 「である」

items.diff: なりとも means “even just a little”; AなりBなり means “A or B, pick one”.

this.tr: I'd like to express my thanks, even if only in a word.

that.tr: I'd like to express my thanks, whether by phone or by letter.

items.explain: なり = である: 「一言なりとも」 = 一言であっても, preceded by a tiny amount like 「一言」 「少し」 「一目」, saying “even just this little”; 「電話なり手紙なり」 = 電話であれ手紙であれ, naming a few options to pick from.

groups.note: なりとも ↔ たりとも: only one kana differs

items.diff: なりとも means “even just a little”, followed by a wish; たりとも means “not even one…”, followed by a negative.

this.tr: I'd love to see them, even if just for a glimpse.

that.tr: I didn't take a single day off.

items.explain: The only difference is な vs. た; look at the end of the sentence: たりとも follows 「one + counter」 and is always followed by a negative (休まなかった, 許さない), stressing “not even one”; なりとも follows words for a tiny amount like 「一目」 or 「少し」, and is followed by a wish or request (会いたい), saying “even just this little”.

groups.note: なりとも has two jobs, each with a similar alternative: “even just a little” ≈ ないまでも; “anything at all” (何なりと) ≈ 何でも

items.diff: なりとも only names the bare minimum; ないまでも first states a high standard that can't be reached, then falls back to “at least…”.

this.tr: I'd be glad if I could be of even a little help.

that.tr: Maybe not the full amount, but I'd like you to pay back at least half.

items.explain: Look at how many standards the sentence has: なりとも only attaches to words for tiny amounts like 「少し」 「多少」 「一目」, and is a formal written expression, equivalent to colloquial 「少しでも」; ないまでも has one standard on each side (全額 → 半分), “stepping back by comparison”.

items.title: 何でも (anything)
items.diff: Same meaning, “anything at all”; 何なりと is a formal service expression, 何でも is everyday language.

this.tr: If there is anything you need, please don't hesitate to ask.

that.tr: If you're ever in trouble, just tell me — anything.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting: hotels and shops speaking to customers use 「何なりと (お申し付けください)」; friends and family use 「何でも」. The なり in 何なりと is just the classical 「である」, playing the same role as the 「で」 in 何でも.

groups.note: Both come from the classical adjective 「なし (without)」

items.diff: なしに can mean “without…, (went ahead and) did…”; なくして only says “without…, it would be impossible”, and is more formal.

this.tr: He took the day off work without telling anyone.

this.tag: なしでは · can't do without
this.tr: Without everyone's help, this job can't get done.

that.tr: Without everyone's help, this success would not have been possible.

items.explain: 「なし」 just means “without”. Look at the second half: followed by an action that's already been done (休んだ) → only なしに works, “did… without going through…”, often with blame; followed by a negative (できない, ありえない) → both なしでは and なくして work, saying the first part is indispensable; なくして is more formal, mostly used in speeches and writing. なしには is the same as なしでは.

groups.note: Both mean “without (doing)…, … / never…”

items.diff: Same meaning; なしに follows a noun (休みなしに), ことなく follows a verb in dictionary form (休むことなく) and is more literary.

this.tr: He kept working from morning till night without a break.

that.tr: He kept working from morning till night without stopping to rest.

wrong.why: なしに can't come directly after a verb; you need to add 「こと」

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the word before: a noun (休み, 連絡, 断り) → なしに; a verb (休む, 迷う) → ことなく (or ことなしに), more literary. Since English says “without…” for both, it's easy to write ✗休むなしに.

groups.note: にあって ↔ にあたって: only one 「た」 differs

items.diff: にあって means “in the midst of… (a situation)”; にあたって means “on the occasion of doing…”.

this.tr: Even in a difficult situation, he didn't lose his composure.

that.tr: On launching the new business, they gathered the employees together.

items.explain: First check whether there's a 「た」, then look at what comes before: にあって is preceded by a noun for a situation, era or position (状況, 非常時, 現代社会), meaning “being in the midst of it”; にあたって is usually preceded by a verb in dictionary form or an event like 「出発」 or 「開会」, meaning “at the time of (just before) doing this”. にあたり is the same.

groups.note: Both mean “in… (a place or situation)”

items.diff: において just objectively states where something happens; にあって stresses being in a special situation that affects what follows.

this.tr: In times of emergency, calm judgment is called for.

that.tr: The meeting will be held in Conference Room 1.

wrong.why: にあって can't be used for a simple venue

items.explain: Look at whether what comes before is an ordinary place or a special situation: a venue like a conference room or a convention → において (the written form of 「で」); a special situation like 非常時, 困難な時代 or 責任ある立場 → にあって, usually followed by how one should be or act in that situation.

groups.note: Both mean “worthy of, deserving”

items.diff: に恥じない follows a title or expectation, saying a performance “lives up to it”; に値する follows an action, saying something “deserves to be…”.

this.tag: Title → lives up to the name
this.tr: It was a fight worthy of the name “champion”.

that.tr: His efforts deserve praise.

items.explain: Look at what comes before に: a title or others' expectations like 「名」 「期待」 「伝統」 → に恥じない, saying the actual performance does it justice without disgrace, often used to state resolve (名に恥じないよう頑張ります); an action like 「称賛」 「一読」 「注目」 → に値する, saying the thing itself deserves to be treated that way.

groups.note: Both are used to contrast two situations

items.diff: にひきかえ says the two situations are exact opposites, with the speaker's praise, criticism or feelings; に比べて neutrally compares degree.

this.tr: In stark contrast to his serious older brother, the younger brother does nothing but play.

that.tr: Compared with his older brother, the younger brother studies harder.

items.explain: With にひきかえ, the two people are one good and one bad, exact opposites (真面目な兄／遊んでばかりの弟), and the sentence carries the speaker's dissatisfaction or exclamation; it's a written expression; に比べて just says who has more or less of something, with no judgment.

items.title: 〜に対して (contrast)
items.diff: にひきかえ carries a strong subjective judgment, with one side good and the other bad; に対して just objectively sets out how the two differ.

this.tr: Unlike her hardworking older sister, the younger sister is a lazybones.

that.tr: The older sister studies humanities, whereas the younger sister studies science.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a judgment of good and bad: に対して just objectively sets out how the two differ (文系／理系), without praise or criticism; with にひきかえ, one side is good and the other bad (働き者／怠け者), the sentence carries the speaker's praise, dissatisfaction or feelings, and it isn't used for purely objective explanations.

items.diff: にひきかえ contrasts two different people or things; 反面 talks about two sides of the same thing.

this.tr: In contrast to the convenient city, the countryside is inconvenient.

that.tr: City life is convenient, but on the other hand it's also stressful.

items.explain: Look at whether one thing or two is being contrasted: with 反面, both halves talk about the pros and cons of the same thing (都会の生活); with にひきかえ, the two halves are different people or things (都会 ↔ 田舎), and their situations are exact opposites.

groups.note: Both come from 「至る」 — originally “to reach”

items.thisTitle: 〜に至って (only when it came to…)
items.diff: に至って (初めて) means “only when it reached the point of… (finally took action)”; に至っても means “even when it reached the point of…, (still didn't act)”.

this.tr: It was only when people died that measures were finally taken.

that.tr: Even when it got to the point that people died, no measures were taken.

items.explain: The two sentences differ by just one 「も」: に至って is often followed by 「初めて」 or 「ようやく」, saying it took things getting that serious before action was finally taken, with the criticism of “too little, too late”; に至っても is followed by a negative (取られなかった), saying that even at that point nothing changed, a harsher criticism.

items.thisTitle: 〜に至って (only when it came to…)
items.diff: に至って means “only when it reached the point of…”; に至っては picks out the most extreme item in a list: “as for…, they even…”.

this.tr: It was only when the company was on the brink of bankruptcy that the president finally admitted his mistakes.

that.tr: Everyone in my family is bad at getting up in the morning, and as for my father, he even sleeps until noon.

items.explain: The two differ by just one 「は」: に至って is preceded by the point a situation has reached (倒産寸前), and followed by 「ようやく」 or 「初めて」; に至っては is preceded by a person or thing; it first says “everyone is…”, then picks out the most extreme one and is followed by something even more shocking (昼まで寝ている), with criticism or surprise.

items.diff: に至る says a situation “ends up reaching” a certain point; に至るまで describes a range “all the way to…”, stressing how far it extends.

this.tr: After repeated discussions, an agreement was finally reached.

that.tr: From children to the elderly, everyone in town enjoyed the festival.

items.explain: Both mean “to reach”: に至る means things develop step by step until they finally reach a result (合意に至った, 倒産に至った); に至るまで is often paired with 「〜から」, describing a range that stretches from one end all the way to the other (an extreme or a fine detail), followed by a stress on “all of them…”.

groups.note: Both mean “going through a process and finally reaching a certain point”

items.diff: に至る stresses the situation finally reached (usually something serious); 末に stresses the long period of thought or effort before getting there.

this.tr: The conflict between the two countries finally escalated into war.

that.tr: After agonizing over it for ages, I finally decided to study abroad.

items.explain: Look at where the focus is: 末に is preceded by a verb in た-form or 「noun + の」, describing a long stretch of agonizing or discussion (さんざん悩んだ), usually followed by a decision you made yourself; に至る is preceded by the point a situation finally reached (戦争, 倒産, 合意), and is mostly used to objectively report a serious outcome.

groups.note: All come from the verb 「至る (いたる)」 — “to reach”

items.diff: に至るまで describes a range “stretching all the way to…”; に至る／に至って say a situation “finally developed to the point of… / only at the point of…”.

this.tr: From the president to new hires, everyone attended the meeting.

that.tr: Business went downhill, and it finally ended in bankruptcy.

that.tag: に至って · only when it came to…
that.tr: It was only when people died that the government finally took action.

items.explain: All three are 「至る = to reach」. Look at the context: 「Aから」 before and 「まで」 after, naming both ends to show how wide the range is → に至るまで; preceded by a situation (倒産, 死者が出る), saying things developed step by step to this point → に至る, and 「に至って、ようやく」 means “only when it got to this point…”.

items.diff: に至るまで describes a range “including even…”, without judgment; に至っては first talks about the whole, then picks out the most extreme one to comment on, usually with dissatisfaction.

this.tr: I was given detailed warnings about everything from my clothes to the way I speak.

that.tr: My older brother and sister are both bad at cooking, and as for my younger brother, he can't even crack an egg.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: 「Aから」 before and 「まで」 after, saying everything from A to B is included → に至るまで; first a group of similar people or things (兄も姉も), then the most serious one is picked out as the topic, followed by a surprised or dissatisfied comment → に至っては.

groups.note: Both describe a range (from where to where, how wide)

items.diff: から〜まで just objectively marks a start and end point; から〜に至るまで stresses how far or fine-grained the end point is, with an exclamatory sense of “even…”, and is more literary.

this.tr: This shop has everything, from stationery to furniture.

that.tr: This shop is open from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.

items.explain: Look at what the two ends are: an ordinary start and end in time or place (９時から９時まで, 東京から大阪まで) → から〜まで; listing kinds of things or groups of people, where the end point is surprisingly far-reaching or detailed, often followed by 「何でも」 「すべて」 「全員」 → に至るまで, mostly in writing, advertising and speeches.

items.diff: にわたって is preceded by a whole period or area, describing how long or wide the range is; に至るまで is preceded by an end point, saying it stretches all the way to that end.

this.tag: End point · all the way to
this.tr: From the founding of the shop to this day, we've kept this same flavor.

that.tr: The festival was held over three days.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: something that is itself a whole period or area, like 「３日間」 「10年」 「全国」 → にわたって; an end point like 「今日」 「現在」 「細部」, often paired with 「Aから」 → に至るまで.

groups.note: All come from the verb 「至る (いたる)」 — “to reach”

items.diff: に至っては means “as for…, even more so…”, picking out the most extreme case; に至る／に至って say a situation “finally developed to / only at the point of…”.

this.tr: My older brother and sister are both bad at cooking, and as for my younger brother, he can't even crack an egg.

that.tr: The negotiations broke down, and it finally went to court.

that.tag: に至って · only when it came to…
that.tr: It was only when an accident happened that measures were finally taken.

items.explain: Check whether 「至って」 is followed by 「は」, then look at what comes before: a person or thing (弟), after a group of similar ones (兄も姉も), followed by a comment on how bad it is → に至っては; a situation (裁判, 事故が起きる), saying things developed to this point → に至る, and 「に至って、ようやく」 means “only when it got to this point…”.

items.diff: に至っては means “as for…, even more so…”; に至っても means “even when it reached the point of…, (still not)…”. The only difference is 「は」 vs. 「も」.

this.tr: My mom and dad are both bad with machines, and as for my grandma, she doesn't even know how to make a phone call.

that.tr: Even when the company went bankrupt, the president wouldn't admit responsibility.

items.explain: The only difference is the final 「は」 vs. 「も」. Look at what comes before and after: a person or thing, last in a line of similar ones, followed by how extreme it is → に至っては; a serious situation (倒産する), followed by “still not…” → に至っても.

items.diff: に至っては picks out the most extreme one to comment on, usually with dissatisfaction; に至るまで describes a range that includes everything up to that end, without judgment.

this.tr: Half the class forgot their homework, and as for Tanaka, he didn't even bring his textbook.

that.tr: I was given detailed warnings about everything from my clothes to the way I speak.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: 「Aから」 before and 「まで」 after, saying everything from A to B is included → に至るまで; first a description of the overall situation, then the most serious one is picked out as the topic, followed by a surprised or dissatisfied comment → に至っては.

groups.note: Both bring up someone or something, then make a dissatisfied comment

items.diff: ときたら brings someone up right away to complain about them, and is colloquial; に至っては first talks about the whole, then picks out the most extreme one, and is more literary.

this.tr: Lots of people in this section come in late, and as for the manager, he doesn't show up until noon.

that.tr: Don't get me started on our manager — he doesn't come in until noon every day.

items.explain: Look at whether there's a lead-in: first saying “lots of people…”, then picking out the most serious one → に至っては, also used in the news and writing; no lead-in, bringing up someone close to you right away to complain, with a colloquial feel (うちの〜ときたら) → ときたら.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「至る (いたる)」 — “to reach”

items.title: 〜に至って (only when it came to…)
items.diff: に至って is consequential: “only when it reached the point of… (finally took action)”; に至っても is concessive: “even when it reached the point of…, (still didn't act)”.

this.tr: Even after people had died, the government still took no measures.

that.tr: It was only when people died that the government finally took measures.

items.explain: The first halves of the two sentences are identical, differing by just one 「も」. Look at the second half: 「ようやく」 or 「初めて」 + did something → に至って; “still not…” or 「なお〜ない」 → に至っても, with the criticism of “even after all that, still not…”.

items.diff: に至っても means “even when it reached the point of…, (still not)…”; に至っては means “as for…, even more so…”. The only difference is 「も」 vs. 「は」.

this.tr: Even when the company went bankrupt, the president wouldn't admit responsibility.

that.tr: My mom and dad are both bad with machines, and as for my grandma, she doesn't even know how to make a phone call.

items.explain: The only difference is the final 「も」 vs. 「は」. Look at what comes before and after: a serious situation (倒産する), followed by “still not…” → に至っても; a person or thing, last in a line of similar ones, followed by how extreme it is → に至っては.

groups.note: Both express contrast: “despite…, still…”

items.diff: にもかかわらず is a general “despite…”; に至っても stresses that the situation has worsened to the extreme, yet still nothing changes, with stronger criticism.

this.tag: Worsened to the extreme · still no action
this.tr: Even when the damage had spread nationwide, the government didn't act.

that.tr: Despite the damage that had already occurred, the government didn't act.

items.explain: Look at the first part: just a fact (被害が出ている) → にもかかわらず; a situation that has worsened step by step to an extreme (全国に広がる, 死者が出る), often followed by 「なお」 or 「まだ」 → に至っても. にもかかわらず can also be used for good things (忙しいにもかかわらず来てくれた), while に至っても is almost only used for criticism.

groups.note: Both indicate “whose view this is, who said it”

items.diff: にしたら is the speaker putting themselves in someone's shoes and “guessing” how they feel; に言わせれば is an opinion that person would state outright themselves.

this.tr: According to my mom, it's still too early for me to live on my own.

that.tr: For a mother, her daughter living alone must be a worry.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: にしたら is often followed by 「〜だろう」 or 「〜かもしれない」, with the speaker imagining how the other person feels (にすれば is the same); に言わせれば is followed by a clear opinion (早い, 間違っている); when it's about someone else, 「そうだ」 is often added to report it, and 「私に言わせれば」 means “if you ask me”.

items.diff: から見ると is a neutral “from the point of view of…”; に言わせれば means “if you let… say it”, stressing that this is that person's blunt personal view.

this.tr: Everyone praises it, but if you ask me, that movie is boring.

that.tr: From a foreigner's point of view, Japanese trains are extremely punctual.

items.explain: Look at the first half: に言わせれば is often preceded by a general view like 「みんなは〜けど」, then reveals your own (or someone's) contrary opinion; から見ると just looks at things objectively from a different angle, can be preceded by a category of people like 「外国人」, and doesn't have the tone of “I'm going to say it anyway” (からすると is the same).

items.diff: によると says “where the information came from”, usually followed by 「そうだ」; に言わせれば says “whose personal opinion this is”.

this.tr: According to the experts, this plan was unworkable from the start.

that.tr: According to the weather forecast, it'll rain tomorrow.

items.explain: Look at what the second half is: an objective piece of information (明日は雨), often ending in 「そうだ」 or 「らしい」 → によると (によれば is the same), which can also be preceded by non-human sources like news or surveys; an evaluation or opinion (無理がある, 間違っている) → に言わせれば, which must be preceded by a person.

groups.note: Both mean “do something according to a certain standard or basis”

items.diff: にのっとって means strictly following the rules that already govern the matter; に準じて means taking some other standard and applying it “by analogy”, treating things the same way.

this.tr: Part-timers' transportation costs are also paid on the same basis as for full-time employees.

that.tr: The match is held in accordance with international rules.

items.explain: Check whether the standard and the target naturally belong together: international rules already govern matches, so you simply follow them → にのっとって; rules for full-time staff don't normally cover part-timers, so they are borrowed “by analogy” and applied to another group → に準じて. You also often see 「〜に準じた待遇」 and 「これに準ずる」.

items.diff: に基づいて takes facts, data or experience as its basis; に準じて takes an existing rule or form of treatment as a model and handles something the same way.

this.tr: Absences during a disaster are treated the same as paid leave.

that.tr: Based on the survey results, we reviewed the plan.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: “material” such as survey results, data or experience → に基づいて, drawing a judgment from it; an existing “rule or treatment” such as paid leave, full-time employees or a precedent, applied to something else → に準じて, meaning “handle it as if it were the same”.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「限る（かぎる）」 — “to limit to a certain range”

items.diff: に限らず sits mid-sentence and means “not only… (but also…)”, for good or bad things; に限ったことではない usually ends the sentence and points out that a problem “isn't unique to this case”.

this.tr: The labor shortage is not a problem unique to this industry.

that.tr: This game isn't just for kids — adults can enjoy it too.

items.explain: Look at the position and content: に限らず is mid-sentence and is followed by 「〜も」 to widen the range, for good or bad things; に限ったことではない ends the sentence as a conclusion, usually after a problem (labor shortage, いじめ), meaning “don't think it's only like this here”.

items.diff: に限ったことではない means “it's not just… that's like this” (the scope is wider); とは限らない means “not necessarily…” (partial negation).

this.tr: Long working hours are not unique to Japan.

that.tr: Expensive things aren't necessarily good things.

items.explain: Both are negations of 「限る」; look at what comes before: noun ＋ に限ったことではない negates “only here”, concluding “it's everywhere”; a whole clause ＋ とは限らない negates “always”, concluding “there are exceptions”.

items.diff: に限って means “of all times (just then)”; に限ったことではない means “it's not only this time — it's always like this”.

this.tr: Train delays aren't something that only happens today.

that.tr: Just when I'm in a hurry, the train is late.

items.explain: Both “limit” the range to one point, but the conclusions differ: に限って says “of all times / of all people, just this one”, with a sense of bad luck or surprise, and the sentence continues; に限ったことではない ends the sentence, saying “it's not only at this time”, and is often used to point out that a problem is widespread.

groups.note: Both mean “not only… (it's the same elsewhere)”

items.diff: ひとり〜のみならず is the written “not merely…”, followed by a wider scope; に限ったことではない completes the thought in one sentence and usually ends it.

this.tr: The declining birthrate is not just Japan's problem.

that.tr: The declining birthrate is not merely Japan's problem but a problem for the whole world.

items.explain: The meaning is almost the same; look at the sentence structure: ひとり〜のみならず sandwiches a noun between 「ひとり」 and 「のみならず」 and is always followed by 「〜全体」 or 「〜も」 to widen the scope — it's speech and academic language; に限ったことではない finishes in one sentence, and in speech becomes 「〜に限ったことじゃない」.

groups.note: Both come from 「かかる（掛かる）」 — “to fall on, to hang on…”

items.diff: にかかったら／にかかっては means “once it falls into the hands of… (this happens)”, preceded by a person; にかかっている means “it all depends on…”, and ends the sentence.

this.tag: にかかったら · he can handle anything
this.tr: Once it gets to him, even the hardest problem is solved right away.

this.tag: にかかっては · no match for her
this.tr: Up against her, with that silver tongue, nobody stands a chance.

that.tr: Whether we win the match all depends on your effort.

items.explain: Both are 「かかる」: the matter “hangs on” someone. Look at the position and the word before it: sentence-final にかかっている usually follows things like “effort, weather, skill” and means the outcome depends on it; mid-sentence にかかったら／にかかっては follows a person, and the rest says what happens once things are in that person's hands — either it's easily handled, or nobody can do anything against them.

groups.note: にかかっては ↔ にかけては look almost identical

items.diff: person ＋ にかかっては means “up against this person (nobody stands a chance)”; field ＋ にかけては means “when it comes to… (he's the best)”.

this.tr: Up against her, with that silver tongue, nobody stands a chance.

that.tr: When it comes to arguing, nobody can beat her.

items.explain: Both second halves can say 「かなわない」, so look at the noun in front: a person (彼女, あの先生) → にかかっては, saying you're helpless against this person; a field or skill (口げんか, 数学) → にかけては, saying he's the best in this area.

groups.note: Both mean “with someone's ability, anything can be done”

items.title: 〜をもってすれば
items.diff: をもってすれば follows an ability or skill and is written; にかかったら follows a person directly, is spoken, and often exaggerates.

this.tr: In Tanaka's hands, a breakdown like this gets fixed in five minutes.

that.tr: With Tanaka's skills, this breakdown should be fixed soon.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: 「田中さん」 himself → にかかったら, often with an exaggerated tone like 「こんな〜なんて」 or 「あっという間に」; an ability like 「田中さんの技術」 or 「実力」 → をもってすれば, mostly seen in writing and formal speeches.

groups.note: Both mean “use one thing as an occasion to do another”

items.diff: にかこつけて follows a “reason” given to others, while the real purpose is something else; をいいことに follows a “situation” that happens to favor you, taking advantage of it to do something you shouldn't.

this.tr: Under the pretext of a business trip, I went and enjoyed a hot-spring trip.

that.tr: Taking advantage of my parents being away, I played games until dawn.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a pretext you can tell people, like 「出張」, 「仕事」 or 「病気」 → にかこつけて, with the real purpose after it; a situation that happens to favor you, like 「親が留守」 or 「誰も見ていない」 → をいいことに, meaning “exploit a loophole”.

items.diff: を兼ねて openly means “also serving as, doubling as” — both are real purposes; にかこつけて implies the first one is just an excuse.

this.tag: First part is just an excuse
this.tr: Using a walk as an excuse, I sneaked off to play pachinko.

that.tr: I went shopping near the station, which doubled as a walk.

items.explain: Check for “concealment”: with にかこつけて, the first part is only the official story, often followed by 「こっそり」 or 「実は」 — the real purpose is something to hide, implying criticism or self-mockery; with を兼ねて, both things are true and can be said openly, with no negative nuance.

groups.note: Both mean “only focusing on one thing and neglecting others”

items.diff: にかまけて follows “the thing you're absorbed in”; はそっちのけで follows “the thing that gets neglected”.

this.tr: I was so wrapped up in work that I had no time to spend with my family.

that.tr: Pushing my family aside, I did nothing but work.

items.explain: Both sentences describe the same situation; look at the role of the noun in front: 「仕事」 is what you're absorbed in → 仕事にかまけて; 「家族」 is what's neglected → 家族はそっちのけで. にかまけて often carries an apologetic or reflective tone; letters often say 「忙しさにかまけて、ご無沙汰しております」.

groups.note: Both come from the literary adjective 「難い（かたい）」 — “difficult”

items.diff: がたい attaches to the masu-stem of verbs and means “hard to…”; に難くない attaches to nouns and uses a negative to say “not hard to…”, almost only with words like 「想像」 or 「察する」.

this.tag: Not hard to… · follows a noun
this.tr: It's not hard to imagine how tough it is to raise a child alone.

that.tr: That such a kind person is the culprit — it's hard to believe.

items.explain: Both are 「難い (difficult)」: がたい is voiced and attaches to the masu-stem (信じ＋がたい), meaning something is psychologically hard to do; に難くない is read 「かたくない」 and follows nouns like 「想像」 or 「理解」, or 「察する」, negating the “difficulty” — meaning “it's easy to imagine”.

groups.note: Both mean “about, related to…”

items.diff: に関する is a neutral, formal “about”; にまつわる has a storytelling flavor and is mostly followed by legends, anecdotes or mysteries.

this.tr: I'm researching legends associated with this castle.

that.tr: I'm researching materials about this castle.

items.explain: Look at the noun that follows: story-like things such as 「伝説」, 「エピソード」, 「謎」 or 「怖い話」 → にまつわる; objective, formal things such as 「資料」, 「法律」 or 「調査」 → に関する (に関して when modifying a verb). 「城にまつわる資料」 sounds unnatural.

items.diff: をめぐって is followed by disputes and conflicts; にまつわる is followed by stories and topics, with no conflict.

this.tr: I heard a strange story about this painting.

that.tr: The two brothers are fighting over this painting.

items.explain: Look at the second half: things where parties disagree, like 「争う」, 「議論」 or 「対立」 → をめぐって; stories that circulate around something, like 「話」, 「伝説」 or 「思い出」 → にまつわる.

groups.note: Both mean “too…” — the degree goes beyond the limit

items.diff: にもほどがある is a spoken “there's a limit to…”, said angrily at someone; 極まりない is a written “extremely…”, a calm judgment.

this.tr: Forgetting our plans three times — how rude can you get!

that.tr: That attitude toward customers is rude in the extreme.

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: 「〜なんて、〜にもほどがある（よ）」 is often said to the person in front of you, with surprise and anger; 極まりない is a judgment in writing or formal settings, usually after Sino-Japanese words like 「失礼」, 「危険」 or 「不愉快」 (the same goes for 極まる).

items.diff: すぎる just means “too…”, mild or strong; にもほどがある means it's so absurd you can't stand it: “this is going way too far”.

this.tr: 3,000 yen for a cup of coffee — that's ridiculously expensive!

that.tr: The coffee at this shop is a little too expensive.

items.explain: Look at the degree and tone: すぎる can take 「少し」 or 「ちょっと」 and simply says something exceeds the right amount; にもほどがある is often preceded by 「〜なんて」 — the speaker finds it absurd and is angry — and can't take 「少し」.

groups.note: Both mean “more… than…”

items.diff: より is a neutral comparison; にもまして implies the first item “was already very…” and the second goes even further; it's somewhat written.

this.tag: Last year was hot · this year even hotter
this.tr: This summer is even hotter than last year.

that.tr: This summer is hotter than last year.

items.explain: The two sentences differ by just one word. 「去年より暑い」 only says this year is hotter than last year, with nothing about whether last year was hot; 「去年にもまして暑い」 assumes “last year was already hot enough”, and this year is even more so. Also, にもまして can be used in 「何にもまして (more than anything)」.

items.diff: 以上に usually has an “expectation” as its baseline, meaning it exceeded expectations; にもまして has a baseline that was already high — “before, or something else”.

this.tag: Worked hard before · even more now
this.tr: I'm putting even more effort into practice than before.

that.tr: The exam was harder than I expected.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: expectations like 「予想」, 「想像」 or 「思った」 → 以上に, meaning “beyond expectations”; baselines like 「以前」, 「去年」 or 「何」 → にもまして, implying the baseline itself was already high (I worked hard before, too); 「何にもまして」＝ more than anything.

groups.note: Both mean “not like (someone's) usual self”

items.title: 〜らしくない (not like…)
items.diff: 柄にもなく is a set phrase placed before an action, saying someone did something that “doesn't fit their position or personality”, often self-mocking; 〜らしくない attaches to nouns such as a person's name and judges something as “not like him (me)”.

this.tr: It's so unlike me, but I actually went and bought a bouquet.

that.tr: He's always so calm — panicking like that isn't like him.

items.explain: Look at the form: 柄にもなく doesn't follow a person; the whole phrase goes before the action as an adverb (柄にもなく緊張した, 照れた), mostly about oneself, with a self-mocking “I'm not normally this kind of person”; 〜らしくない is always preceded by a name or noun (彼らしくない, 私らしくない), works as a predicate or modifies a noun (彼らしくないミス), and can describe yourself or others.

groups.note: Both are “same verb ＋ に ＋ same verb”

items.diff: 〜に〜ない means “want to… but can't”; 〜に〜て／た means “…and… again”, stressing repetition or an extreme degree.

this.tr: It was a failure that left me not knowing whether to laugh or cry.

that.tr: I cried and cried all night long.

items.explain: Look at the form of the first verb and the ending of the second: dictionary form (泣く) ＋ に ＋ negative potential (泣けない) → want to but can't; masu-stem (泣き) ＋ に ＋ te-form or ta-form of the same verb (泣いた) → do it over and over, to the extreme. 泣くに泣けない is “can't even cry about it”; 泣きに泣いた is “cried my heart out”.

groups.note: Both mean “want to do something but can't”

items.diff: （よ）うにも〜ない is usually due to objective conditions: “I try, but I can't”; 〜に〜ない is usually due to personal or social considerations: “I don't feel I can”.

this.tr: My boss is still here, so I want to go home but don't feel I can.
