that.tr: Heavy snow stopped the trains, so I can't get home even if I try.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in 「帰る」 vs 「帰ろう」. Look at the reason: objective obstacles like heavy snow or stopped trains, “can't do it even if I try” → volitional form ＋ にも; personal or social considerations like the boss still being there or the other person getting hurt, “I could but don't feel I can” → dictionary form ＋ に.

items.diff: わけにはいかない calmly says “I can't, as a matter of principle or duty”; 〜に〜ない highlights the frustration of “really wanting to but being unable to”.

this.tr: I'm afraid of hurting my friend, so I want to tell the truth but can't bring myself to.

that.tr: I promised to keep it secret, so I can't tell the truth.

items.explain: Look at the reason and the feeling: not allowed on principle or duty, like “I promised” or “the rules” → わけにはいかない, calm in tone, and the speaker doesn't necessarily want to do it; really wanting to but unable to say or do it out of hesitation → 〜に〜ない, with a sense of being torn and helpless.

groups.note: Both are used to list things one by one

items.diff: 〜やら〜やら gives a sense of “a chaotic jumble, too much to handle”, usually negative; 〜に〜に stresses adding item after item, and works for good things too.

this.tag: Adding up one by one · positive
this.tr: The table was laden with a feast — sushi, tempura, cake.

that.tr: What with moving and all the paperwork, I'm run off my feet.

items.explain: Look at the feel of the whole sentence: やら〜やら is often followed by 「で大変だ」 or 「で忙しい」, complaining about “a chaotic jumble”; 〜に〜に adds things one by one and can describe something lavish or complete (ごちそう, プレゼント); you also often hear 「〜に〜にと忙しい」.

items.diff: 〜だの〜だの is mostly used to list other people's complaints or demands, with annoyance; 〜に〜に just adds items one by one without that dissatisfaction.

this.tr: Even on weekends I'm busy with club activities and cram school.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but complain — he's hot, he's sleepy.

items.explain: Look at what's listed and the verb after it: だの〜だの usually lists things others say (暑い, 眠い), followed by 「と文句を言う」 or 「とうるさい」, carrying the speaker's annoyance; 〜に〜に lists nouns (部活, 塾), adding up things to do or things there are, one by one.

groups.note: 泣きに泣いた ↔ 泣くに泣けない, both “same verb ＋ に ＋ same verb”

items.diff: 〜に〜て／た means “…and… again”, stressing repetition or an extreme degree; 〜に〜ない means “want to… but can't”.

this.tr: I cried and cried all night long.

that.tr: It was a failure that left me not knowing whether to laugh or cry.

items.explain: Look at the form of the first verb and the ending of the second: masu-stem (泣き) ＋ に ＋ ta-form or te-form of the same verb (泣いた) → do it over and over, to the extreme; dictionary form (泣く) ＋ に ＋ negative potential (泣けない) → want to but can't. 泣きに泣いた is “cried my heart out”; 泣くに泣けない is “can't even cry about it”.

groups.note: Both mean “do something repeatedly and thoroughly”

items.diff: 〜に〜て repeats a verb (考え, 悩み) and is more emotional; 〜に〜を重ねて repeats a noun (努力, 改良) and is somewhat written.

this.tag: Verb repeated · thought over and over
this.tr: After thinking it over and over, I decided to quit my job.

that.tr: After improvement upon improvement, the new product was finally completed.

items.explain: Look at what's repeated: the masu-stem of verbs like 「考え」, 「悩み」 or 「迷い」 → 〜に〜て, often with the emotional sense of “finally making up my mind” (the same goes for 〜に〜た); nouns like 「改良」, 「努力」 or 「苦労」 → 〜に〜を重ねて, mostly in news reports and speeches.

items.diff: 考えに考える stresses repeating many times and a hard process; 考え抜く stresses sticking with it to the end and being thorough.

this.tr: After thinking it over and over for days, I reached this conclusion.

that.tr: After thinking it through completely, I reached this conclusion.

items.explain: Both sentences work; look at the clue: 「何日も」 or 「何度も」 talk about many times or a long time → 〜に〜て／た, with a “that was tough” feeling; 「最後まで」 or 「徹底的に」 talk about going all the way → 抜く. 抜く is also common with actions carried through to the end, like 「走り抜く」 or 「守り抜く」.

groups.note: Both stress “a large amount”

items.diff: にのぼる says the number actually “reached” this large figure, usually a statistical result; を下らない says “at least…”, usually an estimate.

this.tr: The damage from the earthquake reached ten billion yen.

that.tr: The damage from the earthquake is probably no less than ten billion yen.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: にのぼった is usually in the past tense, reporting a result that has already been counted; を下らない often pairs with 「だろう」 or 「と見られる」 — an estimate before the numbers are clear, meaning “at least this much”.

items.diff: にのぼる ends the sentence and reports a statistical total like a number of people or an amount of money; からある／からする／からの modify the following noun, stressing “a whopping…”.

this.tr: The audience numbered as many as 30,000.

that.tr: I reeled in a fish weighing a good 20 kilos.
I bought a watch that cost a full million yen.
As many as 30,000 spectators gathered.

items.explain: Look at the position: にのぼる is the predicate at the end of the sentence (観客は３万人にのぼった), common in news statistics; からある／からする／からの are directly followed by a noun (３万人からの観客), and divide the work by type of quantity: からある for size and weight, からする for price, からの for numbers of people.

groups.note: Both mean “do something according to a certain standard or basis”

items.diff: にのっとって follows rules or tradition, stressing not deviating from the norm; に即して fits facts or the current situation, stressing not losing touch with reality.

this.tr: The ceremony was solemnly held according to ancient custom.

that.tr: Review the plan in line with the actual situation.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: established norms like 「法律」, 「ルール」, 「古式」 or 「伝統」 → にのっとって, doing things by the rules; actual circumstances like 「現実」, 「実態」, 「事実」 or 「状況」 → に即して, adjusting to reality.

items.diff: にのっとって means strictly following the rules that already govern the matter; に準じて means taking some other standard and applying it “by analogy”, treating things the same way.

this.tr: The match is held in accordance with international rules.

that.tr: Part-timers' transportation costs are also paid on the same basis as for full-time employees.

items.explain: Check whether the standard and the target naturally belong together: international rules already govern matches, so you simply follow them → にのっとって; rules for full-time staff don't normally cover part-timers, so they are borrowed “by analogy” and applied to another group → に準じて.

items.diff: にのっとって takes laws, rules or tradition as the yardstick; に基づいて takes data, materials or experience as the basis.

this.tr: We will deal with it fairly in accordance with the law.

that.tr: We improved the product based on the survey results.

items.explain: Check whether what comes before is a “norm” or “material”: a yardstick that must be followed, like laws, rules or tradition → にのっとって; material used to draw conclusions, like survey results, data or facts → に基づいて. に基づいて is used far more widely; にのっとって only appears in formal settings.

groups.note: Both come from the verb 「及ぶ（およぶ）」 — “to reach”

items.diff: に及んで means “the situation has already reached the point of…”; には及ばない means “it hasn't reached the point of needing…” ＝ there's no need.

this.tr: Only after the accident happened a third time did the company finally start investigating.

that.tr: It's just a mild cold, so there's no need to worry.

items.explain: 及ぶ ＝ to reach. Affirmative に及んで: things really have reached this point, often followed by 「ようやく」 or 「初めて」; negative には及ばない: things haven't reached that point, a polite way of saying “there's no need”. You can tell them apart by whether there's 「は」 and 「ない／ません」.

items.diff: に及んで says “only once it reached the point of…”; 言うに及ばず means “…goes without saying (and even…)”, where 及ばず ＝ no need.

this.tr: Only when there were victims did we first realize how serious the problem was.

that.tr: This song is popular overseas, not to mention in Japan.

items.explain: Both are 「及ぶ」: に及んで is affirmative — things have “reached” a certain point; the 「及ばず」 in 言うに及ばず is negative (＝ 及ばない), “no need to say”, followed by 「〜でも」 or 「〜も」 to add another layer. Check whether what comes before is 「言う」 or a situation, and whether 「も」 follows.

groups.note: Both mean “before…”

items.diff: に先駆けて means “ahead of others or other places”, taking the lead; に先立って means “do something first, before…” in time.

this.tr: We launched the new service ahead of other companies.

that.tr: Before the service launched, we held a briefing session.

items.explain: Look at who or what comes before: others or other places, like 「他社」, 「全国」 or 「世界」 → usually に先駆けて, stressing getting a step ahead of them; an event, like 「開始」, 「発売」 or 「会議」 → usually に先立って, saying something else is done before it. A way to remember: 先 ＋ 駆ける ＝ run out in front; 先 ＋ 立つ ＝ stand in front.

groups.note: Both mean “can't bring oneself to do it, psychologically”

items.diff: 見るに忍びない means too pitiful — you can't bear to look, with sympathy; 見るに堪えない means too poor or vulgar — you can't stand to watch, with disgust.

this.tr: The devastation in the disaster area is too painful to look at.

that.tr: That show is so vulgar it's unwatchable.

items.explain: Both mean “can't bear to look”; check what feeling the object stirs: pitiful, tragic scenes like a disaster area or an injured animal → 見るに忍びない, sympathy; poor-quality things like a vulgar show or clumsy writing → 見るに堪えない, criticism. Mixing them up can be very rude.

items.diff: がたい is a general “hard to…”, for any reason; に忍びない specifically means “can't bear to” out of sympathy or affection.

this.tr: I can't bear to throw away the stuffed toy I've treasured since I was a child.

that.tr: Both plans are good — it's hard to let either one go.

items.explain: Look at why you can't do it: you feel affection or pity for the thing or person and can't bring yourself to → に忍びない (after the dictionary form: 捨てる＋に忍びない); simply because both are good, or it's hard to judge or believe → がたい (after the masu-stem: 捨て＋がたい, 信じがたい).

groups.note: にして ↔ にしては, differing by just one 「は」

items.diff: にして means “only at… (finally)”; にしては means “for… (surprisingly)”.

this.tr: Only at sixty did he travel abroad for the first time.

that.tr: For a sixty-year-old, he looks very young.

items.explain: They differ by just one 「は」, so look at what follows: にして is often followed by 「初めて」 or 「ようやく」, saying something only happened at this age or attempt; にしては is followed by an evaluation that doesn't match the person's status or age (若く見える, 上手だ), expressing surprise.

groups.note: Each shares the meaning of one use of 「にして」 (only at… / both… and…)

items.diff: にして（初めて） follows nouns like an age or a number of times and is written; て初めて follows a verb te-form, saying you only understood after experiencing something.

this.tr: On my third attempt, I finally passed.

that.tr: Only after becoming a parent myself did I truly appreciate my parents.

items.explain: Check whether a noun or a verb comes before: a number of times or an age, like 「３度目の挑戦」 or 「40歳」 → にして, written, saying something was only achieved at this stage; an experience like 「親になる」 (verb te-form) → て初めて, usually followed by a realization like 「分かった」 or 「気づいた」.

items.diff: AにしてB is a written, concise “both A and B”; AでもありBでもある is the ordinary way to say it.

this.tr: He is both a doctor and a writer.

that.tr: He is a doctor as well as a writer.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: 「AにしてB」 is concise and common in writing and profiles (最初にして最後, 医者にして作家); 「AでもありBでもある」 is more common and can also express mixed feelings (うれしくもあり寂しくもある).

groups.note: Both mean “even…”, implying that the rest goes without saying

items.diff: The meaning is almost the same; にしてからが is more written, almost only follows people — specifically “the person who should know best”; からして can also follow things like a name or appearance.

this.tr: Even the principal doesn't follow the rules.

that.tr: This shop looks suspicious from its name alone.

items.explain: Look at the word in front: “people who should set an example”, like 校長, 社長 or リーダー → both work, but にしてからが is more written and sounds more like an accusation; things like 名前, 入口 or 態度, “from this alone…” → only からして.

items.diff: さえ cites “the person least likely to manage it”, for good or bad; にしてからが cites “the person who should do it best”, almost only in criticism.

this.tr: Even the experts don't understand this problem (let alone anyone else).

that.tr: Even a child can understand this problem.

items.explain: Look at what kind of person is cited: even “the least likely person”, like 子ども or 初心者, managed it → さえ (でさえ), for good or bad; even “the person who should do it best”, like 専門家 or 社長, failed → にしてからが, always followed by a negative judgment.

groups.note: Both mean “do something according to a certain standard or basis”

items.diff: に即して fits facts or the current situation, stressing not losing touch with reality; にのっとって follows rules or tradition, stressing not deviating from the norm.

this.tr: Review the plan in line with the actual situation.

that.tr: The ceremony was solemnly held according to ancient custom.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: actual circumstances like 「現実」, 「実態」, 「事実」 or 「状況」 → に即して, adjusting to reality; established norms like 「法律」, 「ルール」, 「古式」 or 「伝統」 → にのっとって, doing things by the rules.

items.diff: に基づいて takes data or materials as the basis and draws conclusions from them; に即して stresses staying close to the actual situation without losing touch with reality.

this.tr: We'll consider how to provide support in line with the actual local situation.

that.tr: We'll consider how to provide support based on the survey data.

items.explain: The second halves are the same; look at the noun in front: material used as a basis, like 「データ」, 「資料」 or 「経験」 → に基づいて; the actual situation at hand, like 「実情」, 「現実」 or 「状況」, stressing “stick close to it, no armchair theorizing” → に即して.

items.diff: に照らして means holding up laws or experience like a mirror and judging “against” them; に即して means handling things close to the facts and situation at hand.

this.tr: Make judgments based on the actual conditions on site.

that.tr: Make judgments in light of past experience.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a “standard” like laws, regulations or past experience, compared point by point with the matter at hand to see if it fits → に照らして; the actual situation at hand, like on-site conditions or reality, going along with it → に即して.

groups.note: Both come from 「堪（た）える」 — originally “to endure, to withstand”

items.diff: に堪えない means “can't withstand” → unbearable to look at, or a feeling too strong to contain (deeply…); に堪える means “can withstand” → worth it, holds up.

this.tr: This text is so full of typos it's unreadable.

that.tr: This book is old, but it's still well worth reading today.

items.explain: Check for 「ない」 at the end, then look at the evaluation in the first half: a flaw before it (誤字だらけで) → に堪えない, unreadable; a concession before it (古いが) and 「十分」 after → に堪える, worth reading. 「感謝に堪えない」 with an emotion noun works the same way: so grateful you can't contain it ＝ deeply grateful.

groups.note: Both mean “can't withstand” — can't bear to watch or listen, or can't hold back a feeling

items.diff: Both mean “just can't bear to listen to or watch it”; に堪えない is written and stiff, たものではない is more colloquial.

this.tr: His singing is so bad it's unbearable to listen to.

that.tr: His singing is so bad you just can't listen to it.

wrong.why: に堪えない attaches to the dictionary form, not the potential form

items.explain: Look at the verb form: に堪えない follows the dictionary form (聞く, 見る, 読む); たものではない follows the ta-form of the potential (聞けた, 見られた, 食べられた). The meaning is the same: reviews and essays use に堪えない, everyday complaints usually use たものではない. たものではない can also say 「食べられたものではない」, whereas に堪えない basically only attaches to 見る・聞く・読む.

items.diff: 見るに堪えない means so bad or disgusting you can't stand to watch; 見るに忍びない means so pitiful your heart can't bear to look.

this.tr: Drunks brawling is really unbearable to watch.

that.tr: The sight of the children in the disaster area is too painful to look at.

items.explain: Look at what you're seeing: embarrassing, vulgar or off-putting scenes (酔っ払いのけんか, 下品な番組) → に堪えない; pitiful, heartbreaking people or scenes (被災地の子どもたち) → に忍びない. 忍びない can also follow other verbs, meaning “can't bring oneself to do” (捨てるに忍びない).

items.diff: に堪えない is mostly used in speeches and letters to formally express one's own gratitude or regret; を禁じ得ない is mostly about feelings like sympathy or anger that well up involuntarily after seeing or hearing something.

this.tr: We are deeply grateful for everyone's support.

that.tag: Seeing or hearing → can't help it
that.tr: Hearing the victims' stories, I couldn't help feeling sympathy.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the clues before it (these are tendencies, not absolutes): に堪えない mostly appears in speeches and letters, after 「感謝、感激、遺憾」, formally conveying one's own feelings to the other party; を禁じ得ない is often preceded by 「〜を聞いて、〜を見て」, describing 「同情、驚き、怒り、涙」 welling up because of something, and is mostly used in written narration.

groups.note: Both come from 「堪（た）える」 — originally “to endure, to withstand”

items.diff: に堪える means “can withstand” → worth it, holds up; に堪えない means “can't withstand” → unbearable to look at, or a feeling too strong to contain (deeply…).

this.tr: This book is old, but it's still well worth reading today.

that.tr: This text is so full of typos it's unreadable.

items.explain: Check for 「ない」 at the end, then look at the evaluation in the first half: a concession before it (古いが) and 「十分」 after → に堪える, worth reading; a flaw before it (誤字だらけで) → に堪えない, unreadable. 「感謝に堪えない」 with an emotion noun works the same way: so grateful you can't contain it ＝ deeply grateful.

groups.note: Both mean “worth it, good enough”

items.diff: に堪える means “has reached a level that can withstand…”; に値する means “has the value of…”, judging in terms of worth.

this.tr: It's an amateur work, but it fully stands up to appreciation.

that.tr: This paper is worth reading.

items.explain: に堪える stresses “the level is high enough to hold up”, often preceded by a concession like 「素人だが」 or 「古いが」, and has limited collocations: 鑑賞に堪える, 読むに堪える, 使用に堪える, 批判に堪える; に値する judges whether something is worth it in terms of value, with a wide range of collocations: 注目, 称賛, 一読, 尊敬に値する, and no sense of “barely good enough”.

items.diff: に堪える means “withstands (scrutiny, use, appreciation)”; に足る means “meets the conditions, is enough to (be trusted, draw a conclusion)”.

this.tr: This data can withstand scrutiny by experts.

that.tr: This data is sufficient to draw a conclusion.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a test applied to it, like 「検証、批判、使用、鑑賞」 → に堪える, meaning “withstands”; something a person will do, like 「信頼する、満足する、結論を出す」 → に足る, meaning “meets the conditions, is enough to”. に足る is also common in the negative 「取るに足らない (not worth mentioning)」.

groups.note: Both are about “worth it or not” — good enough and worthwhile, or not worth it and unnecessary

items.diff: に足る means “qualified, enough to”, focusing on whether the conditions are met; に値する means “has that value”, focusing on whether it's worth it.

this.tr: He is a thoroughly trustworthy person.

that.tr: His brave actions deserve praise.

items.explain: The two are often interchangeable with words like 「信頼、尊敬」. に足る often goes with 「十分」 and usually modifies a noun (信頼に足る人物); its negative is 「取るに足らない (not worth mentioning)」. に値する usually follows evaluative nouns like 「称賛、注目、一読」, judging whether something is worthwhile.

items.diff: に足る means “meets the conditions, is enough to (be trusted, draw a conclusion)”; に堪える means “withstands (scrutiny, use, appreciation)”.

this.tr: This data is sufficient to draw a conclusion.

that.tr: This data can withstand scrutiny by experts.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: something a person will do, like 「信頼する、満足する、結論を出す」 → に足る, meaning “meets the conditions, is enough to”; a test applied to it, like 「検証、批判、使用、鑑賞」 → に堪える, meaning “withstands”.

items.diff: に足らない says the thing itself carries little weight and isn't worth mentioning; には当たらない says the matter is perfectly understandable, so there's no call for that reaction.

this.tr: Our opponent is still a beginner. Nothing to fear.

that.tr: With his ability, there'd be nothing surprising even if he won the title.

items.explain: Look at what the reason says: the thing itself is weak or insignificant (まだ初心者だ) → に足らない, common in 「取るに足らない」 and 「恐るるに足らず」; the matter is understandable and not surprising (彼ほどの実力なら) → には当たらない, usually after reactions like 驚く, 悲観する or 非難する.

groups.note: Both mean “based on…, according to…”

items.diff: に照らして means measuring against a standard to make a judgment; に基づいて means doing something on the basis of materials or facts.

this.tr: In light of the law, his actions were judged illegal.

that.tag: Using it as a base → producing something
that.tr: I wrote a report based on the survey results.

items.explain: Look at the verb in the second half: evaluations that “measure whether something conforms”, like 判断する, 処分する or 明らかだ → に照らして, usually after a “ruler” like 法律, 規則 or 常識; “producing something or taking action on this basis”, like 作成する, 計画する or 行動する → に基づいて, usually after データ, 調査 or 事実.

items.diff: に照らして means comparing and judging against a standard; に即して means acting in line with the actual situation, without losing touch with reality.

this.tr: In light of past experience, this plan probably won't work.

that.tr: We revised the plan in line with the actual situation on site.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front and the action after: に即して follows 「実情、現実、事実、状況」 and is followed by 「対応する、見直す、行う」, meaning the approach fits reality; に照らして follows a “ruler” like 「経験、法律、基準」 and is followed by 「考える、判断する」, meaning measuring with that ruler.

items.diff: に照らして means using rules as a ruler to judge right and wrong; にのっとって means taking rules or tradition as a model and following them.

this.tr: By the standards of common sense, that behavior is very strange.

that.tr: The ceremony was held according to ancient tradition.

items.explain: Look at the second half: にのっとって is followed by things done according to procedure or rules, like 「式を行う、試合をする、手続きを進める」, and preceded by 「伝統、ルール、手続き」; に照らして is followed by judgments like 「考える、判断する、おかしい」, using rules or common sense as a ruler for right and wrong.

groups.note: Both mean “not only… but also…”

items.diff: にとどまらず stresses going beyond a certain range and expanding to a larger one; のみならず just means “not only A, but B too”.

this.tr: Its impact was not limited to Japan but spread overseas too.

that.tr: He is active not only as a singer but also as an actor.

items.explain: Look at the second half: にとどまらず is often followed by 「〜にまで広がる／及ぶ」, with the scope of the same thing growing from small to large (国内 → 海外); のみならず just puts two items side by side (歌手, 俳優), with no sense of “expanding”, and can also start a sentence as a conjunction (のみならず、〜).

items.diff: With にとどまらず, the second part is an expansion of scope; with ばかりか, the second part is something else, even worse or more unexpected.

this.tr: The damage was not confined to the town center but reached the surrounding villages too.

that.tr: Not only did he not apologize, he actually got angry.

items.explain: Look at how the two parts relate: with にとどまらず, both parts are the scope of the same thing (町の中心部 → 周辺の村), saying the impact or activity doesn't stay within the original range; with ばかりか, the two parts are different things, the second even worse or more unexpected (doesn't apologize → actually gets angry), often paired with 「さえ、まで、逆に」.

items.diff: にとどまらず expands from A to a wider range; に限らず means “not just A — others too”, where A is just one example.

this.tr: This movement didn't stay in Tokyo but spread across the country.

that.tag: Static · A is just one example
that.tr: This shop is popular not just with young people but with the elderly too.

items.explain: Check whether the second half is dynamic or static: にとどまらず is usually followed by expanding verbs like 「広がる、及ぶ」, stressing growth outward from a starting point; に限らず is followed by static facts like 「〜にも人気がある、〜も同じだ」, saying “whether A or something else, it's all…”.

groups.note: Both come from 「当（あ）たる」 — originally “to hit, to match exactly”

items.diff: verb ＋ には当たらない means “doesn't warrant it” → there's no need to…; noun ＋ に当たる means “corresponds exactly” → is equivalent to.

this.tr: A mistake of this level is nothing to make a fuss about.

that.tr: One foot is equivalent to about 30 centimeters.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: verb dictionary form (驚く, 悲観する, 非難する) ＋ には当たらない → “the matter doesn't warrant that reaction” ＝ no need to…; a quantity or noun (30センチ, 兄) ＋ に当たる → “corresponds exactly” ＝ is equivalent to.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no need, it's not worth it”

items.diff: には当たらない judges that “this doesn't warrant that reaction”; には及ばない is usually a polite “no need to go to the trouble”.

this.tr: It's a common mistake, so there's no need to criticize.

that.tr: It was nothing at all, so there's no need to thank me.

items.explain: Look at the verb in front: には当たらない follows emotional or evaluative reactions like 「驚く、悲観する、非難する」; には及ばない follows things the other person would do for you, like 「来る、お礼、説明する」, often politely declining with 「〜には及びません」.

items.diff: には当たらない means “it's not that serious, so it doesn't warrant that reaction”; までもない means “it's obvious, so there's no need to bother doing it”.

this.tag: Not serious · doesn't warrant a reaction
this.tr: The result was as expected. There's no need to be surprised.

that.tag: Too obvious · no need to do it
that.tr: The result is obvious. There's no need to check.

items.explain: Look at the verb in front: までもない follows actions like 「言う、調べる、説明する、聞く」, the reason being “it's too obvious or too simple”; には当たらない follows reactions like 「驚く、悲観する、非難する」, the reason being “it's not that serious”. The mid-sentence form 「までもなく」 works the same way (言うまでもなく).

items.diff: には当たらない is a written, calm judgment that something “doesn't warrant…”; ことはない is a spoken way of directly telling someone “you don't need to…”.

this.tr: There's no reason to be pessimistic over a single failure.

that.tr: It's just one failure — no need to be so down about it.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting and tone: ことはない is advice given face to face, often ending with 「よ」; には当たらない is mostly seen in commentary and reports, calmly judging “it hasn't come to that”, and isn't really used to comfort the person in front of you.

items.diff: The meaning is the same — “it's not so bad that…”; には当たらない is somewhat written and usually follows reactions or judgments; ほどのことではない is common in everyday speech and can follow any action.

this.tr: It's just a scratch. There's no need to make a fuss.

that.tr: It's just a scratch. It's not worth making a fuss over.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting: には当たらない is mostly seen in commentary and reports, usually after reactions or judgments like 「驚く、悲観する、非難する、騒ぐ」; ほどのことではない is very common in everyday conversation and can follow any action (医者に行くほどのことではない, 謝るほどのことではない).

items.title: 〜に足らない (not worth)
items.diff: には当たらない says the matter is perfectly understandable, so there's no call for that reaction; に足らない says the thing itself carries little weight and isn't worth mentioning.

this.tr: With his ability, there'd be nothing surprising even if he won the title.

that.tr: Our opponent is still a beginner. Nothing to fear.

items.explain: Look at what the reason says: the matter is understandable and not surprising (彼ほどの実力なら) → には当たらない, usually after reactions like 驚く, 悲観する or 非難する; the thing itself is weak or insignificant (まだ初心者だ) → に足らない, common in 「取るに足らない」 and 「恐るるに足らず」.

groups.note: Both come from 「無理（むり）」 — originally “without reason (理が無い)”

items.diff: には無理がある means “there's something unreasonable in it” → far-fetched, doesn't hold up; のも無理はない means “it's not without reason” → perfectly understandable, no wonder.

this.tr: A plan to finish everything in three hours is a bit unrealistic.

that.tr: He was kept waiting a full three hours, so no wonder he's angry.

items.explain: 「無理」 literally means “no reason”. 無理がある says there's “something unreasonable” in it, used to criticize plans or claims as far-fetched; 無理はない negates that → it makes sense, used to sympathize with someone's reaction (怒る, 泣く). Look at what comes before: a plan, explanation or claim → には無理がある; a person's emotional reaction → のも無理はない.

groups.note: Both repeat the same word as 「AにA」, stressing “again and again, to the extreme”

items.diff: に〜を重ねて repeats a noun, stressing that the number of times keeps building up; 〜に〜た repeats a verb, stressing that the action was taken to the extreme.

this.tag: Noun · built up time after time
this.tr: Through effort upon effort, I finally made my dream come true.

that.tr: The long-awaited summer vacation has finally arrived.

items.explain: Look at the word being repeated: a noun (努力, 改良, 検討, 嘘) → AにAを重ねて, saying it builds up time after time; a verb masu-stem (待ち, 考え) → AにAた, saying the action was taken to the limit (waited and waited, thought and thought). 〜に〜て works the same way (考えに考えて決めた).

groups.note: Both come from 「至（いた）る」 — originally “to arrive at”

items.title: 〜に至る (eventually come to)
items.diff: の至り turns 「至る」 into a noun — a feeling “at its peak” ＝ utmost…; に至る means a situation eventually “reaches” a certain point.

this.tr: It is the greatest honor to receive such an award.

that.tr: After years of losses, the company eventually went bankrupt.

items.explain: Check whether 「の」 or 「に」 comes before 「至」: の至り follows emotion nouns like 「光栄、恐縮、感激」, saying a feeling has “reached its peak”, a formal set phrase in speeches; に至る follows the end point of a situation (倒産, 事故, 結論), saying things gradually “developed into” it. 「若気の至り」 refers to mistakes made out of youthful rashness taken to the extreme.

groups.note: Both mean “at the height of…, utmost…”

items.diff: の至り is used almost only in set phrases for thanks or apologies; の極み can also describe a state at its extreme, good or bad (贅沢の極み, 疲労の極み).

this.tr: It is the greatest honor to have you all gathered here.

that.tr: After working three days straight without sleep, I was utterly exhausted.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: emotions in speeches, like 「光栄、恐縮、感激」, work with both (光栄の極み is fine too); states taken to the extreme, like 「疲労、贅沢、無責任」, generally take の極み. の至り also has the set phrase 「若気の至り」, which can't be changed to の極み.

items.diff: の至り follows Sino-Japanese nouns and is a formal set phrase; 限りだ follows adjectives and directly states how you feel right now, less stiffly.

this.tr: It is the greatest honor to receive such an award.

that.tr: Seeing my former students doing so well makes me so happy.

wrong.why: の至り follows nouns; adjectives need 限りだ

items.explain: Look at the word in front: Sino-Japanese nouns like 「光栄、恐縮、感激」 ＋ の → の至り, mostly in speeches and letters; adjectives like 「うれしい、寂しい、心強い」 → 限りだ, usable in everyday writing too.

items.diff: の至り is the speaker formally expressing their own gratitude or contrition; 極まりない is mostly used to criticize other people or things as “extremely…”.

this.tr: I am terribly sorry for the trouble I have caused you.

that.tr: Breaking a promise and not even apologizing — that's incredibly rude.

items.explain: Look at who it's about: の至り is the speaker talking about their own feelings (恐縮, 光栄), to formally thank or apologize; 極まりない follows na-adjective stems like 「失礼、危険、不愉快」 and mostly criticizes others or things. The same goes for 極まる (失礼極まる).

groups.note: Both come from 「極（きわ）まる／極める」 — originally “to reach the very end”

items.diff: の極み is a noun meaning “the very end”, attached after noun ＋ の, for good or bad; 極まりない attaches directly to na-adjective stems and is almost always critical.

this.tr: It is the greatest honor to receive such an award.

that.tr: Showing up late without even calling — that's incredibly rude.

items.explain: 「極み」 is the noun form of 「極む」, so it needs 「の」 before it (光栄の極み, 疲労の極み), and works for both positive and negative things; 極まりない attaches directly to na-adjective stems like 失礼, 危険 or 不愉快 and is almost always used to criticize. The same goes for 極まる (失礼極まる).

groups.note: Both mean “at the height of…, utmost…”

items.diff: の極み can also describe a state at its extreme, good or bad (贅沢の極み, 疲労の極み); の至り is used almost only in set phrases for thanks or apologies.

this.tr: After working three days straight without sleep, I was utterly exhausted.

that.tr: It is the greatest honor to have you all gathered here.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: states taken to the extreme, like 「疲労、贅沢、無責任」, generally take の極み; emotions in speeches, like 「光栄、恐縮、感激」, work with both. の至り also has the set phrase 「若気の至り」, which can't be changed to の極み.

items.diff: の極み follows nouns and is formal and written; 限りだ follows adjectives and directly states how you feel right now.

this.tr: I am deeply moved by everyone's warm encouragement.

that.tr: Seeing my former students doing so well makes me so happy.

items.explain: Look at the word in front: a noun (感激, 光栄, 贅沢) ＋ の → の極み, somewhat written and solemn; an adjective (うれしい, 寂しい, 心強い) → 限りだ. To use an adjective with の極み, the standard way is to turn it into a noun first (うれしさの極み).

groups.note: Both come from 「やら」 (← classical 「にやあらむ」: “is it perhaps…”), with a sense of “hard to say”

items.diff: のやら〜のやら means “who knows whether… or…”; やら〜やら lists things: “…and… and so on”.

this.tag: Don't know if A or B
this.tr: I can't tell whether he's serious or joking.

that.tr: What with work and housework, I'm busy every day.

items.explain: Check for 「の」 and what follows: のやら〜のやら is often followed by 「分からない」 or 「はっきりしない」, and the two items are usually opposite possibilities (本気／冗談, 行く／行かない); やら〜やら is followed by 「で忙しい／大変だ」, listing several things piling on at once.

groups.note: Both mean “unclear, don't know”

items.diff: のやら〜のやら carries the speaker's confusion and dissatisfaction; かどうか is just a neutral “whether”.

this.tr: He won't give a straight answer on whether he's coming or not.

that.tr: We don't know yet whether he'll come.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's mood: のやら〜のやら states both the positive and the negative, with a dissatisfied “I can't figure him out, it's so frustrating”, mostly used to describe someone else being vague; かどうか just objectively says “whether” and works in any setting (〜かどうか確認する).

groups.note: Both express the doubt of “I wonder…”

items.diff: のやら／ものやら／ことやら are muttering to oneself, with helplessness or worry; のだろうか is a calm self-question, also used in writing to pose a question.

this.tr: Where on earth has my son gone?

this.tag: ものやら · don't know what to do
this.tr: What on earth should one say at a time like this?

this.tag: ことやら · worried about the future
this.tr: Who knows what will happen from here.

that.tr: Why do people work?

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: のだろうか is a calm self-question, often used in writing and speeches to pose a question (人はなぜ働くのだろうか); the のやら family is muttering about the situation at hand, with helplessness: のやら puzzles over what happened, ものやら doesn't know what to do (どう〜ばいいものやら), ことやら worries about the outcome (どうなることやら).

items.diff: のやら is muttering with helplessness or dissatisfaction; かな is a light self-question that can also be said to people nearby.

this.tr: Honestly, where has that guy gone?

that.tr: I wonder where Tanaka went.

items.explain: Look at the tone: のやら is often preceded by 「まったく、いったい」, complaining that someone is causing worry — muttered to oneself; かな is light and neutral, can be half-said to people nearby, and can also express a wish (早く来ないかな).

groups.note: Both mean “carry something through to the end, pull it off”

items.diff: おおせる means “finally succeed despite pursuit or obstacles”; きる means “do it completely, all the way to the end”.

this.tag: Escape pursuit · get away with it
this.tr: The criminal managed to escape the police pursuit.

that.tag: Keep the lead · to the end
that.tr: The front-runner held the lead all the way to the finish.

items.explain: Look at the clue before it: 逃げおおせる means escaping from pursuers without being caught (警察の追跡から); 逃げきる is often used in races, keeping the lead until the finish (ゴールまで). きる can follow many verbs to mean finishing (食べきる, 使いきる), with the negative きれない; おおせる only follows a few verbs like 逃げ・隠し・やり.

items.diff: 隠しおおせる stresses never being found out in the end, and is often used as “can't keep it hidden”; 隠し通す stresses the determination to keep hiding it from start to finish.

this.tr: Lies get found out someday. You can't hide them forever.

that.tr: He kept his illness hidden from his family until the very end.

items.explain: Check whether it's about the result or determination: おおせる says “succeeded in the end, wasn't found out”, so it often goes with negatives or rhetorical questions (隠しおおせるものではない, 逃げおおせると思うな); 通す says a person sticks with one course of action from start to finish (最後まで隠し通した, 意地を通す).

items.diff: おおせる means getting through obstacles and finally succeeding by sticking it out; てのける means pulling off something difficult brilliantly, with admiration.

this.tr: I carried the plan through to the end without anyone noticing.

that.tr: He performed that difficult operation with ease.

items.explain: Look at the adverbs and tone: おおせる is often preceded by 「誰にも気づかれずに、最後まで」, describing getting through obstacles and finally succeeding, commonly for escaping or hiding; てのける often goes with 「簡単に、平然と、見事に」, describing someone casually accomplishing something difficult, with admiration or surprise.

groups.note: Both mean “after a whole process, it finally ended up with a certain result”

items.diff: 始末だ ends the sentence and reproachfully says “in the end it actually came to this”; あげく is mid-sentence, linking the “process” and the “result”.

this.tr: My little brother did nothing but play, and in the end he actually dropped out of school.

that.tr: After agonizing for ages, I ended up going home without buying anything.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: 始末だ is itself the end of the sentence — after describing what happened, it lands directly on “this sorry state”, often together with 「ついには、とうとう」, with a stronger tone of reproach or resignation; あげく follows the “process” (迷ったあげく, 口論のあげく), and the result still has to be stated after it.

items.diff: 始末だ is only used for bad results, with dissatisfaction; 末に means “after a long… finally”, for good or bad results.

this.tr: He kept piling up debt, and in the end he even sold his house.

that.tr: After agonizing for days, I finally decided to study abroad.

items.explain: Look at whether the result is good or bad and the speaker's attitude: 始末だ is only used for troublesome outcomes, with a reproachful “it's disgraceful”; 末に can be followed by a good conclusion (留学を決めた, 完成した), and is neutral in tone.

items.title: 〜に至る (eventually come to)
items.diff: 始末だ is the speaker subjectively complaining “it actually came to this”; に至る objectively narrates how a situation eventually developed to a serious point.

this.tr: My son ran around carousing and in the end actually got himself arrested.

that.tr: That accident eventually resulted in many deaths.

items.explain: Look at who's speaking and where it's used: 始末だ is the speaker complaining about people or things around them, with a “it's disgraceful” feeling; に至る is common in news and reports, calmly narrating how things developed (死者を出すに至った), without personal emotion.

items.diff: 始末だ usually scolds others: “in the end they ended up like this”; 羽目になる usually says that you yourself were “forced into” an unlucky situation.

this.tr: My little brother kept slacking off at work and in the end actually got fired.

that.tr: I forgot my wallet and ended up having to borrow money from a friend.

items.explain: Look at the subject and tone: 始末だ is mostly used to scold others for disgraceful behavior (ついにクビになる始末だ), and is self-mocking when said about oneself; 羽目になる is mostly about oneself, “having to do something you didn't want to” for some reason (借りる, 謝る, 徹夜する), with a frustrated “just my luck”.

groups.note: Both mean “as soon as…, …”

items.diff: そばから means it happens over and over, and the effort is wasted; たとたん is a one-off, unexpected “the moment…”.

this.tr: No matter how much I tidy up, the kids mess it up again the moment I'm done.

that.tr: The moment I finished tidying my room, a friend came over.

items.explain: Check whether it's something that repeats and whether the second part “cancels out” the first: そばから says it's like this every time (いくら〜ても), with the second part undoing what was done, usually ending in the present tense, with resignation; たとたん is about one specific occasion, with the second part being an unexpected thing that happens right after, ending in the past tense.

items.diff: そばから means repeatedly “undone right after doing it”; や否や is written language: the moment one thing happens, the next action immediately follows.

this.tr: Maybe it's my age, but I forget things as soon as I learn them.

that.tr: As soon as the bell rang, the students dashed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Look at the second part: with そばから, it's something that undoes the previous effort (覚える → 忘れる), happening repeatedly, with resignation; with や否や, it's another action that follows immediately (飛び出した), a one-off, common in novels and reports. The shortened 「や」 works the same way (ベルが鳴るや).

groups.note: Both mean “meant to do something but didn't manage to”

items.title: 〜損ねる (failed to do)
items.diff: そびれる means missing the moment and not doing it at all; 損ねる can also mean trying but failing, botching it.

this.tag: Missed the moment · didn't say it
this.tr: I couldn't find the right moment to speak up, so I never got to thank them.

that.tr: My hand slipped and I failed to catch the ball.

items.explain: Look at why it didn't happen: そびれる is “the timing or mood wasn't right”, so the action never happened at all (言う, 聞く, 渡す), often with regret; 損ねる can be trying but failing (受け損ねる, 撃ち損ねる) or missing it (見損ねる, 乗り損ねる). Also, 寝そびれる (missing the moment to sleep, not being able to sleep) is unique to そびれる.

items.diff: そびれる means missing one particular chance; ずじまい means never doing it right up to the end, when it's all over.

this.tr: I was so busy I missed lunch.

that.tr: In the end, I never got to see Mt. Fuji the whole trip.

items.explain: Look at the time frame: そびれる is about missing one occasion (昼ご飯を食べそびれた), and there may be more chances later; ずじまい is often preceded by 「結局、とうとう」, saying the whole thing ended without it happening, with no more chances.

groups.note: Both mean “meant to do something but didn't manage to”

items.diff: 損ねる can also mean trying but failing, botching it; そびれる only means missing the moment and not doing it at all.

this.tr: My hand slipped and I failed to catch the ball.

that.tag: Missed the moment · didn't say it
that.tr: I couldn't find the right moment to speak up, so I never got to thank them.

items.explain: Look at why it didn't happen: 損ねる can be trying but failing (受け損ねる, 撃ち損ねる) or missing it (見損ねる, 乗り損ねる); そびれる is “the timing or mood wasn't right”, so the action never happened at all (言う, 聞く, 渡す), often with regret. 損なう works the same way (言い損なう); 損じる means “to do wrong” (書き損じる), which is different from そびれる.

items.diff: 損ねる means failing on one occasion; ずじまい means never doing it right up to the end, when it's all over.

this.tr: I overslept and missed my usual train.

that.tr: In the end, I never got to see Mt. Fuji the whole trip.

items.explain: Look at the time frame: 損ねる says it didn't work out one time (乗り損ねた), and you can still catch the next train; ずじまい is often preceded by 「結局、とうとう」, saying the whole thing ended without it happening, with no more chances.

groups.note: Both mean “there's no way to do it, unable to…”

items.diff: The meaning is the same — “there's no way to…”; すべがない follows the dictionary form and is more written; ようがない follows the masu-stem and is common in speech too.

this.tr: Since no records remain, there is no means of knowing what happened back then.

that.tr: Since no records remain, there's no way to know what happened back then.

wrong.why: ようがない attaches to the masu-stem (知り＋ようがない)

items.explain: Look at the form of the verb in front: すべがない follows the dictionary form (知る＋すべ); ようがない follows the masu-stem (知り＋よう). The meaning is the same: すべがない is more written, common in essays and news; ようがない is common in both speech and writing. 「なす術もない (at a complete loss)」 is a set phrase with すべ.

items.diff: すべがない means “can't find a means or way”; べくもない means “the conditions are too far off — it's simply impossible”.

this.tr: I don't have his contact details, so there's no way to confirm he's safe.

that.tr: On this salary, owning a home is out of the question.

items.explain: Look at the verb in front: すべがない follows things that need a means to accomplish, like 「確かめる、伝える、防ぐ」 — what's lacking is a method; べくもない usually follows 「望む、比べる、知る」, saying the conditions are too far off, so it's simply impossible. Both are very written.

groups.note: Both mean “even…” — citing an extreme example

items.diff: The meaning is almost the same; すら is more written and stronger in tone, and さえ also has the 「さえ〜ば (as long as)」 usage.

this.tr: He can't even write his own name.

that.tr: He can't even write his own name.

items.explain: The two sentences are interchangeable; the difference is register: すら is mostly written and stronger in tone; さえ is common in both speech and writing. Also, さえ can form 「さえ〜ば (as long as…)」, which すら can't.

items.diff: すら can follow all kinds of nouns; だに is only used in a few set phrases like 「微動だにしない」 and 「想像するだに」.

this.tr: He can't even write hiragana.

that.tr: No matter what was said to him, he didn't budge an inch.

items.explain: Look at the word in front: ordinary nouns (ひらがな, 水, 名前) → すら (さえ in speech); set collocations like 微動, 夢に or 想像する → だに — you generally don't say 「ひらがなだに」. When だに follows a verb, it can also mean “just… is enough to” (考えるだに恐ろしい).

items.title: 〜まで (even…)
items.diff: すら usually goes with negatives, citing “the bare minimum” that can't even be done; まで is mostly used in the affirmative, saying things extend to “an unexpected degree”.

this.tr: He can't even read hiragana.

that.tr: He can even read difficult kanji.

items.explain: Look at the example cited and the end of the sentence: すら cites the simplest, most basic thing (ひらがな), usually followed by a negative (読めない); まで cites the hardest, most unexpected thing (難しい漢字), usually followed by an affirmative (読める), meaning “he can even do this”.

items.diff: The meaning is the same — “even…”; すら (ですら) is written, だって is spoken.

this.tr: This is a problem that even experts can't solve.

that.tr: This is a problem even experts can't solve, you know.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting: すら／ですら is used in writing and formal settings; だって is for casual conversation, often ending with 「よ」. After a person as the subject, すら is often said as 「ですら」 (専門家ですら).

groups.note: Both mean “the second part changes in step with the first”

items.diff: た分だけ says “you get as much as you put in”, one share for one share; ば〜ほど expresses the trend “the more…, the more…”.

this.tag: Amount put in · one for one
this.tr: You improve exactly as much as you practice.

that.tr: The more you practice, the better you get.

items.explain: The two sentences are often interchangeable; look at the angle: た分だけ follows the verb ta-form and focuses on “the share already put in”, often used to encourage (努力した分だけ報われる) or to say “you have to make up for however much you…”; ば〜ほど repeats the same word (すればするほど, 高ければ高いほど), describing a trend where the degree rises along with it, and works with adjectives too.

items.diff: た分だけ follows the verb ta-form and mostly talks about personal effort and reward; に応じて follows a noun and adjusts according to circumstances or conditions, more objectively.

this.tr: You get paid as much as you work.

that.tr: Wages are paid according to hours worked.

items.explain: Look at the word in front: た分だけ follows a verb ta-form (働いた, 頑張った), saying “you get as much as you did”, with the speaker's feelings; に応じて follows a noun (時間, 成績, 収入, 要望), saying things are handled according to this standard, mostly used in rules and explanations.

groups.note: たことにする／たことになる ↔ ことにする／ことになる differ by just one 「た」, but the meanings are completely different

items.title: 〜ことにする (decide)
items.diff: ta-form ＋ ことにする means “treat something that didn't happen as if it did (or vice versa)”; dictionary form ＋ ことにする means “decide to do something in the future”.

this.tr: Let's just pretend this mistake never happened.

that.tr: Let's decide to report this mistake to the boss after all.

items.explain: Look at the form before ことにする: dictionary form (報告する, やめる) → deciding to do something in the future; ta-form or nakatta-form (なかった, 聞かなかった) → knowing it's not true but deliberately “setting it down” as already so, i.e. “let's just say…”. In both, にする means “deliberately decide”.

items.title: 〜ことになる (decided, arranged)
items.diff: ta-form ＋ ことになる means “counts as already… by calculation or rules”; dictionary form ＋ ことになる means “it has been decided, will…”.

this.tr: With this, I'll have earned all my credits.

that.tr: Starting next month, I'll be working at the Osaka branch.

items.explain: Look at the form before ことになる and the clues: ta-form, preceded by a summing-up like 「これで、つまり」 → by calculation or rules, “that amounts to already having…”; dictionary form, preceded by a future time like 「来月から」 → something has been decided or arranged. In both, になる means “it naturally turned out that way”, not decided by oneself.

groups.note: Both mean “it's not necessarily so in reality, but it's treated or counted as already…”

items.diff: たことにする means treating something as an established fact toward others; たつもり means pretending in one's own mind that it was done, usually to console oneself.

this.tr: I told my parents I'd stayed at a friend's place.

that.tr: I pretended I'd gone on a trip and saved that money instead.

items.explain: Look at who it's aimed at: たことにする sets a certain story as fact toward others (親には, 会社には), often to cover something up or bend the rules; たつもり is “treating it as done” in one's own mind, often followed by 「で＋another action」 (貯金した), describing one's own mindset without involving others.

items.diff: たことにする treats something as having happened (or not happened) in how it's handled; ふりをする means putting on an act on the spot for others to see.

this.tag: Agreed afterward · as if it didn't happen
this.tr: I'll pretend I didn't hear what you just said.

that.tag: Putting on an act on the spot
that.tr: My mom called me, but I pretended not to hear.

items.explain: Check whether it's handling things afterward or acting on the spot: with たことにする, both sides usually know the truth and just agree to “treat it as if it didn't happen” (聞かなかったことにする), often to bend the rules or keep a secret for someone; ふりをする means putting on an act in front of someone (聞こえないふり, 寝たふり), who may be fooled.

items.diff: たことになる means officially “counting as” something by rules or calculation; も同然 means the result isn't in yet, but it's practically “as good as…”.

this.tr: Regardless of how the remaining matches go, this means we've won the title.

that.tr: Our opponent in the final is weak. We've as good as won the title already.

items.explain: Check whether the result is already settled: たことになる means by rules or calculation the result is already established, often with 「これで、つまり」; も同然 means the result isn't in yet and just says “it's practically the same as…”, with the speaker's estimate or exaggeration.

groups.note: たなり ↔ るなり differ only in tense

items.diff: たなり means “after…, nothing more came of it”; るなり means “as soon as…, immediately…”.

this.tr: My son went into his room and hasn't come out since.

that.tr: As soon as my son entered his room, he collapsed onto the bed.

items.explain: Check whether 「なり」 is preceded by the ta-form or the dictionary form, then look at the second half: 入ったなり ＋ a negative (出てこない) → after that action nothing more happened, and the state continues; 入るなり ＋ another action that immediately follows (倒れ込んだ) → as soon as…, immediately….

groups.note: Both mean “after doing…, nothing more came of it”

items.title: 〜たきり (never… since)
items.diff: The meaning is the same; たきり is the most common modern Japanese expression, and たなり is written and slightly old-fashioned.

this.tr: My father went out this morning and still hasn't come back.

that.tr: My father went out this morning and still hasn't come back.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: たきり (たっきり in speech) is common in everyday use; たなり is mostly seen in novels and other written texts, slightly old-fashioned. Both are often followed by a negative (帰ってこない, 連絡がない).

groups.note: Both mean “have never… ever”

items.title: 〜たことがない (have never…)
items.diff: たためしがない scolds someone for “never once managing it”; たことがない just objectively says there's no such experience.

this.tr: He has never once been on time.

that.tr: He has never been late.

items.explain: Look at the speaker's attitude: たためしがない scolds someone, following something they should have done (間に合った, 勝った, 当たった), with a dissatisfied “he's hopeless”; たことがない just objectively states an experience and can be used to praise someone (遅れたことがない) or about oneself (富士山に登ったことがない).

items.diff: たためしがない is somewhat colloquial and complains about consistent behavior; 一度として〜ない is written and neutral, simply stressing “not even once”.

this.tr: Our team has never once beaten this opponent.

that.tr: Our team has not beaten this opponent a single time.

items.explain: Look at the register and the word in front: として〜ない is always preceded by 「一 ＋ counter」 (一度, 一人, 一日), is written, and works for any total negation (一人として来なかった); たためしがない follows the verb ta-form, is somewhat colloquial, and carries a resigned or complaining “honestly…”.

groups.note: Both mean “I did do it, but…”

items.diff: After たはいいが comes a new problem that arose from doing it; after たものの comes the fact that, having done it, you didn't follow through or it didn't meet expectations.

this.tr: I bought a guitar all right, but I have nowhere to put it.

that.tag: Did it → nothing came of it
that.tr: I did buy a guitar, but I've never played it even once.

items.explain: Look at the second half: after たはいいが comes a new problem that only arose because you “did it” (置く場所がない), with a tone of self-mockery or regret, very conversational; after たものの usually comes “didn't keep going / didn't live up to expectations” (一度も弾いていない), more written and objective.

items.diff: たはいいが means doing it led to a new problem; 〜ことは〜が means you did do it, but not properly or fully.

this.tr: I went to the party all right, but I didn't know a single person there, which was awkward.

that.tr: I did go to the party, but I came back right away.

items.explain: Look at the structure and the second half: ことは〜が repeats the same verb twice (行ったことは行ったが) and is followed by how it wasn't done fully (すぐ帰ってきた); after たはいいが comes a problem you ran into after going (知り合いがいなくて困った).

groups.note: ただ〜のみ ↔ ただ〜のみならず — the only difference is 「ならず」

items.diff: ただ〜のみ means “only, nothing but”; ただ〜のみならず means “not only… but also…”.

this.tr: All I can do now is pray that I pass.

that.tr: This problem is not only Japan's problem but the whole world's.

items.explain: Look at what follows のみ: if it's 「だ」 closing the sentence → only, nothing but; if it's 「ならず、」 with another half-sentence after it (世界全体の問題だ) → not only… but also. 「ならず」 means “not being”, so 「のみならず」 is “not just this”, which is why the meaning becomes “not only”.

groups.note: Both mean “only, nothing but…”

items.diff: The meaning is basically the same; ただ〜のみ is written and formal, ただ〜だけ is the spoken version.

this.tr: All I can do is pray.

that.tr: The only thing I can do is pray.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; look at the setting: のみ is used in speeches, writing and formal addresses and sounds solemn and determined; だけ is for everyday conversation. Putting 「ただ」 before のみ makes the two ends echo each other, giving a stronger exclusive tone.

items.diff: ただ〜のみ formally states there is nothing else, with determination or the calm of leaving it to fate; しかない means there's no other way and you have to settle for it, with a sense of resignation.

this.tr: I've done everything I can; all that's left is to wait.

that.tr: I missed the last train, so I'll just have to take a taxi home.

items.explain: Look at the situation before it: before ただ〜のみ there's usually “I've done everything I should”, and it says only this one thing is left (待つ, 祈る) — written and formal; before しかない there's usually a situation that leaves you no choice (終電を逃した), and it says “I have to do this” — common in speech.

items.diff: ただ〜のみ formally says “nothing but…”; までだ means “if worst comes to worst, I'll just… — no big deal”.

this.tr: Now all we can do is move forward.

that.tr: If I fail, I'll just do it over again, that's all.

items.explain: Look for a condition before it: までだ is often preceded by 「〜たら、〜なら」, meaning “if it doesn't work out, I'll simply…”, in a blunt, unbothered tone; ただ〜のみ has no such hypothesis and simply says “this is the only thing I can do now”. までのことだ works the same way.

groups.note: ただ〜のみ ↔ ただ〜のみならず — the only difference is the final 「ならず」

items.diff: ただ〜のみ means “only…”; ただ〜のみならず means “not merely…” — adding 「ならず」 flips the meaning.

this.tag: Not only · a wider scope follows
this.tr: This is not merely Japan's problem but a problem for the whole world.

that.tr: The only one I can trust is myself.

items.explain: First check whether 「ならず」 follows 「のみ」: ならず is classical for “is not”, so のみならず = not only. Then look at the structure: のみならず is always followed by a wider scope (世界全体), making the sentence “not only A, but B too…”; ただ〜のみ ends at 「のみだ」 and means “only this”.

groups.note: Both mean “not only… (but also)…”

items.diff: Same meaning; adding 「ただ」 strengthens the “not merely” emphasis and makes it more solemn.

this.tag: ただ＋のみならず · more emphatic
this.tr: This disease is not confined merely to the elderly; it is increasing among young people too.

that.tr: This disease is not confined to the elderly; it is increasing among young people too.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only by 「ただ」. ただ means “merely” and echoes のみならず, further stressing “by no means limited to the first item”; it's common in speeches and papers. のみならず without ただ is also written language but more widely used, and can even start a sentence as a conjunction (のみならず、…＝not only that, but…).

items.diff: ひとり〜のみならず is used only for problems that are “not just one person's or one country's”; ただ〜のみならず has a wider range and can also follow verbs and adjectives.

this.tr: Not only is he a good singer, he also writes his own songs.

that.tag: After one country · not just one party
that.tr: The declining birthrate is not merely Japan's problem but one shared by many developed countries.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: ひとり originally means “one alone” and is followed by a noun like a person, a country or a company, saying “this isn't just one party's problem”; to add actions or qualities, as in “not only sings well but also composes”, use ただ〜のみならず.

items.diff: Same meaning and structure; だけでなく is the everyday phrasing, ただ〜のみならず is the most formal written language.

this.tr: The results of this study can be applied not only to medicine but also to the field of engineering.

that.tr: Tanaka can speak not only English but also Chinese.

items.explain: The structure is the same: 「A＋だけでなく／のみならず、B＋も」. Look at the setting: in chats and everyday writing use だけでなく (in speech also だけじゃなく); ただ〜のみならず is only for formal settings like papers, speeches and addresses — saying 「ただ英語のみならず」 in everyday conversation sounds overblown.

groups.note: Both mean “it worked out, but brought other problems”

items.diff: たら〜たで is a general reflection: “even when it happens, that comes with its own problems”; たはいいが is about one specific thing that already happened: “I did it, but then…”.

this.tag: たら · having it has its own worries
this.tr: Without money you're in trouble, but once you have it, you have a whole new set of worries.
A small room is inconvenient, but a big one is a pain to clean.

that.tr: I bought a car all right, but parking fees are so expensive that I'm struggling.

items.explain: Look at the structure: たら〜たで and ば〜で repeat the same word twice (あったらあったで, 広ければ広いで), often after first saying “not having it / small is no good either”, meaning “there are worries either way”; with たはいいが the two halves are two different things, describing one specific experience: “doing it was fine in itself, but then a problem came up”.

groups.note: Both come from 「ところ（所）」 — a “situation” or point

items.title: 〜ところを (should have… but instead)
items.diff: 本来なら〜ところですが first says what should properly be done, then that you can't do it; 本来なら〜ところを is followed by what actually happened (usually the other person did it for you).

this.tr: Properly we should come to visit you, but unfortunately we really can't find the time this week.

that.tr: Properly we should have come to see you, yet you went to the trouble of coming here — we're truly grateful.

items.explain: The first halves are identical; look at what follows ところ: 「ところですが／ところだが」 first finishes stating “this is how it should be”, then turns to the reason you can't; 「ところを」 connects straight to the second half, which is what actually happened, contrary to what “should” have, often thanks or apologies to the other person like 「わざわざ〜いただき」.

groups.note: Both are counterfactual: “if… then… would have…” (but it didn't happen)

items.diff: 〜ば〜のに usually says a “good result” that should have come didn't, with regret; 〜たら〜ところだった usually says a “bad result” that almost came didn't, with relief.

this.tr: If I hadn't brought an umbrella, I'd have been soaked to the skin.

that.tr: If I'd brought an umbrella, I wouldn't have gotten wet (but I didn't).

items.explain: First think about the speaker's actual situation: didn't bring an umbrella and got wet → regret, “if only…”, use 〜ば〜のに; brought one and stayed dry → relief, “if not for…, it would have been bad”, use 〜たら〜ところだった. Then look at the end of the sentence: 「のに」 carries complaint and regret, 「ところだった」 carries relief.

groups.note: たりとも ↔ なりとも — just one kana apart

items.diff: たりとも means “not even a little”, followed by a negative; なりとも means “even just a little”, followed by a wish.

this.tr: I have never missed practice, not even for a single day.

that.tr: I'd like to be of help, even if only a little.

items.explain: Only た／な differs. Look at the end of the sentence: たりとも is always followed by a negative or prohibition (休んだことはない, 許さない); なりとも by a wish or request (〜たい, 〜てください). Then look before it: たりとも is almost always preceded by “one ＋ counter”, while なりとも is usually preceded by words for small amounts like 「少し」「多少」「一目」.

groups.note: Both can follow “one ＋ counter”, meaning “not even a single…”

items.diff: 一人として〜ない is more objective, usually describing the fact that “there wasn't a single one”; 一人たりとも〜ない is categorical, mostly used for prohibitions and resolve.

this.tr: Not a single person is to be let in.

that.tr: Not a single person was opposed.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: prohibitions and resolve like 「〜てはならない」「〜わけにはいかない」「許さない」 → たりとも is most typical; sentences describing facts like 「いなかった」「なかった」 → として is more common, often together with 「誰一人」「何一つ」.

items.title: 〜も (not even one…)
items.diff: 一円も〜ない is the everyday phrasing; 一円たりとも〜ない means the same but is more written and more resolute.

this.tr: Not a single yen of tax money must be wasted.

that.tr: There isn't a single yen in my wallet.

items.explain: Both mean “not even one”; look at the tone and setting: 一円も and 一人も are everyday phrasing, fine anywhere; たりとも is formal written language, often followed by 「〜てはならない」「〜わけにはいかない」, expressing a strong prohibition or resolve — saying 「一円たりとも入っていない」 in casual talk sounds exaggerated.

items.title: 〜といえども (one ＋ counter)
items.diff: 一円たりとも can only be followed by a negative or prohibition; 一円といえども means “even if it's only one yen” and can also be followed by a positive judgment.

this.tr: Not a single yen can be wasted.

that.tag: Even if only… · can be positive
that.tr: It may be only one yen, but it's still precious tax money.

wrong.why: たりとも must be followed by a negative or prohibition

items.explain: After “one ＋ counter” the two are close in meaning; look at the second half: たりとも can only be followed by a negative or prohibition (無駄にできない); といえども originally means “even though it is…” and can be followed by a negative (一円といえども無駄にはできない) or by a positive judgment like “it's still important”.

groups.note: Both come from たる, the attributive form of the classical 「たり」 — equivalent to modern 「である」

items.diff: たる modifies a noun: “one who is… (ought to…)”; たるや raises a topic: “as for its…, it's astonishing”.

this.tr: Anyone who is a teacher should set an example for students.

that.tr: As for its sheer power, it was beyond words.

items.explain: たる＝である, so 「教師たる者」 is just 「教師である者」, followed by “ought to…”; たるや＝たる＋the exclamatory 「や」, raising the preceding noun as a topic, followed by amazement. Look at what follows: 「者」「べきだ」 → たる; a pause right after the noun followed by an exclamation (言葉では言い表せない, すさまじい) → たるや.

groups.note: Both talk in terms of “status”: as a… (such a person)

items.diff: として just objectively says “in the capacity of…”; たる is preachy: “since one is…, one ought to…”.

this.tr: Anyone who is a doctor ought to put patients' lives first.

that.tr: He works as a doctor at a regional hospital.

items.explain: Look at the second half: simply describing doing something in a certain capacity, like 「働いている」 → として; duties that come with the status, like 「〜べきだ」「〜なければならない」, with a preachy tone → たる. Also, たる only follows weighty roles like teacher, doctor or politician, and is usually followed by 「者」.

items.diff: たる者は is followed by the duties that come with the status; ともあろう者が is followed by behavior unworthy of the status, meaning “of all people, to actually…”.

this.tr: A police officer ought to obey the law.

that.tr: A police officer, of all people, breaking the law!

items.explain: Look at the second half: talking about the duties that come with a status (〜べきだ, 〜なければならない) → たる, often as 「たる者は」; expressing shock or condemnation at a scandal that already happened and is unworthy of the status (〜とは, 〜なんて) → ともあろう, often as 「ともあろう者が」.

groups.note: Both come from たる, the attributive form of the classical 「たり」 — equivalent to modern 「である」

items.diff: たるや raises a topic: “as for its…, it's astonishing”; たる modifies a noun: “one who is… (ought to…)”.

this.tr: As for its sheer power, it was beyond words.

that.tr: Anyone who is a teacher should set an example for students.

items.explain: たる＝である, so 「教師たる者」 is just 「教師である者」; たるや＝たる＋the exclamatory 「や」, raising a noun as the topic. Look at what follows: a pause right after the noun, then an exclamation → たるや; 「者」「べきだ」, talking about status and duty → たる.

groups.note: Both raise something as a topic and then give a strong evaluation

items.diff: Almost the same meaning; たるや is written language, more exaggerated and formal; といったら is spoken, and at the end of a sentence can shrink to 「〜といったらない」.

this.tr: As for the beauty of Mt. Fuji, it left me speechless.

that.tr: Talk about how beautiful Mt. Fuji is — words just can't describe it.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the register: たるや is written language with an exaggerated solemnity, common in reports, reviews and novels; といったら is also common in everyday conversation (the 「よ」 at the end is a chatty tone), and can shrink to 「〜といったらない」 (寒いといったらない).

items.diff: ときたら is mostly used to complain about people and things around you; たるや mostly expresses amazement, and is written language.

this.tr: As for the new product's popularity, it sold out on the very first day.

that.tr: As for my son, all he does every day is play video games.

items.explain: Look at the evaluation that follows and the setting: ときたら is spoken, usually raises people close to you (うちの息子, 部長), and is followed by dissatisfaction or blame; たるや is written, usually raises a degree of something (人気, 迫力, 美しさ), and is followed by amazement.

groups.note: Both come from 「いただく（頂く）」 — originally “to hold above one's head”, i.e. to receive respectfully

items.diff: ていただけるとありがたい doesn't ask a question, it just says “I'd be grateful if you could…”; ていただけませんか asks directly and waits for an answer.

this.tag: Stated as a feeling · no pressure
this.tr: I'd be grateful if you could send me the materials by next week.

that.tr: Could you send me the materials by next week?

items.explain: いただける＝“be able to receive the favor of…”. Check whether the sentence ends as a question: 「〜ませんか」 asks whether the other person can, and they have to answer yes or no; 「〜とありがたいです」 turns the request into your own feeling without pressing them to commit, which is more common in emails and with clients — business emails often use 「〜いただけますと幸いです」 instead.

groups.note: Both express “I'd like you to…”

items.diff: ていただけるとありがたい spells out “I'd be grateful”, so it's clearer; ばと思います doesn't even mention gratitude and is more reserved.

this.tr: I'd be grateful if you could check the materials.

that.tr: I was hoping you could check the materials.

items.explain: Both are very polite requests, at about the same level. Look at how the sentence ends: 「ありがたいです」「助かります」 state your own feeling and are common in speech too; 「ばと思います」 only says “I hope…”, leaving the result completely unsaid, and is common in business emails and formal remarks.

items.diff: てほしい states your wish directly and sounds rude to a superior or client; ていただけるとありがたい is the polite way to ask someone above you.

this.tr: Sir, I'd be grateful if you could look over this document.

that.tr: Tanaka, I'd like you to look over this document.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to: to a colleague or friend you can say 「〜てほしいんだけど」; to a superior or client, saying 「〜てほしいです」 puts your own demand up front and is rude — switch to 「〜ていただけるとありがたいのですが」. 「〜てもらいたい」 is the same as てほしい.

groups.note: Both mean “ever since a certain time, (continuously)…”

items.diff: てからというもの stresses that life changed greatly since then, with deep feeling; て以来 just objectively says “ever since then, …”.

this.tr: Ever since I got a dog, every day has been incredibly fun.

that.tr: Since joining the company, I haven't taken a single day off.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a heartfelt “since then I / my life have completely changed” (毎日が楽しくてたまらない, すっかり変わった) → てからというもの, with a fairly literary flavor; a plain continuation like 「一度も〜ない」「ずっと〜ている」 → て以来.

items.title: 〜てから (ever since…)
items.diff: てから just plainly says “since…”; てからというもの is written language, stressing that ever since then things have stayed greatly changed.

this.tr: Ever since our child was born, my husband has come home early every day.

that.tr: It's already been three years since I came to Japan.

items.explain: てから can be followed simply by how much time has passed (３年になる) or by a one-off event; てからというもの must be followed by a new state that has continued ever since (毎日早く帰ってくる), with a feeling of “what a change”, and isn't used to say “it's been three years”.

items.diff: というもの follows a stretch of time like 「この一年」; てからというもの follows a verb て-form and means “ever since a certain event”.

this.tr: Ever since moving here, I've been sleeping well.

that.tr: This whole past year, I've hardly taken any time off.

items.explain: Both stress “throughout this whole period…”; look at what comes before: a time period like 「この一年」「ここ数か月」 → add というもの directly; an event (引っ越してくる, 結婚する) → use て-form ＋ からというもの, meaning since that event.

groups.note: Both mean “even if…, it's fine”

items.title: 〜てもかまわない (concession)
items.diff: てもかまわない just says “that would be fine”; てもともと also gives a reason: you weren't counting on it anyway, so failing costs nothing — “might as well try”.

this.tag: Nothing to lose → give it a try
this.tr: I've got nothing to lose if they say no — let's take the plunge and ask.

that.tr: I don't mind being turned down; I at least want to get my feelings across.

items.explain: Look at the second half: てもともと means “if it fails, I'm just back where I started”, and is almost always followed by something encouraging action like “let's try” (in speech, 「だめもとで〜」); てもかまわない just means you can accept that outcome, and is followed by what the speaker really cares about — it can also give permission (ここに座ってもかまいません).

groups.note: Both mean “it's only worth something if…”

items.diff: てこそ is standard language and must be followed by a result like “then it has value”; てなんぼ has a Kansai colloquial flavor, is itself the conclusion, and ends the sentence on its own.

this.tr: Tools are only worth anything if you use them.

that.tr: Only when tools are used do they have value.

items.explain: Check whether the result is spelled out afterward: てこそ is followed by 「価値がある」「意味がある」「〜と言える」; てなんぼ already carries the meaning “only then is it worth it” and just takes 「だ」 to end the sentence — blunt, with a Kansai feel; in formal writing use てこそ.

groups.note: Both express relief or gladness about an outcome

items.diff: てよかった is the most general, usually about yourself; て何よりだ is more formal, mostly used to express gladness about the other person's situation.

this.tr: It's wonderful to see you looking so well.

that.tr: I'm really glad I joined this company.

items.explain: Look at whose situation it is: your own experience or choice (この会社に入って) → てよかった is most natural; gladness about the other person's safety, health or circumstances (お元気そうで, ご無事で) → 何よりです, a set phrase in greetings and letters. て何よりだ is the evaluation “this matters more than anything”, and sounds more formal than てよかった.

items.diff: だけましだ means “at least…, better than worse”, while still fretting over the loss; て何よりだ means “this matters more than anything”, with genuine relief.

this.tr: The car got wrecked, but nobody was hurt, and that's what matters most.

that.tr: The car got wrecked, but at least nobody was hurt.

items.explain: Both are “a blessing in disguise”; look at where the speaker's focus is: だけましだ means “a little better than a worse outcome”, still thinking about the loss, consoling oneself; 何よりだ means “this matters more than anything”, making light of the loss with genuine relief, and is often used to show concern for or comfort others (ご無事で何よりです).

groups.note: Both explain the reason for an action or phenomenon

items.diff: 〜のは〜からだ gives a reason in general; 〜てのことだ stresses the intention or consideration behind an action, and is often used to explain or defend someone.

this.tr: Your dad is strict with you because he's thinking of your future.

that.tr: The train was late because there was an accident.

items.explain: Look at what the reason is: objective causes like accidents or weather → 〜からだ; a person's feelings like “thinking of you”, “worry” or “hopes” → 〜てのことだ, usually preceded by 「思って」「考えて」「心配して」, meaning “there was a good intention behind what he did”.

groups.note: Both mean accomplishing a (difficult) task

items.diff: 抜く is gritting your teeth and sticking it out to the end; てのける is doing it neatly and effortlessly.

this.tr: He performed that difficult surgery with the greatest of ease.

that.tr: He never gave up and ran the full marathon to the end.

items.explain: Look at the adverbs: 「いとも簡単に」「見事に」「あっさり」 → てのける, stressing ease and flair; 「最後まで」「諦めず」 → 抜く, stressing a hard process and seeing it through. The connection differs too: 抜く follows the ます-stem (走り抜く), てのける follows the て-form, most often as 「やってのける」.

items.diff: おおせる means “managed to keep it hidden / get away to the very end”, focused on persisting over a long time until success; てのける focuses on doing something boldly and nonchalantly in one go.

this.tr: He told a lie without batting an eye.

that.tr: He kept that secret for a full ten years without it ever coming out.

items.explain: Look at the time span and the verb: おおせる is used for things you have to hide or escape from for a long time (隠しおおせる, 逃げおおせる), meaning “in the end, not found out / not caught”; the negative 「〜おおせない」 is also common. てのける is about a single act or statement done boldly and neatly (平然と言ってのける).

groups.note: Both mean “ought to…, should…”

items.diff: べきだ is the general “should”, and can be used to give advice; てしかるべきだ is more written, stressing “it's only right by reason”, often with dissatisfaction at the current state of things.

this.tag: Only right · unhappy with the status quo
this.tr: His achievements deserve to be valued more highly.

that.tr: If you're tired, you should go to bed early tonight.

items.explain: Look at what's being said: advising someone (早く寝るべきだ) → べきだ; commenting that a person or organization “hasn't received the treatment they deserved” → てしかるべきだ, usually preceded by a passive form or 「あって」 (評価されて, 認められて, 謝罪があって); it isn't used for everyday advice.

groups.note: Both come from 「たまる（堪る）」 — “to endure, to bear”

items.diff: てたまるか is a rhetorical question, “can I put up with this?”, meaning “I absolutely won't allow it”; てたまらない means “so… I can't stand it”, expressing a strong feeling.

this.tr: No way am I losing in a place like this!

that.tr: I lost the match, and I'm so frustrated I can't stand it.

items.explain: たまる＝to bear. たまらない (can't bear) → “so… I can't stand it”, preceded by a feeling or sensation (悔しくて, うれしくて); たまるか is the rhetorical “can I bear it?” ＝ absolutely not, preceded by something you don't want to happen (負けて, だまされて). Look at the ending: 「ない」 describes a feeling, 「か」 declares resolve.

groups.note: Both express a strong refusal: “never…”

items.diff: ものか is preceded by your own action: “I'll never…”; てたまるか is usually preceded by something you don't want to befall you: “I won't let…”, and is more heated.

this.tr: No way am I letting a guy like that look down on me!

that.tr: I'm never going to that shop again!

items.explain: Look at the verb before it: an action you decide whether to do (行く, 許す) → ものか (spoken もんか), meaning “I'll never…”; a passive form or an outcome you don't want (馬鹿にされる, 負ける) → てたまるか, meaning “I can't let this happen”, with anger and fighting spirit.

items.title: 〜まい (will never…)
items.diff: まい is a calm, written resolve not to do something; てたまるか is blurted-out speech, full of emotion.

this.tr: No way am I giving up here!

that.tr: I made up my mind that I would not give up here.

items.explain: Look at the tone and setting: まい is written language, mostly found in calm narration like 「〜まいと決めた」「〜まいと思う」; てたまるか is blurted-out speech, often as heated as an exclamation mark, used to psych yourself up or show anger.

groups.note: Both mean “without hesitation, not caring”
