items.diff: もかまわず follows a noun and means “doing something without regard to (people watching, one's surroundings)”; てはばからない follows verbs of speaking and means “openly saying what others wouldn't dare”.

this.tr: He openly declares that he is the true genius.

that.tr: She cried out loud, without caring who was watching.

items.explain: Look at the structure: もかまわず is preceded by what's being ignored (人目, 雨, 周りの迷惑), with the action coming after; てはばからない is preceded directly by the action, usually a speaking verb like 「公言する」「断言する」「言う」, describing someone who speaks with no restraint, often with criticism or surprise.

groups.note: Both can mean “I can't stand…”

items.diff: てたまらない describes your own sensation or feeling being extremely strong; てはかなわない means “if this keeps up, I can't take it”, complaining about a situation.

this.tr: It's this hot every day — I can't take it.

that.tr: I'm so hot I can't stand it — I really want some cold water.

items.explain: Both talk about “heat”; look at the speaker's focus: てたまらない describes a physical or emotional feeling right now at its extreme (暑くて, 眠くて, and also good things like 「うれしくて」); てはかなわない complains “this situation can't go on”, often with 「こう」「毎日」「こんなに」, and only for unpleasant things.

groups.note: Both express a strong, uncontrollable feeling

items.diff: てならない is a feeling that wells up involuntarily, usually worry or anxiety; てやまない is a long-held, earnest wish or admiration, mostly used in speeches and writing.

this.tr: I sincerely wish you all good health and every success.

that.tr: I can't help worrying about my daughter, who's studying abroad.

items.explain: Look at the preceding word and the setting: てやまない is usually preceded by 「願う」「祈る」「期待する」「愛する」, expressing a lasting, earnest wish, common in speeches and letters; てならない is usually preceded by 「心配」「気になる」「〜気がする」, expressing an emotion you can't hold back, and is fine in everyday use too.

items.diff: てたまらない is more colloquial, for physical sensations or a strong passing feeling; てやまない is written language, only for lasting feelings like wishes and admiration.

this.tr: He is a mentor I have always deeply admired.

that.tr: I didn't sleep last night, so I'm unbearably sleepy.

wrong.why: てやまない doesn't go with physical sensations

items.explain: Look at what comes before: physical sensations like 眠い, 暑い, お腹がすいた, or passing emotions like 「うれしい」 → てたまらない; lasting feelings like 「尊敬する」「愛する」「願う」 → てやまない, which also often modifies a noun (尊敬してやまない恩師).

groups.note: Both mean “since…, (then)…”

items.diff: 以上は is about principle and responsibility: since…, one ought to…; 手前 is about saving face: having said it (or in front of others), you can't back out.

this.tr: Having made a promise in front of everyone, I can't very well quit now.

that.tr: Since we've signed the contract, we should take responsibility and see it through.

items.explain: Look at the nature of the reason: 以上は is grounded in principle, contracts or responsibility, and is often followed by 「〜べきだ」「〜なければならない」; 手前 is grounded in things you've said or done while others were watching, usually followed by 「〜わけにはいかない」, with an awkward feeling of being stuck. からには works basically the same as 以上は.

groups.note: Both warn that “doing that will lead to a bad result”

items.title: 〜ては (hypothesis → bad result)
items.diff: ては points out a bad result fairly calmly; ても知らない is emotional, a sulky warning of “if something happens, don't come to me”.

this.tr: Eat that much and get fat — don't say I didn't warn you.

that.tr: If you eat that much, you'll get fat.

items.explain: Both warn that “eating too much will make you fat”. Look at how the sentence ends: ては is followed directly by the result (太るよ), an objective warning; ても知らない puts the bad result before ても and ends with the speaker's “not my problem” attitude, often used when someone won't listen and you're a little annoyed.

groups.note: Both mean “added to that…” as a factor

items.diff: に加えて just adds two things together; と相まって stresses that two factors interact to produce a stronger effect.

this.tr: Set off by the beautiful scenery, the food tasted all the more delicious.

that.tr: On top of the rain, the wind has gotten stronger too.

items.explain: Look at the result: after に加えて there's just “one more thing” (風も強い), the two being independent; after と相まって comes the “even more…” effect of the two combined (いっそう, ますます, 〜効果を生む), with a strong written flavor.

items.diff: こともあって just lightly mentions one of the reasons; も相まって stresses that this factor combined with others to make the result more pronounced.

this.tr: With the long weekend and the fine weather on top of it, the tourist spots were packed.

that.tag: After a clause · one of the reasons
that.tr: Partly because the weather was nice, the tourist spots were packed.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: も相まって follows a noun (好天も相まって), implying another factor (連休) is also at work, with a strong written flavor; こともあって follows a clause (天気がよかったこともあって), just giving one reason, fine in both speech and writing.

groups.note: All come from 「と＋ある」 — “it being the case that…”

items.diff: とあれば means “if it's for…, (I'm willing to)…”; とあって means “because it's…”; とあっては means “since it's…, there's no choice but to…”.

this.tr: If it's for my children, I'll gladly endure any hardship.

that.tr: Because it was a long weekend, the holiday spots were crowded everywhere.

that.tag: とあっては · no choice but
that.tr: Since it's the president's order, I have no choice but to obey.

items.explain: All three are 「と＋ある」: the conditional form of ある, あれば → “if it's…”; the て-form あって → “because it's…”; あっては → “if it's… (there's nothing to be done)”. Look at the second half: willing resolve → とあれば; an objective scene that has already appeared → とあって; being forced, no choice (〜しかない, 〜わけにはいかない) → とあっては.

groups.note: Both express a hypothesis: “if it's…”

items.diff: なら is the most ordinary hypothesis; とあれば implies the first part is an especially important reason, usually followed by “I'd do anything for it”, in a formal tone.

this.tr: If it's what our customer wishes, we'll handle it even in the middle of the night.

that.tr: If you're going to the station, this road is shorter.

items.explain: Look at both halves: なら can follow any topic and is usually followed by advice or a judgment (この道が近い); とあれば is preceded by a special reason like 「〜のため」「ご希望」「必要」 and followed by a resolve to spare no effort (夜中でも対応する, どんなことでもする).

items.diff: となれば means “if it really comes to that, then…”, usually followed by a guess or judgment; とあれば means “if it's for…, I'm willing to…”, followed by the speaker's resolve.

this.tr: If it's for my child, I don't mind taking time off work.

that.tr: If you really go study abroad, it'll probably cost quite a lot.

items.explain: Look at the second half: となれば／となると is usually followed by a guess or judgment like “then it'll probably…” (費用がかかるだろう); とあれば is followed by the speaker's resolve to “be willing to…” for the sake of the first part (いとわない, 何でもする).

groups.note: All come from 「と＋ある」 — “it being the case that…”

items.diff: とあって means “because it's…”; とあっては means “since it's…, there's no choice but to…”; とあれば means “if it's for…, (I'm willing to)…”.

this.tr: Because it was a long weekend, the holiday spots were crowded everywhere.

this.tag: とあっては · no choice but
this.tr: Since it's the president's order, I have no choice but to obey.

that.tr: If it's for my children, I'll gladly endure any hardship.

items.explain: All three are 「と＋ある」: the て-form あって → “because it's…”; あっては → “if it's… (there's nothing to be done)”; the conditional form あれば → “if it's…”. Look at the second half: an objective scene that has already appeared → とあって; being forced, no choice (〜しかない) → とあっては; willing resolve → とあれば.

groups.note: Both express a reason: “because it's…, so…”

items.diff: とあって just states the result brought about by special circumstances; だけあって means “as you'd expect from…”, with praise.

this.tr: Because it's a famous restaurant, a long line had formed even before it opened.

that.tr: As you'd expect from a famous restaurant, the food really is delicious.

items.explain: Look at the second half: after とあって comes an objective scene caused by the special circumstances (行列ができていた, 混んでいた), common in news reports; after だけあって comes an evaluation — it lives up to its name (さすがにおいしい), often used with 「さすが」.

items.diff: とあって stresses that the first part is an unusual, special circumstance; こともあって just gives one of the reasons, for ordinary situations.

this.tr: Because a popular singer was coming, the venue was overflowing with young people.

that.tr: Partly because it was raining, the venue wasn't crowded.

items.explain: Check whether the first part is “something special”: an unusual situation like a star coming, a long weekend or a limited release → とあって, followed by a description of the resulting scene; an ordinary reason like rain or feeling unwell, implying there are other reasons too → こともあって.

groups.note: Both come from 「ばかり」 expressing degree — “almost to the point of…”

items.diff: とばかりに follows an unspoken line, meaning “as if to say…”; んばかりに follows a verb, meaning “almost about to…”.

this.tr: The clerk started turning off the shop lights, as if to say “hurry up and leave.”

that.tr: She begged him, practically in tears.

items.explain: Here ばかり means “almost to the extent of…”. Look at what comes before: a verb's ない-form with ない dropped ＋ ん (泣か＋んばかり) → almost about to do that action; a line (早く帰れ, 待ってました) ＋ と → an attitude so obvious it's as if saying that line. 「と言わんばかりに」 is just 言う＋んばかり, and means the same as とばかりに.

groups.note: Both mean “just as if…”

items.diff: かのように is a general comparison and can follow all kinds of situations; とばかりに specifically “reads” an unspoken line from someone's attitude or actions.

this.tr: The dog wagged its tail and dashed out, as if to say “I've been waiting for this!”

that.tr: He was smiling calmly, as if nothing had happened.

items.explain: Check whether what comes before と is a “line”: before とばかりに is what the other person seems to want to say (待ってました, ここぞ, 帰れ), used to describe someone's actions and demeanor; before かのように is a situation that isn't actually true (何もなかった), simply making a comparison.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 plus a contrastive ending — “although it's said to be…”

items.diff: とはいえ is widely used, in both writing and speech, and can even start a sentence; といえども is more classical and usually stresses “even… is no exception”.

this.tr: Even children must follow the rules.

that.tr: Although it's spring, mornings and evenings are still cold.

items.explain: Look at the second half: といえども is often followed by a principle like 「〜なければならない」「〜べきだ」, stressing “no matter how special one's status, no exception”, common in law and speeches, often paired with 「いかに」「たとえ」; とはいえ is mostly used to acknowledge a fact and then add “but in reality…”, is fine in everyday use, and can stand alone at the start of a sentence (とはいえ、…).

items.diff: といえども is written language for “even… (is no exception)”; といっても means “although it's…, it's actually not that…”.

this.tr: Even teachers make mistakes sometimes.

that.tr: He may be a teacher, but he's actually just out of university.

items.explain: Look at the second half: saying “however special the status, it's the same” (間違うことはある, ルールは守るべきだ) → といえども, with a strong literary flavor; downplaying the impression (まだ…たばかりだ, 簡単なものだけ) → といっても, which is spoken.

groups.note: Both mean “even…, still…”

items.diff: とて usually follows a noun for a person and carries emotion (“I too…”); といえども is more objective and formal, usually about principles.

this.tr: Even a minister is the same as anyone else before the law.

that.tr: I feel just as frustrated, you know.

items.explain: Look at the preceding noun and the tone: とて is usually preceded by people like 「私」「彼」「親」, expressing “I (he) have feelings too”, with a defensive, pleading tone; といえども is usually preceded by roles like 「大臣」「プロ」「子供」 and followed by an objective judgment of principle, in a solemn tone.

items.diff: 一円といえども means “even if it's only one yen” and can also be followed by a positive judgment; 一円たりとも can only be followed by a negative or prohibition.

this.tag: Even if only… · can be positive
this.tr: It may be only one yen, but it's still precious tax money.

that.tr: Not a single yen can be wasted.

wrong.why: たりとも must be followed by a negative or prohibition

items.explain: After “one ＋ counter” the two are close in meaning; look at the second half: たりとも can only be followed by a negative or prohibition (無駄にできない); といえども originally means “even though it is…” and can be followed by a negative (一円といえども無駄にはできない) or by a positive judgment like “it's still important”.

groups.note: All come from 「と言う」 — “saying” A and B in turn: といい＝whether you say A, といわず＝not just saying A, というか＝should I call it A

items.diff: といい〜といい gives examples from several aspects to evaluate the whole; といわず〜といわず means “whether A or B, everywhere…”, stressing there's no exception.

this.tr: Whether it's the taste or the price, this restaurant is beyond reproach.

that.tr: The child was covered in mud — face, hands, everywhere.

items.explain: といい＝speaking of (A, and B too), listing several aspects, followed by the speaker's evaluation (文句なしだ, さすがだ); といわず＝not just (A or B), followed by an objective “everywhere, all of it” (泥だらけ), usually preceded by body parts, places or times.

items.diff: といい〜といい lists several aspects and says they all share the same quality; というか〜というか is searching for the right expression: “should I call it A, or B…”.

this.tr: Her taste, the way she talks — she's truly charming.

that.tr: Her actions — bold, or reckless, I'm not sure which — are astonishing, anyway.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: before といい come several aspects of a thing (センス, 話し方, 味, 値段), saying they're all good or all bad; before というか come several evaluative words for the same thing (大胆, 無謀), showing you're unsure which word fits, often followed by 「とにかく」.

groups.note: Both list two aspects, meaning “both… and…”

items.diff: も〜ば〜も directly lists two facts side by side; といい〜といい first lists the aspects and then gives one overall evaluation, with a stronger subjective, exclamatory tone.

this.tr: Both in its closeness to the station and its sunlight, this apartment is beyond reproach.

that.tr: This apartment is close to the station, and it gets good sunlight too.

items.explain: Look at the sentence structure: in も〜ば〜も each item has its own predicate (駅にも近ければ, 日当たりもいい), just laying out two facts; in といい〜といい only nouns come first (近さ, 日当たり), and the evaluation comes together at the end (申し分ない), with the speaker's exclamation of “all satisfying / all hopeless”.

groups.note: Both mean the amount or degree is “not much, only so-so”

items.diff: といったところだ is a rough estimate, “at most about…”; にすぎない is a verdict on a known fact, “merely…”.

this.tr: Tomorrow's turnout will probably be around 50 people at most.

that.tr: The actual turnout was a mere 50 people.

items.explain: Check whether it's an estimate or a fact: an uncertain estimate with 「せいぜい」「〜だろう」, saying “probably about this much” → といったところだ; an established fact with 「実際は」「たった」, with a dismissive tone → にすぎない. といったところだ can also give a rough assessment of the current state (まあまあといったところだ); にすぎない can't.

groups.note: Both come from the conditional form of 「と言う」 — “speaking of…”

items.diff: といったらない closes the sentence itself, “incredibly…”; といったら first raises the subject, then describes the degree afterward.

this.tr: Mt. Fuji was incredibly beautiful that time.

that.tr: The beauty of Mt. Fuji that time — words simply can't describe it.

items.explain: Look at what follows といったら: if 「ない／なかった」 follows right away and ends the sentence → といったらない, itself meaning “to the extreme”; if a description like 「言葉にできない」「〜ほどだ」 follows → といったら. The meaning is the same; only the sentence structure differs.

groups.note: Both express an extremely high degree, “indescribably…”

items.diff: といったらない is said with feeling, for good or bad; 極まりない is written and stiff, usually follows Sino-Japanese words like 「危険・失礼」, and is mostly used for criticism.

this.tr: The first aurora I ever saw was indescribably beautiful.

that.tr: Looking at your phone while driving is extremely dangerous.

items.explain: Look at the preceding word and the tone: 「〜さ」 nouns like 「美しさ」「寒さ」 or い-adjectives, said with feeling → といったらない; Sino-Japanese words like 「危険」「失礼」「不愉快」, calmly criticizing → 極まりない (極まる is the same).

items.diff: といったらない usually follows a 「〜さ」 noun and can also be used in writing; のなんのって follows the plain form of an adjective and is purely spoken.

this.tr: It was incredibly cold yesterday.

that.tr: It was freezing yesterday — I couldn't even go outside.

items.explain: Look at the form before it: the noun 「寒さ」＋といったらない; the adjective's dictionary form 「寒い」＋のなんのって. のなんのって is only used when chatting, and the second half is often a concrete situation or simply left out; といったらない can also be used in writing.

items.diff: といったらない attaches directly to a noun or adjective, meaning “indescribably…”; ことか uses a rhetorical question, “how… it was!”, and needs a question word.

this.tr: The frustration when I lost was indescribable.

that.tr: When I lost, you can't imagine how frustrated I was.

items.explain: Look at the structure: ことか is preceded by 「どんなに／どれほど」, and the sentence takes a question form; といったらない is preceded by a noun or adjective like 「悔しさ」「寒さ」, without a question word, directly saying the degree has reached its peak.

groups.note: All come from 「と言っても」 — “even if you call it…”: followed by 「過言ではない」＝it's no exaggeration, 「いい」＝it's fine to, or the actual facts＝it's actually not that…

items.diff: と言っても過言ではない stresses “it's no exaggeration to say this”, solemn and forceful; と言ってもいい just means “you could say”, in a softer tone.

this.tr: It's no exaggeration to say this work is his greatest masterpiece.

that.tr: You could say this work is his greatest masterpiece.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only at the end: と言っても followed by 「いい」 → just “it's fine to put it this way”, common in casual talk too; followed by 「過言ではない」 → deliberately stresses “this is in no way overstated”, a weightier evaluation, common in speeches, reviews and writing.

items.diff: と言っても過言ではない pushes the evaluation up: “it's no exaggeration to call it…”; といっても pulls expectations down: “although it's…, it's actually not that much”.

this.tr: It's no exaggeration to say his cooking is better than a professional chef's.

that.tr: I may be good at cooking, but I can only make simple things.

items.explain: Both are 「と言っても (even if you call it…)」; look at what follows: 「過言ではない」 → saying so is no exaggeration, a high evaluation; a comma and then the actual situation (〜しか〜ない, 〜だけだ) → even so, it's actually not that impressive. When you read 「と言っても」, don't jump to conclusions — look at the second half.

groups.note: Both are the speaker's evaluation: “you could say…”

items.diff: と言っても過言ではない means “it's no overstatement to say…”, deliberately putting it strongly for emphasis; と言える is a plain, calm conclusion.

this.tr: It's no exaggeration to say smartphones have become part of our bodies.

that.tr: You could say smartphones have become indispensable to daily life.

items.explain: Check whether what's said is exaggerated: deliberately strong (体の一部だ), for emphasis → と言っても過言ではない, mostly in speeches and writing; a reasonable judgment (生活に欠かせない) → と言える.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 — “calling” something by a word: というか〜というか＝should I call it… or…, といい〜といい＝whether you say… or…

items.diff: 〜というか〜というか searches for two ways to describe the same thing; 〜といい〜といい lists two aspects and then gives one overall evaluation.

this.tr: The food at this restaurant is nostalgic, or maybe new — it's a curious flavor.

that.tr: Both the food and the service at this restaurant are beyond reproach.

items.explain: Look at what kind of words A and B are: evaluative words like 「懐かしい」「新しい」 → というか〜というか, weighing how to describe it; “aspect” nouns like 「料理」「サービス」 → といい〜といい, always followed by an evaluation of the whole (申し分ない, 最高だ).

groups.note: Both can list two feelings to express mixed emotions

items.diff: 〜というか〜というか means “I can't find the right word for it”; 〜やら〜やら means “several feelings rush in at once”.

this.tr: Being praised in front of everyone — happy, or embarrassed, I can't quite describe the feeling.

that.tr: Being praised in front of everyone, I was so happy and embarrassed that I turned bright red.

items.explain: Look at what follows: phrases like 「何とも言えない気持ち」「とにかく」 → というか〜というか, the focus being “not knowing which word to use”; what happened as a result (顔が真っ赤になった) → やら〜やら, the focus being several feelings existing at once, all jumbled up.

groups.note: Both are written 「というもの」 but mean completely different things

items.diff: Time period ＋ というもの means “throughout this whole period…”; sentence-final というものだ is an assertion, “that's what… is”.

this.tr: For this whole past week, I've hardly slept.

that.tag: End of sentence · asserting the essence
that.tr: Things not going your way — that's life.

items.explain: Look before and after というもの: if it's preceded by a time expression like 「一週間」「この十年」 and continues after a comma → stresses how long the period was; if it's at the end as 「〜というものだ」, preceded by an abstract noun like 「人生」「愛」 or a truth → asserts “that's what… is”.

groups.note: Both stress “all through this period…”

items.diff: Time period ＋ というもの just stresses how long it's been; てからというもの takes an event as the starting point, saying “ever since…, it's been…”.

this.tr: For the past six months, I've had one sleepless day after another.

that.tr: Ever since our child was born, I've had one sleepless day after another.

items.explain: Look at what comes before というもの: a time expression like 「半年」「この一週間」 → というもの, stressing “for so long, continuously”; a verb て-form ＋ から, like 「生まれて」 → てからというもの, stressing that things completely changed after a certain event. Both are followed by an ongoing state, not a one-off event.

groups.note: Both pair with 「からだ」 to explain a reason

items.diff: というのも has a light tone, like filling in the background or inside story; なぜなら is like a logical argument, used to support your own claim.

this.tr: I haven't been sleeping well lately. The thing is, there's construction going on next door.

that.tr: I'm against this plan. The reason is that it costs too much.

items.explain: Look at the purpose: just filling in how things came about → というのも, common in narration and conversation; persuading others and supporting your own claim (反対だ) → なぜなら, common in essays and debates.

items.diff: というのも starts a new sentence after the previous one to add the reason; 〜のは〜からだ puts the result and reason in the same sentence.

this.tr: I was late this morning. The thing is, the trains had stopped.

that.tr: The reason I was late this morning is that the trains had stopped.

items.explain: Look at where the result goes: if the result is finished with a period first and the reason is added starting with 「というのも」 → というのも; if the result becomes the topic as 「〜のは」 and the reason is given in the same sentence → 〜のは〜からだ.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 — といわず＝whether you call it A or B, といい＝whether you say A or B

items.diff: といわず〜といわず means “regardless of A or B, everywhere…”, describing a state; といい〜といい means “whether you look at A or B…”, giving an evaluation.

this.tr: The children were covered in mud — faces, hands, everywhere.

that.tr: Both the food and the service at this inn are beyond reproach.

items.explain: Look at the second half: describing a state found everywhere (usually bad) (泥だらけ, ほこりだらけ) → といわず〜といわず, where A and B are usually body parts or places; giving an evaluation of a person or thing (申し分ない, 最高だ) → といい〜といい, where A and B are aspects being evaluated. Literally, 「言わず」 is “whether you call it A or B”, and 「言い」 is “whether you say A or B”.

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…, all…”

items.diff: といわず〜といわず gives two concrete examples to describe the situation at hand; を問わず is preceded by one general word (昼夜, 年齢, 男女) and is mostly used in notices and rules.

this.tr: The construction goes on day and night alike.

that.tr: The construction continues around the clock.

items.explain: Look at how many words come before: 「昼」 and 「夜」 each followed once → といわず〜といわず, with the exclamatory feel of “practically all the time, everywhere”; combined into one general word 「昼夜」 followed once → を問わず, objective in tone, common in job ads and notices like 「年齢を問わず」「経験を問わず」.

items.title: 〜という〜 (every single…)
items.diff: といわず〜といわず gives two different things as representatives; NというN repeats the same noun, meaning “every single…, without exception”.

this.tr: After the typhoon, the garden, the road — everywhere was covered in fallen leaves.

that.tr: After the typhoon, every single window was broken.

items.explain: Check whether the noun is the same: the same noun with 「という」 in between (窓という窓, 店という店) → every one of that kind, without exception; two different nouns each followed by 「といわず」 (庭, 道) → giving representatives to say the whole area is like that.

groups.note: Both are built on 「決（き）まる」 — “to be settled, unchanging”

items.diff: と決まって is a regular pattern, “whenever…, always…”; に決まってる is a verdict on one thing, “it's bound to be…”.

this.tr: Whenever it rains, I always get a headache.

that.tr: You practiced so much — you're bound to pass.

items.explain: Only 「と」 and 「に」 differ: in 「〜と決まって〜」, 「決まって」 is actually an adverb meaning “always, without fail”, preceded by the conditional 「と」, describing something that happens every time; 「〜に決まってる」 comes at the end of the sentence and is a strong verdict on one thing.

groups.note: Both mean “whenever…, …”

items.diff: と決まって stresses “without exception, without fail”, usually about a person's habits or quirks; たびに stresses “every single time”, and can also follow 「noun＋の」.

this.tr: Whenever my father drinks, he invariably starts bragging about the old days.

that.tr: Every time my father goes on a business trip, he brings back souvenirs.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun＋の like 「出張の」 only works with たびに; と決まって is preceded by a verb's dictionary form＋と, usually followed by an unshakable habit or quirk (starts talking about the old days whenever he drinks). When the two are interchangeable, と決まって emphasizes “not a single exception” more.

groups.note: Both come from the colloquial 「〜と来る」 — “(the topic, the situation) has come to…”

items.diff: ときたら raises a person or thing as the topic at the start and then complains; ときている adds a striking condition that leads to a natural result.

this.tr: As for my son, all he does every day is play video games.

that.tr: This place is cheap and, on top of that, tasty, so there's always a long line.

items.explain: Look at the position and what follows: noun＋ときたら＋comma, followed by dissatisfaction with that person or thing → ときたら; adjective or clause＋ときている, often followed by 「から」「のだから」 leading to a result → ときている. One is “the topic comes to…”, the other is “the situation has, of all things, come to this”.

groups.note: Both raise someone or something and then express dissatisfaction

items.diff: ときたら has a stronger tone of dissatisfaction and blame, and can follow both people and things; ったら usually follows someone close to you, with exasperation and affection.

this.tr: As for trains these days, they're always late.

that.tr: Oh, Mom! She tidied up my room without asking again.

items.explain: Look at who comes before: someone close like family or friends, in an “oh, honestly!” tone → ったら, mostly spoken by women and children; seriously complaining about a person or thing (最近の電車, うちの会社) → ときたら, with a heavier tone.

groups.note: Both come from the colloquial 「〜と来る」 — “(the topic, the situation) has come to…”

items.diff: ときている adds a striking condition that leads to a natural result; ときたら raises a person or thing as the topic at the start and then complains.

this.tr: This place is cheap and, on top of that, tasty, so there's always a long line.

that.tr: As for my son, all he does every day is play video games.

items.explain: Look at the position and what follows: adjective or clause＋ときている, often followed by 「から」「のだから」 leading to a result → ときている; noun＋ときたら＋comma, followed by dissatisfaction with that person or thing → ときたら. One is “the situation has, of all things, come to this”, the other is “the topic comes to…”.

groups.note: Both mean adding one more condition “on top of” another

items.diff: 上に just objectively adds one more item; ときている deliberately singles out the last condition with an exclamatory “and on top of that…”, then leads to a result.

this.tr: This apartment is small and, on top of that, far from the station — no wonder nobody will rent it.

that.tr: This apartment is not only small but also far from the station.

items.explain: Check whether a “conclusion” follows: 上に just lists two facts, and the sentence can end there; ときている is placed on the last condition, with an exclamatory “and on top of that…”, often followed by a natural result like 「〜わけだ」「〜のも無理はない」「〜から」.

groups.note: Both come from 「見る (to see)」 — here 「みる」 means “to judge, to regard as”

items.diff: とみられる is the news phrase “is believed to…”, objective and not saying whose judgment it is; とみえる is the speaker's own guess after seeing signs.

this.tr: According to the police, the cause of the fire is believed to have been a cigarette.

that.tr: The book on the desk is still open. Looks like he was studying until just now.

items.explain: Look at the tone: a guess by the police or experts in a news report, without saying who's guessing → とみられる (the passive of 「みる」, “is regarded as”); the speaker judging for themselves from signs → とみえる.

groups.note: Both are objective, non-committal judgments in written language: “(is) believed to…”

items.diff: とみられる is a guess based on signs at hand, not yet confirmed; とされる is a generally accepted view or an official determination.

this.tr: Judging from the scene, the cause of the accident is believed to be speeding.

that.tr: It is generally held that eight hours is the ideal amount of sleep.

items.explain: Look at where the judgment comes from: signs at hand like 「現場の状況から」「調べによると」, with the conclusion not yet settled → とみられる; a generally accepted view like 「一般に」「古くから」, or a determination by law or rules → とされる.

items.diff: とみられる is mostly used in the news, reporting a guess by the police or experts; ものと思われる is mostly used in reports and papers, as the writer's own careful judgment.

this.tr: According to the police, the culprit is believed to still be in the city.

that.tr: From the above results, this drug appears to be effective for the elderly as well.

items.explain: Look at who's judging: the news reporting the views of police or experts, often with 「〜によると」 → とみられる; the conclusion of a report or paper, where the author judges based on evidence like 「以上の結果から」 without wanting to be too definitive → ものと思われる.

groups.note: Both mean “as soon as…, …”

items.diff: と見るや is preceded by “a situation one has judged”, followed by an action taken quickly in response; や否や is preceded by an action that actually happened, immediately followed by something else.

this.tr: As soon as he saw his opponent was tired, he launched an all-out attack.

that.tr: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a judgment about the situation like 「相手が疲れた」「勝てない」, followed by the subject's quick-witted action → と見るや (と見ると is the same, slightly weaker); an action that actually happened like 「ベルが鳴る」「ドアが開く」 → や否や, just saying two things happened almost simultaneously.

items.diff: と見るや is followed by the subject's deliberate, quick action; たとたん is usually followed by an unexpected change.

this.tr: As soon as it looked like rain, the clerk immediately put the goods away.

that.tr: The moment I stepped outside, it started to rain.

items.explain: Look at who does what in the second half: the subject seizing the moment and acting right away on their own (すぐ片付けた) → と見るや; an uncontrollable, unexpected change (雨が降り出した) → たとたん. Also, と見るや is preceded by a judgment (〜そうだ, 〜だ), while たとたん is preceded by a verb's た-form.

groups.note: The same 「との」, written the same way, with completely different meanings

items.title: 〜との (with…)
items.diff: The との in 中止との連絡 is a quotation, “saying that…”; the との in 友達との約束 means “with…”.

this.tr: We received word that the match was canceled.

that.tr: I forgot my promise with my friend.

items.explain: Look at what comes before との: the content of a statement (試合は中止) → quotation, usually followed by 連絡, 知らせ, 返事, 意見; a person (友達, 先生) → “with…”, usually followed by 約束, 関係, 会話.

groups.note: Both give the specific content of news, opinions and the like

items.title: 〜という (stating the content)
items.diff: との is more concise and written, and only follows nouns for news or opinions like 「連絡・知らせ・意見」; という works in both speech and writing and is far more widely used.

this.tr: The department head notified us that the meeting was canceled.

that.tr: The department head notified us that the meeting was canceled.

wrong.why: Only 「という」 can introduce a name

items.explain: When giving the content of news or an opinion, both work, and との is more concise, common in news and official documents; but との is usually followed by nouns like 「連絡・知らせ・返事・意見・声」, and to introduce a name (田中という人) only という works.

groups.note: Both come from 「と思う」 — “to think that…”; in 思いきや, 「き」 is a classical past auxiliary and 「や」 is rhetorical: “I thought…, right? (but no)”

items.title: 〜かと思ったら (I thought… but)
items.diff: For “I thought…, but actually…”, かと思いきや is the written phrasing, common in writing; かと思ったら is spoken.

this.tr: I thought the exam would be easy, but it turned out to be surprisingly hard.

that.tr: I thought the exam would be easy, but it turned out to be surprisingly hard.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same; look at the setting: かと思いきや is common in news, essays and other writing, with a slightly classical flavor (と思いきや is the same); in conversation say かと思ったら. Also, かと思ったら／かと思うと can mean “no sooner had… than…”, but かと思いきや can't.

items.title: 〜かと思った (I thought…)
items.diff: かと思いきや must be followed by a fact contrary to expectations; かと思った just says “I thought…”, and the outcome can be left unsaid.

this.tr: I thought nobody would come, but the venue was packed.

that.tr: Oh, it's you. I thought you were a burglar.

items.explain: Look at where the sentence ends: かと思いきや is always followed by a comma and a surprising outcome (会場は満員だった), mostly in writing; かと思った often ends the sentence, just stating your own misunderstanding a moment ago — it's spoken, and the actual situation is clear from context.

groups.note: Both mean the result was contrary to expectations

items.title: 〜のに (even though… still)
items.diff: と思いきや is preceded by your own expectation and focuses on “contrary to what I expected”, and also works for pleasant surprises; のに is preceded by a fact and is often followed by dissatisfaction or regret.

this.tr: I thought it would rain today, but it's been fine weather since the morning.

that.tr: The forecast said it would be sunny, and yet it rained.

items.explain: Look at the first half: the speaker's own expectation in their mind (雨かと思った) → と思いきや, and the result can be good or bad; an existing fact (天気予報は晴れだと言っていた), with a result that leaves you dissatisfied → のに.

groups.note: Both come from 「AをBとする」 — “to set or regard A as B”

items.diff: AをBとする says who set A as B; in the passive 「AはBとされる」, the one who decided is hidden, making it sound objective.

this.tr: Under this law, those 18 and over are defined as adults.

that.tr: The state made a law defining those 18 and over as adults.

items.explain: Look for 「を」 and the person deciding: 「国は〜を〜とする」 makes clear who set it → AをBとする; change 「を」 to 「が／は」 and make the verb passive 「される」, and who decided disappears → とされる, which is why it's common in laws, news and papers.

groups.note: Both objectively report in written language that “it is believed…”

items.diff: とされる is usually a determination or rule from research or authorities, and is formal; と言われている is a saying that circulates in society or among people, and is common in speech too.

this.tr: Among experts, the main cause of this disease is considered to be stress.

that.tr: Since olden times it has been said that dreaming of Mt. Fuji brings good luck.

items.explain: Look at where the claim comes from: a determination by experts, law or authorities (専門家の間では, 法律で) → とされる, mostly in papers and news; something passed down among people that everyone says (昔から) → と言われている, fine in both writing and speech.

items.diff: とされる is an already accepted view or official determination; とみられる is a guess based on signs at hand, not yet confirmed.

this.tr: It is generally held that eight hours is the ideal amount of sleep.

that.tr: Judging from the scene, the cause of the accident is believed to be speeding.

items.explain: Look at where the judgment comes from: a generally accepted view like 「一般に」「古くから」, or a determination by law or rules → とされる; signs at hand like 「現場の状況から」「調べによると」, with the conclusion not yet settled → とみられる.

groups.note: Both mean “for someone of… status or ability, to actually…”

items.diff: としたことが is mostly used about yourself (私としたことが), with regret and self-mockery, in a light tone; ともあろう criticizes someone of status or standing, in a heavy tone.

this.tr: How careless of me — I left important documents at home.

that.tr: A police officer, of all people, arrested for drunk driving!

items.explain: Look at the subject and tone: 「私」「僕」 or someone usually reliable who unexpectedly makes a mistake, with regret or pity → としたことが; a role with social standing like 「教師」「警察官」「大臣」, followed by 「者が／人が」, doing something they shouldn't, with condemnation → ともあろう.

groups.note: Both come from 「とする／にする」 (to take as, to suppose) — plus the concessive 「ても」「たところで」

items.diff: としたところで is negative in tone, stressing “even so, it's no use”; としても is a neutral hypothetical concession, and the second half can be good or bad.

this.tag: Negative · no use even if done
this.tr: Even if I went to apologize now, I probably wouldn't be forgiven.

that.tag: Neutral · can be followed by something good
that.tr: Even if I fail, it'll be good experience.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a negative conclusion, “it's no use, it won't change anything” (許してもらえない, 無駄だ) → としたところで, with a sense of “wasted effort”; the result can be good or bad (いい経験になる) → としても.

items.diff: にしたところで is almost always followed by a negative, “no matter who, it's impossible”; にしても can be followed by good or bad.

this.tag: Negative follows · anyone would be the same
this.tr: Even Tanaka, a veteran, couldn't get through this much in a single day.

that.tr: As for Tanaka, he must be pleased with the results this time too.

items.explain: Both are 「person＋に＋する」, bringing up someone's standpoint. Look at the second half: a negative “can't be done” judgment like 「無理だ」「分からない」 → にしたところで is most natural; a neutral or positive guess like 「うれしい」 → use にしても.

groups.note: Both mean “even if…, (it's no use)”

items.diff: たところで attaches directly to an action, “even if you do it, it's no use”; にしたところで is preceded by a person, としたところで by a hypothetical situation.

this.tag: にしたところで · after a person
this.tr: Even experts don't know tomorrow's stock prices.

this.tag: としたところで · hypothetical situation
this.tr: Even supposing we left right now, we wouldn't make it in time.

that.tag: たところで · after an action
that.tr: Even if I ran there now, I wouldn't make it in time.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「ところで」: a verb's た-form (走った) → たところで, “doing it would be in vain”; a person (専門家)＋にした → it'd be the same no matter who; a clause＋とした, often with 「仮に」 before it → first suppose a situation, then say “even so, it won't work”. All are followed by a negative or “no use” result.

groups.note: Both come from 「と言う」 — “although it's said to be… (but)”

items.diff: とはいえ is more written, and can be followed by anything that doesn't match expectations; といっても is more spoken, focusing on “the actual degree isn't that high”.

this.tr: Although it's already spring, the cold days are continuing.

that.tr: I say “trip”, but I just stayed one night at a hot spring nearby.

items.explain: Look at the second half: just pointing out another side that differs from expectations, common in writing and news → とはいえ; correcting the listener's idea of scale or degree (〜だけだ, 〜ぐらいだ) → といっても. In speech, to lower someone's expectations, people generally say といっても.

items.diff: といえども is more classical and stiff, usually followed by principles like “must still” or “is not allowed”; とはいえ works in both writing and speech, usually followed by the actual situation.

this.tr: It may already be March, but mornings and evenings are still chilly.

that.tr: Whatever the reason, violence is not permitted.

items.explain: Look before and after: “whatever” expressions like 「いかなる」「たとえ」, followed by a principle or obligation like 「〜は許されない」「〜なければならない」 → といえども, common in speeches and law; just stating a reality different from expectations (まだ冷える) → とはいえ.

groups.note: Both express concession: “although…, still…”

items.diff: とはいえ can attach directly to a noun (春とはいえ); ものの must follow a verb or adjective (春になったものの).

this.tr: Although it's spring, the cold days continue.

that.tr: Although spring has come, the cold days continue.

wrong.why: ものの can't attach directly to a noun

items.explain: Look at the word before it: a noun (春, 子ども) can take とはいえ directly; ものの must be preceded by a verb, adjective or 「noun＋である」 (春になった, 春であるものの). Also, ものの is often used for “did it but it didn't work out as hoped” (買ったものの、まだ使っていない).

groups.note: Both come from 「比べる」 — “to put two things side by side and compare”

items.diff: とは比べものにならない means the gap is too large, “there's simply no comparison”; に比べて compares to find something “a bit higher or lower”.

this.tr: This year's heat is nothing like last year's.

that.tr: Compared with last year, this year is a little hotter.

items.explain: Look at what follows: とは比べものにならない is itself the conclusion — the gap is so large they can't be mentioned in the same breath, so no comparison result follows; に比べて is followed by the result of the comparison, often with 「少し」「ずっと」 to say by how much.

groups.note: Both mean one side “can't match” the other

items.title: 〜には及ばない (can't match)
items.diff: とは比べものにならない is only for a huge gap; には及ばない just says “can't match”, and works even when it's only slightly short.

this.tr: My cooking is still nowhere near as good as my mom's.

that.tag: Can't match · can be just slightly
that.tr: My cooking is still just a step short of my mom's.

wrong.why: 比べものにならない itself means “so far apart there's no comparison”, so it can't mean “only slightly short”

items.explain: Look at how big the gap is: far apart, not even in the same league → とは比べものにならない (the better side can also be the subject: 母の料理は私のとは比べものにならない); just saying “can't match”, which can take 「あと一歩」「少し」 before it to say it's only slightly short → には及ばない.

groups.note: Both mean two things — before and after, surface and reality — are “exactly opposite”

items.diff: とは裏腹に usually follows 「言葉・見た目・表情」, talking about a gap between surface and reality; に反して usually follows 「予想・期待」, and can also mean going against rules.

this.tr: Contrary to his harsh words, his eyes were kind.

that.tr: Contrary to most people's expectations, a newcomer won the championship.

items.explain: Look at the preceding noun: surface things like 「言葉」「見た目」「表情」, exactly opposite to the true feelings or reality → とは裏腹に; 「予想」「期待」 work with both, with に反して more objective; 「規則」「命令」, meaning violation → only に反して.

items.diff: とは裏腹に follows a noun (見た目, 言葉); ようでいて follows a clause describing appearance, “seems…, but actually…”.

this.tr: Contrary to his laid-back appearance, he actually thinks things through carefully.

that.tr: He seems laid-back, but he actually thinks things through carefully.

items.explain: Look at the form before it: a noun like 「見た目」「言葉」＋とは裏腹に; a clause describing appearance like 「のんびりしている」＋ようでいて. Both mean “on the surface it's like this, but in reality the opposite”.

items.diff: とは裏腹に is about the surface versus the reality of the same person or thing; にひきかえ compares two different people or things.

this.tr: Contrary to his gentle appearance, he's a very strict teacher.

that.tr: Unlike his serious older brother, the younger brother does nothing but play.

items.explain: Look at how many things are being compared: the appearance and reality of the same person → とは裏腹に; two different things put side by side, like an older and younger brother or last year and this year → にひきかえ, often carrying the speaker's evaluation.

items.diff: とは裏腹に means expectations or appearance are opposite to reality; とはうってかわって means the same thing has suddenly changed completely from before.

this.tr: Contrary to the forecast of rain, it was sunny all day today.

that.tr: In complete contrast to yesterday's heavy rain, it was sunny all day today.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「とは」: an expectation or surface like 「予報」「期待」「見た目」 → とは裏腹に, saying things turned out contrary to hopes or the surface doesn't match the reality; a past state like 「昨日」「以前」 → とは打って変わって, saying how greatly the same thing changed from before.

groups.note: All express a change or contrast: before vs. after, appearance vs. reality, or between two things

items.diff: とはうってかわって means the same thing has suddenly changed completely from before; とは裏腹に means expectations or appearances turn out the opposite of reality.

this.tr: In complete contrast to yesterday's heavy rain, it was sunny all day today.

that.tr: Contrary to the forecast of rain, it was sunny all day today.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「とは」: a past state like 「昨日」 or 「以前」 → とは打って変わって, describing how dramatically the same thing has changed; an expectation or surface like 「予報」, 「期待」 or 「見た目」 → とは裏腹に, describing things going against expectations, or appearance not matching reality.

items.diff: とはうってかわって compares the same thing before and after; にひきかえ compares two different people or things.

this.tr: In complete contrast to his slump last year, he's in top form this year.

that.tr: Unlike his serious older brother, the younger brother does nothing but play.

items.explain: Check whether the comparison is about the same subject: the same person or place, comparing “before / last year” with “now” → とは打って変わって, stressing how drastic the change is; two different subjects such as an older and a younger brother → にひきかえ.

items.diff: Before とはうってかわって comes “what it was like before the change”, stressing that it's now completely different; before を境に comes the “turning point” (an event, a particular day).

this.tr: He's a completely different person from before — he's started working seriously.

that.tr: Since getting married, he's started working seriously.

items.explain: Look at what comes before 「とは／を」: a state before the change like 「以前」 or 「昨日」 → とは打って変わって, highlighting “completely different from back then”; an event or point in time that caused the change, like 「結婚」 or 「その日」 → を境に, highlighting “from this point on, things changed”.

groups.note: Both are 「status noun ＋ とも ＋ …」; only the ending differs: あろう vs. なると

items.diff: ともあろう means “someone of such standing, of all people, would…” and is used only to condemn; ともなると means “once you reach such a position, naturally…”, a neutral observation.

this.tr: A principal, of all people, laying hands on a student!

that.tr: Once you become a principal, work chases you even on your days off.

items.explain: Look at what follows 「とも」: 「あろう者が／人が」 followed by something shocking and unbecoming of that position → ともあろう, condemning; 「なると／なれば」 followed by what naturally comes with that position (忙しい, 責任が重い) → ともなると, no criticism.

groups.note: Both mean “not befitting one's status”

items.diff: ともあろう criticizes someone of social standing, in a strong tone; としたことが is mostly used about oneself (私としたことが), with regret or self-mockery, in a lighter tone.

this.tr: A police officer, of all people, getting caught drunk driving!

that.tr: How careless of me — I left the important documents at home.

items.explain: Look at the subject and tone: a position of social standing like 「教師」, 「警察官」 or 「大臣」, followed by 「者が／人が」, having done something they shouldn't, with condemnation → ともあろう; 「私」, 「僕」 or someone normally reliable who unexpectedly slipped up, with regret → としたことが.

items.diff: ともあろう modifies a “person”, stressing the gap between position and behavior; まじき modifies an “act”, saying the act itself is unacceptable.

this.tr: A police officer, of all people, driving drunk!

that.tr: Drunk driving is conduct utterly unbecoming of a police officer.

items.explain: Look at the noun that follows: 「者が」 or 「人が」 → ともあろう, then say what they did; 「行為」, 「発言」 or 「態度」 → まじき, directly judging the act. The two often appear together: 教師ともあろう者が、教師にあるまじき行為をした.

groups.note: Both are concessive: “even if…”

items.diff: とも is written language and attaches only to an adjective's く form, a verb's volitional form, etc.; ても・でも is the everyday form and attaches to anything.

this.tr: No matter how hard it gets, I won't give up until the end.

that.tr: No matter how hard it gets, I won't give up until the end.
Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; the difference is register and how they attach: とも is common in speeches, writing and song lyrics, and attaches only to an adjective く form like 「苦しく」 or a volitional form like 「行こう」; in speech you'd normally say ても. A noun can't take とも directly — in writing you'd say 「雨であろうとも」, in speech simply 「雨でも」.

items.diff: Volitional ＋ とも is a more formal, more forceful version of ようと／ようが.

this.tr: No matter who says what, my resolve won't change.

that.tr: No matter who says what, my resolve won't change.

items.explain: Only the final 「も」 differs: volitional ＋ と (言おうと) is the common form, and 「言おうが」 means the same; adding 「も」 to get 「言おうとも」 makes it more formal and forceful, typical of speeches and novels. All three mean the same.

groups.note: Both come from 「となる」 — “become…, reach a situation of…”

items.diff: Before ともなると comes an “out of the ordinary” position, age or period; となると is more neutral and can follow any ordinary situation or hypothesis.

this.tr: Once you become a company president, you can't relax even on your days off.

that.tr: If the business trip starts tomorrow, I have to get ready by the end of today.

items.explain: Both come from 「となる」 (reach a situation of…); the difference is the 「も」: the 「も」 in ともなると stresses that the first part “has reached such a high level”, so it usually follows a position, age or period like 「社長」, 「大学生」 or 「年末」 (same with ともなれば); if you're simply raising an ordinary situation or hypothesis (出張, 雨) → となると.

groups.note: Both are 「status noun ＋ とも ＋ …」; only the ending differs: なると vs. あろう

items.diff: ともなると means “once you reach such a position, naturally…”, neutral; ともあろう means “someone of such standing, of all people, would…”, used only to condemn.

this.tr: Once you become a principal, work chases you even on your days off.

that.tr: A principal, of all people, laying hands on a student!

items.explain: Look at what follows 「とも」: 「なると／なれば」 followed by what naturally comes with that position (休みの日も仕事, 責任が重い) → ともなると, no criticism (same with ともなれば); 「あろう者が／人が」 followed by something bad that doesn't befit that position → ともあろう, condemning.

groups.note: Both mean you can't tell whether it's A or B

items.diff: 〜とも〜ともつかない describes something that is itself somewhere between the two; 〜のやら〜のやら means the speaker can't figure out which it is, with a sense of bewilderment.

this.tag: Neither A nor B quite fits
this.tr: He wore an expression that was hard to call either joy or sorrow.

that.tr: I have no idea whether he's happy or sad.

items.explain: Look at the structure and what follows: two nouns each followed by 「とも」, ending in 「つかない」, usually before a noun like 「表情」 or 「声」 → describes the thing itself as hard to pin down; two clauses each followed by 「のやら」, often followed by 「分からない」 → the speaker can't make sense of it, often with some irritation.

groups.note: Both come from 「とて」 — i.e. 「と言って」, originally “saying that…”

items.diff: とて is written language; the spoken だって derives from it (だとて → だって), with the same meaning: “even…”.

this.tr: Parents are human too; they make mistakes as well.

that.tr: Parents are human too, you know. They make mistakes as well.

items.explain: Both sentences mean the same; look at the register: sentences ending in 「だ」 or 「である」, in writing or speeches → とて; everyday conversation with 「よ」 or 「じゃない」 at the end → だって. だって is simply 「だとて」 said quickly, so it also attaches directly after a noun (私とて＝私だって).

items.diff: たとて is a formal, literary expression; the spoken たって derives from it (たとて → たって); both mean “even if…”.

this.tr: Even if I apologized now, I probably wouldn't be forgiven.

that.tr: Even if you apologize now, they're not gonna forgive you.

items.explain: The meaning and how they attach are the same (謝った＋とて → 謝ったって); look at the register of the ending: a classical-sounding ending like 「〜まい」, in novels and writing → たとて; talking with friends, 「よ」 at the end → たって.

items.diff: からとて is a classical contraction of からといって, with the same meaning: “just because… doesn't mean…”.

this.tr: Being rich does not, in itself, make one great.

that.tr: Just because someone is rich doesn't mean they're great.

items.explain: とて＝と言って, so からとて＝からといって, and both are followed by negatives like 「わけではない」, 「〜とは限らない」 or 「〜てはいけない」. からといって works in any writing or conversation; からとて only appears in literary written language — when writing yourself, just use からといって.

items.diff: Noun ＋ とて is concessive: “even…”; こととて, however, gives a reason: “since it's… (please forgive)”.

this.tr: Even if it's a child, I won't go easy on them.

that.tr: It was just a child's doing, so please forgive them.

items.explain: Both sentences have 「子ども」 and 「とて」 — look at the second half: an unsparing conclusion like 「容赦しない」 → “even…”; a request for forgiveness like 「お許しください」 or 「ご了承ください」 → “because it's…”. If 「こと」 comes before it (〜のこととて, 〜したこととて), it's こととて giving a reason, preserving the old classical use of 「とて」 meaning “because”.

groups.note: Both mean “even…”

items.diff: とて is emotional, often used in personal statements or self-justification like 「私とて」 or 「親とて」; といえども is more formal and objective, common in news and regulations.

this.tr: It's not that I don't feel frustrated, either.

that.tr: Even a minister must obey the law.

items.explain: Listen to the tone: talking about your own or those close to you's feelings or justifying yourself (私とて, 親とて) → とて, often with a sense of grievance or emotion; reasoning objectively in news, speeches or regulations (大臣といえども, 子どもといえども) → といえども. といえども can also follow a clause meaning “although…” (冬といえども暖かい); とて generally isn't used that way.

items.diff: The meaning and how they attach are almost identical — both mean “even if you do it, it's no use”; たところで is common in both speech and writing, while たとて is a literary written form.

this.tr: However much one may regret it now, lost time will not return.

that.tr: It's too late to regret it now.

items.explain: Both attach to the た form and are followed by a “no use / wasted effort” result. The difference is register: everyday speech and ordinary writing use たところで; たとて has a classical flavor and appears mostly in novels, poetry and speeches. Also, たところで has another use, “at the point when…” (一段落したところで休憩する), which たとて doesn't.

groups.note: つ〜つ ↔ つつ, both 「ます form ＋ つ」

items.diff: つ〜つ needs two verbs, each with its own つ, meaning “now… now…”; つつ attaches to just one verb, meaning “while…” or “although…”.

this.tr: He was pacing back and forth in front of the station.

that.tr: I knew it was wrong, but I lied anyway.

items.explain: Count the verbs before つ: 「行きつ戻りつ」 is two opposite verbs each with a つ, often followed by 「する」, describing two actions alternating back and forth; 「知りつつ」 has just one verb with つつ joined together, followed by something else (while…, even though I knew…).

groups.note: Both express actions “alternating repeatedly”

items.diff: つ〜つ is a classical remnant, used only in set phrases like 「行きつ戻りつ」; たり〜たりする is the modern form and works with any verb.

this.tr: Deep in thought, he paced back and forth in the room.

that.tr: Thinking it over, he walked back and forth around the room.

items.explain: Both sentences can mean “walk back and forth”; the difference is context and range: つ〜つ appears only in a handful of set phrases like 「行きつ戻りつ」, 「浮きつ沈みつ」, 「持ちつ持たれつ」 and 「抜きつ抜かれつ」, mostly in written description; in everyday speech or with other verbs, always use たり〜たりする (食べたり飲んだりする).

groups.note: All attach to the ます form and mean “do completely, all the way”

items.diff: 切る means doing “one thing” from start to finish; 尽くす means doing it to “every target” until none is left.

this.tr: I've read pretty much every book in the town library.

that.tr: I read a thick novel all the way through in one night.

items.explain: Look at the object: “one” thing done from beginning to end, like a book or a race → 切る (読み切る, 走り切る); a whole mass of targets all used up, like “the library's books” or “all the food” → 尽くす (読み尽くす, 食べ尽くす). The negative of 切る, 切れない (食べ切れない = can't finish eating), likewise means “can't finish one thing”.

items.diff: 抜く stresses “sticking it out to the end” through a hard process; 尽くす stresses “having done everything there was to do”, leaving nothing out.

this.tr: I did everything I possibly could.

that.tag: See it through · don't give up
that.tr: Hard as it was, I saw it through to the end.

items.explain: Both are 「やり〜」 — look at the clues: 「全部」, 「あらゆる」 or 「できることは」 say nothing in the range was left out → 尽くす; 「最後まで」 or 「苦しくても」 say you didn't give up along the way → 抜く (走り抜く, 戦い抜く, 考え抜く).

groups.note: Both come from 「うち（内）」 — “within a certain range”

items.diff: うちに入らない is about being “within” a category — “doesn't even count as…”; うちに is about “within” a time span (while…).

this.tr: Five minutes late doesn't even count as being late.

that.tr: Let's head home while it's still light.

items.explain: うち simply means 「内」 (inside). Check whether 「入らない」 follows: if it does, it's about “whether it counts as part of this category” → the degree is too low to count at all; if not, what comes before is a span of time or a state → while….

groups.note: Both downplay something as “not worth mentioning”

items.diff: にすぎない admits “it is X, just a small one”; うちに入らない flatly says “it doesn't even count as X”.

this.tr: Walking fifteen minutes a day doesn't even count as exercise.

that.tag: That's what it is · nothing more
that.tr: Walking fifteen minutes a day is nothing more than a light stroll.

items.explain: Look at how the noun before it relates to the thing: before うちに入らない comes the category being denied (運動, 料理, 遅刻), meaning “doesn't qualify for this category”; before にすぎない comes what it actually is (散歩, 噂, 言い訳), meaning “it's just this, nothing more”.

items.diff: うちに入らない follows a noun, meaning “doesn't count as this kind of thing”; ほどのことではない follows an action, meaning “not serious enough to need to…”.

this.tr: A fever like this doesn't even count as being sick.

that.tr: A fever like this isn't bad enough to go to the hospital.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: noun ＋ の (病気の, 運動の) → うちに入らない, denying that it “belongs to this category”; a verb's dictionary form (行く, 騒ぐ, 心配する) → ほどのことではない, denying that it's “necessary to do this”.

groups.note: Both come from 「あれ」, the imperative of 「ある」 — “let it be however it is”, expressing concession

items.diff: はどうあれ follows a noun like “reason” or “result”, meaning “whatever it may be”; であれ follows a concrete noun or a question word, meaning “whether it's…”.

this.tr: Whatever the reason, violence is unforgivable.

that.tr: Whoever it is, violence is unforgivable.

items.explain: あれ is the imperative of 「ある」: “let it be whatever it is” → no matter what. Look at what comes before あれ: 「どう」 (how) after an abstract noun like 「理由」 or 「結果」 → はどうあれ; 「誰」, 「何」 or a concrete noun directly followed by 「で＋あれ」 → であれ (same with 子どもであれ大人であれ).

groups.note: Both mean “regardless of…”, setting a factor aside

items.diff: はどうあれ expresses the speaker's own judgment or stance; いかんにかかわらず is official language used in rules and notices.

this.tr: Whatever your reasons, breaking your promise was your fault.

that.tr: Regardless of the reason, fees already paid will not be refunded.

items.explain: Look at who is speaking to whom: criticizing someone or stating your stance (君が悪い, 応援する) → はどうあれ; laying down a rule that applies to everyone in a notice, contract or regulation (返金いたしません, 受け付けます) → いかんにかかわらず (same with いかんを問わず).

items.diff: はどうあれ means “however A turns out”, with the conclusion unaffected by A; はともかく means “setting A aside”, then turning to evaluate a different aspect.

this.tr: Whatever the result, what matters most is that you gave it your all to the end.

that.tag: Setting aside · talk about something else
that.tr: Looks aside, it does taste good.

items.explain: Look at the second half: if it evaluates a different aspect (味はいい, 量は多い), often with a contrastive 「は」 → はともかく, implying A itself isn't great; if whether A is good or bad can't change the judgment or stance that follows (大切だ, 許されない) → はどうあれ.

groups.note: Both come from 「及ぶ（およぶ）」 — “to reach”

items.diff: 言うに及ばず sits mid-sentence, meaning “… goes without saying”, followed by something further; には及ばない sits at the end, meaning “there's no need to…”.

this.tr: This singer is popular not only at home, of course, but overseas as well.

that.tr: It'll heal soon, so there's no need to worry.

items.explain: 言うに及ばず is the classical form of 「言うに及ばない」 (needn't even be said) → of course. Look at the position: mid-sentence, followed by 「〜でも」 or 「〜も」 to add another layer → 言うに及ばず; at the end, politely brushing aside someone's worry or kindness → には及ばない.

groups.note: Both mean “A goes without saying, and B too…”

items.diff: Same meaning; は言うまでもなく is standard written language, while は言うに及ばず uses the classical negative 「ず」 and sounds stiffer and more formal.

this.tr: This festival draws not only the locals, of course, but also crowds of visitors from overseas.

that.tr: This festival draws the locals, needless to say, and also lots of visitors from overseas.

items.explain: The two sentences mean exactly the same; only the feel differs: 言うまでもなく is common in writing and formal speech; 言うに及ばず has a classical tinge and appears mostly in news and formal addresses. Both are too formal for casual chat — just say はもちろん.

items.diff: Both share the “A goes without saying” use; but 言わずもがな also has the original meaning “better left unsaid, superfluous”, which 言うに及ばず lacks.

this.tr: Foreign tourists are increasing not just in Tokyo, needless to say, but even in small regional towns.

that.tr: I let slip something I shouldn't have said and made the other person angry.

items.explain: Look at what follows 言わずもがな: 「の＋こと」 and then 「言う／口にする」 → the original meaning, “words better left unsaid” (もがな = “would that…”), often with regret; after a noun, followed by 「〜も」 or 「〜でも」 → “A goes without saying”, and here it's interchangeable with 言うに及ばず, though 言わずもがな is more literary.

items.diff: 言うに及ばず is mostly used to build up something positive or neutral; はおろか is mostly used with negatives or bad things, with surprise or dissatisfaction.

this.tr: This shop is packed with customers on weekdays, never mind weekends.

that.tr: I'm so busy I don't even have time to rest on weekends, let alone travel.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: はおろか is almost always followed by a negative like 「〜もない」 or 「〜もできない」, with surprise or dissatisfaction at how bad things are; 言うに及ばず is mostly used in positive listings in affirmative sentences (にぎわっている, 人気がある), with a formal tone.

groups.note: Both mean “A goes without saying, and B too…” or “it goes without saying”

items.diff: Same meaning, and both can mean “it goes without saying”; 言うまでもない is general written language, while 言わずもがな is more literary.

this.tr: It goes without saying that health is important.

that.tr: Needless to say, health is important.

items.explain: The two are interchangeable; only the feel differs: 言うまでもない (言うまでもなく) is common in writing and formal speech; 言わずもがな contains the classical 「もがな」 and sounds refined, mostly appearing in essays and commentary. Also, 言わずもがな has the original meaning “better left unsaid” (言わずもがなのことを言う), which 言うまでもない lacks.

items.diff: Both share the “A goes without saying” use; but 言わずもがな also has the original meaning “better left unsaid, superfluous”, which 言うに及ばず lacks.

this.tr: I let slip something I shouldn't have said and made the other person angry.

that.tr: Foreign tourists are increasing not just in Tokyo, needless to say, but even in small regional towns.

items.explain: Look at what follows 言わずもがな: 「の＋こと」 and then 「言う／口にする」 → the original meaning, “words better left unsaid” (もがな = “would that…”), often with regret — 言うに及ばず has no such meaning; after a noun, followed by 「〜も」 or 「〜でも」 → “A goes without saying”, and the two are interchangeable, with 言うに及ばず more common in news and speeches.

items.diff: 言わずもがな is mostly used to list positive things; はおろか is mostly used with negatives or bad things, with surprise or dissatisfaction.

this.tr: He speaks French, never mind English.

that.tr: He can't even read the alphabet, let alone English.

items.explain: Look at the second half: piling up abilities or strengths (も話せる) → 言わずもがな (same with 言うまでもなく); a negative or bad thing like 「〜も読めない」 or 「〜もない」 → はおろか, with surprise at how absurd it is.

groups.note: Both mean “never mind A, even B…”

items.diff: Both can say “let alone A, not even B…”, with はおろか more formal; but どころか can also mean “far from…, on the contrary…”, which はおろか can't.

this.tr: He can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji.

that.tr: I took the medicine, but far from going down, my fever went even higher.

wrong.why: はおろか has no “on the contrary” meaning

items.explain: Look at the direction of the two parts: if the second adds a further step in the same direction (can't do kanji → can't even do hiragana) → either works, with はおろか stiffer; if the two go in opposite directions (下がる ↔ 上がる) → only どころか. Also, はおろか generally follows only nouns.

items.diff: はおろか is used almost exclusively with negative or bad things, with surprise or dissatisfaction; はもちろん works in both affirmative and negative sentences.

this.tr: I'm so busy I don't even have time to rest on weekends, let alone travel.

that.tr: This shop is crowded on weekdays too, not just weekends of course.

items.explain: Look at the end of the sentence: はおろか is almost always followed by a negative like 「〜もない」 or 「〜もできない」, with surprise or dissatisfaction at how outrageous it is, and can't be followed by a request or intention; はもちろん (はもとより) is neutral and works in affirmative sentences and requests alike (パスポートはもちろん、お金も忘れないでね).

items.diff: はおろか dismisses the lesser A in passing to stress how extreme B is, mostly negative; ばかりか means “not only A but also B” and works for good or bad things.

this.tr: I hurt my leg and can't even walk, let alone run.

that.tag: Good things too · not only… but also
that.tr: Not only is he a good student, he's also great at sports.

items.explain: Check whether the second half is good or bad: praising someone (スポーツも得意だ) sounds natural with ばかりか; はおろか is usually followed by something bad or extreme like 「〜さえできない」. Also look at what comes before: ばかりか can attach directly to verbs and adjectives (できるばかりか), while はおろか usually follows a noun or 「こと」.

groups.note: Both are sentence-final particles expressing the speaker's assertion or feeling

items.diff: よ “tells the listener” something they don't know; わ voices your own feeling or decision, more like talking to yourself, with a soft tone.

this.tr: Oh, it's so cold today.

that.tr: If you're going out, it's cold today, you know.

items.explain: Look at who the remark is aimed at: aimed at someone else, pointing out something they don't know yet (出るなら〜よ) → よ; your own exclamation or decision, like talking to yourself (ああ、〜わ) → わ. A rising わ is feminine speech in standard Japanese; the two are often combined as 「わよ」, voicing a feeling while also alerting the listener.

groups.note: Both mean “focusing on one thing and neglecting another”

items.diff: They mark opposite things: before そっちのけで comes “what gets neglected”; before にかまけて comes “what you're absorbed in”.

this.tr: My son has pushed his studies aside and is completely absorbed in video games.

that.tag: Before it = what you're absorbed in
that.tr: My son is so caught up in video games that he's neglecting his studies.

items.explain: Both sentences describe the same situation — check whether 「勉強」 or 「ゲーム」 comes first: the neglected “studies” first → 勉強はそっちのけで, followed by what he's absorbed in; the absorbing “games” first → ゲームにかまけて, followed by what's being neglected (おろそかにする, 顧みない).

items.diff: Before そっちのけで comes something that should be done or someone who should be the focus; before をよそに usually comes other people's “worry, expectations or opposition”.

this.tr: The relatives were whooping it up, completely ignoring the bride and groom.

that.tr: Despite his parents' worries, he set off overseas on his own.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: serious business that should be done, like 「勉強」 or 「仕事」, or someone who should be at the center, like 「本人」, 「主役」 or 「客」 → そっちのけで; other people's feelings or attitudes like 「心配」, 「期待」, 「反対」 or 「批判」 → をよそに.

groups.note: The 「わ」 in わ〜わ ↔ the sentence-final 「わ」: written the same

items.title: 〜わ (sentence-final particle)
items.diff: わ〜わ says the same verb twice in a row, meaning “one after another”; a single sentence-final わ is a soft-toned particle.

this.tr: When I cleared out the closet, old photos kept turning up one after another.

that.tr: I'd better be heading home. See you.

items.explain: Count how many わ there are and whether the same verb comes before each: the same verb said twice, like 「出るわ出るわ」 → amazement at how many there are, used by men and women alike; a single わ at the end, stating your own intention or feeling → sentence-final particle. When reading fiction, don't take 「出るわ出るわ」 as feminine speech.

groups.note: Both list things happening one after another, with surprise or complaint

items.diff: わ〜わ can end the sentence on its own, exclaiming “there's an amazing amount”; わ〜わで must be followed by a summing-up like “it was awful as a result”.

this.tr: When I looked into it, problem after problem kept popping up.

that.tag: わで → sums up the outcome
that.tr: What with the rain and the wind, the trip was a total disaster.

items.explain: Look at what follows the last わ: if the sentence stops there, simply marveling at how much there is → わ〜わ; if 「で」 follows, with a summing-up like 「散々だった」 or 「大変だった」 → わ〜わで, meaning “because things kept happening like this, the result was…”.

items.diff: わ〜わ attaches only to verbs and adjectives, with strong surprise or complaint; やら〜やら has a flatter tone and can also take nouns.

this.tr: On moving day, things got broken, it started raining — it was a total disaster.

that.tr: Before the move, I'm busy with packing, cleaning and so on.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: nouns (荷造り, 掃除) can only take やら〜やら; わ〜わ always follows a verb or adjective clause (壊れるわ, 降るわ), and carries surprise or complaint along the lines of “how unlucky can you get”. The repeated-verb 「出るわ出るわ」 also only works with わ.

groups.note: The 「わ」 in わ〜わで ↔ the sentence-final 「わ」: written the same

items.title: 〜わ (sentence-final particle)
items.diff: わ〜わで lists things happening one after another: “what with… and…”; sentence-final わ is a soft-toned particle.

this.tr: What with the rain and the wind, it was just awful.

that.tr: Oh, it's started raining. I'll need to take an umbrella.

items.explain: Look at what follows わ: if another item follows, then 「で」 and a summing-up (散々だった) → listing a string of events, used by men and women alike; if わ is at the end and the sentence stops there → sentence-final particle. When you read 「降るわ、吹くわで」, don't take it as feminine speech.

groups.note: Both list several things that happened in a row, implying “it was rough”

items.diff: わ〜わで must be followed by a summing-up like “it was awful as a result”; わ〜わ can end the sentence on its own, exclaiming “there's an amazing amount”.

this.tag: わで → sums up the outcome
this.tr: What with the rain and the wind, the trip was a total disaster.

that.tr: When I looked into it, problem after problem kept popping up.

items.explain: Look at what follows the last わ: if 「で」 follows, with a summing-up like 「散々だった」 or 「大変だった」 → わ〜わで, meaning “because things kept happening like this, the result was…”; if the sentence stops there, simply marveling at how much there is → わ〜わ.

items.diff: わ〜わで mostly lists a run of bad luck, with stronger complaint; やら〜やら has a flatter tone and can also take nouns or list mixed feelings.

this.tr: I lost my wallet, the train was late — what a miserable day.

that.tr: Being praised in front of everyone, I was both happy and embarrassed.

items.explain: Look at what's being listed: a string of misfortunes (落とす, 遅れる) → わ〜わで captures it best; mixed feelings like happiness and embarrassment, or nouns (宿題やら掃除やら) → usually やら〜やら.

items.diff: わ〜わで grumbles about things that have already happened, with strong surprise and complaint; し〜し calmly lists reasons that lead to a conclusion.

this.tr: What with the rain and the wind, it was just awful.

that.tr: It's raining and windy, so let's not go out today.

items.explain: The first halves are almost identical — look at the second half: し lists reasons for a decision, followed by a conclusion like 「やめよう」 or 「行きたくない」; わ〜わで grumbles about what has already happened, followed by 「散々だった」 or 「ひどい目にあった」, with a much stronger tone.

groups.note: Both mean “based on…”

items.diff: を踏まえて means “taking… into account” before thinking about the next step; に基づいて means acting “in accordance with” rules or data.

this.tr: Taking the lessons from last time into account, we revised the plan.

that.tr: Penalties are decided in accordance with the law.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: facts that need to be digested and taken into account, like 「反省」, 「経験」, 「現状」 or 「意見」 → を踏まえて, usually followed by forward-looking actions like 「見直す」 or 「検討する」; a basis you can follow and act on, like 「法律」, 「規則」, 「データ」 or 「資料」 → に基づいて.

items.diff: を踏まえて treats facts as a “premise” for making a judgment; をもとに uses something as “material” to create something.

this.tr: Based on the survey results, we'll consider our future policy.

that.tr: This film is based on a true story.

items.explain: Look at the verb that follows: thinking about the next step on top of a premise, like 「検討する」, 「判断する」 or 「見直す」 → を踏まえて; turning material into a work, like 「作る」, 「書く」 or 「描く」 → をもとに (実話をもとにした小説).

items.diff: The first part of を踏まえて is a fact that has already happened; the first part of を前提に is usually a condition that hasn't come true yet but is assumed.

this.tr: Based on the outcome of our discussion, we set a time for the wedding.

that.tr: The two of them are dating with a view to marriage.

items.explain: Check whether the thing before it has already happened: 「結果」, 「反省」 or 「経験」 are facts already in front of you → を踏まえて; 「結婚」, 「合格」 or 「参加」 are conditions that will only come true in the future and are assumed in advance → を前提に (same with を前提として).

groups.note: Both mean “before some important event”

items.diff: を控えて describes the state or feelings when an important event is “just around the corner”; に先立って says some activity is “done first” before that event.

this.tr: With the match tomorrow, the players are all nervous.

that.tr: Before the match, an opening ceremony was held.

items.explain: Look at the second half: a state or feeling as the event approaches, like 「緊張している」 or 「準備に追われている」, often with 「明日に」 or 「目前に」 before it saying how close it is → を控えて; a specific activity carried out before that event, like 「開会式が行われた」 or 「挨拶する」 → に先立って.

items.diff: を控えて only says the event is “coming up soon”; にあたって says what you do “when setting about” that event.

this.tr: I'm leaving to study abroad next month, and I can't settle down at all these days.

that.tr: In preparing to study abroad, I got a passport.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and what's said after: を控えて takes only a noun, often with a time like 「来月に」, followed by feelings or a state during that period; にあたって can follow a verb (留学するにあたって), followed by preparations made for it or a formal address (パスポートを取った, 一言ご挨拶申し上げます). (Same with にあたり, which is more formal.)

groups.note: Both mean “using an opportunity to do what you want”, with criticism

items.diff: をいいことに means exploiting a “favorable situation” like someone's absence or leniency; にかこつけて means using something as an “excuse” to do something else.

this.tr: Taking advantage of their parents being away, they invited friends over and partied till midnight.

that.tr: Under the pretext of a business trip, I enjoyed some sightseeing in Kyoto.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: a situation that gives someone an opening, like 「留守」, 「優しさ」 or 「黙っている」 → をいいことに, followed by something one shouldn't do; a legitimate-sounding reason like 「出張」, 「病気」 or 「仕事」 → にかこつけて, ostensibly for that purpose but really to do something else.

groups.note: Both mean “disregarding…, doing it anyway”

items.diff: を顧みず means “without considering” one's own risk or cost; をものともせず means “making nothing of” difficulties, with praise.

this.tr: Heedless of the danger, he jumped into the river and saved the child.

that.tr: Undaunted by the heavy snow, the runners ran all the way to the finish.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: 「危険」, 「命」, 「家庭」 or 「健康」 are costs one might pay → を顧みず, can be praise or criticism; 「大雪」, 「けが」, 「逆境」 or 「批判」 are obstacles in the way → をものともせず, usually followed by an achievement that overcame them, used only as praise. も顧みず means the same, with a stronger tone.

items.diff: を顧みず means “paying no heed” to consequences like danger or family; を押して means “pushing through” illness or opposition to do something.

this.tr: My father neglected his family and devoted himself solely to work.

that.tr: My father had a high fever but pushed himself to attend the meeting.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: resistance weighing on you right now, like 「病」, 「熱」, 「けが」 or 「反対」 → を押して, meaning forcing yourself through; things that should have been considered but weren't, like 「危険」, 「家庭」 or 「周りの迷惑」 → を顧みず, meaning “heedless of” when used as criticism. (Same with も顧みず, with a stronger tone.)

items.diff: も顧みず disregards serious things like health or family, and is more formal; もかまわず doesn't care about others' eyes or the setting, and is more conversational.

this.tr: Without regard even for his own health, he carried on with his research.

that.tr: Not caring who saw, she cried out loud.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: everyday small matters or others' eyes, like 「人目」, 「服が汚れる」 or 「時間」 → もかまわず; weighty matters like 「危険」, 「健康」 or 「家族」 → を顧みず (も顧みず has a stronger tone).
