groups.note: Both come from 「限る」 — “to draw a boundary”

items.diff: を限りに means “with… as the last”, never again after that; に限り means “limited to…”, available only within that range.

this.tag: Up to here · no more after
this.tr: This store will close its doors as of today.

that.tr: Today only, everything in the store is half price.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in 「を〜に」 vs. 「に〜」: 本日を限りに = today is the final boundary, followed by an ending like 「閉店」, 「引退」 or 「やめる」; 本日に限り = the range is limited to today, followed by special treatment available only within that range, like 「半額」 or 「無料」.

groups.note: Both mark a boundary at a certain point in time

items.title: 〜をもって (deadline)
items.diff: を限りに stresses a resolution or farewell — “never again after this”; をもって just formally marks the time something ends.

this.tr: Today is the last day — I'm quitting smoking for good.

that.tr: Reception will close as of today.

items.explain: Listen to the tone: the speaker says “that's it as of today” with resolve or emotion (きっぱりやめる, 引退する) → を限りに; a notice or announcement calmly declaring a cutoff (終了いたします, 閉店いたします) → をもって (more politely, をもちまして).

items.diff: を限りに says something “ends there” as of that point in time; を境に says things “changed” before and after that point.

this.tr: This year is my last; after it I'll retire from competition.

that.tr: Ever since that accident, his personality has completely changed.

items.explain: Look at the second half: something ongoing that stops here, like 「引退する」, 「やめる」 or 「閉店する」 → を限りに; a change contrasting two periods before and after, like 「変わった」 or 「増え始めた」 → を境に.

groups.note: Both put A first, implying a whole series of similar things follows

items.diff: を皮切りに means things unfold in sequence, “starting” from A in time; をはじめ puts A first as the “representative” when listing.

this.tr: The exhibition opens in Osaka, then moves on to Nagoya and Tokyo in turn.

that.tr: The exhibition will be held across the country, in Osaka, Nagoya, Tokyo and elsewhere.

items.explain: Look at the second half: 「順に」 or 「次々と」 describing a sequence → を皮切りに, with A as the first stop in time; 「〜など」 grouping similar things together without any order → をはじめ, with A merely the most representative one.

groups.note: Both mean “taking… as an opportunity”

items.diff: を機に is mostly used for decisions made at life milestones like marriage or retirement, and is more formal; をきっかけに is more conversational, and even a chance little event can be the trigger.

this.tr: When I retired, I took the opportunity to move to the countryside.

that.tr: A movie I happened to see got me started learning French.

items.explain: Look at what kind of event it is: a life milestone like 「結婚」, 「就職」 or 「定年」, followed by a new start you chose yourself → を機に (speeches often say 「これを機に」); a chance little event like 「たまたま見た映画」 or 「友達のひと言」 → をきっかけに sounds more natural, and can also be followed by an involuntary change.

items.diff: を機に is mostly used for personal decisions and in business; を契機に is the most formal, mostly used for major social or historical changes.

this.tr: I quit smoking when I got married.

that.tr: The oil crisis spurred major advances in energy-saving technology.

items.explain: Look at who it's about and how big it is: a decision “I” made because of marriage or a new job → を機に; a major shift in “society, technology or institutions” brought about by war or crisis, common in reports and academic papers → を契機に.

groups.note: Both describe a welling-up of emotion: “can't help…”

items.diff: を禁じ得ない follows an emotion noun like 「同情」 or 「怒り」 and is stiff written language; ずにはいられない follows a verb, meaning you can't help “doing” something.

this.tr: Hearing the victim's story, I couldn't help feeling deep sympathy.

that.tr: Hearing the victim's story, I couldn't help crying.

items.explain: Look at what kind of word comes before: an emotion noun like 「同情」, 「怒り」, 「驚き」 or 「涙」 ＋ を → を禁じ得ない, common in news and speeches; a verb like 「泣く」, 「笑う」 or 「言う」 (泣か＋ずにはいられない) → ずにはいられない, also common in everyday speech.

items.diff: を禁じ得ない is an emotion that suddenly wells up about something; てならない is a feeling you just can't shake.

this.tr: I can't help feeling angry about that ruling.

that.tr: I can't stop worrying about my mother living alone.

items.explain: Look at how it attaches and what it's about: emotion noun ＋ を, usually about a public event or someone else's misfortune (判決, 事故) → を禁じ得ない; the て form of an adjective or verb (心配で, 残念で, 気がして), describing a feeling of your own that lingers for a long time → てならない.

items.title: 〜に堪えない (overwhelmingly…)
items.diff: Both follow emotion nouns: を禁じ得ない is mostly used with 「同情」, 「怒り」 or 「驚き」; に堪えない is mostly used with 「感謝」 or 「感激」 in formal speeches.

this.tr: I couldn't help being shocked at the news of the sudden accident.

that.tr: I am deeply honored to receive such an award.

items.explain: First look at the particle: を禁じ得ない uses 「を」, に堪えない uses 「に」. Then look at the emotion: 「同情」, 「怒り」, 「驚き」 or 「涙」 in the face of someone else's misfortune or injustice → を禁じ得ない; 「感謝」 or 「感激」 on receiving an award or help, mostly in speeches and letters → に堪えない. に堪えない also has the meaning “unbearable to…” (見るに堪えない).

groups.note: Both stress a large amount

items.diff: を下らない is mostly used for statistics or estimates in news and reports; からある／からする／からの are used for concrete things, prices or numbers of people right in front of you, and work in speech too.

this.tr: The number of demonstrators is estimated at no fewer than 50,000.

that.tr: I caught a huge fish a good two meters long.
I bought a watch worth a whopping one million yen.
As many as 50,000 spectators gathered.

items.explain: Look at where it's used: calmly estimating “at least…” in news or reports → を下らない, often followed by 「と見られる」 or 「と推定される」; how big or heavy a concrete thing is (からある), how expensive (からする) or how many people came (からの), with a sense of “that's a lot”.

items.diff: を下らない gives an estimate of “at least” a certain amount, possibly more in reality; にのぼる says actual figures from statistics “reached” a certain amount.

this.tr: The damage is estimated at no less than 10 billion yen.

that.tr: The investigation found that the damage reached 10 billion yen.

items.explain: Look at what follows: an estimate like 「と見られる」 or 「と言われる」 → を下らない, meaning “at the very least”; a result from an investigation or statistics (調査の結果, 〜にのぼった) → にのぼる, simply saying it reached this large figure.

groups.note: Both mean “disregarding…, doing it anyway”

items.diff: をものともせず means “making nothing of” difficulties, with praise; を顧みず means “without considering” one's own risk or cost, and can be praise or criticism.

this.tr: Undaunted by the heavy snow, the runners ran all the way to the finish.

that.tr: Heedless of the danger, he jumped into the river and saved the child.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: 「大雪」, 「けが」, 「逆境」 or 「批判」 are obstacles in the way → をものともせず, usually followed by an achievement that overcame them, used only as praise; 「危険」, 「命」, 「家庭」 or 「健康」 are costs one might pay → を顧みず, can be praise or criticism.

items.diff: をものともせず means effortlessly “making nothing of it”, as praise from an onlooker; を押して means barely “pushing through”, implying a cost was paid.

this.tr: Undeterred by his leg injury, he won the championship in fine style.

that.tr: Despite his leg injury, he forced himself to play in the match.

items.explain: The first halves are the same — look at the second half and the tone: if a fine achievement follows (見事に優勝した), the speaker is praising someone “not at all defeated by the difficulty” → をものともせず; if it just says “took part, attended”, with concern or admiration that “it was clearly a strain” → を押して, which also sounds natural about oneself (熱を押して出勤した).

items.diff: Before をものともせず comes a difficulty or danger, with praise; before もかまわず come others' eyes or the setting, usually with criticism.

this.tr: Undaunted by the heavy rain, the rescue team continued the search.

that.tr: He was talking loudly on the phone on the train, not caring who was watching.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it and the evaluation: difficulties like 「雨」, 「けが」 or 「逆境」, with the speaker praising someone's courage → をものともせず; others' eyes or the setting that should be considered, like 「人目」, 「周りの迷惑」 or 「場所」, with the speaker usually criticizing → もかまわず.

groups.note: Both express a means — “by/with…” — or a deadline — “as of…”

items.title: 〜で (tool/method)
items.diff: をもって is formal and usually takes abstract nouns like 「書面」 or 「誠意」; で is everyday and works with any tool.

this.tr: You will be notified of the results in writing at a later date.

that.tr: I'll let you know the results by email later.

items.explain: Look at the setting and the wording that follows: in notices or formal speeches paired with polite forms like 「〜いたします」 → をもって (書面をもって, 誠意をもって, 拍手をもって); in ordinary speech, with a concrete tool (メール, ペン, バス) → で.

items.diff: をもって just formally marks the time something ends; を限りに stresses a resolution or farewell — “never again after this”.

this.tr: Reception will close as of today.

that.tr: Today is the last day — I'm quitting smoking for good.

items.explain: Listen to the tone: a notice or announcement calmly declaring a cutoff (終了いたします, 閉店いたします) → をもって (more politely, をもちまして); the speaker says “that's it as of today” with resolve or emotion (きっぱりやめる, 引退する) → を限りに.

groups.note: Both invoke an “impressive” person or means to say “can…” or “even… can't”

items.title: 〜にかかったら
items.diff: Before をもってすれば comes an ability or skill, in written language; before にかかったら comes a person, in speech, with a slightly teasing tone.

this.tr: With his skills, he could probably fix even this car in no time.

that.tr: In his hands, any car gets fixed in no time.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: an ability noun like 「技術」, 「実力」 or 「才能」, with a formal tone → をもってすれば; directly after a person (彼, 母, あの先生) → にかかったら, common in speech, with a half-joking “he's really something” tone.

items.title: 〜さえ (even…)
items.diff: Before をもってしても comes a powerful ability or means, in written language; でさえ can follow a person or any noun and is common in everyday speech.

this.tr: Even with the latest science, predicting earthquakes is difficult.

that.tr: Even experts say earthquakes are hard to predict.

items.explain: Both sentences say “even something this powerful can't do it” → it's really hard. Look at what comes before: an ability or means like 「科学」, 「技術」 or 「彼の力」, in a formal sentence → をもってしても; a person or ordinary noun like 「専門家」, 「子ども」 or 「先生」 → でさえ (さえ) is more common.

groups.note: をおいて ↔ をおして, just one kana apart

items.diff: をおいて means “no one/nothing other than…”; をおして (押して) means “pushing through, despite…”.

this.tag: None other than · the only one
this.tr: There's no one but him we can entrust this job to.

that.tr: Despite being ill, he attended the meeting.

items.explain: First check whether it's 「い」 or 「し」: をおいて comes from 「置く」 (set aside) and is always followed by 「ほかに〜ない／いない」, praising “only him”; をおして comes from 「押す」 (push against), usually preceded by 「病」, 「熱」 or 「反対」 and followed by something done despite it. They're easiest to misread when written in kana.

groups.note: Both stress “only A, nothing else”

items.diff: をおいて is used to single out the only suitable person or place; にほかならない is used to assert a cause or essence: “is precisely…”.

this.tr: There's no city better suited to host the Olympics than this one.

that.tr: His success is nothing other than the result of hard work.

items.explain: Look at what the sentence is doing: picking the single best one out of many candidates (〜にふさわしいのは〜をおいてほかにない) → をおいて; explaining that the cause or essence of something is precisely this (成功は努力の結果だ) → にほかならない, ending in an assertion, not followed by 「ほかに〜ない」.

groups.note: をおして ↔ をおいて, just one kana apart

items.diff: をおして (押して) means “pushing through, despite…”; をおいて means “no one/nothing other than…”.

this.tr: Despite being ill, he attended the meeting.

that.tag: None other than · the only one
that.tr: There's no one but him we can entrust this job to.

items.explain: First check whether it's 「し」 or 「い」: をおして comes from 「押す」 (push against), usually preceded by 「病」, 「熱」 or 「反対」 and followed by something done despite it; をおいて comes from 「置く」 (set aside) and is always followed by 「ほかに〜ない／いない」, praising “only him”. They're easiest to misread when written in kana.

groups.note: Both mean “disregarding…, doing it anyway”

items.diff: を押して means “pushing through” illness or opposition to do something; を顧みず means “paying no heed” to consequences like danger or family.

this.tr: My father had a high fever but pushed himself to attend the meeting.

that.tr: My father neglected his family and devoted himself solely to work.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: resistance weighing on you right now, like 「病」, 「熱」, 「けが」 or 「反対」 → を押して, meaning forcing yourself through, often with sympathy or admiration; things that should have been considered but weren't, like 「危険」, 「家庭」 or 「周りの迷惑」 → を顧みず, meaning “heedless of” when used as criticism.

items.diff: を押して means barely “pushing through”, implying a cost was paid; をものともせず means effortlessly “making nothing of it”, as praise from an onlooker.

this.tr: Despite his leg injury, he forced himself to play in the match.

that.tr: Undeterred by his leg injury, he won the championship in fine style.

items.explain: The first halves are the same — look at the second half and the tone: if it just says “took part, attended”, with concern or admiration that “it was clearly a strain” → を押して, which also sounds natural about oneself (熱を押して出勤した); if a fine achievement follows (見事に優勝した), praising someone “not at all defeated by the difficulty” → をものともせず.

groups.note: Both mark an event as a turning point after which things changed

items.diff: を境に says that with that event as the dividing line, things changed of their own accord; を機に says you took that opportunity to deliberately do something new.

this.tr: After his hospital stay, my father suddenly lost his confidence.

that.tr: My father used his hospital stay as an opportunity to quit smoking.

items.explain: The first halves are the same — look at the second half: 「弱気になった」 is a change that happened on its own → を境に, focusing on how different things were before and after; 「たばこをやめた」 is an action one decided on → を機に, treating the event as a good opportunity. を境に can also describe a spatial boundary (川を境に); を機に can't.

items.diff: を境に follows a noun and highlights the contrast before and after that point; てからというもの follows a verb's て form and stresses that the state has continued ever since.

this.tr: From that day on, the two stopped speaking to each other.

that.tr: Ever since that fight, the two haven't spoken to each other at all.

items.explain: First look at what comes before: a noun like 「あの日」 → を境に; a verb's て form like 「けんかをして」 → てからというもの. てからというもの is usually followed by an ongoing state with 「ずっと」 or 「毎日」, often with the speaker's emotion; を境に just marks the dividing point, stressing that before and after are different.

groups.note: Both mark an event or point in time as the boundary where something ends or begins

items.diff: を潮に carries a sense of “the time has come to call it quits”, mostly used for endings; を機に simply means taking an opportunity, common for both beginnings and endings.

this.tr: On turning sixty, I closed the shop I'd run for many years.

that.tag: Taking the opportunity · starting something new
that.tr: On turning sixty, I took the opportunity to open a new shop.

items.explain: Look at the second half: “calling it quits” things like closing a shop, retiring or breaking up a meeting → を潮に fits best, as if you'd judged the moment the tide turned; starting something new (店を開いた) → usually を機に. を機に also works for endings (結婚を機に退職した) and has a wider range of use.

items.diff: を潮に follows an event, treating it as a good moment to call it quits; を限りに follows a point in time, declaring “this is where it ends”.

this.tr: When the company president changed, I took that as my cue to quit too.

that.tag: A point in time → this is the end
that.tr: This store will close at the end of this month.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: a point in time like 「今月末」 or 「今日」 → を限りに, announcing a final deadline like a public notice; an event like 「社長の交代」 → を潮に, meaning “taking this as the right moment”.

groups.note: Both mean “have no choice but to…” — not something one wants to do

items.thisTitle: 〜を余儀なくされる (be forced to)
items.diff: を余儀なくされる follows a noun and objectively reports being forced, like a news report; ざるを得ない follows a verb, expressing the speaker's own conclusion after weighing things up that there's no other option.

this.tr: The match was forced to be called off due to heavy rain.

that.tr: With rain like this, I'm afraid they'll have no choice but to call off the match.

items.explain: First look at how it attaches: 「中止を」 is a noun → を余儀なくされる; 「中止せ」 is a verb's ない form → ざるを得ない. In tone, 余儀なくされる objectively describes something that has already happened, common in news and reports; ざるを得ない is usually the speaker's own judgment and resignation.

items.thisTitle: 〜を余儀なくされる (be forced to)
items.diff: を余儀なくされる is formal and objective, forced by outside circumstances; 羽目になる is conversational, usually about one's own bad luck or own doing, with self-mockery.

this.tr: Due to the typhoon, the plane was forced to turn back.

that.tr: I missed the last train and ended up having to walk home from the station.

items.explain: Look at the cause and the setting: an external cause like a typhoon, disaster or economic conditions, written in news or reports → を余儀なくされる; an awkward situation caused by your own blunder (乗り遅れて), told to a friend with a bit of self-mockery → 羽目になる. They attach differently too: noun ＋ を余儀なくされる, verb dictionary form ＋ 羽目になる.

groups.note: Both mean “disregarding…” and doing it anyway

items.diff: をよそに ignores other people's feelings, such as their worry or expectations; もかまわず doesn't care about things one should be mindful of, like others' eyes or the setting.

this.tr: Despite his parents' worries, he went traveling on his own.

that.tr: Not caring who saw, she cried out loud.

items.explain: Look at the noun before it: others' feelings or attitudes toward him, like 「心配」, 「期待」 or 「反対」 → をよそに, usually told by an onlooker, with criticism or emotion; external circumstances one should care about, like 「人目」, 「場所」 or 「服が汚れるの」 → もかまわず, describing behavior heedless of the setting.

items.diff: をよそに ignores other people's worry, often with criticism; をものともせず isn't daunted by difficulty or danger, with praise.

this.tr: Despite his family's worries, he went mountain climbing in winter.

that.tr: Undeterred by his leg injury, he kept going and ran all the way to the finish.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: other people's 「心配」 or 「反対」 → をよそに, with the speaker usually finding the person willful; a difficulty or danger like 「けが」, 「嵐」 or 「困難」 → をものともせず, with the speaker praising his courage.

items.diff: をよそに ignores other people's feelings or the surrounding situation; はそっちのけで pushes aside something one ought to be doing oneself.

this.tr: Despite Mom's worrying, my little brother is hooked on video games.

that.tr: My little brother has pushed his studies aside and is hooked on video games.

items.explain: The second halves are the same — look at what comes before: 「母の心配」 is someone else's feeling → をよそに; 「勉強」 is something he ought to be doing himself → はそっちのけで. Also note the particle: をよそに takes 「を」, while そっちのけ is usually preceded by 「は」.

groups.note: Both mean thinking or acting on the basis of something

items.diff: The basis of を前提に is a condition set in advance that hasn't happened yet; the basis of を踏まえて is facts or results that already exist.

this.tr: We drew up the budget on the assumption of a price increase next year.

that.tr: We drew up the budget based on this year's sales.

items.explain: The second halves are the same — look at what comes before: 「来年の値上げ」 is something assumed to happen, with the whole plan conditional on it → を前提に (same with を前提として); 「今年の売り上げ」 is a result that's already in, used as a reference → を踏まえて.

groups.note: Both come from questions with 「否（いな）」 — “is it… or not”

items.diff: や否や means “as soon as…”; か否か means “whether or not…”; they differ only in や vs. か.

this.tr: As soon as he saw my face, he burst into tears.

that.tr: We still don't know whether he'll come or not.

items.explain: Both come from the question pattern “… or not (否)?”: か否か keeps the original meaning = whether or not, often followed by 「分からない」 or 「決める」; や否や is generally thought to mean that before you could tell whether it was (finished) or not, the next thing had already happened — hence “as soon as…”, followed by something that has already happened.

groups.note: Both mean “as soon as…”

items.diff: With や否や the two parts can have different subjects; with なり both parts are done by the same person, usually followed by a surprising action.

this.tr: The moment the door opened, the cat dashed in.

that.tr: The moment he entered the room, he collapsed onto the sofa.

items.explain: Look at who does each action: the door opening and the cat dashing in are two different subjects → use や否や; entering the room and collapsing onto the sofa are both done by “him” → both なり and や否や work, with なり highlighting how unexpected the action is.

items.diff: Same meaning, but different attachment and register: や否や follows the dictionary form and is written language; たとたん follows the た form and is common in speech too.

this.tr: The moment I got home, it started to rain.

that.tr: The moment I got home, it started to rain.

wrong.why: や否や takes the dictionary form: 着く

items.explain: Check whether it's 「着く」 or 「着いた」: dictionary form ＋ や否や, common in novels and reports; た form ＋ とたん, fine in everyday conversation. Dropping 「否や」 and saying just 「着くや」 means the same, with a more literary feel.

items.diff: With や否や, the second event follows immediately once the first one happens; with か〜ないかのうちに, the second event starts before the first has even fully finished.

this.tr: As soon as the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.

that.tr: The bell had barely finished ringing when the students rushed out of the classroom.

items.explain: Check whether there's 「〜か〜ないか」: 鳴り終わるか終わらないか = “you can't even tell whether it had finished ringing”, stressing that the two are almost simultaneous, or the second even jumps the gun; with や否や, the second event follows right after the first happens.

groups.note: Both list a string of things one after another, often with annoyance

items.diff: Similar meaning — look at the position: やれ goes before each item, listing them in exasperation; やら goes after each item and can also express mixed feelings.

this.tr: What with meetings and business trips, my father doesn't even have time to rest.

that.tr: With meetings and business trips and so on, my father doesn't even have time to rest.

items.explain: The two sentences mean much the same — look at where the marker goes: やれ comes before the noun (やれ会議だ), followed by 「だ」 or 「と」; やら comes after the word (会議やら), usually followed by 「で」. やら〜やら can also list mixed feelings (うれしいやら恥ずかしいやら); やれ〜やれ can't.

items.diff: Almost the same meaning: やれ goes before each item; だの goes after each item. The two are often used together: やれ〜だの、やれ〜だの.

this.tr: Mom keeps nagging me — study, go to bed early — it drives me crazy.

that.tr: Mom keeps nagging me — study, go to bed early — it drives me crazy.

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same — look at where the marker goes: やれ comes before each item, as if they pop up one by one; だの comes after each item, as if quoting someone's nagging line by line. Combining them as 「やれ勉強しろだの、やれ早く寝ろだの」 makes it even stronger.

items.diff: やれ〜やれ mostly lists nouns: things to deal with one after another, or other people's demands; 〜わ〜わで follows verbs, listing misfortunes that actually happened.

this.tr: At year's end, what with the big cleanup and year-end parties, I'm really busy.

that.tr: On the trip it rained and I lost my wallet — it was a total disaster.

items.explain: Look at what's being listed: nouns like 「大掃除」 or 「忘年会」, things to deal with one by one → やれ〜だ; verbs like 「降る」 or 「なくす」, misfortunes that actually happened → 〜わ〜わで, often followed by 「散々だった」 or 「大変だった」.

groups.note: Both mean “just at that moment, something else happened”

items.diff: 矢先に is usually followed by an unfortunate surprise; ところに／ところへ is neutral and works for good things too.

this.tag: Just then, of all times · bad thing
this.tr: Just as I was about to go out, it started pouring.

that.tag: ところに · good things too
that.tr: Just as I was lost and at a loss, a kind person came over and spoke to me.
Just as we were talking about him, he showed up himself.

items.explain: Look at the second half: an unfortunate surprise like 「大雨が降ってきた」 → 矢先に, with an “of all times” tone; a good thing like 「親切な人が声をかけてくれた」 → use ところに／ところへ. Also, 矢先に is usually preceded by 「〜ようとした」, 「〜と思っていた」 or 「〜た」.

items.diff: たとたん is the very instant an action is completed; た矢先に can be a short while after (days or weeks), with regret that it happened “of all times”.

this.tr: No sooner had I bought a house than I got transferred.

that.tr: The moment I opened the door, the cat shot out.

items.explain: Look at how much time separates the two events: opening the door and the cat shooting out happen in the same instant → たとたん; buying a house and being transferred can be days or weeks apart, and the speaker feels “I'd only just…, and then of all things…” → た矢先に. 矢先に can also follow 「〜ようとした」, meaning it hadn't been done yet; たとたん can't.

groups.note: Same meaning as one of the uses on this page: strong negation (not at all, not even, can't possibly), worry about “might…”, or “incredibly…”

items.diff: はしない／やしない means “not at all, never”; もしない means “not even…”.

this.tr: My son just won't listen to me at all.

that.tr: My son won't even look at me.

items.explain: Both sandwich a particle between the ます stem and 「しない」: with 「は」 (which becomes 「や」 in speech: 聞きはしない＝聞きやしない), the action is singled out and flatly denied → not at all, never; with 「も」, it means “won't even do something this basic”, often with surprise or dissatisfaction. Check whether しない is preceded by や／は or by も.

items.diff: っこない only means “can't possibly”; やしない can also describe something that has actually happened — “just won't (do it)” — with dissatisfaction.

this.tr: No matter how many times I teach that kid, it just won't sink in.

that.tr: There's no way I can memorize such a long passage in one day.

items.explain: Look at what's being described: an annoying fact that has already happened (何度教えても) → やしない, with dissatisfaction — “just won't…”; asserting that something that hasn't happened yet is “impossible” → っこない, often attached to the potential form (覚えられっこない, できっこない).

items.diff: Both やしないか and のではないか express worry that “something might…”; やしないか attaches to the ます stem and is conversational and a bit old-fashioned, while のではないか attaches to the plain form and is more common.

this.tr: I'm worried I might oversleep on the day of the exam.

that.tr: I'm worried I might oversleep on the day of the exam.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at how they attach: 「寝坊し＋やしないか」 takes the ます stem; 「寝坊する＋のではないか」 takes the plain form. やしないか is almost always followed by 「と心配だ」 or 「とはらはらする」; のではないか can also express a guess or a tactful opinion, so it's used more widely.

items.diff: ったらありゃしない is mostly used to complain that something is “incredibly…”; といったらない works for good and bad things alike and is also more formal.

this.tr: The noise from the construction next door is unbearably loud.

that.tr: The joy when I found out I'd passed was beyond words.

items.explain: Check whether it's good or bad: annoying things like noise, hassle or something you dislike → ったらありゃしない, very casual speech; good things like joy or beauty → use といったらない, often after a nominalized 「〜さ」 (うれしさ, 美しさ).

groups.note: Both mean “I hear that…”

items.diff: 由 is a refined expression used in letters and greeting cards; とのこと is used in general writing and business emails.

this.tr: I was delighted to hear of your marriage and offer my heartfelt congratulations.

that.tr: I heard you got married — congratulations!

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the style: formal wording like 「申し上げます」 in letters, cards and speeches → 由, usually as 「noun ＋ の由」; emails and general writing use とのこと. 由 is almost never used in speech.

items.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
items.diff: 由 is used only in formal settings like letters; hearsay そうだ is the most ordinary “I hear”, fine in everyday conversation.

this.tr: I was relieved to hear that your mother has been discharged from the hospital.

that.tr: According to a friend, Tanaka's mother has been discharged from the hospital.

items.explain: Look at the setting and honorifics: within letter-style honorifics like 「お母様」, 「ご退院なさった」 or 「安心いたしました」 → 由, mostly used to mention news of the recipient or their family; passing on something you heard, between friends → そうだ (after the plain form).

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — “how something appears”

items.diff: ように見える just says “looks like”; ようでいて has a built-in contrast: “seems…, but actually…”.

this.tr: He seems cold, but he's actually very kind.

that.tr: He looks cold.

items.explain: ように見える only describes appearance — to reveal the truth you'd need to add 「が、実は……」; ようでいて contains the whole contrast “it looks this way, but it isn't” in one expression, immediately followed by the opposite fact, mostly used to describe the nature of people or things.

groups.note: Both express a contrast: what follows goes against the impression given by what came before

items.diff: ようでいて describes a gap between how something looks and what it really is, a lasting quality; と思いきや describes one particular expectation of your own falling flat.

this.tr: This problem seems simple, but it's actually quite profound.

that.tr: I thought this problem would be easy, but it turned out to be surprisingly hard.

items.explain: Look at the tense and viewpoint: と思いきや is about “my” judgment on one occasion turning out wrong, usually with a past-tense second half (難しかった); ようでいて is about two sides of the thing itself, always so, usually in the present tense (奥が深い). と思いきや works the same with or without 「か」 before it.

items.title: 〜ながらも (although… but)
items.diff: The first part of ながらも is a fact that really holds true; the first part of ようでいて only looks that way and may not actually be so.

this.tr: This room seems spacious, but there's actually very little usable space.

that.tr: This room may be small, but it's very comfortable to live in.

items.explain: Ask yourself: is the first half true? ながらも admits “it really is small” and then mentions an unexpected upside; ようでいて says “it looks spacious, but it actually isn't”, overturning the impression from the first half.

groups.note: 〜うか〜まいか ↔ 〜うが〜まいが, differing only in か／が

items.diff: ようが〜まいが means “whether you do it or not, it makes no difference”; ようか〜まいか means “whether to do it or not (hesitating)”; they differ only in が vs. か.

this.tr: Whether you go or not has nothing to do with me.

that.tr: I can't decide whether to go to the party or not.

items.explain: Written almost the same, differing by just one voicing mark: followed by が (regardless) → doing it or not gives the same result, followed by an unaffected conclusion; followed by か (or) → can't make up one's mind, often followed by 「迷う」 or 「悩む」. Check whether が or か comes after まい, then the second half makes it clear.

groups.note: Both mean “whatever happens, the result is the same”

items.diff: ようが on its own means “even if…”; adding まいが lists both doing and not doing, meaning “it doesn't matter either way”.

this.tag: Rain or not · same either way
this.tr: Rain or shine, the match will go ahead.

that.tr: No matter how hard it rains, the match will go ahead.

items.explain: Count how many cases are listed: just one 「降ろうが」, often paired with 「どんなに」 or 「何を」 → even if…; the same verb in positive and negative side by side (降ろうが降るまいが) → neither raining nor not raining affects the outcome. Replacing が with と works the same.

items.diff: ようが〜まいが lists only “doing / not doing” of the same action; にしろ〜にしろ can list any two different options.

this.tr: Whether you agree or not, the plan will go ahead.

that.tr: Whether you're for or against it, please explain your reasons.

items.explain: Look at the two items listed: the same verb in positive and negative (賛成しようがしまいが) → ようが〜まいが, with a forceful tone, often implying “suit yourself”; two different words (賛成・反対) → にしろ〜にしろ (same with にしても〜にしても).

items.diff: ようが〜まいが is an emotional “I don't care whether you do it or not”; にかかわらず is a neutral “regardless of” used in notices and rules.

this.tr: Whether you join or not, I'm going anyway.

that.tr: Please reply whether or not you will attend.

items.explain: Look at the setting: formal, objective texts like notices and rules → 〜するしないにかかわらず; stating face-to-face, with emotion, “I don't care what you do” → ようが〜まいが.

groups.note: All express concession: “even if…”

items.title: 〜ても (even if…)
items.diff: ても is the most ordinary “even if…”, calm in tone; ようと／ようが is more formal and forceful, with a defiant “it makes no difference who says what”.

this.tr: No matter who says what, I'm quitting this job.

that.tr: No matter who says what, I'm quitting this job.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the connection and the tone: volitional form (言おう) + と／が sounds harder, and is common in strong declarations, formal writing and speeches (と and が are the same); te-form (言って) + も is the most ordinary everyday way to say it.

items.diff: ようが on its own means “even if…”; ようが〜まいが lists both sides: doing and not doing.

this.tr: No matter how much opposition I face, I'm going.

that.tr: Whether people oppose it or not, I'm going.

items.explain: Check whether the negative of the same verb follows: only 「されようが」, often with 「どんなに」 → even if…; followed by 「されまいが」 → both the positive and negative cases are listed, meaning “whether or not”.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — meaning “appearance, manner”

items.diff: masu-stem + よう is a noun, “the way someone…”; plain form + ようだ is a guess, “seems…”.

this.tr: The way he rejoiced when he learned he had passed was really something.

that.tr: He passed, and he seems very happy.

items.explain: Both 「よう」 are 「様」 (appearance). Look at the form in front: masu-stem (喜び) + よう becomes a noun meaning “the way someone rejoices”, often in 「〜ようといったら」 or 「大変な〜ようだ」 to stress an astonishing degree; plain form (喜んでいる) + ようだ is the speaker's guess, “it looks like…”.

groups.note: For ichidan verbs, masu-stem + よう and the volitional form are spelled exactly the same

items.diff: 考えよう in 物は考えようだ is a noun, “way of thinking”; 考えよう at the end of a sentence is the volitional “let's think”.

this.tr: It all depends on how you look at it — it's not all bad.

that.tr: Let's all think about it together once more.

items.explain: For ichidan verbs, the masu-stem + よう (考え＋よう) and the volitional form (考えよう) are spelled exactly the same. Look at the context: with 「物は」 before it and 「だ」, 「によっては」 or 「がない」 after it, it's the noun “the way of…”; at the end of a sentence expressing a suggestion or resolve, it's the volitional “let's…”. Godan verbs never get mixed up: 言いよう (way of saying) ≠ 言おう (volitional).

groups.note: Both express the way or manner of doing something

items.diff: 〜方（かた） is an objective method or way of saying; 〜よう in the sense of “manner” mostly appears in set phrases, stressing “change the approach and the result changes”.

this.tag: How you say it · different result
this.tr: Even the same thing — it all depends on how you put it.

that.tr: Speaking to a teacher that way is very rude.

items.explain: 〜方 attaches to almost any verb and means a concrete method or way (読み方, 言い方, 作り方); 〜よう meaning “manner” mostly appears in set phrases — 物は言いようだ, 考えようによっては, やりようはある — with the point that “change the approach and the result changes”.

groups.note: Both end in 「〜ものなら」; they differ only in whether the volitional or potential form comes before

items.diff: Volitional form + ものなら is “if you were to do it, there'd be trouble”; potential form + ものなら is “if only I could…”.

this.tr: If I took time off at such a busy time, who knows what my boss would say.

that.tr: If I could take time off, I'd love to rest for about a week.

items.explain: Look before ものなら: volitional form (休もう) → supposing you actually did it, followed by a dreadful consequence (何を言われるか分からない); potential form (休める) → a hard-to-fulfil wish, followed by 「〜たい」. Just one or two kana apart, but completely different meanings.

groups.note: Both mean “once you do it, there will be serious consequences”

items.diff: ようものなら warns by supposing “if you were to do it”; が最後 says “once it happens, there's no undoing it”, mostly about things that are inevitably so.

this.tr: If you dare to touch that dog, it'll bite you.

that.tr: Once that dog bites, it never lets go.

items.explain: Look at the connection and the second half: volitional form (出そう) + ものなら is followed by a warning or worry addressed to the listener (かみつかれるよ); ta-form (かみついた) + が最後 is followed by a result that can't be stopped or undone once it starts, often describing a fixed habit of a person or thing. たら最後 is the same, more colloquial.

groups.note: Both come from 「よう（様）」 — here meaning “method, way”

items.diff: ようによっては is “depending on how you do it (or see it), it's possible…”; ようがない is “there's simply no way”.

this.tr: Depending on how you go about it, you can still make it in time.

that.tr: I know neither the phone number nor the address, so there's no way to contact them.

items.explain: Both よう mean “way, method”. Followed by 「によっては」 → a different method might give a different result, usually an optimistic “it's still possible”; followed by 「がない」 → there isn't even one way, so “there's no way to…”.

groups.note: ようによっては ↔ によっては, differing only by 「よう」

items.diff: によっては attaches to nouns, meaning “some … may”; ようによっては attaches to a verb's masu-stem, meaning “with a different view or approach, it might…”.

this.tr: Looked at another way, failure is also a good experience.

that.tr: Some people may find this movie boring.

wrong.why: The verb must become masu-stem + よう: 考えようによっては

items.explain: Look at what comes before: a noun (人, 場合, 地域) → によっては, referring to some of the cases; a verb's masu-stem + よう (考えよう, 見よう, やりよう) → ようによっては, meaning the same thing can lead to a different conclusion if you see it or do it differently.

groups.note: Both mean “depending on…, the result will differ”

items.title: 〜いかんによっては (depending on…, possibly)
items.diff: いかんによっては attaches to nouns and is formal and written; ようによっては attaches to a verb's masu-stem, usually meaning “with a different approach or way of thinking”.

this.tr: Depending on how you use it, even an old box can become handy storage.

that.tr: Depending on the test results, surgery may be needed.

items.explain: Look at what comes before: nouns like 「結果」 or 「対応」 → いかんによっては, common in notices, news and other formal contexts; verb masu-stems like 「使い」 or 「考え」 → ようによっては, stressing how people go about doing or seeing something.

items.title: 〜次第で (depending on…)
items.diff: 次第で means the result depends entirely on the first part; ようによっては means “with a different approach, it might…”, more tentative in tone.

this.tr: Depending on how you do it, even this job can become fun.

that.tr: It all comes down to effort — anyone can pass.

items.explain: Look at what comes before and the tone: noun (努力, 天気) + 次第で means the result is determined by it, and can be stated quite firmly (誰でも合格できる); verb masu-stem + ようによっては means “if you do it or see it a different way”, usually followed by a hedged statement like “it's also possible that…”.

groups.note: Both express a reason: “because…”

items.title: 〜ために (reason)
items.diff: ために is the general written way to give a reason, common in reports and notices; ゆえ（に） is more archaic and solemn, mostly found in essays and commentary.

this.tr: Due to lack of experience, the plan ended in failure.

that.tr: Due to lack of experience, the plan ended in failure.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the connection and register: ゆえ can attach directly to a noun (不足ゆえに), and also appears in set expressions like 「〜がゆえに」 and 「ゆえの + noun」 (若さゆえの過ち), sounding archaic and dignified; ために needs 「の」 after a noun, and is the most common way to give a reason in reports and notices.

items.diff: ばかりに is only used for bad results, with regret; ゆえに simply states the reason objectively and works for good results too.

this.tr: Because he is honest, he is trusted by everyone.

that.tr: Just because I blurted out the truth, I made him angry.

wrong.why: ばかりに can't be followed by a good result

items.explain: Look at the result in the second half: being trusted is a good thing → only ゆえに (がゆえに) works; making someone angry is bad, and the speaker regrets “just because of that one thing” → ばかりに, often followed by 「〜てしまった」.

items.diff: Both がゆえに and からこそ can stress “precisely because”; がゆえに is solemn and written, からこそ is used in both speech and writing.

this.tr: Precisely because he loved her, he chose to break up.

that.tr: Precisely because he loved her, he chose to break up.

items.explain: Almost the same meaning; the difference is register: solemn narration in novels and essays uses がゆえに; everyday speech and ordinary writing use からこそ. からこそ is also often placed before 「〜だ」 or 「〜です」 for emphasis (あなただからこそ頼むんです), which がゆえに doesn't do.

groups.note: Both mean doing something to your heart's content, nonstop

items.diff: 三昧 attaches to nouns, meaning wholly immersed in an activity; 放題 attaches to a verb's masu-stem, meaning without limits, doing as much as you like.

this.tr: Since retiring, I spend every day fishing to my heart's content.

that.tr: At this shop, it's all-you-can-eat cake for 2,000 yen.

items.explain: Look at the word before it: nouns like 「釣り」, 「読書」 or 「ゴルフ」 → 三昧, the point being you're immersed in it all day; verb masu-stems like 「食べ」 or 「飲み」 → 放題, the point being there's no limit, as in 「食べ放題」 and 「言いたい放題」. 「贅沢三昧」 and 「わがまま放題」 both carry criticism.

items.diff: 三昧 is happily immersing yourself in something; てばかりいる is “always just doing…”, as seen by a disapproving onlooker.

this.tr: I spent my summer vacation happily soaking in hot springs every day.

that.tr: My son does nothing but play all summer vacation.

items.explain: Look at the tone: 三昧 is usually the person themselves happily enjoying something (温泉三昧, 読書三昧); てばかりいる is often a complaint from an onlooker such as a parent or boss (遊んでばかりいる). The connection differs too: 三昧 attaches to nouns, てばかりいる to a verb's te-form.

groups.note: Both are sentence-ending particles that add emphasis

items.diff: ぞ・ぜ are forceful and strongly masculine, and normally only follow the plain form; よ is used by everyone, is gentler, and can follow polite forms too.

this.tr: If you don't hurry up, you'll be late!
Come on, let's go together!

that.tr: If you don't hurry, you'll be late, you know.
Hey, let's go together.

items.explain: Look at who you're talking to and the connection: to a boss, an elder, or when speaking politely, only 「〜ますよ」 works; ぞ is mostly used to psych yourself up (よし、やるぞ) or to warn juniors or peers, and ぜ to call out to or assert something forcefully to close friends (行こうぜ). ぞ・ぜ sound very masculine; women generally say よ.

groups.note: ずには + おかない／いられない／すまない, differing only in the final verb

items.diff: ずにはおかない says something “is bound to make people…”, with a work or event as the subject; ずにはいられない says “I can't help…”, with yourself as the subject.

this.tr: This movie is bound to move its audience.

that.tr: Watching this movie, I couldn't help crying.

items.explain: Look at the subject and the verb: 「この映画は」 as the subject with a causative verb (感動させ) → ずにはおかない, meaning “is bound to make people…”; 「私は」 as the subject with your own action (泣か) → ずにはいられない. Memory aid: おく (put down) — won't let it go until…; いる (stay) — can't stay still without…. ないではおかない is the same, more colloquial.

items.diff: ずにはおかない is a strong will, “I won't rest until…”; ずにはすまない is “it wouldn't be right not to…”, based on what is reasonable or proper.

this.tr: That criminal — I will track him down, no matter what.

that.tr: Since I broke someone else's property, it wouldn't be right not to pay for it.

items.explain: Look at who is demanding it: the speaker's own resolve (あの犯人だけは) → ずにはおかない, often about pursuing or getting revenge; what social norms or decency require (breaking someone else's property) → ずにはすまない. Memory aid: おく — won't let it go until…; 済む — the matter can't be settled without….

groups.note: Both come from 「済む（すむ）」 — meaning “the matter is settled, it's acceptable”

items.title: 〜ずに済む
items.diff: ずにはすまない is “you have to do it”; ずに済む is “you get away without doing it” — the difference is just one 「は」 and the negative at the end.

this.tr: Since I caused trouble, it wouldn't be right not to apologize.

that.tr: The other person didn't mind, so I got away without having to apologize.

items.explain: Both use 「済む」 = the matter is settled. ずに済む: it can be settled without doing it = no need to do it, often with relief, and usually in the past tense (済んだ); ずにはすまない: it can't be settled without doing it = must do it. Look at 「は」 and the ending: with 「は」 and ending in a negative → must; without 「は」 and ending in 「済む」 → no need.

items.diff: ずにはすまない is “it won't be settled unless you…”; ではすまない is “just … won't settle it”.

this.tr: After a mistake like this, I'll have to report it to my boss.

that.tr: After a mistake like this, an apology alone won't settle it.

items.explain: Both use 「済む」 (to be settled). Look at what comes before: verb nai-form (報告せ) + ずには → it can't be settled without doing this = must do it; a noun or 「〜ただけ」 + では (謝っただけでは, 冗談では) → going only this far isn't enough; the problem is more serious than that.

groups.note: ずには + すまない／おかない／いられない, differing only in the final verb

items.diff: ずにはすまない is “it wouldn't be right not to…”, based on what is proper; ずにはおかない is a strong will, “I won't rest until…”, or “is bound to cause…”.

this.tr: Since I broke someone else's property, it wouldn't be right not to pay for it.

that.tr: That criminal — I will track him down, no matter what.

items.explain: Look at whose demand it is: social norms or decency require it (if you break someone's property, you pay) → ずにはすまない; the speaker's own resolve → ずにはおかない. Memory aid: 済む — can't be settled without…; おく — won't let it go until….

items.diff: ずにはすまない is having to do something because it's proper; ずにはいられない is being unable to stop yourself emotionally.

this.tr: Since I broke my promise, it wouldn't be right not to apologize.

that.tr: His story was so funny that I couldn't help laughing.

items.explain: Look at the motive: a moral obligation like “breaking a promise” → ずにはすまない, something you must do even if reluctant; an emotional impulse like “so funny” → ずにはいられない, being unable to control yourself. Memory aid: いる (stay) — can't stay still without….

groups.note: Both mean “can't not…, must…”

items.diff: Similar meanings: ないわけにはいかない is common in both speech and writing; ずにはすまない is more formal and stiff, stressing “the situation can't be resolved unless you do it”.

this.tr: Having caused the company such a huge loss, he probably won't escape taking responsibility.

that.tr: It's my best friend's wedding, so I can't not go.

items.explain: Look at the situation and consequences: everyday social obligations like a friend's wedding or a boss's invitation → usually ないわけにはいかない; serious situations like causing a loss or an accident, which can't be resolved without acting → ずにはすまない, which sounds very written and often comes with 「だろう」. ないではすまない is the same, slightly more colloquial.

items.diff: ずにはすまない focuses on social norms and outside demands; ざるを得ない focuses on the speaker's reluctant choice, forced by circumstances.

this.tr: Since I scratched someone else's car, it wouldn't be right not to pay for the repairs.

that.tr: The rain is so heavy that we have no choice but to cancel the trip.

items.explain: Look at the reason for “having to”: you did something that wronged someone, so you should take responsibility as a matter of what's right → ずにはすまない; circumstances like the weather or budget leave no other choice → ざるを得ない, with no moral element.

groups.note: Both come from the classical negative 「ず」 — the equivalent of modern 「ない」

items.diff: ずに is the general modern “without…”; ずして is archaic and stiff, mostly used in proverbs and set phrases, and often pairs with a negative later in the sentence.

this.tr: To win without fighting.

that.tr: I went to school without eating breakfast.

items.explain: Both are 「ず + particle」, meaning “without…”. Ordinary narration uses ずに (= ないで); ずして appears only in writing, proverbs and set phrases (戦わずして勝つ, 労せずして), and is often used as 「〜ずして〜ない」 meaning “you can't… without…”.

items.diff: ずして is “without…, (still achieved it)” or “can't… without…”; ずとも is “even without…”.

this.tr: The opponent withdrew, so we won without fighting.

that.tr: We've known each other so long that I understand without you saying it.

items.explain: Both are built on the negative 「ず」 — look at the particle that follows: して (= て) expresses manner or condition, often paired with a later negative (〜ずして〜ない); とも (= ても) expresses concession, usually followed by a result that still holds, like 「分かる」 or 「よい」.

groups.note: Both mean “without…, (you can't)…”

items.diff: Same meaning, different connection: なくして attaches to nouns; ずして attaches to verbs (nai-form minus ない).

this.tr: You won't succeed without making an effort.

that.tr: Without effort, there is no success.

wrong.why: ずして attaches to verbs: 努力せずして

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in what comes before: a noun (努力) takes なくして directly; a verb must first change to the nai-form (努力しない → 努力せ) before ずして. ずして can also mean “achieved it without…” (戦わずして勝つ), a use なくして doesn't have.

items.diff: ことなしに attaches to the dictionary form and is modern written language; ずして attaches to the nai-form, is more archaic, and mostly appears in set phrases.

this.tr: Without hardship, you can't achieve great results.

that.tr: Without hardship, you can't achieve great results.

items.explain: Same meaning — look at the connection: dictionary form (苦労する) + ことなしに; nai-form (苦労せ) + ずして. ことなしに is the general written style of papers and speeches; ずして has the classical flavor of kanbun reading and is common in set phrases like 「労せずして」 and 「戦わずして」.

groups.note: Both come from the classical negative 「ず」 — the equivalent of modern 「ない」

items.diff: ずとも is “even without…”; ずして is “without…, (still achieved it)” or “can't… without…”.

this.tr: We've known each other so long that I understand without you saying it.

that.tr: The opponent withdrew, so we won without fighting.

items.explain: Look at the particle after ず: とも (= ても) is concession, “understand even without being told”; して (= て) is manner, “won without fighting”, and also often pairs with a negative to mean “can't… without…”.

items.diff: ずとも is “even without…” (= なくても); ずに is “without… (doing)” (= ないで).

this.tr: If you leave now, you'll make it in time even without hurrying.

that.tr: We had plenty of time, so I didn't rush and walked there slowly.

items.explain: Replace ず with ない and it's easy to understand: ずとも = なくても (even without…, it's fine / it still holds); ずに = ないで (doing the next action without doing…). ずとも is a written, archaic expression; in everyday speech you'd say なくても.

groups.note: Both mean “you don't have to…”

items.diff: Same meaning; ずともよい is a written, archaic version of なくてもいい.

this.tr: There is no need to come if it is difficult for you.

that.tr: You don't have to push yourself to come, OK?

items.explain: The two sentences mean the same, differing only in register: ずとも uses the classical 「ず」 and is mostly found in writing, period-drama dialogue, or a formal tone from a superior to a subordinate; in everyday conversation you say なくてもいい. Note the connection: 来ない → 来（こ）ずとも, しない → せずとも.

groups.note: Both come from 「尽く（つく）」 — meaning “to use up, all”

items.diff: ずくめ is “nothing but, all the same”, usable for both good and bad; づくし mostly lays out good things one after another, “a lavish spread of all…”.

this.tr: Life in this dorm is nothing but rules.

that.tr: At the inn, we enjoyed a full crab-themed feast.

items.explain: Both come from 「尽く」 (to use up), so both mean “all, entirely”. Look at what they're used for: things good or bad, or clothing colors, like 「規則ずくめ」, 「黒ずくめ」, 「いいことずくめ」 → ずくめ; cuisine or programs that go all out on one good thing (カニづくし, 花づくし) → づくし, which is almost always positive.

items.diff: ずくめ attaches to nouns, describing a state of “nothing but…”; 〜尽くす attaches to a verb's masu-stem, describing an action “done completely, leaving nothing”.

this.tr: Passing my exam, getting married — this year has been nothing but good things.

that.tr: The children ate up every bit of the cake.

items.explain: Both come from 「尽く」 = to use up. 〜尽くす follows a verb and means doing the action until nothing is left (食べ尽くす, 言い尽くす); ずくめ follows a noun and means everything around is the same kind of thing. Check whether a noun or a verb masu-stem comes before.

groups.note: Both mean “full of, nothing but”

items.diff: だらけ means covered in bad things, with distaste; ずくめ works for good or bad, including good things.

this.tr: My pay is going up and I'm getting more days off — it's nothing but good news.

that.tr: I wrote it in a hurry, so the essay is full of mistakes.

items.explain: Look at whether the things are good or bad: unwanted things like mistakes, scratches, mud or trash → だらけ, meaning “all over, far too many”; when it can describe good things too → ずくめ (いいことずくめ), meaning “nothing but”.

items.diff: まみれ is a surface covered in a liquid or powder; ずくめ isn't “covered in” — it means the same kind of thing from head to toe.

this.tag: Head to toe · all the same
this.tr: That man was dressed all in black, from his hat to his shoes.

that.tr: After working in the field all day, I was drenched in sweat.

items.explain: Look at the noun in front: things that “stick” to you, like sweat, mud, blood or oil → まみれ; things that are “all of the same kind”, like colors, rules or good things → ずくめ. 黒ずくめ means dressed all in black, not smeared with black.

groups.note: Both come from 「尽く（つく）」 — meaning “to use up, all”

items.diff: づくし mostly lays out good things one after another; ずくめ is “nothing but”, usable for good or bad, and also for clothing colors.

this.tr: At the inn, we enjoyed a full crab-themed feast.

that.tr: Life in this dorm is nothing but rules.

items.explain: Both come from 「尽く」 (to use up). づくし originally means “listing one by one, presenting all of them”, and is mostly used for cuisine, program titles and ads, almost always positively (カニづくし, 花づくし); ずくめ is “all of it, from start to finish”, which can be unwelcome things (規則ずくめ) or clothing colors (黒ずくめ).

items.diff: づくし attaches to nouns, meaning “all…”; 〜尽くす attaches to a verb's masu-stem, meaning “doing it completely”.

this.tr: I was given some spring-like sweets covered in flower designs.

that.tr: That beauty is beyond words.

items.explain: づくし is simply 「尽くし」, the masu-stem of 「尽くす」, attached to a noun and voiced: カニづくし = crab done every way, all crab. A verb's masu-stem + 尽くす means doing the action until nothing is left (言い尽くす, 食べ尽くす). Check whether a noun or a verb comes before.

groups.note: Both mean “full of, nothing but”

items.diff: づくし is full of good things; だらけ is full of bad things.

this.tr: Today's dinner was one delicious dish after another.

that.tr: I wrote it in a hurry, so the essay is full of mistakes.

items.explain: Look at whether they're wanted or unwanted: pleasing things like ごちそう, flowers or good things → づくし; unwanted things like mistakes, scratches or dust → だらけ.
